15914-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
The American Missionary for November 1889, volume forty-three, number eleven. Editorials treat Free Once More, the National Council, the coloured delegates, and the Mohonk Conference. Notes from New England follow, with deaths of Superintendent Hall and Dr. Lane. The magazine served the American Missionary Association's friends.

A general survey covers the South, educational work, church work, mountain work, the Indians, and the Chinese, with enlargements, woman's work, finances, and the Daniel Hand Fund. The Chinese review of the year and woman's work in North Carolina close the survey. The issue gives mission work in 1889 in full: schools, churches, and a wide, hopeful field.
16083-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
January 1889 opens volume forty-three of The American Missionary with New Year greetings, money news, and a look at the Southern situation. Editorials note large gifts from the wealthy, systematic spending, and the death of Mrs. George A. Woodard, beside a portrait of Mr. Daniel Hand. Chinese correspondence scraps, women's state groups, mountain white work, and the needs of colored women and girls fill the later pages.

The number sets the association's tone for the year: fundraising, schooling, and church planting, with women's work given full weight. Receipts close the issue, listing the gifts behind the plans. Readers can use it as a New Year snapshot of mission hopes and hard facts in 1889.
16084-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
Issued in New York in February 1889, this number of The American Missionary speaks for the American Missionary Association, a Protestant body that ran schools and churches. Its pages list the association's officers and field workers, then mix editorials with notes from New England, the Tennessee mountains, and missions to Chinese immigrants. A list of good Samaritans and a table of receipts close the business side.

The issue shows what the association cared about that month: freed Black Southerners, Roman Catholic outreach, the death of Professor Hatch, and the work of women through their own bureau. Modern readers can use it as a window on church charity, schooling, and race relations in America a generation after the Civil War.
16103-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
Published in New York in March 1889, this number of The American Missionary carries the monthly voice of the American Missionary Association. Editorials urge pastors and churches to enlist in the work, discuss race and power in the postwar South, and note the training of Black students for church ministry. Field reports follow, from a revival at Lemoyne Institute to crowded schoolrooms and everyday Southern life.

Other pages turn to Chinese missions, a Christmas at Fort Yates, women's work, children's stories, and the monthly receipts that kept the whole effort afloat. Together the contents show a church body juggling schools, missions, and fundraising across a divided country. The issue is a useful primary source on religion, schooling, and race in 1889 America.
16104-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
April 1889 brings volume forty-three, number four of The American Missionary, the monthly of the American Missionary Association in New York. Editorials ask who will furnish the remedy for Southern troubles, note curious and suggestive facts, and print school echoes, book notices, and a doctrinal sermon. Southern reports mark the dedication of the Ballard building, ten years at the front, and progress in Southern schooling.

Indian, Chinese, and women's work follow, with a visit to Park Street Church station, a San Diego Chinese mission, temperance work in Tennessee, and Christmas at the Skokomish reservation. Receipts close the number. The issue shows mission schools and churches growing, building, and counting their gifts in the spring of 1889.
16118-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
May 1889 brings volume forty-three, number five of The American Missionary, the monthly of the American Missionary Association. Editorials cover money, a centennial, Congregational work in Georgia, notes from the South, illuminated spots, the government and the Indians, and what the world says. Southern echoes and a book notice round out the front pages, with news of the Georgia association and evangelistic labors.

Indian perils of missionary life, a Los Angeles Chinese mission, women's home mission groups, three new Southern organizations, and a young folks' piece on how the pennies grew follow. Receipts close the number. The issue shows mission giving, schooling, and church planting as a single, busy enterprise in the spring of 1889.
16141-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
The June 1889 American Missionary, volume forty-three number six, mixes editorials with field news from the association's schools and churches. Editorials weigh the financial outlook, the line between two centuries, and notes on Frederick Douglass. Southern reports cover church building in a day and Tougaloo University. Work at Hampton and a Black girl's prose poem also appear. Items from Whitley County add local color.

Indian, Chinese, and women's work fill the later pages, with a day's missionary work, Chinese Sunday schools, state women's meetings, and a teacher's letter from Georgia. Receipts close the number, naming the gifts that kept schools and churches running. The issue offers a detailed snapshot of mission charity in the postwar South.
16147-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
July 1889 brings volume forty-three, number seven of The American Missionary, published in New York by the American Missionary Association. Editorials discuss money, Congregational work in Georgia, Atlanta University, the industry and skill of Black Americans, and caste in the churches. Southern reports then cover mountain work in Tennessee, academies in Kentucky, and schools and churches from Marshallville to Wilmington.

Indian out-stations, Chinese work under Dr. Dana, women's state meetings at Meridian and Macon, and work among children round out the number, with receipts at the end. The issue shows a mission network teaching, preaching, and fundraising across the South and West. It is a rich source on race, schooling, and church life in 1889.
16153-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
August 1889 finds the American Missionary reporting an annual meeting, improving figures, letters, and civil rights in court. Southern pages describe what one writer found in the Cumberland Mountains. Cuts show cabins, a native church, and the Williamsburg academy. Anniversary exercises at Fisk, Talladega, Straight, Le Moyne, and Avery also appear. A new church at Alco and children's day at Chattanooga add cheer.

Indian letters from Miss Collins, the Ramona school, Chinese stations at Oroville, Marysville, and Petaluma, and women's local societies round out the number, with receipts at the end. The issue shows mission schools celebrating a year's work across the South and West. It is a warm, detailed record of 1889 mission life.
16154-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
September 1889 brings volume forty-three, number nine of The American Missionary, the monthly of the American Missionary Association. Editorials cover the annual meeting, the treasury, methods, five questions, a mid-summer catechism leaf, and Rome and the Negro. Southern reports feature the Hand Fund, Howard University, Tillotson Institute, missionary visits, and a call from Aunt Mary.

Indian letters from Oahe School, evangelistic work at Petaluma among the Chinese, women's state groups, a visit to a missionary Sunday school, and young folks' letters round out the number. Receipts close it, as usual, with the gifts that funded the work. The issue is a detailed record of mission schools, churches, and fundraising in 1889.
16159-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
At year's end, the October 1889 American Missionary takes stock of the association's work. Editorials report the annual meeting, voting members, the close of the financial year, letters from givers, and compromises in Georgia's Congregational churches, plus Indian contract schools and a minister's testimony. Field items, a vacation at Tougaloo, and a teacher's letter from the Tennessee mountains follow.

Fort Yates in Dakota, Chinese workers in China, women's state groups, and school incidents for young folks complete the contents, with receipts to close. The number shows the association taking stock at year's end, counting money, workers, and progress. It serves as a clear annual snapshot of mission work in 1889.
16172-the-american-missionary-volume-43-:
Closing the year, the December 1889 American Missionary devotes most of its pages to the association's annual meeting. Proceedings, a summary of the treasurer's report, Secretary Strieby on the association's place and work, and Secretary Beard on the missionary view of the Southern situation lead the number. Committee reports and addresses by Wright, Woodbury, Taylor, Hiatt, Fisk, Foster, Riggs, Stimson, Goodwin, and Salisbury follow, with a closing address by Dr. Taylor.

Women's work and receipts close the issue, as the association counts a year of schools, churches, and gifts. The number reads like a yearbook for a mission movement, formal yet full of local detail. Historians of American missions will find it a complete annual record.
16972-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This August 17, 1889 issue of the Scientific American Supplement mixes farm notes, lab work, and new electric gear. Readers find hints on raising turkeys, a life of a famed pear tree, notes on embryo growth, and a curious sunfish hatchery tale. Carey Lea's work on silver forms and Davies on turpentine add weight for chemists.

Electric light at the Paris show leads the applied side, with full notes on the Oerlikon plant and gear. The mix shows the magazine's aim: plain, pictured reports that a farmer, a chemist, or a shop owner could all use. As a record, the number captures 1889 science in mid-stride, keen on light, metals, and farm craft alike.
17755-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 717, dated New York, September 28, 1889, volume twenty-eight, offers the week's popular science and engineering. Scientific American itself dated from 1845, and the supplement cost five dollars a year, or seven with the parent paper. Its table of contents opens with civil engineering, including the Girard hydraulic railway.

That railway, a curiosity of the Paris exposition, ran almost without friction, and eight pictures show its structure in section. Readers get a single weekly number of late Victorian technical journalism, wide-ranging and illustrated. The issue suits readers of invention, engineering, and the Paris exposition year.
19362-in-the-year-2889:
Jules Verne and Michel Verne wrote this short futuristic piece, In the Year 2889, first printed in the Forum in February 1889. A redactor notes it is now thought chiefly Michel's work, though its topics echo Jules. It imagines people of the twenty-ninth century, surfeited with marvels, living as if in fairyland.

Towns hold ten million souls, streets run three hundred feet wide, houses rise a thousand feet, and pneumatic tubes carry travellers at a thousand miles an hour. Reporters with telephones and telephotes send news and pictures, even phototelegrams from Mars. Readers get a charming Victorian forecast of media, travel, and city life.
25726-the-pretty-sister-of-jose-1889:
Frances Hodgson Burnett writes this 1889 tale, The Pretty Sister of Jose, published by Scribner's Sons. Jose, slow and dull yet kind and faithful, laboured long to prepare a tiny home outside Madrid for his aged grandmother and Pepita, bringing them there in triumph one hot summer day.

Vine leaves and orange trees stood dusty in the heat, and Jose, big as an ox in body and heart, proved slow in everything except carpenter work. From boyhood in his uncle's vineyards, tilling fields and feeding flocks, he kept a fancy and knack for woodwork. Burnett builds a Spanish family story on his patient love.
26656-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Nature Study Publishing Company of Chicago issued this August 1897 number as volume two, number two, of Birds, a monthly serial illustrated by color photography. The series aimed to promote knowledge of bird-life through accurate colored portraits and popular biographical text, including juvenile autobiographies approved by high ornithological authority. Volume one had entered public schools as a textbook.

This issue opens with bird song from June morning excursions, then profiles the American osprey, the sora rail, the Kentucky warbler, and the red-breasted merganser, among others. Praise from Elliott Coues, John Burroughs, and Frank M. Chapman is quoted for the pictures' faithfulness in color and pose. It is a gentle introduction to common North American birds.
31684-belford-s-magazine-volume-ii-no-8-:
Belford's Magazine, volume two, number eight, for January 1889, opens with an essay called Wicked Legislation, on mankind's patient submission to tyrants' demands. The number also carries the Honor of an Election, Andy's Gift, and a piece from the windows of a great library. The Root of the Spoils System follows, with Uncle Scipio and a piece on silk culture.

Its editorial department takes up the communism of capital, the infamy of it, and the pulpit cult, and the number closes with reviews and the passing of the year. The magazine mixes politics, fiction, and comment, and this issue shows its range from legislation to literature in a single monthly bundle.
32282-elevator-systems-of-the-eiffel-tow:
Robert M. Vogel's Elevator Systems of the Eiffel Tower, 1889, issued as a Smithsonian museum paper, traces the powered lift. It follows the lift from its mid-nineteenth-century beginnings to the three separate lifts fitted in the Eiffel Tower in 1889. Vogel was a curator at the Smithsonian's National Museum. He writes for engineers and general readers alike.

The tower's elevators, Vogel explains, faced problems of capacity, height of rise, and safety beyond any met before. The equipment that resulted was the first able to meet the ways to move people up in the new tall building. Its sections cover early work for the tower, how it stands, lift development before the tower, the tower's lifts, and an epilogue. Readers get a Smithsonian history of lifts, where a thousand-foot tower forced the lift to grow up.
4859-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
After the Armada crisis, the war slackens into sieges and expeditions, and John Lothrop Motley follows the years 1588 and 1589 through their mixed results. Alexander besieges Bergen-op-Zoom until fury and failure force him to raise the siege, while Gertruydenberg is betrayed to Parma and the States rage at the treachery.

Schenk attacks Nymegen, is defeated, and drowns, and an English-Dutch expedition to Spain achieves meagre results. The deaths of Guise and the queen mother, and then the murder of Henry III, reorder French politics. Motley captures the exhaustion after crisis, when Europe breathed again but found no settled peace.
613-the-constitution-of-the-empire-of-ja:
The Meiji Constitution of 1889 sets out Japan's imperial government in this short legal text, fronted by an imperial oath. The emperor swears in the palace sanctuary to keep the ancient form of rule, yet to give his subjects a wider range of action and his heirs a clear guide. An Imperial House Law accompanies the constitution.

Articles define the throne, the Diet, ministers, courts, and subjects' rights in formal, solemn language. The text marks Japan's step from feudal rule to a modern state on imperial terms. It serves as a key document for readers tracing Japan from Meiji reform to war and, later, to a new charter.
9477-spalding-s-baseball-guide-and-offic:
Spalding's Base Ball Guide and Official League Book for 1889 served fans of America's young national game. The book pairs the official league record with Spalding's own trade in bats, balls, and athletic goods. Depot lists name supply houses east, west, south, and abroad. Club presidents, league clubs, and city teams fill the front matter.

Inside, readers find batting and fielding records by position, pitchers' marks, club totals, and notes on coaching signs and overrunning bases. The American Association gets its own records, with Chicago games set out in full. A reader gets a rich snapshot of 1889 baseball, when the game was fast becoming a national pastime.
a-book-of-golden-deeds-pg6489:
Charlotte M. Yonge asks first what a golden deed is, then answers with a long table of them. Alcestis and Antigone stand early in her contents. The pass of Thermopylae, the two friends of Syracuse, and Regulus join them. The keys of Calais and the battle of Sempach follow. Her preface notes that the noblest deeds are often the best known, grown hackneyed by fame.

The stories run from Greek and Roman heroes through medieval saints and burghers to soldiers in the snow, heroes of the plague, and the Vendeans. Each is told briefly, as an example for young readers of courage, loyalty, or self-sacrifice. Yonge, a beloved Victorian writer for the young, chose deeds across all centuries and ranks, and her book stayed in print for generations.
alexander-moral-order-progress-1889:
Moral Order and Progress, published in 1889, is Samuel Alexander's first book, an analysis of ethical ideas from an evolutionary standpoint. The young Manchester philosopher asks how moral ideals arise, change, and claim their hold over human conduct.

Alexander treats moral judgment as a balance struck by a society at a time, like an equilibrium in nature, and ideals as its forward pressure. Goodness is therefore real but historical, growing with the social organism. The book's naturalism prepared his later account of emergence. It remains a clear, early statement of evolutionary ethics in Britain, still worth reading.
appletons-cyclopaedia-american-biography:
Volume Six of Appletons' work, from 1889, completes the set, covering Sunderland to Zurita. A general index to all six volumes closes the work. Wilson and Fiske had finished the largest American book of lives of their century.

The final alphabet stretch holds Washington's officers, western explorers, and the editors' own contemporaries. Washington himself receives one of the longest lives in the set. The index lets readers trace families and find every portrait. Appletons' remained the standard national biography until the twentieth century's greater dictionaries replaced it, and it is still mined for lost details. The last pages let a reader find any name in the whole set in a few short steps.
arxiv-2412-02489:
Felix Bartel and four co-authors use an old statistics trick, picking points that maximize a determinant, to build tight frames and exact sampling rules. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. In statistics the trick picks the best places to measure. In numerics it has served for integration and fitting.

The team turns the trick toward a clean goal: capture a function's total energy from few samples. For any space of functions of a set size, they build points and weights that do this exactly. The count of points stays modest, near the square of the space size. The same build lets users rebuild functions from their key modes with least squares. It works on spheres and on wave-like functions in many variables. Tests suggest the point count cannot be much improved.
arxiv-2412-03589:
Valentina Anita Carriero and co-authors use large language models to turn written procedures into knowledge graphs, then ask people to judge the output, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Procedures live in recipes and manuals as plain text, which machines cannot run directly. Prompts pull out steps, actions, objects, tools, and timing into a set graph form.

A user study scored the pulled graphs for quality and for felt use. Models gave output of fair quality by those scores. Judges also shared how they view AI help in such tasks. The work sets up digital aids for people who must follow or run procedures. Readers get human grades, not just machine scores.
arxiv-2412-04989:
Dimitrios Bozanis and colleagues used light to locate users for programmable wireless rooms in a 2024 paper. Future networks will steer signals with reconfigurable surfaces on walls and ceilings, but steering needs to know exactly where each user stands, even when a handset tilts randomly and hardware is imperfect. Their framework pairs ordinary ceiling LEDs with light-emitting versions of those surfaces, which add extra signal paths from more angles.

Equations for signal-strength positioning are derived with random receiver orientation built in, plus placement rules for the lights that guarantee a unique answer. Simulations show the added paths improving accuracy and cutting errors under varied orientations. Smart surfaces that also shine become beacons for the network they serve.
arxiv-2412-05489:
Pingwei Liu and co-authors wrote a physics paper in 2024 on the exotic properties of a two-dimensional semimetal, a manganese boron hydroxide compound not yet made in the lab. Most useful materials have one single strong trait, which limits them to one purpose. A material whose many traits can be controlled would be far more useful for electronics.

The math finds eighteen distinct electrical polarizations in the material, with three sizes across twelve directions. Switching it is linked to a split of the band structure between spin states and to ferroelastic change, a spring-like switch of the crystal's shape. These traits can be shifted by controlling how the chains line up in the sheet. The boron layer forms a near honeycomb lattice, which hints at superconductivity. The authors propose it as a strong candidate for sensing uses at the two-dimensional limit.
arxiv-2412-06789:
Hernan Gustavo Solari and Mario Alberto Natiello rebuild quantum mechanics from electromagnetism in this 2024 paper. Their construction aims to harmonize quantum theory with classical mechanics. Puzzles such as wavefunction collapse and Schroedinger cat are absent by design. The unifying rule is Hamilton principle of least action, which also secures energy conservation.

Part one builds the theory for a single charged entity and its interactions with other charges and matter. Part two tests the theory on the hydrogen atom. The electron proton relation is derived systematically, without analogy or ad hoc steps. Standard quantum equations tied to measurement can be recovered as a special view. The authors also argue the usual notion of isolation in time evolution is flawed.
arxiv-2412-08889:
Yu-Yang Songsheng and co-authors measure distances to binary stars in other galaxies by pure geometry, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The method answers the call for fresh distance ladders amid the Hubble tension. Spectroastrometry, radial velocity, and light curves are fitted jointly to one binary model.

Mock data tests show how data quality and binary traits sway the errors. A typical eclipsing pair in the Large Magellanic Cloud yields about six percent distance error. Single systems generally land under ten percent. No empirical calibration enters, and nearby known binaries can check the systematics. Repeated measures could pin whole galaxies, they argue.
arxiv-2412-09489:
Fulvio Melia compares two views of the cosmos ahead of a new kind of test, in a letter from two thousand twenty-four. The test watches how the red shift of far objects drifts over years. That drift gives a direct check on how the universe expands, free of model bias.

Melia weighs the standard model against an alternate model in which a set horizon grows with time. Three planned ways to take the measure are covered. A giant new telescope should split the two views after twenty years of watching far sources. A second planned tool could do the same in ten years, using nearer sources.
arxiv-2412-10389:
Wei-Ting Chen surveys reliability problems in a hardware design that runs spiking neural networks on memory chips that also compute. Spiking networks mimic the brain's event-driven style and promise low energy use, which suits small edge devices. ReRAM chips store data as resistance and can compute in place, dodging the bottleneck between memory and processor. Joining the two ideas creates a promising but fragile platform.

The survey reviews the basics of spiking networks and ReRAM crossbar arrays. It then catalogs the failure sources on both sides: device variation, drift, and operational errors in the memory, plus sensitivity in the networks themselves. Existing fixes are gathered and compared. The author aims to give designers a clear map of what can go wrong and which remedies the field has tried so far.
arxiv-2412-11289:
Paulina Stevia Nouwou Mindom and three co-authors tested ways to keep bug finding tools sharp as code changes. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with links between bug reports and the code changes that caused them. Deep learning tools find those links well at first. But as code shifts over time, their aim fades, a drift that hurts real use. The team asked if continual learning can hold the line.

They tried continual learning on many sub tasks with steady and shifting data. They set it against a BERT based tool, a reinforcement learning tool, and a function level learner. Readers who build code tools learn if step by step retraining beats one off training. Fresh proof can guide how bug hunters are maintained.
arxiv-2412-13989:
Candace Ross, Melissa Hall, Adriana Romero Soriano, and Adina Williams ask, in a 2024 paper, what makes a good automatic score for whether an image matches its text prompt. Four popular scoring methods all lean on language or question-answering models as parts. The authors set out clear traits such a score should have, then test each method against them.

No method met all the traits, and all were too blind to some changes in words or images. Three methods added new signal beyond the simplest one, yet they tracked each other closely. Tests also showed parts of the methods could be dropped with little loss, and that question-based scores lean on text shortcuts like a bias toward yes answers.
arxiv-2412-15689:
Zihan Ding and his eight co-authors, publishing in 2024, make AI video generation dramatically faster without draining its quality. Diffusion models build video over many sampling steps, which is slow. Cutting steps usually costs sharpness or variety. The team's method, DOLLAR, trains a small student model to imitate a big teacher in very few steps, blending two distillation styles to keep both quality and diversity.

A second trick fine-tunes the student against a reward score computed in compressed space, which saves memory and works with any scoring rule. On a standard benchmark, the student scored 82.57 for ten-second videos, beating its own teacher and three rival systems. One-step generation ran up to 279 times faster than the teacher. Human judges also preferred the four-step student over the teacher's fifty-step output.
arxiv-2412-15989:
Sébastien Clesse, Virgile Dandoy, and Sonali Verma wrote a 2024 astrophysics paper asking whether merging primordial black holes could explain part of the gravitational wave background hinted by pulsar timing arrays. These arrays time ultra-precise pulsars to detect ripples in spacetime at very low frequencies.

The authors ran a Bayesian search of the international pulsar timing data release for a combined background. One part comes from scalar perturbations in the early universe, the other from unresolved mergers of primordial black holes across a broad mass range. Constraints from the cosmic microwave background and from black hole overproduction sharply limit the merger share. They find the scalar-induced waves dominate at nanohertz frequencies, leaving black hole mergers a smaller role.
arxiv-2412-16189:
Brandon Le studies two artificial neurons wired together, in a 2024 preprint, and the wild geometry of their possible fates. The neuron model is the Rulkov map, here set in a calm, nonchaotic mode. The pair is coupled electrically, but the coupling is lopsided: one direction is stronger than the other. Even simple neuron pairs can settle into more than one long-term behavior. Which fate arrives depends on where the system starts.

Le maps the sets of starting points for each fate. Those basins turn out to have fractal edges of great complexity. A strange extra state appears: a chaotic spiking-bursting pattern that acts almost like an attractor. He calls the resulting picture quasimultistability. Using uncertainty exponents, he shows tiny changes in the start can flip the final state. Such extreme sensitivity, he argues, could matter for how real neural systems behave.
arxiv-2412-16589:
Hitesh Sagtani, Rishabh Mehrotra, and Beyang Liu improve in 2024 the AI that fills in missing code. Fill-in-the-middle models read code before and after a gap to suggest what belongs there. They must answer fast, which favors small models, but small models stumble on hard patterns.

The team mined code repositories for the patterns that most often break completions, and built extra context using compiler analysis. Fine-tuning models of several sizes on this curriculum helped all of them, and helped small ones most. Live A/B tests on real users showed more accepted and kept completions, with no added delay. The work balances accuracy against the strict speed coding tools demand.
arxiv-2412-18689:
Ehsan Faridi, Se Kwon Kim, and Giovanni Vignale compute, in a 2024 preprint, how a magnetic wall inside an insulator can throttle heat carried by spin waves. The material is an antiferromagnetic insulator, which conducts no charge but passes magnons, the quanta of spin waves. A domain wall is a narrow seam where the magnetic order flips. Heat flow through such a seam matters for future magnon-based devices. The authors apply a magnetic field along the material's easy axis and track what changes.

The wall's own spin couples to the field, which alters how spin waves pass through. The field also splits the two magnon modes so they carry unequal shares of heat. With a narrow wall reflecting part of the waves, the heat current shifts markedly. The effect is a thermal magnetoresistance: field-tunable heat flow. The authors propose the wall as a control knob for magnonic circuits.
arxiv-2412-19489:
Zhilei Shu and colleagues made live animation from diffusion models practical in a 2024 system called RAIN. Streamers and virtual hosts want endless, steady animated video, but diffusion generators are slow and drift in quality over long runs, especially on home hardware. RAIN rethinks how attention is shared across frames at different noise levels and across long time spans.

By denoising many more frame tokens at once, it cuts delay while keeping long-range consistency. A standard image diffusion model, fine-tuned briefly with RAIN, then streams video in real time on a single high-end consumer card, with little loss in quality. Streams can in principle run without limit. Live creators gain a cheaper path to stable animation.
arxiv-2501-00889:
Syamantak Datta Gupta benchmarks, in a 2025 paper, the new breed of time series foundation models on a deliberately plain test: repeating patterns buried in noise. These large pretrained models promise strong forecasts with no task-specific training, yet hard-nosed tests lag behind the claims. The author builds two synthetic data sets of noisy periodic series and varies the noise, the cycle length, and the sampling rate.

As yardsticks he uses two classical tools, a Fourier-based method and a linear autoregressive model. The big models matched or beat the classics when cycles were bounded and sampling dense. Their edge melted as periods lengthened, noise rose, sampling thinned, or shapes grew complex. The study gives practitioners a sober map of where zero-shot forecasting can be trusted and where simple statistics still win. It also argues for tougher, more basic test beds in this field.
arxiv-2501-00989:
Jacob Adamczyk, Volodymyr Makarenko, Stas Tiomkin, and Rahul Kulkarni wrote a machine learning paper in two thousand twenty-five on helping agents learn when rewards are rare. In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trial and error. When rewards come seldom, learning is slow. A known fix adds shaped rewards, extra signals that guide the agent without changing the best strategy.

Shaping needs a guide function, and a poor guide can hurt training. The authors let the agent use its own current guess of state value as that guide, a move they call bootstrapped reward shaping. They prove the method settles in simple settings and show faster training on Atari games.
arxiv-2501-02189:
Zongxia Li, Guangyao Shi, and four co-authors survey the fast-moving field of vision-language models. Their survey, from twenty twenty-five, tracks models that read images and text together. The field has moved from paired encoders to native multimodal giants. A few big model families now lead the frontier.

The survey maps how designs evolved step by step. It also charts how tests grew harder, from caption quizzes to long video and embodied tasks. Post-training tricks and agent uses get their own review. Domain uses, from medicine to robotics, are weighed with their risks. The authors close on open challenges like calibration and trust.
arxiv-2501-02789:
Goo Ishikawa and Yoshinori Machida study a classic shape problem first set out by Cartan in 1893. The shape is a rule that limits how a system can move in space, known as a distribution. This one has a rare symmetry tied to the algebra called F4. The authors look at its odd paths, called singular curves, through the lens of control theory and curved space measures.

From facts about those paths, they build an extension of Cartan's model. The extension yields a graded algebra built from nilpotent parts. That algebra turns out to match the negative part of the graded algebra of type F4. The work links a historic model to modern tools for paths with strict motion rules.
arxiv-2501-05289:
Gritz, Hoppe, and Ewerth ask in twenty twenty-five how the visual clutter of web pages affects people who search in order to learn. Searchers judge pages within a second of seeing them, past work shows. Yet little was known about how clutter shapes learning itself, a gap that matters for building search tools that truly support study.

They modelled page clutter and beauty with a wide set of layout traits. They linked those traits to behaviour in a lab dataset where people learned how thunderstorms form. Fit with the topic was the strongest driver of learning gains. Still, sessions with simpler pages led to better learning, and layout traits mattered more than simple counts like image numbers. They share their code openly.
arxiv-2501-06589:
Muru Zhang and co-authors reshape neural network architecture so big models can talk and compute at the same time, in a 2025 paper. Splitting a model across graphics cards speeds it up, but the cards must swap data constantly, and that chatter eats the gains. Their ladder-residual tweak changes the wiring of residual blocks so communication can hide behind computation. The idea needs no exotic systems tricks.

Applied across a 70-billion-parameter transformer, it cut end-to-end inference time by 29 percent over eight devices. Ladder models of one and three billion parameters, trained from scratch, matched standard models. A large open model was partly converted with barely any quality loss after light retraining. The authors release their training and inference code.
arxiv-2501-08389:
In two thousand twenty-five, Atharv Belsare, Zohre Karimi, Connor Mattson, and Daniel Brown present VOSA, a shared autonomy framework that lets a robot guess what its user wants without prior training. Shared autonomy should let high-degree-of-freedom robots assist people rather than hinder them.

VOSA uses only end-effector vision to estimate user intent on the fly, then blends robot and human control. Installed on a Kinova Gen3 arm, it matched an oracle baseline that knew all possible intents in advance. In user studies on three tabletop tasks it also demanded less effort and time than existing approaches, and most participants preferred it.
arxiv-2501-12089:
Maryia Zinouyeva and a large team of co-authors measure electron-phonon coupling in cuprates in twenty twenty-five. Cuprates are layered copper-oxide superconductors. How strongly electrons couple to lattice vibrations, and how that varies with momentum, is an open experimental problem. Phonon peaks in X-ray scattering spectra can reveal the coupling, under approximations that need checking.

The team measured scattering intensity across several cuprates, varying photon energy and momentum transfer. Phonon symmetry and electronic structure both shape the signal. Their care with the approximations matters for trusting the numbers. Readers in condensed matter get a firmer handle on a coupling that may help explain high-temperature superconductivity. The work spans calcium, lanthanum, and yttrium based cuprate families.
arxiv-2501-13189:
Alexander Spinos and co-authors give, in a 2025 paper, a team of exploring robots a way to imagine the rooms they have not entered. Robot scouts act only on what their sensors have already mapped. This team's map predictor paints plausible completions of the unknown space, using a fine-tuned image-generation model that filled in simulated city blocks quickly and coherently. Where the model's guesses disagree most, a measure the authors call generative entropy runs high.

The trick is where to send the robots next. Instead of chasing the spots promising the most new information, the team sent its three simulated vehicles toward high-entropy spots, the places the model could not make up its mind about. The imagined map converged on the true scene significantly faster that way. The authors frame uncertainty about the unseen, not just ignorance of it, as the compass for exploration.
arxiv-2501-13689:
Anirudh Sivakumar and co-authors simulate colliding dark matter condensates in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Some theories model dark matter as a self-gravitating quantum condensate. The team merges two such condensates in a computer model and watches the flow patterns that result.

The merging speed sets the regime. Collisions spawn dark solitons whose decay creates vortices and drives the system into turbulence. Energy spectra follow a classic turbulence law at large scales and a steeper one at small scales. Over time, vortices drift to the edge and the turbulence fades. The authors say the self-gravitating trap shapes the density waves in ways that differ from trapped atomic gases, with lessons for star mergers.
arxiv-2501-15089:
Zhan Ling and eight co-authors build LongReason, a synthetic benchmark that stretches short reasoning questions into long-context trials. Their paper from twenty twenty-five answers a lag: models read ever longer inputs, but reasoning tests stayed short or shallow. Context expansion pads proven questions with surrounding material. The set holds 794 multiple-choice items across reading comprehension, logical inference, and math word problems.

Twenty-one models are put through it. Most sag sharply as context grows, including the state of the art. The analysis shows robust long-context reasoning remains unfinished business across task types. The benchmark is open-sourced for the community. Designers of long-window models gain a yardstick that measures thinking, not just retrieval.
arxiv-2501-16689:
Edward Chang builds MACI, a framework that lets groups of AI agents plan tasks with care for time and limits. His paper from two thousand twenty-five says large language models often plan by pattern alone. They check their own work poorly and handle limits in uneven ways.

MACI splits the job three ways. A meta-planner lists roles and limits, adds common-sense fixes, and draws a graph of task order. A set of agents then does the task work, while a run-time monitor adjusts the plan as things change. By keeping planning apart from checking, MACI did well on two scheduling tasks, such as wedding planning.
arxiv-2501-17489:
Xiaowei Jiang and co-authors build a brain-based spelling system for people who cannot speak or move well, in work from 2025. Their system reads brain waves through the scalp, with no surgery. Past systems of this kind could not cover the full set of letters, which capped their use in daily life.

The new system first decodes the brain signs of handwriting, letter by letter, across all twenty-six letters. A large language model then cleans up and sharpens the spelled text. The team reports strong exactness in tests. They frame the tool as a broad, friendly path to plain speech for users with severe speech loss.
arxiv-2501-18189:
Yingjie Zhao and Zhiping Xu test how well two kinds of neural networks learn the growth of fine inner shapes in matter, when taught from stored sets of past runs. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Inner shape change is most often faked with field or edge tools. Those match the twin forms such change takes: grid data and drawn forms. The team checks both plain nets and spiking nets, whose units fire in bursts. Their tasks are crack growth from stress and the rise of Turing patterns. The spiking form, with a leaky fire rule, won on care while using fewer terms and less memory. Its narrow weight range and sparse links drive the gain.
arxiv-2501-18589:
Nathan L Foulk, Silas Hoffman, Katharina Laubscher, and Sankar Das Sarma propose a new kind of spin qubit. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The design, called SAGE, stores one qubit in the spins of four electrons. It stays on at all times and can be run with baseband control alone.

Older exchange-only qubits leak and pick up errors from local magnetic fields. The SAGE space is shielded from those field shifts, and leaks are held down by the always-on exchange forces. When magnetic noise rules, the team finds far longer coherence and far fewer gate errors. Two-qubit gates need just one pulse between qubits, with a much simpler pulse shape.
arxiv-2502-01889:
Peter Chen, Yue Xie, and Qingpeng Zhang teach optimal transport maps that move mass with few nonzero shifts, making them readable in high dimensions, in work from twenty twenty-five. Neural transport solvers beat classic ones on speed and memory for tasks like drug response modeling. Their dense maps, though, are hard to interpret.

Earlier sparsity tricks worked only for exact solvers. Their new formulation brings displacement sparsity into neural solvers, with a smoothed counting penalty that beats the usual absolute value version. A flexible network design lets sparsity strength adapt during training. On large, high dimensional runs, the adaptive setup improved accuracy and stayed practical for downstream use.
arxiv-2502-02889:
Barker, writing solo in twenty twenty-five, surveyed AI advances in dynamic spectrum sensing and open radio networks. Wireless spectrum is scarce, so systems must spot free bands fast and share them well. Artificial intelligence increasingly does that spotting.

His reading report starts with DeepSense, which uses neural networks on spectrogram images for wideband monitoring in real time. Follow-ups add parallel sweeping and signal stitching to handle scale, delay, and varied data. The report then turns to Open RAN, the open, mix-and-match network design. AI there supports drone testbeds, digital twins, network slicing, and self-healing apps. Barker argues joining smart sensing with open networks points toward resilient, self-tuning 5G and 6G systems.
arxiv-2502-03589:
Zeyu Zhang and co-authors shrink the memory traffic that slows split large language model serving. Splitting a model run into a prefill stage and a decode stage uses hardware better. The snag is shipping key-value data between the two stages for long prompts. Shrinking that data by quantization helps, but restoring it costs heavy compute.

Their HACK system computes directly on the compressed data instead. The math mimics the full step closely enough to skip dequantization entirely. Trace-driven tests cut job completion time by up to about seventy-one percent. Gains over top quantization methods reached about fifty-two percent. Long prompts gain the most from the trick.
arxiv-2502-04389:
Shue Shiinoki, Ryo Koshihara, Hayato Motegi, and Masumi Morishige propose a text-driven workaround for diagram understanding in business documents. Vision-language models still struggle to extract structures and relationships from diagrams reliably. Office files, however, store diagram shapes, lines, and annotations as editable textual metadata.

The team extracted shape data from spreadsheet-based system design documents and fed it as text to a large language model. Compared with a vision-based method, the text-driven framework answered detailed structural questions more accurately. The approach extends to presentation and word-processing files with similar source data. The authors argue it can improve workflow efficiency and information analysis in real business settings.
arxiv-2502-04889:
Han Bao, Shinsaku Sakaue, and Yuki Takezawa prove that gradient descent can converge with any step size for a broad family of losses. Their 2025 paper studies training on data that a linear model can separate cleanly. Standard theory demands small steps, yet practice shows training often rides at the edge of stability and still works.

Earlier work proved any-step convergence for logistic loss, leaning on a special property that loss has. This team generalize through a wider loss family built from entropy-like functions. Borrowing the classic perceptron argument, they derive convergence rates for most losses in the family. Two named entropies give especially fast rates. The result widens the theory of why big steps do not break training.
arxiv-2502-05489:
Tak and co-authors open up how large language models infer emotions from text, step by step. Models can guess human feelings well, but the inner path they take was mostly unknown. The study finds emotion signals sit in set spots inside the model.

The result held across model families and sizes, backed by robustness checks. The spots also made sense under cognitive appraisal theory, which says feelings arise from judging a situation. By nudging those appraisal concepts, the team steered model outputs in expected ways. Precise control like this could aid safety in sensitive feeling-based uses.
arxiv-2502-07489:
Klötergens and five co-authors built a benchmark for forecasting messy medical-style time series in twenty twenty-five. Irregularly sampled series with missing values arise throughout medicine and engineering, yet models were being judged on just four datasets. Embarrassingly, a naive constant forecast beat recent equation-based models on three of them.

Their method generates benchmark data from real biological differential equations, then uses rejection sampling to keep only challenging instances. The resulting Physiome-ODE benchmark holds fifty datasets, an order of magnitude more than before. On it, differential-equation-based models finally play to their strengths, and the benchmark cleanly separates good forecasters from weak ones, reversing the old datasets' verdicts. The authors expect the benchmark to revive research on equation-based time series modeling.
arxiv-2502-07789:
Alfredo Capozucca and three co-authors test whether ChatGPT helps undergraduates write formal specifications in the B-method. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Formal methods demand precise, checkable descriptions of software. AI help is well studied for coding, but not for this stricter craft.

Students wrote B-specifications with and without the chat model's aid. The aid did not improve the correctness of their specs. Trust mattered in a surprising way: students who trusted the output less did better. The team also spotted a pattern in how students chatted with the model that tracked spec quality. The study warns against assuming AI lifts all technical writing. For formal work, skepticism seems to be part of the skill. The findings can guide teachers of rigorous software methods.
arxiv-2502-11389:
Jner Tzern Oon and three co-authors release a Python package in twenty twenty-five. The package, TEMPO, simulates pulse sequences for quantum systems. Pulse sequences are used across quantum computing, magnetic resonance, and quantum metrology. TEMPO builds on QuTiP, the Quantum Toolbox in Python, and its master equation solvers.

Users can define pulse structures in a straightforward way. Time-dependent Hamiltonians and pulse timing are part of that definition. Simulations run faster than naive QuTiP implementations of the same sequences. The package stays compatible with the existing QuTiP ecosystem. Readers who design control pulses get an accessible tool that removes boilerplate. The authors stress its immediate relevance to a wide range of research.
arxiv-2502-12089:
Alessandro Favero and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how diffusion models learn to create new combinations. Real data is built in layers: parts make features, features make wholes, and a good generator must learn the recipe, not just the samples.

The team models the data with a tree-like grammar and proves a tidy result. A diffusion model learns the grammar's rules once it has seen enough data to cluster features that share a context, much like the old word2vec trick. Big structures need more data than small ones, so learning climbs the tree level by level. A half-trained model thus makes outputs that hang together locally but fall apart globally. Tests on text and images match the theory well. The authors link the climb to the renormalization idea from physics.
arxiv-2502-13689:
Two authors, Raicher and Lv, solved the quantum path of a fast electron in two opposed laser beams. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with beams that run head on. In the electron's rest frame, one wave's pitch far tops the other's. That split sets this case apart from the known Compton scatter regime. The pair first built a classic limit trick for this set up.

They then solved the Klein-Gordon and Dirac forms in the WKB near classic frame. The Dirac wave ties the electron's momentum and spin in one knot. Spin flat momentum still matches the classic path. Readers in strong field physics get waves fit to count photon trades next.
arxiv-2502-14789:
Yoel Levy, David Shavin, Itai Lang, and Sagie Benaim propose, in twenty twenty-five, a way to split three-dimensional scene features into separate fields for editing. Past work distills features from big two-dimensional image models into a single three-dimensional field. That single field assumes features do not change with view angle. Their method instead uses several fields, each capturing a distinct structural part of the features. Some parts depend on view, such as reflections. Others do not. All are learned from two-dimensional supervision alone.

Each part can then be controlled on its own. With a single click, a user can select the features of one object, then segment, edit, or remove its reflective traits. Tests cover three-dimensional segmentation and new editing tasks.
arxiv-2502-16289:
Tuan-Anh Yang, Truong-Son Hy, and Phuong Dao classify hyperspectral images by looking at objects at several scales at once, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Hyperspectral cameras record hundreds of wavelengths per pixel, letting analysts tell materials apart, but pixel-by-pixel classifiers are noisy and speckled.

Object-based analysis groups pixels into meaningful regions first, yet a single segmentation scale misses details at other levels. Their network, MOB-GCN, builds a dynamic hierarchy of graphs across multiple segmentation scales. A multiresolution graph network then models both fine detail and global context together. Features from each scale are extracted and integrated before classification. Experiments show the multiscale fusion beats pixel methods and single-scale object methods. Land cover mapping, crop monitoring, and mineral surveys all lean on such classification. Seeing the scene at several resolutions mirrors how human photo interpreters actually work.
arxiv-2502-16989:
Davide Testa, Giovanni Bonetta, Raffaella Bernardi, Alessandro Bondielli, Alessandro Lenci, Alessio Miaschi, Lucia Passaro, and Bernardo Magnini wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents MAIA, an Italian benchmark that tests vision language models on video with two matched tasks at once.

For each video question, a model must both judge a claim as true or false and answer in its own words. A dozen reasoning kinds sort the questions, set to pull apart what the eyes give from what the words give. A joint score grades both tasks as one. The videos show Italian life and the text comes from native speakers. Scores run low across models, which exposes how shaky their grounded sense still is.
arxiv-2503-00889:
Xiaoxue Xu, Decong Yi, Xing Li, and Da-jun Zhang derive exact solutions in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. Their system is the discrete Chen-Lee-Liu system, a nonlinear integrable model on a lattice. They build the solutions with tools from algebraic geometry.

They first construct a symplectic map whose flows act as discrete phase flows. Compatibility of maps with different parameters yields the system itself. Special functions on the phase flow then let them rebuild the discrete potentials in terms of Riemann theta functions. The method extends to three dimensions, giving solutions of a discrete modified Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation. Genus one solutions are illustrated.
arxiv-2503-02089:
Jugal Garg and Parnian Shahkar improve fair division guarantees in a 2025 paper. They study splitting indivisible goods under the maximin share idea, where each person should get a fair share of what they could guarantee by dividing it themselves. When agents fall into a few types with identical tastes, exact fairness may fail once there are two types, so approximations matter.

Their new algorithms guarantee a stronger share for two agent types and a better one for three types than the best known before. The approach starts from the majority type's own fair partition and adapts it. The setting matches many real cases where people cluster into a few preference groups.
arxiv-2503-02789:
Paul Zivich and four co-authors show how to fill gaps in public health data when some groups are never measured at all. Standard fills rest on each trait mix having some measured cases, a rule called positivity. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The case in point is blood pressure in US youth from a national survey. Children under eight were never measured, so the rule breaks by design. The team blends the survey with outside knowledge through a mix of stats and math models. The blend gave a mean value lower than both a plain case only read and a stats based stretch. A check on the math model in the measured range backed the blend.
arxiv-2503-02889:
Wheeler extends a theory of gambles to choices made again and again over time in twenty twenty-five. The desirable gambles framework grounds imprecise probability in coherence rules. Its standard version assumes gambles add up in a straight line. That fails when rewards build on themselves, as in long run investing.

He swaps out the rule for adding with a nonlinear operator working in the log domain. The operator preserves the time average, or geometric, growth rate. That choice addresses the ergodicity problem, where group means mislead about one person's fate. He proves the key algebraic properties of the new operator. Examples show effects on coherence, risk assessment, and representation. The approach bridges mean values and time averages in decision theory.
arxiv-2503-03889:
Muhammad Waseem and co-authors wrote this manufacturing paper in 2025. They ask whether a pretrained language model, GPT-4, can run a robot production line in real time. Lines that pair machines with mobile robots need fast, knowing choices about which robot goes where. Old rules are hand-built and opaque, and learning methods need long retraining.

Their frame lets the model assign robots to machines as orders flow. It beat the classic rules: first-come-first-served and shortest or longest job first. It matched a top multi-agent learning method on throughput, yet needed no retraining and can explain its calls. The authors say such control fits plants short on experts and cash but keen on clarity and growth. The test bed was a serial line run by robots.
arxiv-2503-04889:
König and five co-authors classified phases on nonorientable spaces in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Non-Hermitian band structures can live on parameter spaces like a Möbius strip, which lack a consistent orientation. Such spaces arise when symmetries fold the parameter space back on itself. The authors sorted the gapped phases and the special nodal points there.

The gapped side exposed deep puzzles from braid group theory, including torsion and conjugacy. Gapless systems hosted exceptional points that break the usual fermion doubling rule, even in two-band models. Moving those points around the space flipped their non-Abelian charge. Braided phases left fingerprints as bulk Fermi arc degeneracies. The authors point to these as experimental signatures.
arxiv-2503-04989:
Ali Aghababaei and six co-authors open the black box of a classifier that scores psychological traits in text, word by word. Sentence-level classifiers for markers like agency are popular, but users cannot see which words drive a score. Integrated gradients, an attribution method, can assign each word its contribution.

The team applies the technique to agency, one of few markers with a verified deep classifier, BERTAgent, available. They tune how the attribution model is trained, test alternatives, and check usefulness in a real application scenario. A second scenario uses the method with only a small labeled dataset, deliberately encouraging overfitting to sharpen class-distinctive words. The goal is explainable sociopsychological text analysis that researchers can audit.
arxiv-2503-06089:
David C Jeong and co-authors present a model that rebuilds a person's 3D body mesh from a wearable camera view. Their 2025 paper uses first-person video from head-mounted fisheye lenses. Such views distort the image and hide parts of the body, which makes mesh recovery hard.

Their model, Fish2Mesh, is built on a transformer and adds a position block tuned to the first-person view. That block helps undo fisheye distortion inside the network. Heads in the model output body shape terms, camera shifts, and joint spots in 3D and 2D. Training data was scarce, so the team made weak labels with a prior model and third-person cameras. Tests beat earlier best models for this task, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-08289:
Ranjith Mudimadugula and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-five, neural networks inside simulations of merging neutron stars. Neutron star mergers shed light on how heavy elements form and on the state of ultra-dense matter. Simulations are costly and need big computers. One costly step converts conserved variables, the tracked bookkeeping values, into physical values such as pressure and density. The team asks if a neural network can do that step.

They ran what they report as the first merger simulations that use such a method for this step. The runs stayed stable and matched classic methods in accuracy. Total cost was comparable. The authors call it a proof of principle, and say more speed gains are needed before the method pays off.
arxiv-2503-09689:
Liangtao Peng and six co-authors explained in twenty twenty-five how magnetism arises in twisted double layers of two semiconductors, WSe2 and MoTe2. Stacking two sheets with a slight twist creates moiré patterns that flatten electron bands and boost interactions. Recent experiments found ferromagnetism in twisted WSe2, and the team set out to explain it.

Using a self-consistent Hartree-Fock theory, they trace the magnetism to a Stoner-like instability of the reshaped bands. Their model matches the observed shift between layer-mixed and layer-split regimes as filling and electric field change. Maps over twist angle and interaction strength reveal a zoo of states: valley-polarized ferromagnets, a triangular antiferromagnet, stripe order, and a multiferroic phase. The framework should apply across moiré materials.
arxiv-2503-09789:
Dickson Akuoko Sarpong and colleagues published an engineering paper in 2025 on identifying NFC tags by radio signals. NFC cards guard doors and hold identity data. Attackers can copy the digital data onto a clone card. Radio fingerprinting instead checks tiny physical traits of each card's signal, which cannot be copied.

The team built a software radio testbed for one common NFC standard. It sampled signals across channels and speeds to gather richer fingerprints. Deep learning and random forest models named the tags. A statistical method called conformal prediction measured confidence for each call. That let the system stop early once confidence was high. The result was fast identification with high accuracy.
arxiv-2503-10089:
Biaogang Wu, Zhanduo Tang, and Ralf Rapp compute how fast bound states of heavy quarks break up in the hot soup made when heavy nuclei crash. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Heavy quarks and their bound states probe how this soup, called quark-gluon plasma, moves matter. A sound count of their traits needs one frame for both free and bound heavy parts. The team uses a many-body T-matrix frame. Its core force is set by grid-based data on strong forces, with no weak-force shortcut. The summed chain gives a much stronger force than past weak takes. Bound traits, such as how tight the states are at each heat, come out of the same frame.
arxiv-2503-11889:
Oliver Gorton and Konstantinos Kravvaris build a way to fit the terms of the nuclear shell model to data, with trust-worthy bounds on the doubt. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The shell model foretells how nuclei are built, but its terms are fit to lab data. To reach far nuclei, by the drip lines, fits must be fast and their doubt true. Past ways cost too much and can play the doubt down. The team joins a fast stand-in, built by a stretch method, with a chance-based sampler. The stand-in remakes a known shell case with scant error. The sampler then fits the terms and gauges their doubt in full.
arxiv-2503-13689:
Stef Baas and three co-authors build exact tests for comparing two rates, such as success rates in medical trials, with the most power math allows. Common tests are either too loose or too strict, which wastes power. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team uses whole number programming to draw the best decision edge for a test. Their test lifts average power as high as it can go while holding false alarm rates in check across the full null range. Number trials showed steady power gains over the classic exact test and over strong rivals. For large samples where the build gets heavy, a mid value variant is the best looser option, and a web tool aids use.
arxiv-2503-14089:
A quantum Otto cycle runs a heat engine in rounds, trading heat for work or pumping heat as a cooler. Katoorani and co-authors study such a cycle built on a two-dimensional Ising model, a grid of interacting spins. Starting from the exact solution for the model's calm states, they pick the best settings for work extraction and cooling in very slow cycles. In those cycles the calm states sit in different phases, dodging the phase change.

Finite-time cycles deliver real power, but the authors warn that energy changes during the heat-exchange strokes include work spent linking and unlinking the fluid from its baths. That coupling work should not be mistaken for heat. For very fast cycles it wrecks performance, so an ideal cycle length maximizes work or cooling per unit time. Even transitions with no net energy change can heat the cold bath.
arxiv-2503-14189:
Yongqi Li and co-authors make AI assistants that see and read safer in their 2025 paper. Models that take in images and text can be tricked into harmful replies through either channel. Teaching them safety needs examples of good and bad replies, ranked by humans.

The team built such a data set with image-based prompts and ranked answer pairs. They noticed two quirks: the two channels can guard each other, and a model can cheat by leaning on one channel only. Their fix, called Blind Preference Optimization, trains the model while hiding parts of the input. Safety scores jumped by forty-five percent over the base model, beating the standard method. The data and code are public.
arxiv-2503-14889:
Kenjiro Ishizuka, writing solo, tracks three solitary waves in a damped wave equation over long times. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The model is the nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation with a friction term. Solitary waves keep their shape while traveling. With damping, their dance changes slowly. Three waves interact in ways hard to foresee.

Ishizuka proves the trio settles into a line-like arrangement. The waves act as if all three sat on one line. Their signs alternate along that line. Gaps between neighbors grow like the logarithm of time. The result holds across dimensions one through five. Wave theory gains an exact long-time portrait of a damped trio.
arxiv-2503-15489:
Elvis Kimara, Kunle Oguntoye, and Jian Sun introduce PersonaAI, a system that builds digital avatars imitating a real person's personality. Their paper came out in 2025. The system runs as a cloud-based mobile application.

Rather than training a huge model from scratch, the avatar draws on stored facts about the person at answer time, a method called retrieval-augmented generation. User data is collected through the app and kept in a secure database for that retrieval. A prompt-tuned open language model then answers in character, with context drawn from the person's own data. The authors argue this approach is lighter and more sustainable than full model training. They open-source their implementation to invite community development of personalized avatars.
arxiv-2503-15589:
Connor Hainje, Oren Slone, Mariangela Lisanti, and Denis Erkal present a 2025 simulation study of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy and its star stream. The dwarf is being torn apart by our galaxy, leaving a wide ribbon of stars. If dark matter particles can bump into each other, the tearing should run faster. The team ran a large suite of world models to test that idea.

With strong self-bumping, the dwarf lost most of its stars and near all its dark matter by today. A new trick that lets only set particle pairs bump traced the loss to a ram-pressure-like drying of the dwarf. The star stream also changes: a spur on its trailing arm fades as the dwarf lightens. Stream shapes could thus betray the nature of dark matter.
arxiv-2503-16789:
Seven researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on why chatbot users often get weak answers. Many people do not know how to phrase a prompt that states what they need. The authors study real chats between people and AI systems to see where user questions fall short.

They test a fix in which the language model itself rewrites a poor prompt before answering. The rewritten prompts drew better replies while keeping the user's original intent. The study is, they say, the first of its kind centered on real human-AI conversations at scale. It points to prompt rewriting as a built-in help for everyday users.
arxiv-2503-17989:
Yuan Zhou and co-authors simulate how a model micro-swimmer moves in fluids filled with flexible polymers. Their 2025 paper studies a squirmer, a simple self-propelling sphere, in solutions at varied flow regimes. Real microbes live in such messy fluids, and their motion matters for medicine and industry.

Simulations show striking effects for swimmers with active surface stresses. Rotation speeds up enormously, by up to a thousandfold in some cases, while forward speed falls. The cause sits in how polymers gather: they wrap ahead of pushers and collect behind pullers, twisting and braking the swimmer through contact and flow. A neutral swimmer instead sweeps polymers backward and feels little effect. The findings help explain how microbes navigate mucus and other polymer-rich fluids.
arxiv-2503-18389:
Alba Aguilera, Nardine Osman, and Georgina Curto fused agent-based modeling with the capability approach in twenty twenty-five. They simulate homelessness policy with the mix. The capability approach underpins the United Nations development goals. It judges policy by real chances it gives people. Shelter counts, but so do health, agency, and development. They turned it into a form a computer can use.

They cast the approach as a Markov decision process. Values and needs join the decision model as motivators. On that base they build an agent-based simulation where policies can be tested. It shows how each policy grows or gives back people's capabilities, with no test on real lives. Nonprofits and domain experts helped build it around health inequity and homelessness. It is meant to transfer to other social contexts.
arxiv-2503-19389:
Zahra Hamed-Labbafian and three co-authors propose three ways to solve a graph puzzle in a 2025 note. The puzzle asks for the largest set of points with a special property. On any shortest path between two points in the set, no other set member may sit in between. Such sets matter in several parts of graph theory.

Their three methods take different routes to the same goal. One solves the problem exactly through a whole-number program. The other two search by guided trial, borrowing ideas from evolution and from heating and cooling in metal work. Examples from different areas of graph theory show how each method performs.
arxiv-2503-19689:
Uttam Cadambi Padmanaban, Bharathram Ganapathisubramani, and Sean Symon blend lab data into flow models in two thousand twenty-five. Their case is flow that splits from a wing at a steep angle. They use flat plane data from a particle image method. The aim is to fix a known turbulence model with real data.

Their new frame adds three dimensional rules to the blend. A force term in the flow equations soaks up the mismatch. Flat blends force that term to cover both model flaws and data flaws. The full frame splits those two sources apart. It gave a better match for pressure, lift, and shear stress in the test case.
arxiv-2503-20489:
Hristo Sariev studies traits of probability kernels and how they relate to each other, in work from twenty twenty-five. A kernel gives the chance of events based on some prior data. Standard conditional forms can clash with what intuition expects from simple conditioning.

A stricter form, called proper, was coined to fix that clash. Sariev asks how properness links to four other traits: staying the same over time, fitting with other kernels, running in reverse, and covering all cases. He shows what each link says about kernel structure. He also solves the reverse task, giving tests for when a kernel is the proper form for some data split. The work is pure measure theory.
arxiv-2503-20589:
Wenchao Gu and eight co-authors ask what retrieval actually helps code generation in twenty twenty-five. Generating code for a whole repository is hard: dependencies are complex and contexts are long. Retrieval-augmented generation is widely used to cope. But which retrieved material helps had not been rigorously tested.

Their empirical study covered two benchmarks and three source types. In-context code and potential API information significantly improved model performance. Retrieved similar code, by contrast, often added noise. It degraded results by up to fifteen percent in their tests. Building on that, they propose AllianceCoder. It uses chain-of-thought prompting to split a query into implementation steps. It then retrieves APIs by matching semantic descriptions. Readers get evidence-based retrieval, not retrieval by habit.
arxiv-2503-20889:
Pranav Kukreti, Dominika Wylezalek, Marco Alban, and Bruno DallAgnol de Oliveira study feedback from dim to mid radio galaxies using the MaNGA galaxy survey. Bright centers can stir the gas in their host galaxies across wide spans. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team picked a large sample of radio active galaxies across a wide radio power range. They traced warm gas motion from a bright oxygen line in cube spectra and set it against star motion. Stirred gas clustered near galaxy centers, most of all when both radio and optical signs of activity were present and radio power was high. With only one sign, the stir was milder, which points to jets and light acting together.
arxiv-2503-22989:
Gabriel Recchia, Chatrik Singh Mangat, Issac Li, and Gayatri Krishnakumar introduce FindTheFlaws in a 2025 paper. Their project tackles a growing problem: as AI systems solve harder problems, people struggle to check the answers. Oversight methods such as debate and critique need test data with known errors.

FindTheFlaws bundles five datasets covering medicine, mathematics, science, coding, and the Lojban language. Each set holds long questions and long worked answers. Experts marked each answer as correct or flagged the exact spots where the reasoning goes wrong. The authors then tested leading AI models on spotting the flaws. Scores varied widely by topic, and experts still beat the models in some areas. The data gives researchers a fair yardstick for oversight tools.
arxiv-2504-00089: Houjun Zhang, Dajun Liu, and Yu-Zhe Liu wrote a short algebra paper in two thousand twenty-five on string algebras. String algebras are a class of algebras defined by combinatorial data, and the Gorenstein property is a key homological trait. The authors give a description of the self-injective dimension of string algebras. From that description, they obtain a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for a string algebra to be Gorenstein. The result gives algebraists a direct test for this property in a widely studied class.
arxiv-2504-00289:
Wang, Jo, and Mimno ask in twenty twenty-five whether language models built in China actually serve the languages spoken in China. Top open Chinese models have cemented China's lead in AI. Yet global test sets reward English skill, which may skew what builders prioritise, at the cost of local language needs.

They compared Chinese and Western open models across twenty-one language variants, from Mandarin to minority and European tongues. Scores tracked closely between the two groups, except that Chinese models led in Mandarin. Chinese models did well in French and German, yet sometimes failed to even name minority languages like Kazakh and Uyghur. The authors blame shared global benchmarks and training sources for the sameness.
arxiv-2504-01389:
Hou built a new way in twenty twenty-five to design fresh drug-like compounds, swapping trial re-ward learning for choice-based train-ing. Word tools gain from such preference train-ing, which scores pairs of good and bad outputs. A staged learning plan, easy tasks first, speeds the train-ing up.

The trained maker scored high on a known drug-design bench-mark set. On one blood-press-ure drug task it beat ri-val models by six per-cent. Later bind-ing tests on a tar-get protein backed its real-world use. The route looks like a strong, cheap path for data-led drug hunts.
arxiv-2504-01989:
Yi Yao and colleagues survey how machines reason out lane topology for high-definition maps, the invisible grammar self-driving cars navigate by. Knowing lanes exist is not enough; a vehicle must know how they connect, split, and merge. The survey organizes the young field into three paradigms. Procedural methods model roads by rules, aerial imagery methods read topology from above, and onboard sensor methods infer it live from the car.

The review traces the arc from rule-based beginnings to transformer and graph network systems. Standard metrics are explained, at road level and lane level, with benchmark comparisons on a leading data set. Dataset scarcity and model efficiency stand out as open challenges. Promising directions close the survey. For practitioners, it is a map of the mapping field.
arxiv-2504-03189:
Rohith Reddy Mada and Rajasekhar Anguluri wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It learns the wiring of a network from flow samples, for systems where what flows in must flow out, with a fast split algorithm.

The hidden wiring sits in the sparsity pattern of a Laplacian matrix that links flows to potentials. Past work set up a penalized likelihood fit but solved it with a slow general tool. The new method uses ADMM, the alternating direction method of multipliers, which is clear and fast. A Riccati equation turns out to run the core update. Tests on fake and real power and water nets show the speed.
arxiv-2504-03589:
Badhan Kumar Das, Gengyan Zhao, Han Liu, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It presents AdaViT, a vision transformer model built for three-dimensional medical scans, where different patients often arrive with different sets of scan types.

Most models assume every case has the same inputs, so a mismatch between training and new data hurts accuracy. AdaViT instead turns each scan type into tokens with a flexible tokenizer, then lets attention work across however many tokens a case has. In tests on brain infarct and brain tumor segmentation, the model carried pre-trained knowledge to new datasets with different scan sets. It did well with no extra training, with a little fine-tuning, and when moved back to older tasks.
arxiv-2504-03889:
Pedro Sandoval-Segura and co-authors hunted for dead weight inside large language models: attention heads that contribute almost nothing. Attention heads are meant to focus on relevant words, but some park most of their focus on the first token, a behavior called an attention sink. The team tested twelve scoring functions that flag inactivity in different ways, then removed the flagged heads to see whether the models noticed.

More than twelve percent of heads proved inactive on average. Removing them in the right contexts kept test accuracy within one percent of the original model. Scores based on a head's output size found slack heads that attention weights alone missed, while sink-based scores missed over seven percent of the inactive set. Fine-tuning, they also found, barely changes attention habits.
arxiv-2504-04389:
Zi-Ming Zhou, Zhi-Bin Du, and Chang-Xiang He present a 2025 math paper on extreme graphs, the networks that push a measure to its edge. The measure here mixes a network's edge count with the sum of its top two signless Laplacian values, a spectral gauge of shape. A recent result named the star graph with one added edge as the sole minimizer among networks with a set node count.

The new paper moves the contest to networks with a set edge count. The same star-plus-edge form, sized by edges, is again the sole minimizer. Proofs of this kind pin the exact shape where a spectral gauge turns. Such pins feed the wider study of how network shape rules signal flow.
arxiv-2504-05489:
