Harrison Katz and Robert Weiss wrote this econometrics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on forecasting many linked time series at once. Vector autoregression models do this well but drown in parameters when the series count and lag count grow.

The authors stage a fair race among shrinkage methods that pull wild estimates back toward zero. Three Bayesian priors, horseshoe, lasso, and normal, face two frequentist rivals across three simulation setups: a small overfit model, a sparse large one, and a mix of both traps. The horseshoe prior wins on accuracy of estimates and honest coverage of its intervals. Ridge forecasts points well but understates its own doubt. A run on Canadian macroeconomic data echoes the simulations. The paper guides analysts who must choose a prior before they see the data.
arxiv-2504-05789:
Bose and co-authors estimate infant body poses without any labeled infant training data in this 2025 paper. Pose tracking helps infant healthcare, but labeling baby images is scarce and costly. Adult pose models transfer poorly because infant bodies and movements differ.

Their system, SHIFT, starts from synthetic adult datasets. A teacher-student setup generates pseudo-labels for infants and enforces agreement between the two networks. A learned prior on plausible infant poses penalizes impossible predictions. A visibility module helps the model notice body parts hidden behind others. Across benchmarks, SHIFT beat unsupervised adaptation methods by 5 points and even supervised infant methods by 16. The approach frees infant studies from hand labeling.
arxiv-2504-07489:
Nipun Batra, Baradhwaj Coleppa, Akshat Khanna, Santosh Kumar Rai, and Agnivo Sarkar map the allowed space, in a 2025 preprint, for a model with three Higgs doublets. Extending the Higgs sector is a standard way to look beyond the Standard Model. In the version studied here, each doublet couples to only one type of fermion. The particle list grows rich: four charged Higgs bosons, two odd scalars, and three even scalars. One of those even scalars must match the known 125 GeV Higgs.

The team applies all current theory and experiment limits to the model's masses and couplings. Machine learning, in the form of active learning, speeds up the scan. They study three cases: the known Higgs as the lightest, middle, or heaviest even scalar. One lighter extra Higgs below the known one remains possible. Two lighter ones are ruled out.
arxiv-2504-07789:
Guzmán, Chatzikos, and Ferland warn, in a 2025 astronomy paper, that glow line strengths computed for hydrogen and helium plasmas can go badly wrong if the atom model is too small. Such lines are used to measure the early universe's helium share, where small errors matter. The team ran a standard plasma code with varied numbers of energy levels.

With too few levels resolved, some infrared hydrogen lines were off by more than thirty percent at thin space densities. Helium lines erred by ten to twenty percent. The fix is to match the level count to the target lines and to the plasma's heat and density. The paper is the fifth in a series on these spectra.
arxiv-2504-08189:
Ming Hsiao and Man-Chun Lee prove a gap theorem for a class of curved spaces in a 2025 mathematics study. Their spaces are locally conformally flat, meaning small patches can be rescaled to look flat, and they carry non-negative Ricci curvature. The question is how close such a space can come to curved without being curved at all.

Running a Yamabe flow that instantly tames the curvature gives the leverage. If curvature decays fast enough in an averaged sense, the space must be exactly flat. The result extends earlier gap theorems, sharpening the border between flat and genuinely curved geometries.
arxiv-2504-09489:
Hong Duc Bui wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It trims a classic proof on packing a large square with unit squares, by showing only near-flat squares need be weighed.

The waste in such a packing, the area left bare, grows at a set rate. Roth and Vaughan proved a floor for that growth, with a split of squares into good ones, tilted by no more than a hair, and bad ones. Bui proves the growth rate can be found from packings of good squares alone. The bad squares can be dropped, which makes the old floor proof much simpler. The paper is a neat step in packing theory.
arxiv-2504-09789:
Chao Liu and Arash Vahdat analyze warped noise, a training trick for video diffusion models that aims at smooth, consistent motion. Video-to-video tasks like style transfer need frames that stay coherent over time. Their theory explains why warping the noise during training works so well.

Pairing warped noise with the standard training objective quietly teaches the model to mirror spatial changes in its input noise. Motion placed in the noise then appears naturally in the generated video, with no extra modules. A bonus is speed: good results arrive in far fewer sampling steps. One-step distilled versions keep the property and beat comparable baselines on benchmarks.
arxiv-2504-09989:
Sarthak Joshi and Sathish Vadhiyar build a safety net for the world's biggest computers. In the exascale era, parts fail so often that the standard fix, saving checkpoints and restarting, would waste too much time. Their library, FTHP-MPI, instead runs copies of each process: when one copy dies, its twin carries on and the job never stops.

The trick is doing this inside a standard MPI library that was never built for fault tolerance, keeping its fast, platform-tuned communication. The team added efficient messaging between replicas and support for partial copying and checkpointing together. On three real applications, the library beat checkpoint-only methods when failures came at least hourly, and it cost almost nothing when nothing failed. The authors present it as resilience that fits the libraries scientists already use.
arxiv-2504-10089:
Boyi Hu, Zhongjian Wang, Jack Xin, and Zhiwen Zhang analyze a computer method for models of chemotaxis, where living things move toward chemical signals. Their paper appeared in 2025. The model, called the Keller-Segel system, pairs equations for the creatures' density and for the chemical field. In three dimensions it can focus sharply and may blow up in finite time. The team's method tracks swarms of particles for the density and a smooth field for the chemical.

A random batch shortcut keeps the cost down by skipping the usual limit step. The authors prove the particle cloud settles toward the true solution, measured in a standard distance, with high chance. Lab-style computer tests back the predicted rates. They also use the method to probe when the model blows up, which depends on how much mass starts in the system.
arxiv-2504-10489:
Vikranth Udandarao and colleagues built a browser extension that plans trips with language models in a 2025 paper. Roamify, a Chrome extension, generates personalized itineraries from user preferences, and the team experimented with several large language models, including Llama and T5 variants, as its engine. Two design choices anchor the system: scraping current news and blog articles about destinations so suggestions stay fresh, and a recommendation layer that reshapes the itinerary as user needs change.

Surveys of users found a preference for AI-powered planning over existing methods across all age groups, which the authors take as validation of demand for such assistants. The study, published in a human-computer studies journal, presents Roamify as evidence that travel planning is ripe for conversational, preference-aware tools.
arxiv-2504-12389:
Nayoung Lee and colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on keeping steel blast furnaces at the right heat. A blast furnace melts iron ore, and its inner heat swings in complex ways. Steady heat means better steel and less waste, but plain prediction tools often miss the swings.

The team mixes quantum computing with standard machine learning in one neural network. Their hybrid design aims to predict heat more exactly than older tools. They pair the forecasts with control of coal injection, one lever that steers furnace heat. Tests check whether the quantum-classical mix beats classic methods alone. The work points to new tools for heavy industry.
arxiv-2504-13489:
Kuowen Chen, Jian Li, Yuval Rabani, and Yiran Zhang present a 2025 paper on a broad class of optimization problems. Many tasks ask for the cheapest set under a norm, a size gauge that can bend in many ways. Gauges that treat all entries alike and grow with them form the class here. The authors recast the whole class as a multi-goal problem with log-sized budgets, at only a fixed loss in quality.

That one bridge yields near-best methods for several cover problems at once. Interval cover and multi-size knapsack cover get fixed-factor methods, and set cover gets a log-factor one. For matching and path problems, a natural relaxed form proves too weak, a useful warning. One reduction thus sorts a whole shelf of problems.
arxiv-2504-15589:
Hitesh Poddar, Tomoki Yoshimura, and Art Ishii report tests of a wireless signal model in a 2025 arXiv paper. They check a standard model for how signals lose strength indoors, known as the 3GPP indoor hotspot model. The checks support work on standards for 6G networks.

Their team measured real signals at four frequencies, from 6.75 to 73 gigahertz, in both clear and blocked paths. They compared the standard model with two fitted models. The results show the standard model holds for the 7 to 24 gigahertz range in both path types. The findings feed into the standard-setting work for future networks.
arxiv-2504-16589:
Norihiro Iizuka, Simon Lin, and Mitsuhiro Nishida extend a mathematical measure of genuine multipartite entanglement, quantum linkage that truly involves all parties at once. Their earlier work defined such a measure for any number of parties; this paper gives a systematic recipe for building it. The construction turns on a counting pattern from number theory, the partition numbers, which fix how many free parameters each measure carries.

For four parties, the recipe reproduces the known diagnostics and adds a new one. The authors then test the measures for four and five parties in holographic settings, where entanglement mirrors the shape of a dual spacetime. The values come out large in the expected way, both in formulas and in numerics. They read this as evidence that genuine multipartite entanglement is everywhere in holography. They discuss links to quantum error correction and bulk reconstruction.
arxiv-2504-16789:
Yu Jeffrey Hu, Jeroen Rombouts, and Ines Wilms keep fleets of forecasting models honest with MLMA, a monitoring agent built for digital platforms. Their paper from twenty twenty-five starts from scale trouble: platforms run huge, unstable counts of data streams, so hand-supervised monitoring collapses and firms retreat to weak unmonitored models. Their design science answer automates test-based retraining. A data-adaptive reference loss batch anchors the tests.

The human engineer stays in the loop through key metrics, acting proactively or after the fact. A large-scale trial at a last-mile delivery platform validates the framework in production. Performance holds in streaming settings without labor exploding. Model governance gains a scalable middle path between neglect and babysitting.
arxiv-2504-18289:
Beltrán and Shao wrote in twenty twenty-five a group theory paper on supersolvable subgroups. Groups are sets with a rule for combining elements, central to abstract algebra. A supersolvable group has a chain of subgroups with simple steps between them. The authors study finite groups that are not solvable, yet whose largest subgroups with order divisible by three are supersolvable. They pin down exactly what such groups can look like.

Either the group avoids factors of three in a key part, or a certain quotient has a named simple form. That form is a projective special linear group over a field of prime-power size. In that case a large normal subgroup is nilpotent, meaning its parts commute nicely. A smaller part lies in the group's center. The result completes a clear classification.
arxiv-2504-20189:
Cynthia Marcelino, Sebastian Gollhofer-Berger, Thomas Pusztai, and Stefan Nastic build a cost model for serverless workflows spread across edge, cloud, and space. Serverless computing rents code by the run, with no servers to manage. Spreading it over three layers adds wild swings in price and speed. Even one cloud's price list can hide traps.

Their model, Cosmos, names the factors that move cost for each function in a workflow. A case study prices real workflows on the two leading clouds. For data-heavy functions, moving and storing data ate up to three quarters of the bill. For AI-style compute, helper services behind the scenes dominated instead. Knowing which driver rules a function, the authors argue, is the first step to taming serverless bills.
arxiv-2504-20489: Kaoru Ono wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a sign and orientation problem in Lagrangian Floer theory. The paper works in the Bott-Morse setting and uses a de Rham model. It first gives the definition of filtered A-infinity operations in a Fukaya category. It then verifies the filtered A-infinity formulae with the signs fixed. Such sign conventions are the kind of careful groundwork that later calculations in Floer theory rest on.
arxiv-2504-20989:
Monbroussou and a large team build and run in twenty twenty-five the first light-based quantum neural network of the convolutional kind with adaptive state injection. Quantum circuits made of light keep a fixed particle count, a quirk lately used to design leaner networks. Adding injection, swapping fresh states in mid-circuit, gives extra control without breaking that thrift.

The chip used a semiconductor single-photon source and programmable interferometers of two sizes. It classified simple images in a binary task on real hardware, matching the design's promise. Simulations on larger datasets probed how the design scales. The authors also show a simple adaptive trick for a harder sampling task, aimed at near-term quantum devices.
arxiv-2504-21089:
Vervoort, Tang, and Bultinck present a paper from twenty twenty-five on averaging results for messy magnet chains. Such chains have random fields at each link, so each chain differs from the next. The usual way to find an average is to test many random chains one by one. Their new method skips that sampling step. It works with a grid method that treats the chain as if it had no end.

The method leans on the fact that the mess looks the same on average at each spot. They test it on a known odd point of a random chain model. That test case is famed for strong random effects. The authors show their method finds the average traits well. It offers a direct route for messy quantum systems.
arxiv-2505-00489: Lasse Grimmelt and Jori Merikoski prove a theorem on weighted averages of automorphic kernel sums in this 2025 paper. The sums are parametrized by congruence subgroups of the modular group. Their method applies spectral tools directly to the automorphic kernel. That route avoids passing through sums of Kloosterman sums, the usual detour. Symmetries of the problem survive better this way.
arxiv-2505-01689:
Samer Lahoud and Kinda Khawam propose a smarter way to receive long-range radio signals in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A frequency-hopping variant of LoRaWAN spreads packets into fragments for capacity and resilience. Today, though, one gateway must collect a whole packet alone.

Their macro-diversity scheme lets several gateways pool the fragments each of them hears. A stochastic geometry model captures header repetition, fragmentation, and coding redundancy. Closed-form formulas give success rates under interference. Simulations show large capacity gains over single-gateway reception. The authors argue fragment sharing could scale future low-power wide-area networks. The method uses gateways already deployed, turning overlap from waste into strength.
arxiv-2505-01889:
Sandro Coriasco, Alexandre Kirilov, Wagner de Moraes, and Pedro Tokoro studied a smoothness question for systems on open spaces in two thousand twenty-five. The spaces pair a non-compact manifold, a space that stretches without end, with a torus. The system acts on differential forms, which are tools for measuring change.

The question is global hypoellipticity, whether rough inputs that give smooth outputs must in fact be smooth. The authors show the answer depends on number traits of the closed one-forms that define the system. Their proof uses microlocal tools adapted to scattering spaces and a form of the Hodge theorem. The result extends earlier work done on compact spaces.
arxiv-2505-02889:
Komolafe, Mei, Zarate, and Spangenberg proposed a transfer learning method in twenty twenty-five for predicting sepsis early. Sepsis, the body's extreme response to infection, can kill within hours, so early warning saves lives. Existing prediction models use inconsistent sets of vital signs and lab values, and most train on narrow patient groups, which limits their reach.

Their method, Feature-Aligned Transfer Learning, first aligns models on the features most studies share, like heart rate and temperature. It then blends models trained on diverse populations, weighted by each model's contribution. The aim is a predictor that travels across hospitals and patient mixes. The authors present it as a practical route for early sepsis detection, especially in hospitals with few resources.
arxiv-2505-03089:
Lalitwadee Kawinwanichakij and eleven co-authors examine massive quiescent galaxies seen when the universe was young, in a two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. The seventeen galaxies are spectroscopically confirmed and lie at redshifts between three and four.

Using JWST imaging and Sérsic profile fits, the team derives a size-mass relation showing compact galaxies around zero point six to zero point eight kiloparsecs across. Formation history and shape jointly affect size: late-forming bulge-dominated systems run compact, disk-dominated ones larger. A random forest finds local environmental density the strongest predictor of bulge fraction in the data, while simulations point instead to merger history, suggesting several bulge growth pathways.
arxiv-2505-07989:
Matias Cattaneo, Rocio Titiunik, and Ruiqi Yu deliver rd2d, a software package for causal inference where treatment is assigned along a border. Their paper appeared in 2025. In boundary discontinuity designs, eligibility turns on crossing a line drawn in two scores, as in geographic programs bounded by a map line. The package, offered for three statistical languages, estimates effects with local polynomial fits using either the two scores or the signed distance to the border.

It handles sharp and fuzzy designs, picks bandwidths automatically, and gives bias-corrected intervals, uniform bands, and cluster-safe errors. An application to Opportunity Zones finds eligibility strongly raised designation rates but shows no early effect on workplace job growth. The authors aim to make border designs routine and reliable.
arxiv-2505-08389:
Rahmatullah Musawi and Sheng Lu propose benchmarks that resist contamination by training data in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Test sets leak into model training, inflating scores. A resistant test should stay hard even if seen before.

Their example uses Caesar ciphers, letter shifts like turning ab into bc. The task is simple to state but hard to fake from memory. Tested on popular large language models under varied settings, the cipher test tripped the models once contamination was controlled. The authors say the stumble raises doubts about what headline scores really measure. They offer the idea as a base for tougher evaluation.
arxiv-2505-10789:
Eppstein, Goodrich, and Liu introduced a new graph measure in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Bandwidth asks how narrowly a graph's connections can be laid along a line. It matters for reordering matrices and drawing graphs. The authors define BFS width, based on how a breadth-first search spreads through the graph.

They prove tight bounds tying BFS width to bandwidth within logarithmic factors. Unlike older width measures, this one is easy to compute in polynomial time. Small BFS width forces small bandwidth, pathwidth, and treewidth, which unlocks fast algorithms for hard problems. The team gives the first quality guarantees for a classic matrix reordering heuristic. They also rebuild bounded-bandwidth graphs from distance answers with few queries.
arxiv-2505-12489:
Shaobin Zhuang and co-authors teach a model to treat video as a language, in a 2025 paper. Text models like GPT predict the next word; video, though, carries the space and motion that words miss. Their Video-GPT predicts the next clip instead. It cleans up a noisy clip by leaning on the clean clips before it, one step at a time, which serves both short generation and long-range forecasting.

On a physics-based video prediction benchmark, the model scored well above two strong commercial rivals. It also adapted to six mainstream video tasks, spanning making and understanding clips. The authors argue next-clip training is a clean path toward world models that grasp how scenes unfold. They present the design as simple but broadly capable.
arxiv-2505-13389:
Peiyuan Zhang and co-authors present VSA, a faster attention method for video generation, in this 2025 paper. Video diffusion models pay a high cost for full attention, which grows with the square of size. Most attention weight lands on a small set of positions anyway. VSA keeps only those key positions, and it learns which ones matter.

A coarse stage pools tokens into tiles and picks the critical ones. A fine stage runs full attention only inside those tiles. The whole step trains end to end with no extra profiling. Tests ranged from small models to 1.4 billion parameters. Training cost fell by more than half at equal quality. Added to an open video model, it cut generation time from 31 to 18 seconds.
arxiv-2505-13489:
Wenkang Han, Wang Lin, Liya Hu, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It improves knowledge tracing, the task of predicting how a student will do next, by letting what a learner does in one course inform the model of another.

Most tracing models look at a single course, so they miss how skills overlap. The authors' method, TransKT, first builds a graph linking related concepts across courses, using a large language model to spot the links. That graph guides the transfer of knowledge signals between courses. A pipeline then feeds summarized text features into the graph network to sharpen the transfer. A contrastive step lines up the single-course and cross-course views of each learner. The result is a fuller picture of what each student knows.
arxiv-2505-13989:
Yanzhe Wen and six colleagues tackle a weak spot in graph learning with large language models, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Their setting is the open world, where a text-attributed graph holds nodes whose classes were never seen in training and labels are scarce.

Older fixes lean on word meaning alone or graph shape alone to reject unknown classes, and they lack a good way to label new finds. The proposed framework, called OGA, joins both signals to trace where a label came from before trusting it. A second part, a graph label annotator, labels fresh nodes so the model can update itself. Broad tests show the system works well in practice. It offers a path for graph tools that must keep learning as new kinds of data appear.
arxiv-2505-14889:
Soyeon Kim sets out the cluster automorphism group of braid varieties, in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. Braid varieties are algebraic varieties picked out by positive braid words. Past work showed they carry a cluster structure. That is a rich combinatorial geometry brought in from mathematical physics. The group at stake here acts on such a variety and leaves its core shape as it was.

Gekhtman, Shapiro, and Vainshtein first set out this group. Lam and Speyer then studied it in their own work. Kim puts forth a description of the group for braid varieties. She also sets out how it acts on them. A few cases are worked out in full, step by step. Such maps show a variety's hidden symmetries. So to pin them down is to make the geometry more clear. The paper joins braid theory, cluster algebras, and symmetry in one concrete family.
arxiv-2505-15389:
DongGeon Lee, Joonwon Jang, Jihae Jeong, and Hwanjo Yu wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It tests whether image-and-text AI models stay safe when the image is a meme, the kind of picture real users actually share.

Most safety tests use artificial images, which may flatter the models. The authors built a benchmark of over fifty thousand cases pairing real memes with harmful or harmless instructions, generated under a detailed safety taxonomy. Across several models, and in both single chats and multi-turn talks, memes raised harmful answers and lowered refusals compared with text alone. Longer conversations helped somewhat, but the weakness persisted. Model size related to safety in complicated ways. The authors release the benchmark publicly and urge testing that reflects the wild, not the lab.
arxiv-2505-16289:
Yan Zhao, Yang Li, Zhengxue Cheng, Hengdi Zhang, and Li Song tackle a data problem in robot hands. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is called TacCompress. Skilled robot hands carry many touch sensors, since fingers block the view of what they hold. All those sensors send more data than the link can easily carry.

The team first builds a data set of touch signals from many grasps and objects. They then turn the signals into images and test common image codes. Lossless codes shrink the data to a tiny share with no loss at all. Lossy codes go further at some cost to detail. The bench gives hand builders a shared yardstick.
arxiv-2505-20489:
Luke Edholm and Vikram Mathew wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on the Bergman kernel, a key function in complex analysis. It is studied on regions of space, and one open problem asks when the kernel has zeros inside its region. Zeros can change how the region's geometry behaves.

The authors work on a class of quotient domains with a curved, ring-like shape. For rational shape values above one, they write an exact formula for the kernel. The formula turns on number traits of the shape value. They then build a chain of values nearing one where each kernel has zeros, though the limit case has none. That chain settles the open question for this class.
arxiv-2505-21289:
Nurbek Tastan and four co-authors present LoFT, a low-rank tuning method that mimics full fine-tuning of large models by fixing how the optimizer's memory is handled. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Low-rank adapters train tiny matrices instead of the whole model, saving memory. But they often trail full tuning and converge slowly.

LoRA-style methods learn the update in a small subspace yet leave the optimizer's momentum and variance in the full space. LoFT projects those moments into the same small subspace too. The low-rank update then truly shadows the full update. That alignment removes the need to tune the usual scaling knob. Tests show LoFT closing much of the gap to full tuning. It beat standard adapter methods without adding run-time cost. The work suits teams adapting big models on modest hardware.
arxiv-2505-21689:
Five researchers wrote a computer science paper in two thousand twenty-five on ranking court petitions in India. A huge backlog of unresolved cases slows the delivery of justice. Sorting petitions by hand can be slow and shaped by personal bias, which adds to the delay.

Their system, called LLMPR, ranks petitions by how urgent their content seems. It learns from a data set of more than seven thousand annotated petitions. Text is turned into number form by three language models, then joined with simple counts such as days elapsed and word count. Among the models they trained, random forest and decision tree methods gave the best results.
arxiv-2505-22089:
San Jiang and colleagues speed up the matching of features across drone photos, a step that dominates the cost of building three-dimensional models from images. Their method, from twenty twenty-five, first picks likely image pairs with a fast retrieval search. It then groups images into compact blocks using a matrix reordering trick that follows image connections, so the graphics card wastes less time loading data. Matching runs inside each block with an accelerated hashing scheme, and rough matches are cleaned with local geometry checks plus a standard robust fitting step.

On large drone data sets, the schedule ran far faster than tree-based matching, with speed gains reported in the dozens of times. Accuracy in later camera and model adjustments stayed comparable. The authors offer the approach for survey teams facing very large aerial photo collections.
arxiv-2505-22589:
Bychkov and Litvinov uncover a dual regime in deformed sigma models in twenty twenty-five. Sigma models map fields onto spheres and anchor much of quantum field theory. Yang Baxter deformations bend them while keeping them solvable. In the high energy view, the models look like free fields with extra nudges.

Those nudges hide solvable systems keyed by one dial. A duality flips the dial, and odd sized spheres are self dual. Even sizes are not, which births fresh nudges of sigma type. The pair computes the matching curved metric and field. Both solve a generalized Ricci flow, they show.
arxiv-2505-22889:
Hamidreza Montazeri Hedesh, Moh Kamalul Wafi, and Milad Siami study how to prove stability for systems steered by neural networks, in a research paper from 2025. Such feedback systems are nonlinear, and their safe zone around a steady state is called the region of attraction. The work uses positivity constraints that the system obeys.

Their base is a local form of the Aizerman conjecture, which gives conditions for fast settling inside a bounded set. Two methods then estimate the safe zone. One builds bowl-shaped energy sets through a matrix condition, and the other tightens local bounds on the network layer by layer. Trials showed larger certified safe zones and better scaling than leading past methods based on integral constraints.
arxiv-2506-01189:
Emmanuel Hartman and Nicolas Charon build learning tools for data made of shapes in a 2025 study. Each observation might be a curve, graph, or surface, and shape spaces do not behave like flat number spaces. A model must also ignore how a shape is parameterized, or it will fail on the same shape described differently.

Their method represents shapes as varifolds, measures that pair position with direction. Duality with test functions turns shape comparison into operations a linear machine can use. Support vector style learning then handles classification and regression on geometric data. Keeping the right invariances should help the learned rules transfer to new shapes.
arxiv-2506-01789:
Genta Indra Winata and a large team of co-workers argued that data set records needs binding quality metrics in a 2025 position paper. Data sets drive machine learning, yet many data set papers lack newness, variety, or rigorous quality control, and reviewers often overlook the gaps. Datasheets, the standard transparency tool, describe a data set but offer no set. Scored way to judge its quality, and meeting metadata rules are imposed in mixed ways.

The authors advocate DataRubrics: full rubric-based scores for data quality, built-in into the review process itself so accountability has teeth. As submission volumes climb, they argue, only scored rubrics will keep data set standards real rather than for show. Above all for data sets built on hard-won huma tagging.
arxiv-2506-01889:
Simone D'Onofrio, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on neutron stars that hold a dark energy fluid. Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a city sized ball. How stiff their matter is shapes three traits: spin inertia, bulge under spin, and stretch under a partner's pull. A known set of links, the I-Love-Q relations, ties those traits in a way that hardly cares about the matter recipe.

D'Onofrio asks if those links hold when dark energy seeps into the star's core. He works out all three traits for such models in full. The links hold in this wider class too. That widens the reach of a tool used to test dense matter with wave data.
arxiv-2506-02989: Mahdi Anbarloei wrote this algebra paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a class of structures called multiplicative hyperrings. The paper addresses the notion of (u,v)-absorbing primary hyperideals within commutative multiplicative hyperrings. It belongs to the part of abstract algebra that generalizes ring ideals to hyperstructures, where operations can return sets of values rather than single ones. The abstract is a single line, so the entry is presented at this level: a specialist study of how this named kind of hyperideal behaves in that setting.
arxiv-2506-03389:
Tommaso Lorenzi and Kevin Painter extend a classic model of self-organizing cell crowds to crowds whose members differ, in a 2025 paper. In chemotaxis, cells chase a chemical they release themselves, clumping into patterns. Standard models assume identical members. Real populations vary: some sense the chemical keenly, some secrete more of it, and members can switch types.

Their framework spreads the population across a trait space and lets sensitivity and secretion vary independently. A Turing-style stability analysis shows the switching rate shifts both the threshold for patterning and the pattern's later life. Whether keen sensing and heavy secretion travel together or oppose each other changes the outcome. The authors say trait structure is not decoration; it steers the pattern.
arxiv-2506-04489:
Lukas Exl and Sebastian Schaffer present a solver for a physics equation in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The free-space Poisson equation asks for the potential from a smooth source with compact support. Their method restates the task through a super-potential. First they convolve with the biharmonic Green's function, then get the potential by spectral differentiation, applying the Laplacian in Fourier space. A separable Gaussian-sum near call makes the convolution fast for FFT-based work.

The biharmonic kernel has better regularity, and that pays off: the Gaussian-sum cut-off error is fourth-order and uniform across target points. That wipes out the near-field fixes and Taylor expansions that Ewald-type methods need. Tests on Gaussian, oscillatory, and compactly supported densities hit the double-precision limit. At matched exactness on hardware, the method cut error and run time, beating the team's past scheme.
arxiv-2506-04689:
Thao Nguyen and six colleagues propose recycling discarded web text to feed language model pretraining, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Pretraining consumes nearly all public web data, yet compute supply grows faster than the pool of natural text. Filtering pipelines discard up to ninety-nine percent of crawls to reach high quality. The discarded material is their raw resource.

Their method, REWIRE, rewrites low-quality documents under guidance so they become useful for training. Experiments on a standard benchmark at three model scales mixed rewritten text with high-quality raw text. The mixes beat training on filtered web data alone across twenty-two tasks. They even beat having twice as much raw web data. Most mixed-in text came from documents that filtering would have thrown away. REWIRE also outperformed other synthetic data approaches the authors compared.
arxiv-2506-05189:
Javier Goicoechea and five co-authors model a charged molecule's glow in a young planet-forming disc that is lit hard from outside. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A space scope may have caught this molecule, in a hot form, in a disc in Orion that sits in hard far light. That raises a key doubt: is the charge in such discs fed by cosmic rays, or by other paths? The team models the disc's lit skin and its wind that boils off. They trace gas reactions with hot hydrogen that can build the molecule. They add a path where hard light frees a charge from hot hydrogen, not used in such models before.
arxiv-2506-05589:
Sara Shields-Menard and colleagues wrote a 2025 report on a system that answers doctors' questions from health records. The system entered the ArchEHR-QA shared task, a contest on clinical question answering. Good answers must rest on the patient's own record, with proof.

Their system works in two steps. First, a language model picks the record sentences that matter for the question. Then it drafts a short answer backed by those lines. Tricks like self-consistency checks sharpen the picking step. A smaller model beat a much larger one at finding the right lines. The report shows careful prompting can matter more than raw model size.
arxiv-2506-06789:
Gang Huang and co-authors test a physical picture of how deep neural networks store what they learn, in a research paper from 2025. Theory had predicted that in wide networks, the weights near the input and output ends are pinned down by training data. The middle weights, by contrast, should stay mostly free, giving a solid-liquid-solid layer pattern.

The team built a thermal version of a deep learning machine and trained it with a physics simulation run at very low temperature. The trained machine still scored well on real benchmark data. Measures of how weights moved over time showed the end layers had ordered, layered design spaces, while the middle layer stayed formless. The authors sum up the results in a phase diagram that maps storage load against network depth.
arxiv-2506-07389:
Guanming Qiao and Partha Protim Paul published this empirical study in 2025. Fuzzing tools bombard smart contracts with random inputs to expose security flaws before attackers do. Adoption by working developers has lagged, though. The authors asked what makes these tools hard to use in practice. They analyzed 381 GitHub issues from two popular contract fuzzers, Echidna and Foundry. A follow-up user study compared smart contract developers with traditional security professionals.

The team sorted the complaints into a taxonomy covering the whole fuzzing workflow. Some problems are technical, such as trouble emulating blockchain behavior. Others are human: thin documentation and weak automation of routine steps. The two practitioner groups felt these pains differently, and each had evolved its own workarounds. The authors offer the findings as a design brief. Better defaults, clearer guides, and smoother automation, they argue, would widen the use of contract fuzzing and improve blockchain security.
arxiv-2506-08589:
Demircan and co-authors interpret a new particle state in two thousand twenty-five as a molecule made of two mesons. The LHCb experiment found bumps in pairs of J/psi particles from proton collisions, including a narrow peak near six point two gigaelectronvolts. The state, called X six thousand two hundred, is built only from charm quarks.

The authors model it as a bound pair of two eta-c mesons with scalar quantum numbers. Using thermal QCD sum rules, they track how the state's mass and decay constant shift as temperature rises. Both quantities fall with heat. At zero temperature their values match figures already in the literature. The authors expect the thermal picture to guide future experiments on this fully charmed state.
arxiv-2506-11189:
Ish Kaul and co-authors explain in 2025 slow waves of heat seen rippling through the disks around black holes. Telescopes have caught temperature changes drifting inward and outward at a few percent of light speed. Light echo effects cannot explain them.

Using large three-dimensional simulations of these disks, the team found matching waves near the disk's mid-plane. The waves moved exactly at the local fast magnetosonic speed, a speed set by gas and magnetic pressure together. Their size, a few percent in temperature, also matched the observations. Disks dominated by orderly magnetic fields showed no such waves. The authors note the waves must survive a damping layer to be seen, which itself teaches something about the disk.
arxiv-2506-11389:
Singh, Band, and Adeli present a study from twenty twenty-five on a curriculum-guided way to pretrain language models. Pretraining costs keep rising, so learning efficiency matters more each year. Inspired by how children's brains mature alongside growing knowledge, their method grows model depth as data difficulty rises. Layers are stacked in stages during training rather than all at once. At a small scale, data moves from made-up short stories to web text. At a larger scale, a classifier sorts a big corpus by technical depth.

Growing depth alongside difficulty beats baseline methods on two question-answering benchmarks. Gains hold at the larger scale across downstream tests. Generalization and zero-shot skill both improve in their runs. The authors frame staged growth as a simple, effective efficiency lever.
arxiv-2506-11589:
Sardo Infirri and a large team of colleagues report a search for QCD axions using the QUAX haloscope. Axions are candidate dark matter particles, and post-inflationary models favor masses above forty micro-electronvolts. The team scanned a thirty-eight megahertz band near 10.2 gigahertz, corresponding to an axion mass near forty-two micro-electronvolts.

The apparatus uses a one-liter tunable cavity inside an eight-tesla magnetic field with a quantum-limited detection chain. No signal candidate appeared. The resulting limits on the axion-photon coupling rule out viable hadronic axion models in a preferred post-inflationary mass region. The work tightens the experimental net around a leading dark matter candidate.
arxiv-2506-11889:
Colin Decker, Dehan Kong, and Stanislav Volgushev developed a statistical test in 2025 for data where every subject provides many curves rather than single numbers. Such repeated functional recordings are now common in medical imaging and environmental science. The challenge is comparing average curves between two paired groups across all recordings at once, without letting false alarms multiply.

Their paired two-sample test controls the family-wise error rate while comparing many functional means simultaneously, and it allows the number of recordings to grow much faster than the sample size. The test works directly on the curves, with no dimension reduction, no principal component step, and no tuning choices. To justify it, the authors prove new results on Gaussian approximation for maxima of curve-based statistics, and they illustrate the method on brain imaging data from the Human Connectome Project.
arxiv-2506-13889:
Francener and four co-authors proposed this experiment in twenty twenty-five at the Large Hadron Collider. Detectors placed far forward there already catch neutrinos with huge energies. The same detectors are flooded by muons, usually treated as a nuisance background. The authors show those muons can serve as a probe in their own right.

When a muon smashes into a nucleus, the scattering pattern reveals the target's inner structure. The team predicts over one hundred thousand such events in one detector during the current run. Up to ten thousand would involve charm quarks. Those events could test whether protons hold a built-in charm component. The setup overlaps with a planned electron-ion collider, giving two views of the same physics.
arxiv-2506-13989:
Johan Östman, Edvin Callisen, Anton Chen, Kristiina Ausmees, Emanuel Gårdh, Jovan Zamac, Jolanta Goldsteine, Hugo Wefer, Simon Whelan, and Markus Reimegård wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents AMLgentex, an open suite that makes fake money flow data so laundering detectors can be built and tested.

Real transaction data is locked away, yet launderers hide in plain sight and proven cases are rare. Past fake sets miss core traits: partial views, time flow, sly actors, shaky labels, class skew, and network links. The suite can dial all of these. It ships country sets and plain set-up guidance. The aim is a shared ground where banks and scholars can grade anti-laundering tools under life-like strain.
arxiv-2506-15089:
Yuning Zhang, Dandan Xu, Chengzhe Li, and Wei Cui model stray X-ray glow along long sight lines in a 2025 arXiv paper. When astronomers measure hot gas around a distant target, gas in between adds its own emission. Surveys subtract this contamination by varied tricks, but its size was untested.

Using the TNG100 simulation, the team built wide light cones and split the in-between gas into three kinds. Diffuse gas in the cosmic web produced strong oxygen and iron lines at many redshifts. Its soft X-ray glow could match the target's own halo emission. The results warn that foreground gas can bias halo measurements.
arxiv-2506-15889:
Yifan Hu and colleagues tackled a basic step in language models in 2025: splitting text into small pieces called tokens. The common method joins the most frequent letter pairs, which works poorly for Chinese, where words have no spaces. Joins based only on frequency often cut across real word edges.

Two fixes use measures of surprise and order in text to find likely word edges before joining. One reads patterns inside the text itself, and the other borrows a small trained model. Tests on a Chinese dataset beat the standard method on precision, recall, and overall score. Better first cuts could help models for many languages with few resources.
arxiv-2506-16089:
Sean Moushegian, Taposh Banerjee, and Vahid Tarokh present a study from twenty twenty-five on tests that spot a change in a data stream. Score based tools, drawn from diffusion models, can run such tests with no full chance model. They tend to trail the classic likelihood tests in power. A weighted twist on the score gap can close that gap.

The team builds diffusion forms of both the fixed test and the change point rule. They work out how well each form can do and when the best mark can be hit. A numeric search finds the best weight matrix for a case. Fake data tests show the diffusion forms beat plain score forms.
arxiv-2506-16189:
Putri van der Linden, Alexander Timans, and Erik Bekkers make uncertainty guarantees survive rotated or flipped data. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, extends conformal prediction. That method wraps any model with error bars backed by coverage promises. Geometric shifts, like a turned image, break both the model and its promises.

Their fix feeds pose information into the procedure. A canonicalization step first rotates each input to a standard pose. Tests cover sudden and gradual shift patterns. Rivals include symmetry-aware models and heavy data augmentation. The geometry-aware version restores coverage while staying model-agnostic. Black-box predictors can adopt it without retraining.
arxiv-2506-16489:
Zeno Capatti, Lucien Huber, and Michael Ruf build a perturbative model for collisions where several partons interact at once. Multi-partonic contributions matter for collider observables, but organizing them without infrared divergences is delicate. Their model arranges cross sections from building blocks that are separately finite, courtesy of the KLN theorem.

Those blocks turn out to have compact forms: double discontinuities of Feynman-type integrals carrying extra topological information. The framework is applied to next-to-leading order structure functions in deep inelastic scattering. The authors discuss the scale dependence of the results and whether a scheme change connects them to parton model quantities. Next steps toward higher orders in two processes are laid out.
arxiv-2506-17389:
Antonios Nathanail explains a long radio transient as a precessing black hole in two thousand twenty five. ASKAP J1832-0911 bursts for two minutes every forty four minutes. Magnetar and white dwarf models compete for the source. He tests an intermediate mass black hole with a tilted disk.

Lense-Thirring precession of the disk sets the forty four minute clock. A Blandford-Znajek jet from the hole supplies the power. Predicted jet light matches the radio and X ray fluxes. Fast variability under one hundred seconds would be a smoking gun. Timing and polarimetry tests can separate the rival models.
arxiv-2506-17989:
Mattioli, Ait-Hadichou, Chaouche, and Gonzalez warned in twenty twenty-five that models trained on raw table data turned into text codes can fail in a stark way. The failed models guess one class for all inputs, no matter what comes in. Same settings on the raw tables did not fail that way.

They coin gauges for how far that collapse has gone in a model. The gauges double as a quality check on the text codes. Collapse can also fake good shift scores that look sound but are not. Care in code choice and checks is thus a must, they show.
arxiv-2506-18089:
Walter Smith and nine colleagues trace the early death of a promising ferroelectric memory material to missing nitrogen atoms, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The material, aluminum boron nitride, offers large polarization and chemical toughness for high-temperature and in-compute memory, but devices wear out before roadmap targets.

The team cycled devices while watching their defect states with electronic measurements and optical spectroscopy. Ultra-thin metal contacts let light reach the very regions that switch. Photoluminescence revealed a new defect signature growing with cycling. The evidence points to nitrogen vacancies as the fatigue driver: each switching cycle creates more of them, degrading the response. Naming the culprit defect turns a vague endurance problem into a concrete materials target. Growers can now try to suppress vacancy formation or heal it. The study blends device testing with spectroscopy to catch degradation in the act.
arxiv-2506-18289:
Saurabhsingh Rajput, Mootez Saad, and Tushar Sharma argue that energy efficiency should be a first-class design goal in AI pipelines, in work from 2025. Practitioners already use many tuning knobs to save energy, but they apply them late, one at a time, without knowing how the choices interact.

The team organises optimisations across five pipeline phases: data, model, training, system, and inference. Because the knobs act on different parts of the pipeline, their savings cascade rather than collide. In experiments, chosen combinations cut energy use by up to about ninety-five percent while keeping nearly all of the original accuracy score. The authors offer the framework as a practical guide for building AI that balances performance with environmental cost.
arxiv-2506-18689:
Saviolo and Loianno presented this robotics paper in twenty twenty-five. It introduces NOVA, a system that lets a drone follow a moving target at high speed. The drone works in places where GPS signals fail, such as forests, city mazes, and inside buildings. It carries only a stereo camera and a motion sensor, with no map and no outside help.

NOVA judges the world from the target's point of view rather than its own fixed position. It spots the target, estimates distance, and plans safe paths in real time. Built-in safety rules steer it around obstacles as they appear. In field tests the drone kept up with targets at over fifty kilometers per hour. The work shows fast tracking is possible with onboard sensing alone.
arxiv-2506-20989:
Eric Zhang, Leshem Choshen, and Jacob Andreas ask whether fine-tuning can mimic prompting in twenty twenty-five. A language model takes in new information in two main ways. A user can change the prompt, or training can change the parameters. Parameter updates cost nothing to store long-term. Yet prompting often generalizes far better, even from a single example.

Prompted models also draw inferences that standard fine-tuning misses. The authors meta-train models so gradient updates emulate conditioning on new facts. Their targets are the model's own prompted predictions, so no ground-truth labels are needed. Later gradient training recovered some, and at times all, of the prompted performance. Gains showed on reversal curse tasks and on question answering.
arxiv-2506-21589:
Mao, Wei, Fang, and Chau built a tool in twenty twenty-five to spot text and facts made by large chat models. Such text now floods social and shop sites, and false claims can spread fast. Old spot tools work on known models and topics but fail on new ones.

Their tool pairs twin memory nets with a part that learns how to spread to new cases. It is guided by a theory of what marks machine text in broad terms. On real data sets it beat top rival tools in wide tests and case checks. The team notes gains for trust and safety on web platforms.
arxiv-2507-01889:
Sebastian Wissel and six colleagues use deep learning, in a 2025 preprint, to read crystal orientations straight from electron microscope patterns. Knowing which way each tiny grain points helps explain how a material behaves. The test material here is a lithium nickel oxide used in advanced batteries. Older mapping methods, like hand indexing or template matching, are slow and suffer from noise. Overlapping patterns make them worse.

The team trained three network types on real diffraction patterns labeled by a commercial tool. A plain convolutional network served as the baseline. Two richer designs, DenseNets and Swin Transformers, did better. The Swin Transformer scored highest and gave the steadiest maps. Its maps showed sharp grain borders and smooth orientation inside each grain. The authors argue that attention-based models paired with microscope data can speed up fine-scale material studies.
arxiv-2507-02189:
Ricardo Fitas, Heinz Schaffrath, and Samuel Schabel wrote a paper in 2025 on the design of corrugated board, the fluted cardboard used in packaging, through new modeling and lab tests. Simple finite element models exist for the board, based on homogenization, in which the flute shape is replaced by a like elastic material. Those models work well for large structures and custom packaging. They fail, however, when the board undergoes large deformation.

The authors extend the simple model with correction factors drawn from two Weibull distributions. The corrections cover two failure mechanisms under large deformation: contact pressure and buckling. Parameters for the corrections were fitted from two series of experiments. The new model stays fast while matching how real board behaves under load. Experiments confirm that the extended model predicts the board's response accurately. The work aims to help improve packaging design.
arxiv-2507-02289:
Wangbin Ding and eight colleagues present CineMyoPS, a network that segments heart muscle damage using only cine cardiac magnetic resonance images. Heart attacks leave scars and swelling that normally require contrast-enhanced or T2-weighted scans to identify. Those extra sequences take time and may be impossible when contrast agents cannot be given.

Cine imaging is fast and contrast-free, and it shows both motion and structural abnormalities. CineMyoPS extracts motion and anatomy features, trains them jointly through a consistency loss, and aggregates information across the cardiac cycle. On a multi-center dataset it performs promisingly at pathology segmentation, motion estimation, and anatomy segmentation alike.
arxiv-2507-03089:
Lucas Desoppi and Bertrand Reulet connect two ways of describing electrical noise in parts whose resistance changes with voltage. Their paper came out in 2025. One description treats noise as a smooth random process, and the other treats it as a stream of single charges.

They show that basic heat rules force a specific reading of the smooth model when noise depends on voltage. Under that reading, a classic noise formula holds with one term swapped for a ratio of current to voltage. The discrete model, when built to obey the same heat rules, leads back to the smooth one. The shared formula holds exactly only at low voltage.
arxiv-2507-03489:
Yang Liu and Jun-Bao Wu report the first chiral boundary states that are integrable in a certain spin chain. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The chain is the SU(4) alternating chain, which comes from a part of ABJM theory. All such states found before were achiral, that is, they lacked this twist of handedness.

The authors use a known test for when a state can be called integrable in the untwisted sense. With it, they pick out two-site and four-site base states as chiral and integrable. Counts from tests suggest the rest are not. They also work out how these states overlap with Bethe states that solve the chain.
arxiv-2507-03789:
Andrii Dzhoha and five co-authors built a rank model that uses query context in sequence based picks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with next item tools built on transformers. Such tools mix speed with quality well. But the scene of a click, like the browse class it sat in, is a rich hint of aim. That hint does not line up with the item chain, and at run time it may be gone for privacy rules.

Their model folds that past query scene in with care at low cost. It stays apt when the scene is thin or gone. Readers in recommender work get a rank boost from a hint most tools throw out.
arxiv-2507-04789:
Yinuo Zhao and co-authors present a way to score robot actions without new training, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Big vision and language models can break a goal into steps, but their scores can jump around over time. Steady scores matter when a robot learns by trial and error.

Their method asks the model for steps and a first guess of progress before each round. A tracking method then updates progress as the scene changes. Tests on two robot task sets gave top scores with less compute than rivals. The steady scores also helped the robot recover when a step went wrong.
arxiv-2507-05089:
Satoshi Nishimoto tests in 2025 how sturdy a protected quantum phase is when electrons can also move and interact. The Haldane phase is a symmetry-protected state with telltale signs: string order, an energy gap, and paired entanglement patterns. He studied ladder-shaped materials with strong magnetic coupling between electrons.

In spin-only ladders, the phase switched on at once and grew stronger with coupling. Adding charge motion changed the picture: the phase survived, but only inside a bounded region set by both repulsion and coupling. Outside lay a plain insulating phase. The maps tell experimenters where to look for this physics in real ladder materials.
arxiv-2507-06189:
Maximilian Heil and Dionne Bang report their entry to a shared lab task on spotting slanted sentences in English news text. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The task sorts news lines as slanted or straight. The team matched two ways to teach a model: tuning a fresh base model, and moving a model tuned on a kin task. They also built a set pipeline that uses a large model to reword lines in set slants. The same model then checks and fixes the new lines, to keep tags and style true. Task-tuned models beat fresh ones, and the clean added data made the tool more firm. Their entry placed mid-field.
arxiv-2507-06989:
Juna Kollmeier, Hans-Walter Rix, and a large collaboration describe the fifth phase of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey in a twenty twenty-five paper. The survey, known as SDSS-V, maps the sky with spectroscopy, splitting star and galaxy light into spectra. The paper's title calls the setup panoptic, meaning it watches the sky in many ways at once.

The work presents the survey's facilities and plans as a resource for the field. Spectroscopic surveys of this scale trace how stars, galaxies, and black holes form and change. By laying out the design in one place, the paper lets other teams plan work that builds on the data.
arxiv-2507-08889:
Bek Herz and Ivan Contreras build a toy model of supersymmetric quantum mechanics on graphs. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Supersymmetry pairs two kinds of particle in one frame. On a graph, points and links stand in for space, which gives a clean test bed for such ideas.

With a discrete form of Witten-Morse theory, they show finite graphs bear a natural supersymmetric build. They fold that build into a known graph quantum model. Key traits of the smooth case hold on plain finite graphs, yet supersymmetry cannot break on its own there. They also prove how these systems act when links are rewired.
arxiv-2507-09189:
Jun Eshima and co-authors find, in a 2025 paper, that soapy films can make the droplets from a bursting bubble bigger, not smaller. When a bubble at a liquid surface pops, a jet shoots up and sheds droplets that become aerosol. Earlier work said surface-active agents, the soaps, shrink those droplets for bubbles preceded by surface waves. The authors test bubbles without such waves, the regime of small bubbles.

There the trend flips: soap enlarges the ejected droplet. The cause lies in surface tension gradients, the Marangoni stresses, which refocus the collapsing cavity that launches the jet. Lab measures of jet speed and drop size match computer simulations fed with the measured tension curve. The result matters for predicting spray from the ocean and other real, contaminated surfaces, where bubbles rarely burst clean.
arxiv-2507-09389:
Chris Davis Jaldi and four co-authors test, in a 2025 paper, how the shape of stored knowledge sways an AI agent that looks facts up as it writes. Such retrieval-augmented generation agents pick sources, interpret them, and query them in reply to natural language prompts. Clear design aids trust, while fitness for new domains aids use. The team ask whether those two aims pull against each other.

They run tests in which the same facts are stored in different shapes, from flat lists to rich structured webs. The agent must query a knowledge store in each shape. Both structure and complexity left marks on how well the agent did. Some shapes made queries precise but brittle, while others traveled better to new questions. The authors weigh what the trade-off means for systems that must be both interpretable and flexible.
arxiv-2507-09789:
Bowen Xie and co-authors study matching systems in a 2025 mathematics paper. In such a system, a task starts only when several kinds of agents meet at the same moment. Agents wait in separate lines, grow impatient, and may leave. Each line also has a size cap.

Because matches happen at once, at least one line is always empty, which makes the system hard to analyze. The authors use a tool called the infinitesimal generator to build a simpler smooth model for busy periods. They show their limit matches one found in earlier work by a different route. The result helps designers of matching platforms predict delays and losses under heavy load.
arxiv-2507-09989:
Xiaoyang Yu, Youfang Lin, Shuo Wang, and Sheng Han wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on teams of unlike agents learning together. In such multi-agent learning, steady step-by-step improvement is prized, but sharing parameters across grouped agents tends to break it.

The conflict has a name in their tests: baseline drift, where a shared update scheme's yardstick slides mid-step. Their algorithm, OMDPG, swaps the sliding yardstick for an optimal marginal value built from the best joint action sequence. A pessimistic critic supplies stable scores, and a grouped actor layout lets agents share parameters by group while a central critic sees the whole game. On standard strategy and robot-control testbeds, the method beat strong rivals. The authors frame it as a way to keep both sharing and steady gains.
arxiv-2507-10989: Mikolaj Sienicki and Krzysztof Sienicki critique a defense of Bohmian mechanics in a 2025 reflection. Bohmian mechanics reads quantum theory through particle paths guided by a wave. A recent experiment was read as a challenge to that picture, and Hrvoje Nikolic answered with a revision. The Sienickis argue the fix restores the continuity equation but brings back assumptions it aimed to avoid. It also passes over key facts of the experiment and the nonlocal side of the system. Tensions remain for Bohmian mechanics in complex, interacting settings.
arxiv-2507-11889:
Adnan Abdullah and co-authors build an underwater robot that takes new orders mid mission through a faint magnetic electric link, in work from twenty twenty-five. Ocean robots work without GPS and with weak contact, so most run fixed scripts. Changing course mid dive is rare and slow.

Their system pairs a mission code format with a control stack built for quick retasking. A digital twin tested task switches in under fifty milliseconds with lean computing overhead. Tank tests and open water trials confirmed steady control and clean mission runs. The team frames the robot as a step toward responsive, goal driven exploration with a remote operator in the loop.
arxiv-2507-11989:
Alexander Zhuravlev and five co-authors design coatings that stop reflections from thick glass-like slabs in a 2025 paper. Any sharp change in a material's traits bounces part of a wave back, and for thick slabs the bounce depends strongly on the incoming angle. Standard anti-reflection coatings fail that test once a slab grows thick in wave terms.

The team coats both faces with metasurfaces whose response shifts with angle, a trait called nonlocality. That angle sense proves to be the key for wide-angle calm on thick slabs. They built a version from linked split-ring parts and checked it in simulation and in the lab. Transmission rose across a broad span of angles, which points to thin, easy coatings for lenses and panels.
arxiv-2507-13489:
Meredith Stone and co-authors study a distant quasar whose black hole looks far too heavy for its galaxy. Seen as it was when the universe was young, at redshift seven point zero eight, its host galaxy is oddly light. Such mismatches are common in early quasars, and it is unclear how they settle into the tight local balance between galaxy and hole.

Using the Webb telescope, the team searched for companion galaxies that could later merge and bulk up the host. They found twenty-two candidate companions in a crowded field, an overdense neighborhood for that era. Even summing every nearby galaxy's stars and gas, the host could not dilute the hole below about two and a half percent of its mass, still far above local norms. The authors note such oddballs may simply hide locally.
arxiv-2507-17489:
Minglong Xue, Aoxiang Ning, Shivakumara Palaiahnakote, and Mingliang Zhou build a network that cleans flare from night photos. Bright lamps at night cast flares that spoil image quality and hurt later vision tasks. Large flares near a lamp are the hardest to remove, and fixes can damage fine detail. The team notes flares stand out more in the frequency view of an image than in the plain view.

Their network works in that frequency view to split flare from scene content. One part tunes global frequency traits to guide the split. A second part uses contrast-based learning to guard local detail near the lamp. Tests show the method beats the best prior tools on shared measures. The team posts its code for others to use.
arxiv-2507-19189:
Shota Tankano and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a machine learning model that can predict a key property of crystals without the slow calculations that give exact values. The property is the band gap, the energy step electrons must clear in a solid. A cheap standard method, the local density approximation, gets this step wrong, while an accurate method called QSGW takes huge computing time.

The team ran QSGW on 1,516 materials from the Materials Project database. They then trained a model to map a cheaper fingerprint, the partial density of states from the cheap method, onto the accurate QSGW gap. The learned model significantly outperformed linear regression approaches. The authors present it as a first model of its kind, and a step toward fast screening of new materials by their electronic structure.
arxiv-2507-19689:
Pablo Donato brings in a new way to write logical proofs in this two thousand twenty-five paper on logic. Scroll nets stand for proofs in propositional logic. Their base construct, the scroll, is a topological notation for implication. Charles Sanders Peirce made it in the late nineteenth century for his diagrammatic existential graphs. Donato takes scroll nets from those graphs with the Curry-Howard methodology. Inference rules are taken in, inside judgments. That is how typed terms take in deduction rules.

The work centers on the intuitionistic implicative fragment. It starts from a natural diagrammatic representation of scroll nets. It then pulls their combinatorial essence into a pure graph-theoretic definition. A notion of detour backs a sketched elimination procedure like cut elimination in proof theory. The author also shows how to simulate normalization in the simply typed lambda calculus. That shows the frame's logical and computational expressivity.
arxiv-2507-20989:
Kulkarni, Noll, Kausch, and Bhattacharjee propose reading the neutral fraction of the Milky Way's warm ionized gas from a faint nitrogen line, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Most ionized mass in the Galaxy sits in this diffuse warm medium, not in bright nebulae, and it is usually traced by pulsar dispersion and hydrogen recombination light.

The warm ionized medium is thought to be lit by ultraviolet light leaking out of the bright H-two regions in the Galactic plane. Where those rays strike neutral gas, they grow an ionized skin. Unlike sharp nebular boundaries, this transition is gradual, and the in-between gas stays warm enough to excite oxygen and nitrogen atoms. A forbidden nitrogen line at fifty-two hundred angstroms glows from exactly that layer. Measuring it can reveal how much of the medium remains neutral, for a Galactic component that hides in plain sight.
arxiv-2507-21389:
Huang and six co-authors taught language models to ask questions before answering in twenty twenty-five. Real requests are often ambiguous or missing key facts, yet today's models tend to answer passively or ask shallow clarifications instead of gathering what they need.

The team defines a new task, proactive information gathering, and generates partially specified real-world tasks by masking key information. Their training strategy uses reinforcement learning that rewards questions uncovering genuinely new, unspoken user knowledge, such as hidden expertise or fine-grained requirements. A trained seven-billion-parameter model beat a strong commercial mini model by eighteen percent on automatic metrics. Human judges preferred its clarification questions by forty-two percent and its final outlines by twenty-eight percent. The authors argue proactive questioning turns models into collaborative partners.
arxiv-2508-00889:
Hagyeong Shin and six co-authors build FECT, a way to check if claims made by smart tools from call center chats are true to the chat. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such tools can state things with no base in the source, and in firms that error can hurt real choices. Worse, claims about mood or root cause have no set truth to check. The team first sets out a three-step plan whose name joins the acts of breaking a claim down, parting its strands, and standing back from it. On that base they build their check. The work aims to make machine-made claims from service chats fit for trust.
arxiv-2508-02989:
Ninh Pham, Yingtao Zheng, and Hugo Phibbs reframed a grouping problem in 2025. Real data sets mix dense and sparse regions, and density-based grouping handles that variety but scales poorly to millions of high-dimensional points. The authors recast varied-density grouping as label propagation over an area graph whose links adapt to the local density, formally tying density-based grouping to graph connectivity.

That reframing unlocks fast propagation methods from network science. A density-aware propagation method, along with random projection methods that build rough area graphs cheaply, keeps the computation down while keeping group quality. In tests the method processed data sets of millions of points in minutes. It matched the accuracy of current baselines. This offers a useful route to density-aware grouping at scales where classic methods stall.
arxiv-2508-03489:
Zhao, Balaji, and Lee answered carbon questions buried in PDF reports in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Product sustainability reports mix tables and text in wildly inconsistent layouts. Parsing them into clean data is error-prone. The team built a question-answering dataset over one thousand seven hundred thirty-five such reports, with human-checked answers.

A leading commercial model stumbled badly on the inconsistencies. Their system, CarbonPDF, fine-tunes an open model on the new training data. Retrieval augmentation grounds the answers in the documents. The method beat existing question-answering systems tuned for tables and text. The authors release the dataset openly for footprint research.
arxiv-2508-03689:
Morales-Rivera and four co-authors modeled this question in twenty twenty-five: how often did the first stars produce gamma-ray bursts? Population III stars were the first to form, before any heavy elements existed. Some massive ones may have collapsed into black holes and fired bright jets. The rate depends on unknowns such as their masses and spin.

The team ran a grid of star models across mass, spin, and wind strength. For each, they computed the black hole left behind and whether a jet could break out. With modest winds, the burst rate could reach a few dozen per year across the sky. Most would lie at great distances. If real rates prove far lower, the authors argue, the first stars likely needed partners to make bursts.
arxiv-2508-04289:
Hong Su proposes, in a 2025 paper, a way to make language models reason with explicit, reusable methods instead of raw pattern memory alone. Each method is stored as a problem paired with its solution, drawn from training text, past answers, and user exchanges. Feedback ranks the store over time.

When a fresh query arrives, the system fetches the closest methods and steers the model's reply with them. Tests showed gains in fact checking and in generalizing to hard prompts. New methods, refined by users, could overtake older ones, giving the system a learning loop beyond its frozen weights. The author frames methods as the unit of steady improvement.
arxiv-2508-04789:
Gary Lazzaro, Max Wakefield, and Jason Weiss wrote this math note in 2025 on matroids, structures that capture the idea of independence in sets. From chain counts on a matroid they build a family of polynomials that widen the classic characteristic polynomial, a famed counter of colorings. The new polynomials' coefficients alternate in sign, and a recursion builds them for any matroid.

To show what the counts mean, the pair of new graph ideas matters: coupled multicoloring, a beefed-up vertex coloring, and coupled multicommodity flow, a beefed-up nowhere-zero flow. The polynomials count exactly those objects on a graph. The note ends with open problems on the counts' traits. The authors frame the family as a bridge between matroid theory and graph coloring counts.
arxiv-2508-04989:
Rahul Kumar Anand and co-authors wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on dust around dying carbon-rich stars. As such stars shed their layers, aromatic molecules in the outflow glow at set infrared bands, and those bands carry clues about the chemistry at work.

The team observed five well-known objects at stages from post-giant to planetary nebula. They took photos through nine optical and infrared filters and added mid-infrared spectra from an archive instrument. All five objects show strong aromatic bands, but the band shapes differ from star to star. One key molecule feature at a set wavelength appears in four of them and is missing in the fifth, hinting at a distinct molecular mix or harsher conditions there. The authors read the variety as a sign that no two of these shells evolve the same way.
arxiv-2508-05889:
AS Sathe and three co-authors study side flows over rough walls made of many posts, in churning boundary layer flow. Such side flows shape drag, heat flow, and how gases carry scents and dust. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Most past work used neat, even spaced roughness, but real walls are clumped and messy. The team ran large eddy simulations over post clusters with varied density and layout. Shifts in layout flipped the side flow's direction. A key factor was the gap between the edge posts of near clusters, scaled by the channel depth. The authors also track how flow direction shapes fast, snap by snap motion.
arxiv-2508-07389:
QH Liu and three co-authors argue that a second kind of system can exist near absolute zero. It would stand apart from the normal kind that fits all forms of the third law of heat science. The usual view holds that heat capacity must fade to zero as cold nears its limit. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The authors note that the law's forms are not fully the same once that quiet premise is dropped. A system might fit one or two forms but not all, and still be fit for the real world. They call such a case a singular zero temperature system. Past models from other authors are checked and found to belong to this new class.
arxiv-2508-08389:
Eyles-Ferris and four co-authors find nine candidate events where a black hole tore a star apart. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses data from the eROSITA X-ray survey. When a star is shredded, some gas falls in and can glow with soft X-rays. The team searched the first German data release for just such soft sources.

Five of the nine are brand new X-ray finds. All faded in later checks, as this kind of event should. Two have visible light matches, and four flare in infrared data. That high infrared share hints that soft X-ray events may often come with warm dust around them.
arxiv-2508-09189:
Madan Baduwal presents a hybrid neural network for segmenting colonic polyps in colonoscopy images. Accurate segmentation is hard because polyps vary in size and shape and often have ill-defined boundaries. Lighting, imaging protocols, folds, and fluid add further difficulty for existing networks such as U-Net variants and PraNet.

The model combines transformer and convolutional components. Boundary-aware attention targets polyps with unclear margins, while the architecture resists artifacts like specular highlights, motion blur, and fluid occlusions. In evaluations, recall improved to 0.9555 and accuracy to 0.9849, beating state-of-the-art methods. Baduwal argues the hybrid design offers more robust polyp segmentation for clinical screening.
arxiv-2508-09289:
Necir, Guesmia, and Meraghni improved how tail heaviness is gauged when data are censored in twenty twenty-five. The tail index gauges how heavy a data spread's tail is. It matters for insurance losses and survival data. With right-censored data, classic integral-based gauges worked only when over half the largest values were uncensored. That shut out many real datasets.
