Their fix adds a tuning value above one. It reweights the gauges built on Kaplan-Meier and Nelson-Aalen integrals. The fix stretches its reach to the whole censoring range. Under standard terms, they prove the gauges stay consistent and settle into a bell shape in the limit. Computer trials showed clear gains in bias and accuracy over older methods. The gains stood out most under strong censoring. Use on insurance loss data and AIDS survival data showed it at work in weak and strong censoring alike.
arxiv-2508-10189:
Jakub Černý, Garud Iyengar, and Christian Kroer wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It plans delivery routes where a foe waits to strike the truck along its path, and answers with routes that are sound yet hard to guess.

A fixed safe route is still a known route, which a smart foe can plan around. The team frames the choice as a two-player zero-sum game. Randomness, dosed with care, makes the plan both strong and less easy to foresee. Exact game solving is out of reach, but a double-oracle loop lands plans in seconds. The scheme takes plug-in routing tools as its oracles. On real scenes it scales well, and tests show the foe model itself earns its keep.
arxiv-2508-10389:
Wenlin Li and co-authors propose a lab tool to hunt for a smallest length in nature, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Some theories that join quantum physics and gravity say space has a finest grain. That grain would bend a basic quantum rule in a small, testable way.

Their tool uses a light-and-motion device with bright and dark modes. The bright mode boosts the tiny bend, and the dark mode reads it out as noise. The read does not hinge on how clean the device rings. With workable settings, the reach beats the prior scale by ten orders, the authors say.
arxiv-2508-10689:
Matteo Luperto and four co-authors help exploring robots spend their time on the parts of a space that matter most. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A mapping robot picks each next spot to visit from the edge of what it has seen. Most rules just chase the largest unseen area.

The team's insight is that some edges open onto wide unknown ground and deserve a head start. A neural network reads the current map and marks these high-value zones. The marks come from a model trained to judge when a space counts as fully explored. Feeding the marks into standard exploration rules changed the robots' paths for the better. A broad test campaign backs the claim. The method suits search, mapping, and inspection tasks in unknown buildings.
arxiv-2508-13889:
Chuang Li, Weida Liang, and colleagues improve chat-based recommendation by adapting outside recommenders in a 2025 study. A conversational system built on a language model can chat freely but often suggests items outside the store's real catalog. It also leans on dialogue alone when reranking, missing the strength of dedicated recommender engines.

Their approach adapts an external recommender to the conversation's context, then lets the language model rerank with that domain knowledge in hand. Grounding suggestions in the true item space raises accuracy. The design keeps the fluency of chat while borrowing the hard-won expertise of specialist recommendation systems.
arxiv-2508-15189:
Jiahao Xu, Changchang Yin, and colleagues built a benchmark for diagnosing surgical wounds in a 2025 medical study. Infections at surgical sites are among the most common and costly hospital-acquired infections, and early screening could speed treatment. Deep learning has been tried for first-pass wound checks, but privacy limits on patient photos and the cost of expert labels have stalled progress, leaving no public test set.

SurgWound-Bench fills that gap so models can be compared fairly. A shared benchmark lets hospitals judge whether an automated screener is safe to trial, instead of trusting each vendor's private numbers.
arxiv-2508-16989:
Fu-Chieh Chang, Yu-Ting Lee, and Pei-Yuan Wu probe how reflection lives inside a language model's activations. Their 2025 paper studies reflection, the habit of checking and revising one's own reasoning. Most prior work shaped reflection through prompts or training goals, leaving the inner mechanism unclear.

The team build steering vectors between states of no reflection, self-driven reflection, and triggered reflection. With those vectors they can find new instructions that spark reflection, and they can dial reflective behavior up or down directly. Turning reflection off proved much easier than turning it on. Tests on math and code tasks with two model families showed clear layers across reflection levels. The authors note both a defense opportunity and a risk: attackers could suppress reflection to weaken a model.
arxiv-2508-17189:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim expanded math rules in probabilistic special groups in a 2025 paper. Frobenius-Euler math rules are a classic sequence with number-theoretic roots, and recent variants attach them to a random variable. They weight the definition by that variable's moments, or deform it with a degeneration setting. Higher-order versions stack the building further, and the zoo of formulas can be hard to navigate.

The authors use umbral calculus, a symbolic tool set for math rule sequences. With it they derive explicit formulas. The formulas write any math rule as a combination of these probabilistic and degenerate groups, including higher orders. Worked cases for several concrete random variables illustrate the expansions. The results give researchers ready-made dictionaries between plain math rules and the new special groups.
arxiv-2508-20089:
Ross Gardiner and five co-authors classify moth species from field camera photos by borrowing knowledge from a big foundation model. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Automated cameras can track insect decline, but their messy field images differ sharply from clean reference photos.

The team worked with one hundred one Danish moth species caught by camera systems. A large model called BioCLIP2 beat other methods by a wide margin. The authors then distilled its skill into a small network that runs cheaply. The small model matched the big one's accuracy at far lower cost. Expert-labeled field examples were the bridge between the two image worlds. The paper gives practical guidance for cheap, accurate insect monitoring.
arxiv-2508-20489:
David Eppstein, Michael Goodrich, Abraham Illickan, and Claire To present a computing paper from 2025 on geometry algorithms. Some algorithms run faster when the input is partly sorted or has low disorder. Disorder can be measured by entropy, a score of how mixed the data is.

The authors define a new entropy measure based on how points split across ranges. Their measure covers past ones used for sorting and for geometry in one frame. They give simple algorithms for flat maxima, hulls in two and three dimensions, and some line-of-sight tasks. Each algorithm's run time tracks the new entropy of its input. Sorted inputs thus finish fast, while mixed inputs cost more. The work aims to make such adaptive methods easier to design.
arxiv-2508-20689:
Konstantinos Karathanasis, Spyros Kontogiannis, and Christos Zaroliagis sped up Pareto filtering for multi-objective tuning in a 2025 paper. When no option wins on every criterion, the Pareto frontier keeps the non-dominated trade-offs. Work it for unions or Minkowski sums of two partial frontiers is a narrow point inside many tuning methods. Their new tree data forms index non-dominated vectors so dominance checks run fast in three or more criteria.

Three matching methods filter dominated points out of unions and sums fast. On synthetic and real data sets the methods beat the state of the art and scaled well as problem size grew. Faster frontier arithmetic widens every design search that trades cost against quality.
arxiv-2508-20889:
Dmitri Bykov and Andrew Kuzovchikov solve a sigma model by tying it to a spin chain. Sigma models map a line or surface into a curved target space and show up across physics. Their target is a flag manifold, a space of nested planes, with the most general even metric allowed. The spin chain link is to a Gaudin model, a classic system of linked spins.

Through that link, they write all shortest paths in the space with elliptic functions. They also show the spectrum of the Laplace-Beltrami operator follows from polynomial equations of Bethe type. Those equations are far easier to solve than the raw spectrum problem. The mapping is shown to hold for the wider unitary family as well, not just the three-level case.
arxiv-2508-20989:
Andrea Corti and co-authors hunt for signs that neural networks truly learn features, in work from 2025. Feature learning, the grasp of what matters in data, drives deep learning's wins, yet no shared account of it exists. The team studies a one-hidden-layer network in a physics-style frame, where width and data size both run large.

Two signs stand out. The gap between class clouds in feature space bends in a non-steady way as noise shifts, which mirrors a known training effect. The weights also shift by a finite, data-set amount from the endless-width case and grow linked. The authors read both as real feature learning at work.
arxiv-2508-21389:
Tanguy Herserant and Vincent Guigue audited how summary quality is measured in a 2025 paper, written in French. Automatic metrics for text summarization range from the classic word-overlap score ROUGE to recent methods that ask large language models to grade. Running six representative metrics in one open framework on a standard human-rated dataset, the authors found reported scores in the literature often failed to reproduce in their setting.

Metrics that agreed best with human judgments also cost the most compute and wobbled most between runs. Because model-based grading adds randomness and hidden dependencies, the authors argue for exhaustive documentation and standardized protocols. Their unified framework supports fair, transparent comparison for future summarization research.
arxiv-2509-00189:
Jinzhou Tang and six co-authors present HiVA in 2025, a self-organizing agent framework for general intelligence tasks. Agents break problems down and call tools through language models. Fixed workflows are reusable but need hand rework when settings change, while loose reactive loops fail to save progress in reusable form.

HiVA models workflows as graphs that organize themselves. An evolution algorithm tunes both the meaning of nodes and the graph's topology, using textual gradients, which are feedback phrased in words, in place of numeric backpropagation. Forward routing borrows from multi-armed bandit methods, which balance trying new paths with using known good ones. Diagnostic feedback from the environment then drives joint updates.
arxiv-2509-00289:
BESIII Collaboration, represented by M. Ablikim and 720 co-authors, measures helicity amplitudes and branching fractions for chi_cJ decays to a lambda and an antilambda in 2025. Chi_cJ states are bound states of a charm quark pair. Helicity, the spin projection along motion, shapes how their decay products fly apart.

The study uses about two thousand seven hundred million psi(3686) events held by the BESIII experiment in China. A partial wave analysis of the decay chain yields the ratio of same-helicity to opposite-helicity amplitudes for the chi_c2 state for the first time, near zero point five eight in value. Angular distribution terms and the chi_c0 width, about twelve point three MeV in size, are also measured, along with branching fractions for all three states.
arxiv-2509-00689:
Vera Serganova and Arkady Vaintrob study almost inner derivations of Lie superalgebras. A derivation is a rule for differentiating inside an algebra. Inner derivations come from elements of the algebra itself. An almost inner derivation matches an inner one on each single direction. The question is whether such derivations must be inner as a whole.

For simple finite-dimensional Lie algebras, the answer is yes. Lie superalgebras add odd, sign-flipping elements to the picture. Outer derivations can exist there, so the question is not trivial. Serganova and Vaintrob still prove the answer is yes for finite-dimensional simple cases. Their proof works over the complex numbers. They also give natural examples of the opposite kind. Those examples arise for certain pseudo-reductive superalgebras.
arxiv-2509-00889:
Biaoyan Hu, writing alone, introduces auxiliary functions for f electrons. These electrons sit in the f shell of heavy atoms. Such systems mix strong spin-orbit coupling with crystal-field effects. The mix produces complex energy landscapes that are hard to compute. Hu aims for a faster way to read those landscapes.

His functions extend hydrogen-like wave functions. They do so through a changed Legendre function. The new functions often have a Mobius-like topology. They flip sign after one full turn. Their squared modulus still respects inversion symmetry, though. By aligning that modulus with the crystal field, eigenstate structures can be read fast. No elaborate calculations are needed. Agreement with known results suggests the physics is captured well.
arxiv-2509-00989:
Josef Grun leads a team of six authors on integrating multi-spectral imaging with Gaussian Splatting. Splatting is a fast method for high-fidelity three-dimensional reconstruction. It works from multi-view images of a scene. It excels on color data, but extra spectra are a problem. Naive per-band optimization yields poor reconstructions there.

The team evaluates three strategies for the integration. One does separate per-band reconstruction with no shared structure. One splits optimization, fitting color geometry first and bands second. One optimizes all modalities jointly, optionally after a color-only phase. Their dedicated joint strategy wins on spectral reconstruction. It also enhances color results through spectral cross-talk. They suggest modeling multi-spectral reflectance directly in spherical harmonics components. Trade-offs in when to introduce bands are analyzed.
arxiv-2509-01089:
Watches and fitness bands record steps, sleep, and daily rhythms for millions of people, yet the data are hard to turn into clear health insight. Jinjoo Shim, Jacob Hunecke, Elgar Fleisch, and Filipe Barata present CosinorAge, an open tool that estimates biological age from those records. Biological age reflects how old the body acts, not just years lived.

CosinorAge joins rest and activity rhythms, movement, and sleep in one shared workflow. The Python package takes raw data, cleans it, computes features, and gives an age estimate, and a web version widens access. Earlier tools were split up or closed, so a single open pipeline helps researchers study aging in a way others can repeat and check.
arxiv-2509-01389:
Task-based chatbots book flights and answer bank questions. They handle other set jobs too. But testing every conversation path they support is hard. Diego Clerissi, Elena Masserini, Daniela Micucci, and Leonardo Mariani extend MUTABOT. That is a mutation testing approach for such bots. Mutation testing injects small faults on purpose, to see whether a test suite catches them.

The extension now covers two platforms, Dialogflow and Rasa. It makes faulty chatbot versions that mimic real conversational defects. Experiments show mutation testing can expose weaknesses in test suites. Those suites were made by Botium, a leading test generator. The team argues a suite that misses injected faults may also miss real bugs. Mutation scores thus give builders a sharper measure of true test quality.
arxiv-2509-01489:
A nova is a sudden stellar eruption, and polarized light from it can reveal whether the ejected material spread unevenly. Isabel J. Lima, with five co-authors, measured the linear polarization of Nova Vel 2025, also called V572 Vel, on two nights in mid 2025, soon after its eruption was found. Their readings came through a red filter band.

The nova showed an average polarization near one point six percent of its light, at a set angle. To test whether that signal was the nova's own, the team also measured eighty-six nearby field stars. Those stars averaged a similar level at a nearly identical angle, pointing to interstellar dust between Earth and the nova as the main source. No clear intrinsic component was found, and the authors recommend more observations across several bands to confirm.
arxiv-2509-01889:
Yu Tsao reviews neural tools that grade speech quality and clarity, then feed back into speech systems. Human listening tests are the gold standard but cost much time and do not scale. Classic scores need a clean reference signal, which real settings rarely provide. Neural graders predict quality without that reference and score well in recent work.

The review traces two growing uses beyond grading alone. First, graders act as trainable stand-ins for human judgment to tune enhancement and synthesis systems. Second, they flag salient speech traits to guide leaner downstream processing. Limits and open paths close the survey. The shift turns assessment from a final check into an active design tool.
arxiv-2509-01989:
Jon Links solves a bosonic lattice model with all-to-all interactions by the Bethe Ansatz, a method famed for one dimensional systems. Bosons are particles that can share states freely, unlike fermions. His model lives on a square lattice, breaking the one dimensional mold. Global range interaction, where every site talks to every other, opens the door to exact solutions in higher dimensions.

Exact solutions are given for open, cylindrical, and toroidal edge setups. A generalization to an integrable defect, a flaw that preserves solvability, also follows. That defect case resists a neat closed form, unlike the clean cases. The result widens where exact methods can reach in quantum many body theory. It may guide studies of long range interacting cold atom systems.
arxiv-2509-02189:
Aditya Bhardwaj and Peter Kutas give a gentle introduction to blind signatures from RSA to lattice based cryptography. Blind signatures let a signer sign a message without seeing it, protecting user anonymity. Voters and digital cash users benefit most from that property. The user blinds the message, the signer signs the blinded form, and unblinding yields a publicly verifiable signature.

An envelope analogy carries the intuition throughout the exposition. Quantum computers would break the traditional schemes behind such features. Lattice based constructions aim to restore security against quantum attacks. The review starts from classical digital signature foundations before climbing to lattice designs. It serves newcomers entering post-quantum privacy protocols.
arxiv-2509-02389:
Matilde Gianocca wrote a 2025 solo analysis paper on whether every harmonic map between two spheres can be approached by critical points of the Ginzburg-Landau energy, a standard approximation scheme. Harmonic maps minimise a stretching energy, and degree counts how many times one sphere wraps the other.

Gianocca proves a rigidity result: among degree-one harmonic maps, only rotations arise as such limits. For small parameter values, any critical point with energy below a stated threshold must be, up to conjugation, a scaled rotation. So the approximation misses most harmonic maps entirely. The finding limits a common route for building harmonic maps and sharpens knowledge of the approximating energy landscape.
arxiv-2509-02589:
Xuan Qi and three co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on mitotic figures. These are images of dividing cells. The task is to sort them as normal or atypical. It forms part of the MIDOG 2025 challenge. Atypical division patterns can signal aggressive cancer behaviour.

Their classifier uses EfficientViT-L2. It mixes convolutional and transformer parts for speed and accuracy. Training data merged two public sets. The sets cover seven cancer types. Atypical cases form a small minority. To test generalisation, the team held out one cancer type at a time. They also ensembled five model folds. Stain deconvolution supplied augmentation. It separates dye colours in the images. The test model posted strong balanced accuracy and ranking scores. Performance held across cancer types.
arxiv-2509-03089:
Rajrupa Banerjee and 3 co-authors studied in 2025 how wave-particle duality extends to neutrinos, ghostly particles that shift flavor as they travel. Duality says quantum objects act partly like waves and partly like particles, and gaining one kind of information costs the other. Neutrino oscillation gives a rich, real setting for that trade-off.

The authors treat flavor change as an open quantum system and track links between the traveling neutrino and its detector. They extend the old duality relation into a three-way balance among predictability, visibility, and entanglement. Their measures sum to a fixed total, suggesting entanglement holds wave-like information that visibility alone misses. Applied to two major long-baseline experiments, the framework shows a point where particle and wave traits can be probed together.
arxiv-2509-03189:
Georg Schwefer presented a 2025 analysis of diffuse gamma-ray glow across the Milky Way using eight years of HAWC data. The HAWC observatory in Mexico watches very high energy gamma rays from the ground. This glow arises when cosmic rays strike interstellar gas and radiation, so mapping it traces how those fast particles spread through the galaxy.

A newer data processing version sharpened sensitivity and resolution. After subtracting known sources with a survey-style algorithm, strong leftover emission remained all along the galactic plane. Profiles across and along the plane were compared with models and with results from a Chinese observatory. Emission well above the plane matched the shape expected from cosmic rays hitting gas. The study also weighs several sources of uncertainty.
arxiv-2509-03389:
Dario Fasone and 7 co-authors used machine learning in 2025 to detect correlations in noise affecting two coupled qubits. Noise correlations, whether linked across space or across time, can spoil quantum hardware in distinct ways. Their system holds two ultrastrongly coupled qubits, quantum bits interacting more strongly than usual, exposed to classical noise.

Six noise classes are considered, mixing memoryless Markovian types with memory-carrying non-Markovian ones. A coherent population transfer protocol, run under three driving conditions, reacts differently to each class. Only the final transfer efficiencies are measured, and a shallow neural network classifies the noise from those few numbers. Accuracy reached about ninety-four percent or better, with near-perfect separation between the two broad families. The method needs no time-series monitoring.
arxiv-2509-03789:
Muratkhan Abdirash and one co-author survey a decentralised safety-critical controller for direct-current microgrids in a 2025 research paper. Microgrids mix solar panels, batteries, and power electronics, while cyber threats against them rise. Controllers must be provably safe and resilient, yet common droop-based designs are empirical and offer no rigorous guarantees.

Their Distributed Safety-Critical Controller joins global steadying with formal safety, with no central coordinator. Control barrier functions, fences that keep voltages and currents inside safe sets, are combined with port-Hamiltonian system theory, an energy-based modelling framework. The design stays scalable and fast enough for real-time use. Tests on switched circuits check the controller under varied contingencies, where it shows clear advantages over standard practice. The authors present it as a path toward robust, safety-critical control for future microgrids.
arxiv-2509-03989:
An injectivity property of vertex superalgebras, and on how Hopf algebras can act on algebras with that property is what Chao Yang examines in a 2025 mathematics paper. Vertex superalgebras are structures encoding two-dimensional quantum field theories, with even and odd parts tracked by signs. Injectivity, modelled on module theory, singles out algebras with extension properties.

Two large classes are shown to qualify. Simple superalgebras have no nontrivial ideals. Others admit a PBW basis, a basis of ordered monomials named for Poincaré, Birkhoff, and Witt. The symmetry result is restrictive. Any finite-dimensional Hopf algebra that acts inner faithfully here must in fact be a group algebra, the classical case. Hopf algebras generalise groups by relaxing symmetry rules, so the theorem says that extra freedom buys nothing here. A direct consequence follows for fixed-point subalgebras: their structure and representation theory under Hopf actions reduces to the group-action case.
arxiv-2509-04389:
Alec L Riso and three co-authors built a classroom device that acts out a famous quantum encryption protocol with ordinary light in a 2025 research paper. Quantum key distribution lets two parties create a shared secret key guarded by physics rather than hard math. The BB84 protocol encodes bits in photon polarization, the orientation of light waves. A true version needs single photons, but this fiber-optic apparatus uses many-photon beams to show each step visibly.

Encoding, transmission, and the basis-sifting stage, where mismatched measurement settings are discarded, all happen in the open. The design favors accessibility and visual clarity over real security. Students can watch the logic of quantum key exchange unfold step by step, making an abstract protocol tangible.
arxiv-2509-04689:
Timing the length of electron bunches shorter than a hundred femtoseconds is a standing problem at modern accelerators. Joseph Wolfenden, lead author with seven co-authors, demonstrate a new monitoring approach in a 2025 paper. Their method images coherent terahertz radiation produced by the bunches, bunch by bunch.

Proof-of-principle results cover relative compression monitoring using broadband imaging. The team show both standard intensity checks and a newer approach based on spatial distribution changes. Tests used invasive and non-invasive coherent radiation sources. The authors argue the results point toward a future monitor of longitudinal bunch profiles that never touches the beam.
arxiv-2509-04789: A new combinatorial proof of Cramer's rule, the classic formula for solving linear systems using determinants, is given by Sudip Bera in a solo-authored 2025 mathematics note. The proof is graph theoretic in character. It rests on the Gessel-Viennot-Lindström lemma, a result that counts families of non-intersecting paths in a directed graph using determinants.
arxiv-2509-04889:
Fear of spiders could be estimated from a picture before a patient ever sees it. Dominik Pegler, lead author with six co-authors, test that idea in a 2025 paper on vision models and phobia treatment. Scalable computerised exposure therapy needs automatic fear prediction to adapt stimulus choice and treatment intensity.

Pretrained convolutional and transformer models, adapted by transfer learning, predict group-level perceived fear for spider images. Their errors stay small on a hundred-point scale, even for new people and new images. Explanation analyses show predictions rely on spider-specific regions. Errors grow at extreme fear levels, a limit the authors report openly.
arxiv-2509-05089:
In biased positional games, who moves first can change everything about the outcome. Ali Deniz Bagdas, lead author with three co-authors, present constructions exploring that behaviour in a 2025 combinatorics paper. They show outcomes can differ arbitrarily depending on which player starts, and that fair biased games can behave in highly non-monotonic ways.

A gadget they build transfers such results to Maker-Breaker domination games, extending a recent theorem about game length. They also introduce Waiter-Client domination games, solve them tightly on trees and cycles, and show their length can diverge arbitrarily from the Maker-Breaker analogue.
arxiv-2509-05189:
Protein models with several conformations can tangle, with states wrongly intertwined during refinement against density maps. Avinash Mandaiya and one co-author present an automated method to avoid that failure in a 2025 structural biology paper. The method refines all conformations at once. Their approach uses iterative projections inside a divide-and-concur framework.

Geometric constraints and experimental density constraints are integrated seamlessly. Each atom satisfies the density constraints independently. That independence circumvents tangling artifacts in their tests. States stay apart instead of merging. Refinement stays robust even for models starting from poor agreement factors. The authors compare the advance to how that method transformed phase retrieval in crystallography. They aim it at probing protein dynamics.
arxiv-2509-05289:
Event histories where effects bend and drift over time need richer models, Martina Boschi and two co-authors propose in a 2025 statistics paper. Relational hyper-events link two or more actors at a time stamp, such as teams forming or messages sent within groups.

Standard models for such data assume effects are straight-line and constant, which the authors relax. Their model lets each effect vary both non-linearly and with time, using smooth surfaces built from products of simpler curves. Tests on synthetic and real data check the approach. Applied to scientific collaboration, the model tracks how patterns of teamwork and impact change, including effects that rise and then fall.
arxiv-2509-05589:
Inequality problems with a moving feasible region are solved by a new iterative method from Watanjeet Singh and Sumit Chandok in a 2025 optimisation paper. Variational inequalities model equilibria in economics, traffic, and engineering, and the pseudo-monotone case is a weakened form that is harder to handle.

Older methods project onto the full feasible set, which can be expensive, or onto a half-space that may leave the set entirely. Their scheme projects instead onto a ball sitting inside the feasible set, where the projection has an explicit formula. It also needs no advance knowledge of the operator's Lipschitz constant, a measure of smoothness. Numerical experiments illustrate that the scheme converges as claimed.
arxiv-2509-05989:
The Sun's surface magnetic field is tested against its own fingerprint in a 2025 paper by Yukun Luo and two co-authors. Surface flux transport models describe how magnetic patches drift and spread across the Sun, but their grip on fine structure was unverified. The authors compare observed and simulated magnetic power spectra, summaries of how much magnetism lives at each spatial scale.

Simulations match observations well at large scales but drift away at small ones, likely because the model treats supergranulation, the Sun's boiling surface motion, as simple diffusion. Source flux rules the middle scales, while transport settings steer the largest. Comparing specific multipoles suggests the poleward flow high above sixty degrees latitude is very weak. The study is the first quantitative check of these models by power spectra.
arxiv-2509-06089:
Thin shear layers near a wall can destabilize the full three-dimensional Navier-Stokes flow, construct Cheng-Jie Liu and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. They study boundary layer profiles as viscosity shrinks toward zero. When the streamwise and spanwise velocity profiles near the boundary are linearly independent, trouble follows.

The authors build an unstable mode whose amplitude grows at a rapid exponential rate tied to the square root of viscosity. The instability is analytic, not numerical, and it springs from the interplay between spanwise flow and three-dimensional perturbations; purely two-dimensional flows escape it. The result marks generic boundary layers as genuinely unstable in three dimensions, a caution for high-speed flow prediction.
arxiv-2509-06489:
Listening for a faint background hum of gravitational waves is the setting for a 2025 statistics paper by Rutger van Haasteren and two co-authors. Pulsar timing arrays watch steady radio pulsars for tiny timing shifts that follow a known sky pattern. Current evidence sits below the usual five-sigma bar for a claim.

The standard detection statistic squeezes cross-correlations between pulsar pairs, yet the authors show it does not give the best detection chance at a fixed false-alarm rate. A fully optimal version would use each pulsar alone too, but that invites errors from poorly modeled pulsar noise. Their compromise stays as close as possible to the optimal form while using only cross-correlations. In simulations matched to the NANOGrav fifteen-year data, the new statistic lifts detection probability by nearly half.
arxiv-2509-06589:
Slow drift along repeating cycles in fast-slow systems is given a coordinate-free treatment by Bob Rink and two co-authors in a 2025 dynamical systems paper. Bursting behavior in many sciences follows this pattern. Classic averaging theory, through the Pontryagin-Rodygin theorem, approximates the slow drift, but its link to geometric singular perturbation theory is often left vague.

The authors use the parametrisation method, which solves for a surface's embedding and the flow on it together. Their self-contained account shows how this yields averaged systems that stay consistent with the persistent invariant manifold to any order. Floquet theory, spectral analysis, and the Fredholm alternative turn the theory into a concrete computing recipe. Worked examples, both by hand and numerically, show how to build high-accuracy averaged models in practice.
arxiv-2509-07589:
Rachel Nixon leads a 14-author study in 2025 of unusual magnetic order in the intermetallic compound Eu10Hg55. Europium atoms in solids can carry mixed valence, taking two charge states at once, especially when they sit at several distinct crystal positions. This compound has 65 atoms per unit cell, with four europium positions and seventeen mercury positions, arranged in a cage-like structure.

Measurements on large single crystals suggest europium indeed appears in two valence states, leaving a fragile magnetic ground state. The widely spaced europium atoms couple weakly and ferromagnetically, ordering below about 5.5 kelvin, with a spin re-orientation near 4.3 kelvin and no sign of frustration. The sublattice ordering produces a magnetization pole reversal with a weak ferrimagnetic ground state. A modest external field can induce further magnetic phases, making the compound a rich test case for mixed-valence magnetism.
arxiv-2509-07689:
Paul Moujaes and 2 co-authors design a numerical scheme in 2025 for the M1 model of radiative transfer. The scheme never lets the computed states leave the physically allowed set. Radiative transfer tracks how radiation flows through matter. The M1 model follows its two lowest moments, summaries of the radiation field. An entropy-based rule closes the system. If computed moments step outside the realizable set, the model stops making physical sense.

The authors first build a low-order method that provably preserves the invariant domain. It uses intermediate bar states drawn from averaged exact solutions of Riemann problems. They prove these states are realizable in any number of space dimensions. High resolution comes from nonlinear correction terms. A two-step monolithic convex limiting algorithm constrains those terms. Reactive terms get a diagonally implicit treatment. The result is a scheme that stays physical by construction.
arxiv-2509-07789:
Jiayang Shi and 2 co-authors build a unified benchmark in 2025 for filtered approximate nearest neighbor search. In filtered search, a query must return the closest points that also satisfy label constraints, such as a category or attribute, while keeping both recall and queries-per-second high. Many algorithms exist, but comparisons were unreliable: parameters couple to datasets, key factors go unanalyzed, and workloads differ across studies.

The authors propose a taxonomy that divides methods into families such as filter-then-search, design a fair evaluation, and run a systematic experimental study of when each algorithm performs well. The benchmark aims to clarify relative strengths and weaknesses that biased setups had hidden. Such shared yardsticks matter because filtered search sits inside modern recommendation, retrieval, and AI database systems.
arxiv-2509-08589:
Cells signal to their surroundings through molecular chains that unfold over time, and simulators try to reproduce those chains faithfully. Lena Cibulski and 3 co-authors present a visual analysis design study in a 2025 research paper. Modelers must tune parameters until simulated responses match known cell biology. Biologists, meanwhile, want to see how receptor trafficking affects signal efficiency inside the cell.

Their design embeds time series plots inside parallel coordinates, a chart that shows many parameters at once. Parameters and temporal outputs can then be read together, side by side. A usage scenario walks through judging whether outputs look plausible and how sensitive they are to settings. The approach turns calibration from blind number-crunching into guided exploration. Better-calibrated signaling models support drug research and basic cell biology alike.
arxiv-2509-08689:
Riccardo Bovo and 3 co-authors present a system that enriches VR speech transcripts with gaze and pointing data in a 2025 paper. In virtual reality, words like it or there often point to things only seen in the scene. Plain transcripts lose that context, making coreference hard.

Eye tracking, laser pointing, and scene data are turned into text notes about non-verbal cues and objects of interest. Data come from twelve participants in pairs doing a design critique of a 3D apartment model. A language model resolves references far better with the enriched transcript than with speech alone. The gain supports better tools for immersive meetings.
arxiv-2509-08989:
An AI that explains itself can still mislead users about how much to trust it. Carina Newen and 5 co-authors study that trust calibration problem in a 2025 research paper. Their focus is uncertainty explanations, which say how unsure a model is, and global explanations, which describe the whole model rather than one decision. Both are understudied compared with local explanations.

The team picked an algorithm combining uncertainty, robustness, and global explanation in one scheme. They tested whether it calibrates user trust appropriately. They also asked whether a visually intuitive but complicated display could beat simpler ones on satisfaction and interpretability. Guidelines for explanation design are derived from the results. The stakes are practical: overtrust invites accidents, undertrust wastes good tools, and explanations are the dial meant to set trust correctly.
arxiv-2509-09489:
Children whose soft palate cannot seal against the throat speak with excess nasality. The standard tests are invasive and unpleasant. Saba Tabatabaee and 4 co-authors pursue a kinder measurement in a 2025 research paper. Speech inversion estimates how the mouth moves from sound alone, with no instruments in the body. Their system targets nasalance, the acoustic mark of nasal coupling.

The model was trained on healthy adults' data, then enriched with voice-source data from throat sensors and acoustic estimates. That enrichment improved correlation with reference readings clearly. Fine-tuning on speech from children with velopharyngeal insufficiency improved it further. A noninvasive, child-friendly nasality measure could change how speech therapy for these children is tracked. Progress could be tracked from recordings made in ordinary rooms, instead of procedures children dread.
arxiv-2509-09689:
Himanshu Thakur and 2 co-authors build cheap stand-ins for real users in a 2025 paper on recommendation systems. Simulating shoppers is hard because human choices are tangled and random, and large language models that mimic them are costly to tune for millions of people. Raw history tables must also be parsed again and again, and a general model's built-in habits can fight against learning one person's taste.

Their route first reads a frozen large model to draw sturdy text portraits of users. Small language models, fine-tuned with low-rank adapters grouped by persona, then act out behaviour at far lower cost. Grouping adapters this way balances scale against fidelity, and experiments support the design as a practical way to staff user simulators.
arxiv-2509-09989:
Priyanka Rushikesh Chaudhary and 4 co-authors build a camera-spotting system in a 2025 network security paper. Its decisions come with reasons a human can check. Learning models can flag odd traffic from smart home devices. Yet their black-box verdicts stall the staff who must act on them. The team's tool is called rCamInspector. It sorts each traffic flow into broad groups first. It then names the exact camera type behind flows marked as camera traffic. It does not lean on addresses or ports.

Eight models were compared on a large bank of captured traffic. A gradient boosting model won both stages. Its scores were high on each. The authors then test how much trust the verdicts deserve. A common importance score cannot certify them, they show. Tools such as SHAP and LIME do better. They surface traits an analyst can audit.
arxiv-2509-10089:
Marco Andrea Bühler and Gonzalo Guillén-Gosálbez introduce KAN-SR in a 2025 paper, a tool that hunts for the equation behind a data set. Symbolic regression usually relies on genetic programming to evolve formulas. Their framework instead builds on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks and a divide-and-conquer plan, then simplifies what it finds by using symmetries and by splitting problems into separable parts.

The method recovered the true equations behind the Feynman benchmark data set, a standard test drawn from physics formulas. Paired with neural differential equations, it also modeled the behavior of a simulated bioprocess system with high precision. The authors suggest the same pairing could model other engineering systems where the governing equation is unknown but the data are rich.
arxiv-2509-10389:
Does having true beginners on a science team help or hurt? Mahdee Mushfique Kamal and Raiyan Abdul Baten analyze over twenty-nine million articles from 1941 to 2020 in this 2025 scientometrics paper. Beginners are authors with no prior publications, and teams are now where most advances happen.

Across fields and team sizes, a higher share of beginners tracks with more disruptive, innovative work, a pattern the authors call beginner's charm. Such teams draw on wider, less canonical sources and recombine ideas in unusual ways. The effect strengthens when beginners work beside early-career colleagues or proven disruptors. Disruptive papers usually collect fewer citations, yet the highly disruptive ones from beginner-heavy teams are heavily cited, giving departments a concrete reason to mix newcomers into research teams.
arxiv-2509-10589:
Debarshi Mukherjee, writing alone, presented this 2025 paper on signs of QCD phase changes inside neutron stars. He then withdrew it. The arXiv record says the work is withdrawn by the author. It does not meet the standards the author wishes to keep in the permanent record. The results are called preliminary. The record also says the work should not be cited.

The withdrawn text claimed several effects. It claimed paired star branches of twin stars. It claimed shifts in merger waves after two stars collide. It claimed extra neutrino output during phase changes. It said these claims fit current data only roughly. Since the author has retracted the work, those claims now stand as part of the self-correcting record. They are not findings to rely on.
arxiv-2509-10789:
Sudhamshu Hosamane and 3 co-authors examine whether safety tools on social platforms work for blind and low-vision users in this 2025 paper. Platforms hand more and more moderation to users. The tools include reporting, blocking, and filters. If those tools are hard to use, the burden of staying safe falls hardest on those least able to carry it.

The team ran interviews and task walkthroughs with 15 people with vision loss, on Facebook and X. They sort the costs into three kinds. One is learning what the tools do. A second is carrying out long steps through a screen reader. A third is stress and self-blame when things fail. One user blamed herself before she blamed the design. A list of breakdowns and fixes follows.
arxiv-2509-11189:
Two identical chaotic Lorenz oscillators, linked together, are the subject of this 2025 physics paper. Pavel S. Komkov and three co-authors wrote it. As the link between the oscillators strengthens, odd regularities appear. Their wild motion shows coherence and anti-coherence resonances.

The authors read different output signals of the pair. Both effects show up at the same coupling values. This holds below the level of complete synchrony. In that range the system behaves hyperchaotically. It also shows bursts of on-off intermittency. Computer simulations revealed the pattern first. Bench-top circuit experiments then reproduced it closely. The match suggests a robust effect, not a numerical accident.
arxiv-2509-11289:
The energy appetite of sixth-generation mobile networks is the subject of this 2025 survey. Rashmi Kamran and five co-authors wrote it. Networks for vastly more users risk unsustainable power use. Data-heavy services add to the risk. Efficiency is becoming a design goal in itself.

The survey gathers the main tools for energy-aware design. It covers harvesting ambient energy. It covers models and parameters describing consumption. It classifies energy-aware services. It reviews machine learning methods that trim power without hurting service. Use cases show how energy information improves network decisions. The authors review standardization work in 3GPP, the ITU, and IEEE. They close with open problems. Those include the overhead of exposing energy data and user consent.
arxiv-2509-11589:
Yanyun Pu and 4 co-authors release a richly annotated dataset for judging video quality in a 2025 paper. As video generation models improve, quality assessment matters for selecting the best material for pretraining, yet single numerical scores say little about why a video looks good or bad.

Their dataset, MVQA-68K, covers tens of thousands of videos annotated across seven quality dimensions, from camera movement and texture detail to factual consistency. Each annotation includes chain-of-thought reasoning explaining the judgment. Experiments showed the dataset significantly improved several multimodal models on quality assessment, reaching state-of-the-art results on internal and public benchmarks. Training with explicit reasoning also boosted zero-shot generalization to new settings.
arxiv-2509-11689:
Jeremiah Fadugba and 4 co-authors compress ensembles of retinal vessel models into one network in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Mapping tiny eye vessels aids diagnosis, and doubt estimates are key for reliability. Deep ensembles improve results but multiply training and testing costs.

Their method, ensemble distillation, moves the joint knowledge of several trained networks into a single model. Wide tests on two retinal datasets compared calibration and segmentation quality against common uncertainty methods. The distilled model matched those methods on both kinds of metrics while cutting compute sharply. The findings suggest ensemble distillation is an efficient and reliable route to uncertainty-aware segmentation, with promise for clinical imaging use.
arxiv-2509-11789:
Timilehin B. Aderinola and 7 co-authors build a real-time fall detector for older adults in a 2025 health technology paper. Falls carry severe health consequences, and timely intervention matters. Earlier detectors often relied on simulated falls or assumed the system knew when falls could occur, limiting real-world use.

Their framework monitors accelerometer streams continuously with no prior knowledge of fall events. Training used over sixty hours of real-world wearable data from a falls dataset containing genuine incidents. Efficient classifiers compute fall probabilities in streaming mode. A cost-sensitive strategy tunes the decision threshold, weighting missed falls as costlier than false alarms. The system detected every fall with low false alarms and very fast per-sample inference, suiting wearable deployment.
arxiv-2509-11889:
Lorenzo Carosini and 9 co-authors send quantum dot photons through a hollow-core fiber in a 2025 quantum communication paper. Quantum dots are promising single-photon sources, but their best devices emit near a wavelength where standard fibers lose too much light over distance.

The engineered hollow-core fiber transmits at those wavelengths with low measured loss, and potentially far lower. It also carries strong classical signals at the usual telecom wavelength without adding Raman noise. The team transmitted all four polarization states of a standard quantum key protocol from an indium arsenide quantum dot over hundreds of meters. Error rates stayed very low, and single-photon purity and indistinguishability survived alongside the classical signal. Tailored fibers could extend quantum networks beyond standard limits.
arxiv-2509-12189:
JSON databases like MongoDB are everywhere, yet they have no shared formal standard for how queries should behave. Elena Botoeva and two co-authors draft a candidate core in 2025 by writing down a precise syntax and semantics for a chosen slice of MongoDB's aggregation framework.

The report shows how that slice lines up with known relational query languages and flags where their clean semantics parts ways with what MongoDB actually does, with reasons for each choice. It also supplies algebraic rewrite rules that a database engine could use to optimize queries. The hope is a common starting point for an industry standard.
arxiv-2509-12589:
Garima Agrawal and 7 co-authors present a case study of agentic AI in customer support in a 2025 paper. Customer experience still suffers from long handling times, low first-call resolution, and poor satisfaction. A key driver is cognitive load on human agents, who navigate fragmented systems, troubleshoot manually, and often place customers on hold.

The authors introduce Minerva CQ, a real-time agent assist product deployed in voice-based support. It integrates real-time transcription, intent and sentiment detection, entity recognition, contextual retrieval, and dynamic customer profiling. Unlike reactive tools driven by static rules or simple retrieval, the system identifies intent, triggers modular workflows, and adapts to the evolving conversation state. The case study argues that goal-driven, tool-using agents can proactively support human agents.
arxiv-2509-12689:
Jonas Ohnemus, Marta Fochesato and two co-authors improve in 2025 a safe choice method that guards plans against data error. The method builds a zone of likely spreads around past data with a transport cost, then picks the plan that stays best inside that zone.

Standard use fixes the zone first and plans second, which can be too strict. The new end-to-end flow learns the zone shape from the loss of the final task, so plans stay safe but less strict. Math shows the learning step settles at a sound point. Tests on fund choice and line fitting support the gain.
arxiv-2509-12789:
Ayush Dixit, Chunheng Zhao and three co-authors explain in 2025 why thin liquid sheets tear even when they are far thicker than the scale where tiny forces act. Sheets in sprays, waves, and breath films often break at the scale of a hair width, and the rule for break or heal was not clear.

Computer models of a draining sheet with a trapped air pocket show break needs two things at once: a strong outward push and a bent pocket shape. If either is weak, surface pull heals the hole. Timing depends on the mix of flow force and thickness. The rule gives clear levers to control spray breakup.
arxiv-2509-12889:
Romane Giard, Yohann de Castro and Clement Marteau estimate in 2025 mixtures of bell curves with unknown spread per part. Past sparse methods needed known, shared spreads. Real mixtures vary spread by part, so that curb hurt use.

A convex sparse frame now learns count, centers, spreads, and weights at once. Recovery bounds come close to the best rate for all parts. A clear split rule between parts lets proof tools be built. Fisher geometry and a new semi-distance drive the proof. The work links part split, space shape, and recovery in one view.
arxiv-2509-13089:
Jonas Werheid, Shengjie He and three co-authors pipe fake image data for assembly checks in small factories in 2025. Vision checks cut faults, but photos, labels, and training cost block small firms. Fake data can cut that load if it transfers to real views.

Scenes are built from CAD files and fed to a detector. On fake gear parts scores near the top were reached. On real camera tests scores stayed high, above nine in ten. The pipe saves time and fits plant floors with ease. Small firms gain a lean path to vision control.
arxiv-2509-13189:
Zhao Feng, Bicheng Yan and five co-authors invert buried flow data in 2025 with a surrogate-guided generative frame called SURGIN. Buried multi-phase flow must be inferred from sparse well data. Old inversion needs retraining for each new sensor layout.

SURGIN pairs a Fourier operator surrogate with a score-based generator. The generator learns rock priors alone, with no labels. Posterior draws then use the fast surrogate to judge unseen data on the fly. No retraining is needed per layout. Broad tests infer mixed rock fields and forecast flow with doubt bands across layouts.
arxiv-2509-13489:
Chester J. F. Gould and William J. Bowman present work in progress on comparing type equality checking methods in a 2025 extended abstract. Every dependent type checker must decide, again and again, whether two types count as equal. That single step sits at the heart of checking. A piece of folklore surrounds it. Equality driven by syntax is said to run faster. Equality driven by types is said to say more.

Real systems pick one road or the other, never both, so the two can never be raced on the same track. Gould and Bowman are building that track: a realistic platform where both approaches run side by side, apples to apples. With it they can measure how much slower the type-directed road really is. They can also study where the time goes, and what might win some of it back.
arxiv-2509-13589:
Will Dolphin and Peter Dukes improve a bootstrap percolation problem in a 2025 combinatorics paper. In the three-neighbour process on a three-dimensional grid, an empty cell fills once at least three neighbors are filled. A percolating set is a starting set that eventually fills everything. The puzzle is finding the smallest such sets for thin grids.

Through several new constructions, the pair show that optimal percolating sets exist for many grids. These are sets matching the known lower bound. They exist whenever the smallest grid dimension is at least seven. As a step toward that, every grid with smallest dimension at least four has such a set. It hits the bound exactly whenever the bound is a whole number. The result narrows a long-standing gap.
arxiv-2509-13689:
Oem Trivedi proposes the Thermodynamic Split Conjecture in a solo 2025 theoretical physics paper. String theory explains black hole entropy beautifully. It counts the microscopic states behind the famous area law. But Trivedi argues the structures enabling those derivations do not carry over. Realistic expanding cosmologies have horizons of their own.

The conjecture states a clean claim. In any complete quantum gravity theory, black hole and cosmic horizon thermodynamics are, in general, different things. He states a formal criterion for the split. He also discusses how the idea could be falsified. And he proposes a scaling test on sky maps. It compares entropy proxies from tomographic sky maps against the black hole prediction. The aim is a sharper account of when the area law holds.
arxiv-2509-14089:
Luca Aceto and three co-authors settle complexity questions about characteristic formulae in a 2025 logic paper, presented as an extended abstract. In process algebra, a characteristic formula is a single modal logic formula. It captures exactly one behavior up to a chosen equivalence. Here the equivalence is nested simulation, a refined way of saying one process can mimic another with extra lookahead.

Deciding whether a given formula is characteristic amounts to checking it is satisfiable and prime. The team show the primality problem is coNP-complete for the logic of two-nested simulation. The overall decision problem sits in the class DP. For n-nested simulation with n at least three, deciding characteristic formulae is PSPACE-complete. That jump in difficulty maps exactly where automated reasoning about these specifications stays feasible.
arxiv-2509-14289:
Lanxiao Huang and four co-authors test language model agents at penetration testing in 2025, the authorised probing of computer systems for weak points. Models are being tried as test helpers, but skill across attack phases is uneven and failures repeat.

The team compared single and modular agents on realistic test scenarios and logged where each design failed. They then added five supports one by one: shared memory, messaging between agents, careful tool choice, adaptive planning and live monitoring. Each support targets a clear weakness, from losing context to poor recovery after errors. Findings show raw model skill alone does not predict field performance. Scaffolding around the model decides much of what a testing agent can actually finish.
arxiv-2509-14389:
Sarbari Mitra and Soumya Bhoumik study graph polynomials in 2025 built from permanents, a determinant like sum over matchings of rows to columns. For a graph, the Laplacian and signless Laplacian matrices encode degrees and links. Their permanental polynomials package graph structure into one formula.

A graph is determined by such a polynomial if no differently shaped graph shares it. Being fixed by both polynomials together is a stronger property. The authors investigate permanental characterisations for several well known graph families. They check which families are pinned down by one polynomial or by the pair. Such results matter for graph identification, where a compact algebraic fingerprint that is unique to one shape is valuable.
arxiv-2509-14789:
Michael Neri and Tuomas Virtanen build a way to fake the sound of a room so that fake-speech detectors can be trained, in a 2025 audio paper. Replay attacks play a recording of a voice to fool voice-based locks and assistants. Multi-mic recordings carry clues about where sound came from, and those clues help expose fakes. Most data sets, though, use just one mic.

Their tool fakes multi-mic replay setups from public sound files, so training data can cover many rooms. They train a top detector on faked data only and test it on real tapes. They also add phase-gap clues between mic pairs, which point to where sound came from. The faked data sets are shared in public for others to use.
arxiv-2509-14889:
Nan Sun and four co-authors introduce CollabVLA in a 2025 robotics paper. Vision-language-action models turn camera input and instructions into robot actions, but they often overfit their training domain, reason in ways humans cannot follow, and run slowly when extra generative models help them. CollabVLA aims to turn such a controller into a collaborative assistant.

Reflective reasoning from a vision-language model is combined with diffusion-based action generation in a mixture-of-experts design. Training proceeds in two stages, action grounding and then reflection tuning. The system can explain itself, and it asks a human for guidance when it is uncertain or keeps failing. Compared with generative agents, it finishes tasks faster with fewer internal dream steps, while reaching higher success rates and lower delay.
arxiv-2509-14989:
Benedikt Kolbeinsson and Krystian Mikolajczyk teach drones to spot wires and judge their distance in a 2025 computer vision paper. Wires are among the hardest obstacles for autonomous drones: thin, low-contrast, and deadly to miss. Safe navigation needs both detection and depth from a single camera.

Their end-to-end model performs wire segmentation and depth estimation jointly. A temporal correlation layer, trained on synthetic data, lets the model compare views across time, which helps reveal thin structures that single frames hide. Tests show the method beating existing competitors on the combined task of finding wires and estimating their depth. The authors argue the design can raise drone safety and precision in real flights near power lines and other wire hazards.
arxiv-2509-15489:
Athira Unni leads a team building the data pipeline for a new Keck telescope tool. The tool, SCALES, will take heat based light from the sky and spread it into spectra. It is an imager and spectrograph for the Keck II telescope, built to study planets around other stars. Raw reads from such a tool need much care before they become science data.

The pipeline stacks reads into a ramp, pulls out spectra in two ways, and builds a three way data cube. It leans on fix maps made from test shots that track how each tiny lens bends light. Each point in the cube carries a value and its doubt. The code is in Python, open on GitHub, and still growing.
arxiv-2509-15689:
Jay Park leads a team that reads speech sounds from scans of the moving mouth and throat. Real time MRI films the vocal tract as a person speaks, giving a full view of how sounds are made. The signals are large and noisy, though, which hides their meaning. The team seek compact codes for these motions that still name each sound.

They compare three views: raw video, motion flow between frames, and six zones tied to speech parts like tongue and lips. Mixed views beat any single view. The best mix joins zone traits with raw video. Removing zones one by one shows the tongue and lips matter most. Fine timing in the motion proves key as well.
arxiv-2509-15989:
Grouping nodes in a network into clusters helps reveal hidden structure in the data. Bertrand Cloez and three co-authors offer a new family of fast methods for this task in graphs built with block models. Their methods need no fixed model of the links and grow out of a classic grouping method used for points.

Tests on many data sets show much faster run times than leading tools, with errors that stay low. The authors also prove their estimates hold up under a clear condition. In a final test, they use real animal network data to infer social roles, which shows the methods work outside pure theory.
arxiv-2509-16089:
A newborn strange star, made of loose quarks, could shine with pairs of particles at a huge rate if its surface stays hot. Mikalai Prakapenia and Gregory Vereshchagin ask whether such a star can keep that heat for long. They model how heat flows through quark matter and how neutrinos carry energy away from its core.

Their runs show a steep heat drop near the surface forms fast. Within about a hundred seconds, the surface cools and the pair output falls by a huge factor. The result holds even when a neutrino layer is present. So the bright phase of such a star would be brief.
arxiv-2509-16289:
A charged particle near a strange, horizon-free space-time held up by electric charge alone faces a wall of singular shells. Abdullah Guvendi and three co-authors chart how such particles move in this geometry, which comes from a massless charged wormhole model. They build the effective potential from exact conserved values and read off orbit sizes, wobble rates, and precession.

Far away, the motion looks like a hydrogen atom's, with small curve-driven shifts that push orbits backward. Near the outer shell, the potential soars and traps the particle. Heat measures shift as well, with energies raised by the curvature.
arxiv-2509-16589:
Qiongqiong Wang and co-authors build a test for speech models in a 2025 paper. Speech models can transcribe and translate well. Yet they often miss tone, feeling, and other cues that ride along with words. Those cues matter for social and emotional sense. The team call the skill of mixing words with such cues contextual paralinguistic reasoning.

Their benchmark, CP-Bench, uses real-world recordings rather than clean studio clips. Models are scored on how well they read both content and delivery. The best two models were tested further with varied settings. Results show a wide gap in current tools. The benchmark points to what builders must fix for more human-like speech systems.
arxiv-2509-16689:
Bethany Davies, Guus Avis, and Stephanie Wehner check a common shortcut in quantum networks in a 2025 paper. Chains of repeaters pass entanglement from link to link. Analysts often simplify noisy states into tidy forms called twirled states. The team ask how much error that shortcut adds to end results.

They bound the gap in final fidelity for a key swapping step. The bound holds for states with general noise. They then test secret key rates over a chain as a use case. The lesson is when the shortcut is safe and when it misleads. Network designers can plan with firmer error bars.
arxiv-2509-16789:
Mojtaba Hosseini, working alone, tests a dark matter model against two classic problems in a 2025 theory paper. The model adds a hidden sector with four new fields. One scalar field links the hidden part to the known Higgs field. Dark matter lives in the hidden part.

Hosseini checks whether the vacuum stays stable in this setup. He also checks a set of conditions that ease the fine-tuning of the Higgs mass. One spot in the allowed range passes both checks at a set energy scale. That point suggests the extra fields could solve the tuning problem. The model stays a theory claim, not a measured fact.
arxiv-2509-16989:
He Xiao and co-authors squeeze large language models to trit-planes in a 2025 paper. Shrinking a model after training cuts memory and boosts speed. At extremely low bit widths, quality usually drops or retraining costs explode. Their method stores weights in ternary planes, a middle path between binary and full precision.

The approach rivals a leading training-based method in quality. It needs only about an hour of quantization, not many GPU days. Inference runs several times faster than a half-precision baseline. Code will be shared in public. Practical low-bit models could run strong assistants on modest hardware in clinics, schools, and field sites.
arxiv-2509-17289:
Sydney Anuyah and five co-authors built a pipeline that turns text into knowledge graphs on its own. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes CoDe-KG, an open-source system that works sentence by sentence. It pairs coreference resolution, which links pronouns to the things they name, with a step that breaks tangled sentences into simpler ones.

Language models do the extraction, guided by prompts tuned for five grades of sentence complexity. The team releases a data set of well over a hundred thousand knowledge triples, plus smaller gold sets checked by humans. On standard relation extraction tests, the pipeline beat the prior best score by a clear margin on one benchmark and matched or beat rivals on others. Adding the coreference and splitting steps lifted recall on rare relations by a wide margin.
arxiv-2509-17389:
Lois Liow and six co-authors printed soft sensors shaped like real corals in a 2025 arXiv paper. Conservation teams catalogue, digitize, and care for fragile samples from threatened ecosystems. Handling such samples by robot risks damage, and learning-based handlers need safe ways to gather training data without harming the real thing.

The team's method prints free-form soft structures filled with liquid metal sensors, copying scans or models of natural objects. A design workflow builds these sensor-rich physical twins on demand. The twins recreate tangled natural shapes faithfully and sense touch well. As sensing corals, the printed replicas stand in for live coral in handling tests. That swap removes the need to experiment on live coral, raises data quality, and gives soft manipulation research an ethical, scalable test bed.
arxiv-2509-17489:
Woongkyu Lee, Junhee Cho, and Jungwook Choi squeeze a team of coding agents into one small model. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a known split: multi-agent coding systems solve hard programming tasks, but they lean on very large models or fall apart when shrunk. Small open models are cheap, yet they stumble on format, retrieval, and debugging.

Their framework, MapCoder-Lite, distills the multi-agent reasoning into a single modest model with three pillars. Trajectories from strong teachers fix fragile formats and cut debugging failures. A supervisor's global feedback sharpens the planning and coding roles. Agent-wise low-rank tuning then gives each role its own memory-light specialty. On three coding benchmarks, the small model more than doubled accuracy on one. It also wiped out format failures. It used just a fraction of the memory and time of a model four times its size.
arxiv-2509-17689:
Žiga Babnik, Deepak Kumar Jain, Peter Peer, and Vitomir Štruc grade face image quality by watching the recognizer itself. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves face recognition in high-stakes settings, where a bad sample can cause a costly error. Quality tools let a system reject samples too poor to trust, but the best ones need heavy supervised training, while training-free ones run slow and score worse.

Their method, FROQ, reads specific intermediate representations inside a given recognition model. A light calibration step with pseudo-quality labels finds which representations carry quality signal. The result is semi-supervised and training-free in practice, joining the speed of supervised tools with the freedom of unsupervised ones. It can be fitted to any modern recognition model. The authors present it as a practical quality gate that travels with the recognizer it serves.
arxiv-2509-17889:
Phuong Mai Dinh and Van-Nam Huynh offer a softer way to learn trade-off fronts with many goals. Their 2025 method, GaussianPSL, deals with cases where the best trade curve is broken, bent, or thin. Past tools that learn the whole front at once can miss such shapes.

Their plan splits the choice and goal space into soft zones. Small plain nets learn each zone, then their outputs are pooled for the final guess. The split helps search, steadies starts, and cuts the pull of local traps. Tests show steadier wins over standard front learners, while the model stays simple.
arxiv-2509-18089:
Xiaosheng Huang leads a very large DESI team that follows up strong lens candidates with spectra. Their 2025 paper, part two of the Strong Lens Foundry series, deals with candidates found in DESI survey images. Lens and source distances are key for any lens model that yields physical values.

The catalogue holds dozens of candidate systems from an early DESI data set. Spectra confirmed a score of them as true lenses, and ruled a few out. The rest await more data from runs still to come. The team also draws lessons for net-based lens hunts in current and future surveys.
arxiv-2509-18189:
Daxiang Dong leads a large team that built a family of vision-language models with extra domain skill. Their 2025 series, Qianfan-VL, spans small to very large sizes. A staged training plan and a high-grade data making pipe drive the gains, the team reports.

Broad bench scores match top open models, the team reports. Scores on text-in-image and document tasks stand out as a clear strength. Larger sizes add long step-by-step thought, with strong maths and logic scores. All models were trained on Baidu chips, at high scale and with high yield across thousands of chips.
arxiv-2509-18289:
Akrati Saxena, Gaurav Kumar, and Chandrakala Meena give a tutorial on homophily, the pull to link with folk like oneself. Their 2025 piece is a survey, not a new data study. That pull shapes how social networks grow, and how gaps in them form and harden over time.

The tour covers core senses of the term, its key traits, and the flaws of common scores. It moves past pair links to group forms such as hypergraphs. Models that grow networks with a tunable dose of the pull are set out. Open snags and fresh paths close the survey.
arxiv-2509-18389:
Some learning agents pick up new tasks with no retraining, just by reading their own past actions. Jiuqi Wang, Rohan Chandra, and Shangtong Zhang ask why that trick, called in-context reinforcement learning, works at all. Their 2025 paper studies agents whose settings stay fixed while context grows. As the context holds more of the agent's history in a new task, its play improves.

The authors guess that the settings that enable this trick are ones that minimize the pretraining loss. They back the guess with a case study and a proof. In their setup, a transformer is pretrained to judge policies. One best-fit setting of that training can support in-context temporal difference learning, a step-by-step value update done inside the context. The work is a first step toward a full theory of how such flexible agents emerge from standard training.
arxiv-2509-18489:
When no perfect reference test exists, judging new medical tests gets tricky. Enzo Cerullo and five co-authors compare two statistical models for that job in this 2025 simulation study. Both models assume a hidden true state and let test results depend on each other. One, the latent trait model, forces a simple link structure. The other allows a full web of links.

The team simulated data under five patterns, from no links to rich, varied ones. They also tried varied prior settings, including new priors that keep correlation guesses readable. Their software fits these slow models at graphics-chip-like speed. The full-web model won overall. The simple trait model did fine on its own kind of data but failed badly on rich patterns, sometimes worse than assuming no links. High test sensitivity could mask poor link recovery. The authors advise the flexible model for real use.
arxiv-2509-18789:
A classic theorem of Weyl says a polynomial with an irrational slope spreads its fractional parts evenly. Ethan Ackelsberg proves a function field version of that statement in this 2025 paper. Function fields swap the real numbers for ratios of polynomials, a parallel world with its own arithmetic. The result had been conjectured by Lê, Liu, and Wooley.

Ackelsberg confirms their conjecture in full. The paper is short and proof-centered, with the abstract stating the claim and its source. Such equidistribution results say that polynomial sequences leave no corner of the unit interval favored. They feed into number theory questions about counting and randomness in arithmetic settings. A function field analog matters because many rational-number problems have cleaner twins in that world. The proof closes an open case named by three other researchers.
arxiv-2509-18889:
Survey pipelines mislabel spectra, and those mistakes can hide rare objects in plain sight. Helmut Meusinger mines one such error pile in this 2025 paper. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey pipeline had tagged about four thousand spectra as quasars at very high redshift. He re-examined all of them by hand and by class.

After dropping poor spectra and three special plates, the true picture emerged. Only about a quarter were really quasars at that distance. Half were quasars at lower redshift, and the rest split between galaxies and stars. Many of the misfits proved unusual and were reassigned to rare types. The results are gathered into a catalogue. The study is a reminder that automated labels at the extremes are shaky. It also shows error piles are treasure pools for odd objects.
arxiv-2509-19289: Ilya V. Vyugin, writing alone, studies solutions of the Markoff-Hurwitz equation when arithmetic is done modulo a prime. Equations of this kind generalize the classic Markoff equation, whose whole-number solutions form a well-known tree. He proves that almost all solutions over the residue field can be reached from one another. A chain of natural transformations does the connecting, so the solution set is nearly one family. The paper also examines recurrence sequences taken modulo a prime. The abstract is brief, and this summary stays close to it.
arxiv-2509-19489:
Firms often ask a language model the same prompt many times and blend the replies to gain trust in the result. Robert Nowak studies how to judge that self-agreement under a fixed budget of calls. His short note weighs two uses of the budget: more distinct prompts, or more repeats of each prompt. The math treats the total as the product of those two counts.

The analysis favors a rough even split, with each count near the square root of the budget. Spending all calls on repeats of a few prompts wastes information. Spreading them too thin leaves agreement untested. The note gives builders a simple rule for planning tests. It also frames agreement itself as a thing that can be measured with care, not just assumed.
arxiv-2509-19889:
Cancer risk maps at town level can mislead when sharp local jumps are smoothed away. G. Santafé, A. Adin, and M. D. Ugarte build a two-step method that respects those jumps. A fast scan-statistic search first finds clusters of towns with unlike risk. A greedy hunt inside the scan window keeps the search feasible over large domains.

The found clusters then enter a Bayesian space-time model as explicit discontinuities. Applied to cancer mortality across mainland Spain, the method beat a standard tool at cluster detection. Model fit and risk accuracy improved by several standard criteria. Public health teams use such maps to target screening and study causes. Honoring real boundaries keeps hot spots visible instead of averaged away.
arxiv-2509-19989:
Directed graphs, where edges run one way, resist the curvature tools built for symmetric networks. Shuliang Bai and three co-authors define Ricci flow for weighted directed graphs. The flow evolves edge weights while preserving distances, and solutions exist and are unique, they prove. A node-wise balancing factor tunes the tug between inflow and outflow, capturing asymmetry directly.

A discrete version of the flow runs on real machines. Numerical studies test the machinery. Ricci flow on undirected graphs already serves community detection and representation learning. Extending it to directed settings covers citation webs, traffic, and follower networks as they are. The balancing factor is the design's signature: direction is information, and the flow now respects it.
arxiv-2509-20089:
Yahya Mohammadi and three co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on gravity theory. They work inside the local limit of nonlocal gravity, a theory that modifies Einstein's general relativity. The change adds a scalar field that measures how strongly spacetime responds to matter. The paper asks whether the classic Schwarzschild solution still solves the modified equations.

They show that Schwarzschild spacetime is an exact solution when the new scalar stays constant. Its mass is then the general relativity mass divided by a factor set by that constant. Reading the solution as a black hole fails, though. Key torsion measures blow up at the Schwarzschild horizon.
