The result maps both where the modified theory agrees with Einstein and where it parts ways.
arxiv-2509-20389:
Growth that saturates, like a population nearing its limit, is classically described by the logistic equation. M. O. Aibinu, A. Shoukat, and F. M. Mahomed generalize that model in a 2025 arXiv paper aimed at industrial modeling. Real growth often remembers its past, which the classical equation cannot express. Their version adds memory in two ways.

Fractional derivatives of Atangana-Baleanu type in the Caputo sense supply the memory effect. A proportional time delay adds a second, explicit lag. Free parameters let the model bend toward complex growth in industrial, medical, and social systems. The authors solve it with a hybrid Sumudu variational method that yields semi-analytical solutions efficiently. Their results chart how fractional order and delay jointly reshape the growth curve.
arxiv-2509-20789:
Models learn better from little data when their built-in assumptions match the task. Qiyu Chen and Guozhang Chen study that match for state space models in a 2025 paper listed for NeurIPS 2026. State space models process sequences, but their inductive bias is usually fixed and task-blind.

The authors describe the bias of a linear time-invariant state space model through a kernel the model implies. They show, in theory and in experiments, that a misaligned bias forces the model to spend samples unlearning its own prior. Their framework then aligns the bias with the task structure. The goal is data-efficient generalization, learning more from less at a time when high-quality data is running short.
arxiv-2509-21089:
Spectrometers on space telescopes need gratings that split light finely in a small package. Dhwanil Patel and four co-authors design one in a 2025 paper published in Optics Express. Their grating sits immersed in silicon, a high-index medium that boosts resolving power inside a compact device.

Standard immersed gratings use blazed profiles. Those work best at one design wavelength and react strongly to the light's polarization. The team instead shapes a pattern of sub-wavelength structures with an evolutionary search algorithm. The test case targets the third short-wave infrared band. The metagrating aims for high diffraction efficiency across the band with less polarization dependence. Such designs could shrink and sharpen future spectrometers for astronomy and Earth observation.
arxiv-2509-21189:
People entering an unfamiliar office building read signs, spot landmarks, and ask for directions instead of searching every room. Bhargav Chandaka and five co-authors give robots the same strategy in ReasonNav, a 2025 paper for the CoRL 2025 conference. Existing robot navigation lacks those human-like skills and searches inefficiently.

ReasonNav is a modular system built around a vision-language model. Compact input and output abstractions, framed in terms of navigation landmarks, let the model focus on understanding and reasoning rather than raw control. The robot can interpret signage and decide when to seek information, cutting wasted wandering in large buildings. The work targets real indoor spaces designed for people, where the environment itself is full of guidance cues.
arxiv-2509-21389:
Keeping attack detection private across many sites is the theme of a 2025 survey by Devashish Chaudhary and 2 co-authors. Federated learning trains a shared model without centralizing sensitive traffic data. That fits network intrusion detection, where traffic cannot be pooled freely. The survey maps how federated methods are tailored to intrusion detection in depth.

Coverage spans architectures, deployment strategies, protocols, and aggregation methods. Privacy preserving techniques and model compression are examined in detail. Attack specific solutions cover denial of service floods, man in the middle attacks, and botnets. A pioneering section treats quantum federated learning. It covers quantum feature encoding and quantum machine learning algorithms for detection. The goal is clear: spot attacks fast, keep raw traffic at each site, and share just the learned model. It stays local by design, and that is the point of the whole survey.
arxiv-2509-21689:
Autoregressive protein making is powerful but slow, since each token waits for the last. Thomas Walton and 3 co-authors speed it up with biologically guided speculative decoding in a 2025 paper. A draft model proposes tokens and a target model verifies them. Protein draft models usually ignore form and functional constraints. Implausible outputs and shifted odds follow.

SpecMER guides drafting with k-mer motifs extracted from multiple sequence alignments. K-mers are short sequence fragments that carry biological signal. Candidate series are scored in parallel, and promising ones are selected. Form and functional priors enter the decoding loop directly. Fast protein making for high throughput screening is the goal, without abandoning biological plausibility.
arxiv-2509-21889:
Judging a language model by answer correctness alone misses how the exchange actually feels. Yijin Guo and seven co-authors present QoNext in this 2025 paper, the first frame that brings Quality of Experience thinking to human-AI interaction. That idea comes from networking and media, where speed and smoothness shape satisfaction. With chat models, how fast text appears and how it pauses can matter as much as what it says.

The team lists the experience factors that shape satisfaction, then runs controlled studies in simulated chats. Human ratings were gathered under many service setups, from quick and smooth to slow and uneven. From those studies they built a database and trained a neural predictor. The predictor estimates how a user will feel from measurable system settings alone. The authors say the model uncovers what drives satisfaction and predicts it well across varied conditions.
arxiv-2509-21989:
Generated portraits of the same person often drift: a face changes subtly from one image to the next. Abdelrahman Eldesokey, Aleksandar Cvejic, Bernard Ghanem, and Peter Wonka present a way to catch that drift in this 2025 paper, a NeurIPS spotlight. Their starting point is the inside of a pre-trained image generator, which holds both meaning-based and purely visual features, tangled together.

The team built an automatic pipeline that makes image pairs with labeled matches of both kinds, using existing subject-driven generation data. A contrastive network then learns to separate the visual features from the semantic ones. From the separated features they define a new score, Visual Semantic Matching, which measures visual inconsistency. The score beat global comparison methods based on popular vision models. It can also point to where in the image the inconsistency sits, which the authors say is a first for this task.
arxiv-2509-22289: Ken Nagai, writing alone, introduces a family of functionals. They generalize the Euler-Mascheroni constant, one of the classical constants of analysis. His short 2025 note defines regularized functionals. They are built from weighted sums of Clausen-type trigonometric sums. The classical constant appears as a special case. Nagai gives explicit integral formulas for the family. He also gives differential relations and ladder relations that connect its members. An umbral generating function packages the whole family in one object.
arxiv-2509-22489:
Jaouhar Slimi, Tristan Le Gall, and Augustin Lemesle extract readable automata from recurrent neural networks. Such extraction shows what language a network has learned, but large or infinite alphabets break older tools. Their passive method watches network behavior rather than probing it with chosen inputs. It blends overapproximation methods from abstract interpretation with passive learning from grammatical inference.

First, they compared their tool with the best known extractor on networks trained on classic Tomita grammars. Then they moved to regular languages with infinite alphabets. They propose those languages as a new benchmark for the field. The results show extraction can reach cases that were out of bounds before.
arxiv-2509-22689:
Ha-Hieu Pham and 4 co-authors enforce shape-level consistency when segmenting tissue images with few labels. In pathology, dense annotations are costly, so semi-supervised methods must learn from mostly unlabeled slides. Pixel-level consistency can spread noisy pseudo-labels and yield broken, topologically wrong masks. Their framework, Topology Graph Consistency, adds graph-theoretic constraints on top.

Prediction graphs are aligned with reference graphs on three traits: Laplacian spectra, component counts, and adjacency statistics. That alignment enforces global topology, not just local agreement. On the GlaS and CRAG benchmarks, the method reached state-of-the-art results with only five to ten percent supervision. It also narrowed the gap to full supervision by a wide margin.
arxiv-2509-22789:
Debosmita Pathak leads a large team that weighed eighteen thousand star-forming regions across nineteen nearby galaxies. The data combine JWST, Hubble, and ground and radio telescopes from the PHANGS survey. For each HII region, they measured young stars, ionized gas, and older disk stars at ten-parsec scales. Lower-resolution data added the molecular and atomic gas, plus swept-up shell material.

Older stars dominate the mass at those scales, while ionized gas outweighs young stars in most bright regions. Star-formation efficiencies per region ran from about six to seventeen percent. Most bright regions are over-pressured and likely expanding. Self-gravity takes over only at much larger scales, and the ambient pressure always dominates on region scales.
arxiv-2509-22889:
Sets of images can share a theme while each image looks quite distinct. Federico Chinello and Giacomo Boracchi design the Convolutional Set Transformer, or CST, for such sets. Older set networks take plain vectors, so a separate image model must first turn each image into numbers. CST works on the raw image tensors instead, learning traits and cross-image links at the same time.

That joint design beat older tools on set classification and set anomaly detection. CST also works with Grad-CAM, a tool that shows which image parts drove a choice. The pair pre-trained CST on ImageNet and adapted it to new tasks. They release the trained model, called CST-15, for other researchers.
arxiv-2509-22989:
Language models can persuade people about as well as humans can, which brings both promise and risk. Zirui Cheng and Jiaxuan You build a theory-led test bed for that skill. They ground the work in Bayesian persuasion theory. Human persuasion data sets become arenas where models act as strategic persuaders. Scores measure how much a model gains by shaping what others learn.

Top models earned high persuasion gains and used tactics that match theory. The pair then trained models with reinforcement learning inside these arenas. Even small models raised their gains a lot after training. The setup gives a scalable way to study machine persuasion.
arxiv-2509-23089:
Network foundation models promise broad skill, but their hidden knowledge is rarely inspected. Sylee Beltiukov and 4 co-authors audit four such models on five network data sets. Their review has three parts. One checks how the embedding space is used. One compares hidden features with expert domain features. One tests causal sensitivity to protocol changes.

All four models showed strong anisotropy, meaning codes bunch in narrow directions. Feature sensitivity was inconsistent across models. None separated high-level context or payload dependence cleanly. Fixing the flagged flaws lifted scores a lot without architecture changes. The study maps where these models still fall short.
arxiv-2509-23389:
Factories merging IT and control networks need management that adapts faster than static rules allow. Tuğçe Bilen and Mehmet Ozdem present a modular framework on knowledge-defined networking. Four modules form a closed loop. A telemetry collector watches the system, and a knowledge builder extracts context. A decision engine weighs actions, and a control enforcer applies them.

A graph abstraction holds the system state for the loop. Utility optimization guides choices under changing conditions. Three metrics judge the design: decision latency, control effectiveness, and system stability. Results show gains in resilience and response speed. Programmable endpoints across the plant receive the policies.
arxiv-2509-23489:
Virtual reality headsets drain power on bright displays, yet the eye adapts to slow color shifts without noticing. Ethan Chen and 3 co-authors exploit that trait of chromatic adaptation to save power on OLED screens. Their method needs no gaze tracking. A new test setup models how the viewer's adaptation state follows the scene's light color over time.

From that model they compute a shift path for the scene light that cuts power while staying inside a set budget for visible loss. Gradual shifts looked far better than the instant shifts of prior work. Paired with brightness dimming from earlier work, the method cut display power by about a third with no measured drop in perceived quality.
arxiv-2509-23989:
A fluid pressing on an elastic body sets up a coupled dance whose long-term fate depends on the body's shape. Karoline Disser, the sole author, extends work by Avalos and Triggiani on the fluid-elastic semigroup for the coupled Stokes-Lame system. That semigroup was known to be strongly stable when the structure's domain is not a bad domain, in a precise geometric sense. Disser handles the bad domains.

For them, the dynamics split into a strongly stable part plus a pressure wave, a special solution fixed by the starting values, which fully characterizes long-run behavior. She also shows that being a bad domain is equivalent to the Schiffer problem, tying the question to geometric analysis.
arxiv-2509-24189:
Ask a model what a user likes and it will name the popular picks, while niche tastes vanish. Luyang Zhang and 6 co-authors built SPECTRA to recover the full spread of preferences. Instead of generating one ranked list, it probes the tuned model's output distribution over clear preference categories.

On movie, review, and short-video data, SPECTRA matched the true spread of tastes far better than list generation. It raised the exposure of long-tail categories and helped tail-taste users more than head-taste users. Rankings built from its distributions also improved a lot on public data. In a live deployment test, long-tail ranking improved several-fold against a head-tuned production system.
arxiv-2509-24489:
Learning a constraint model from examples can overfit, inventing global rules that the true model never had. Vasileios Balafas and 3 co-authors built a hybrid acquisition framework to fight that failure. Passive learning drafts candidate constraints first. A query-driven phase then refines them, using confidence scores seeded by machine learning priors to hunt the over-fitted ones.

A subset exploration step rescues valid parts from rejected candidates, and a final active phase ensures completeness. On diverse benchmarks, the interactive refinement proved crucial for coverage and accuracy from few examples. Query counts stayed manageable. The design targets robust modeling where data is scarce.
arxiv-2510-00489:
Alihan Hadimlioglu and Siddharth Linga published this 2025 paper on interfaces that read a user's face and adapt in real time. Static screens ignore mood, yet emotion shapes how people judge software. Their system, Face2Feel, watches expressions through a webcam or built-in camera. Image processing, face recognition, and emotion detection then personalize the interface on the fly.

A case study built an emotion-based book recommendation system on the framework. Recommendations shifted with the reader's detected feelings during the session. After trying the working model, surveyed users responded with clear enthusiasm. Nearly eighty-six percent called such systems very engaging and user-friendly. The authors see demand extending to chatbots, banking sites, and corporate help pages. They frame emotion-aware design as a route to comfort and satisfaction in daily computing.
arxiv-2510-00889:
Shpilrain surveys recent progress on automorphic orbits in free groups in this 2025 arXiv paper, written for a volume honoring Alexei Myasnikov. Free groups sit at the heart of combinatorial group theory, and their automorphisms connect algebra with topology, geometry, and dynamics. An automorphic orbit collects every image of one group element under all possible automorphisms. Whitehead began studying these orbits in classical work nearly a century ago.

The survey covers counting problems, including how many potentially positive elements appear at a given length. It also reviews the complexity of Whitehead's automorphism problem under worst-case, average-case, and generic-case measures. A further topic is orbit-blocking words, elements whose orbits avoid certain patterns. Shpilrain ties these threads together as a progress report for researchers entering the area.
arxiv-2510-01189:
De Ninno, Inverardi, and Belotti use a role-playing game plus a language model to learn what moral choices people actually make. Laws set hard limits, but daily behavior follows softer personal preferences that surveys capture poorly. Immersive stories about digital privacy let players reveal those preferences through action.

A customized model, nicknamed the GPT Anthropologist, interprets the session data afterward. Cross-validation showed richer stories and better interpretive framing both sharpen behavior prediction. The approach suits early software design, where value conflicts surface before products harden. Automated interpretation makes a slow ethnographic method fast enough for engineering teams. Anthropology supplies the fieldwork stance that requirements interviews lack. Digital privacy scenarios gave the games their ethical charge. Prediction of situated choices beats asking for abstract principles. Software teams gain a window into values before building. Context, in this account, is the data.
arxiv-2510-01389:
Karli, Shangguan, and Fitzgerald teach robot brains to know when they are out of their depth and ask a human for help. Vision-language-action models generalize impressively, yet they plow ahead through situations they cannot read. Their framework, INSIGHT, mines the model's own token stream for doubt.

Entropy, log-probability, and uncertainty decompositions flow from every generated token. Compact transformer classifiers read those sequences and fire help triggers at the right moments. Watching uncertainty evolve over time beat any static summary score decisively. Dense human labels work best, but cheap weak labels remain competitive when annotation is scarce. Aleatoric and epistemic doubt are separated, since they call for different remedies. Out-of-distribution tasks stress the trigger where it matters most. Real-time checks confirm the introspection keeps pace with action. Help-seeking becomes a learned skill for robots, not an add-on alarm.
arxiv-2510-01589:
Schaefer and Myers close a four-decade timing campaign on U Scorpii, another recurrent nova once cast as a future supernova. The star's white dwarf sits near the critical mass and feeds quickly, which made the candidacy plausible. Everything depends on whether eruptions remove more mass than feeding replaces.

Eclipse timings gathered since 1989 measure how the orbital period jumped across eruptions. The ejected mass comes out about twenty-six times the mass accreted between outbursts. Older emission-line estimates carried errors of a hundredfold or more, which the timing method avoids. The dwarf is losing ground, so no supernova awaits. Amateur observers supplied much of the photometry across the four decades. Space telescope data from TESS sharpened the recent eclipse timings. A factor of twenty-six leaves no room for optimistic bookkeeping. Prototype status made the negative verdict especially consequential. Archives made the answer possible.
arxiv-2510-01889:
Da Silva Barros and three co-authors argue that choosing smaller models can cut AI's energy bill in this 2025 paper. The field's habit says bigger models are always better, whatever the power cost. The authors push the opposite slogan, that small is often sufficient. Their lever is model selection at inference time, which needs no new hardware or architectures.

They surveyed popular models on hubs like Hugging Face and Papers with Code. Across several tasks, they measured how usefulness grows as model size increases. The gains shrank steadily with size, leaving a fat margin where smaller models do nearly as well. Picking the smallest adequate model exploits that margin directly. The authors frame this as energy sobriety that practitioners can adopt today. It complements efficiency work on chips and training with a simple deployment habit.
arxiv-2510-02089:
Chen and eight co-authors build efficient couplers between optical fibers and lithium niobate on sapphire chips in this 2025 photonics paper. The LNOS platform promises wide transparency, strong nonlinearity, and powerful electro-optic effects for integrated circuits. Grating couplers are the standard bridge, but none existed for this platform.

Their design uses a self-imaging grating with fixed period and a linearly shrinking fill factor. That shape diffracts light at a negative angle matched to fiber arrays and suppresses higher orders. Simulations predicted forty-two percent coupling efficiency at the telecom wavelength. Fabricated devices on a thin X-cut lithium niobate film were tested with a fiber array on a precision stage. Measured single-end efficiency exceeded twenty percent, confirming the design works. The result unlocks practical LNOS circuits for information processing, sensing, and nonlinear optics.
arxiv-2510-02289:
Jiang, Monserrat, and Ku propose a fresh origin story for charge order in certain metals. Their 2025 physics paper challenges the standard account. Charge order means electrons settle into a repeating uneven pattern. The usual story blames a wobble of the Fermi surface. That story works well for good metals. It fits poorly for ionic materials with strong local forces. The authors suggest a different driver. Long-lived Frenkel excitons, which are tight bound pairs of charge, can freeze into a crystal-like array. That freezing itself creates the charge pattern.

They test the idea on kagome superconductors, a family named for its woven lattice. The model reproduces local charge links seen in experiments. It also matches the long-range order in cesium vanadium antimony compounds. It further explains distinct patterns in a related scandium compound. One mechanism thus covers cases the old story split apart.
arxiv-2510-02589:
Huang and co-authors benchmark five reinforcement learning methods on container ship loading. Their 2025 operations paper studies the stowage planning problem. Loading containers decides how fast ports turn ships around. Bad plans force reshuffles during the voyage. Human planners have carried this puzzle for decades. The team built a Gym environment capturing the core task. A crane scheduling layer extends it in two forms. Five algorithms then faced scenarios of rising complexity. Value based and actor methods both entered the contest.

Simple scenarios left all five methods close together. Complexity pried their performance far apart. A2C and the value based methods degraded badly at scale. PPO stayed strong across the harder settings. TRPO took the best results in the toughest cases. Formulation choices mattered more as settings grew complex. Ports gain a reusable test bed for planning research. Algorithm choice deserves care before any deployment.
arxiv-2510-02689:
Zhang, writing for the STAR Collaboration, images the shape of uranium nuclei from collision debris. Their 2025 nuclear physics paper reports measurements at the RHIC collider. Nuclear shape steers the plasma born in heavy collisions. Flow patterns carry fingerprints of that starting geometry. The team collided uranium with uranium at high energy. Gold on gold collisions supplied the comparison system. They measured elliptic flow and momentum fluctuations. Correlations between flow and momentum added another handle. Central collisions showed the clearest differences between systems.

Hydrodynamic models pointed to strongly deformed uranium nuclei. The result agrees with older low-energy experiments. A small break from axial symmetry also appeared. The method images ground state shapes at collider energies. It links nuclear structure across very different energy scales. Other nuclei can now get the same imaging treatment. Quark-gluon plasma studies gain better starting conditions.
arxiv-2510-02789:
Seo and co-authors at KAIST take on a hard problem in medical imaging. One detector must find lesions in scans of very different kinds. The mix can include chest X-rays, CT scans, MRI scans, and pathology slides. Each kind has its own look and its own statistics. A single model trained on the mix usually loses accuracy.

Their fix adds small text-based tokens that name the scan type. A new attention step, called MoCA, blends those tokens into the detector queries. A short pre-training stage, called QueryREPA, then tunes the queries to fit their scan type. The pair raised detection scores across all four scan types. The cost was tiny, and the base detector stayed the same. That makes the method easy to adopt in real clinics.
arxiv-2510-02889:
Doostmohammadian, Ramesh, and Aghasi make group optimization survive slow messages. Many agents share one task in distributed optimization. Each agent holds part of the data or the cost. They swap updates over network links as they work. Real links add delays, and delays differ by link. Most older methods assume instant or uniform timing. This team handles mixed, fixed delays that stay within a bound.

Their method rests on an augmented consensus design. Extra state variables absorb the effect of late arrivals. The network may be directed, so links can run one way. It must merely stay strongly connected overall. Proofs draw on matrix theory and algebraic graph theory. They show the group still reaches the true optimum. Simulations back the proofs with live runs. The method runs beside delay-free rivals without breaking down. Open work includes finding the largest delay the scheme can take.
arxiv-2510-02989:
Hori and co-authors recover hidden phase patterns using an event camera. Phase retrieval means rebuilding a wave's phase from brightness alone. A classic route uses how brightness changes along the light axis. Measuring that change fast and steadily is the hard part. An event sensor reports brightness jumps pixel by pixel. It works over a huge range of light levels.

The team slides the sensor along the axis to create defocus. Each slide logs events where brightness shifted. They derive a new equation, the transport of event equation. It links those events to the phase in a linear way. Fast Fourier methods then solve for the phase at once. Tests showed the sensor beat a normal camera on speed and stability. Accurate phase maps came through in those hard conditions. The method should strengthen adaptive optics for astronomy and microscopy.
arxiv-2510-03089:
Devulapally and co-authors shield personal images from AI copycats. A few photos now suffice to teach a model someone's face. Owners may not want their pictures used that way. Poisoned training images can block the lesson. Older poisons worked in pixel space and left visible noise. This method works in the latent space of diffusion models instead. It shifts the path that the denoising process follows.

The shift alternates between denoising and inversion steps. A small network crafts the perturbation for each image. The result looks nearly identical to the original photo. Downstream models, though, fail to invert or copy it. Four benchmark data sets tested the defense. Perceptual quality scores rose by a clear margin over pixel methods. Robustness across five attack settings rose as well. Even a strong purifier called DiffPure could not wash the guard away.
arxiv-2510-03189:
Ndir, Pfefferle, and Schirrmeister train a medical image segmenter that learns from simulated clicks. Interactive segmentation lets a user correct outlines step by step. Three-dimensional scans make that loop costly to train. Their strategy generates prompts dynamically during training. It mimics how real users box and click to fix errors. Content-aware cropping focuses the encoder where it matters. One graphics card sufficed for the whole regimen.

Training started from public nnInteractive weights, a strong base. A foundation-model competition supplied the test arena. The system reached solid average overlap scores overall. Well-initialized cases scored far higher across several modalities. Microscopy, PET, and ultrasound all cleared a high bar there. One weakness stood out sharply in the results. Missing bounding boxes caused accuracy to collapse. Clicks alone could not rescue a cold start. Robust initialization is therefore the key open problem.
arxiv-2510-03289:
Researchers at WhaleTech.ai wrote a 2025 arXiv paper that asks why mask diffusion language models fail to deliver their main promise. These models are meant to write text in parallel, filling in many words at once. They should also use context from both sides of a sentence. The authors test whether open mask diffusion systems really do either of those things in practice.

Their tests show that the models fall back on simple word by word guessing. Predictions shrink to basic word odds, so words picked side by side do not fit together well. In effect, the writing process turns into the same step by step method the models were meant to replace. The team then offers training and use tricks that work better with this limit. The lesson guides future work toward designs that truly write in parallel.
arxiv-2510-03389:
Jäger, Elsässer, and Torabian present a 2025 arXiv paper on teaching quantum computers to build their data encodings with less quantum effort. Quantum machine learning turns classical data into qubit states through circuits called feature maps. Searching for circuits normally burns quantum time on trial runs. Their method, Q-FLAIR, shifts most of that search onto a classical computer. Small analytic rebuilds of the model let each trial gate be judged without new quantum runs.

Built into both a quantum neural network and a quantum kernel classifier, the method matched benchmark scores in the study. It then trained a model on a real IBM quantum device in only four hours. That model scored above ninety percent on full resolution handwritten digit data with hundreds of features, a scale earlier methods could not reach on hardware. Cheaper circuit search brings quantum learning closer to real tasks on today's machines.
arxiv-2510-03589:
Bhardwaj, Balashankar, and Subramanian present a 2025 arXiv paper introducing FieldFormer, a transformer that rebuilds physical fields from sparse sensor readings. Weather, pollution, and fluid fields are known through a few noisy sensors, and older methods either ignore the equations or fail to scale. FieldFormer gathers a neighborhood for each query point using a velocity scaled distance. An expectation maximization loop refines those neighborhoods as the scales evolve. Physics enters through equation residuals and boundary penalties computed by automatic differentiation.

On three benchmarks, covering heat flow, shallow water, and a pollution simulation, FieldFormer beat baselines by more than forty percent. It stayed accurate with sensors covering under two percent of the field and noise at ten percent. Errors stayed below one hundredth in root mean square terms. City air monitors and river gauges produce this sparse data. Better reconstruction means better forecasts and faster warnings from the sensors that already exist.
arxiv-2510-03889:
Yao wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in theoretical physics, on symmetries that change across a crystal lattice. Ordinary symmetries act the same everywhere, but modulated ones are twisted by translations through space. Such symmetries help classify exotic phases of quantum matter. Yao seeks a general language for them in one space dimension, including the newer non-invertible kind.

The paper describes these symmetries using tensor networks, a standard tool for quantum lattice systems. The twisting is captured by special maps, called autoequivalences, between mathematical categories. Although modulation breaks the usual topological behavior, Yao still builds a bulk theory, assembled by inserting domain walls between regions. The framework recovers known results for the simpler invertible cases. It also extends them to the general setting. The work gives physicists a unified way to handle modulated symmetries and the phases they protect.
arxiv-2510-04189:
Panda and Bhatnagar present this 2025 arXiv paper giving the first finite-time guarantees for a natural critic-actor algorithm under safety constraints. Actor-critic methods dominate reinforcement learning, but their convergence theory often lags practice. A recent critic-actor variant for discounted problems received only asymptotic analysis. Nothing covered the natural-gradient version with function approximation, average costs, and inequality constraints together.

The authors introduce exactly that algorithm for the long-run average cost setting. Their non-asymptotic analysis establishes optimal learning rates for the iterates. They also propose a modification that improves the sample complexity further. Experiments on three Safety-Gym environments show the algorithm competing well against established baselines. Finite-time guarantees matter most where constraints encode safety limits that agents must respect during learning itself. This work closes a theoretical gap for constrained, natural actor-critic methods.
arxiv-2510-04389:
Faye Jackson wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the hidden size of a symmetry group. The setting is a Lefschetz fibration, a way of viewing a four dimensional shape as a family of surfaces over a sphere. Each such map has a group of braids that can be lifted to symmetries of the whole shape. Jackson asked how large that braid group is inside the full braid group of the sphere.

 For genus one fibrations, the gap is infinite. The same holds for maps built by gluing a fibration to itself when the genus is two or more. It also holds for a class of complex genus two maps whose special curves do not separate the surface. For genus one, she links the braid group to a character variety from algebra. The work sharpens tools that topologists use to tell four dimensional shapes apart.
arxiv-2510-04489:
Jiachen Xu, Jian Qian, and Zijun Gao wrote this 2025 paper on designing experiments with many treatment levels. Dose trials and online tests often compare several treatments against one control group. In practice, analysts first pick a winning treatment, then estimate the effect of that winner alone. Standard designs ignore that two step habit and waste budget. The team built a design, named MUSE, around the habit itself.

MUSE sets one objective that balances picking the right winner and estimating its effect well. It then assigns subjects to treatments and control by optimizing that objective under a budget. The authors prove finite sample guarantees for the design. In the long run, their allocation matches the classic Neyman allocation for the best treatment. Simulations and a real data study favored MUSE over standard alternatives on both tasks. The work matters wherever trials are costly and the winner is what counts.
arxiv-2510-04689:
Chengwei Liu and six coauthors wrote this 2025 roadmap paper on a self improving system for software threat intelligence. Attack warnings no longer arrive only through official databases and vendor notices. Signs now surface in blogs, forums, code repositories, social posts, and underground communities. Channels struggle to keep up, and their records arrive late or incomplete. The authors propose Evolaris, a platform of cooperating software agents. Each agent owns one job in a workflow.

The jobs cover finding new signals, reasoning over them, filling gaps, checking claims, and flagging risks. Agents share context, so the system learns from each round and refines its knowledge base. Over time it should adapt to threat patterns on its own. The roadmap argues this design improves precision, speed, and scale together. Security teams drown in scattered reports and need that combination. The paper lays out the architecture and research path rather than a product.
arxiv-2510-05089:
Amira Abbas, Yanlin Chen, Tuyen Nguyen, and Ronald de Wolf speed up a classic learning trick with quantum computing in this 2025 arXiv paper. Boosting combines many weak classifiers into one strong one. Each weak learner only needs to beat random guessing slightly. Classical boosting is well understood but still costs time.

Their algorithm, QuantumBoost, computes key projection steps on a quantum computer. It also borrows a lazy strategy from convex optimization, projecting rarely instead of every round. Together the two ideas give the best known runtime among boosting methods. The authors prove the lazy schedule still reaches tiny training error. QuantumBoost is the first boosting algorithm, classical or quantum, to make lazy projections work.
arxiv-2510-05189:
Maksym Zavhorodnii, Dmytro Dehtiarov, and Anna Konovalenko sort AI fabrications into types in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language models hallucinate in different ways, from subtle distortions to wholesale invention. Treating every error alike makes detection harder. A good taxonomy could guide targeted defenses for medicine, law, and finance.

The authors build a classification framework around the geometry of model outputs. In their experiments, different hallucination types formed separable clusters in a reduced-dimensional space. That separation held across sample sizes and random seeds. They also measure distances between correct-answer clusters and each hallucination cluster. Such a classifier could anchor practical detectors in industry settings. The distances may even hint at deeper semantic differences between hallucination kinds.
arxiv-2510-05389:
Robert Hołyst and five co-authors extend thermodynamics to fluids that keep moving in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classical thermodynamics assumes equilibrium, with no macroscopic motion at all. Their global non-equilibrium framework covers stationary states instead. They apply it to Rayleigh-Bénard convection, the rolling flow in a fluid heated from below.

The theory folds macroscopic kinetic energy into the global energy balance. A new potential, built from the inertial term of the flow, acts as a state function. It determines the direction of spontaneous changes between stationary states. The external work needed for a transition depends only on the endpoints, not the path. The authors expect the same potential to appear across many hydrodynamic problems.
arxiv-2510-05489:
Batley and Saha question a basic habit in training neural networks. Training normally proceeds through many small update steps, each guided by a local gradient. That step-by-step pattern dates back to work by Cauchy and Newton. Their 2025 paper asks whether a well-built model could jump straight to the best answer.

Their method, Infinite Descent, rewrites training as one direct equation for the update step. The trick works only for models with a special closed structure. The authors design such a model, called AION, to meet that requirement. In a simple test problem, AION reached the optimum in a single step. The authors call that wider family the Infinity Class. The paper also sets out clear membership conditions for the class. If the idea scales, it could point toward learning without long chains of small steps.
arxiv-2510-05689:
Ahmadi and Tahmasebi compute option sensitivities under a self-exciting jump model. The delta measures how an option's price moves with its underlying asset. Here the asset follows a Hawkes jump-diffusion, where jumps excite further jumps. Their 2025 paper derives the delta through Malliavin calculus.

Stochastic jump intensity is the central complication for the hedge formula. The authors relate integrals under the Hawkes process to an associated Poisson process. That bridge yields a new duality between Skorokhod integrals and Malliavin derivatives. From it, they build a Wiener-Poisson weight for the delta. Controlling exponential moments of the Hawkes solution makes the machinery rigorous. The formula covers both European and exotic Asian options. Monte Carlo tests check the weight's convergence in practice. Numerical simulations compare it against exact solutions and finite differences. Reliable deltas keep hedging books balanced when markets jump.
arxiv-2510-06289:
Hepworth and a large collaboration report a new ultracold neutron guide-coating facility at the University of Winnipeg in a 2025 instrumentation paper. Ultracold neutrons move so slowly that coated tubes can transport and store them for precision experiments. Diamond-like carbon is prized because it reflects these neutrons well, absorbs few, and rarely flips their spin.

The facility uses pulsed laser deposition to coat cylindrical guides up to one meter long. A first full-length aluminum guide and flange received carbon films measured by X-ray reflectometry. The guide's film reached an optical potential of two hundred nano-electronvolts, with no delamination. Adding a plume collimator and ion-probe feedback raised it to about two hundred forty, though that film adhered poorly. The results set the facility's baseline. Future work targets richer diamond content and stronger adhesion, supplying guides for the TUCAN experiment at TRIUMF.
arxiv-2510-06389:
Zanardi, Dallas, and Andreadakis introduce mereological quantum phase transitions in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Standard phase transitions track changes in a system's state. Their concept tracks changes in subsystem structure itself, asking how a system best divides into parts.

The framework varies the operator algebras that define tensor product structures. A scrambling score picks the structure with least scrambling for each Hamiltonian parameter. Pulling the information-geometric metric back to parameter space defines an algebra susceptibility. Its singularities in the thermodynamic limit mark the transitions. Worked examples involve quantum coherence and operator entanglement. Spin-chain simulations test the idea in code. The susceptibility responds sharply at an integrability point and grows across disorder-induced localization. Those signatures suggest critical reshuffles of emergent subsystems where physics expects change. The concept reframes phases as properties of parthood, not only of states.
arxiv-2510-06789:
Haoran Zhang and Yunxiao Chen combine many people's rankings into one fair overall ranking. Their 2025 paper studies rank aggregation from raters who score items in several ways. Classic models, like Bradley-Terry, assume every rater's tastes follow one neat formula. Real raters differ wildly, and those models can fail badly.

Their method, called MASTER, makes no such parametric assumption. It follows a maximum score approach borrowed from robust regression work. The authors prove the method is consistent, with ranking errors vanishing as the number of raters grows. Its error bounds nearly match the best possible ones in some regimes. The optimization is provably hard in the worst case, as expected. Simulations tell a friendlier story in practice. The algorithm stays robust and produces high-quality rankings. It beats existing methods when raters are highly diverse. It also stays competitive when the classic models happen to be exactly right.
arxiv-2510-06889:
Zaid Alyafeai, Maged Al-Shaibani, and Bernard Ghanem build small models that pull bibliographic details out of scientific papers. Their 2025 paper presents MeXtract, a family of lightweight language models for metadata extraction. Titles, authors, and venues must be harvested accurately to index the literature. Rule-based tools break whenever journals change their formats or schemas.

The models range from half a billion to three billion parameters, fine-tuned from Qwen 2.5 bases. Training used data distilled from a much larger teacher model, plus preference optimization. On the MOLE benchmark, MeXtract reached the best scores in its size class. The team extended that benchmark with model-specific metadata as a harder, out-of-domain test. Training on one schema transferred surprisingly well to schemas never seen. That robustness matters for libraries facing hundreds of publisher formats. All code, data, and models are released openly for the community.
arxiv-2510-06989:
Pengyue Yang and five co-authors redesign the documentation that ships with AI models. Their 2025 paper introduces CRAI-MCF, a framework for responsible AI model cards. Model cards today are inconsistent, incomplete, and hard to compare across platforms. Users cannot easily judge which specialized model fits their needs or risks.

The framework organizes documentation into eight modules holding 217 atomic parameters. The design came from analyzing 240 open-source projects, grounded in Value Sensitive Design. Each parameter carries priors and baselines, turning narrative text into auditable data. A coverage check and a practitioner study tested the format. Documentation prose shrank by about thirty-eight percent on average with no facts lost. Practitioners strongly preferred the new cards for quick understanding and review. Technical and governance ownership became clearer as well. Adopting the grid is meant to be light work for model publishers.
arxiv-2510-07089:
Federico Gonzalez, Estefania Talavera, and Petia Radeva teach computers to find objects in images without any labeled examples. Their 2025 paper presents DADO, a self-supervised method for unsupervised object discovery. Attention maps can suggest where objects are, but they are often noisy. Depth estimates add a second cue, though scenes mix many depth planes.

DADO fuses the attention and depth signals into one decision. A dynamic weighting scheme leans on whichever cue suits each image. The balance adapts from the image's characteristics, using an entropy-based rule. On benchmarks, DADO beat state-of-the-art discovery methods in accuracy. It also proved more robust across scenes. No fine-tuning was needed to reach those results. The method needs no training labels at all, which suits domains where annotation is scarce. Combining mid-level cues like attention and depth looks like a strategy. It may extend toward instance segmentation.
arxiv-2510-07189:
Li and co-authors present Secure-Instruct, a recipe that teaches language models to write safer code. Their 2025 paper starts from a known flaw. Models often produce code with security holes. Older fixes relied on small, lopsided hand-built data sets. This framework instead creates its own training examples automatically. It generates matched vulnerable and secure code, then turns them into tuning lessons.

The team tested the recipe on four well-known models. They also built CWEBench, a fresh test with ninety-three scenarios across forty-four weakness types. Tuned models wrote safer code and also worked better on plain function tests. The average share of secure outputs rose by a wide margin over the base models. The recipe also beat the leading prior method, SafeCoder, on the new bench. Because the data is synthetic, the method can extend to new weakness types without huge manual effort.
arxiv-2510-07389:
Ugolini investigates how intermediate-mass black holes assemble inside dense star clusters. The 2025 paper bridges two worlds. Stellar-mass black holes are well observed, and so are supermassive ones. The middleweights between them remain poorly confirmed. Two complementary tools attack the question. Direct N-body simulations from the Dragon-II project follow clusters of up to a million stars in full detail. A semi-analytic code, BPop, calibrated on those runs then sweeps far wider conditions than any direct simulation could afford.

The combined models match the observed rate of merging black hole pairs. Roughly a third to three fifths of mergers form dynamically, mostly in globular and nuclear clusters. About two to three percent of mergers involve an intermediate-mass black hole, producing distinctive slow inspirals. The middleweight mass spectrum runs continuously from a few hundred to tens of thousands of solar masses.
arxiv-2510-07589:
Viguera Diez, Schreiner, and Olsson teach a generative model to leap through molecular time. Their 2025 paper confronts the timescale wall of molecular dynamics. Simulations resolve femtosecond steps, but the conformational changes that decide chemical function unfold over vastly longer spans, unreachable by brute force. Their framework learns the statistics of time-integrated dynamics directly from simulation data. Once trained, it propagates molecules over long lag times in single generative steps. The claimed acceleration is four orders of magnitude at retained physical realism.

On small organic molecules and peptides, the method recovers equilibrium ensembles quantitatively, not just plausible shapes. It also reproduces the rates and mechanisms of conformational exchange, the kinetic content brute-force runs are too short to measure. The authors frame it as molecular dynamics fidelity at generative-model cost.
arxiv-2510-07689:
Kumar wrote this 2025 paper in algebraic geometry and representation theory on loop groups and K-theory. Loop groups arise by letting a symmetry group vary around a circle. Their geometry connects to a space called the affine Grassmannian. That space is layered by Schubert varieties, which give a natural basis for its K-theory. Multiplication and comultiplication in this setting produce structure constants whose signs matter deeply.

Kumar states a positivity conjecture for those constants under the Pontryagin product. Positivity means the constants should be nonnegative in a suitable sense, reflecting hidden geometry. Using results of Kato, he shows the conjecture matches an equivalent one in quantum K-theory. That second setting concerns the flag variety of the group and its Schubert basis. Proving either version would link loop group geometry to quantum Schubert calculus. The paper is dedicated to Daniel Nakano on his sixtieth birthday.
arxiv-2510-07989:
Le, Münger, Andriulli, and Cools wrote this 2025 paper on simulating electromagnetic waves off dielectric objects. Engineers model such scattering with boundary integral equations marched forward step by step. The favored formulation is accurate but numerically fragile. Fine meshes break it, large time steps break it, and late times drift unstable. The authors rebuild the formulation to cure all three failures at once.

A Calderón preconditioner built from a modified static operator fixes the fine-mesh breakdown. Rescaling with quasi-Helmholtz projectors separates the loop and star parts of the current. Time differentiation and integration, used as rescaling operators, suppress the late-time instability and restore accuracy at large steps. Tests on smooth and rough dielectric shapes, simply and multiply connected, confirmed the claims. The scheme stayed accurate, stable, and efficient across them. Reliable transient scattering matters for radar and antenna design.
arxiv-2510-08689:
James Johnson, Miqaela Weller, and Ryan Cooke show how hydrogen and helium isotopes can break a modeling deadlock for the Milky Way in a 2025 arXiv paper. Star formation fuses hydrogen and helium into heavier elements, reshaping galactic composition over time. Metal yields from stars are degenerate with gas flows: raising both yields and inflow speed gives similar metallicities. Gas ejection rates create a matching degeneracy as well.

Precise isotope ratios cut through the confusion, they demonstrate. At fixed oxygen abundance, higher metal yields push deuterium-to-hydrogen ratios up and helium-3 to helium-4 ratios down. Current measurements are too few and too imprecise to settle the question confidently. Only about four more helium isotope measurements within three kiloparsecs of the Sun are needed, they forecast. Those would pin down the primordial helium ratio and test Big Bang nucleosynthesis directly.
arxiv-2510-08889:
Jia and co-authors give programmers a safer way to handle resources that change state, in this 2025 arXiv paper on programming languages. Files, locks, and network sessions must be used in the right order: open before reading, never use after closing. Block-based tools enforce order by tying permissions to a code block, which is easy to reason about but blocks clever patterns. Manual tracking is flexible yet demands heavy analysis to stay safe.

Their system grows out of capabilities, tokens that stand for permission to use a resource. They free those tokens from fixed blocks, letting functions hand them out, take them back, and return them as the program's flow demands. Built into the Scala 3 compiler, the approach uses its type machinery to keep the bookkeeping invisible. The prototype handled file operations, intricate locking schemes, web page construction, and communication protocols, all checked statically.
arxiv-2510-08989:
McClelland explores a loophole in the most famous limit in thermodynamics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Carnot limit caps how efficiently any heat engine between two temperatures can turn heat into work. McClelland works in a generalized thermodynamics read through information theory, where a system may store order in several independent quantities at once, not just energy. An engine that can draw on all of them, he argues, behaves like a battery with a larger total entropy capacity.

Using engines that evolve without leaking, called unitary engines, he shows work can be extracted past the Carnot efficiency while still running at maximum power, with no exotic heat sources required. He develops spin, the built-in angular momentum of particles, as one such extra reservoir. Spin baths mirror heat baths closely in their response laws and statistics. The ideas target spin-based electronics and condensates with near-degenerate spin energies.
arxiv-2510-09289:
Mecheri proves that several prized traits of an operator survive small, tame nudges, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Local spectral theory asks how an operator acts near each point of its spectrum. Two strict conditions, Bishop's property and the decomposition property, mark the best-behaved cases. Operators holding them are called decomposable. A famous open problem asks whether such traits persist when operators that commute are added or multiplied.

Rather than sums of two operators, Mecheri studies perturbations of one. All three traits prove stable under three tame kinds of commuting perturbations. The allowed nudges are quasinilpotent operators, whose spectrum is just zero, compact operators, and algebraic ones, which satisfy a polynomial equation. The traits, the result shows, are robust features, not accidents destroyed by small modeling errors.
arxiv-2510-09589:
Aflatoun Amouzandeh, Klaus Jansen, Lis Pirotton, Rob van Stee, and Corinna Wambsganz study job scheduling with restarts in a 2025 arXiv paper. A single machine processes jobs, and any job may be interrupted, but an interrupted job must start again from zero rather than resume. The goal is to minimise the weighted makespan, the largest weighted finishing time, without knowing future jobs.

The authors first prove a lower bound of about one point four seven on the competitive ratio that any deterministic online algorithm can achieve. Competitive ratio compares the online result with the best offline schedule. For the special case where all jobs take the same processing time, they design a deterministic algorithm that beats a ratio of one point two eight. They also prove that no algorithm for that case can go below about one point two four, narrowing the gap between the possible and the impossible.
arxiv-2510-09689:
Haoran Ou, Kangjie Chen, Xingshuo Han, Gelei Deng, Jie Zhang, Han Qiu, and Tianwei Zhang red-team language models that browse the web in a 2025 arXiv paper. Search gives models fresh facts beyond their static training, but the retrieval and citation process can expose users to harmful or low-credibility pages. Older red-teaming, the practice of attacking a system to find flaws, targets standalone models and unsafe generation, missing the search workflow itself.

Their framework, CREST-Search, introduces three attack strategies that craft innocent-looking queries yet induce unsafe citations. An iterative refinement loop strengthens the attacks under black-box conditions. The team also built WebSearch-Harm, a search-specific harmful dataset, and used it to fine-tune a specialised red-teaming model. Experiments show the framework slips past safety filters and systematically exposes weaknesses in search-based systems.
arxiv-2510-09889:
Huijts and Jom Luiten review the ultracold electron source in this 2025 arXiv paper in accelerator physics. The source is a distinct way to make high-brightness electron beams, the tight, well-ordered beams needed for sharp imaging and diffraction work. It cools the electrons at birth to keep the beam quality high.

The review traces twenty years of development of the technique. It covers the physical principles behind the source, the technical details of how such sources are built, and recent experiments that use them. The authors also look ahead to what the method may enable next. Their account marks the source as a mature tool, no longer just a lab curiosity.
arxiv-2510-10189:
Wang and Mohammad Abdulaziz certify unsolvable planning problems in this 2025 arXiv paper on automated planning. Temporal planning schedules actions over time, and sometimes no plan exists. Proving that negative result, rather than merely failing to find a plan, is what certification adds.

Their approach encodes the planning problem as a network of timed automata, formal models of timed behavior. An efficient model checker explores the network, and a separate certificate checker verifies its verdict. The certificate can be checked inside a formally verified framework, so the unsolvability claim does not rest on trusting the solver. Such guarantees matter when planners control real systems and a false claim of impossibility, or of success, carries cost.
arxiv-2510-10389:
M Hanzer settles a conjecture about the theta correspondence in this 2025 arXiv paper. The theta correspondence is a method that moves representations, meaning symmetry descriptions of a group, from one group to a partner group. Hanzer studies dual pairs formed by a symplectic group and an even orthogonal group. The work is set over a local field that is not based on the real numbers.

The focus is the big theta lift, the largest representation produced by this transfer. Hanzer proves that, starting from a discrete series representation of one group, its big theta lift to the partner group is irreducible whenever it is nonzero. Irreducible means the result cannot be split into smaller pieces. This proves a conjecture of Muić about how the correspondence behaves. The result sharpens what is known about a central tool in the theory of automorphic forms.
arxiv-2510-10489:
Jiaye Li and five co-authors improve how image generating transformers keep track of position, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Transformers need positional encoding, added signals that tell the model where each piece of an image sits. The standard rotary method works well for text but struggles with fine spatial detail, color cues, and counting objects in images. The team traces this to rigid frequency choices and to treating every attention head the same way.

Their fix, called HARoPE, adapts the encoding separately for each attention head. It inserts a small learnable transformation, built through singular value decomposition, before the rotary step. This lets the model shift frequencies, align its rotary planes with meaning, and give each head its own positional reach, while keeping the rotary method's key relative position property. In tests on ImageNet generation and text to image systems such as Flux and MMDiT, HARoPE beat strong baselines.
arxiv-2510-10589:
Rohit Mukherjee and Asutosh Dubey compute how magnetic impurities interact on the surface of a Weyl semimetal nanowire, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The interaction, known as RKKY, is mediated by itinerant electrons that carry influence from one impurity to another. In a Weyl semimetal, unusual surface states called chiral Fermi arcs host those electrons at low energies. Because these states lock spin to momentum, spin structure shapes the resulting spin to spin correlations.

The authors untangle which states produce which coupling channels. The azimuthal coupling arises only from Fermi arc states with identical spin polarization. The couplings along and across the wire instead come from arc states with opposite spin polarizations. They further show that purely surface mediated contributions scale differently from those mixing arc and bulk states. They present Weyl semimetal nanowires as a versatile platform for engineering a broad class of spin models.
arxiv-2510-11089:
Companies use modular product design to offer variety without losing efficiency, yet assembly problems often surface only after the design is fixed. Fabio Marco Monetti and co-authors tackle that gap in this 2025 arXiv paper on product architecture. They extend Modular Function Deployment, a standard method for defining modular architectures, by building Design for Assembly thinking into it from the start.

The extended method adds structured heuristics, assembly-oriented module drivers, a coded taxonomy for interfaces, and numbers that score assembly feasibility and automation readiness. It still fits standard Modular Function Deployment workflows, so teams can compare early design options through an assembly lens. A case study on a handheld leaf blower shows the payoff clearly. The redesigned architecture needed less assembly effort, used simpler interfaces, and offered more automation potential during production, supporting continuous improvement over the product life cycle.
arxiv-2510-11289:
A financial shock does not land the same way on a rich household and a poor one. Ciganović, Scola Gagliardi, and Tancioni trace who gains and who loses after such shocks across the euro area in this 2025 arXiv economics paper. They work with survey records on what people earn, not country averages. Then they follow each income group as a shock unfolds.

When financial conditions jump upward, the gap between high and low incomes grows wider. Most of that change sits at the two ends of the income scale, not in the middle. Pay from assets turns more uneven, likely because richer homes hold far more assets. Pay from work also spreads out, as skilled workers pull ahead through a skill premium. Bad shocks push the gap the other way, and middle income homes respond only to those, which marks them as exposed.
arxiv-2510-11389:
Werewolf, the party game of hidden werewolves and suspicious villagers, is a natural test of whether language models can deceive, persuade, and read other players. Zirui Song and co-authors argue that earlier evaluations relying on model self-play produced templated speech and flimsy metrics in this 2025 arXiv paper. 

The team curated a human-verified multimodal Werewolf dataset with over one hundred hours of video, 32.4 million utterance tokens, and fifteen rule variants. Their evaluation uses the winning faction's actual strategies as ground truth in two stages. A speech evaluation casts tasks as multiple-choice questions across five dimensions of social ability. A decision evaluation covers voting choices and inferences about opponents' hidden roles. State-of-the-art models performed very unevenly, with roughly half scoring below 0.50, exposing clear gaps in deception and counterfactual reasoning. They release the dataset and the WereAlign framework to support multi-agent interaction research.
arxiv-2510-11589:
Neural search advanced along two separate roads: models that exploit knowledge graph entities, and multi-vector models that keep a separate vector for every token. Shubham Chatterjee and Jeff Dalton merge the two in QDER, presented in this 2025 arXiv information retrieval paper. The model's defining choice is late aggregation: instead of compressing a document and query into single embeddings before comparing them. QDER keeps individual token and entity representations alive through the whole ranking process.

Learned attention transforms the representations before scoring, with aggregation only at the end. Across five standard benchmarks QDER posted significant gains, including a thirty-six percent improvement in the nDCG ranking metric over the strongest baseline on the TREC Robust 2004 collection. The advantage was largest on hard queries: QDER reached an nDCG score of 0.70 in cases where traditional approaches scored zero.
arxiv-2510-11689:
A robot trained to push objects in simulation often fails in reality because the object's mass distribution is not what the simulator assumed. Maggie Wang and co-authors close that gap by letting the robot measure the physics in Phys2Real, a 2025 arXiv robotics paper. It reconstructs the scene with 3D Gaussian splatting, estimates physical parameters with a vision-language model, then refines them from interactions.

Policies are conditioned on the interpretable physical parameters. The vision-language priors are fused with online estimates through ensemble uncertainty quantification. On pushing tasks the gains over domain randomization were large. A bottom-weighted T-block was pushed every time, against seventy-nine percent for the baseline. The hard top-weighted block succeeded fifty-seven percent of the time, against twenty-three percent. A hammer with off-center mass was pushed fifteen percent faster on average. Ablations showed both sources are essential.
arxiv-2510-11789:
Shai Zucker, Xiong Wang, Fei Lu, and Inbar Seroussi ask how efficiently machines can learn the interactions inside attention models. Attention is the mechanism that lets each token in a sequence weigh the others, the heart of modern language models. In their simplified single-layer version, tokens interact through one weight matrix plus a nonlinear activation. The team's 2025 arXiv paper proves a minimax rate, the best worst-case learning speed anyone can guarantee.

The rate depends only on the smoothness of the activation function and on the sample size. Strikingly, it does not depend on the number of tokens, the ambient dimension, or the rank of the weight matrix. That independence holds even though the matrix and activation cannot be separately identified from data. The authors call this a fundamental dimension-free efficiency of attention-style models.
arxiv-2510-11889:
Bernhard Kliem and three colleagues link the speed of solar eruptions to the shape of the magnetic field they escape through. A coronal mass ejection hurls billions of tons of solar plasma into space. How fast it goes may depend on how quickly the overlying magnetic field weakens with height, measured by the decay index. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests this on fifteen very fast and twenty-two slower halo events from Solar Cycle 23.

For the very fast group, ejection speed correlates strongly, at about zero point eight, with the decay index's slope above the height where the torus instability sets in. The link supports the idea that this instability drives the acceleration. The full sample correlates more weakly, unless events with a broad stabilizing dip in the profile are excluded. Simulations of erupting flux ropes confirm that such dips brake eruptions.
arxiv-2510-11989:
C. Freijo and F. A. Tal develop a theory of rotation for randomly shuffled surface motions. A cocycle applies a sequence of homeomorphisms, smooth reshufflings, of the two-dimensional torus, chosen by a shifting random environment. Classical rotation sets measure the average drift of such motion. Their 2025 arXiv paper defines a new version of the rotation set, inspired by the Misiurewicz-Ziemian approach, suited to this random setting.

The authors compare several notions: rotation sets for the whole cocycle and for measures kept invariant by the base shift. They present initial results on the possible shapes these sets take. Continuity holds when the invariant measure varies. For irrotational cocycles, those with no average drift, displacements stay bounded. A handful of worked examples shows the phenomena the definitions must accommodate. The paper lays groundwork for a fuller theory of rotation in random dynamics.
arxiv-2510-12189:
Ryuji Hashimoto, Takehiro Takayanagi, Masahiro Suzuki, and Kiyoshi Izumi let language models trade stocks to see if they inherit human quirks. Real markets show path dependence: prices sag near historical highs in ways fundamentals cannot explain, plausibly because loss-averse investors anchor on personal reference points. Traditional simulated agents cannot capture such subtleties. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds the Fundamental-Chartist-LLM-Agent.

In the framework, language models make each agent's buy and sell decisions from its individual situation, while order prices and volumes follow standard rules. Simulations recreate path-dependent patterns conventional agents fail to generate. Behavior analysis shows the agents' loss-aversion reference points shift with market trajectories, purchase prices and past peaks gaining or losing grip as prices move. That is precisely the human mechanism behavioral finance posits. LLM agents, the study suggests, can serve as wind tunnels for market psychology.
arxiv-2510-12289:
Kikuchi develops a flexible method for finding where the effects of a treatment fade out across space, in a 2025 arXiv economics paper. Pollution from a coal plant spreads with distance, and policy needs to know the boundary of its impact. Standard theory assumes effects decay exponentially, but that rests on idealized conditions like steady winds and flat terrain.

Kikuchi shows spatial boundaries can be identified without a fixed formula, under weak smoothness and monotonicity assumptions. He proposes a kernel based estimator whose bandwidth is chosen from the data. It is applied to forty two million satellite observations of nitrogen dioxide near coal plants from 2019 to 2021. Kernel regression cut prediction errors by about one percentage point on average against the exponential model, with gains of nearly three points near plants and almost four at long range. The pandemic also served as a natural check, with concentrations falling in 2020 and rebounding in 2021.
arxiv-2510-12389:
Teklehaymanot and Nejdl measure how unevenly language models charge different languages for the same content, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Tokenization splits text into subword units, and models bill and process text by the token. The authors compare how efficiently text is tokenized across more than two hundred languages, with uniform preprocessing and the same tokenizer throughout.

They collected statistics such as tokens per sentence and relative cost, benchmarked against English. Latin script languages tokenized most efficiently throughout. Languages with non Latin scripts or complex word forms suffered large token inflation, often costing three to five times more than English for equivalent text. Those gaps raise computing costs and shrink the usable context for speakers of low resource languages. The authors call this infrastructure bias. They urge strategies informed by language typology, plus adaptive vocabularies, so multilingual systems share costs more fairly.
arxiv-2510-12689:
Fulay, Zhu, and Bakker ask whether an artificial intelligence representing a person should mirror their stated preferences or act on their long term interests, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Political theory calls these the delegate and trustee styles of representation. The question matters because language models are increasingly used to predict survey responses and policy preferences, and sycophantic models may validate choices that harm the user later.

The authors simulate votes on US policy issues under a temporal utility framework. It weighs short and long term interests. They compare with behavior cloning models that act as delegates. Trustee style predictions aligned more tightly with expert consensus on well understood issues. They also showed greater bias toward the models' default stances on topics lacking clear agreement. Delegate models preserved user autonomy yet diverged more from well supported positions. They frame this as a fundamental design trade off involving welfare, autonomy, and paternalism.
arxiv-2510-12889:
Da and Kalyvianaki introduce Dodoor in this 2025 arXiv paper, a scheduler that assigns computing tasks to data center servers without a central coordinator. Decentralized schedulers usually probe remote servers in real time, and that probing traffic grows heavy at scale. Dodoor instead decides from cached server information that is refreshed in batches, cutting communication sharply.

To handle tasks with shifting, multidimensional needs on mixed hardware, the authors score each server with a novel load measure. It captures how poorly a task fits that server, rather than merely counting pending tasks. On a cluster of about one hundred heterogeneous nodes, tested with simulated Azure placements and real serverless Python functions, Dodoor cut scheduling messages by well over half. It also raised throughput and reduced both average and tail completion times.
arxiv-2510-13189:
Desai, Cervantes, and Banerjee derive scaling laws for wildfire plumes in this 2025 arXiv paper, a companion Lawrence Livermore study to their canopy plume simulations. Managing smoke hazards needs predictions of plume geometry: tilt angle, centerline trajectory, height, and curvature. A vegetative canopy complicates all of these through the turbulence it creates.

The authors ran suites of large-eddy simulations with and without canopy. They collapsed the forcing parameters into two dimensionless groups. One compares buoyancy strength to wind forcing. The other measures plume turbulence intensity against upstream conditions. Near-surface plume slopes were an order of magnitude higher with canopy drag. There they rose with turbulence intensity following a one-fourth power law. The results offer a physics-based route to better smoke prediction.
arxiv-2510-13289:
Prasad reviews dark sector searches at the BESIII experiment in this 2025 arXiv report, presented on behalf of the BESIII Collaboration. Dark matter explains galaxy rotation curves and other cosmic anomalies. Many extensions of the Standard Model let it couple to ordinary matter through portals. They predict new light particles such as dark photons, light Higgs bosons, and axion-like particles. A dark baryon tied to the matter-antimatter asymmetry is also possible.

If those particles weigh only a few billion electron volts, high-intensity electron-positron colliders like BESIII in Beijing can produce and detect them. The report surveys recent BESIII results across these search channels. Prasad frames the program as a direct experimental attack on the dark sector's lightest corner, complementary to astrophysical evidence that so far reveals dark matter only through gravity.
arxiv-2510-13789:
Uddin, Changani, and Coskunuzer classify whole time-evolving graphs with a transformer fed by topological and spectral descriptors. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses temporal graph classification, used in security, neuroscience, and traffic analysis. Snapshot and recurrent methods either blur fine timing or miss long-range patterns. Local message passing also oversmooths, washing out the structures that matter.

Their model, T3former, slides windows over the graph's life and computes shape descriptors for each. Persistent homology and spectral curves become first-class tokens for the transformer. A special descriptor-attention mechanism fuses those tokens with the graph's own signals. The design avoids rigid time slicing, preserving temporal fidelity throughout. Benchmarks span dynamic social networks, brain connectivity data, and traffic networks. T3former sets new state-of-the-art results across them, the authors report. Theory further guarantees stability when the graph wobbles slightly in time or structure.
arxiv-2510-13889:
Hu and Zhuang recognize foods in images through multi-agent chats between vision and language models, with no training on the target foods. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces MultiFoodChat for smart food quality inspection. Trained rivals need large tagged datasets and fail on unseen dishes. Zero-shot recognition promises inspection that adapts to new menus freely.

Agents converse over several rounds, mixing visual evidence with textual thinking. An Object Perception Token captures fine-grained visual traits of the dish. An Interactive Reasoning Agent reads those cues in context and refines the verdict step by step. The loop mimics how a human checker looks, looks again, and settles. Tests span several public food datasets with varied styles. The system beat no-label and few-shot rivals on recognition scores. Its chat trail also makes each verdict clear after the fact.
arxiv-2510-14589:
Sundararajan and Rithwik, in a 2025 arXiv paper, put Apple's Find My location network under a formal microscope. Find My helps users locate lost devices, even ones with no cellular signal or GPS, by using other people's Apple devices as relays. Apple says the system is private and secure. But the code is secret, so those claims normally rest on trust.

The authors built a symbolic model of the protocol, a mathematical sketch of its messages and steps. They also wrote precise formal statements of the privacy and security properties the system should have. Then they proved those properties automatically with the Tamarin prover, a tool that checks protocol logic exhaustively. The proofs are machine-checkable, so anyone can rerun them. The work matters because logical flaws can hide in protocols even when the underlying encryption is perfect.
arxiv-2510-14789:
Mustafa and Guvendi solve, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an exact quantum problem in a curved, magnetized universe model. The setting is Bonnor-Melvin spacetime, a universe threaded by a magnetic field, corrected by rainbow gravity, a proposal where geometry depends on a particle's energy. Into this arena they place scalar bosons and antibosons, governed by the Klein-Gordon equation, confined by a uniform magnetic field and a positive cosmological constant.

The cosmological constant slices spacetime into endless confinement domains walled off by impenetrable barriers. Inside the first domain, the equation reduces to a hypergeometric one, giving closed-form energies and wavefunctions. Two rainbow gravity models produce spectra that are bounded at the Planck scale and symmetric between particles and antiparticles. Strangely, all magnetic quantum states collapse onto a single level, a degeneracy flat space lacks, and stronger fields squeeze the bosons into ring-shaped configurations.
