arxiv-2510-15189:
Xiangyu Chen, Chuhao Zhou, Yuxi Liu, and Jianfei Yang teach robots delicate manipulation without asking humans for demonstration videos first. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets tasks like handling cell plates in a lab, where a small slip, such as spilling a reagent, ruins the whole job. Collecting expert demonstrations for such precision work is slow, and offline learning from fixed data often drifts out of sync with the real robot.

Their framework, RM-RL, treats a near-optimal example action as a role model and uses it to label data the robot gathers live. A hybrid scheme reuses that labeled online data for offline training as well, squeezing more value from each trial. In real-world tests the method learned faster and more stably than rivals, improving translation accuracy by 53 percent and rotation accuracy by 20 percent. It also completed a precise cell plate placement that earlier methods failed.
arxiv-2510-15489:
Miguel A. Rodríguez and Piergiulio Tempesta convert differential equations into discrete step-by-step maps without breaking their special structure, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The equations have variable coefficients, meaning their terms change with position, and they cover linear and nonlinear cases. Naive discretization usually breaks the delicate structure that makes such systems integrable.

Their construction rests on Rota's finite operator calculus, where difference operators behave like derivatives inside an algebra of power series. By building categories for both the algebra side and the dynamical systems side, they link each equation to its discrete analogues as objects of one framework. Under mild regularity assumptions the resulting maps share a wide set of exact solutions with the original equations. In linear cases they even share the Picard-Vessiot group, a symmetry group that encodes solvability. The authors present the method as a vast, principled factory for integrable discrete models.
arxiv-2510-15589:
Harkaitz Goyena, Peter M. Atkinson, Unai Pérez-Goya, and M. Dolores Ugarte make satellite image fusion easier by standardizing mismatched inputs first. Their 2025 arXiv paper explains that spatio-temporal fusion blends images from different sensors to get fine detail at frequent times. The inputs must first match in spatial and spectral resolution, which in practice they rarely do.

Two standardization routes are compared. The first simply upscales the fine-resolution images in the traditional way. The second, called ABSIS, sharpens by blending the broad features of the fine image series with the distinctive traits of one coarse image, mimicking what aggregation would produce. Both routes significantly improved the accuracy of a chosen fusion method on their tests. The sharpening route did better, lifting spectral accuracy by up to about forty-nine percent and spatial accuracy by up to about seventy-eight percent.
arxiv-2510-15689:
Harmonic maps extend analytic functions, and their behavior near the unit disk edge is delicate. Gebreslassie Atsbha, Weldegebrial Hunduma, and Legesse Geleta extend earlier work in this 2025 arXiv paper. Laugesen and Bshouty studied how one-to-one harmonic maps behave near the disk's edge. The present authors work under varied conditions on the maps and their dilatation. Dilatation measures how far a harmonic map stretches in different directions.

They pin down angular limits for arguments and logarithms of related analytic functions. They also show this stretching has only finitely many zeros inside any Stolz angle, under a condition on derivatives. That condition needs the map's first derivative to blow up at the edge point.
arxiv-2510-15989:
Keshav Sood, Sanjay Selvaraj, and Youyang Qu build a headset-side filter that stops intimate behavioural data from leaking out of immersive apps. Virtual, augmented, and mixed reality need biometric and behavioural tracking to feel immersive, yet that stream is deeply sensitive. Reviews of the privacy problem, the authors say, rarely address real-time filtering inside the headset itself.

Their system, Meta-Guardian, is a Unity software kit that classifies biometric signals with machine learning models inside the headset and blocks the sensitive ones before transmission or storage. The modular design fits major immersive platforms, so developers can embed privacy by design into varied headsets and applications. This early evaluation frames the work as a practical guard for psychography, the profile of mind and behaviour that raw tracking can reveal to outsiders.
arxiv-2510-16089:
William Hoy and Nurcin Celik gate each proposed edit to a large language model against a stability budget, so the model can keep learning without forgetting. Sequential updates cause catastrophic forgetting, where new edits erode older knowledge. Their STABLE framework performs the edits with low-rank adaptation and checks every candidate before accepting it.

Three gates are offered: exact match drop for factual loss, bits increase for falling confidence, and KL divergence for distributional drift from the base model. An edit that crosses its threshold is clipped down or rejected outright. On a seven-billion-parameter Qwen model, gating curbs forgetting while adaptability survives, and exact-match gating gives the best cumulative score on short update sequences. Different gates can yield equal drift yet different accuracy, which makes gate choice itself a design lever, the pair conclude.
arxiv-2510-16189:
Rico Huhnstock and three co-authors present a chip that sorts tiny magnetic beads by how they move. Lab-on-a-chip tools use such beads for medical tests, but beads vary in size and strength from the factory. A pre-sort step can cut that spread before the real test starts.

Their chip carries a striped magnetic pattern whose stripes widen step by step. Pulses from an outside magnet make the beads hop along, and wider stripes mean longer hops at slower speeds. Beads with unlike size or magnetic pull drop out of the dance at unlike spots. So they end up sorted across the chip. All beads sort at once under one pulse train, giving high throughput with sharp local sorting.
arxiv-2510-16289:
Yoonho Lee and five co-authors bring category theory to bear on learning from hypergraphs. A hypergraph links groups of nodes at once through hyperedges, like genes grouped in one pathway. Untangling a hyperedge's hidden traits, called disentanglement, could expose unlabeled links that matter for labels.

The team studies the problem through category theory, a branch of math about structure and maps between structures. From its naturality condition, a rule about maps playing well together, they derive a test for true disentanglement. Their proof-of-concept model then reads gene pathways and recovers real working links between genes. The result hints that deep math can guide hypergraph models toward meanings that data alone rarely annotates.
arxiv-2510-16689:
Luca Claude Gino Lebon and Claudio Altafini, writing together, solve a network control problem: how to shield chosen nodes from disturbances while touching as few input and output nodes as possible. Disturbance decoupling means feedback cancels the effect of troubled nodes on protected targets. It is a classic goal in control theory.

Rewriting the problem in terms of sets of nodes, rather than vector spaces, gives the key invariance conditions a simple graph meaning. For state feedback and dynamical feedback, the pair shows the smallest node choices can be found exactly and quickly with min-cut and max-flow methods. Output feedback laws are also given. The results suit large networks where each added sensor or actuator costs money.
arxiv-2510-17389:
School pupils need answers pitched at their own reading level, yet large language models often reply with words that are too hard or too vague. Numaan Naeem, Abdellah El Mekki, and Muhammad Abdul-Mageed build EduAdapt, a test set for that grade level fit. Their benchmark holds nearly forty-eight thousand question and answer pairs across nine science subjects, labelled for grades one through twelve and grouped into four bands.

Naeem and his co-authors test a range of open models on the set. Bigger models generally did better, but all of them struggled to write suitably for the youngest pupils in grades one to five. The team offers the data and scoring framework as a first standard for judging grade level adaptability, hoping it guides training toward answers children can actually use.
arxiv-2510-17489:
Texts written together by people and AI are now common, and telling how a mixed text was made matters for fighting falsehoods and cheating. Yongxin He and four co-authors note that the mixing takes many forms: AI text polished by a person, human text edited by AI, or AI text refined by another AI. Simple detectors that sort text into just human or AI miss that variety, and treat each blend crudely.

He and his co-authors model the blends as branches of a family tree, and train text representations to sit near their proper branch. They also built a benchmark covering many such hybrid texts. Their DETree method improved detection scores and held up better on unfamiliar text types, especially when only a few training examples were available.
arxiv-2510-17589:
A. Ya. Maltsev asks how likely the strangest current patterns in metals are to appear in a 2025 arXiv paper. In his model, electrons move through a crystal in a simplified energy pattern called the tight binding picture. In strong magnetic fields, some electron paths on the energy surface grow highly complex. Those paths would make electrical conductivity, meaning how well current flows, change in unusual scaling ways as the field grows.

Theory has mapped these regimes well, but no experiment has seen them yet. Maltsev estimates the chance that they occur across a wide class of conductors. He also points out the conditions under which a lab could detect them. The work gives experimentalists a guide for where to look.
arxiv-2510-17889:
Eilene Tomkins-Flanagan and Mary A Kelly build a full Lisp programming language out of vectors that stand for symbols. The idea follows a suggestion by Kanerva that such a build should be possible. Their version covers the five basic Lisp functions, lambda forms, and helper functions from the classic Lisp 1.5 guide.

That small set is enough for full computing power, which the authors stress. A cleanup memory based on lookup tables keeps the vector codes readable. The paper links coding theory with the math of closed categories, and it shows that a vector-symbolic system can host a real language.
arxiv-2510-18089:
Paul-Tiberiu Miclea, with five co-authors, explores machine learning for spotting microplastic bits caught on filters. These pollutants are everywhere and may harm ecosystems and health, yet their tiny size makes counting them slow by hand. Microscopes give sound images, but manual reading blocks large screening studies.

The team pairs electron microscope images with object detection models in a simple filtration setup. The study weighs what works, what fails, and what should come next for finding and counting particles and fibres. Environmental labs get an early map of how far automated microplastic hunting can go today.
arxiv-2510-18589:
Alessandro Allegrezza and his sixteen co-authors study colonies of human bone marrow cells. The colonies hold skeletal stem cells. Those cells show real promise for regenerative medicine. Yet colony behavior in the body is hard to predict. The authors ask why colonies differ so much. Pure random noise should wash out at colony scale. A million cells should average to uniformity. Colony traits persist, so noise alone cannot explain them.

The team proposes that traits pass down cell lineages. They define a new measure called inheritance entropy. It tracks how inactive cells spread across a colony's family tree. They grew thirty-two colonies from single cells. The entropy was decisively low in most clones. Their conclusion is direct. Heritable traits govern when cells stop dividing. Those traits shape each colony's structure. The result gives a new handle on a long-standing puzzle for skeletal therapies.
arxiv-2510-18689:
Hiromi Ebisu, Bo Han, and Weiguang Cao link two ideas about quantum matter. One is modulated symmetry. Such symmetries act in distinct ways at distinct places. They can trap excitations in place. The other is the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis anomaly. Such anomalies forbid certain simple phases on a lattice. In one dimension, gauging was known to link the two ideas. Gauging makes a symmetry act locally. Higher dimensions lacked a general picture.

The authors show where modulated symmetries come from. They arise when plain symmetries are gauged near generalized anomalies. Their dipole algebras arise the same way. The team builds explicit lattice models in two and three dimensions. They give field theory accounts for any dimension count. Anomaly inflow is tied to higher-group structures there. Those structures govern the modulated symmetries. The result is one unified framework across dimensions.
arxiv-2510-18789:
Erik Horsdal, writing alone, works out the internal forces inside a swinging counterweight trebuchet. The machine hurls projectiles with a falling weight and a sling. Forces in the arm, counterweight, and sling depend on the machine's motion. The motion is given by angles that change over time, taken from experiment or theory. Horsdal derives explicit formulas for those forces. They use the angles and their first and second rates of change.

A useful shortcut follows. Forces right after a shot starts can be read from the equations of motion, without solving them in full. They can be compared with the static forces just before release. Builders care because the strength each part needs follows from these forces. Sliding friction losses follow from them too. Worked results for one specific trebuchet show the method in action.
arxiv-2510-18989:
Yifei Sun studies neural operators, fast stand-ins for solvers of partial differential equations. Sun asks two things. How well does a learned operator generalize? And how well does it resist attack? The view is tied to the solver. Both outputs tend to shift as one when inputs are nudged.

Sun defines generalization through a model-solver error map at fixed inputs. Robustness is defined through bounded rises in attack loss. This gives operator learning its own safety terms. They differ from the terms used for image tasks. Users can judge when a fast stand-in is safe to trust.
arxiv-2510-19089:
Érik Martin-Dorel presents three related tools that bring Docker-based continuous integration to Rocq and OCaml software projects. Rocq, formerly called Coq, is a proof assistant whose projects need reliable build checks, and container images make those checks reproducible across machines.

The projects cover ready-made Docker images, a GitHub action that uses them, and a keeper tool that maintains them. The article explains their main features to encourage adoption, and records the requirements and design choices behind the tools so future maintainers can keep the system running and extend it sensibly.
arxiv-2510-19289:
Kefeng Huang and seven co-authors introduce TARMAC, a taxonomy of manipulation skills for robots working in chemistry laboratories. Lab automation promises faster, safer, more repeatable experiments, yet many systems still need frequent human help because their skills were built for one task and do not transfer to the next.

Existing experiment descriptions list protocol steps but not the robotic actions needed to carry them out. TARMAC defines and organizes those manipulation skills in a shared framework, so builders can specify what a lab robot must do and reuse skill blocks across setups. A common language is a first step toward general chemistry robots.
arxiv-2510-19389:
Lin Xv and four co-authors present ARA. It allocates rank in an adaptive way for model compression. Singular value decomposition does the compressing. Each linear module must be compressed on its own. Nonlinear parts sit between the modules. So the real problem is the rank budget. Each module must keep the right amount under one global limit.

Older heuristic searches explore narrow regions only. Mask-based training captures module relations poorly. Adaptive allocation searches the trade-off more fully. Key modules get more rank, and the rest are squeezed harder. Smaller models then lose less of the original skill.
arxiv-2510-19489:
František Bartoš, Samuel Pawel, and Björn S. Siepe propose living synthetic benchmarks as a fairer way to judge statistical methods. Simulation studies usually test methods on data-generating setups invented by the methods' own authors, which rewards favorable setups. Results also fragment across mismatched setups, so studies are hard to compare.

Under their proposal, benchmarks stay open and keep growing: whenever a new data-generating mechanism, method, or performance measure appears, it joins the benchmark. Method development and benchmark design are kept apart to protect neutrality. The authors lay out a blueprint for building and running such benchmarks and show feasibility with a working prototype for publication bias adjustment methods.
arxiv-2510-19589:
David Békollè, Hugues Olivier Défo, and Edgar L. Tchoundja study when Toeplitz operators with operator-valued symbols are compact on vector-valued Bergman spaces. These spaces consist of analytic functions on the unit ball whose values lie in a sequence space, and the symbols take values in operators on that space. Compactness of such operators is a basic structural question in operator theory.

One strategy restricts the problem to finite dimensions, letting earlier results of Rahm and Wick apply, and the paper gives an explicit compact example. The authors then test two sufficient conditions for compactness in infinite dimensions, one using a Toeplitz algebra and one using localized operators. They close by asking whether the second condition actually implies the first.
arxiv-2510-19689:
Guilin Zhang and ten co-authors lay out a production blueprint for running enterprise human-resources analytics on serverless graphics processors. Large firms and agencies need workforce analytics that are fast, cheap, and auditable, while classic distributed frameworks like Spark add coordination and compliance overhead for moderate workloads. Their design pairs a single-node serverless GPU runtime with TabNet, an interpretable model for tabular data.

Benchmarks on human-resources and public datasets showed up to about four and a half times the throughput of Spark baselines, far lower latency, and about ninety percent lower cost per thousand inferences. Compliance mechanisms added only a few milliseconds, and the model's feature-mask explanations stayed stable under peak load, keeping the system auditable for regulated settings.
arxiv-2510-19789:
Guowei Xu and eight co-authors present OmniMotion-X, a single framework for generating whole-body human motion from many kinds of input. One model handles text-to-motion, music-to-dance, and speech-to-gesture. It also handles control tasks like prediction and in-betweening. The design is an autoregressive diffusion transformer in a unified sequence-to-sequence form. Reference motion can be supplied as a signal, to keep style and timing consistent.

Training such a model needed a matching dataset. So the team built OmniMoCap-X from twenty-eight public motion capture sources across ten tasks. The data was standardized to a common body format, with captions made from rendered videos. A staged training strategy, weak conditions first and strong ones later, resolves clashes between input types. The system beat existing methods across the tasks tested.
arxiv-2510-19889:
Mostafa Ameli and three co-authors replace the optimization machinery of traffic assignment with a transformer that predicts equilibrium flows directly. Assigning trips to routes under the equilibrium principle is a classic transportation problem, but the mathematical programs behind it grow prohibitively slow on large networks. Their model predicts path-level flows, a finer view than the usual link-level output.

Trained on networks including a Manhattan-like synthetic grid, Sioux Falls, and Eastern Massachusetts, the model ran orders of magnitude faster than conventional solvers. It adapts to changed demand or network structure without solving the problem again, and it handles multi-class traffic. The authors pitch the approach for rapid what-if analysis in planning and policy.
arxiv-2510-20089:
Constance Crozier studies a hard choice in running a power grid. Grid staff must pick switch states for lines and gear. When those picks are added to a power flow plan, the math turns hard to solve at full scale in time. A fast linear plan, called DC-OPF, can give picks, but some picks fail when checked in full.

Crozier uses a search that builds many near-best plans for the linear task. More plans mean a much lower chance that all of them fail the full check. She tests the search on 13 grids where the linear picks fail. The search finds a plan that works in all 13 cases. The search rules used change how many good plans turn up and how strong they are.
arxiv-2510-20389: Bjorn Remseth holds that symmetry is a core design rule for software platforms. In his view, a platform acts as a shape-keeping system. It gives steady hooks and acts that stay the same under a set of shifts, which he calls symmetries. Firmness of build grows, he argues, from strict care for such shared rules. Keep those rules whole, and the platform stays sound as it grows and shifts.
arxiv-2510-20689:
Darij Grinberg, writing alone, gives a teaching account of matrix traces, determinants, and adjugate matrices, centered on a trace form of the Cayley Hamilton theorem. That classic theorem says a matrix obeys its own characteristic equation, and the trace version links its powers to the equation coefficients.

While the results are known, several proofs here are new and chosen to display broad techniques for linear algebra over general commutative rings, not just over numbers. Grinberg proves the trace identity for every size and works through the supporting facts on traces and determinants step by step. The account serves readers who want firm ground under formulas often used without proof in advanced work.
arxiv-2510-21389:
Stefan Kraft and four co-authors test whether explained AI advice actually helps sleep specialists at work, rather than only scoring well in the lab. Eight professional practitioners scored brief arousal events in overnight brain recordings under three setups: alone, with an opaque AI assistant, or with a transparent one that shows its reasons.

Help arrived either from the start of scoring or later, as a quality-control review of finished work. Against the clinical standard, both AI setups and human-AI teams beat unaided experts, and teamwork also narrowed disagreement between scorers. Transparent help used as a targeted review lifted event scores by roughly thirty percent over opaque help, though it took more time. Seven of the eight specialists said they would adopt the system with minor changes or none.
arxiv-2510-21489:
Nouredine Medjoudj and Abdelkrim Moussaoui prove that a coupled system of singular quasilinear elliptic equations admits at least three real solutions. The system carries zero values on the boundary. Such systems model steady states where two quantities act on each other. The equations can blow up or degenerate at some points.

Their toolkit joins three parts. A topological degree method counts solutions by how a mapping wraps around its target. An order method sandwiches the system between a lower and an upper trial solution. Cut-off arguments tame the singularities. Two of the solutions keep one strict sign throughout, in opposite directions. The third solution changes sign. Its two components switch in opposite patterns. For systems whose coupling ties the signs together, the components switch in step.
arxiv-2510-21889:
Marios Andreou and Nan Chen extend a method called assimilative causal inference, which blends real observations with a working model of a system to trace causes from effects. Knowing that two things are causally linked is only half the answer; the pair also asks when an influence began and how long it lasts.

They define two influence ranges for each moment in time. The forward range measures how long a cause keeps mattering after it acts, and the backward range reaches back to find when the trigger of an observed effect first emerged. Clean mathematical formulas and objective measures for both ranges remove the need for arbitrary cutoffs. The framework ties causal detection to prediction and attribution, separating what can be forecast from what can be explained afterward.
arxiv-2510-21989:
Lucas Adams Cowan, Ronja Eilfort, Kerry Seekamp, and Julianna Tymoczko prove a matching between two operations in a corner of algebra where diagrams do the counting. Web graphs, flat directed drawings with boundary points, model certain symmetry-respecting vectors, and tableaus, grids of numbers following strict rules, label the natural basis for those graphs.

Evacuation is a standard reshuffling of a rectangular tableau, and reflection flips a web drawing. The team shows the two moves correspond exactly, up to a stated set of local edge-flip equivalences, for rectangular tableaus of any height. Earlier work covered only the smallest cases. A bridge object, a multicolored noncrossing matching, carries the argument, tying the result to a broader pattern in which tableau moves mirror diagram moves.
arxiv-2510-22089:
A. Padoan, J. Eising, and I. Markovsky extend behavioral systems theory, which describes systems purely through the signals they can produce, from straight-line linear systems to affine ones, whose behavior includes a constant offset. The shift sounds small, but many identification methods that read a system's rules straight from data rest on exact structural results for the linear case.

The authors rebuild the main representations, kernel, input-output, state-space, and finite-horizon data-driven forms, for affine time-invariant systems and show where the parallels with the linear theory hold. They then craft a persistence of excitation condition matched to the affine class, yielding a fundamental lemma, the data-driven workhorse result, that provably needs less data than borrowing the linear condition would. The moral is that excitation demands should fit the model class, or experiments collect more data than the job requires.
arxiv-2510-22489:
Pruning, or cutting unneeded parts from a large language model, can make such models cheaper to run. Yuanhe Tian, Junjie Liu, Xican Yang, Haishan Ye, and Yan Song present a task aware pruning method in a 2025 paper, noting older methods protect general fluency but neglect specific jobs.

Their approach scores each model part twice, once with general text and once with task specific text. Parts are split into shared and task only groups, then the scores are merged to guide cutting. The design plugs into several existing pruning methods, aiming to keep special skills while the model shrinks under compression.
arxiv-2510-22689:
Explaining why a retrieval augmented language system gave an answer matters when sources drive the output. Joel Rorseth, Parke Godfrey, Lukasz Golab, Divesh Srivastava, and Jarek Szlichta present in 2025 the first proposal to explain such systems with if then rules about which sources were retrieved.

A rule might say that when a ranking article is retrieved, the model ranks a given university first. Testing every source combination would be far too slow. Their optimizations adapt pruning ideas from frequent itemset mining to cut the search. Qualitative and quantitative experiments show the rules are useful and can be generated efficiently.
arxiv-2510-22789:
Legged robots need full body motion forecasts to avoid collisions. Abhijeet M Kulkarni, Ioannis Poulakakis, and Guoquan Huang present a learning frame in 2025. It predicts motion at the limb level. Simple kinematic models miss closed loop dynamics. Those dynamics include the low level controller.

Their neural observer reads past body sensor data. It gives a stable latent state estimate. Stability comes with a proven boundedness guarantee. A fast predictor then scores many paths in parallel. That suits sampling based planners. The team tested it on a Vision 60 quadruped. It planned through a narrow passage. It also stepped over small objects safely.
arxiv-2510-22989:
L.-H. Li and 28 co-authors report optical observations of supernova 2017ckj in a 2025 paper. They followed the Type IIb event for about 180 days after it exploded. Stars of this type explode after losing most of the hydrogen in their outer layers.

Its brightness rose in about five days, then fell in a straight line at late times, with no clear early cooling tail. Models of the total light point to more nickel and a heavier hydrogen layer than is usual for this class. Early spectra looked blue and showed narrow hydrogen and helium lines from gas the star had shed. Later spectra grew broad lines, and the final one still showed strong hydrogen, which fits a fairly massive envelope.
arxiv-2510-23089:
Nicolas Allegra applies tensor network methods to image processing and classical optics. Tensor networks borrow ideas from quantum systems to compress large classical data and speed up operations within that compressed form. Their strength is strong compression plus a rich set of efficient algorithms.

Allegra focuses on basic problems: compressing and processing images, propagating wave fronts, and forming optical images. Parallels with quantum mechanics guide the methods, directly or indirectly. The work shows that tools built for quantum states can also sharpen everyday tasks in imaging and lens design, often at lower cost than brute-force computation.
arxiv-2510-23289:
Lukas Ostrowski and Christian Rohde construct an energy-stable numerical method for a model of compressible two-phase flow. The Navier-Stokes-Allen-Cahn system governs a viscous, immiscible two-phase fluid at constant temperature, and its weak solutions dissipate a natural energy. A good scheme should mirror that behavior discretely.

Their fully discrete discontinuous Galerkin method conserves mass, stays energy stable, and gives high-order accuracy in space with second order in time. It rests on an equivalent reformulation and a special splitting. Reliable two-phase simulation supports work on fuel, cooling, and materials processing. The authors present their evidence and methods in full for readers to judge.
arxiv-2510-23389:
Edoardo Manino, Bruno Farias, Rafael Sa Menezes, Fedor Shmarov, and Lucas C Cordeiro verify neural networks at the software level, with explicit reasoning about floating-point arithmetic. Safety-critical systems need proof that network components behave correctly, yet existing verifiers cannot certify the absence of faults in the actual software implementation, where rounding errors live.

They build NeuroCodeBench 2.0, a benchmark of nine hundred twelve verification examples covering activation functions, common layers, and full networks up to one hundred seventy thousand parameters. Their methods specify and verify safety for the floating-point code itself, closing a real deployment gap.
arxiv-2510-23989:
Shangde Gao and two co-authors learn how individuals change their movement after urban disruptions, and how reliance on social infrastructure shapes those shifts. After floods, outages, or closures, people's travel patterns reveal new demands on community resources. Predicting the shifts in advance is hard: resilience is rarely measured, standard features are scarce, and movement data are sparse and tangled with place.

The study builds a measure of each person's social infrastructure reliance and feeds it into a conditioned deep learning model alongside spatial context. Large-scale individual-level data drive the training. Experiments show the added reliance measure and context improve predictions of post-event movement. The model separates people whose pre-event patterns look identical but whose resilience differs — they diverge after disruption, and the model sees it coming. The authors aim the tool at planners who must pre-position community resources before the next shock.
arxiv-2510-24089:
Fuyu Dong and Changbom Park use the shape of galaxy clustering to test what dark energy is doing over time. They apply an extended Alcock-Paczynski test to data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The test compares the full shape of the two point pattern in redshift space against a standard shape to read the expansion history.

Their checks use large simulations to set the standard shape and test for bias. Using the test alone, they find values that favor a thawing quintessence field, where dark energy was frozen early and now slowly changes. Combined results are also reported. The paper is the second in a series using this tomographic method.
arxiv-2510-24189:
Ayan Chatterjee and two co-authors extend the laws of black hole mechanics to rotating black holes in five dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity. This theory adds a Gauss-Bonnet term to Einstein's gravity, which changes the rules that govern black hole horizons. The authors work within the isolated horizon framework, which treats the horizon as an internal boundary.

They show the first law needs two corrections from the Gauss-Bonnet term: one to the area of horizon cross sections and one to the formula for horizon angular momentum. With those changes, the Hamiltonian correctly generates evolution on the solution space. The boundary conditions may also help the search for exact rotating black hole solutions in this theory.
arxiv-2510-24489:
Liqian Qin, Yuchao Tang, and Jigen Peng, three authors, design an algorithm. The task is a monotone inclusion, a math problem of finding a zero. Such problems mix three kinds of operators with distinct traits. Operators are rules that turn one input into a set of outputs. The team extend a known splitting method by adding momentum.

Splitting methods break a hard problem into steps for each operator. Momentum reuses past steps to speed the search, here in nonlinear form. With the right step size, their method is proved to converge weakly. Under a strong trait, the error shrinks at a linear rate. A random version cuts variance for sums of many terms. Tests on portfolio tasks beat rival methods in practice.
arxiv-2510-24889:
Shakeel Abdulkareem, Bora Yimenicioglu, Khartik Uppalapati, Aneesh Gudipati, Adan Eftekhari, and Saleh Yassin built a brain wave tool to sort stroke cases fast at the bed side. Brain wave reads are cheap and quick, yet rare at first touch for stroke. Their tool reads thirty two wires of brain waves and turns them into wave power traits.

A mixed net that joins loop and coil parts then calls the stroke type, side, and weight of the case at once. A learn based step tunes the call lines in real time for each case. On a small set of stroke and calm cases, the tuned tool hit a high right rate for stroke type. A second, sparse wire set checked its hold.
arxiv-2510-25189:
Ana M Rodriguez, Jaime Acosta, Anantaa Kotal, and Aritran Piplai built AgentCyTE, a frame that makes cyber drill worlds with a chat model kept on a leash. Hand made threat scenes for train and tests take much work. Free chat model drafts oft fail checks or will not run at all.

AgentCyTE pairs model thought with a strict, schema bound fake net engine. A loop reads the run's end, checks it, and hones the scene for more truth and fit. That mix keeps the model's bend while it forces the scene to run. Scenes for threat models and live train can then be made at scale, with facts to back each build.
arxiv-2510-25389:
Meng Hua, Haotian Wu, and Deniz Gunduz present AirCNN. Their 2025 paper implements convolutional networks over the air. It uses reconfigurable intelligent surfaces for analog computation. The environment itself then emulates a network layer. That offers a novel computing paradigm for contacts.

They consider classic 2D convolution first. Lightweight depthwise separable convolution is also covered. Two transmission architectures are proposed and studied. One uses multiple inputs and multiple outputs. The other uses multiple inputs and single output. They jointly optimize transmitter, receiver, and surface settings. Power budgets and phase shift limits are respected. Runs show satisfactory classification results for AirCNN. The single-output design beat the other across settings. Multiple surfaces better results over a single surface. Gains were strongest in line-of-sight dominated environments.
arxiv-2510-25589:
S Haemmerich led thirty co-authors compiling the eROSITA blazar catalog. A Gokus, F McBride, and P Weber helped. Their 2025 astronomy paper presents BlazEr1, a blazar census. eROSITA performed its first X-ray all-sky survey. That survey ran during 2019 and 2020.

It detected about nine hundred thirty thousand sources overall. The team compiled blazar candidates from literature sources. They matched that list with the eRASS1 catalog. Sources with over fifty counts got spectral properties. Multiwavelength data span radio to gamma-ray regimes. Spectral indices and redshifts were compiled for sources. The catalog contains five thousand eight hundred sixty-five sources. Confirmed blazars number about two thousand of them. For nearly three thousand sources, eROSITA gives first X-ray data. Contamination from non-blazar sources stays below eleven percent. Most candidates exhibit typical blazar properties throughout. The catalog provides follow-up targets for future surveys.
arxiv-2510-25689:
Tibor Jordan, Xuemei Liu, and Soma Villanyi study degree settings for graph rigidity. Their 2025 math paper seeks sufficient settings for generic rigidity. Settings are expressed through minimum degree of graphs. Another setting sums degrees of nonadjacent vertex pairs. For each case, smallest forcing thresholds are sought. Those thresholds guarantee rigidity in d-dimensional space.

Krivelevich, Lew, and Michaeli conjectured a degree bound. A constant times dimension plus half vertices suffices, they guessed. The authors answer that conjecture affirmatively here. Constant one suffices for the bound, they prove. For large vertex counts, exact threshold values follow. The nonadjacent degree sum gets similar bounds. Exact values hold when vertices are sufficiently many. Low dimensions two and three are fully determined. Another conjecture is confirmed in those cases. Uses include Erdos-Renyi random graph rigidity. Random graphs are almost surely rigid in high dimensions. The first linear lower bound for dimension is given.
arxiv-2510-25889:
Kang Chen leads thirteen co-authors in a method to fine tune robot models with online reinforcement learning. The models, called vision language action models, let a robot turn images and words into actions. Flow based versions are hard to train with reinforcement learning because the chance of each action, needed for learning, cannot be computed directly from the flow process.

Chen and the team offer two fixes. One turns the denoising steps into a decision process with a learned noise network that allows exact chances. The other merges denoising with interaction through a two layer process for faster exploration. Across benchmarks, reinforcement learning improved results both in familiar and in new settings.
arxiv-2510-26289:
Zijing Xu, Yunfeng Kou, Kunming Wu, and Hong Liu propose a fusion method for multi source learning that treats each data source according to its input value. Models that combine image, text, and other data types often suffer from data type uneven split, where one source wins out, and from noisy data. Prior fixes suppress the leading data type, which can waste its information value and lead to weaker solutions.

Their Input value Guided Uneven Learning raises the input value of strong data types while shrinking weak ones so their input value grows. A input value metric blends information amount with certainty for each data type. An uneven gradient device speeds updates unevenly, and an information choke point shrinking step cuts noise in low input value data types. Tests span five benchmark data sets.
arxiv-2510-26489:
Artur Avkhadiev, with eight co-authors, pins down a key piece of the strong force's behaviour in moving particles. The piece is the Collins-Soper kernel, a function that guides how parton patterns shift with energy in transverse-momentum-dependent distributions. Those distributions describe how a proton's parts spread in sideways motion as well as along its path.

Avkhadiev and the team combine lab data with lattice QCD, the grid-based form of the strong force theory, in a single joint fit. A neural network shapes the unknown functions, and a Bayesian reweighting step folds the lattice results in. Adding lattice input moved the kernel's central value by about ten percent. It also cut the uncertainty by forty to fifty percent. The work shows how grid calculations can sharpen fits built on lab data alone.
arxiv-2510-26689:
Abhinav Roy and Niti Singh build a low-cost spectrometer for student astronomy. Their module pairs a diffraction grating of six hundred lines per millimetre with a monochrome CMOS sensor in a 3D-printed mount. It attaches to the reflecting telescopes many schools already own.

Roy and Singh calibrate the device with a helium lamp in the lab and with the star Vega as a standard. A custom Python pipeline handles wavelength calibration and stacks spectra. The spectrometer recorded usable spectra of bright stars including Vega, Sirius, Procyon, Capella, and Betelgeuse, spanning spectral types A through M. The authors present it as a practical frame for student-led instrumentation projects at institutions with modest budgets.
arxiv-2510-26789:
Shao-Hua Hu, Po-Sung Liu, and Jun-Yi Wu blend two routes to distributed quantum computing. One route uses shared entanglement to perform nonlocal operations directly, but it eats entanglement fast. The other, circuit knitting, cuts a big circuit into pieces with no entanglement at all, but pays an exponential sampling cost.

Hu and his two co-authors propose entanglement-assisted circuit knitting, which knits circuits with a limited amount of entanglement as help. They build the general theory, find the best sampling overhead for a class of operations, and bound it for general ones assisted by one Bell pair. A black-box extension removes the need to know the whole circuit in advance. Under a dynamic, probabilistic supply of entanglement, they reveal a trade-off between sampling overhead and entanglement cost, and give an algorithm for the best mix of protocols.
arxiv-2510-27189:
Sutirtha Sengupta, Das Sujit, and Arkaprabha Sarangi model the dense gas shells thrown off by dying red supergiant stars before they explode. Such shells power interacting supernovae, where blast waves crash into surrounding material and shine brightly. The study covers stars born at twelve to twenty times the Sun mass and focuses on pulsation-driven mass loss late in life.

Using detailed MESA stellar evolution models with a recipe for pulsation-driven superwinds and shock ejections, the team builds the surrounding medium before explosion and computes density profiles as the wind accelerates. Bursts in the final centuries to decades reach high loss rates and form dense shells matching multi-wavelength observations of recent events like SN 2023ixf. The work links late stellar pulsations to supernova appearance.
arxiv-2510-27389:
John Southworth remeasures the totally eclipsing binary star UZ Draconis to high precision in the twenty-seventh paper of a long series. The system holds two late-F stars in a circular orbit of about three and a quarter days. The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed it in many sectors, yielding hundreds of thousands of high-quality flux measurements, which Southworth models together with published radial velocities.

Total eclipses, previously unrecorded, enable exceptionally precise radii alongside masses modestly above the Sun values. Light curves show spot modulation at the orbital period, and both stars rotate synchronously with the orbit. The derived distance agrees very well with the Gaia parallax distance. System properties match theoretical predictions for an age near six hundred million years and slightly super-solar metallicity.
arxiv-2511-00389:
Fan Zhang and eleven co-authors ask how well multimodal large language models read faces. Facial expression recognition is moving from narrow specialist models toward general models that answer visual questions. Their benchmark, FERBench, runs twenty leading multimodal models across four widely used expression datasets to see where the new approach stands.

The models classify expressions well but reason poorly about them and explain themselves weakly. To close that gap, the team built two large training sets: one of chain-of-thought examples for a cold start, and one for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Their unified model, UniFER-7B, trained on those sets, beat many larger open and closed generalist models. The study maps both the promise and the current limits of general models for affective computing.
arxiv-2511-00689:
Berk Atil, Rebecca Passonneau, and Fred Morstatter ask whether jailbreaks and their defenses travel across languages. Language models receive safety alignment after training, yet attacks still bypass it, and almost all testing happens in a few major languages. Their study is the first systematic multilingual evaluation: ten languages spanning high, medium, and low resources, six models, and two established harm benchmarks.

Two attack families are tested, logical-expression-based and adversarial-prompt-based. Success and defense strength vary widely by language: high-resource languages look safer under plain queries yet more vulnerable to adversarial ones. Simple defenses can work, but their value depends on the language and the model in question. The authors call for language-aware, cross-lingual safety benchmarks as a standing requirement, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2511-00789:
Darshan Kumar, Deepak Jain, and Shobhit Mahajan close a two part study of how the universe expands, using distance ratios from strong gravitational lensing. Lensing ratios, joined with other data, can test expansion and spatial curvature without first assuming one fixed model of the cosmos.

They combine the lensing ratios with three supernova samples and with baryon acoustic oscillation data from the DESI survey's second release. Expansion is tracked through parameters that describe slowing, jerk, and snap. A flat universe stays consistent with the data, and the DESI data tightens the ranges while keeping that agreement. The slowing and jerk values match the standard model, while the snap value remains loosely pinned down.
arxiv-2511-00889:
Pawan Singh Mehta and Biswajyoti Saha study multiple polylogarithms, a family of functions built from nested series that appear across number theory and physics. The region where the defining series converges absolutely is known, but the wider region of conditional convergence has been little explored, especially at depth two and beyond.

Using translation formulas satisfied by these functions, they exhibit a larger open domain where the series converges and defines a holomorphic function. They then build a regularisation process, extending earlier work by Saha, which needs a generalized Euler-Boole summation formula proved in an appendix. The process extends the domain further at integer points, setting up a study of local behavior there.
arxiv-2511-00989:
Asal Meskin and colleagues present Hydra, a model for forecasting several related time series at once, such as readings from many sensors or prices of many assets. Popular backbones have real gaps here: some ignore time order, some treat each series separately, and some are too slow for long histories.

Hydra is a two headed memory module that learns, at test time, which patterns are worth memorizing, favoring the ones that say the most about the data. Its recurrence runs in two dimensions, across time and across series at each step, capturing cross series dependence that single sequence models miss. The design also targets the efficiency problems of attention based models on long series, while avoiding the error build up of purely additive recurrence.
arxiv-2511-01489:
Qurat-ul-ain Shaheen, Katarzyna Budzynska, and Carles Sierra design a structured dialogue system for medical experts who must reach a joint recommendation despite holding different knowledge. Their starting point is a requirement analysis of how such collaborative conversations among specialists actually need to work.

On that base they build an inquiry dialogue game. Each move in the game carries an explanation. So the system records a rich trace of why a recommendation was reached, not just the outcome. The game was implemented as a prototype web application and checked in a formative user study. The study confirmed the design fits the experts' collaboration needs and suggested where dialogue tools could add value in real medical practice.
arxiv-2511-01589:
Wenjie Hua, Hoang Nguyen, and Gangyan Ge bring language modeling to ancient Chinese bronze inscriptions. These texts were cast into ritual vessels. They survive in fragments and are hard to date. They introduce BIRD, a fully encoded dataset for the twin tasks of restoring missing characters and assigning dates, built from standard scholarly transcriptions and labels for their dates.

On top of the data they propose a masked language modeling framework that knows about allographs, the variant shapes a single character can take. A component called Glyph Net links graphemes with their allographs, after domain- and task-adaptive pretraining. In experiments, Glyph Net improved restoration accuracy, while a glyph-biased sampling strategy improved dating, showing that the script's visual structure carries real chronological signal.
arxiv-2511-01689:
Sharan Maiya, Henning Bartsch, Nathan Lambert, and Evan Hubinger open up a stage of chatbot development. Industry uses it, but academia has barely studied it. It is character training: the deliberate shaping of an AI assistant's persona. That covers its apparent values, beliefs, and manner. They present the first open implementation, built on Constitutional AI.

Their pipeline fine-tunes models on synthetic introspective data, text in which the assistant reflects on its own character, rather than relying on system prompts or activation steering. Three open-weights models were trained into 11 example personas, from humorous and deeply caring to malevolent. A revealed-preference analysis shows the personas took hold coherently. They held up against adversarial prompting better than the prompt- and steering-based alternatives. Standard capability benchmarks were barely affected. The full method is released as open source.
arxiv-2511-01889:
Alberto Rojo revisits a 1931 thought experiment of Paul Dirac. Its subject is the magnetic monopole, a particle carrying a lone magnetic charge. Its existence would explain why electric charge comes in discrete units. Dirac's version comes with a solenoid of zero thickness attached: the Dirac string. That subtlety makes even the force between two such monopoles a delicate exercise.

Rojo shows that despite the string's complications, the force between two Dirac monopoles follows a Coulomb-like law, the magnetic mirror of the familiar inverse-square attraction and repulsion between electric charges. The derivation is deliberately basic. It is pitched as a teaching exercise in electricity and magnetism, for college and early graduate students. It clarifies a corner of Dirac's model that textbooks often skip. Those books focus on later, non-Dirac versions instead.
arxiv-2511-01989:
Tuğçe Bilen and Mehmet Özdem design the management layer for 6G networks. In 6G, slices are virtual networks carved from a shared physical plant. They come with guaranteed quality of service. They must be set up and repaired in real time. Static orchestration cannot promise ultra-low latency and high reliability across such shifting demand.

Their framework offers digital twins as a service. Every slice gets its own synced digital twin. The twins are fed by multi-domain telemetry. Deep sequence models predict traffic evolution. They flag service-level risks before they bite. Modular intelligence layers, programmable interfaces, and edge-embedded decision-making enable proactive provisioning, adaptive scaling, and closed-loop assurance, with mathematical formulations for twin fidelity and predictive control. In evaluation the framework improved the service compliance ratio, cut resource over-provisioning, and lowered the average probability of violations.
arxiv-2511-02289:
Gaurav Kottari, Qazi Azhad, and Niteesh Sahni build a tool for governments deciding which of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals to push first. The goals' many indicators are interlinked, so progress on one can accelerate others. Most research studies those links at the level of whole goals while policy is made at the level of individual indicators and targets. The authors review the existing prioritisation methods and find important drawbacks in them.

Their model represents the indicators as a network and uses network theory to quantify each indicator's importance for maximum combined benefit. The method is generic, meant to work for any country, and the team illustrates it with data from India, naming the indicators that matter most there. Supporting evidence from the published literature backs several of the key observations.
arxiv-2511-02389:
Gianluca Giacomelli, Danilo Saccani, Siep Weiland, Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate, and Valentina Breschi train neural controllers for nonlinear machines within hard limits on states and inputs. Their starting point is performance boosting, a design where the controller is a stable neural operator. Closed-loop stability is guaranteed by construction, and training only lifts performance. Constraints, though, were earlier handled with soft penalties instead of hard bars.

The authors fold the alternating direction method of multipliers into the training: extra state and input trajectories are brought in. Training alternates between a gradient update of the controller and a projection step that pushes the trajectories toward feasibility. Stability guarantees survive unchanged, since they are built into the controller's design, though the authors are candid that constraint satisfaction still depends on the method converging. In tests, the method produced fewer constraint violations than penalty-based training, at the cost of more cautious action.
arxiv-2511-02889:
Lucian Mathes and seven colleagues present LIMPID, a free Python tool for reading positron annihilation data in layered materials. Positrons fired into a sample slow down, wander, and annihilate, and the pattern reveals defects. Modeling that walk means solving a diffusion equation for each layer, with its own implantation profile, diffusion traits, and positron affinity.

Their method uses a Markov chain approach to compute annihilation chances layer by layer, and it can fit experimental line-shape data directly. To prove it works, the team analyzed depth-resolved Doppler broadening measurements of a copper layer on silicon. The fit matched the measured profiles very well. The authors say a shared open tool will help labs compare defect results on equal footing.
arxiv-2511-02989:
R. Hill, A. Abghari, and the Euclid Collaboration measure the dusty glow of ordinary star-forming galaxies in the telescope's first data release. Euclid sees millions of galaxies in visible and near-infrared light, but dust shines in the far-infrared, covered by older Herschel and SCUBA-2 surveys. Their 2025 paper stacks those far-infrared maps at the positions of 2.6 million Euclid galaxies, binned by mass and distance.

Fitting the stacked light gave average dust temperatures, dust masses, and star formation rates per bin. Dust share relative to stars fell from redshift one to today. Dust temperature barely depended on stellar mass and drifted toward a floor value over time, which the authors read as heating by older stars taking over. Euclid's catalog alone accounts for over sixty percent of the cosmic infrared background at key wavelengths.
arxiv-2511-03089:
Premananth and Espy-Wilson return to disordered speech in schizophrenia with a second 2025 study, this time on the text of what patients say. Disorganized speech and loose discourse are known signs of the illness and may mark its severity. The pair measure two things with computational language models: surprisal, how unexpected each word is in context, and semantic coherence, how well the meaning holds together across an utterance.

They compare both measures between people with schizophrenia and healthy controls. Then they ask how the measures shift as symptom severity varies. The goal is an objective, number-based read of language disruption that could support diagnosis and track severity over time, rather than resting only on a clinician's impression during a short visit.
arxiv-2511-03689:
Pradeep Niroula and colleagues run a quantum streaming algorithm on a trapped-ion machine whose qubits live long enough to talk with an outside data server. Streaming algorithms face data one item at a time, and quantum versions promise exponential space savings in theory. The catch is keeping qubits coherent while the stream flows past.

Their run implements a pair sketch, the primitive under many streaming methods, and solves a hidden matching problem famed for that space gap. The machine used is Quantinuum's Helios system, chosen for its long-lived ions. The team also compiles the method for fault-tolerant hardware to come. A working demo moves quantum streaming from blackboard promise toward laboratory fact.
arxiv-2511-04189:
Pengyu Yu, Fridtjof Brauns, and M Cristina Marchetti model how feedback between active forces and stress alignment shapes epithelial tissue mechanics. Catalog evidence used a slightly different title; the arXiv record gives the vertex-model title used here. How tissue-scale ordered patterns emerge from cell-scale processes, and how they change flow behaviour, has stayed unclear.

A minimal vertex model couples cytoskeletal active forces to local elastic stress alignment. That loop drives a transition into an ordered solid showing soft elasticity. Stronger activity then triggers collective self-yielding, with flows correlated across the whole tissue. This plastic nematic solid, the authors argue, suits active remodelling during morphogenesis far better than a simple fluid picture.
arxiv-2511-04289:
Antonio Maglio and Fabricio Valencia define basic sections for LA-groupoids whose core-anchor map is injective, objects that blend Lie algebroid and groupoid structure. Sections are the working tool for describing such geometries, and a simpler model than the standard multiplicative sections would ease many arguments.

The new notion turns out to be invariant under Morita equivalence, the natural sameness for groupoids. Basic sections therefore model sections of the stacky Lie algebroids these groupoids present, while remaining equivalent to the well-known multiplicative model. Simplicity without loss is the contribution: results proved with basic sections transfer directly to the stacky objects geometers actually study.
arxiv-2511-04789:
Xiaoda Wang leads eleven authors forecasting Parkinson's progression with a Conditional Neural ODE. The disease reshapes brain structure over time, but each patient follows a distinct path. Onset, speed, and severity vary enough to defeat one-size models.

Recurrent and transformer tools also demand regular, dense MRI scans that clinics rarely have. Their CNODE models each person's trajectory as a continuous curve instead. Conditioning captures individual differences while handling irregular, sparse visits. Such individualized forecasts could act as digital twins, helping clinicians test treatment plans against a patient's own projected course.
arxiv-2511-04889: Jiahe Wang, writing alone, proves that the moduli space of stable n-pointed rational curves is algebraically hyperbolic. The space collects all ways to mark n points on a sphere-like curve, up to deformation. Its boundary divisor, where curves split into joined pieces, is part of the statement. Algebraic hyperbolicity limits the rational and elliptic curves the space can contain, in the spirit of Kobayashi hyperbolicity for complex manifolds. The result adds a central moduli space to the list of spaces with this strong restriction on their internal geometry.
arxiv-2511-05289:
Marius Fracarolli and co-authors test whether added synthetic data can shield clinical time series models from membership inference attacks. Such attacks probe a model to tell if a given patient's record was in its training set, a direct privacy risk.

Their augmentation works in embedding space and aims to make fresh samples close to real ones, yet novel enough to help the model learn. Retraining with that data cut the attacker's true-to-false positive ratio a lot. The work weighs how to keep forecast skill high on health records while proof of membership fades.
arxiv-2511-05889:
Zeyuan Feng, Haimingyue Zhang, and Somil Bansal let people state safety rules for a robot in plain words, and have the robot obey them. As robots enter human spaces, they must follow instructions and respect limits. Older work mapped language to rewards, or covered only narrow limits like avoiding obstacles.

Their framework has three parts. A large language model turns free-form instructions into structured safety rules. A perception module tracks objects in 3D so the rules attach to real things. A predictive controller then filters the robot's motion in real time, enforcing both the worded rules and plain geometry. Tests in simulation and on hardware showed the system held diverse rules across many scenes.
arxiv-2511-06089:
M S S Manasa, Praful Mankar, and Sundaram Vanka study stacking smart radio surfaces in a row to boost MIMO wireless links. Such surfaces reshape signals by tuning many small elements. Placing several in series raises a design question: how should they and the sender be set jointly for the best effect?

The authors derive closed-form best settings for the stacked surfaces under two sender plans, water-filling and flat power. Strikingly, the simpler flat plan nearly matches water-filling once the surfaces are tuned, hinting stacks can cut sender complexity. They also derive the mean capacity and a high-power shortcut form. The results expose a clear trade-off among send power, surface size, and capacity, guiding real setups.
arxiv-2511-06589:
Hua Wang proves interpolation results linking three families of function spaces used across analysis and partial differential equations. Lorentz spaces refine ordinary integrability scales, Morrey spaces track local concentration, and BMO collects functions of bounded mean oscillation. How their intersections embed into plain Lebesgue spaces, and at what cost, is the paper's core question.

Intersecting a Lorentz space with BMO lands continuously inside every Lebesgue space above the base index, and Wang computes the exact growth rate of the embedding constant as the target index grows. A new Lorentz-Morrey family receives the same treatment. New bilinear estimates follow, with applications to global existence and regularity for weak solutions of elliptic and parabolic equations.
arxiv-2511-06689:
Sudip Bera proves the trace Cayley-Hamilton theorem by counting walks on a graph built from a matrix. Every square matrix over a commutative ring defines a weighted directed graph whose structure mirrors the algebra. Determinants and characteristic polynomials already admit elegant readings as signed sums over the graph's cycle covers.

Building on that link, Bera's combinatorial argument produces explicit trace identities. The coefficients of the characteristic polynomial connect directly to traces of the matrix's successive powers. The proof shows how a cornerstone identity of linear algebra, usually reached through algebraic manipulation, can instead be read off the combinatorics of an associated graph.
arxiv-2511-07189:
Marc Jayson Baucas and Petros Spachos strengthen remote patient monitoring with a fog-based Internet of Things platform that understands speech. Remote monitoring eases pressure on scarce healthcare resources, but as patients and sensing devices multiply, server load, data flow, privacy, and ease of interaction all become problems. Their platform pushes computation into a fog layer between devices and the cloud, allocating resources so central servers are not overloaded.

Speech recognition gives patients and clinicians an interactive way to query and control the monitoring system by voice. The authors built a testbed simulating the platform and measured accuracy, latency, and throughput. The results support the design as a viable basis for sound-based healthcare services, showing fog designs can keep remote monitoring responsive as it scales.
arxiv-2511-07389:
Xiaoyou Chen and Mark L Lewis generalize a circle of results about monomial characters and M-groups in group representation theory. Taketa's theorem and Isaacs' generalization of it relate a group's structure to features of its irreducible characters. The authors first extend the definitions of pseudo monomial characters and M-groups into two newer settings: Brauer characters, which live in positive characteristic. Isaacs' pi-partial characters, which see only part of a group.

Within each setting they prove an analogue of Isaacs' generalization of Taketa's theorem, so the structural conclusions survive the move to partial information. They also consider other analogues of classic M-group results in these settings. The work extends a well-developed theory of plain characters to the partial character systems that finite group theorists increasingly use.
arxiv-2511-07689:
Zain Muhammad Mujahid, Dustin Wright, and Isabelle Augenstein stress-test the tools that grade summary honesty. Factual consistency metrics were built for short texts, but long documents strain their input limits and long-range links. A metric that wobbles under harmless rewriting cannot be trusted.

Six widely used reference-free metrics face seven meaning-preserving attacks, from paraphrase and simplification to synonym swaps and compression. Sensitivity patterns show which scores stay steady and which flip without cause. Long-document summarizers are entering law, medicine, and research, so dependable honesty checks are safety equipment. The study tells builders which gauges deserve trust today.
arxiv-2511-07989:
Taja Kuzman Pungersek and colleagues compare fine tuning against prompting for text classification in South Slavic languages. Smaller languages often lag behind English in language technology research. The team tests sentiment in parliamentary speeches, topic labels in news and speeches, and genre identification in web texts across several languages.

Large language models did well with no task specific training, often matching or beating fine tuned BERT style models. Their results were also similar across South Slavic languages and English. Still, the authors note slower speed, higher cost, and less predictable outputs, so fine tuned models remain practical for large scale annotation.
arxiv-2511-08089:
Giacomo Cordoni, Sajay Sunny Mathew, and Christoph Federrath compare simulated and observed rotation in young star clusters. How fast young stars spin shapes their later evolution, so the starting spin pattern matters. High resolution magnetohydrodynamic simulations of star forming clouds with different properties produce initial period distributions for newborn stars.

Simulations reproduce the observed rise of period with stellar mass, especially with weak turbulence relative to gravity or solenoidal driving. Still, simulated stars spin about ten times too fast, likely because the runs capture an earlier stage. Matching observations would require losing most initial angular momentum within the first million years.
arxiv-2511-08289:
Vojtech Novak and co-authors study how sampling noise undermines tuning in variational quantum algorithms, above all the variational quantum eigensolver. With finitely many measure shots, the cost landscape warps, false minima appear, and a winner curse bias rewards lucky noise. Eight classic optimizers, spanning gradient based, gradient free, and metaheuristic families, are benchmarked on chemistry Hamiltonians for small molecules and chains.

Gradient methods often diverge or stall under noise. Tracking the population mean, rather than the biased best individual, corrects the estimator bias in population methods. Adaptive metaheuristics, notably CMA-ES and iL-SHADE, prove most resilient, and the guidelines extend to hardware lean circuits and condensed matter models.
arxiv-2511-08789:
David Pfau writes a teaching note on the bias-variance decomposition, the identity that splits prediction error into a systematic part and a fluctuation part. Textbooks usually prove it only for squared error, yet the same split exists when error is measured by any Bregman divergence, the family tied to maximum likelihood in exponential families.

The generalized result was already known, but no clear standalone derivation existed, so Pfau supplies one for pedagogical purposes. An earlier version sat on his personal website without context; this version adds discussion and points readers to the prior literature. The note is aimed at students and practitioners who use losses beyond squared error and want the same clean intuition about why models err.
arxiv-2511-09289:
J. R. Callingham and seventeen co-authors report the first clear radio evidence of a coronal mass ejection from another star. Such eruptions blast magnetized plasma into space and drive space weather, possibly eroding planets' atmospheres. Until now, stellar eruptions were only inferred indirectly from other flare-like events.

The team caught a burst from the M dwarf StKM 1-1262 matching a solar Type II burst in frequency, timing, and polarization. Type II bursts come from shock waves as an ejection plows through the corona. The detection gives the first observational handle on how often such events strike exoplanets. The authors estimate similar bursts from M dwarfs occur only rarely per star each day.
arxiv-2511-09389:
Lorenzo Branca, Rune Rost, and Tobias Buck present Ray-trax, a fast ray tracer for light moving through turbulent astrophysical gas. Radiative transfer is a notorious bottleneck in computational astrophysics because it is nonlocal, stiff, and coupled to the fluid motion. Their solver targets the time-dependent emission and absorption problem directly on simulation data.

Written in JAX and built for GPUs, Ray-trax is fully differentiable, exposing end-to-end gradients for tuning and inverse problems. It vectorizes across rays and sources and handles any number of frequency bins without redesign. The authors check it against analytic solutions and show light spreading through turbulent media. A gradient-based inverse problem demonstrates the differentiable design in action.
arxiv-2511-09589:
Changjian Xie and Cheng Wang prove convergence for a fast numeric scheme. It solves the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, which governs how magnetization evolves in magnetic materials. The equation is highly nonlinear, and physical solutions must keep the magnetization's length fixed on the unit sphere. Their method combines a third-order backward differentiation formula with one-sided extrapolation from earlier steps.

A projection step restores the length constraint after each solve. The analysis introduces two families of approximate solutions to bridge the discrete and continuous problems rigorously. They establish third-order accuracy in time and fourth-order in space under matched step sizes, plus unique solvability with no step-size assumptions. 1D and 3D numeric examples confirm the theory.
arxiv-2511-09989:
Fushuo Huo, writing alone, examines why multimodal neural networks that shine in the laboratory often falter in the open world. Models that combine text, vision, and audio have advanced reasoning and decision making, yet real settings bring shifting environmental composition, missing modality inputs, and spurious distribution patterns. Humans adapt to such ambiguity naturally, while artificial systems show sharp limits in robustness when signals arrive incomplete or skewed.

The study frames open-world multimodal robustness as the central problem to close the gap between controlled benchmark performance and practical deployment needs. It sets out the failure conditions that matter most, including unpredictable mixtures of inputs and broken cross-modal relationships, as the basis for judging whether a multimodal system is ready for real-world complexity.
arxiv-2511-10189:
Gertian Roose and Erez Zohar take gauged tensor network states off the lattice and into the continuum. Physical states of a gauge theory must obey the Gauss law, and on a lattice the gauge-invariant subspace is spanned exactly by gauged tensor networks. Whether those discrete constructions survive the continuum limit, where lattice spacing vanishes, was not established.

Roose and Zohar demonstrate that the continuum limit of certain gauged tensor networks is well defined. The limit produces a new class of states defined directly in the continuum. Such states could help the non-perturbative study of gauge theories without a lattice, where strong-coupling behavior is otherwise hard to reach. The paper is a bridge result between tensor network methods and continuum field theory.
arxiv-2511-10289:
Sreyan Ghosh and ten co-authors present Music Flamingo, a large audio-language model built to understand music deeply rather than caption it shallowly. Music is layered and information dense, and open models have been held back by scarce high-quality music data and annotations. Their answer starts with data. MF-Skills, a large data set built by a multi-stage pipeline, carries rich captions and question-answer pairs. They span harmony, structure, timbre, lyrics, and cultural context.

An enhanced Audio Flamingo 3 backbone was fine-tuned on that data set. It was then strengthened with a chain-of-thought data set grounded in music theory, followed by reinforcement learning with custom rewards. Across more than ten benchmarks for music understanding and reasoning, Music Flamingo set state-of-the-art results, which the authors offer as a foundation for more human-like musical perception.
arxiv-2511-10389:
Hui Zheng, Jia-Rui Dong, and Si-Hong Zhou update predictions for how charm mesons decay into a light pseudoscalar meson plus a vector meson. New high-precision measurements motivated the rework. Their method, called factorization-assisted topological-amplitude analysis, sorts decay diagrams into a small set of shared parameters fitted to data all at once.

Allowing flavor symmetry breaking inside those parameters lets them pin down contributions that earlier fits had to leave vague. That includes parts of the leading diagram once assumed simple. The fitted strong phases shift a lot compared with the earlier analysis. Branching ratios now match current data well. Several predicted charge-parity asymmetries also differ clearly from older values, awaiting tests at LHCb, BESIII, and Belle II.
arxiv-2511-10489:
Matías G. Gonzalez and Johannes Reuther study spin liquids, exotic magnetic states in which atomic spins keep fluctuating instead of settling into order. They focus on the tetratrillium lattice, a network of tri-coordinated tetrahedra recently proposed to explain the behavior of the langbeinite compound K2Ni2(SO4)3.

Combining classical Monte Carlo simulations with large-N theory, they find a gapped spectrum with flat bottom bands, the signature of a fragile classical spin liquid whose correlations decay exponentially. The same picture holds for the more realistic Ising and Heisenberg versions, with no phase transition at any finite temperature. Quantum calculations for spin one-half then probe which ground states quantum fluctuations might select.
arxiv-2511-10689:
Ashish Kattamuri and five co-authors study what happens to gender bias when text datasets are generated recursively, with language models repeatedly prompted to produce more data from earlier output. The worry is runaway amplification, but their experiments across three generations tell a subtler story.

Starting from three initial bias levels, they track bias with rule-based matching, embedding similarity, and downstream task performance. Instead of amplifying forever, bias moves toward the model's own inherent level: a low starting bias rose by about a third, while a high one fell by about a quarter. Among four mitigations, contrastive augmentation with gender-swapped variants cut downstream bias the most, by roughly 91 percent on average. Embedding metrics scored it worse, a paradox the authors flag for evaluators.
arxiv-2511-10989:
Prab Prasertying, Paulo Garcia, and Warisa Sritriratanarak present a method for guiding a swarm of robots from one formation into another with care. Each robot must know when and where to move, and that joint choice is hard to compute. Real robots add sensor error and control lag, which make a clean plan harder to carry out.

Their algorithm uses shape-based rules to plan the shift, then maps those rules onto the real robots through control, position tracking, and mapping tools. The result is a smooth move from one shape to the next. The authors argue this opens the door to richer joint tasks for swarms.
arxiv-2511-11489:
Jay Shen, Yifeng Tang, and Andrew Ferguson propose power-law attention biases for molecular transformers. The bias is a cheap way to tell the model how atoms sit in space. Transformers lead in many data types. They do not lead in molecular property prediction, though. One cause may be weak structural cues about atom relations.

Their bias weighs attention by the log of the gap between atoms. The form follows power laws from physics. It stays low in complexity. On the QM9 and SPICE data sets, it beat positional encodings and graph attention. It stayed level with costlier Gaussian kernel biases. Good biases even made up for removing the core attention step. That hints at a low-cost path to molecular transformers that users can read.
arxiv-2511-11789:
Jiayi Li, Xiao Liu, and Yansong Feng investigate whether giving language model agents personas quietly biases how groups of agents treat each other. Personas are a standard trick to diversify behavior in multi-agent simulations, but a persona may also change how much an agent is trusted and how forcefully it pushes its views.

Controlled experiments in collaborative problem solving and persuasion measure both effects: trustworthiness, how others receive an agent's opinion, and insistence, how strongly it advocates. Biases appear on both dimensions. Since such systems increasingly simulate human societies and teamwork, persona-driven skew is a methodological hazard that simulation designers need to measure, not assume away.
arxiv-2511-12289:
