Drones and other multi-radio Internet-of-Things devices move across LoRaWAN, cellular, mesh, Wi-Fi, satellite, and proprietary links such as DJI OcuSync. Each hop crosses a trust boundary, potentially voiding authentication, device attestation, and contextual trust signals.

Current zero-trust frameworks assume fairly stable networks and say little about frequent, dynamic radio switching in mobile deployments. This paper frames the problem and its stakes for the first time, arguing that trust-boundary management across heterogeneous wireless environments needs its own treatment. It is a conceptual ground-clearing for securing roaming, multi-radio fleets.
arxiv-2602-09089:
Particle physics now has far more models than signals, and navigating them is its own problem. Conrado Albertus and ten co-authors compile WISPedia, an encyclopedia of Weakly Interacting Slim Particles, light and feebly coupled particles proposed beyond the Standard Model. It systematically gathers theoretical models, effective field theories, and frameworks in one concise reference.

Rather than reviewing every model in depth, entries define essential traits and point to original sources, reviews, tools, and bound compilations. The direct, encyclopedic style aims to help researchers find their way through a crowded landscape quickly. As a community tool, it favors orientation over exhaustive detail.
arxiv-2602-09189:
India runs the world's most complex quota system, mixing upright quotas, where each seeker belongs to at most one group, with cross-cutting quotas, where seekers may qualify for several at once. Orhan Aygün and one co-author study handing-out when cross-cutting quotas follow a layered structure inside a one-to-all matching setup.

They bring the layered choice rule and show it picks the most worthy seeker set. Looking at the combined rule across upright groups, they prove that broad delayed acceptance paired with it is the one steady and cheat-proof setup that kills justified envy. The result gives India's tangled quota design a strict base.
arxiv-2602-09289:
Christine de Kock and one co-author study how real-world events shape online extremist communities, using seven years of records from two ideologically unlike forums, Stormfront and Incels. The mainstream community r/News serves as a reference. Three questions guide the work: how extremist violence affects community behavior, whether news coverage of political entities predicts conversation shifts, and whether language diffuses between mainstream and extremist spaces.

Counterfactual synthesis estimates event-level impacts, while vector autoregression and Granger causality model ongoing links among news signals, behavior, and language change. Results show Stormfront and r/News react more to external stimuli, while Incels shows less cross-group tongue sway and less reply to news and violence. Extremist communities, the authors conclude, are not homogeneous in their coupling to the wider information ecosystem.
arxiv-2602-09389:
Live voice conversion and speaker anonymization must run causally with low delay, yet most systems inject speaker identity as one fixed global embedding while content changes frame by frame. Waris Quamer and three co-authors introduce a streamable synthesizer in their 2026 paper that matches identity to content in time, through a time-varying timbre representation. A global timbre memory expands one timbre instance into compact facets that frame-level content can attend to.

A gate regulates how much the timbre varies, spherical interpolation keeps identity geometry smooth during local changes, and a factorized quantized bottleneck curbs leftover speaker leakage in the content stream. The full system streams end to end with latency well under a tenth of a second on graphics hardware. Trials show gains in naturalness, speaker transfer, and anonymization over leading streaming baselines, framing time-varying timbre as a scalable route to private, expressive speech.
arxiv-2602-09589:
Joint comms and sensing is seen as a core 6G radio power, merging data transfer and outdoor sensing in one system sharing spectrum, waves, and hardware. Wali Ullah Khan and four co-authors survey a key enabling tech in their 2026 paper: send-and-reflect tunable smart panels, which program EM waves across full space.

The survey first lays out basics of joint comms and sensing and of the panel tech. It then sorts recent research across system designs, wave and beam shaping, resource sharing, tuning plans, and learning-based control. Tradeoffs between comms and sensing goals, limited control over travel, and strict hardware limits drive the tech throughout. The paper closes with open tasks and future paths toward smart, flexible, and aware radio networks.
arxiv-2602-09689:
Tuning large ready-made models for a target often lifts in-spread score. Out-of-spread toughness falls as pictures narrow to tuning data. Alireza Abdollahpoorrostam and three co-authors note that blending methods like Model Soups ease the effect by mixing checkpoints. Training and storing dozens of tuned models costs too much. Their 2026 paper offers MonoSoup, a simple data-free post-hoc method using one checkpoint.

MonoSoup splits each layer's update by single value. High-energy ways hold task-single tuning; low-energy ways add noise yet maybe hold left signals good for toughness. Entropy-based rank then alone re-weighs these parts with layer weights for spectral and shape structure. Tests on CLIP models tuned on ImageNet under natural spread shifts, and Qwen models on thought and choice tests, show a usable swap keeping much of multi-checkpoint gains without their cost.
arxiv-2602-10189:
Entanglement percolation aims to create maximal linkage between any two network nodes using only local moves and classic messages between the nodes. A 2026 paper led by Alessandro Romancino, with three co-authors, extends the method to networks where shared linkage varies at random between node pairs. Network shape matters, as in classic spread, but so does the linkage each link carries.

For classic link spread, only the average initial linkage proves key. The quantum link spread method, within the q-swap setup, weakens as the spread widens, hinting that random classic spread may become the optimal local plan in very mixed quantum networks. The study thus splits what chance changes from what it leaves the same.
arxiv-2602-10489:
Wei Chen and six co-authors tackle a useful frustration in graph domain adaptation in a 2026 paper. Methods that transfer knowledge from labeled source graphs to unlabeled targets usually align hand-picked elements, like node attributes or structural statistics. Those choices depend on scenario-exact heuristics and break when the dominant mismatch changes.

Their system, ADAlign, drops the manual selection. It uses a neural characteristic function to identify the most relevant discrepancies in each transfer scenario automatically, then aligns them jointly. By learning what differs instead of assuming it, the method adapts across transfer settings without redesign. The paper places this as a more flexible route to graph transfer in the wild.
arxiv-2602-10589:
Alessandro Andrea Zecchi and five co-authors give a stated quantum circuit for block encoding a class of sparse matrices in a 2026 paper. Block encoding underpins many strong quantum recipes, but general-purpose methods scale exponentially for dense matrices. Matrices with cyclic diagonal structure deserve better.

Built on the linear combination of unitaries system, the circuit projects a complex exponential at a given rate. An fast unitary rule splits it into real and imaginary parts. Gate hardness grows polynomially in qubit count in the worst banded case, and linearly for a simple diagonal matrix. The paper discusses uses to solving ordered linear systems, where the construction turns an abstract subroutine into a concrete, fast circuit.
arxiv-2602-10689:
Changjian Xie and two co-authors design a stable number method for the Landau-Lifshitz equation in a 2026 paper. Micromagnetics simulation faces intertwined difficulties. The magnet force must keep unit norm. Stated integrators demand impractically tiny time steps, and implicit integrators require solving complicated coupled systems. Projection methods add their own instability worries.

The paper presents a first-order structure-keeping method combining Gauss-Seidel iteration, double spread iteration, and Crank-Nicolson iteration. The combination preserves norm constraints while keeping the scheme stable and useful. The method gives micromagnetics simulators a rigorously grounded option that respects the physics of magnet force without paying the usual machine price.
arxiv-2602-10889:
Semra Gurtas Dogan and three co-authors study wave propagation in Lorentz-violating wormhole geometries in a 2026 paper. They analyze massless scalar waves in static, spherically symmetric wormhole spacetimes within a shaped-optical system. The starting point is a general metric with arbitrary lapse function and areal radius.

Deriving bend invariants and regularity settings at the throat, the authors reduce the Klein-Gordon equation to a Helmholtz-type radial wave equation. A place- and rate-dependent strong refractive index emerges from spacetime shape and Lorentz violation, producing rate-dependent wave-optical conduct. Divergences of the index coincide with Killing horizons, while bend-induced turning points control reflection, transmission, and confinement. Analyses of constant, linear, and quadratic lapse profiles map the wave physics.
arxiv-2602-11389:
World models need to understand how objects interact, not just what they look like. Heejeong Nam and four co-authors propose C-JEPA, an object-centric world model that extends masked joint code forecast from image patches to object forms. Masked object states must be inferred from surrounding context.

That structured partial observability creates counterfactual-like queries, discouraging shortcuts and forcing contact-dependent forecast. Visual question answering improves, with a large absolute gain in counterfactual thinking over the same design without object masking. Agent control planning grows far more fast, using a tiny fraction of latent traits at similar results. Formal analysis shows object masking induces useful inductive bias by controlling observability.
arxiv-2602-11489:
The Zeroth Law says systems in balance with a third system are in balance with each other. Jonathas N. da Silva and two co-authors look beyond that endpoint, studying middle stages on the way to balance with classic molecule motion. Ideal gases separated by heat-conducting walls are modelled in two- and three-region setups with argon atoms.

Fluctuations, links, and heat spreads are tracked, showing how heat conduction shapes the time to balance. The part is its detailed focus to the journey, not just the destination: middle stages reveal structure that a final-balance statement alone hides. The work connects a textbook law to the motion that actually enforce it.
arxiv-2602-11689:
Coding agents promise to automate fluid dynamics workflows, but can they actually set up and run simulations in OpenFOAM with little hand-holding? Ke Xiao and five co-authors test tool-using agents with a light configuration that steers them toward reusing tutorials and repairing from logs. The evaluation uses FoamBench-Advanced, covering tutorial-derived cases and flat two-dimensional obstacle-flow tasks.

For tutorial-derived cases, prompt guidance sharply raises completion rates and cuts needless tool calls. For obstacle flows, stronger models markedly improve mesh generation and overall completion over earlier models. The findings show agents can already run a range of simulations with minimal setup, while model capability still decides success on tasks that demand geometry and mesh creation.
arxiv-2602-11789:
Decentralized optimization spreads machine learning across a network of nodes that work together through local links. Stochastic gradient noise often differs from node to node, but its effect on design and cost has stayed unclear. Hongxu Chen and two co-authors propose D-NSS, a method with node-specific sampling. Its sample cost depends on the simple average of local standard deviations, not worst-case or root-mean-square measures.

That link gives tighter bounds than existing methods. The authors also derive a matching lower bound under uneven variance, proving their link is optimal. A variance reduction extension, D-NSS-VR, improves sample cost further under mean-squared smoothness while keeping the simple-average link. Tests confirm the theory and show both methods work well for network learning with uneven noise.
arxiv-2602-11889:
Singular elliptic problems driven by mixed local-nonlocal operators combine a local term with a fractional term and a spiky term that blows up near zero. Dhanya and one co-author study such a problem with a parameter that tunes the spiky term, proving a global result on many answers. A sharp threshold separates regimes where answers exist, do not exist, or come in multiples. That threshold result is new for spiky problems with mixed terms.

A Hopf-type strong comparison principle adapted to this nonlinear setting provides the main math tool for the many-answers result. The authors also investigate fine properties essential for variational analysis, including a uniform bound on answers and a result comparing Sobolev and Hölder local minima. The tools developed here interest others beyond this problem, working across a broader class of mixed problems.
arxiv-2602-12089:
When people negotiate alongside AI, does it matter whether the AI advises, coaches, or simply acts for them? Kehang Zhu and four co-authors ran an online experiment with 243 participants playing three three-person bargaining games, each game offering one form of language-model help: proactive advice, reactive coaching, or autonomous delegation.

Participants strongly preferred the advisor, chosen 44 percent of the time, over the delegate at 19 percent. Yet only groups with delegate access significantly raised their collective surplus. The gap traces to a human filter: AI proposals created more joint value than manual ones in every mode, but advised and coached users often edited, overrode, or ignored them. The delegate's edge came from bypassing that filter, not from a different AI capability.
arxiv-2602-12389:
Forecasting a temporal knowledge graph means predicting future facts from both structure within each snapshot and change across time. Siyuan Li led this work with seven co-authors, noting that most methods are stateless. They rebuild entity views at each timestamp from a narrow query window, forgetting long-term links and suffering episodic amnesia. That decay hurts long-horizon forecasts most.

Their framework, Entity State Tuning, gives forecasters persistent, evolving entity states, independent of the encoder used. A global state buffer is updated in a closed loop. A topology-aware perceiver injects state priors into structural encoding. A temporal module merges state-enhanced events with a sequence backbone. A dual-track update writes context back to memory, balancing plasticity and stability. Tests show consistent gains across backbones and top scores overall.
arxiv-2602-12589:
His robust mean tool, from 2012, handles heavy-tailed data while matching old scores for sub-Gaussian data, yet its limit action was largely open. Zhijun Cai led this work with two co-authors, looking at Catoni-type robust tools in two settings. The first is mean guessing for heavy-tailed data. The second is linear fitting with heavy-tailed shocks.

His frame has spread across stats, random methods, and machine learning, but Central Limit Theorem and rare-event questions stayed open. For mean guessing, the team proves Berry-Esseen bounds and mid spread rules, covering both known and unknown variance settings. For linear fitting, the linked tool proves steady and meets a multi-way Berry-Esseen bound. Readers get the first full limit picture for Catoni-type guessing, grounding a widely used robust tool in precise limit theory for heavy-tailed data.
arxiv-2602-12789:
Plasma wakefield accelerators promise compact particle acceleration, and surface plasmons on a cylindrical surface offer a new route to drive them. Bifeng Lei and seven co-authors study resonant plasmon excitation from the beating of two co-moving laser pulses on a smooth plasma-vacuum cylinder. They derive formulas for the plasmon dispersion, field strength, geometric coupling, and resonance conditions, then validate them with full three-dimensional particle simulations.

Curvature turns out to matter: geometric effects shift the dispersion and allow resonance by beat waves, which flat surfaces or a single laser cannot achieve. Under matched resonance, a few-gigawatt laser pair can drive a strong plasmon wakefield, within reach of modern fibre lasers. The mechanism points toward portable laser-driven accelerators built on tabletop-scale hardware.
arxiv-2602-12989:
Keyphrases help organise documents, and generative models can predict phrases that never appear in the text, called absent keyphrases. Maël Houbre and two co-authors test whether that ability makes models more homogeneous: for two documents on the same subjects, does a model predict the same keyphrases for both? Current benchmarks ignore homogeneity, so the team introduces a method to measure it.

Surprisingly, extraction methods, which only pick phrases from the text, compete with generative models on homogeneity. Worse, generating absent keyphrases can actually harm homogeneity rather than help it. The finding challenges a natural intuition: associating documents with unmentioned notions does not automatically yield consistent indexing. Data, code, and prompts are public for others to build on.
arxiv-2602-13189:
Sterile neutrinos at keV scale are a popular dark matter candidate, produced in the early Universe by the Dodelson-Widrow mechanism, yet that production faces tight astrophysical constraints. Debtosh Chowdhury and Md Sariful Islam study sterile neutrinos with mass varying through a scalar field coupled to both active and sterile neutrinos. That novel mechanism opens new parameter space that generates the observed dark matter relic while addressing the Hubble tension.

Future X-ray missions can probe the resulting parameter space fully. If X-ray searches find nothing in that space, the mass-varying scenario faces serious trouble; if they find a signal, it would support both the sterile neutrino and the Hubble-tension resolution. The paper thus ties a dark matter candidate to a testable cosmological payoff.
arxiv-2602-13289:
Shrinking vision-language models for edge devices saves memory, but it can also make their confident answers less trustworthy. This study is the first to map that trade-off in full for visual question answering, testing two models across bit widths with data-free and data-aware quantization methods. Both accuracy and reliability fell as models were compressed, though data-aware methods softened the damage.

A confidence estimator called the Selector, adapted for quantized multimodal models, clawed back much of the lost reliability across quantization levels and shifted data. The best mix, four-bit data-aware quantization plus the Selector, neared uncompressed performance while using about 75 percent less memory. Paul Jonas Kurz leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13389:
Light from distant galaxies carries a fingerprint of the early universe, but neutral hydrogen between galaxies can dim the Lyman alpha line, even far from its core. Reading that dimming demands knowing what spectrum left the galaxy in the first place, and that emergent spectrum varies wildly with the gas around each galaxy. This paper builds a flexible empirical model for it, describing emergent Lyman alpha brightness, line velocity offsets, and hydrogen alpha brightness as probability distributions tied to ultraviolet magnitude.

Fitted to galaxy observations near redshift 5 to 6 from VLT MUSE and JWST NIRCam, the model matched independent Subaru equivalent-width data better than prior models. Survey selection effects were modeled forward in the fit. Its broad width and offset distributions could ease Lyman alpha transmission early in reionization, and it flags GN-z11-like outliers. Samuel Gagnon-Hartman leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13489:
Recording brain electricity and brain imaging together gives both timing and location, but combining EEG with fMRI is artifact-prone, especially the heartbeat-driven ballistocardiogram artifact. This proof-of-concept study tests simultaneous EEG-fMRI at a low field of 0.55 tesla during a visual task, characterizing gradient and heartbeat artifacts in that environment. Lower field strength appears to shrink the heartbeat artifact relative to high-field systems at 1.5, 3, and 7 tesla.

That shrinkage promises cleaner denoising with signal integrity intact. A joint pipeline using the EEG power envelope to predict the BOLD response further shows EEG-based estimation of blood-flow coupling is feasible at 0.55 tesla, opening a gentler environment for joint imaging. Parsa Razmara leads the work with eight co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13589:
Long-time behavior of waves under the defocusing nonlinear Schrodinger equation with a finite-genus algebro-geometric background is the subject of this paper, which derives asymptotics in four space-time regions. The leading term is, up to a constant, the background solution shifted in its parameter, while the subleading term decays at different rates across regions.

In the two transition regions, the decay is of order t to the minus one-third, with coefficients involving an integral of the Painleve XXXIV transcendent. The results come from a nonlinear steepest descent analysis of the associated Riemann-Hilbert problems, a standard but demanding technique for such asymptotics. Engui Fan leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13689:
Insertion tasks demand precise contact-rich interaction that vision alone cannot resolve, yet naive fusion of vision and touch often fails to help consistently. This paper proposes a Cross-Modal Transformer for visuo-tactile fusion, combining wrist-camera views with tactile signals through structured self- and cross-attention. A physics-informed regularization further stabilizes tactile embeddings by encouraging bilateral force balance, reflecting principles of human motor control.

On the TacSL benchmark, the transformer with symmetry regularization reached 96.59 percent insertion success, beating naive and gated fusion baselines and nearly matching the privileged wrist-plus-contact-force configuration at 96.09 percent. Two lessons stand out: touch is indispensable for precise alignment, and principled fusion unlocks the complementary strengths of vision and touch. Wonju Lee leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14089:
Zhizhao Luo and three co-authors present a 2026 arXiv system for reasoning over tables with language models. Prompt-only methods lack step-level checks, while agent methods check only locally and rarely backtrack. Both routes let errors spread and waste tokens on redundant paths.

Their system, TabTracer, tracks table states step by step, with typed operations and light numeric and format checks for reliable rewards. A search tree over candidate states uses reflection scores to guide selection and rollback via versioned snapshots. Budget-aware pruning, deduplication, and state hashing cut token cost. Tests on TabFact, WikiTQ, and related benchmarks gauge its gains.
arxiv-2602-14189:
Samir Abdaljalil and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv problem: when should a language model refuse to answer science questions? Models now verify scientific claims, but tests usually force a definite answer. In science, an unsupported answer can do more harm than abstaining, the authors argue.

Their framework splits claims into minimal conditions, audits each against evidence with natural language inference, and then chooses to support, refute, or abstain. Tests on SciFact and PubMedQA, in closed-book and open-domain settings, cover six diverse models. Raw accuracy varied only modestly across models, while confidence-based abstention cut error risk substantially, showing restraint as a safety lever for scientific AI.
arxiv-2602-14589:
Gabriel Roccabruna and two co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv benchmark for temporal reasoning and planning in vision-language models. Agents must plan hard goals by joining sight, sub-goal splits, and runs, with steps ordered by a Time Run Order graph ensuring each step runs only after its needs hold. Prior work on time run lore leaned on auto notes, straight-chain guesses, or text-only inputs.

MATEO, or MultimodAl Time Run Order, fills that gap with a pro mixed recipe corpus, penned through a set editorial plan that splits instructions into discrete steps paired with images. Time run notes were gathered as graphs via a scalable crowd-sourcing line. Six top vision-language models were tested on MATEO, probing temporal reasoning and planning skills needed for real-world agent tasks.
arxiv-2602-14989:
Shrivastava and colleagues build a benchmark for vision-language models on thermal images, a domain where strong RGB models often fail. Thermal sensing matters where visible light fails, from night surveillance and search and rescue to self-driving cars and medical screening. Thermal images encode temperature rather than color or texture, so they demand skills that RGB benchmarks never test. The team introduces ThermEval-B, with roughly 55000 thermal question-answer pairs.

ThermEval-B joins public sets with ThermEval-D, a new set giving dense per-pixel temperature maps with body-part labels across indoor and outdoor scenes. Testing 25 open and closed models, the team finds steady failure at temperature-grounded reasoning, decay under colormap changes, and fallback to language priors. Prompting and fine-tuning help only slightly, showing that thermal understanding needs its own dedicated evaluation.
arxiv-2602-15189:
Brach and colleagues offer ScrapeGraphAI-100k, a data set for schema-constrained generation. Fitting output to a given JSON schema powers tool use, extraction, and knowledge base building. Yet public data sets stay small, synthetic, or text-only, rarely pairing real pages with real prompts and schemas. This corpus offers 93695 schema-constrained events from opt-in telemetry in mid-2025. It was deduped and evened by schema from 9 million events.

The corpus spans 18000 schemas across 15 named languages plus a long-tail Other group. English and Traditional Chinese make 88 percent of found content. Each instance pairs Markdown pages with a prompt, schema, response, and structural conformance labels. The team maps diversity of structure and finds sharp failure thresholds as complexity grows. As a case study, a small student fine-tuned on this data tracks its GPT-5-nano teacher. It still trails a 30-billion-size model with about 3 billion active weights.
arxiv-2602-15389:
Lin and colleagues offer a random Schrödinger rule to study the motion of giant atoms coupled to a waveguide. It covers two gaps in current work: thin study of steady coupling and many bursts. A key result is that steady coupling, not like point coupling at set spots, snaps the fixed gap rule, thus dulling clash hits in these systems.

A handy edge of the method is that auto- and cross-link tools can straight show tangled light output and intake flows and time-delay hits in these systems. Also, the method plainly takes many bursts, without growing tangle as the count of bursts rises. This trait allows study of multi-burst initial states of the waveguide, such as warm and pressed initial states. All told, the method gives a strong tool for probing giant atoms coupled to a waveguide, notably for steady coupling and multi-burst systems.
arxiv-2602-15489:
Solomonik and colleagues study whole social media lives, not single platforms in isolation. They draw on a quota sample of one thousand people in the United States, and they coin the phrase social media journeys to cover each person's full path across platforms. The aim is to learn what people have used, why they moved, and what pushed them away or pulled them in.

The team finds push and pull forces at work across the whole landscape, and it shows how each generation took up platforms to meet its own needs. The work shifts the field toward a whole-life view of social media use, with lessons for design, for rules, and for how platforms are run. It will suit readers who want to see platform choice as a life story, not a single sign-up.
arxiv-2602-15689:
Linder and colleagues argue that refusal rules for cybersecurity requests in large language models need a rethink. Current rules lean on broad topic bans or offence-focused taxonomies, which yield inconsistent calls, over-restrict legitimate defenders, and break under obfuscation or split requests. The authors insist that good refusal must weigh offensive risk against defensive benefit explicitly, rather than resting on stated intent or offensive labels alone.

Their content-based frame scores requests on five dimensions: offensive action contribution, offensive risk, technical complexity, defensive benefit, and expected frequency among legitimate users, all grounded in what the request technically asks for. They show the frame resolves inconsistencies in current frontier model behaviour and lets organisations build tunable, risk-aware refusal policies. The paper offers auditors a concrete way to design and check cyber refusal rules.
arxiv-2602-15789:
Solyaev and colleagues review and extend general answers for shift fields in static problems of uniform strain gradient elastic theory. They not only review existing answers but derive new forms, showing that all classic elastic answers, including Boussinesq-Galerkin, Papkovich-Neuber, Naghdi, Lamé, Love, and Boussinesq, extend simply to the strain gradient frame. In general, strain gradient elastic theory allows any classic general answer form joined with a Helmholtz split for the gradient part of the shift field.

Match is also shown between the given Papkovich-Neuber form and earlier general answers put forth by Mindlin in 1964, Lurie et al. in 2006, and Charalambopoulos et al. in 2020. The team further shows links between stress functions of varied general answers and shows their wholeness. The paper serves both as a survey of the field and as a source of new forms that unify classic and strain gradient answers.
arxiv-2602-16689:
Ferdinand Kapl and co-authors ask if object-centric vision aids compositional generalization, the skill of reasoning about new mixes of known concepts. That skill is core to human thought and a hard test for machine learning. Object-centric codes split a scene into objects, and many claim they aid such generalization. Yet systematic proof in visually rich settings was thin.

The team builds a visual question answering benchmark across three controlled visual worlds, CLEVRTex, Super-CLEVR, and MOVi-C. They compare vision encoders with and without object-centric bias, controlling for data mix, sample size, code size, downstream size, and compute. Object-centric routes win in harder settings and learn from fewer images, while dense codes win only in easier settings at much higher downstream cost.
arxiv-2602-16789:
Herold Dehling, Daniel Vogel, and Martin Wendler compare two CUSUM-type change-point tests built from U-statistics, called first-vs-full and first-vs-last. Both routes appear in the literature, raising the natural question of whether they truly differ and which wins in which data setting. In large samples, the tests are similar: asymptotically equivalent under the null and under local alternatives.

In small samples, notable gaps can appear, matching varied behavior under fixed alternatives. The authors derive a simple criterion for which test is more powerful. Detailed examples cover Gini's mean difference, sample variance, and Kendall's tau. For scale changes judged by Gini's mean difference, first-vs-full wins exactly when scale shifts from smaller to larger, regardless of distribution or change location. Simulations and data examples illustrate the results.
arxiv-2602-16889:
Thomas Descamps and co-authors show in situ calibration of microwave loss and gain using a cryogenic on-chip attenuator. Accurate in situ calibration of microwave attenuation and amp chain noise is essential for superconductor quantum circuits. The compact, self-calibrating noise source is a chromium loss device on chip. It is heated by current with nanowatt-level power and built directly into a coaxial microwave line at the mixing-chamber stage.

By comparing Johnson-Nyquist noise from Joule heating and microwave heating, measured through the amplification chain, input line attenuation is determined. Chain gain follows from that, with no need to know the loss device temperature. The device responds in milliseconds. Gain and added noise of a cryogenic amplification chain are determined over the four-to-eight gigahertz band. That gives a simple, accurate route to characterize near-quantum-limited parametric amps for superconductor-qubit readout.
arxiv-2602-16989:
Chentong Hao and Minmao Wang present a low-cost retrieval system for the WSDM Cup 2026 multilingual retrieval task. English queries must retrieve relevant documents from about ten million news articles in Chinese, Persian, and Russian, outputting the top one thousand ranked results per query. The system follows a four-stage pipeline.

It combines language-model-based query expansion with BM25 candidate retrieval, dense ranking using long-text representations, and pointwise re-ranking of the top twenty candidates, preserving dense order for the rest. On official evaluation, the system achieves strong normalized discounted cumulative gain and judged scores at rank twenty. Ablation experiments quantify each stage's contribution and analyze query expansion, dense ranking, and top-k reranking under limited compute budgets.
arxiv-2602-17089:
Xinghao Dong led a three-author team comparing generative models for a hard physics task: learning stochastic closure models for turbulent flow. Diffusion models, borrowed from generative AI, produce diverse, high-quality samples, but their slow iterative sampling is a drawback. The paper tests transport-based alternatives on two-dimensional Kolmogorov flows to find a faster route.

Flow matching in a lower-dimensional latent space came out ahead, allowing single-step sampling far faster than diffusion-based methods. To keep the sampled closure term physically faithful, the authors compare joint training against two explicit guards: metric-preserving and geometry-aware constraints. Both routes kept key topological information from the original system, so good closure models could be learned without huge training sets.
arxiv-2602-17489:
J. Phillips led a four-author team predicting two-dimensional pi-electron half-metallic ferrimagnets. The team sketches a route to organic conductors with a fully spin-polarized Fermi surface at a singular flat band. Their spins live in pi-orbitals of nanographenes, pointing in opposed ways. The crystal is a honeycomb lattice whose cell pairs two spin one-half molecules: Aza-3-Triangulene, with orbital degeneracy, and 2-Triangulene.

The system is half-metallic, with ferrimagnetic order yet zero net moment per cell. Density functional theory plus a Hubbard model give its magnetic links, bands, intrinsic Anomalous Hall effect, and spin excitations. Links between molecules prove very large, near fifty-nine millielectronvolts. Spin excitation spread points to stability near one hundred kelvin. With magnetization off-plane, spin orbit coupling in graphene opens a tiny topological gap, giving quantized Hall conductance at tens of millikelvin, though heat smears it above one kelvin.
arxiv-2602-17589:
Philip Mannheim revisits the simple harmonic oscillator and finds it less simple than textbooks claim. Beside each familiar normalizable energy state sits a non-normalizable partner with the same positive energy. That partner is built not on the usual vacuum, but on the vacuum killed by a distinct operator product.

Those stationary states come with companions whose wave functions grow linearly in time. The Hamiltonian's eigenbasis is thus incomplete, and each energy level becomes an exceptional point of non-diagonalizable Jordan-block form. A probability-conserving inner product survives the growth and yields zero-norm states. A shift into a Stokes wedge domain restores normalizability, backing Mannheim's case for antilinearity over Hermiticity.
arxiv-2602-17789:
Maximilian Meyer-Mölleringhof and team cast Förster resonance energy transfer, or FRET, theory for ultrafast nonlinear response of tiny systems. They introduce an exact time-dependent split of the molecular stats operator into system and bath parts. With plain bath evolution, that split extends the old Förster master rule.

Where the old rule tracked only state odds, the new one covers the full reduced stats object of the system. Old FRET theory applies when coupling between molecules is weak and system-bath coupling is strong, yet the new time non-local master rule stays valid even as system-bath coupling vanishes. It predicts rapid initial in-step evolution of populations from a brief coherence link, causing a slippage of the initial setup that persists during later rate-controlled transfer. Check against exact results confirms a clear gain over earlier forms and maps the range of reach.
arxiv-2602-17889:
Noah Oyeniran and Chongze Hu predict order-to-disorder shifts in mixed MXenes with an improved basic-physics Monte Carlo frame. Improvements include shape settling and picked atom swapping during Monte Carlo rounds for more accurate and fast forecasts. Ti-Mo-based double transition metal carbide MXenes serve as the model system. Simulations reveal surface termination and layout settings as key drivers of chemical order.

Out-of-plane MXenes with molybdenum drift to outer metal layers form only under oxygen coating at prismatic sites. In contrast, oxygen coating at octahedral sites and fluorine coating at both sites always promote out-of-plane MXenes with titanium drifted to outer layers. Changing the fluorine-to-oxygen ratio at prismatic sites or swapping atomic layout within MXene grids can induce an order-to-disorder shift, giving readers a predictive map of order in these materials.
arxiv-2602-18389:
Pinki Pradhan and two co-authors improve clustering when distance information is scarce and noisy. Their 2026 paper works in the weak-strong oracle model of Bateni and co-authors, where a cheap weak oracle and a costly strong oracle both answer distance queries. The goal is strong guarantees for k-means and k-center grouping while rationing strong queries.

The team adapts k-means++ to the weak-strong setting, reaching a constant approximation for k-means with only a small number of strong queries, far fewer than Bateni's method. For k-center, a simple ball-carving method gives a six-times-approximation using a comparable query budget, improving on the earlier fourteen-times bound. Real-world tests confirm the new methods beat Bateni's algorithms in practice. The work makes clustering under limited distance information markedly cheaper.
arxiv-2602-18589:
Jiayang Shi and two co-authors benchmark diffusion models for CT. Their 2026 paper notes diffusion models have emerged as strong priors for inverse problems. While computed tomography is theoretically linear, practical challenges include correlated noise, artifacts, reliance on geometry, and misaligned ranges. That makes direct use harder than in image generation.

To test diffusion models and compare them with established methods, the team introduces DM4CT, a broad benchmark with medical and industrial data in sparse and noisy setups. They acquire a high-resolution CT set at a high-energy synchrotron site and evaluate all methods in real conditions. Ten recent diffusion methods are benchmarked with seven baselines, including unsupervised and supervised methods. Analysis details behavior, strengths, and limits, with data public and code open-sourced.
arxiv-2602-18689:
Finding bugs by fuzzing a software library needs test harnesses that can call functions in realistic orders, not just fixed scripts. Harrison Green, with two co-authors, introduces stitching in 2026. It builds those orders on the fly from small, reusable pieces.

A static type system governs how objects pass between pieces. A checked typestate tracks facts such as object state and cross-function preconditions. So one specification can describe a wide space of valid uses. Built into the STITCH tool, the method uses language models to set up projects and triage crashes. It beat four rivals on benchmarks. It found 131 new bugs across widely used open-source projects.
arxiv-2602-18889:
The thymus trains T cells to tolerate the self, yet its three-dimensional architecture remains poorly understood. Haochen Yang, with seven co-authors, introduces SampEuler in 2026. It is a shape descriptor based on the Euler characteristic transform, built to resist noise.

Theory shows SampEuler is stable. Tests on a benchmark dataset confirm it through pairwise similarity analysis. The team then applies it to new two-dimensional images of mouse thymi by age group. SampEuler beats both persistent homology methods and deep learning models at detecting subtle, localised differences linked to aging. A vectorisation and visualisation frame keeps the results easy to read. It helps pinpoint structural features that distinguish thymi by age. In short, shape can reveal age. That is the promise here.
arxiv-2602-19089:
Photorealistic 3D human animation still eludes most methods. Qi Sun, with four co-authors, closes the gap in 2026 with Ani3DHuman. Kinematic methods miss non-rigid motion, like cloth movement. Video diffusion methods capture it, but add artefacts and lose look.

The framework marries both approaches. A layered representation splits rigid motion from residual non-rigid motion. Kinematics generate rigid motion and a coarse rendering. That render guides a video model to restore non-rigid detail. Standard deterministic samplers fail here, since initial renders sit out of distribution. A self-guided stochastic sampler fixes the problem. Random sampling supplies photorealism. Self-guidance preserves look. Restored videos then supervise optimisation of the motion field left over. Tests show lifelike results ahead of existing methods.
arxiv-2602-19189:
Splitting graphs into atoms simplifies hard problems. Pei Heng, with two co-authors, links atom splitting to maximum size search order in 2026. Applying a convex push to the first-numbered node and its neighbours in such an order yields an atom. That result anchors a recursive splitting method.

The method needs no minimal filling and avoids finding clique minimal separators. It aligns closely with chordal graph splitting results. Combined with two existing convex expansion methods, it significantly outperforms prior methods on efficiency. Divide and conquer thus gains a leaner graph-decomposition tool.
arxiv-2602-19289:
Finding where a molecule settles on a catalyst surface is a bottleneck in catalyst work done by computer. The hard part is not only the cost of accurate energy math, but proposing starting spots that relax into the right low-energy basins. Diffusion-based tools improved success rates, yet they need about a hundred steps per sample, which adds up fast.

AdsorbFlow, from Jiangjie Qiu and four colleagues, replaces that slow sampling with a direct flow model. It learns an energy-guided flow over the rigid spots of an adsorbate, its shifts and turns, so a spot can be made at once rather than cleaned up step by step. Energy data steer the flow toward realistic, low-energy shapes. The result is faster spot generation for catalyst screening, where many candidate surfaces must be tried.
arxiv-2602-19389:
Pricing a fusion power plant means turning physics and geometry into auditable costs. Simon Woodruff and three co-authors document the 2024-2025 work of the Clean Air Task Force International Working Group on Fusion Cost Analysis. The paper also covers its extensions to the CATF-supported branch of the pyFECONs costing framework. The work builds on the standards-aligned account chart and physics-to-economics workflow set by ARPA-E.

The group reorganizes the framework around three cost-driver tracks: magnetic, inertial, and magneto-inertial fusion energy. In Account 22.1.3, a generic driver placeholder is treated as a controlled swap-point, replaced by a full cost-account treatment of the dominant driver in each class. A probabilistic layer then folds materials price, maturity, and learning-curve uncertainty into cost distributions, tracing plant costs back to requirements and geometry.
arxiv-2602-19689:
Two-sided platforms match users to users, where a match, called a date here, needs mutual interest and action on both sides. Kazuki Sekiya and four co-authors note that naive ranking by guessed dating odds piles views onto a few highly active users, causing jams and puffed-up efficiency. They frame matching users as a many-to-many task, designing mixers that turn guessed login, like, and reply odds into tips under focus limits.

They introduce effective dates, a score that docks matches with swamped receivers to adjust for jams. Their exposure-capped deferred acceptance (ECDA) caps receiver views in expected likes or dates, not headcount. Tuned test runs on guesses from a large Japanese dating site show ECDA lifts effective dates and dating odds for receivers despite fewer total dates. A large regional field trial confirms the effects in practice.
arxiv-2602-19889:
Fitting a model to time-series data is often easy, but saying how much to trust its forecasts is much harder. A 2026 arXiv paper by Mohamed Akrout and Dan Wilson frames that trust problem through inverse problem theory.

Building on Koopman-inspired identification methods for nonlinear dynamics, the authors treat a forecast as a rough measurement. In principle that measurement should let one work back to the starting state. Prediction error then becomes the error of solving the inverse problem that would produce that prediction. Tests on numerical models and on experimental data show the approach gives a robust gauge of model performance. Readers gain a principled uncertainty measure for data-driven dynamical models.
arxiv-2602-19989:
Graham conjectured that any set of nonzero residues modulo a prime can be arranged with all partial sums distinct. That claim was recently proved for large primes, but it stays open for general abelian groups. A 2026 arXiv paper by Simone Costa and Stefano Della Fiore improves the best known result for cyclic groups.

The prior result, by Bedert and Kravitz, used rectification plus a two-step probabilistic argument. It handled sets up to a certain size governed by the least prime divisor. Costa and Della Fiore replace the second step with a one-shot probabilistic approach, again after rectification, improving the exponent in the size bound. The same one-shot approach also works in the weaker setting, where only local constraints are imposed, and the Lovász Local Lemma then yields weak sequencings. The paper thus sharpens cyclic-group sequenceability on two fronts at once.
arxiv-2602-20689:
Crisp edge maps, one pixel wide, remain a challenge for edge detection in classic and learning methods. Bedrettin Cetinkaya and two co-authors note that approaches lean on two post-processing steps, Non-Maximum Suppression and skeleton-based thinning, which block end-to-end learning, being non-differentiable. Worse, all crisp edge methods depend on post-processing. Their module removes that dependence.

MatchED is a lightweight, plug-and-play supervision module with about twenty-one thousand parameters, appendable to any model for end-to-end crisp edge learning. Each iteration matches predicted and ground-truth edges one-to-one by distance and confidence, aligning training with testing. Tests on four data sets show MatchED lifts models, raising Average Crispness by two to four times over baselines. It boosts baseline scores by twenty to thirty-five percent in ODS under crispness-emphasized tests. Similar gains appear in OIS and AP.
arxiv-2602-20789:
Giovanni Covone and one co-author ask how much useful work starlight can do for photosynthesis on other worlds. They build a radiative-thermodynamic model that caps the power a planet can harvest and sets limits on the longest wavelengths that can still drive high-energy photochemistry.

Applied to Earth-like planets getting the same total starlight, the model confines single-photon oxygenic photosynthesis to near-infrared bands around Sun-like stars. Around late M dwarfs it points to bluer light. Around Sun-like stars the usable photon supply runs about five times higher. Cool M dwarfs pay twice: fewer usable photons and a smaller share of shortwave energy.
arxiv-2602-20889:
Elliptical galaxies hold both stars and dark matter, and separating the two takes precise gravitational lensing. Tian Li and nine co-authors analyze a rare double-source-plane lens, nicknamed the Jackpot lens, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their two-component model pairs a stellar mass model with a generalized dark-matter halo, using the double geometry to break a stubborn degeneracy.

The model lets the stellar mass-to-light ratio vary with radius and the halo shape vary. Even so, the data favor the standard picture: a near-constant mass-to-light ratio with a Salpeter-like initial mass function, and a halo consistent with the standard NFW form. The inferred stellar mass sits slightly above typical literature relations, within their scatter. The method offers a template for future dark-matter studies with large lens samples from Euclid.
arxiv-2602-20989:
Pulling apart the layers of a real photo, like a logo from the surface beneath it, is hard because shading, shine, and slant tangle up. Zheng Gu, Min Lu, Zhida Sun, Dani Lischinski, Daniel Cohen-Or, and Hui Huang present a layer-splitting setup in this 2026 arXiv paper, built on large diffusion base models. A pretrained model is tuned lightly, and cycle-steady tuning trains splitting and joining at once.

That two-way guidance keeps split and rejoined images in line, which helps most where layers mix in hard ways. A stepwise self-improving loop then grows the training set with high-grade model-made cases. Tests show true, coherent splits that carry over to other layer types, pointing toward one shared setup.
arxiv-2602-21089:
Catalytic methods promise small workspace with lent memory, but matching the best non-catalytic bounds in poly-time has been elusive. Petr Chmel, Aditi Dudeja, Michal Koucky, Ian Mertz, and Ninad Rajgopal achieve it in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their arrow-link method runs in poly-time with log-size workspace and below-linear catalytic space, matching state-of-the-art non-catalytic bounds.

A coin-flip variant using only log-size many random bits nearly matches the fastest free-space time bounds. The same catalytic budget also covers edit distance, longest shared run, and discrete Frechet distance in poly-time. The work pushes catalytic work onto the frontier before held by plain space-bounded methods.
arxiv-2602-21189:
Optimizing for pass-at-k, success within k tries, can quietly damage pass-at-one, success on the first try. Anas Barakat and three co-authors explain why in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pass-at-one often remains a hard constraint from latency, cost, imperfect verifiers, and the need for a reliable single-shot fallback, so the trade-off matters practically.

The cause is prompt interference: shared parameters couple prompts, so gains on some prompts hurt others. Pass-at-k gradients reweight prompts toward low-success ones, and when those prompts interfere negatively, the update rotates away from the pass-at-one direction. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and coding illustrate the mechanism. Readers learn when multi-sample optimization helps and when it backfires.
arxiv-2602-21289:
Red giants stripped by companions just before the helium flash should produce a continuum of binaries, from hot subdwarfs to undermassive red clump stars. Pranav Nagarajan and six co-authors test those models against Gaia data in this 2026 arXiv paper. They simulate a Milky Way-like galaxy with realistic star formation and dust, generate epoch astrometry with Gaia's scanning law, and fit it with the Gaia DR3 model cascade.

The model significantly overpredicts hot subdwarfs with binary solutions, partly because predicted flux ratios are more unequal than observed. It also predicts over one hundred RR Lyrae with orbital solutions, while none are observed, suggesting such binaries are far rarer than predicted. Red clump stars with high mass functions fit plausibly as black hole impostors, with about ten times more stripped binaries expected in DR4.
arxiv-2602-21589:
Haoxiang Fu and nine co-authors offer SEF-MAP, a subspace expert fusion design for multi-mode HD map prediction. High-definition maps are vital for self-driving cars, yet camera-LiDAR fusion often suffers mode mismatch, hurting scores in low light, blocked views, or sparse clouds.

The idea splits bird's-eye-view features into four zones: LiDAR-private, Image-private, Shared, and Interaction, each with one expert. That keeps mode-specific cues while catching shared view. A doubt-aware gate at the bird's-eye-view level down-weights shaky experts by spread, with a balance rule to prevent expert collapse. Spread-aware masking fakes mode-drop cases in training with EMA-statistical stand-in features, and a role loss forces habits of private, shared, and interaction experts across full and masked inputs. On nuScenes and Argoverse2, SEF-MAP leads older methods by about 4 and about 5 percent in mAP.
arxiv-2602-21689:
Sokea Sang and six co-authors study landscape-guided tuning in divide-and-conquer QAOA. Divide-and-conquer methods ease limits for QAOA on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices by splitting large graphs into smaller, hardware-compatible sub-problems. But that creates a severe classical training bottleneck. Splitting across m boundary nodes generates 2 to the m sub-problems needing independent tuning.

Across varied synthetic and real-world graphs, reduced QAOA landscapes show robust universality. Adapting the replica-overlap design of spin-glass physics, the team defines a landscape-overlap order parameter q to gauge geometric correlations between landscapes, revealing a sharp similarity transition as connectivity is tuned. Doubly Optimized QAOA collapses 2 to the m sub-problems into K landscape classes. Optimizing one representative sub-problem and passing parameters to the rest lowers runtime and measurement overhead by orders of magnitude while keeping a strong Approximation Ratio Gap.
arxiv-2602-21789:
S. K. Saroj and one co-author present a novel approach for magnet-driven deposit patterns in a drying iron-fluid droplet. Field strength and mix stay fixed while drive rates vary from under 1 to 5 hertz. Without a field, the coffee-ring pattern appears. A time-varying field changes the deposit pattern, making multiple ring circles as it dries.

Ring count first rises with drive rate, then falls beyond a tipping rate near a fifth of a hertz. At higher rates, iron bits settle in the droplet center, killing the coffee-ring effect. Inner ring thickness and spacing shrink with rising rate up to the tipping point. The shift from multi-ring buildup to coffee-ring cutoff reflects rivalry among magnet forcing, wicking flow, and particle spread, with spread leading. A unit-free magnet switching number based on magnet nudge timing serves as control gauge for rate-linked patterns.
arxiv-2602-21889:
Otto Nyberg and three co-authors study how people learn from machine-learning forecasts guiding health-care and court choices. Little is known about what decision makers take from such support. The team offers the 2-Step Agent, treating a forecast as a clue to training data and the causal process.

Their scheme tracks how a forecast shifts a rational Bayesian agent's views. It then tracks how that shift shapes the causal-effect estimate, the next choice for a fresh case, and the result that follows. They solve the Bayesian inference problem in workable form for the multivariate linear-Gaussian case, and pin down by experiment when aided choice beats unaided choice. They prove one off-kilter prior belief can suffice to make aided choice worse than no aid, even with a sound model and a fully rational agent. So in ideal cases, decision aid can hurt more than help.
arxiv-2602-22289:
Do biological foundation models learn real structure, or just training artifacts dressed as biology? Ihor Kendiukhov tackles that question for models like scGPT and Geneformer through autonomous large-scale hypothesis screening. An AI loop proposed, tested, and refined over a hundred geometric and topological hypotheses across dozens of iterations, with null controls and disjoint gene splits.

Three findings emerge, starting with real geometric structure: gene-neighborhood topology holds up in nearly all model layers across domains. The screening also covers distance ranks, cross-model alignment, and community structure, all under explicit controls. The paper gives biologists a graded map of what these models actually know.
arxiv-2602-22489:
Models of hunters and prey often add randomness through diagonal noise terms picked for ease, without a firm basis in tiny-scale events. Jiguang Yu and Louis Shuo Wang show that this common habit twists the shape of population swings. Building a stochastic Rosenzweig-MacArthur model straight from an integer-valued, Bernoulli-coupled Markov chain, they pin down the exact noise link pattern set by event counts.

They prove that linked hunt-and-convert events must yield a below-zero hunter-prey cross-link, showing sharp limits of simple-noise guesses. The paper also settles an old puzzle by spelling out the split between open-domain models for survival-only dynamics and absorbed models that allow extinction, backed by a two-stage Lyapunov case for soundness. Ecology teams gain an exact guide for noise that respects both links and edges.
arxiv-2602-22789:
Cynthia Ihuoma Osuala and four co-authors study heat-to-power behaviour in light-hit zigzag tungsten diselenide ribbons. A six-orbital tight-binding model with built-in spin-orbit coupling covers charge flow. Regular driving enters through a Peierls swap and maps, at high rate, to a static Floquet energy model with light-angle-dependent hops.

In-step transport follows from wave-function matching in the Landauer picture, and lattice heat flow from density maths plus repeat phonon Boltzmann maths. Light remakes bands and flow near the Fermi level, shifting the sums that set charge and heat flow and the Seebeck number. Combined with spin-orbit splitting and lowered lattice heat flow from uneven bouncing, the heat-power figure of merit tops one over a broad heat range.
arxiv-2602-23189:
Cassandre Lebot proves a low-Mach-number limit for a compressible two-phase flow model. It is a bi-fluid isentropic Navier-Stokes system in which both phases share one pressure and one velocity. The question is whether the model settles into the familiar incompressible picture as the Mach number tends to zero, and under what conditions that passage can be made rigorous.

Under well-prepared initial data, the main result shows the partial densities converge to constant states. The velocity field converges to a divergence-free field, recovering the incompressible non-homogeneous fluid system. The volume fractions stay nontrivial and are carried along by the limit flow. The proof leans on tailored modulated quantities and two relative entropy functionals: a standard one, plus a logarithmic one that proves essential where the standard form falls short.
arxiv-2602-23289:
Yipeng Liu and three co-authors introduce WAIR, a workload-aware method for incremental reclustering in cloud data warehouses. Modern warehouses store data in micro-partitions and use metadata such as zonemaps to prune data during queries. Keeping a large table well clustered matters for pruning, but existing auto-clustering tools lack flexibility under continuous ingestion and shifting workloads.

The paper argues for a clean split between reclustering policy and clustering-key choice. It defines boundary micro-partitions, those sitting on the edges of query ranges, and WAIR reclusters only the boundary partitions most critical for pruning efficiency. The result is near-optimal query performance, judged against fully sorted layouts, at far lower reclustering cost, with a theoretical upper bound. Tests on TPC-H, DSB, and a real-world workload confirm better query speed at lower total cost.
arxiv-2602-23489:
Anton Bochkarev and four co-authors tackle materials science for chemically varied, multi-element systems spanning much of the periodic table. Older work favored high-purity, few-element systems, but a circular economy and extreme planetary and industrial conditions demand mastery of so-called Mendeleev materials.

Current broad machine-learning atom potentials often fail here, largely because training sets stress low-energy, near-balance structures. The authors introduce a chemistry-blind, entropy-max protocol for making data. It separates structural sampling from thermodynamic bias. Training a Graph Atomic Cluster Expansion model on the resulting SMAX dataset markedly improves toughness on strict benchmarks. These include large-strain phase changes in tin, defect growth in tungsten alloys, and catalyst barrier prediction.
arxiv-2602-24189:
Raluca M. Balan and two co-authors prove an almost sure central limit theorem for the hyperbolic Anderson model driven by Lévy colored noise. The 2026 paper builds on a central limit result for the model's normalized spatial integral. It also uses a Malliavin derivative estimate for the solution, from recent companion work.

For the noise, the team assumes a spatial correlation kernel that is either integrable or given by the Riesz kernel, covering two important correlation classes. The almost sure version strengthens the ordinary central limit theorem: it asserts convergence along almost every single realization, not merely in distribution across realizations. The result adds a strong probabilistic limit law to the theory of stochastic wave equations with colored noise. Hyperbolic dynamics and heavy-tailed jumps interact in ways that ordinary Gaussian theory does not capture.
arxiv-2602-24289:
Shengqu Cai and ten co-authors present a training paradigm for fast long video generation, where mode seeking meets mean seeking to decouple local fidelity from long-term coherence. The 2026 paper addresses a data bottleneck: short-video data are abundant and high-fidelity. Coherent long-form data are scarce and confined to narrow domains, blocking the scaling of video generation from seconds to minutes.

The approach uses a decoupled diffusion transformer with two heads. A global flow matching head trained on long videos captures narrative structure, and a local distribution matching head aligns sliding windows to a frozen short-video teacher through a mode-seeking divergence. That combination lets the system learn long-range coherence and motion from limited long videos, yielding a few-step generator for minute-scale videos. Tests show the method closes the fidelity-horizon gap.
arxiv-2603-00089: Neumann, Pi and Singh study how end users view system prompts, the hidden instructions that shape generative AI behaviour and override user inputs. Users remain largely unaware of this steering mechanism, since prompts are rarely public and models are told to conceal them. The paper reports user views on benefits and risks, preferred prompt-design values, comfort with different prompt types, and desired transparency and control. From these views the authors draw design and governance guidance for aligning prompt mechanisms with user expectations.
arxiv-2603-00289: Chen and colleagues ask which signals in combined medical scans and data are truly needed, and which alone settle an outcome. They argue features meeting both tests should predict better and stay useful when a data type goes missing. Their method splits each combined representation into shared and modality-specific parts, then builds learnable necessity-and-sufficiency goals for each part. Tests on synthetic and real medical data show the approach works.
arxiv-2603-00489: Gao and four colleagues build a language model helper that flags when a pull request should trigger a README update, where the change belongs, and what event caused it. Tested on more than twenty five thousand pull requests from hundreds of popular repositories, the best setup recovers half of the requests that historically came with README updates. Manual review finds about a fifth of matched suggestions spot updates developers missed, suggesting reported accuracy understates real performance. The team also traces failures and sketches how such tools fit open source workflows.
arxiv-2603-00889: Zhu and seven colleagues release CHIMERA, a compact synthetic dataset of nine thousand reasoning examples built to generalize across fields. Long step-by-step solutions come from strong reasoning models, span eight scientific disciplines and over a thousand topics, and pass automated cross-checks for problem and answer validity. Post-training a four-billion-parameter model on it rivals far larger systems on hard reasoning tests, easing the cold-start, coverage, and annotation bottlenecks.
arxiv-2603-01289: Guo and five colleagues test whether language models can simulate one specific person, using a volunteer archive of private chats spanning more than ten years. They propose the Individual Turing Test: can the volunteer's acquaintances pick which reply in a pool most plausibly came from the volunteer? Current simulation methods fail that test, though they do substantially better with strangers to the target. Fine-tuning improves daily-chat style imitation, while retrieval-augmented and memory-based approaches perform stronger on questions.
arxiv-2603-01489:
Aman Desai presents a small software tool in this 2026 work for particle physics studies. Event files in the Les Houches format hold records of particle crashes made by simulation programs. Many teams study those records with ROOT, a common analysis toolkit, but the two formats do not match directly.

The tool, LHEReader, turns a Les Houches file into a ROOT file so the study can proceed in ROOT. Desai tests the change on a few standard crash types, such as pairs of jets and Higgs-related events. One full case tracks a Higgs event from first generation through fast simulation, all handled in ROOT. The code is shared in public, so other groups can use the same bridge in their own work.
arxiv-2603-01789:
Andreas Happe and Jurgen Cito document how to rebuild a study that asked if AI can hack business networks. Their 2026 report is a replication package, not the original study itself. The source study tested language models on penetration tests of Microsoft Active Directory networks under an assumed-breach setup.

The report lists the artifacts used, walks through building the evaluation setup, and highlights the analysis scripts. Most setup effort goes into installing a third-party testbed that mimics a real company network. Log data from the original test runs ship with the prototype for teams that cannot build the full testbed. With those logs, the data analysis can still run as the report describes. Such packages let other groups verify security claims about AI attackers on shared ground.
arxiv-2603-01889:
Sebastiao Amaro, Joao Goncalves, and Miguel Matos speed up programs that use persistent memory without changing their safety rules. Their 2026 work studies a storage type that is fast, byte-addressable, and keeps data through crashes. To stay consistent after a crash, coders add flush and fence instructions by hand.

Those guards are hard to place well, so coders often add more ordering than needed and lose speed. The team tests which mixes of persistency instructions help across several real programs. One specific mix lifts performance while keeping the exact crash-consistency meaning of the code. Their tool, Bento, rewrites program binaries automatically to apply that mix, with no source edits. Gains reach a solid margin with minimal effort from the programmer, the tests show.
arxiv-2603-01989:
David Gentile, Joshua Huang, and James Murphy find stable states in time series by watching how data patterns shift. Their 2026 work uses the Wasserstein metric, a transport cost between two patterns, to spot change points. Stable states are long-lived modes that a system keeps coming back to, as in molecule simulations.

Their method tracks how fast that cost changes along a path with many measures at each step. Sharp shifts mark borders, which split the series into a few clear stretches. Each stretch is then grouped with like stretches, with the same cost used to judge how close two stretches are. No fixed form is assumed for the data at any step. Cost grows in a straight line with data size, which keeps large paths cheap to treat. Tests span fake paths, molecule runs, and sound traces from under the sea.
arxiv-2603-02289:
Kwangho Kim and Hajin Lee build a framework for cause and effect on shapes in this 2026 paper. Outcomes sometimes live in complex spaces, like networks or images, not plain numbers. Standard causal methods then miss how the shape itself changes. Their approach compares the topological structure of outcomes under treatment and control.

Shape is summarized by persistence diagrams, which record features across scales. Weighted silhouette functions turn those diagrams into curves that can be compared. The team gives an efficient estimator that stays robust if one part is mis-modeled. They prove it settles into a stable pattern as data grows, and build a formal test for no effect. Trials show the method measures shape-level treatment effects reliably across varied outcome types.
arxiv-2603-02389:
Radiative corrections in supergravity models of inflation are examined in this 2026 paper, with Keith Olive among the authors. Supergravity is the natural supersymmetric frame for early universe cosmology. Many no-scale models in it mimic the successful Starobinsky model at first pass. Quantum loop corrections, though, can distort that clean picture.

The authors derive conditions that keep the gravitino mass finite during inflation. They also require loop effects on the potential to stay finite or small. In the original no-scale model, corrections grow at large field values and can take over. Predictions for the cosmic microwave background then become unreliable. A class of Starobinsky-like models, including the Cecotti model, stays safe. There corrections remain tiny across the relevant range, preserving agreement with Planck data.
arxiv-2603-02489:
Gal Ben-Itzhak and Ender Ayanoglu tune smart radio surfaces to clean up wireless signals in this 2026 paper. These surfaces are passive arrays that reshape how signals travel. Wideband links suffer pulse distortion when signals bounce along many paths. A surface inside the channel could fix that distortion before reception.

Their classic method tunes surface settings from full channel knowledge. It cuts multipath effects while boosting signal strength at the receiver. No delay elements are needed, unlike classic adaptive filters. Learning-based control offers an alternative that skips channel estimation entirely. Three learning methods were tested across channel conditions and array sizes. One, SAC, converged fast and stably. It matched the classic method's quality with far less channel knowledge.
arxiv-2603-02589:
Krutika Tawri, Roger Temam, and Xinwu Yang analyze a wave equation shaken by random jumps. Their 2026 paper studies the damped KdV equation, a classic model of shallow water waves, on a ring-shaped domain. Random forcing arrives as sudden jumps rather than smooth noise, which makes long-run behavior harder to pin down.

First they prove that, for any positive damping, the equation has exactly one well-behaved solution path. Then they turn to the long term and ask whether the system settles into a steady statistical state. Using methods from Maslowski and Seidler, they show such a steady state exists when damping is strong enough. Jump noise can disturb averages, so the damping threshold is the key condition.
arxiv-2603-02689:
Joakim Blikstad, Yannic Maus, and Tijn de Vos speed up edge coloring for networks where nodes can only swap short messages. Edge coloring assigns colors to links so that no node touches two links of the same color. Their 2026 algorithm works in the CONGEST model and never uses randomness.

The method colors any graph with only slightly more colors than the busiest node degree demands, in few communication rounds. For mid-sized degrees it beats the classic two-times-degree color count in fast rounds for the first time. The trick came from an online coloring algorithm with very low locality, adapted and derandomized for distributed use. A side result also improves the round count for the classic color bound in all degree ranges.
arxiv-2603-02789:
Jiyuan Shen, Peiyue Yuan, Atin Ghosh, and colleagues ask whether document reading software still needs a separate OCR step. Their 2026 study benchmarks ready-made multimodal language models on pulling data from real business documents. The simpler image-only pipeline is attractive, but its true standing against OCR-assisted setups was unclear.

Across a large set of real-world documents, image-only input matched OCR-enhanced pipelines when the model was strong. The team also built an automated tool that sorts errors into a hierarchy, using language models to spot failure patterns. Careful design of the output schema, examples, and instructions lifted scores further. Their guidance helps teams decide when OCR can be skipped and where effort pays off instead.
arxiv-2603-02889:
Jarosław Pawłowski and Mateusz Krawczyk teach a neural network to read a quantum device's rulebook from its measurements. Their 2026 paper targets solid-state quantum simulators, whose behavior follows an energy rule set called a Hamiltonian. Finding those rules from lab data is normally slow, expert work.

Their physics-informed autoencoder bakes the scattering rules of quantum transport straight into its decoding half, so learned summaries must stay physically sensible. Trained on simulations, it characterized a chain of three quantum dots from transport data alone. The model generalized beyond its training range and coped with noisy measurements, as real labs require. It did weaken when the parameter space grew too large or varied, marking where the method needs care.
arxiv-2603-02989:
Jiayi Wang and Steve Tonneau plan footsteps for two-legged robots in real time without chopping the world into a grid. Classic A-star search needs reachability chopped into discrete steps, while exact optimization handles smooth constraints but slows down fast, especially with turning. Their 2026 framework, CASSR, keeps the constraints continuous inside the search.

Convex, smooth descriptions of the robot's leg reach travel through the search tree as it grows. A new cost-to-go estimate, built on a geometry algorithm, keeps the search aimed well. In tests, plans of up to thirty steps arrived in well under a second. The method beat grid-based A-star by up to one hundred times and also outperformed a commercial optimization solver.
arxiv-2603-03289:
Ji-Eun Byun and Se-Hyeok Lee offer a new way to judge how reliable an industrial process plant is. Plants for chemicals, gas, and energy must keep material flowing through linked stages, yet older tools like fault trees often ignore flow continuity and layout. Their 2026 system function measures the maximum flow a plant can still process, given its structure and stage order.

The function builds on maximum-flow methods and is solved with linear programming, then feeds estimates of failure probability and component importance. Two benchmark cases test it, including a gas supply plant. Layout changes guided by the importance scores cut the failure probability by up to one fifth. The authors present the framework as a practical aid for risk-informed plant planning.
arxiv-2603-03489:
Raz Heppner and four colleagues simulate a shock wave squeezing through a narrow spot in a pipe. Such constrictions appear in engines and natural channels, and the reflected and transmitted shocks they create decide downstream behavior. Their 2026 study varies blockage, constriction length, and shock strength systematically, comparing two shapes: an abrupt rectangular step and a smooth sinusoidal narrowing, the two limiting cases.

Validated large-eddy simulations resolve the full transient, not just the end state. For rectangular steps, the reflected shock's strength depends mainly on blockage, barely on length, while the transmitted shock does feel length. Smooth constrictions couple the two strongly, governed by the wall's local slope. The start-up inside the constriction unfolds far more slowly than the shock's passage, through reflections, separation, and reorganization. Simple semi-empirical formulas fitted to the trends predict both shock strengths across the whole parameter range.
arxiv-2603-03589:
Arnab Phani, Elias Strauss, and Sebastian Schelter sketch infrastructure for machine learning pipelines written by agents rather than people. Language models now generate, test, and refine whole data science pipelines, producing thousands of executions. The popular Python ecosystem was built for humans working interactively, one step at a time, and its slow interpreted core buckles at that scale. Their 2026 vision paper proposes stratum, a system that splits planning from execution.

Stratum accepts pipelines from agents or humans through the usual Python libraries, then compiles batches of them into optimized execution graphs. Those graphs run across heterogeneous backends, including a new runtime written in Rust for speed. Early prototype experiments speed large-scale pipeline search by more than sixteen times. The paper lays out the architecture, key design decisions, and open research problems.
arxiv-2603-03689:
A measurement from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider listens for the spin of gluons inside particle jets. Gluons, the carriers of the strong force, are spin-one particles, and their polarization should imprint angular patterns when a gluon splits into a quark-antiquark pair inside a jet. This 2026 analysis, using proton collisions recorded by CMS in 2022, goes hunting for that imprint.

Jets are unclustered step by step to expose their inner branching history, and a novel selection isolates the intermediate gluon splittings of interest. The measured polarization-sensitive observable is then compared against two standard shower simulators, each run with and without spin-induced angular correlations. The data side clearly with the models that include gluon polarization, and strongly disfavor those that leave it out.
