The system must find the edited target. No labeled training triplets exist. Lightweight projection methods are cheap. But they treat the edit text as a label for the target image. They miss that it is a change applied to the source.

The authors show that one adapter trained for both jobs creates a conflict. Endpoint matching fights transition learning. DeCIR separates them. Paired forward and reverse edit tuples are built from image-caption pairs. They train distinct low-rank modules for endpoints and for semantic transitions. The bottleneck goes away.
arxiv-2605-08489:
Musabbir Ahmed Arrafi, Malik Ali, Nicholas Stiffler, and Krishna Bhavithavya Kidambi model race car dynamics with a memory that respects physics. At the handling limit, simulators built on simple assumptions miss nonlinear behavior. Purely learned models can drift into states no real car can reach. They can also fail when track conditions change, and a race car gives no second chances at speed.

DynSSM couples two learned parts with a structured vehicle model at the core. State-space sequence modeling and recurrent encoders capture long and short dynamic patterns. Tire and vehicle settings adapt inside bounded ranges to stay plausible. A small patch term absorbs what the physics misses. The hybrid targets accurate, adaptable dynamics for high-speed racing controllers.
arxiv-2605-08689:
Xiaodong He and four coauthors build graph foundation models that treat network structure itself as the transferable knowledge. Graphs from different domains clash in both shape and node features, blocking one model for all. Their structure centric approach views graphs as metric measure spaces and learns geometric bases that form a shared coordinate system for structure.

Graphs align to those bases through optimal transport distances, while a structure aware re-encoding unifies node features without fixed dimensions or per dataset preparation. Across graph level and node level tasks, the model generalizes within and across domains better than earlier graph foundation approaches. Graph learning gains a path toward general models grounded in shape rather than surface features.
arxiv-2605-09089:
Abhishek Kumar, Riya Tapwal, Carsten Maple, and Mark Hooper build a detector for forged identity documents, the kind uploaded when people open bank or telecom accounts online. Attackers may swap the photo, edit text fields, or do both, and general forgery detectors are not built for the fixed layout of such documents.

Their system, FLiD, first finds the face and text regions with a tuned detector, then reads each region with a small frozen image model and a compact classifier. Tested with repeated cross-checks, it beat a whole-document baseline by a wide margin on error rates. It also used far fewer trainable parts and far less computing than general detectors, suiting places with tight resources.
arxiv-2605-09289:
Roback and four colleagues study moving geometric modes in non-Euclidean plates, where prestress plus geometry yield many ground states. Continuum elastic shells under prestress can show geometric zero modes: complex motions needing no elastic energy to excite, drivable by weak generic inputs. Non-Euclidean plates modelled on minimal surfaces offer one example, explored through a geometric zero mode.

The team shows a plate matching Enneper's minimal surface metric shows the predicted continuous stability, but aging ultimately lifts this degeneracy. Even after settling on a preferred setup, the zero mode stays the softest mode, and its motion is captured by a damped pendulum's dynamics. Periodic driving reveals resonance effects in this pendulum mode, with small swings and steady rotations, but blends with an extra flapping mode at high frequencies. Combining theory and experiments, the work maps the motion traits of a mode class previously understood only statically.
arxiv-2605-09489:
Li resolves exercise 7.2.2.4–224 of Knuth's Pre-Fascicle 8a, research-rated, showing SB(3,n) lacks a Hamiltonian cycle for even n. The proof turns on a sign-of-permutation argument. Writing the successor map of a candidate cycle as fS equals Ab composed with sigma, the sign of Ab is plus 1 when m is odd. So the sign of fS equals the sign of sigma for every S. A dihedral Burnside computation shows the sign of sigma is minus 1 on 3-to-the-n strings for even n, contradicting the sign plus 1 required of a 3-to-the-n cycle.

That yields the claim that SB(m,n) lacks a Hamiltonian cycle whenever m is odd with m congruent to 3 mod 4 and n is even. That restricts the residue classes where Knuth's hint to exercise 225, on Hamiltonian cycles in SB(m,n) for m greater than 3 and n greater than 2, can hold.
arxiv-2605-10089:
Coste and four co-authors offer a unified atom-level view of lithium electrolytes, the liquids that carry charge inside cells. Separate frames usually cover local coordination chemistry, electrostatic screening and ionic transport. That split works when dilute but fails at higher concentration, where bonding, ion pairing, clumping and group motion couple together.

Their multiscale frame links local bonding motifs, mid-scale ionic layout and large-scale transport in one real picture. Across carbonate liquids, polymer electrolytes, concentrated systems and tight spaces, rising concentration shifts the picture from solvent-led lithium bonding toward ion pairing, clumping and linked domains. Screening and transport then emerge from the same linked shapes, so reasoned liquid design must control short-range bonding, mid-scale layout and collective charge response as one.
arxiv-2605-10889:
Mohammadreza Armandpour and eight colleagues probe on-policy distillation, a way to train reasoning models with dense, token-by-token guidance from a teacher. It is often unclear when that signal helps and when it harms, which teacher to use, and whether the best choice changes from token to token.

Instead of costly training runs that hide token-level effects in aggregate scores, the team builds a training-free diagnostic. They define an ideal per-token gradient, estimate it with targeted rollouts, and score any distillation setup by how closely its gradient aligns with the ideal. Across self-distillation and outside-teacher settings, the score reveals where the signal helps and where it hurts. Trainers get a cheap lens for choosing teachers token by token.
arxiv-2605-10989:
Haoyu Huang and eight colleagues present SURGE, a learnable gradient-compensation framework for training binary neural networks. Binary networks approximate gradients through non-differentiable sign operations, and hand-crafted estimators like the straight-through estimator suffer gradient mismatch and information loss from fixed clipping.

SURGE adds a Dual-Path Gradient Compensator, a parallel full-precision branch per binarized layer that decouples gradient flow and estimates terms beyond first-order approximation. An Adaptive Gradient Scaler then balances branch contributions by norm-based scaling. Tests on image classification, object detection, and language understanding show SURGE beating established estimators. Binary-network builders get theory-grounded training that keeps accuracy while keeping weights to one bit.
arxiv-2605-11289: Kaya and three colleagues tackle average-reward learning, where bias is defined only up to an added constant. This makes direct distributional versions ill-posed. They identify bias laws up to a common shift, and pair this quotient space with a categorical form that respects the symmetry. On it they define a projected operator that is well-defined, non-expansive and has fixed points. They then prove convergence for sampled updates, with and without a known gain.
arxiv-2605-11689: Margaret Li and three colleagues run the first broad sweep of mixture-of-experts design choices, varying expert counts, sizes, shared experts, and load balancing across more than 2,000 pretraining runs up to 6.6 billion parameters. They find performance keeps rising with total expert parameters, optimal expert size tracks active parameters alone, and most other choices matter little beside expert count and granularity.
arxiv-2605-11889: Rachael Hwee Ling Sim and five colleagues design the first system that locks in group fairness and rewards honesty in Bayesian learning. Current data valuation rewards sources for data as given, letting sources inflate rewards with copied or noisy data. Their design joins semivalues such as the Shapley value with an honest scoring rule based on a check set hidden from sources. Theory plus tests on mock and real data confirm it.
arxiv-2605-11989: Nermeen Abou Baker, Nico Zengeler, and Uwe Handmann evaluate how to pick the best pre-trained model for image classification in a new domain. They refined output layers and general parameters to transfer eleven ImageNet models to five target datasets. They compared accuracy and accuracy density, plus training time and model size, across single-episode and ten-episode training sessions, giving a practical guide to model selection by transfer learning.
arxiv-2605-12089: Wolfgang Rolke's 2026 study presents simulation studies of power for goodness-of-fit and two-sample tests on multivariate data. In two dimensions both continuous and discrete data appear, while higher dimensions use continuous data only. No single method reliably provides good power: any method may excel for one null-alternative combination and fail badly for another. Based on these studies he proposes a small set of methods chosen so at least one performs well for every included case study, implemented in the R packages MD2sample and MDgof.
arxiv-2605-12289: Junyu Xiong and three colleagues bridge language priors and world models for choices with PriorZero. Language knowledge cannot adapt to change: fixed priors limit search range, blind to world change, while tuning suffers wobble and credit problems. It injects priors only at the root of the MCTS tree during rollout, aiming search while keeping foresight. During training it splits model learning from language tuning, tuning model, policy, and value guesses, then using scores for fine-tuning in turns. Tests on Jericho games and BabyAI tasks show better speed and scores.
arxiv-2605-12389: Miller and Lee shrink image segmentation for small, sparse structures by leaving the pixel grid behind. Their SEMIR framework learns a compact graph minor, a topology-preserving sketch of the image built by contracting and deleting edges and nodes, with an exact map back to pixel labels. Minor construction becomes a few-shot learning problem driven by boundary alignment, replacing hand-tuned preprocessing. The design decouples compute cost from image resolution and protects boundary evidence exactly where rare structures carry the most information.
arxiv-2605-12489: Duan and Gan show how to tame contact forces between polarisable particles by tuning asymmetry. Charged colloids, ions and soft nanomaterials can depart sharply from simple Coulomb behaviour when dielectric mismatch and sharp geometry amplify polarisation. Using charged dielectric spheres as a model, they extend an image-charge formula to contacting spheres and derive rules for cancelling the polarisation part. Two-sphere checks agree within three percent, and many-body simulations then self-assemble much like pure Coulomb systems.
arxiv-2605-12689: Castellani, Turco and Prattichizzo combine reinforcement learning with the Dynamic Window Approach for 3D local navigation of many-degree robots. Sparse point cloud data let the method adjust both motion and shape of a deformable microrobot, steering toward a goal in complex, constrained spaces while maximising occupied volume. Tests in a simulated vascular network, over 1080 trials, show the hybrid beats pure reinforcement learning and model-based methods on deformation and path completion.
arxiv-2605-12989: Drouin and Kahmeyer construct a sharp lower bound on the self-intersections of fold singularities, the smooth curves where a fold map from a surface to the plane goes singular. They first bound the self-intersections of the boundary of a surface immersed in the plane. They then view the singular set's components as boundaries of smaller surface pieces and invoke that bound, yielding a sharp lower bound for simple stable fold maps.
arxiv-2605-13189: Fiorellino and Somigliana review mass accretion onto young stellar objects, which sets final stellar masses and starting conditions for planet formation. Later-stage Classical T Tauri stars are well understood. But the earliest protostellar phases, Class 0/I, where most mass gathers, remain patchy. They survey ways to measure accretion on protostars. They show how method differences affect parameter estimates, discuss pitfalls in comparing with number models, and suggest next steps toward a fuller picture of the protostellar phase.
arxiv-2605-13389: Guy Foghem proves optimal convergence for solutions to integro-differential equations governed by symmetric p-Levy operators, under nonlocal Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions. He treats the fractional p-Laplacian with power s between zero and one as an example case. Under suitable domain and data rules, solutions converge strongly as s nears one from below, in the optimal norm. He also shows nonlocal trace spaces converge, in the right sense, to the local trace space.
arxiv-2605-13689: Jan Linnenbrink, Jakub Nowosad and Hanna Meyer call for situation-aware evaluation in environmental modelling. Map scores are ideally gauged from a fresh chance sample of the map area. Random checks suit spread training points, while spatial checks suit new areas, yet most cases sit between those extremes. Situation-aware methods freely adapt to the map setting, giving the most sound map scores across scenarios. The authors ground the case by redoing an earlier test study and weighing check methods.
arxiv-2605-13789: Kaiwen Shi and Carlos Oliver introduce Ensembits, the first coder of protein shape sets. Current protein shape coders capture only local shapes of static structures, missing linked motions and other shape states shown by sets. Trained with a spare VQ-VAE using a frame boiling goal on a large atom motion corpus, Ensembits beats all related methods on RMSF guesses. It further matches or exceeds static coders on EC, GO, binding site and grip guesses, and zero-shot change-effect guesses despite far less prep data.
arxiv-2605-13889: Mingi Hong proposes Calibrated Adversarial Stain Augmentation, performing adversarial augmentation in Macenko stain parameter space with a budget set from multi-center statistics. On Camelyon17-WILDS over 5 seeds, CASA reaches 93.9 percent plus or minus 1.6 percent slide-level accuracy. That beats HED-strong at 88.4 percent plus or minus 7.3 percent, RandStainNA at 85.2 percent plus or minus 6.7 percent, and ERM at 63.9 percent plus or minus 11.3 percent.
arxiv-2605-13989: Santillana offers VectraYX-Nano, a decoder-only language model of about 42 million weights, trained from scratch in Spanish for cyber defense. It keeps a Latin-American focus and calls tools natively via the Model Context Protocol. Its text set, VectraYX-Sec-ES, holds 170 million tokens, built by an eight-machine line for about 25 dollars of cloud compute. The set splits into chat, cyber defense and attack-tool phases.
arxiv-2605-14089: Zhang and six co-authors offer SkillFlow, a flow-driven framework for recursive skill growth in agentic orchestration. Current orchestration methods suffer strategy collapse under reward maximization, high gradient variance with opaque credit assignment, and skill growth guided by raw model prompting rather than principled training signals. SkillFlow pairs a trainable Supervisor agent with a world holding a dynamic skill library and a frozen executor. A Tempered Trajectory Balance loss, a regression-based flow-matching loss, samples trajectories for multi-turn tasks.
arxiv-2605-14189: Deng, Henrich, Kawano and Tawfeek introduce KnotMosaics, a SageMath package for building, viewing and analyzing knot mosaic diagrams. An n-mosaic becomes a matrix of standard tile labels. The package enforces local link rules to check mosaics, trace strands and parts, compute planar diagram codes, make random examples, and build rational tangle mosaics. A planar diagram link joins the mosaic form to existing knot and link software, opening up computations like Jones polynomials and knot Floer homology checks.
arxiv-2605-14289: Jiang, Chen and Pan propose MetaMoE, a privacy-preserving framework unifying independently trained, domain-specialized experts into one mixture-of-experts model using public proxy data. Client data stay spread out and unshareable under privacy rules, making unified training hard. Diversity-aware proxy selection picks relevant and diverse public samples to stand in for private data and guide router learning. Proxies also align expert training, improving coordination at unification, while a context-aware router improves expert choice across varied inputs.
arxiv-2605-14389: Das and team present Nexus, a system that joins event thinking with number-based models for time-series work. Nexus first distils history into a timestamped causal-temporal profile and a forecast anchor. It then makes split macro and micro outlooks. Finally it merges anchor and outlooks by Bayesian synthesis using past error patterns. Across eight data sets in three benchmarks, spanning rich event contexts, abrupt shocks and purely numerical series, Nexus beats leading time-series base models and LLM rivals. It also supplies clear causal thinking with its outlooks.
arxiv-2605-14489: Vanegas, Lensu and Ruiz present a stability-ensuring, backpropagation-compatible Schur projection scheme for linear discrete-time state-space layers. The methods project the quasi-triangular factor of the real Schur decomposition onto its nearest stable peer. Tests on synthetic linear systems show accuracy and convergence matching state-of-the-art methods, despite higher compute cost. The lower weight count speeds convergence during training without losing accuracy.
arxiv-2605-14589: Tian and colleagues stretch a language model's context window using only short training sequences. Their EndPrompt keeps the short context intact as a first segment. It appends a brief terminal prompt, forming a second segment, with positional indices near the target length. This exposes long-range distances without full-length inputs. Applied to LLaMA-family models from eight thousand to sixty-four thousand tokens, it is claimed to top rival methods on LongBench.
arxiv-2605-14789: Chen, Young, Ahmed and Cant simulate flat lean hydrogen-air flames under high-frequency sound forcing. A monopole sound source at the inflow provides the forcing. Frequencies from thirty-five to five hundred kilohertz are tested at two fuel ratios. Flames evolve from weakly stretched states through fast perturbation growth and wrinkle mixing to nonlinear cellular patterns. At the leaner ratio, thermodiffusive instability drives uniform cells, splitting and merging. At the richer ratio, hydrodynamic instability and large-scale wrinkle growth dominate.
arxiv-2605-15089: Dong Xiao, Zahra Sharif Khodaei, and M. H. Aliabadi replace blind tracking of viscoelastic wave dispersion curves with transport between manifolds. Local trackers follow branches by continuity alone and fail quietly near exceptional points, where eigenvector match fades. A lossless helper problem supplies an anchor manifold where each branch holds a unique global identity. Step-by-step homotopy then carries those tags to the lossy target, swapping labels only when an exceptional point crosses the real axis.
arxiv-2605-15189: Adi Zitrin surveys strong gravitational lensing, the bending of distant light by massive foreground objects from general relativity. The 1919 eclipse deflection first proved the theory, and modern telescopes have since made lensing a main astronomical tool. Lensing reveals the matter, mostly dark matter, inside lensing galaxies and clusters, while magnifying background sources. Strong lensing boosts sources substantially and images them many times, aiding distance checks and studies of variable sources.
arxiv-2605-15289: Mainak Mukhopadhyay and Shunsaku Horiuchi propose that accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs can power ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. A rapidly rotating, highly magnetized dwarf near the Chandrasekhar limit can collapse into a proto-neutron star or newborn magnet star. It drives a magnetism-ruled relativistic outflow that well forms heavy nuclei. Simulating heavy-nucleus acceleration, the pair finds crashes could mostly supply observed cosmic rays if most host near-light outflows. They add a few times ten to the 43rd to 45th power erg per cubic megaparsec yearly.
arxiv-2605-15389: Alexander Zotov and three others extend radio-frequency reflectometry, a high-bandwidth cryogenic readout for quantum devices, to large-area silicon carbide transistors. Such devices carry stray capacitances orders of size larger than tiny forms, settings hoped to hinder readout. The gate-linked RF response drops and dies as heat falls, even though DC switch working persists to deep-cold levels. Carrier freeze-out in the drift region changes impedance, and the authors propose a tweaked circuit to restore sensitivity.
arxiv-2605-15989: Philippe Gigon and three colleagues ask how much remote entanglement a single driven two-level system can stabilize between distant qubits fed by a correlated photon source. Their framework bounds the entanglement any such source can sustain, and they find shared entanglement in the Mollow sidebands of an unadorned two-level system. Near-maximal entanglement, however, needs extra filter cavities that boost the useful correlated emissions over competing processes.
arxiv-2605-16089: Medjadji and three colleagues run head-to-head tests of centralized, decentralized, and semi-decentralized federated learning. Federated learning trains models on edge devices with no raw data pooled in one place, which suits privacy and rule limits. Few past studies had tested all three layouts side by side. With the Fedstellar simulator, MNIST data, and a small perceptron classifier, they weigh what each layout does well, where it falls short, and what it trades away.
arxiv-2605-16189: Rodenas-Ruiz, Zhao, and Lee present a quantum method for Riccati matrix problems used in quantum chemistry. The method encodes stable answers with Riesz projectors onto fixed spaces. For m-particle, m-hole RPA, it yields an encoding of the amplitude answer and estimates correlation energy. With local orbitals, cost grows in line with system size and as a power of rank m, suggesting an exponential edge in rank over classical rules of thumb.
arxiv-2605-16489: Arnaudo and Withers trace the bound on the region where the Schwarzschild quasinormal-mode sum converges at real times to a singularity in the complex time plane. That singularity is a bouncing kind, in AdS/CFT language, produced when a light ray rebounds off the black hole singularity itself. The same ray picture explains a second bound: a null ray scattered at r_* = 0 matches the bouncing singularity's distance from the origin. The same singularities set an annular convergence zone for the Matsubara mode sum near the horizon.
arxiv-2605-16989: Garriga and team target treatment selection with ongoing actions under proximal methods, where proxies and bridge functions find effects despite hidden bias. Building a global response surface and then picking its peak wastes effort on regions that do not decide it, since standard goals follow seen treatments. Their weighted bridge loss stresses choice regions while keeping balance. They prove a regret bound tying selection regret to a weighted ill-posed constant. Choice-aware versions of several proximal solvers cycle fitting, mapping, update, and tuning, and in tests cut regret.
arxiv-2605-17089: Tang and Toh speed up a classic solver for semidefinite programming, a class of optimization with matrix constraints. They add a preconditioner built from a projection onto the feasible region's tangent space, which helps most when problems are badly conditioned. Paired with their earlier feasible solver, the result is SDPF+, a tool that also handles curved objectives. Tests show it usually beats rivals on large low-rank problems.
arxiv-2605-17189: Yang and Ma close a gap in noisy inductive matrix completion, where side information about rows and columns should shrink the problem but prior guarantees did not deliver in noise. They analyze projected gradient descent with spectral start and prove linear convergence and stable recovery at sample sizes set by side-information dimension, not matrix size. The analysis extends to imperfect side information, and a penalized blend balances efficiency against robustness.
arxiv-2605-17289: Mozaffari and colleagues introduce LEAP, a learnable method for pruning large language models end to end without structure. It replaces an unwieldy mask parameterization with a per-weight Bernoulli relaxation via a Gumbel-sigmoid, making unstructured mask learning tractable. Across five model families at 50 and 60 percent sparsity it lifts six-task average zero-shot accuracy by about two and a half points over the best layer-wise baseline.
arxiv-2605-17389: Puhan analyzes parton distribution functions for the kaon and heavy pseudoscalar mesons in the light-cone quark model. Starting from initial-scale quark and antiquark distributions, he evolves them with next-to-leading-order DGLAP equations and computes average momentum fractions at model and evolved scales. He also predicts kaon structure functions for the Electron-Ion Collider and Drell-Yan cross sections for COMPASS++/AMBER, finding heavier constituents dominate momentum share in heavy mesons.
arxiv-2605-17589: Samuel Gómez Gómez, Jimenez Forteza and Palenzuela Luque estimate how axion-like self-interactions in gravitational atoms affect LISA inspirals. Ultralight self-interacting bosons can form condensates around stars or compact objects. Using a recent halo formation mechanism, they show LISA can tell waveforms from binaries inside halos apart at signal-to-noise ratios near 100. LISA can then probe boson masses between 10^-17 and 10^-15 eV and decay constants between 3 times 10^10 and 6 times 10^12 GeV for solar-mass binaries of 10^4 to 10^5. One tuned case recovers particle parameters at percent level.
arxiv-2605-17689: Bhanu Suraj Malla and Yuqing Hu test a common forecasting habit: reshaping a time series to make its statistical behavior steady over time. Across 35,099 controlled trials covering eighteen synthetic processes, ten reshaping methods, five models, and three horizons, they find that careful, structure-matched changes help, while blanket differencing hurts. Choosing by out-of-sample checks beats fixed rules or unit-root pretests, a finding confirmed on nine real series.
arxiv-2605-17789: Olukunle Owolabi argues that AI memory systems built for one user break down in social groups. Group memory must tie facts to shared history, tell group norms apart from personal exceptions, and credit facts rightly even after a member leaves. His SocialMemBench covers five group types and sizes from 4 to 30 members, with 430 personas and 7,355 conversation turns yielding 1,031 test questions. A full-context Gemini 2.5 Flash reference scores just 0.721 against a blind-critic mean of 0.98 on small networks. Four open-source memory frameworks cluster far lower, near 0.12 to 0.18, showing a wide gap.
arxiv-2605-17989: Wuyang Zhang and Shichao Pei propose predictive prefetching for retrieval-augmented generation. That grounding helps language models but suffers latency from sync retrieval. Async methods rely on heuristic coordination and assume stable information demands during decoding. Their framework predicts when to retrieve and what to retrieve, using a predictor, a monitor, and a query maker. It exploits early signs that appear several tokens before uncertainty turns critical. Tests show up to 43.5% lower overall latency and 62.4% better first-token time, with quality matching baselines.
arxiv-2605-18089: Florent Dupont's 2026 paper studies Hall states at fractional filling with quasihole excitations on curves of any genus. For m quasiholes they build a bundle over the m-fold symmetric product of the curve, with each fibre the state for quasiholes at those spots. Its Chern character follows from Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch, and at maximal filling the bundle meets the projective flatness condition. In genus zero and one, explicit wave functions confirm the predicted curvature, matching the Berry phase split into an Aharonov-Bohm part and a fractional statistics part.
arxiv-2605-18189: Alejandro Gonzalez Garrido's 2026 paper frames fast 5G signal acquisition as inference over delay and Doppler, not full waveform rebuild. A multi-coset sampling design keeps only the samples needed for detection and estimation, shrinking the correlator bank that runs on them. An offline search picks the coset pattern by balancing peak isolation against even energy cover across the delay range. On 5G NR sync signals under worst-case Doppler, mean acquisition time falls by 2.8 times to 34.2 times versus uniform sampling, at a cost in delay and Doppler error.
arxiv-2605-18389: Pierre Houédry and three co-authors show a heat based cost for comparing measures closing in on the transport cost. As its time scale shrinks to zero, that closing holds for balanced and unbalanced cases. On the two sphere, its Sinkhorn divergences keep the geometric and analytic traits of classic transport gaps. The sphere's harmonic toolkit then yields a Sinkhorn routine storing only a linear amount of data. They close by sketching its use for judging global climate models, with spatial and seasonal reads on performance.
arxiv-2605-18589: Saraswati Pandey and two co-authors present, in a 2026 paper, a likelihood analysis of deeply virtual exclusive meson production off the proton. Using Jefferson Lab cross sections plus beam and target spin asymmetries, they derive a joint likelihood for twist-two chiral-odd helicity amplitudes and Compton form factors. Joint analysis constrains the form-factor space far beyond either measurement alone. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods explore the full space, extracting uncertainties, correlations, and credible intervals.
arxiv-2605-18789: Philipp Stecher and three colleagues trace the life history of features inside language models during training. They find a stable backbone of about fifty sparse features in two Pythia models, around which structure organizes. The backbone forms early, carries more load than matched rivals under joint ablation, and its future members can be predicted from firing at training onset. Function, they argue, comes before direction in how these features settle.
arxiv-2605-18989: J. Martin and twenty-eight colleagues measure the Virgo cluster core's chemistry with XRISM/Resolve spectroscopy. Most cool-core clusters show near-solar iron ratios, but earlier Virgo work hinted at super-solar values. Four regions show super-solar ratios throughout, though the northwest pointing sits closer to solar. Modeling finds cool metal-rich gas lifted by black hole jets beside hotter, more uniform ambient gas. The authors read this as enrichment from M87's old stars plus a limited cold gas reservoir, distinct from other cool-core clusters.
arxiv-2605-19089: Yunan Wang and three colleagues propose reachability-augmented dual dynamic programming for planning trajectories along a path under motion constraints. Classical dual dynamic programming assumes complete recourse; the new method uses backward reachable sets instead, building value cuts and trial paths only inside them. The authors prove global optimality for convex problems and KKT convergence for non-convex ones, with versions for second- and third-order cases. Experiments show objective values matching convex baselines while cutting time by 28.6 times for second-order and 5.8 times for third-order problems.
arxiv-2605-19189: Rodrigo Labouriau extends inference functions to spread models, where each measure is a distribution kernel pair. The move rests on one insight: good likelihood results converge and follow a normal shape because the result is the root of a regular rule, not peak likelihood. He adds viewing operators mapping models to a viewing space, and defines new rules from them. The frame covers point data, censored interval data, convolutional measures, and transform stats. He proves convergence and a normal shape, with Godambe optimality and Fisher bounds beating operators and rules.
arxiv-2605-19589: Shende and Popov present ELGIN, a physics-informed graph surrogate for nanoparticle dispersion in dental clinics, where tiny nuclei from aerosol procedures linger airborne. Standard flow simulations with particle tracking run too long per scenario for clinical support. ELGIN jointly predicts carrier-flow dynamics on a mesh and per-parcel spray motion, coupling a graph transformer and pressure projection to a Lagrangian network. In a test it beats a Lagrangian-only baseline on parcel displacement and cloud radius errors, and a 26-second rollout runs about 37 times faster.
arxiv-2605-20189: Nitin Vetcha and Dianbo Liu present SOLAR, a self-optimizing autonomous agent that learns across its lifetime. It treats its own weights as a space to explore, using parameter-level meta-learning to improve without retraining from scratch on each new stream. Multi-level reinforcement learning lets it find adaptation strategies at test time, while a growing base of valid modification strategies balances plasticity against stability. Tests on common-sense, maths, medical, coding, social and logical reasoning tasks beat strong baselines.
arxiv-2605-20289: Xinzhe Yuan and three co-workers present spiking operators for spiking transformers. ANN-to-SNN conversion gives a training-free path to spiking language models, but pipelines cover mainly linear steps. That gap limits neuromorphic runs, where nonlinearities need division, exponentiation, or norms. Their method splits these into division, exponentiation, and l2 norms, built with leaky integrate-and-fire neuron groups and bit-shift scaling. These blocks support Softmax, SiLU, and normalization without fine-tuning. Tests show replacing nonlinear operators costs less than one percent accuracy on all tasks.
arxiv-2605-20389: Kramer and three co-workers test models built on neural integral operators for fMRI encoding and decoding. Their latent framework iterates to a fixed point in an auxiliary space, then decodes stimuli or predicts brain activity from that space. Longer time windows mostly improve results and yield clearer latent groupings across two open datasets. Wider brain context helps both prediction and representation, though encoding scores stay modest given the task difficulty.
arxiv-2605-20489: Farias and Sills present D-CAF, a tool linking how stars form to young stellar dynamics. Stars form bit by bit inside a shifting gas potential, with gas motion taken from realistic magneto-hydrodynamical runs. Across all setups gas keeps shrinking while stars form, lifting central crowding and speed scale before expulsion. Today's spread still bears the dynamical birth imprint, with spread speed capped by the pre-blowout speed scale.
arxiv-2605-20889: H. Deguchi and five colleagues present Map-Mono-Ego, a map-grounded method for global human pose estimation from monocular egocentric video. One-camera egocentric pose estimation matters for activity monitoring, yet absolute location within an environment remains hard. Existing methods track relative motion from a start point and ignore absolute place. Scale ambiguity in one-camera vision also causes severe translational drift. Their method uses a pre-scanned 3D point cloud to achieve globally consistent poses from one camera alone, with tests on a new dataset.
arxiv-2605-20989: Mehmet Yigit Balik and Harri Lahdesmaki model temporal single-cell RNA sequencing data with a latent Gaussian process and optimal transport. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals gene expression at single-cell detail, yet inferring time processes from static snapshots remains hard. Current methods using neural differential equations and streams are sensitive to overfitting and lack careful treatment of biological variability. Their design models population shifts using a latent heteroscedastic Gaussian process, aligned by an optimal transport goal.
arxiv-2605-21189: Stefan Hoffelner builds a generic extension of L that meets Martin's Axiom, with the continuum equal to aleph-three. The model has a lightface Delta-one-three wellorder of the reals, which orders all real numbers in a definable way. It also meets Sigma-one-n uniformization for every n at least two at once. In one model, then, a large continuum, a definable wellorder, and global uniformization all hold together.
arxiv-2605-21389: Luca Mikadze, Peter M. Oppeneer, and Markus Weißenhofer report a huge ultrafast spin Seebeck effect from laser-excited magnon currents. Subpicosecond laser pulses drive nonequilibrium dynamics of electrons, phonons, and magnons, which three-temperature models capture poorly. Their microscopic method, parameterized ab initio, models magnon scattering via the quantum Boltzmann equation and predicts a strong burst of fast magnonic spin current in iron films.
arxiv-2605-21489: Jesse Bettencourt and co-authors present variance reduction for averages with diffusion teachers. Trained diffusion models feed later pipelines such as text-to-3D, distillation, and attribution. Teacher gradients are Monte Carlo averages over noise levels and Gaussian samples. Estimator variance drives compute cost, since each draw needs costly upstream work. They introduce CARV, a compute-aware framework motivating a layered estimator. It spreads upstream work over cheap resamples, sharpened by importance sampling and a stratified inverse-CDF build, giving two to three times effective compute gains.
arxiv-2605-21689: Gomes asks whether friction-like losses can tame the runaway ghost modes that plague theories with higher derivatives. Coupling the ghost sector to dissipative baths, he shows, creates effective masses and damping widths that split the dynamics into two branches above a critical coupling. In one branch a heavy ghost survives as a particle-like excitation, while in the other strong damping washes that character out entirely, suggesting that loss itself can quiet the instability.
arxiv-2605-21789: Aaron Wang and co-authors introduce PHAT-JeT, a transformer for real-time jet tagging at the Large Hadron Collider. Trigger systems must decide in microseconds which events to store, yet standard transformers pay a quadratic self-attention cost that strains that budget. PHAT-JeT pairs a geometric message-passing module for local detector-plane structure with hierarchical patch attention, exact inside small particle groups and globally linked through patch tokens. Under a restricted budget it leads resource-constrained rivals on accuracy and background rejection across four benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-22389: Li and colleagues propose High-Entropy Sum, a training-free metric for judging language model reasoning. It sums only the entropy of the top 0.5 percent highest-entropy tokens in each reasoning sample. Training on the top 20 percent of HES data matches full-dataset performance in supervised fine-tuning, while the lowest data degrades it. In rejection fine-tuning, HES-based training beats baselines. In reinforcement learning, HES-picked successful trajectories teach strong reasoning patterns. The metric thus unifies data selection across three paradigms at far lower compute cost.
arxiv-2605-22589: Ding and team propose SCALE, a federated unlearning model mixing past input analysis with freshness thinning. Unlearning enables picked removal of client data to address taint and meet privacy rules. Old methods suffer low care and lack time view, giving weak loss. SCALE first uses past input analysis to find layers most shaped by target clients. It then performs fine removal through tuned thinning to balance freshness with loss. Theory shows settling and speedup gains. Tests and testbed results show better removal versus rivals, with much better loss.
arxiv-2605-22689: Dobrodey and others measure K shell X ray emission from charge exchange between fully ionized argon and neutral gas targets at low collision energies within an electron beam ion trap. The same trap resolves the capture quantum number in extreme ultraviolet spectra from bare and hydrogen like oxygen ions. Comparing these and earlier measurements with multichannel Landau Zener models exposes discrepancies the paper analyzes in detail. The work thus tests charge exchange theory against precision trap spectra for two highly charged ion systems.
arxiv-2605-22889: Chen and seven colleagues systematically review remote robotic assistance for endovascular intervention, where catheters treat blood vessels from a distance. Screening 2501 records down to 16 studies, they found teleoperated catheters and guidewires navigated up to 7000 kilometers. Latency ran from 30 to 163 milliseconds, and small human trials reported full procedural success. Most evidence still comes from animal or phantom models. Multi-center trials are needed to confirm safety and reach.
arxiv-2605-23089: Sonigra and Kumar propose GPLD, a gradient-based latent dynamics penalty for the DreamerV3 world model. Existing latent world models do not enforce local smoothness in learned transition dynamics. GPLD applies a row-wise Jacobian cost to the posterior latent distribution. The penalty mirrors finite-difference smoothing of state laws in discrete MDPs, estimated cheaply with Hutchinson-style stochastic probes. Across DeepMind Control proprioceptive tasks it improves sample efficiency, most strongly on complex locomotion, and reaches high-return quadruped behavior earlier.
arxiv-2605-23189: Zeng and four coauthors present Bayes conformal prediction for vision and language. Conformal prediction gives free coverage but ranks from one unstable score, while average variants smooth scores. Both discard inconsistency that can flag stable picks. Their method uses r-values to turn score spread into an uncertainty score, estimating top-group odds from mean and spread. It offers closed-form and sampling estimators. R-values keep target coverage while cutting noisy false picks. Tests on classification, CLIP, and language show kept coverage and smaller sets.
arxiv-2605-23389: Bai and colleagues build AlignedServe, a serving system that lifts large language model throughput by fixing bubbles inside each decode step. Tokens in one step cost different amounts because their key-value caches differ in length, and long-cache tokens stall the next step. Grouping requests with similar cache lengths in one batch smooths those stalls, backed by large CPU memory for in-flight requests and one GPU prefetching cache for another. Throughput rises up to 1.98 times, and latency falls up to 7.4 times.
arxiv-2605-23589: Santosuosso and Wogrin tackle generation expansion planning, the NP-hard problem of choosing future power capacity under storage limits over long horizons. Prior work leans on heuristic time series aggregation, which compresses time steps to cut compute. Their marginal-cost aggregation instead builds an aggregated model that preserves the active limits of the full model, aiming at exact temporal aggregation. Embedded in algorithms that refine validated error bounds step by step against full-scale optimization, it offers a formal guarantee, and tests recover tractability where full-scale optimization stalls.
arxiv-2605-23689: Tabish and Klus present RaNNDy, a randomized neural network for transfer operators. Hidden weights and biases are randomly set and fixed, with only the output trained, yielding a closed-form solution at far lower cost than optimized networks. But RaNNDy is restricted to its weight and bias selection, which sets the basis functions, so the hidden-layer activation matters. The authors propose optimizing the activation itself while keeping weights fixed, giving a better dictionary. They test it on stochastic differential equations and random walks on graphons.
arxiv-2605-23789: Kay and Kalliadasis derive thin-film equations for surfactant films that treat surfactants as polar rod-like particles rather than symmetric dots. Surfactants can weaken a film by changing surface tension, the Marangoni effect, which can induce flows in the film. Starting from dynamic density-functional theory under the long-wave approximation, the authors derive rules governing film height, surfactant concentration, and polarisation field. They preserve gradient dynamics form through a well-defined free energy.
arxiv-2605-23889: Chong Cheng and colleagues rebuild streaming 3D reconstruction around a simple insight. Geometric evidence lives on mixed timescales, but current systems impose one blunt influence pattern. Their HorizonStream transformer factorizes an evidence influence kernel. It learns per channel decay for long range geometry. It uses local attention with space time position codes for short range matching. Readout tokens recover stable scale and pose. Trained on 48 frame clips, it holds steady past ten thousand frames with constant memory and linear time.
arxiv-2605-24089: Mescia and Gil-Marín constrain a dark-radiation framework with free-streaming and fluid-like parts, extending the radiation sector. From Planck CMB data alone, fluid-like radiation stays below 0.66 at 95 percent confidence, while adding BAO data gives free-streaming radiation near 2.93 and fluid-like near 0.36. The framework eases the Hubble tension through faster early expansion that shrinks the sound horizon, cutting SH0ES disagreement to non-significance. Bayesian comparison shows no decisive preference without SH0ES, but decisive support for dark radiation once SH0ES is included.
arxiv-2605-24489: Yuhang Zhang and colleagues present TIGER, a 2026 framework for matching enzymes to the reactions they catalyze and back again. Existing tools generalize poorly across tasks and data splits, with lopsided accuracy between the two directions. TIGER draws textual knowledge out of enzyme sequences with protein-to-text models, then blends it with sequence features through a gating network. A shared projector aligns enzyme and reaction representations, and tests show clear gains over leading baselines.
arxiv-2605-24689: Chong Zheng introduces the Morse ensemble polynomial of a simplicial complex. It sums over acyclic matchings, each giving a monomial counting critical simplices by dimension. It records the full distribution and is an isomorphism invariant. For graphs it recovers a Chari-Joswig graph formula. A top-face recursion handles a new top simplex, with a term ruled by the incidence graph. A tree-like regime yields a correction-free rule, including stacked balls. An independence variant refines the graph version and separates examples others miss.
arxiv-2605-24789: Yuli Wang and others adapt Vision Transformers to cardiac MR classification with self-supervised contrastive learning. Pretrained vision features transfer poorly to cardiac MR, since general datasets lack medical domain knowledge. Tests on an in-house cardiac MR dataset find self-supervised contrastive learning beats traditional supervised training. The adapted model also generalizes strongly to outside MR datasets like BraTS and ADNI. Ablation studies probe batch size and dataset scale. Ultimately the adapted model reaches classification AUC above 0.75 across the four commonest cardiac MR sequences.
arxiv-2605-24989: Moyu Zhang leads UTTSI, spending test-time compute where click calls waver. Test-time scaling helps language models, but click models face asymmetry: known mixes stay confident, while sparse mixes waver. Training-phase fixes learn one fixed rule, no per-case recourse. UTTSI pairs logit confidence with a frequency prior to separate true uncertainty from ambiguity. All cases get adaptive filtering; uncertain cases get stochastic exploration pooled by consistency. Sure cases skip exploration, holding overhead near three times base cost. Four data sets confirm consistent gains.
arxiv-2605-25689: Zhu and colleagues hunt changing-look active galactic nuclei, where a galaxy's central engine transforms, using extreme color-magnitude variability. They select candidates from Type-2 AGNs in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey by the slope of color-magnitude variation. They favor strong bluer-when-brighter behavior plus optical and mid-infrared amplitudes. Spectra from two telescopes confirm seven turn-on changing-look AGNs among twelve candidates. Four sources show flare-like brightenings tied to turn-on within three to seven years, suggesting accretion boosts behind the transitions.
arxiv-2605-25789: Hou, Zhong and Tan study bandit problems, where an agent chooses among options with unknown payoffs. They add a free exploration phase before losses start counting. The authors name a class of policies that probably save regret, meaning lost reward. Their two-phase method explores freely first, then exploits with a history-aware rule. Bounds show it beats policies denied the free phase and is near-optimal for two-valued bandits.
arxiv-2605-25889: Tai proves a hard ceiling for vision-language-action models, which turn images and words into robot actions. Such models score highly on clean inputs yet collapse under tiny hostile pixel changes. Tai shows capability plus robustness cannot exceed a budget set by task uncertainty and attack strength. The proof uses a classic information-processing inequality twice. Tests across 308 cells find no violation, and the construction yields three label-free checks.
arxiv-2605-25989: Martins asks why short chains stray from Gaussian statistics while long chains return to it. That pattern is a bell curve for end-to-end distance. Simulations of polyethylene melts show a patchwork at the Kuhn scale, the stiff segment length. Stretched, aligned segments mix with coiled runs and chain ends. End-to-end distances fit a q-Gaussian curve for free and entangled chains. Its index rises from 0.67 for short chains to 0.99 for long ones. That rise tracks coiled runs, absent in short chains.
arxiv-2605-26189: Cheng and six colleagues diagnose two hidden faults in low-bit quantisation training. Delayed tensor scaling masks faults that plain metrics miss. First, amax saturation quietly corrupts key knowledge representations via forward clipping when scale guesses lag. Second, catastrophic forgetting wipes already-trained commonsense knowledge when the learning rate runs high. It is fixed with a cautious max scaling rule over a 64-step window. Forgetting is fixed with a 500-step BF16 warmup. The study uses OpenPangu-Embedded-1B at eight-bit weights and activations.
arxiv-2605-26389: Ning Sun and Yanting Cheng stretch the thermalization picture for chaotic quantum systems to cover quantum many-body scars. The usual hypothesis says lone energy states act like random vectors, but scar states are non-thermal and spoil that account. The pair frame a scar version of the full hypothesis that tracks links among matrix entries touching scar states. Typicality reasoning backs its scaling shapes, and multi-time correlations split into thermal and scar parts. Numerical tests on the PXP model, the classic scar system, support the frame.
arxiv-2605-26489: Hongtao Zhang and four colleagues identify a spectral marker for the two-phase shape of pretraining: a fast early loss drop, then slow improvement. Their Stability of Singular Distribution says the trace-normalized singular-value spectrum settles early even as weights keep changing. This settling lines up with the slow-descent regime across GPT-2 and LLaMA models, varied schedules, weight decays, and AdamW and Muon optimizers. A simplified transformer analysis proves growing weight norms force an early threshold. After that point, loss-decline speed is bounded by singular-distribution change.
arxiv-2605-26589: Yusuf Brima and six colleagues test tabular anemia models across countries under distribution shift. Anemia affects around 40 percent of children globally, with varied causes. Survey data from 16 countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, plus the Caucasus and the Middle East, feed comparisons of logistic regression, XGBoost, LightGBM, and TabPFN v2.6. LOCO, reverse-LOCO, and few-shot settings probe generalization. TabPFN wins in low-data regimes, with better discrimination and strong calibration. AUC-ROC spans from 0.59 to 0.76 across countries, and subgroups show no bias.
arxiv-2605-26889: Huang resolves a puzzle about orbital magnetization, the response to a uniform magnetic field, in a quantum Hall ferromagnet. A uniform field makes momentum operators that do not commute and Landau-quantizes electron motion. She computes magnetization two ways: from local Hartree-Fock response to a periodic field with zero net flux, and from the grand potential along the Středa line. Both routes agree, tying orbital magnetization to spectral flow behind the Středa formula.
arxiv-2605-27189: Kopar and co-authors test how speech signals line up with staged scores for mild cognitive impairment. They use 5754 German assessment recordings across six tasks and three score levels: task, domain, and global. Learned speech embeddings beat hand-built acoustic features at the lower levels, but that edge flips for impairment classification. Freer tasks lose signal as levels rise, while tightly set tasks gain, a split the authors read as specialist versus generalist patterns.
arxiv-2605-27389: Junsoo Park and colleagues test two ways to tailor a teacher-facing recommender: from memory or from current context alone. Memory-based suggestions track learner history and tell learners apart on the same input, while context-only ones track the current question. Scores capture question reaction but miss history-based tailoring, so tests of behavior are needed.
arxiv-2605-27589: Kunlin Cai and colleagues test whether video world models change their output the way physics predicts when one detail changes. Their What-If World benchmark pairs 319 prompts on the same scene with one physical variable varied, scored on prompt adherence, physical consistency, scene preservation, and outcome difference. No tested model tops 52 percent on the paired score, while open-source models sit near 28 percent.
arxiv-2605-27689: Meghana Bhange, Ulrich Aivodji, and Elliot Creager propose test-time collective action, letting user groups correct algorithmic harms without platform retraining. The collective pools query access to build a proxy of the platform, then tune a per-class universal perturbation that each member applies at submission time. Small collectives narrow most of the subgroup accuracy gap and carry across architectures, improving worst-group accuracy.
arxiv-2605-27989: Sun and colleagues ask how a fixed parameter budget should split between a network's depth and width. Tracing a gradient-based measure of response strength, they find it tracks test error closely, including a shared peak at interpolation. The work links scaling behavior to amplified error responses, offering a practical guide to shaping models.
arxiv-2605-28189: Mohamed Fkirine and Lassi Paunonen build watcher-based regulators that steady abstract linear boundary control systems. Their main findings set rules for fast, firm, and slow-decay steadiness, plus sound behavior of the closed loop. Regulators are built for one- and two-dimensional wave equations and an uneven beam model.
arxiv-2605-28289: Rozhin Yousefjani and Saif Al-Kuwari propose a levitated mechanical gravimeter built from a squeezed-Fock qubit. Gravity couples to the anti-squeezed quadrature, boosting the gravity-driven transition rate while keeping direct mass scaling. Sensitivity grows as effective qubit splitting shrinks, while squeezing trades signal gain against anisotropic noise from damping.
arxiv-2605-28489: Felix Rupprecht and Sabine Wölk cut the cost of preparing matrix product states on quantum computers using symmetry-induced block sparsity. Particle-number and spin symmetries make tensors block-sparse, a property long used in classical renormalization methods. Row and column permutations turn block-sparse matrices into block-diagonal form, with unitaries synthesized at a cost set by the largest block. Cheaper synthesis for real-valued unitaries yields Toffoli cost gains of ten to thirty times over the state of the art.
arxiv-2605-28589: Zonghao Chen and four colleagues cut the cost of mean-field Langevin dynamics with kernel thinning. Learning tasks minimize an entropy-regularized goal over distributions, with the distribution as the fixed point of a McKean-Vlasov process run with N particles at N squared cost. Their KT-MFLD lets particles link only to a coreset of square root N size, dropping cost to N to the three halves. Under mild regularity it keeps the convergence guarantees within log factors, confirmed on neural-network training, quantization, and posterior computation.
arxiv-2605-28789: Xi Chen and Enno Lenzmann study finite-time blow-up for the Calogero-Sutherland NLS on the torus. For finite-gap inputs, the answer formula reduces motion to shrinks. Near blow-up time, every case splits into shared shapes plus a smooth rest. Each bubble carries one unit of mass with stepped rates. Within a subclass, an exact echo rule yields blow-up. A direct build gives single- and multi-bubble cases with rate one. In the non-echo regime they prove global life with uniform Sobolev bounds.
arxiv-2605-28889: Ziyang Zheng and seven colleagues frame context distillation as latent memory handling, packing each context into a solo LoRA adapter to form a modular memory bank with open memory choice. Given a query, their framework fetches near items, routes the query to the best adapter, and uses a Self-Gating switch to decide whether latent memory should be used. Cache sharing reduces handling load during use. Tests show the method clearly beats rivals with lookup, while Self-Gating improves toughness by switching off spare latent items.
arxiv-2605-29089: Xinyu Liu and team present on-policy inner self-distillation for language models, called OISD. During rollout and GRPO tuning, the final layer acts as policy and solo teacher for selected middle layers. Two tools align middle layers with the final layer: logit alignment for thinking habits, and attention match for attention patterns, both without special information. Advantage-weighted Jensen-Shannon training trains middle layers while keeping policy match under one acting policy. Tests show great gains over strong thinking rivals across four math thinking tasks.
arxiv-2605-29189: Andrew Womack and Daniel Taylor-Rodriguez develop a Bayesian prior for multiplicity within the forward stepwise view of model-space priors for regression. The prior, built by analogy to the Holm procedure, behaves closely like the Matryoshka doll prior. Against rivals, including recent objective choices, adequate multiplicity correction demands a degree of sparsity many recommended priors fail to provide. They argue multiplicity correction itself gives a principled, transparent rule for setting model-space priors in regression.
arxiv-2605-29389: Hiroki Kobayashi presents an auto design method for soft-rigid hybrid robots for walking. Rigid robots lack give for rough settings, while fully soft robots struggle with scale and loads. Taking a cue from nature, it tunes a soft-body shape, a stiff truss layout, and multi-channel drive. A sim couples a point method for soft bodies with position-based dynamics for truss elements, to search by gradient steps. The built design repeats the walking mode, which does not emerge without the skeleton.
arxiv-2605-29489: Large-model merging becomes a budgeting problem in work by Yuanyi Wang and seven colleagues. Merging is usually treated as pure algebra on saved checkpoints, yet at language-model scale the real limit is reading expert weights. Their MergePipe layer indexes parameter blocks and plans which expert delta blocks to access under a stated budget. It then runs the budgeted merge with replayable manifests. The plan recovers the full merge at full budget, and tests cut expert-read traffic roughly tenfold with speedups up to 11 times.
arxiv-2605-29789: Giulio Crisanti, Hjalte Frellesvig, Andrzej Pokraka, and Sid Smith take a step toward mapping magic relations for Feynman integrals. Magic relations are integration-by-parts rules where every integral in that sector drops out, and their presence breaks pipeline methods. The team finds magic relations always arrive with higher-dimension varieties there. That link yields a test for whether integral groups can host magic relations, built in an attached code file. The paper counts master integrals under such shapes and sorts magic patterns under symmetries and cuts.
arxiv-2605-29989: Jordana Torrico, Romulo A. Silva, S. M. de Souza, and Onofre Rojas study a triangular spin-half cluster with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Energy spectra and ground-state maps show ferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic, and frustrated phases, shaped by spin and DM interaction. At low warmth the system holds a one-third magnetization plateau, while heat wipes order at higher warmth. Entropy and specific heat show leftover entropy, Schottky-type bumps, and low-warmth phase-change features. The DM term deepens magnetocaloric complexity, with direct and inverse regimes shifting entropy with field.
arxiv-2605-30089: Yankai Chen, Hanrong Zhang, Bowei He, Philip S. Yu and Xue Liu tackle set learning when live models meet damaged inputs, such as outliers or missing parts. Standard methods shine on clean data but ignore corruption at test time. Their SW-DRSO method optimizes a stand-in for the worst-case loss across plausible corrupted variants. A barycentric adversary makes that search tractable with differentiable optimization over simplex weights. Across four tasks, it boosts robustness while keeping overall performance high.
arxiv-2605-30289: M. Ross Kunz, John Merickel and Keith Wilson describe numeric tables through survey descriptors. Descriptors enter a shared vector space with a sentence transformer, and likeness is measured via Canonical Correlation Analysis. A penalized CCA method recovers sparse variable matches, showing which descriptors drive matching without shared names or conventions. Differential privacy is applied before embedding, allowing use in private contexts without access to raw records. Across 15 sets spanning general, materials and graphite data, it reaches a P@1 score of nine tenths, with retrieval and cluster structure holding across ablations.
arxiv-2605-30389: Wei Luo frames the task of working out the inclusion depth of a pattern language. Inclusion depth is the length of the longest inclusion chain from the universal language to a given pattern's language. It tracks the mind-change cost of learning patterns from good examples. The open ask is whether inclusion depth can be worked out for each pattern over each finite alphabet, and in polynomial time. A guessed rule, twice the pattern length, minus the count of variables, minus one, would give a linear-time method.
arxiv-2605-30489: Jia-Wei Wang and six co-authors present new continuum polarization observations from JCMT, ACA, and ALMA, tracing magnetic field shape from about 5 parsecs down to about 4000 astronomical units. Their maps show many U-shaped field patterns pointing at the central protocluster, lined up with accreting filaments and meeting at the center. This shape points to colliding flows that trigger massive protocluster birth. Growing curvature of these U patterns measures rising magnetic tension, implying a field strength scaling index of about one half.
arxiv-2605-30589: Shportun builds ImmigrationQA, a question-answering dataset grounded in official sources for United States immigration law, a field too vast for unrepresented petitioners to navigate alone. Assembled from eleven sources including the USCIS Policy Manual and federal regulations, it holds over seventeen thousand pairs across thirteen subdomains. A small Llama model fine-tuned on it beat a larger base model on judged answers, gaining most on procedural topics while staying weak on complex reasoning. All artifacts are public, though the system is no substitute for legal counsel.
arxiv-2605-30889: Osaro and colleagues hand machine-learned interatomic potential building to language-model agents that work under strict physics checks. Building such potentials means balancing accuracy, stable dynamics, and speed, goals no single training loss captures. Their MLIPilot lets tool-using agents propose ideas, edit training code, launch high-performance jobs, and keep or drop changes by a fixed scorecard. Across molecular and copper crystal tests, the strongest agents turn failing baselines into accepted models by finding useful tricks like output scaling, loss changes, staged training, and capacity tweaks.
arxiv-2605-31089: Hadasch and Khangulyan review extreme gamma-ray transients, among the strongest events in space. They show rapid, large change and states near limits on speed-up, cooling, and density. The review focuses on transients above around one hundred MeV, calling extreme events huge changes. Stellar blasts, compact-object mergers, and tidal-breakup events, or extreme particle acceleration, are cases. They are powered by energy release, with shocks and field merging making ultra-fast particles. Classes include gamma-ray bursts, novae, variable jets, and flaring Crab Nebula light.
arxiv-2605-31289: Esterhuysen and Jonsson introduce the terminal representation for reinforcement learning. Successor representations encode states by future trajectories. Default representations weight those trajectories by reward. Both lean on eigenvectors for later tasks. It encodes reward-weighted paths as a smaller object usable at once, with no vector math and no symmetry demands. The authors develop its theory, two learners and zero-shot mix-and-match use. It sits inside the top default vector, and tests show it works with less cost.
arxiv-2605-31489: Sibilla and colleagues test context-conditioned generative models for sharpening sparse humanitarian surveys below the national level. Across eight household surveys from six low- and middle-income countries, the models refine subnational distributions even under severe scarcity, and do better as the conditioning facts grow richer. By learning full conditional distributions rather than single point estimates, the approach yields fine-grained evidence for aid decisions when the thin sample still holds enough support.
arxiv-2605-31589: Hegde and team present Gesture Recognition in the Wild, a dataset of co-speech gestures for a vocabulary of 155 words. Humans gesture during speech, but only a sparse subset of co-speech gestures depict and link to spoken words. The dataset holds 140,000 clips where the word is spoken, with 17,000 semantic co-speech gestures with frame-level boundaries. Clips come from lectures, talk shows, and interviews. The team also presents video models that classify gestures as semantic or not, recognize the word behind one, and localize it in time.
arxiv-2606-00089:
Or asks a question about robot prediction systems in this 2026 arXiv paper: can a predicted motion be accurate on average yet physically impossible? Physical AI models output rollouts and plans, and low prediction error does not guarantee a proposal could run. Or formalizes physical admissibility as a gate before control. Before running, each plan is checked against kinematic and dynamic conditions and horizon consistency rules, with rejections explained by component.

Experiments used the PushT benchmark from the LeRobot collection, with rigged tests. One-step error and dynamics residuals each separated valid from invalid proposals well, while kinematic checks alone performed weakly. The gate scored strongly while adding step-level attribution for its calls. In replay tests, the filters prevented 87 to 89 percent of invalid proposals while keeping progress almost intact. Passing the gate is not a certificate, Or stresses, but failing it identifies a concrete violation.
arxiv-2606-00189:
Kumar and co-authors seek ways to build agent systems that work well in the field. Auto-built agents can beat plain set-ups by a wide mark. Yet field use prizes plain form, firm control, and known costs. Lab wins can miss those needs.

The team gives a frame that keeps agents in clean blocks. Blocks, called pseudo-tools, call a model on a tight slice of context. Hand-made fixed work flows beat free-planned ones on cost and scores in their tests. New learn tricks then beat the hand-made agents. They tune cost and quality at once. They also blend gains from more than one learn route. The frame keeps each block open to checks and swaps.
arxiv-2606-00289:
White and Singal shape shrink tools that keep dot-based sums true, not just raw values close. Shrinking data cuts store size and model weight across tasks. Most end uses take dot sums of shrunk traits with fresh inputs. A shrink that trims plain miss can still skew those sums.

They set goals that prize true dot sums for worst and mean fresh inputs. Their tools adapt to the data and keep no slant in their marks. Math ties these goals to a known scheme, called ASQ. They give provably swift routes, both exact and near, for the new goals. Bench tests show strong marks across work types. Their ASQ tools run two to ten times past past best tools.
arxiv-2606-00589:
Parker and Rodrigues settle which quasisimple groups hold a sub-group with the same vector paths. A group and a sub-group act on the marks of a module. The triple is called immutable when both have the same paths on those marks. Past work left the plain quasisimple case in char two open.

Their case fixes the field at two parts, the GF(2) case. The main group is quasisimple, near a lone form with a mild core. The sub-group is a true part, not the whole group. They list all such triples that meet the same-path term. The work closes that case in the wider hunt for such triples.
arxiv-2606-01889:
Zhao and Haas compute how thick elastic plates stretch and bend. For thin plates, energy splits cleanly into two parts. One part covers stretching, the other bending. That split is often used for thick plates too. It stays oddly accurate beyond its strict range.

The pair impose small midline deformations on thick plates. They derive effective stretch and bend moduli from them. Both moduli soften as plate thickness grows. Yet their ratio stays roughly constant, they find. That fact justifies the thin-plate picture for thick plates. Cases like biological cell sheets fall in this range. The work explains a long-used approximation.
arxiv-2606-02289:
Chauhan sorts LLM hallucinations by whether a scorer could have caught them. Existing taxonomies classify errors by what is wrong. Memorised misconceptions, reasoning failures, and fabrications are typical classes. Those classes cannot say which uncertainty scorer would flag the error. The DECK taxonomy classifies by detectability signature instead.

Two axes split errors into four regimes. Inter-sample consistency is one axis of the split. Token level confidence is the second axis. The regimes are named Drift, Entrenched, Confabulation, and Knotted. A falsifiable blind spot map comes with the taxonomy. Black box consistency scorers see signal in two regimes. White box probability scorers see signal in two others. Only an independent LLM judge can detect the Entrenched regime. Three models and four QA data sets test the map.
arxiv-2606-02389:
Katz and co-authors settle a question in Ramsey theory, a branch of graph theory. An old claim by Burr and Erdős bounds the Ramsey number of any tree. Schelp later asked a degree form of that claim. Take a large graph with high minimum degree. Color its edges blue and red. Must a single-color copy of each small tree appear? The trees have bounded maximum degree.

The authors prove that the answer is yes. Their proof is stronger than the question asked. It drops the extra slack term in the size of the host graph. The host needs only the base vertex count. Every blue-red coloring then yields the wanted trees in one color. The result closes a question open since 2012.
arxiv-2606-02689:
de Giorgi and co-authors revisit metastable cosmic strings as a source of gravitational waves. Pulsar timing arrays report a nanohertz background. Metastable strings offer one account of it. The team uses a minimal dark-sector gauge theory. A complex Higgs doublet breaks the symmetry at a single scale. Metastable Z-strings form, ending on monopole-like defects.

At zero temperature, monopole nucleation sets the decay rate. Once the transition happens in a thermal plasma, that picture changes. Thermally induced nucleation on the string worldsheet dominates. The team computes the nucleation temperature from a finite-temperature effective potential. Daisy resummation enters that step. The worldsheet bounce action is then mapped across parameter space. A pulsar-timing-compatible signal selects a narrow region. Thermal effects shift that region to lower dark coupling and higher monopole-to-string-tension ratio. Heat, not just vacuum physics, shapes the signal.
arxiv-2606-02989:
Gassot, Gérard, and Miller study the long-time behavior of solutions to the Benjamin-Ono equation. This equation models waves, and its Cauchy problem asks how a solution evolves from given initial data. The authors focus on the limit as time grows, in a region where position scales like the square root of time.

They obtain the leading term of the solution in that limit. The decay is faster than that of self-similar solutions. They give an explicit universal profile for the decaying solution. The profile comes from linearizing the profile equation for self-similar solutions. The proof assumes rational initial data in two Lebesgue spaces. The data must also show generic behavior of the reflection coefficient at the origin. The result sharpens what analysts know about late-time wave decay for this equation.
arxiv-2606-03089:
Wen and co-authors tackle a collapse problem in safety training for multimodal language models. On-policy self-distillation uses a teacher with privileged information to give dense token-level supervision. In safety alignment, guidance comes from a constitution, not target answers. Pilot studies show safety distillation still collapses: the teacher drifts toward short, overly conservative replies, and reverse KL deepens the loss of expressiveness.

The team formalizes this as geometric leakage. Under safety boundaries in a non-orthogonal semantic space, safety pressure transfers into the expressiveness dimension. Their method, COPSD, first calibrates the teacher with a cross-SFT cold start. It then runs constitution-conditioned on-policy distillation. Experiments cover three multimodal models and twelve safety and general benchmarks. COPSD improved both safety and helpfulness over baselines. It also reduced the safety tax on general reasoning.
arxiv-2606-03289:
Parisel models how cloud privileges for non-human identities change over time. Cloud permission checks treat sameness of access as a fixed relation. For bots and service accounts, that view misses the time side. Parisel splits sameness into two parts that cannot be merged. Structural sameness means like permission profiles at one snapshot, read through graph fibration.

Temporal sameness means states that recur over time. It is read from strongly connected parts of a fiber transition graph. The classes under temporal sameness are named privilege circuits. A three-layer frame joins both views: a spatial quotient of the permission graph, a lineage split into stable compartments, and windowed cycle analysis inside each lineage. Tests on a large Azure tenant back the frame. Early sight of ratchet-type circuits predicts long-term structural stability in backtests. The work gives cloud teams a way to track privilege drift over time.
arxiv-2606-03389:
McDonald builds spectral dualities for expansions of De Morgan algebras. Duality theory pairs algebraic categories with categories of spaces. Stone and Priestley set the base case for bounded distributive lattices. Cornish later showed the two space categories are in fact isomorphic. McDonald pushes the theory to richer lattice algebras.

The targets are De Morgan algebras with extra structure. One class adds a closure operator, giving S4 De Morgan algebras. Another covers De Morgan groupoids, from residuated groupoid expansions. Spectral duality results are obtained for both classes. The proofs adapt Bimbó's Priestley-style duality for De Morgan algebras. They also adapt Urquhart's duality for relevance algebras, under the match between Priestley and spectral spaces. The work extends a classic duality frame to modal and residuated settings. Logicians gain space-side views of algebras that arise in non-classical reasoning.
arxiv-2606-03589:
Terwel and co-authors analyze the Type Ia supernova 2024gy and test how its dust extinction is measured. Type Ia supernovae serve as standard candles for distances. Dust between us and the event dims and reddens the light. Correcting for that dust needs an estimate of its amount and its wavelength behavior. Optical and near-infrared data on 2024gy support the comparison.

The event is a normal Type Ia with high-velocity silicon and calcium features. Modeling with TARDIS favors a double-detonation explosion over a delayed-detonation one. That preference comes from the calcium high-velocity component. A stable nickel-to-iron ratio, however, favors delayed detonation instead. Host extinction estimates span a notable range across methods. Narrow absorption lines give the low end, and the Lira law the high end. The mean sits near 0.22 magnitudes. The spread shows how hard extinction measurement remains.
arxiv-2606-03689:
Vargas Vieyra adapts tabular foundation models to survival analysis without any training. Survival analysis models the time until an event of interest. It serves healthcare, churn prediction, and other fields. Its core snag is right-censoring, where event times are only partly observed. Tabular foundation models predict in one forward pass, with no dataset-specific fitting. Censoring had kept them from time-to-event tasks.

A training-free method closes that gap. A foundation model builds an accelerated failure time model, fitting just one scalar parameter. A Buckley-James style step then imputes censored values in context, without parameters. The loop predicts event times and refines the censored data in turn. Benchmark tests show the method rivals trained Cox and parametric models. Those rivals need full training runs. Practitioners get a near-instant survival tool for tabular data.
arxiv-2606-03889:
Lv and co-authors build RealClawBench, a live benchmark from real developer-agent sessions. Agent benchmarks should mirror what users actually ask deployed agents to do. Real sessions are hard to score, though. They depend on local environments and carry implicit, underspecified intent. Verification is nontrivial as well. Two mechanisms convert real sessions into scored tasks.

Reconstructed execution environments restore the original working setting. Deterministic scorers then grade outcomes without human judgment.
