Hou and colleagues teach a bipedal-wheeled robot to climb long staircases smoothly. It is a machine that walks on two legs ending in wheels. Earlier teacher-student training setups lose touch with the robot's dynamics. They also encode terrain shape incompletely. So performance on continuous stairs lags behind slopes and single steps. Their 2026 framework, DynaWM, adds two stabilising ingredients to the representation the student controller learns.

A learned world model acts as a regulariser. It forces the internal representation to predict forward dynamics, and so retain full terrain geometry. A momentum target encoder supplies steady distillation targets. That prevents the representation from collapsing when the teacher keeps changing. Visual checks show the encoder organising terrain features in a clear hierarchy. In simulation and on real hardware, Hou's method delivers better terrain adaptability and smoother motion. The robot handles varied continuous staircases that defeated earlier controllers.
arxiv-2606-24289:
Igra, Sopin, and Yu build a flow that pushes dynamical systems downhill from order into chaos, in homage to the second law of thermodynamics. Given any smooth one parameter family of vector fields transitioning from order to chaos, can a single flow realise that transition on its own trajectories? Their 2026 construction, the Entropy flow, answers by coupling the original dynamics to a drift through parameter space.

Defined on the product of phase space and parameter space, the Entropy flow carries each initial condition toward more disordered, complex states. Tested against the three classical routes to chaos, period doubling, the Ruelle-Takens-Newhouse route, and intermittency, the construction behaves exactly as hoped. Using the Conley index from forcing theory, the authors also connect the Entropy flow to bifurcations topologically. Igra's team gives the vague idea of a route to chaos a concrete dynamical vehicle that travels it.
arxiv-2606-24589:
Khandelwal builds a red-teaming pipeline that does not trust its own judge. Scaling adversarial evaluation needs hard inputs, and confirmation that the failures found are real. A single judge is fast, but cannot flag its own leniency or settle close calls. AdversaBench mutates seed prompts with five operators, attacks a target model, then confirms each failure through a three-judge panel with a meta-judge breaking ties.

Dozens of seeds run across reasoning, instruction-following, and tool-use categories, expanded from a pilot to cover temporal reasoning, strict formatting, and tool edge cases. Every seed produces a confirmed failure. Operator effectiveness varies sharply by category, a pattern invisible in totals. Binary failure rates also hide difficulty: instruction-following seeds need more than twice the attacker iterations of the other categories. Writing alone in 2026, Khandelwal argues red-teaming should report effort and category structure, not just whether a model broke.
arxiv-2606-24789:
Juul Sanders, Sebastiaan Brand, Arend-Jan Quist, and Tim Coopmans speed up the normal form algorithm behind a quantum decision diagram. Decision diagrams store vectors compactly by merging equivalent pieces, which speeds linear algebra. In quantum circuit simulation the vectors are quantum states. One variant, the LIMDD, merges vectors up to local invertible maps such as Pauli gates. Theory promises exponential advantages for such diagrams, but the complex normal form procedure is only partly implemented in existing tools.

The new algorithm targets Pauli LIMDDs. For a diagram node with a single child, worst case cost drops from cubic to quadratic in the qubit count. Nodes with two distinct children keep the cubic bound. The authors implement the method inside QolDDer, a simulator written from scratch in C and C plus plus. On Clifford circuits it realises the proven advantages and runs far faster than existing LIMDD simulators.
arxiv-2606-25189:
AI agents in production run inside harnesses, software that is meant to enforce policies like running tests before a commit. Yusheng Zheng and eight colleagues identify the gap. Policy intent is stated in loose natural language. Enforcement, though, must act on concrete system actions. Tool level guardrails miss actions that bypass the tool layer entirely.

Their system, ActPlane, lets the agent declare policies close to the task, then enforces them inside the operating system kernel, covering every execution path. A small information flow control language expresses policies about event ordering and data flow across events. Built with eBPF, ActPlane returns semantic feedback instead of opaque sandbox errors. Across policies from an empirical study, coding benchmarks, and safety benchmarks, compliance improves, including on indirect paths that tool interception cannot see. The overhead runs roughly two to eight percent.
arxiv-2606-25389:
Teams of agents that learn task after task tend to forget old coordination skills or lose the flexibility to gain new ones. Yuchen Xiao and colleagues propose COMAD in 2026, a framework for continual cooperation learned entirely from stored multi agent data. An autoencoder first mines reusable coordination skills from mixed behaviour logs. A density based estimator then judges which skills are worth reusing, and a multi head policy is steered by the skills it selects.

Because the skill library keeps growing instead of staying fixed, new tasks add skills without overwriting old ones as badly. Theory shows the method approximates the optimum of the continual skill discovery problem it defines. Across several multi agent benchmarks, COMAD transferred skills both forward to new tasks and backward to old ones better than the baselines tested.
arxiv-2606-25889:
Gregor Humar and colleagues report an experiment on false vacuum decay, the process where a metastable state collapses into a lower-energy one through growing bubbles of the new phase. Cosmologists use the same picture for the early universe. Instead of a cosmic setting, the team stages the process inside a programmable quantum annealer holding more than four thousand qubits.

A two-dimensional quantum Ising model on the annealer encodes the false vacuum as an aligned spin state. At one chosen field strength, single spin flips along a seeded bubble's edge become resonant, so the bubble expands in a constrained but rapid way. Domain growth turns out nearly ballistic, far outpacing new bubble formation, while the boundary widens more slowly in a pattern matching Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality, a known class of roughening behaviour.
arxiv-2606-26089:
Abdelrahman Elabd, Eilam Gross, Dmitrii Kobylianskii, and Benjamin Nachman release Parnassus, a fast particle detector simulator written in Python. Simulating detectors with Geant4 is accurate but slow. Reconstruction chains add more cost. Parnassus swaps in interchangeable detector models that run on graphics processors. Neural models imitate the expensive simulation chains. Simpler parametric models follow the Delphes recipe of bias and smearing.

Two CMS detector models headline the release. One uses a flow-matching neural network. The other reimplements the Delphes CMS card in PyTorch. ATLAS and ALEPH parametric cards join them, plus a neural ALEPH model for the older LEP setting. Every backend shares one process-agnostic interface. Users pick a detector card and study new physics without retraining. Links to the Pythia event generator and FastJet clustering come built in. No ROOT installation is needed, a break from older tooling.
arxiv-2606-26389:
Jiarong Wu, Bertrand Chapron, and Laure Zanna forecast ocean wave conditions with a diffusion model, the generative approach behind image generators. Numerical wave models are accurate but too slow for ensemble forecasts or live coupling into climate simulations.

Conditioned on five days of global wind history, their model samples full sea states directly, with no step-by-step rollout. Beyond wave height it estimates wave partitions, Stokes drift, and mean square slope. Training used a 30-year hindcast dataset, and it runs far faster than the numerical model while keeping skill on bulk measures and a well-calibrated spread across ensemble members.
arxiv-2606-26489:
Raven Adam, David Maier, and Marie Kogler compare two ways to detect framing in German climate news. Framing is whether a sentence stresses threats from climate change or solutions to it. Coding sentences by hand does not scale to large news collections. The authors test a fine-tuned German BERT model against few-shot prompting of a large language model. Few-shot prompting gives the model a few worked examples in its instructions.

Both approaches run two separate classifiers, one for threat and one for solution framing. The test set holds four hundred forty Austrian newspaper articles coded by hand with expert help. The fine-tuned BERT classifiers scored higher on the standard F1 measure. F1 balances missed cases against false alarms. BERT reached a score the authors report as clearly ahead of the language model. Giving BERT the previous sentence as context helped a great deal.
arxiv-2606-26989:
Nex C. X. Stuhlmüller and Marjolein Dijkstra determine what physical neural networks need in order to learn. Physical computing lets matter itself do the calculating as it relaxes to a steady state, promising huge energy savings. Many proposed physical networks are linear, though. Linear systems cannot perform the nonlinear operations real learning demands. The authors show nonlinearity alone is still not enough.

Simulations reveal two further requirements: amplification and suppression of signals. Without them, the network cannot emphasise useful paths or quieten useless ones, and nontrivial computation fails. The authors present physically plausible circuit designs that include all three features. Their findings set design rules for energy-efficient learning hardware built from real materials rather than transistors alone.
arxiv-2606-27789:
Linear mixed models can face a huge number of candidate covariates. The count can grow faster than the sample size itself. Dependence from random effects and dirty data make screening harder still. Abhik Ghosh and Magne Thoresen propose a robust screening method in 2026. It seeks the fixed effects that matter in very high-dimensional mixed models. Random effects are treated as known.

A proxy-based transformation first decouples the dependence. Screening then runs as a marginal analysis in the transformed model. Marginal utilities are built from minimum density power divergence. That choice keeps the method stable under contamination and model misspecification. The method, called DPD-SISP, keeps all relevant covariates with probability rising exponentially toward one. Influence and breakdown analyses back its robustness. Simulations show it matches rivals on clean data and gains much stability on dirty data. A study of longitudinal data from ADNI2 shows practical use.
arxiv-2606-27989:
The overlap Dirac operator is central to lattice QCD with good chiral symmetry. It needs the matrix sign function, which is costly to approximate. Stephan Dürr, Stylianos Gregoriou, and Giannis Koutsou propose a new formulation in 2026. Diagonal Kenney–Laub iterates approximate the sign function. They need no prior spectral information about the kernel. A partial fraction decomposition makes the scheme practical. Two kernels are tested, the Wilson and the Brillouin operators.

A proof-of-concept run uses quenched lattices. The team examines Ginsparg–Wilson violation and the critical bare quark mass as order grows. Kenney–Laub iterates preserve chiral symmetry better than the Chebyshev approach. They are also more efficient. The approximation converges monotonically with order. The partial fraction form enables multi-shift solvers, cutting costs further. Pairing the method with the Brillouin kernel needed the fewest resources of the combinations tried.
arxiv-2606-28389:
Faisal Altawijri and Ismail Mathkour report their system for the SoccerNet 2026 challenge, which spots ball actions player by player in soccer video. The organizers supplied a two-stage pipeline: a detector that scores each player's actions frame by frame, and a sequence model that converts scores and game state into structured events.

Altawijri and Mathkour improve both stages. A temporal transformer lets the detector reason across frames instead of judging each in isolation, and they fixed a scheduler bug that had frozen the learning rate at its warmup value. The sequence model gains two-stage per-player attention, first across players within a frame, then across time for each player. An agreement-based ensemble combines model variants. Their final submission reached a macro-F1 of about fifty-nine on the challenge set.
arxiv-2606-28489:
Madalina N. Tudorache, Hiranya V. Peiris, Stephen Thorp, Sinan Deger, Daniel J. Mortlock, Gurjeet Jagwani, Anik Halder, Boris Leistedt, Benedict Van den Bussche, and Joel Leja measure how galaxy sizes scale. They relate size to mass and cosmic time, using nearly one hundred thousand galaxies. The catch they probe: conclusions depend on how galaxies are sorted, by star-forming activity or by shape.

Combining population estimates from a generative model with space-based size and morphology measurements, Tudorache and colleagues find the two sorting schemes give quantitatively different slopes, offsets, and scatter. Scatter tracks morphology but not star formation, a clue about the galaxy-halo connection. Both quiet and bulge-dominated galaxies show bent size-mass relations, but the bends sit at different masses. This implies galaxies stop forming stars and change shape on different timescales, plausibly paced by black hole feedback.
arxiv-2606-28589:
Tianlong Wang, Yuhang Wang, Weibin Liao, Xin Gao, Xinyu Ma, Yang Lin, Yasha Wang, and Liantao Ma steer a reasoning model toward truth while it is still thinking. Prompting tricks make models reason longer without guiding them to right answers, and static representation editing, nudging internal activations, ignores how a reasoning chain unfolds and forks over time.

The team first maps the geometry of truth inside chains: truth is encoded at sentence level, tangled with latent reasoning patterns. Interventions work best at early, high-uncertainty forks, with effects that decay. Naive steering vectors carry noise that can damage healthy trajectories. Their DynaSteer framework clusters patterns to purify a truth direction, then watches lookahead uncertainty and steers or rolls back only when needed. Tests on mathematics benchmarks and out-of-domain coding support the approach.
arxiv-2606-28689:
Gabriel P. Paternain and Eric Woolgar ask whether a spacetime that refocuses light must be the standard one. Around a lone system, the conformal structure at infinity encodes both the mass and the causal layout. For asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetimes, spacetimes with a negative cosmological constant, earlier work turned that link into a positive mass theorem needing no energy condition.

The rigidity question: if every light ray leaving a point at infinity returns focused at the opposite point, must the spacetime be anti-de Sitter space itself, up to a conformal factor? Easy cases, given an energy condition or a static spacetime, get simple proofs. The authors settle the harder globally stationary case by quotienting out the time symmetry. That converts light rays into magnetic geodesics on a Riemannian manifold with boundary, where the focusing premise forces the rigid answer.
arxiv-2606-28989:
Chidambaram and Keller show that a few counts of points on an abelian variety, a higher-dimensional analogue of an elliptic curve, can pin down its whole zeta function. The variety lives over a finite field, a number system with finitely many elements. Counting its points over a short ladder of extension fields gives partial data about the Frobenius endomorphism, the symmetry whose characteristic polynomial is the zeta function's core.

When the field is large enough relative to the dimension, the first g point counts determine the zeta function completely, and hence the isogeny class. This count is best possible in dimensions two and four. Dimension three is special: two counts suffice there, while one count never suffices anywhere. The proof pairs the functional equation of the associated polynomial with Newton's identities, using careful error control to recover the hidden eigenvalues exactly by rounding.
arxiv-2606-29289:
Izzo and Acciarini give a neglected spacecraft problem its own formal treatment: the maximum initial mass problem. Mission design usually fixes a spacecraft's starting mass and minimises time or propellant for a low-thrust transfer. This problem inverts the question: given the transfer and its flight time, what is the largest starting mass that can still complete it? The quantity summarises thrust, efficiency and boundary conditions in one number.

Working in Pontryagin's optimal control framework, they derive the necessary conditions. In the nondegenerate case, the best throttle setting is simply full-on, and thrust direction follows a primer-vector law. Their central theorem shows minimum-time solutions are exactly maximum-initial-mass solutions over the same flight time, and conversely. They also show the problem yields a smooth homotopy path to multi-revolution transfers, exposing the funnel-shaped landscape of time-optimal solutions in a worked example.
arxiv-2606-29389:
Domunco and four colleagues at Oxford ask what cryptographic functions a transformer can actually compute inside its layers. Cryptography means methods that keep messages secret or prove they were not changed. The question matters because colluding artificial intelligence agents could hide messages with steganography, which conceals data inside harmless looking text. Such hiding needs the model to compute a hash function on its own.

Following work that views saturated transformers as threshold circuits, the team first builds circuits for three constructions. Those are Keccak functions, Merkle-Damgård constructions, and Merkle trees. They then map the circuits onto transformer designs in two ways. One mapping drops attention entirely. The other treats tokens as circuit gates. Verified scaling laws state how circuit width and depth must grow. Those bounds give evaluators a principled way to judge what a model of a given size could plausibly compute.
arxiv-2606-29489:
Appicharla, Gain, Pal, and Ekbal ask which words in a translation truly need the surrounding sentences. Human translators lean on context for pronouns and helper verbs, while names and concrete nouns mostly stand alone. Existing ways to study this rely on special test sets or on opening up one model's internals, so they stay narrow or model-bound.

The team builds a post-hoc framework, meaning it analyses finished translations without touching any model. Two measures come from word alignments: fertility, how many target words each source word produces, and entropy, how stable those patterns stay across contexts. They study three language pairs under four context conditions, using human reference translations. Context shifts generative responsibility from source words to context words without changing overall fertility. The largest fertility drops appear in function words, while content words stay stable. Context, they conclude, resolves ambiguity rather than adding new information.
arxiv-2606-29589:
Shulman presents EchoHawk, an open pipeline that detects drones by sound. Passive acoustic sensing listens for rotor noise, which makes it covert and cheap. It also works against drones with tiny radar cross-sections or almost no radio emissions. EchoHawk spots a drone through the harmonic structure of its rotor noise, estimates its blade-passing frequency, and locates it with a microphone array.

Classical wideband beamforming methods and time-delay processing feed a recursive Bayesian tracker that follows the drone over time. Evaluation uses a synthetic benchmark with hard low-frequency confusers such as ground vehicles, plus real recorded audio. The lesson concerns data leakage at the session level. A used public dataset arrives pre-cut into short clips, so naive validation puts slices of a single recording in both training and test sets, inflating scores noticeably. Enforcing recording-grouped validation lowers them, and Shulman reports corrected numbers throughout.
arxiv-2606-29689:
Ghiasvand and four colleagues evaluate whether multimodal large language models can critique photographs the way humans do. Open-ended aesthetic critique has no single correct answer. Most earlier evaluation compared models against numeric scores, not against the written critiques people actually give. The team uses the Reddit Photo Critique Dataset, scoring five open-weight models against ranked human critiques for each photo.

Six prompt conditions separate persona framing, aspect hints, and length control. A grounding control feeds each model the wrong photograph. Reference-based similarity turns out to mislead: strict metrics show weak alignment only with human critiques, while a coarse embedding score reports broad overlap that the control traces to a stable house style. Behaviourally, models write two to three times more than humans even under a length cap. The authors argue such metrics reward fluent breadth over human selectivity.
arxiv-2606-29989:
João Ferreira, Spencer Topel, Pierre Fromholz, and James Wootton present a graphics framework for materials whose look changes as light hits them, work prepared for the SIGGRAPH 2026 conference. Standard rendering treats material traits as fixed, which fails for such engineered materials, so the authors merge classical ray tracing with a quantum collision model. Coherent light and matter interaction then drives the shading instead of static tables.

In their model, subsurface scattering, the spread of light inside a material, becomes a sequence of unitary collisions constrained by symmetry, with light modes and material excitations both treated as quantized. This captures chaotic optical responses caused by interference across many layers. The collision operators can be precomputed on near-term quantum computers and converted into the standard reflection functions that renderers use. Images of a coated jade statue and the Stanford dragon show richer color depth as layers and rays increase.
arxiv-2606-30089:
Feiyu Quan, Yitao Xu, Keping Qiu, Xiaodan Fan, and Hua-bai Li ask what dust polarization really reveals about star forming clouds. Polarization maps are used to judge magnetic fields against turbulence. New observations of Orion's Integral-Shaped Filament show varied patterns among dense cores. The authors test whether projection effects could explain that diversity. Their tool is a set of sub-Alfvénic simulation models.

Sub-Alfvénic means magnetic forces dominate over turbulent motion in the cloud. Inside the simulations, dense cores turn slightly super-Alfvénic on their own. Modest tilts of core fields, combined with projection, create polarization spreads. Statistical tests compare observed mean directions and dispersions with the models. The Orion values prove consistent with sub-Alfvénic clouds over many viewing angles. Mean and dispersion alone cannot pin down a cloud's three-dimensional field. They also cannot rule sub-Alfvénic models out.
arxiv-2606-30189:
Xinxin Chen, Yuchen Li, Zihan Wang, Ruixin Liu, and Mingyuan Zhao rebuild multimodal fusion as teamwork among agents. Static mixture-of-experts systems fuse images, text, and other inputs rigidly. Complex real-world tasks need adaptive, efficient collaboration instead. Their network, DAIN, lets specialized interaction agents cooperate dynamically. A context-aware meta-controller schedules which agents activate for each sample.

Sparse activation keeps computation low while agents build consensus. Compressed communication passes between the active agents during reasoning. A multi-objective loss balances accuracy, agent specialization, and cost jointly. Five diverse benchmarks test the framework, from medical data to sentiment. DAIN sets a new state of the art across them. Accuracy on the ADNI medical benchmark gains noticeably over prior work. Ablations confirm dynamic scheduling and communication both matter. The design also exposes agent roles, making them easier to read.
arxiv-2606-30289:
Torkel Loman, Alexander Browning, and Ruth Baker ask when an unknown function inside a differential equation model can be recovered from data at all. The classical question asks whether parameter values can be pinned down uniquely. Machine learning now discovers whole unknown functions and links instead. That expansion raises the same question at that level. Their paper generalizes structural identifiability to that setting.

Broad classes of models forbid unique functional recovery outright. For the rest, differential algebra can assess functional identifiability. It is a standard tool for ordinary equation models. New phenomena appear in passing from parameters to functions. They have no analogue in the classical parametric theory. Several common model classes are characterized completely in the framework. This idea thus grounds modern inverse problems with learned components. Model discovery gains a principled way to know its limits.
arxiv-2606-30489:
Davide Valsecchi, Mauro Donegà, and Rainer Wallny teach a density model to morph smoothly as physical parameters change. Normalizing flows model one fixed probability density very well. Many science problems need how it changes with parameters instead. Training a separate flow per setting explodes in count. Their Factorizable Normalizing Flows sidestep that explosion.

A fixed reference flow handles the base case. A learnable change, polynomial in the parameters, deforms it. That change factorizes over parameters, which is the key move. Each knob's effect is learned from samples varying it alone. Combined responses are recovered by adding at use time. The joint space never needs sampling at all. A controlled test with two known warps validates the idea. The learned map reproduces the true warps and best likelihood. Optional interaction terms soak up leftover correlations. Cost grows in step with the number of knobs.
arxiv-2606-30689:
Subham Panda studies a trade-off in spec-driven development, where language models write code from formal specifications. Frameworks differ in how they tie code back to requirements. One, traceSDD, forces a citation to a numbered requirement on every line. Others trace at the level of whole artefacts, or build trace maps afterwards. Panda ran two controlled studies across two frontier models, with hundreds of implementations per condition.

The pre-registered analysis found the same pattern in both models. Uncited code was more deterministic, meaning independent sessions produced more similar text, than cited code. But only the cited condition allowed automated hallucination detection: software could flag code drifting from its specification. Detection rates reached about eighty-six to eighty-eight percent for cited code, against zero for every alternative, with no false positives. TraceSDD also beat one rival framework on determinism. Panda concludes that citations trade sameness for verifiability.
arxiv-2606-30789:
Rajat Ghosh and six colleagues derive a closed-form model of how GRPO training behaves. Group Relative Policy Optimization is now a standard way to sharpen language-model reasoning. Its training curves are usually fitted with formulas whose constants mean nothing, and hyperparameters are chosen by trial and error. The team reduce the update rule, under one assumption, to a physics system.

The policy's reward obeys the equation of a stochastically forced damped oscillator. Momentum plays the role of inertia. Off-policy lag eats into the damping, and group size acts as a noise temperature. Its constants follow in closed form from the optimiser settings plus one measured curvature scale. The model explains the saturation curve as its overdamped limit and predicts group-size invariance of the mean trajectory. Across three models and two group sizes, its fits matched reward, with a coefficient of determination above zero point nine one.
arxiv-2606-30889:
Abigail Loe, Susan Murray and Zhenke Wu build a predictor for events that alternate with a forced pause. An alternating recurrent event, such as a hospital admission, triggers a refractory period, such as the hospital stay itself, during which the event cannot recur. Predicting the next event-free stretch is statistically delicate: observations are correlated, outcomes repeat, and follow-up can be cut short. The trio combine neural network methods, presented for a statistics audience, with weighted pseudo-observations to update predictions as new information arrives.

Simulations showed good performance. The real application predicted periods of low mood in first-year medical residents, alternating with baseline mood, and performed very well there. The framework suits any field, from health to criminal justice, where episodes and gaps both matter.
arxiv-2606-31389:
Noda and five colleagues compute how hybrid stars cool when their quark cores sit in a new superconducting state. Hybrid stars mix normal hadronic matter outside with quark matter inside. The proposed 2SC plus dd phase links smoothly to neutron superfluidity at lower density, unlike the older 2SC picture.

Stars with the new phase stay hotter than 2SC stars and sit close to the CFL phase in their cooling curves. The inherited neutron superfluidity matters because it suppresses quark beta decay, a key cooling channel. Cool observations of pulsars such as Vela and 3C58 could therefore test whether the phase is real. The study gives observers a clear thermal signature to hunt for in low-temperature data.
arxiv-2606-31589:
Bennaceur and four colleagues present REAL, a requirements engineering framework for machine learning systems that starts from failure. Organisations must check that learning systems are trustworthy and say so clearly to users, engineers, and society. Requirements engineering is built for exactly that stakeholder work, yet learning systems lacked a systematic process of their own.

REAL weaves together requirements for data, models, and the whole system rather than treating them apart. Failure cases drive the search for alternative requirements, and refinement stays iterative and traceable, so each choice can be followed back to a need. An autonomous driving example shows the framework in use. The authors argue that systems built this way align better with what their stakeholders actually require.
arxiv-2606-31889:
Murillo and four colleagues improve path tracking for an articulated tractor-trailer used in precision agriculture. The vehicle steers at two points, which suits seeding, spraying and harvesting in small fields. Guidance systems usually track the tractor, but the trailer swings onto a different path in curves and headland turns, leaving gaps and overlaps.

Their nonlinear kinematic model of the whole articulated system is embedded in a nonlinear model predictive controller. The controller then steers the trailer's own position, not just the tractor's. Simulations run in ROS and Gazebo show trailer deviation reduced substantially along straight paths and through headland turns alike. Better trailer tracking means field operations cover ground more evenly.
aspr-proceedings-vol1-1885-1889:
Volume 1 of the Proceedings of the American Society for Psychical Research appeared in 1889, covering 1885 to 1889. The American society followed the London model, gathering reports of ghosts, trances, and thought transfer. Figures such as Richard Hodgson and William James shaped its early work.

Reports describe sittings with mediums, tests of claimed powers, and cases sent in by the public. The writers weighed fraud, faulty memory, and chance before accepting any claim as real. The volume shows American psychical research at its start, when trained scholars tried to bring strict method to claims that most scientists of the day dismissed.
attar-bird-parliament-fitzgerald-1889:
Farid ud-Din Attar, a Persian Sufi poet of the twelfth century, wrote the Conference of the Birds as a long allegory in verse. Edward FitzGerald, known for the Rubaiyat, rendered it in 1889 as Bird Parliament. His version was the first English translation of the work.

The birds of the world gather and set out under the hoopoe to find their king, the Simorgh, beyond distant mountains. Most fall away on the road, and the thirty who arrive find the king in a mirror of themselves. The poem maps the soul's journey toward God with wit, story, and sorrow.
baco-verulamius-alchemicis-philosophis-q:
Pierre Janet, once a pupil of the École Normale, offered this Latin thesis to the Faculty of Paris, printed at Angers. Its question stands in the title: what did Bacon of Verulam owe to the alchemical philosophers? Janet, later famous in psychology, here works as a historian of ideas in formal Latin, dedicating the piece to his father.

A proem argues that sciences, once grown certain, forget their first workmen. Janet traces Bacon's debts in detail, down to how fire and water should be named: not this is fire, but this is a species of fire. Plato's real and formal species pass through bodies unchanged, as gold stays gold in any setting. The hosted copy comes from Glasgow's Ferguson collection of alchemy, stamped there in 1921.
bentham-principles-morals-1789:
Jeremy Bentham published An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation in 1789. Bentham founds utilitarianism, the view that right acts bring the greatest happiness to the greatest number. His principle of utility judges every law and act by its effects on pleasure and pain. The felicific calculus is his scheme for weighing those effects.

Bentham defines crimes, punishments, and the aims of law with reforming zeal. He attacks vague talk of natural rights and sympathy as guides to legislation. The book became utilitarianism's founding text in English. Law reformers across the world took up its program. Its demand that laws justify themselves by results still shapes policy debate.
bernard-eales-life-works-vol1-1889:
Samuel Eales translated and edited the Life and Works of Saint Bernard, and the first volume appeared in 1889. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux in the twelfth century, was the most commanding churchman of his age. He founded scores of monasteries, preached the Second Crusade, and advised popes and kings across Europe.

Volume 1 opens with Bernard's life, drawn from early accounts by those who knew him. It shows a monk who ruled much of Europe's public life from a cloister cell. His influence rested on preaching, letters, and a fearsome gift for rebuke. Eales made the Latin sources readable for English church readers of the Victorian age. The later volumes of the set carry Bernard's own letters, sermons, and treatises in the same translation.
bernard-eales-life-works-vol2-1889:
The second volume of Eales's Life and Works of Saint Bernard appeared in 1889, the same year as the first. Where the opening volume told Bernard's life, this one gives his letters in English. Bernard wrote to nearly everyone who mattered in twelfth-century Christendom, and his letter bag was enormous.

Popes, kings, bishops, and abbots all received his counsel, his comfort, or his sharp rebuke. The letters show how a monk with no army or office could steer the politics of an age through words alone. They also reveal his pastoral side, guiding monks and laypeople in the life of prayer. Eales's translation opened this correspondence to English readers who had no Latin, and it remains a vivid window on the medieval church.
bernheim-suggestive-therapeutics-1889:
Hippolyte Bernheim made the trance a tool of the ward in Suggestive Therapeutics, in English from 1889. Bernheim led the Nancy school in France. He held that the trance is no strange state, but keen heed to a healer's words. By such words, he claims, pain, dread, and bad wonts can be eased in sick folk of all kinds.

Case past case fills his proof. His school beat the great Paris school in their long row. The book is the flag of that win. It made trance craft a part of true care.
blavatsky-voice-of-the-silence-1889:
H. P. Blavatsky said she took The Voice of the Silence from an old book of gold rules. It came out in 1889, late in her life. The prose reads like verse. Short, grave lines urge the soul to spurn pride, greed, and self love on the path up.

The path leads to a vow to help all who live and strive. That call to pity is the heart of the book. It is the most loved prayer text of her creed. Seekers still read a page a day from it. Short lines make the book fit a coat pouch with ease. Many fans kept it so, as a daily guide for the path.
brentano-vom-ursprung-sittlicher-erkennt:
Brentano delivered the lectures behind On the Origin of Moral Knowledge in Vienna, and the German text appeared in 1889. The work is his ethics in brief, one of the shortest books ever to found a school of moral thought. Brentano asked how we know right from wrong, and answered through the emotions.

He argues that some feelings are felt as correct, the way some judgments are seen as true. Love of the good and hatred of evil, when rightly aimed, give moral knowledge its ground. The analogy between logic and ethics runs through the whole argument. Brentano's students carried the idea across Europe, and the book still anchors debates about whether value can be known rather than merely felt.
burgoyne-light-of-egypt-vol-1-1889:
Thomas Burgoyne set down the lore of a hid band in The Light of Egypt, Vol. I, out in 1889. The band was the Hermetic Brotherhood of Luxor, a foe to the creed of Blavatsky. Burgoyne, its scribe, lays out its scheme of stars, souls, and man's long rise through the ages.

Charts of the stars and rules of fate fill the tome. The band taught by post, in hid grades of drill. This book is its school text, first half. It shows a whole rival scheme of the occult in full dress. The band sold its lore in grades, each locked till paid and sworn. This tome was the prize its keen pupils worked to earn.
burgoyne-light-of-egypt-vol-2-1889:
Thomas Burgoyne rounds out his band's school text in The Light of Egypt, Vol. II, out in 1889. The scan here comes from a print run of 1900. The Hermetic Brotherhood of Luxor taught its lore by post in hid grades. This tome takes up where the first left off, in stars, souls, and fate.

More charts, keys, and rules for growth fill the pages. Read with the first tome, it gives the band's whole creed. The band is gone, yet its scheme still draws fans. These two tomes are its chief mark. The band's foe creeds mocked its claims as mere made up lore. Yet pupils kept the tomes, and collectors now prize them as rare finds.
chelmsford-three-witches-apprehension-15:
Chelmsford saw a third great witch case in 1589, and The Apprehension and Confession of Three Notorious Witches tells it. The pamphlet follows the Essex town's earlier trials of 1566 and 1579. By now the printed trial report was a known form in England.

It records how the three women were taken, what they were asked, and what fate the court gave them. Arrest, questioning, and judgment unfold in order, as the law of the day allowed. The series of Chelmsford prints shows local justice turning into national news. Printers knew fear and wonder sold, and this case fed both.
cia-0000009389:
Quynh Luu district, in Nghe An province, opens a January 1973 report with the sighting of a captured American officer. The heading numbers the item first, suggesting companion items followed in the original file. Quynh Luu lies on North Vietnam's coast, south of Hanoi.

A captured officer sighted at war's end drew close attention, since officers' names were well documented. Officials could test the claim against prisoner lists with unusual precision. If the officer was not listed for release, the sighting stayed alive as a lead. The file preserves that lead at the moment peace was being signed.
cia-0000009589:
Italy's current situation, with strategy for keeping it from communist hands, fills a CIA paper from September 1947. The agency itself was days old in its modern form. Italy's communists were the largest such party in Western Europe, and elections loomed for 1948.

The paper treats Italy as a prize whose loss would shift Europe's balance. That judgment drove one of the CIA's first big covert political campaigns the next year. Reading the analysis now shows the campaign's logic before its launch in that election. The file stands near the very start of Cold War political warfare.
cia-0000012089:
By February 1965 the yearly ritual of judging Egypt's course produced National Intelligence Estimate 36.1-65, on problems and prospects for the United Arab Republic. Egypt still carried the union's name three years after Syria left it. Nasser ruled a state strained by the war in Yemen and by a struggling economy at home.

The estimate returns to the standing questions of the series: the ruler's health, the economy, and the Soviet embrace. It weighs Egypt's problems against Nasser's proven skill at surviving them. The paper shows the community's steady, yearly reckoning with the Arab world's central state.
cia-0000012389:
A second undated paper on the U-2 incident, its year also estimated as 1961, offers another look at the Powers affair. Two staff papers on the same event show how thoroughly the agency picked over the wreckage. The May 1960 shootdown had cost a plane, a pilot's freedom, and a summit meeting between Eisenhower and Khrushchev in a single morning.

This paper assesses the summit's ruins from its own angle. Studies multiplied because the questions did: warning, cover stories, and blame. For readers, the double take shows an institution studying its worst day until the lessons gave out.
cia-0000013189:
North Vietnam's military potential for fighting in the south is measured in a CIA paper from June 1966. American combat troops had been in Vietnam for over a year by then. The question was how much war Hanoi could make. How many men could it train, arm, and send down the trails? How long could its economy and people bear the cost of sending them south?

The paper counts the other side's muscle at the national level. Counting the enemy's strength was the staff officer's eternal task. Here it is done for a war still growing month by month. For readers, it shows the buildup priced by the side that paid for guessing low.
cia-0000013889: One American prisoner was sighted in the Vinh Linh area, and a CIA note dated October 2, 1967, records the sighting. Vinh Linh sat at the top of South Vietnam, hard against the northern border. A prisoner seen there was close to the road into the north. Sightings like this helped confirm which missing men were still alive.
cia-0000014789: The Great Spy Ring, a book by Norman Lucas, is noted in a CIA file dated November 2, 1968. The file says Lucas showed that Soviet spy activity hung together as one story. Books on spying drew agency notes long after the trials ended. This file keeps the reading list of an era hooked on spy tales.
cia-0000024389: Likely communist reactions to certain possible American and South Vietnamese moves are weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1964. GVN in the title means the Government of Vietnam, in Saigon. Gaming the other side's answers was basic planning before any step in the war. The year matters: 1964 brought the Gulf of Tonkin and the road to a much larger war.
cia-0000028489: A threat assessment for El Salvador fills a CIA paper dated in 1979. That year the country's politics cracked open, with a reform coup in October and violence rising fast. A threat assessment named the dangers in order: rebels, death squads, and a state losing control. The paper stands at the door of a civil war that ran twelve years.
cia-0000036489:
A National Intelligence Estimate dated June 2, 1960 takes up the outlook for the Union of South Africa. An estimate is the intelligence community's shared judgment, not one office's private view. South Africa was then ruled under apartheid, and its future was a live Cold War question.

The estimate sets out where the country seemed headed and what that meant for American interests. Such papers tried to look past daily news and judge the deeper forces at work. Readers now can compare the forecast with what followed, and see both its insight and its limits. It was written in a year when African independence was reshaping the map of the continent.
cia-0000042289: Richard N. Cocheo, noted in the title as a civilian, is the subject of a CIA record dated September 2, 1970. The catalog title gives his name and status and little more, and the older record ties him to the DIA book of missing and captured personnel. A thin personal file of this kind still matters, because it keeps one civilian's name inside the accounting built mostly for soldiers. Beyond that, the surviving title supports no further detail.
cia-0000046689: An American plane went down in Laos on December 21, and a CIA item dated November 2, 1972, records the loss. The December date sits oddly against the item's own November stamp, a small clash the file never explains. The loss itself belonged to the air war over Laos, flown in secret beside the war in Vietnam.
cia-0000047389:
The summer 1982 issue of Studies in Intelligence, volume 26, number 2, survives in this CIA item. Studies in Intelligence was the agency's in-house journal, and its pages mixed history, method, and argument. The issue's named feature is the Oxcart story. Oxcart was the code name of the A-12, the spy plane built to outrun every missile of its day.

Telling the Oxcart story inside the journal let officers study a bold program after its secrets had cooled. The A-12 flew higher and faster than any aircraft before it, gathering photos over denied ground. Read today, the piece shows the agency turning its own past into lessons for working spies.
cia-0000048989: President Alfredo Cristiani of El Salvador came to the United States on a visit. A CIA item dated January 2, 1990, holds the trip's file, kept with the Truth Commission records. Cristiani had taken office the year before, as the civil war ground toward its end. Visits like this one were where aid, pressure, and peace terms were argued face to face.
cia-0000049089: ARENA, El Salvador's Nationalist Republican Alliance, and its ties to the right-wing world around it fill a CIA item from 1984. The party stood at the legal edge of a movement whose far end ran to the death squads. Mapping who belonged to that world was basic work for anyone judging the war.
cia-0000049389: Religious groups and their ties to the FMLN are examined in declassified CIA document 0000049389, dated January 1, 1990. The paper carries a Truth Commission note and links religious groups to the Salvadoran guerrilla front by name. Readers find a brief agency item whose title states that connection as its subject, preserved in the declassified Salvadoran files.
cia-0000096489: Sitrep as of 1440 hours local time is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000096489, dated July 2, 1967. The title timestamps the situation report to a single afternoon hour. The brief file is a snapshot record, its value in the precise moment it claims to capture rather than in any subject named in the heading.
cia-0000098089: Spectrum of Courses of Action with Respect to Cuba is the title of declassified CIA document 0000098089, dated January 5, 1964. The heading promises a range of options rather than one plan. The brief file is an options paper on Cuba, preserved under a title that tells readers the choices, not the choice, are its subject.
cia-0000105889: Dated April 5, 1965, declassified CIA document 0000105889 reports a senior Indonesian diplomat's belief that Indonesia would sever diplomatic relations. Its heading spells sever as Server and breaks off at Rela. The belief is attributed to one unnamed diplomat in the title. No country is named as the other side in the heading text. The brief record preserves the belief, the misspelling, and the ending as released.
cia-0000107289: Prospect of Living U.s.mias Unlikely is the heading, in compressed capital style, on declassified CIA document 0000107289, dated June 5, 1991. The title states a judgment: living American MIAs were unlikely to be found. That judgment is the whole message of the short heading. The brief record is an assessment item in the June 1991 MIA cluster as released.
cia-0000126889: Dated February 1968, this CIA report covers Vice President Ky's plan to advise President Thieu about a task force, the heading breaking off at the letter B. Saigon's generals were reshuffling commands while the Tet fighting raged. The paper catches the advice mid-sentence. Command reshuffles mid-offensive were read as signs of strain in Saigon, where the partnership between Thieu and Ky had been uneasy since the junta years.
cia-0000132289: Skirmishing along the border leads Situation Report 598 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 6, 1991. It then turns to a second topic lost where the headline breaks off. Border clashes were among the first signs that the standoff over Kuwait was turning into open war. The short report tracks those early clashes and whatever followed them in the filing that day.
cia-0000132489:
Cuba and the Caribbean pairs the island with its neighbors in a CIA briefing dated April 4, 1960. Fidel Castro had ruled Cuba for about fifteen months, and his revolution was worrying Washington. Rather than treat Cuba alone, the paper places events there in a regional frame.

Briefings in this form gave senior officials a quick regional picture: what Castro's government was doing and how nearby countries might react. The paper shows analysts already tracking the revolution's effects beyond Cuba's shores in spring 1960. Released decades later through the CIA Reading Room, it preserves that wider lens in the agency's own words.
cia-0000132589: Cuba and North Vietnam exchanging ambassadors fills a CIA document dated September 6, 1960. The headline uses the singular ambassador, a small slip in the original. Havana and Hanoi recognized each other as comrades in arms against the United States. Two revolutionary states were making their ties formal. The short document notes the exchange and its timing.
cia-0000135689: Dated 2 November 1960, a Spanish text from the declassified archive of Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained Cuban exile force. That date recurs across this part of the file, marking a heavy stretch of brigade paperwork during training. Nothing in the catalog record singles out this document's subject. It survives in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room. Researchers working on the brigade's training period will find it among the primary records of that month.
cia-0000135889: With a date of 3 January 1954, a CIA report in the open files deals with a contact report from the first days of January 1954. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136189: One CIA cable dated 1 May 1954 handles a report from ONTRICH on the Calligeris meeting, relayed onward for REELFOOT in May. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136289: Marked Instruction 16, this June 1954 LINCOLN cable gave the broadcaster LANGEVIN ready-made propaganda lines for the PBSUCCESS operation. One script claims President Arbenz hid money in Mexico from coffee sales and plans to flee to Switzerland, urging soldiers not to die for him. Another cites foreign reaction, including Brazil's foreign minister calling Guatemala an American problem. The scripts show psychological warfare written word for word at headquarters.
cia-0000136389: Guatemala has quit ODECA, the Central American regional body. This March 1953 cable explains why. Guatemala feared a planned anti-communist resolution. It then made a false claim of foreign intervention. It hoped a world court would back it. That beat submitting to the Organization of American States. The cable quotes Guatemala's reply. The USSR, it said, does not meddle in its internal affairs. The cable also lists points to stress. Labor is led by communists, it says. The supreme court has been packed.
cia-0000136689: The 2506 Brigade records hold this Spanish-language item from 1 January 1961. The date is shared by a run of brigade documents, likely paperwork logged together at the year's start. The brigade was the CIA-trained exile force preparing for Cuba. No subject is recorded for this item in the catalog. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the declassified release.
cia-0000138989: Chinese Communists in Antung secretly move machines and supplies to Korea. The Russian army there receives them, this May 1946 report states. Extreme secrecy shrouds the transactions. Details are impossible to obtain. The sourcing note explains the limits. The Kuomintang can only work underground in Antung. Many of its men had to return to Mukden. The party gathers word there from Antung representatives. A headquarters member is the sub-source. The report catches supply lines between Manchuria and Soviet Korea.
cia-0000139489: Conditions in POW camps east of Manpojin are the subject of this February 1954 report. Camp conditions and communist personnel attitudes are covered. POW hospitals are covered too. The sample kept here is fragmentary. A narrator's group continued on after another group left for the camps. The transcription breaks off before the findings. The report is marked unevaluated information. Its full account of camp life after the armistice cannot be recovered here. No specifics are invented.
cia-03192689:
Current Intelligence Bulletin for 5 December 1957 lists eleven items, opening with Britain's threat to reduce its troops in Europe. The bulletin comments that statements in the WEU and NATO councils on 3 December seemed meant to press West Germany to keep paying local costs. Britain said it would retain a force of 55,000 men if acceptable financial terms could be reached.

Later items report that a French nuclear test might be near, and that a new Communist theoretical journal was to be set up. East German views of the Moscow conference, a Japan-Soviet trade pact, and an expected dissolution of the Japanese Diet follow. The bulletin also covers Indonesia, a reported Soviet oil offer to Iran, a new Egyptian Red Sea base, and Brazilian concern over a Communist bloc campaign.
cia-06862489:
National Intelligence Daily for Monday, 5 May 1986, number CPAS NID 86-104JX, is marked Top Secret. Its lead contents item is USSR: Reactor Accident Update, on the Chernobyl disaster. A map of the Chernobyl area, dated 3 May, marks a 50-mile range ring over Chernigov, Korosten, and Zhitomir.

Other contents cover a new party chief in Afghanistan, East European troops in UNIFIL, and mounting farm problems in Nicaragua. A special analysis at page 10 covers Soviet handling of the Chernobyl accident. It reports Politburo members Ryzhkov and Ligachev sent to the area over the weekend. Official efforts to hush up news raised risks to public health, the analysis states. The Soviet Foreign Ministry told the Finnish ambassador that no special measures to protect the local population were envisaged, it reports.
constitution-iran-1989:
Iran adopted this constitution in 1979, months after its revolution, and revised it in 1989, the version hosted here with later changes. Chapter one gives general principles for an Islamic republic. Twelver Shi'a Islam is the official faith, and Persian is the official language, script, and calendar base. Chapter three lists the rights of the people, framed within Islamic rules.

At the top sits a Supreme Leader, a senior cleric with the last word on major matters, chosen by an Assembly of Experts. A president runs the government and is voted in by the people. The Islamic Consultative Assembly makes laws, but a Guardian Council of clerics and jurists can block them and screen candidates. Later chapters cover the courts, the army, and foreign policy.
english-bill-of-rights-1689:
The English Bill of Rights was passed by Parliament in 1689, its full title an act declaring the rights and liberties of the subject. It closed the Glorious Revolution, which had driven King James II from the throne. The text here comes from Yale Law School's Avalon Project.

The act lists the old king's abuses, then fixes the rules. No standing army may be kept in peacetime without Parliament. No taxes may be levied without its consent, and elections and speech in the House are free. It also settles the crown on William and Mary and bars Catholics from the throne. America's own Bill of Rights drew straight from it.
ephrata-chronicon-ephratense-hark-1889:
Pennsylvania's strangest commune tells its own story in the Chronicon Ephratense, Englished by J. Max Hark in 1889. Brothers Lamech and Agrippa of the Ephrata community wrote the chronicle in German in 1786. Their subject is Conrad Beissel's cloister of Seventh Day Baptists, celibate, communal, and devoted to music and printing.

The insider account follows the cloister's rise, its choir schools, its famous press, and its slow fading. Mysticism and petty quarrels share the record, as honest chronicles allow. The book remains the primary document of America's most famous Pietist commune, told by men who lived its rule.
europmc-pmc10016089:
Reyes and a global team report a prospective cohort study of drug-resistant Pseudomonas infections in a 2023 paper. The germ in question resists carbapenems, a key class of antibiotics. Such infections form a worldwide threat, yet the spread and impact of the enzymes behind the resistance were unclear.

The study followed patients at hospitals in many countries and recorded their traits and outcomes. It also mapped how often each resistance enzyme appeared across regions. The findings give doctors and health planners a firmer picture of a hard-to-treat infection. They also guide the choice of antibiotics in hard cases.
europmc-pmc10144389:
Desai and colleagues review chitosan, a natural polymer with promise for drug delivery and medical use, in a 2023 paper. Chitosan comes from chitin, the material in crab and shrimp shells. It is safe in the body, breaks down naturally, and can be shaped into gels, films, and tiny carriers.

The review covers how chitosan is extracted and how each method changes its properties. It surveys uses in wound care, drug release, and tissue repair. The authors also note quality and safety questions. The paper maps a cheap, green material's path into medicine.
europmc-pmc10507089:
Borges do Nascimento and co-authors pooled reviews in 2023 on what helps or blocks digital health tools at work. Digital tools now touch most parts of care, from records to remote visits. The team searched five data banks for past reviews on barriers and aids. They kept 108 reviews that covered doctors, pharmacists, and nurses.

Weak networks and tech faults were the most cited barrier, Borges do Nascimento reports. Staff also feared more work hours and felt personal strain with new systems. Training and teaching plans stood out as a top aid. Rewards shared across sectors helped too. Staff who saw a tool as useful were far more apt to adopt it.
europmc-pmc10898089:
Astashyn and a large team present a fast screen for stray DNA in genome data in this 2024 paper. Genome assemblies, meaning full DNA readouts of a species, are being produced at a rapid pace. Stray DNA from other species can slip into these files and mislead research. The screen, called FCS-GX, is part of a toolkit from a US national data centre.

The tool scans most genomes in under ten minutes, the authors report. Tests on doctored genomes showed it catches diverse stray species with high accuracy. The team screened 1.6 million public assemblies and found 36.8 billion letters of stray DNA. Half of that came from just 161 files. Cleaned reference genomes then dropped to a tiny share of stray content. The tool is shared freely for labs to use.
europmc-pmc11344989:
Zhang and colleagues review Alzheimer disease mechanisms, trials, and new drug strategies in this 2024 paper. Alzheimer disease is the predominant form of dementia and a growing global challenge. Its causes mix ageing, genetics, and environment. Current theories include the amyloid and tau protein hypotheses, inflammation, oxidative stress, and faulty cell clean-up, among others.

Most clinical drugs of past decades were dropped for weak effect or adverse effects, the authors note. Available drugs mainly relieve symptoms and carry side effects of their own. Two antibodies, aducanumab and lecanemab, won US approval with potential disease-modifying effects. Their long-term efficacy and safety still need validation. The review maps how the many pathological theories interlock. It closes with the hunt for safer, more effective drugs and the open question of which process starts the disease.
europmc-pmc11468589:
van der Koog, Gandek, and Nagelkerke compare two drug delivery systems head to head in this 2022 review. Liposomes are artificial spherical vesicles made of lipid bilayers, the same fat sheets that form cell membranes. They can carry both water-loving and fat-loving cargo. Extracellular vesicles are natural particles secreted by cells and are more complex and body-friendly.

The review evaluates how the two systems differ and match in composition. Critical factors governing pharmacokinetics, meaning how long a carrier circulates and where it goes, are elucidated. Strategies to tweak circulation time, targeting, and cargo release into cells are explored for both. The authors detail the effects of each modification. They close by asking whether a hybrid, built only from the critical parts of each, could offer the best of both worlds.
europmc-pmc1182689:
Turner, Hahn, and Nuzhdin studied the African malaria mosquito in 2005. The species lives as two forms, called M and S. Both forms share the same places yet rarely interbreed. That split makes them a good case for studying how new species form.

Genome scans found just three regions where the forms truly differ. Two regions sit near chromosome centers and hold dozens of genes. The third region holds only five genes. Turner argues these small islands may keep the forms apart. The result shapes how scientists think about species in the making.
europmc-pmc1183189:
Kim and Volsky presented a 2005 method named PAGE for gene data. Labs often test thousands of genes at once on small chips. Single gene changes can look weak or noisy. Grouping genes into known sets gives a clearer signal of change.

PAGE uses standard math on those gene groups instead of slow shuffling tests. In trials it found more truly changed groups than the older method. It also ran much faster. Kim tested it on muscle data from young and old donors. Shared aging themes stood out more clearly at group level.
europmc-pmc1247189:
Armstrong, Hutchinson, Unwin, and Fletcher pooled studies on hydrocarbons and lung cancer in 2004. Hydrocarbon mixtures from work settings are known lung carcinogens. How risk climbs with dose was less clear. Thirty-nine worker cohorts entered the combined analysis.

At a set exposure unit, relative risk averaged 1.20, and that estimate held steady across methods and single studies. Coke ovens, gasworks, and aluminum plants clustered near 1.15 to 1.17, while other trades ran higher. Asphalt work and chimney sweeping showed far higher, though rougher, estimates. Dust exposure did not explain the pattern. Armstrong gives dose-response numbers for workplace limits. The authors say the results give risk checks a firmer base.
europmc-pmc1533889:
Psoriasis, a scaly skin disease, is driven by an overactive immune reply. Arican and co-authors measured immune signals in blood in 2005, hunting a lab marker of severity. Doctors now grade severity by eye, using a skin score. The team compared patients with active disease to healthy controls.

Six signals, including TNF-alpha and interleukin-18, ran higher in patients than controls. Four of them, IFN-gamma, IL-12, IL-17, and IL-18, rose in step with the skin score. Arican suggests blood levels of these signals could grade disease fairly, without relying on a doctor's visual judgment alone.
europmc-pmc1563489:
Genes do not speak at a steady rate; they fire in bursts. Raj and co-authors proved that in 2006 by counting single RNA messages in mammal cells. Cells with the same genes held wildly unlike message counts.

A gene flips randomly between off and on states. While on, it fires a short, intense burst of messages. Neighboring genes in the same stretch burst together. More activator protein made bursts bigger, not more frequent. Raj notes slow protein decay smooths the noise at the protein level. The work raises the puzzle of how cells stay reliable amid such random firing.
europmc-pmc1716189:
Health workers in poor countries catch TB from their patients at high rates. Joshi and co-authors reviewed 51 studies in 2006 on latent and active tuberculosis among staff in low- and middle-income countries.

Latent infection averaged 54 percent of workers, ranging from 33 to 79 percent. Yearly disease incidence ran from 69 to 5,780 per 100,000 workers. Risk ran highest in TB wards, labs, internal medicine, and emergency units. Nurses, attendants, and radiology technicians were among the most exposed roles. Joshi calls for simple, affordable infection controls, since most facilities lack resources to prevent spread. The review covered low- and middle-income countries.
europmc-pmc1847689:
Maldarelli, Mellors, Coffin and co-authors measured in 2007 the HIV that lingers in blood despite strong drug therapy. Modern antiretroviral therapy suppresses the virus below standard test limits but never clears it. Knowing where the residue comes from matters for any cure attempt.

They used a new assay sensitive to a single copy of viral RNA per sample. Over 80 percent of patients on therapy for 60 weeks still had at least one copy per milliliter. The group median was 3.1 copies per milliliter. That stable level matched each patient's viral load before therapy, not the drug mix used. It also did not fall between weeks 60 and 110. The pattern points to long-lived cells infected before therapy began, releasing virus at a steady set point.
europmc-pmc1994989:
Rea, Ventura and Johnson studied in 2007 how faulty mitochondria affect lifespan in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Mitochondria make cell energy through the electron transport chain. Blocking that chain can extend worm life, yet similar faults shorten human life. The team used a new dilution method to reduce five mitochondrial genes by graded amounts.

Each treatment altered several chain components at once. Lifespan showed three phases as inhibition rose. Low levels changed nothing, middle levels lengthened life steadily, and the highest levels shortened it again. Oxidative stress did not track the extension. Instead, larval growth, fertility and adult size shifted together when life began to lengthen. A signal during the L3/L4 larval stage was enough to start the effect.
europmc-pmc2009089:
Wagner, Berry, Skidmore and Timbrell exposed rats to inhaled asbestos in 1974 and tracked lung damage. Wistar rats breathed dust clouds of standard reference asbestos samples. Exposure lasted from one day up to two years across two experiments. The team then examined lungs for scarring disease, called asbestosis, and for tumours.

All asbestos samples caused asbestosis, and it kept progressing after exposure stopped. Control rats showed only slight scarring. Lung tumours from mild growths to squamous cancers appeared with all samples. Twenty tumours spread to other sites, and 16 followed chrysotile exposure. Eleven mesotheliomas, cancers of the lung lining, also occurred. Two followed just one day of exposure. Asbestosis and lung tumours were positively linked.
europmc-pmc2124989:
A. R. Dochez of the Hospital of the Rockefeller Institute reported in 1912 that blood clots more slowly during lobar pneumonia. Through the acute stage the coagulation time runs long. As convalescence sets in, it returns to normal. Circulating fibrinogen, the clot's raw material, rises at the same time.

That pairing needs explaining, and Dochez points to antithrombin. More of that clot-blocking substance, he argues, is probably being formed, and its source is likely the liver. The stimulus, he suggests, comes from the infecting organism itself. His case notes give the scale: severe, fatal cases clotting at thirteen to eighteen minutes in January 1912, against ten to twelve in a mild case after its crisis. Readers get a neat blood puzzle from the pneumonia ward, with a proposed mechanism attached.
europmc-pmc2125189:
James W. Jobling and William Petersen named and dissected serotoxin in 1914, the fourteenth of their ferment studies, from Columbia's pathology department. Serum stripped of its protective lipoids, the unsaturated fatty acids, becomes toxic to the very species it came from. They call the product serotoxin and list its making in ten findings.

Toxicity rises to a definite maximum, then dies away as digestion continues. Anticoagulants like hirudin and citrate give no protection. Heat destroys the toxin, though the isolated proteoses survive boiling. Giving the extracted lipoids back, or adding unsaturated soaps, neutralizes it fully. Animals dosed below the lethal line suffer deep prostration and a marked fall in temperature, and those previously injected resist better. Readers get a poison manufactured from the body's own serum, and disarmed by returning what was taken away.
europmc-pmc2125289:
Alfred E. Cohn, Francis R. Fraser, and Ross A. Jamieson of the Rockefeller Institute hospital traced digitalis's fingerprint on the human electrocardiogram in 1915. Patients took the drug by mouth. When the record's T wave starts upright, the first change is a lowering. The final change is inversion, and the whole stretch from the end of R to the end of T is involved.

The sign is quick to arrive and slow to leave. It can be detected within thirty-six to forty-eight hours of starting the drug. It may persist as long as twenty-two days after the drug is stopped, though five days is also seen. That lingering, they note, explains why a second course needs less digitalis than the first to reach the same effect. Readers get a drug's presence read off a tracing for weeks after the bottle is closed.
europmc-pmc2126289:
A. E. C. Lathrop and Leo Loeb bred mouse strains together to test how tumor tendency passes from parents to offspring. Their paper is the fifth part of a tumor-origin series in the Journal of Experimental Medicine, from 1918. They chose strains watched for generations and steady in their rates. Some lines produced tumors often, others rarely.

Crosses between strains of like rate gave offspring with rates like the parents', and those crosses served as the control pattern. Crosses between Cream mice, a very low tumor strain, and English Sable mice, a high tumor strain, mostly gave hybrids with rates between the two parents. A few leaned toward one side. In crosses between English mice and the Silver strain, split off from English stock yet low in tumors, the high English rate prevailed. Tumor tendency, their numbers say, is inherited in a graded way.
europmc-pmc2131089:
William deB. MacNider asked whether pregnancy unsettles the blood's acid-base balance, and found that age decides the answer. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1926. The measure was the blood's reserve alkali, followed in pregnant animals against non-pregnant controls of the same ages.

In non-pregnant animals the reserve alkali stays constant at every age period, though constancy does not itself prove stability. In pregnant animals an instability may develop, sometimes tied to kidney injury, a retention effect, and sometimes arising independently of any such injury. In the independent group the disturbance grows more frequent, and appears earlier in gestation, as the mother's age increases. In old pregnant animals some mechanism other than the kidney fails to hold the balance, so that as pregnancy advances a normal state turns pathological. Gestation taxes the body's chemistry in proportion to its years.
europmc-pmc2140289:
Jacques Loeb opened his amphoteric colloids series in 1918, in The Journal of General Physiology, with gelatin as his test substance. Amphoteric means a substance can act as acid or base. Gelatin has an isoelectric point, the acidity at which it carries no net charge. Loeb asked on which side of that point gelatin can exist as a charged ion.

For gelatin the point sits at a set acidity. Ionized gelatin exists only as a negative ion on the less acid side, and only as a positive ion on the more acid side. At the point itself it splits into neither. A prior treatment with alkali leaves no trace once the gelatin is moved to the acid side, and the reverse holds for acid treatment. The charge state is fixed by present conditions alone.
europmc-pmc2140789:
Osterhout and Dorcas, at The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, studied how carbon dioxide enters living cells in a 1925 paper, using the alga Valonia. Carbon dioxide is made by every living cell and must cross cell boundaries both ways. Earlier work with hydrogen sulfide had hinted that only uncharged molecules pass. The pair tested that rule for this gas.

Little or no carbon dioxide, their experiments indicate, enters normal Valonia cells except as undissociated molecules. From that rule a forecast follows. When a cell's interior is more acid than the fluid around it, with excess base equal, the total carbon dioxide inside should settle lower than outside at equilibrium. The paper's measurements back the picture.
europmc-pmc2383989:
Eimer and Holmes reviewed brain wave studies of emotional faces in 2007. The method records tiny voltage changes on the scalp as people view faces, letting researchers time each processing step in milliseconds. The question was how fast the brain registers that a face shows emotion.

Across experiments, emotional faces triggered a stronger positive brain wave than neutral faces. The effect began remarkably early, between 120 and 180 milliseconds after the face appeared. It showed for six basic emotions alike, so it does not come from detectors tuned to one emotion. When attention was pulled away from side-presented faces, the effect vanished. With faces at the centre of view it only weakened. The authors placed the effect in a cortex system that builds emotion readings on demand, running alongside deeper brain circuits.
europmc-pmc2519789:
Gilad and colleagues reported in 2008 that tiny RNA molecules in blood could serve as medical biomarkers, meaning measurable signs of body state or disease. The molecules are microRNAs, short regulators that fine-tune gene activity and are already known to circulate in body fluids. The team first built reliable methods to extract and measure them in serum, the liquid part of blood.

Profiles from healthy people proved consistent from person to person, which supports the method's robustness. The team then compared pregnant and non-pregnant women. MicroRNAs tied to the placenta were clearly higher in pregnant women's serum, and their levels rose in step with the stage of pregnancy. The authors present serum microRNAs as a promising new class of blood markers.
europmc-pmc2564789:
Annemans and colleagues compared gout care in the UK and Germany in 2008 using general practice records from 2000 to 2005. Gout is a painful joint disease driven by uric acid crystals, and its companion illnesses and everyday management were poorly charted. The team drew on records of 2.5 million UK patients and 2.4 million German patients.

Gout prevalence came out identical at 1.4 percent in both countries. Other illnesses were common. Obesity led in the UK, at 27.7 percent of gout patients. Diabetes led in Germany, at 25.9 percent. Companion illnesses grew more frequent as uric acid rose. Higher uric acid also predicted more flares. Patients above the top band faced roughly double the flare odds of those kept below 360 micromoles per litre.
europmc-pmc2610389:
Garthwaite reviewed in 2008 how nitric oxide works as a chemical messenger in the mammalian brain. Nitric oxide is a gas, which makes it an oddity among neurotransmitters, yet its signalling role reaches back to the earliest nervous systems. Twenty years of evidence had tied it to a growing list of brain functions, and this review digs into the mechanisms underneath.

The receptors specialised to detect nitric oxide respond by making a second messenger, cGMP. They amplify even brief, faint whiffs of the gas enormously. From there the signal can change neuron excitability and synaptic strength at either side of a synapse, over short and long timescales. Garthwaite also covers signalling to non-neuronal cells and a surprise channel between blood vessel cells and brain cells, judging the gas unusually economical and versatile.
europmc-pmc2615189:
Ojha and colleagues showed in 2008 that Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the tuberculosis bacterium, can grow as biofilms that shelter drug-tolerant cells. Tuberculosis treatment takes six to nine months with several antibiotics, and relapse after incomplete clearance is common, blamed on persistent tolerant bacteria whose hiding place was unknown. In other pathogens such tolerance often comes from biofilms, surface-attached communities wrapped in a self-made matrix.

The team grew defined tuberculosis biofilms in the laboratory. The biofilms need specific conditions, unlike free-floating growth. Their matrix is rich in free mycolic acids, the waxy fats of the bacterial coat. Inside, a population of bacteria survived exposure to high antibiotic levels that would kill ordinary cells. The authors propose these biofilm persisters as a target for shortening therapy.
europmc-pmc2637989:
Perera and colleagues reported in 2009 on a possible chemical mark linking air pollution before birth to asthma in young children. They studied families in New York City, where more than a quarter of children had asthma. Mothers wore personal air monitors during pregnancy to measure soot-like chemicals from traffic, called PAHs.

The team read chemical tags on DNA from cord blood, tags that can switch genes off. In a first group of 20 children, over 30 DNA spots changed with the mother's pollution level. One gene stood out: ACSL3, which helps the body handle fats. In 56 children, heavy tagging of this gene matched high pollution exposure during pregnancy. It also matched asthma symptoms reported before age five, making it a candidate early warning sign.
europmc-pmc2689489:
Bagshaw and colleagues analyzed in 2009 the intensive care of very old patients across Australia and New Zealand, drawing on 120,123 admissions to 57 units over six years. People aged 80 and over made up 13 percent of all admissions staying at least a day, a share growing by about 5.6 percent per year.
