The very old arrived sicker, with more chronic illness, and more often came from long-term care homes. They were less likely to be put on breathing machines. Their death rates ran higher: 12 percent died in the unit and 24 percent in hospital, against 8 and 13 percent for younger patients. Adjusted for other factors, age over 80 still multiplied the odds of hospital death more than fivefold. Survivors were far more likely to leave for rehabilitation or long-term care. Demand, the authors project, could rise over 70 percent by 2015.
europmc-pmc2714989:
Petrides and Pandya traced in 2009 the wiring into the monkey brain areas that match Broca's area, the human frontal zone for speech. In humans, areas 44 and 45 form that zone and sit just in front of face-movement cortex. Whether monkeys held true matches, and how rear brain areas reached them, had long been disputed.

Their detailed tracing in macaque monkeys found two distinct routes into those frontal homologues. One route came from parietal cortex, the upper side area, and one came from temporal cortex, the hearing area, through the extreme capsule fiber bundle. Separate rear inputs reaching one speech-linked zone give clues to how language wiring may have evolved.
europmc-pmc2732489:
Trabulsi, Keller, and Tardelli Gomes compared in 2002 typical and atypical enteropathogenic E. coli, gut bacteria that cause infant diarrhea by attaching tightly to the intestinal wall and flattening its surface. Typical strains are a leading cause of infant diarrhea in developing countries but rare in industrialized ones. Atypical strains seemed to matter more in richer countries, which raised the question of how the two forms differ.

The forms differ in genetics, surface types, virulence traits, and reservoirs: humans alone carry typical strains, while animals also carry atypical ones. Atypical strains sit closer to Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, a dangerous relative, and look like emerging pathogens. Both forms share the attaching lesion machinery, encoded on a shared pathogenicity island.
europmc-pmc2758589:
Craven and co-authors showed in 2009 that alpha-hemolysin switches on the NLRP3 inflammasome in human and mouse monocytes. Alpha-hemolysin is a toxin from community-acquired MRSA Staphylococcus aureus. Monocytes are a type of white blood cell. The toxin is a key virulence factor in severe, tissue-killing lung infections from this drug-resistant bacterium. How it drove inflammation and cell death was not well understood.

Using highly purified toxin, they found inflammasome assembly turns on caspase-1, an enzyme that matures inflammatory signals. Mutant toxin that cannot lyse cells failed to trigger the pathway. Together with other bacterial signals, it drove release of interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-18, and it killed cells through an NLRP3-dependent necrosis that spilled further alarm molecules.
europmc-pmc2780389:
Slaby, Svoboda, Michalek, and Vyzula reviewed in 2009 microRNAs in colorectal cancer, small non-coding RNAs that dial gene activity down. These molecules steer basic cell processes such as programmed death, specialization, and development. In many tumors, including colorectal cancer, their levels shift. Lab studies show individual microRNAs can act as tumor suppressors or as cancer promoters, extending the classic model of how this cancer develops.

Expression profiles of microRNAs can predict a patient's outlook and likely response to chosen treatments. They can also help name the origin of cancers found without a known primary site. MicroRNAs turn up in blood serum and plasma too. As minimally invasive markers, they detected this cancer well, comparing favorably with the stool blood test. The review maps their signaling roles, marker promise, and prospects as drug targets. Blood tests built on them would spare many people a more invasive workup.
europmc-pmc2797089:
Nègre and colleagues built the first full map in 2010 of insulator elements across the fruit fly genome. Insulators are DNA stretches that act as borders, shaping which control regions can reach which genes. The team tracked where six insulator-linked proteins bind in fly embryos, using a method that pulls down bound DNA.

They found more than fourteen thousand likely insulators, including every classic example known before. The sites fell into two main classes, set apart by which proteins they carried. Insulators sat between control regions and their target gene starts, divided genes that switch on at split times, and marked borders between active and quiet genome zones.
europmc-pmc2873589:
Gu and colleagues showed in 2010 that a faulty Parkinson's protein placed only in brain support cells can still wreck movement in mice. The protein, alpha-synuclein, piles up in neurons in Parkinson's disease, but clumps also appear in astrocytes, the support cells. The team switched on the disease-linked mutant form, called A53T, only in astrocytes to see what that alone would do.

The mice developed fast, severe paralysis as protein clumps grew and support cells turned reactive. Normal support jobs failed, shown by tiny brain bleeds and loss of the transporters that clear the signal chemical glutamate. Inflammation surged, most sharply in midbrain and spinal cord, where dopamine and movement neurons died in large numbers. Astrocyte clumps are active drivers of disease, not bystanders.
europmc-pmc2875389:
Andreu and colleagues tuned in 2010 glowing reporter genes so tuberculosis bacteria can be tracked inside living animals without surgery. The reporters are luciferases, enzymes that make light, borrowed from fireflies, sea creatures, and bacteria. Light output had been too dim through tissue, so the team tested vector, promoter, and gene spelling combinations to raise it.

They achieved the first working expression of the full bacterial light operon in the tuberculosis germ and in a fast-growing relative. That version needs no added fuel chemical, since the bacteria make their own. Other tuned versions shone brightly enough for external imaging as well. Brighter, self-lit bacteria open the way to watching infection and drug action in the same animal over time.
europmc-pmc2879389:
Boakes and co-authors warned in 2010 that the records scientists use to map species are skewed by when and where people bothered to look. They assembled about one hundred seventy thousand bird sightings for pheasant-like birds across Europe and Asia, reaching back two centuries. Five sources fed the set: museum collections, journals, bird ringing records, printed atlases, and citizen website reports.

Museum material gave the widest and deepest range coverage but took enormous effort to gather. Journal records grew steadily over time, while ringing, atlas, and website data exist almost only for recent decades. Geographically, records clumped in Western Europe and Southeast Asia. Anyone charting biodiversity change from such data must first correct for these gathering habits, or trends in looking will masquerade as trends in nature.
europmc-pmc2883589:
Sepulcre and co-authors mapped in 2010 how each human brain region balances nearby chatter against long-distance talk. Using resting brain scans, they measured functional connectivity, the tendency of regions to rise and fall together, separately for neighbors within a short radius and for distant partners. The balance turned out to form an orderly map of the cortex.

Basic sensing and movement areas leaned heavily on local links, while higher association areas leaned on distant ones. A few hub regions scored high on both scales, marking them as crossroads. High local connectivity traveled with tight clustering, long network paths, and low wiring cost. When people performed a task, engaged regions shifted toward local coupling, showing the balance flexes with demand.
europmc-pmc2944089:
Krämer and colleagues followed older women in Germany's industrial Ruhr district to test whether traffic pollution raises diabetes risk, reporting in 2010. Earlier hints came mostly from snapshots in time rather than follow-up studies.

Women free of diabetes in their mid-fifties were tracked for sixteen years, with home exposure to traffic particles and nitrogen dioxide estimated at several scales. New diabetes cases appeared more often where exposure was higher, with risk rising notably across the exposure range. The link held after accounting for age, weight, and social factors, and a blood marker of inflammation added context.
europmc-pmc3002989:
Shin and colleagues studied a tuberculosis gene called eis in a 2010 infection study, asking how it helps the bacterium survive inside immune cells. The gene was known to aid a harmless relative's survival, but its actions in real tuberculosis were unclear.

Macrophages infected with bacteria lacking eis filled with self-eating compartments, released more inflammatory signals, and produced extra reactive oxygen from two sources. Despite that fierce response, the infected cells died by a route not using the usual death switch, and blocking self-eating or the oxygen signal saved them. Adding purified Eis protein reversed the effects.
europmc-pmc3009689:
Löytynoja and Goldman launched webPRANK, a web server for aligning DNA and protein sequences with family tree awareness, in a 2010 article. Tree-aware alignment had beaten standard methods in benchmarks and improved studies of gene change, but the underlying program was hard for many users to run well.

The server accepts DNA, protein, and codon data, plus genome-scale models, and exports results in standard formats. Its browser shows the alignment beside the family tree so users can inspect, trim weak sites objectively, and explore alternative evolutionary stories the program scores. Advanced inference thus becomes point-and-click.
europmc-pmc3017089:
Chen built TCM Database@Taiwan, presented in a 2011 article as the world's largest free database of Chinese medicine compounds for computer drug screening. Drug hunters now mine old remedies for fresh leads, yet no free 3D structure set existed.

Volunteers spent years pulling data from medical texts and papers. They logged over twenty thousand pure compounds from hundreds of ingredients. Each entry offers structure files in 2D and 3D forms for download. Searches run by property, part structure, ingredient, or planned action. The set opens old formulas to virtual screening by any researcher.
europmc-pmc3026789:
Fontainhas and colleagues asked in 2011 whether brain chemical signals control the restless motion of immune cells in the retina. The cells, called microglia, constantly wave their fine branches even when tissue looks quiet and healthy. Using living mouse retina kept in a dish, the team filmed labeled microglia and added drugs that boost or block specific signals.

Signals carried by glutamate made branches longer and more active, while signals carried by GABA, another messenger, calmed them down. The effects did not act on microglia directly, since the cells showed no electric response and lacked the matching receptors. Instead, glutamate triggered release of a third chemical, ATP, through channels in nearby cells. The study shows neural activity itself tunes immune surveillance in the central nervous system.
europmc-pmc3087489:
Chell and Brand found in 2010 the missing link between food and the waking of sleeping stem cells in the fruit fly brain. Fly neural stem cells pause during development and restart only when nutrition signals arrive from the fat body, the fly's liver like organ. The team identified a sheet of glial cells, the brain's support cells, as the relay station.

Those glia release insulin like peptides when the larva is fed. The stem cells' insulin receptor pathway proved necessary for them to leave their sleep and resume growth and division. Forcing the glia to release the peptides, or switching the pathway on inside stem cells directly, woke the cells even without dietary protein. The result uncouples brain growth from body nutrition at one defined relay. It shows whole body state reaches stem cells through local support cells, a pattern likely shared with mammals.
europmc-pmc3110189:
Amit Dutt and colleagues published a 2011 study in PLoS ONE hunting for drug targets in squamous lung cancer. This form of lung cancer causes many deaths each year, yet unlike other lung cancers it had no proven gene-targeted treatment. The team scanned tumour DNA for copied gene regions.

A stretch of one chromosome holding a growth receptor gene was copied extra times in about a fifth of squamous tumours and in a small share of other lung cancers. A cancer cell line with that extra copying died back when the receptor was blocked by gene silencing or by small drug molecules. The results mark this receptor as a promising target for a group of patients with few options.
europmc-pmc3161989:
Ryan Noyce and colleagues identified the missing doorway measles virus uses to infect airway lining cells in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Lab strains enter through one known receptor and wild strains through another on immune cells, but the route into respiratory lining cells, key to spread between people, was unknown. Comparing gene activity in infectable and resistant cancer cell lines produced a short candidate list.

Only one candidate, a surface protein also known as a tumour marker, made resistant cells infectable. Blocking it with antibodies or silencing its gene stopped infection, and binding tests confirmed the virus grips it directly. Several measles strains use this doorway, which sits on both faces of lining cells. The discovery explains airway infection and flags a marker shared with lung, breast, and colon tumours.
europmc-pmc3285189:
Carissa Thomas and colleagues found that a gut bacterium calms inflammation by making histamine, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. The probiotic Lactobacillus reuteri secretes something that suppresses the inflammatory signal TNF, but the factor was unknown. Combining chemical profiling of the bacterium's output with targeted gene knockouts, the team isolated and identified the active compound.

The factor was histamine, which the bacterium builds from the dietary amino acid histidine using a three-gene cluster; disabling any of the genes abolished the effect. The team then traced the mechanism in human immune cells triggered through a bacterial sensor. The bacterial histamine acted on the H2 receptor and raised a signaling molecule. Through the PKA pathway, that signal throttled the ERK cascade and cut TNF production. The work shows a gut resident converting food into an immune-regulating signal, a template for anti-inflammatory strategies.
europmc-pmc3317189:
Genc, Zadeoglulari, Fuss, and Genc reviewed how breathing polluted air can harm the brain, in a 2012 article. Air pollution is a worldwide health burden, and its damage to lungs and hearts is well documented. Evidence has been growing that it also reaches the nervous system, with links to stroke, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and developmental disorders in children.

Tiny particles can travel from the nose or lungs into the brain, the authors explain, and inflammation starting in the body can spill over to affect the brain as well. Inside the nervous system, pollution appears to stir immune cells, create damaging reactive chemicals, disturb blood vessels, and weaken the protective barrier around the brain. The exact chain of events is still unclear, and the review calls for work that pins down the mechanisms so at risk people can be protected.
europmc-pmc3338789:
Swarts, Mosterd, van Passel, and Brouns showed how bacterial immune memory expands itself during an active defense, in a 2012 study. Bacteria of the E. coli kind carry a system called CRISPR that stores snippets of invader DNA as a memory bank. Small RNAs built from the bank guide proteins to destroy matching invaders, and new snippets are added after fresh encounters.

Working with a high copy plasmid as the invader, the team watched bacteria cure themselves of it under relaxed conditions. Cured bacteria had added between one and five new memory snippets aimed at the plasmid. All new snippets in a single bacterium targeted the same strand of the plasmid, showing that the first snippet's attack steered later additions. The authors describe a positive feedback loop that lets the memory bank grow fast against an invader already under fire.
europmc-pmc3350489:
Turroni and co-workers mapped the microbes that settle in a newborn baby's gut, focusing on bifidobacteria, among the first and most typical residents. They checked faecal samples from eleven infants to see which species show up in the first stage of life and how these microbes deal with their new home.

Bifidobacteria dominated the samples, with species such as Bifidobacterium longum and Bifidobacterium breve to the fore. The team also looked at how they feed, noting traits that suit them to milk sugars in the infant gut. The results show a specialised gut community forming within days of birth, and they feed interest in these microbes for infant health.
europmc-pmc3359589:
Van Bakel and co-workers produced the first draft genome and transcriptome of Cannabis sativa, a plant cultivated for fibre, food, medicine, and its intoxicating effect. They sequenced the high-potency marijuana strain Purple Kush and compared its gene activity with that of the hemp cultivar Finola, bred for fibre and seed.

The draft genome spans 534 megabases and contains some thirty thousand genes. Genes for cannabinoid production were expressed more strongly in Purple Kush. Crucially, the enzyme making the psychoactive compound's precursor appeared only in Purple Kush. Finola instead carried the enzyme for a non-psychoactive counterpart. That swap neatly explains the chemical split between marijuana and hemp.
europmc-pmc3419089:
Cribbs and colleagues charted immune gene activity across the aging human brain in 2012, comparing young adults, older adults, and Alzheimer's patients. They screened hundreds of immune-related gene probes in four brain regions using tissue arrays. The question was how much of the change blamed on Alzheimer's is really aging itself.

Aging dwarfed the disease: about forty percent of immune probes shifted with normal aging, most switching on, while only a small share changed in Alzheimer's. Nearly every arm of the built-in immune system rose with age, and the brain's resident immune cells showed wide activation, though a few calming factors fell. Responses also differed by sex. Protecting cognition, they argue, means cooling this slow immune burn starting in late midlife.
europmc-pmc3448089:
Brown, DeCoffe, Molcan, and Gibson reviewed in 2012 how diet can unbalance the gut microbiota and thereby feed immune disease. The gut community is the body's largest source of foreign material for the immune system to judge, and the gut must tolerate food and friendly microbes while still attacking invaders. When that balance breaks, inflammation and autoimmunity can follow.

The disturbed state, called dysbiosis, is tied to bowel diseases such as Crohn's and ulcerative colitis and to body-wide troubles including obesity and both kinds of diabetes. A sharp dietary shift in recent decades coincides with rising rates of these conditions. The gut community was once thought fixed from childhood; the review shows diet keeps editing it, for better or worse.
europmc-pmc3496989:
Mold poisons in animal feed rarely break European limits, yet Elisabeth Streit and ten colleagues warn the official picture misleads in this 2012 review. Mycotoxins come from fungi such as Aspergillus, Penicillium, and Fusarium and can contaminate crops in the field or in storage.

Five mycotoxins are covered by EU rules, and breaches are rare in official monitoring. Low-level Fusarium contamination is another story: deoxynivalenol appears in over half of samples. Multi-toxin studies find more than one mycotoxin in 75 to 100 percent of samples. Mixed low doses may still harm animal health, the reviewers argue, so co-occurrence, not single-toxin limits, should frame feed safety.
europmc-pmc3504389:
Parkinson's disease kills dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra with strange selectivity, and J. Paul Bolam and Eleftheria K. Pissadaki propose an architectural reason in 2012. Genes, protein clumps, and toxins linked to the disease are spread across the brain, yet these particular neurons die first.

Each such neuron grows an enormous, branching axon, the fiber that carries its signals, feeding a huge number of connection points. Running that structure leaves the cell on a tight energy budget, living on the edge. Any extra strain, whether from the neuron's own chemistry or body-wide factors, can tip it over. The hypothesis reframes vulnerability as a cost of an extravagant wiring plan.
europmc-pmc3607889:
Lilian Rojas and Marilia Gomes made the case for an old diabetes drug in Diabetology and Metabolic Syndrome in 2013. Metformin remains the first treatment offered in type 2 diabetes after decades of use, while flashier drug classes keep arriving. Their review asks why the veteran still leads, and how far its benefits stretch beyond lowering blood sugar, into blood vessels, clotting, and fat handling.

Trial and laboratory evidence credits metformin with easing insulin resistance, calming oxidative stress, and improving vessel lining function and blood fat profiles. It also reshapes fat stores, a package that may explain fewer heart attacks than sugar control alone predicts. On its own it rarely drives blood sugar dangerously low, and it mixes safely with most drugs. Stomach side effects ease with slow dose increases or the extended-release form. Newer roles in prediabetes and pregnancy are weighed.
europmc-pmc3660389:
Blood thinners are given by habit more than by risk in a world registry of a common heart rhythm fault, Kakkar and a large team report in a 2013 PLoS One study. The registry, called GARFIELD in the text, enrolled 10,614 adults newly told they had non-valvular atrial fibrillation, at 540 sites across the world, between late 2009 and late 2011. Each patient carried at least one stroke risk factor on entry.

Mean age was about 70, and most patients scored high on stroke risk scales: 84 percent sat in the high band of one main scale. Yet 38 percent of high-risk patients got no blood-thinning drug, while 42 percent of low-risk patients got one. The pattern held at the end of the era when one drug family ruled such care. Risk scores, the authors say, were not driving who got protection from stroke.
europmc-pmc3740789:
E. Magda Price and seven colleagues take a hard look at a widely used DNA methylation chip in Epigenetics & Chromatin in 2013. The Illumina Infinium HumanMethylation450 BeadChip measures methylation at more than 485,000 sites, covering 99 percent of known genes. Some of its probes, though, mislead: a common variant at the target site or loose binding can fake a methylation signal.

The team re-annotated the whole array. They flagged probes with documented sequence variants at the target CpG, 4.3 percent of all probes, and probes whose binding is not specific. They also classified each target by its CpG setting and its place in a gene. The result is a filter researchers can apply before trusting any single probe's reading.
europmc-pmc3840689:
Pavel S. Novichkov leads a team in describing a web resource in BMC Genomics in 2013. The resource, RegPrecise, collects gene regulation maps for bacteria. It rebuilds regulons, the gene sets that one switch protein controls, by comparing genomes across species.

Version 3.0 greatly widens the curated set. Maps are sorted by species group, by body traits, and by switch protein, so users can browse in the way that suits their question. The base holds switch maps inferred across many genomes and dozens of bacterial groups. It also covers RNA-based switches called riboswitches. The site serves labs that need a fast start on how a new bacterium runs its genes, without years of bench work.
europmc-pmc3840789:
Joshua G. Dunn, Catherine K. Foo, Nicolette G. Belletier, Elizabeth R. Gavis, and Jonathan S. Weissman report a genome scan in eLife in 2013. Ribosomes build proteins by reading gene copies until a stop signal. At times they read past the stop, making a longer protein. How often this happens in real animals was unclear.

Using ribosome profiling in the fruit fly, the team caught ribosomes in the act across the whole genome. Readthrough proved far more common than gene family trees had guessed. Most cases were new in this fly species. The added protein tails bear marks of natural selection and hold signals that place proteins in cell spots. The team also saw readthrough in yeast and human cells, so the trick looks broad.
europmc-pmc3851189:
Brett S. Abrahams and a team of co-authors describe a gene database upgrade in Molecular Autism in 2013. New genome tools have flooded autism research with candidate genes. Judging the proof for each gene is hard, above all for scientists outside genetics.

SFARI Gene 2.0 adds a scoring module where the research community rates gene proof in a set, shared way. Past lists were patchy, loose, and frozen once made. The new system weighs mixed proof types, such as repeat association finds and rare variant finds, on one scale. Scores can shift as fresh proof lands. The platform aims to give autism researchers a living, trusted map of which genes merit deep follow-up work.
europmc-pmc3851789:
Thalía Harmony wrote a solo review on slow brain waves in Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience in 2013. EEG studies tie brain rhythms to many mental acts, yet the slowest band, delta, has drawn little study during thinking tasks. Harmony asks what delta waves do while the mind works.

Delta power rises in front head areas during mental math, meaning tasks, and memory holding tasks. Her proposal is that steady delta waves quiet brain networks that should stay off during a task, cutting interference. Working memory, on this view, is attention turned inward on held items. The review gathers task data to back the claim and maps where the slow waves rise. It gives the delta band a clear job in focused thought.
europmc-pmc3892689:
Matthias Lienhard, Christina Grimm, Markus Morkel, Ralf Herwig, and Lukas Chavez present a software update in Bioinformatics, with the record dated 2014. Enriching DNA for a trait or mark, then sequencing it, is a core lab method for epigenetic study. Comparing read coverage between groups is the shared core task.

Their package, MEDIPS, now handles any number of samples per group, from a few to the hundreds that wide association studies bring. Fresh statistical tests spot coverage gaps between conditions with more power. New tools check how alike samples are and label genome regions from public databases. The free package runs inside the R and Bioconductor systems that many labs already use, and aims to make such comparisons fast and simple.
europmc-pmc3895189:
Updated guidance on neuromyelitis optica in the Journal of Neurology, with the record dated 2014, comes from Corinna Trebst and co-authors. The disease attacks the optic nerve and spinal cord and was long read as a form of multiple sclerosis. It is now seen as its own disease, since a marker antibody was found.

Testing for that antibody, aimed at a water channel protein, is the core of diagnosis and splits the disease from its look-alikes. Brain scans are a must in work-up, and brain spots do occur and show telling patterns, so they no longer rule the disease out. Eye layer scans add support. The study group sums fresh knowledge on the wider spectrum of the disease and on treatment, from guidelines, papers, and expert meetings.
europmc-pmc3896989:
Andrei Manoliu and a team of co-authors study brain networks in depression in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2013. Major depression involves tangled links within and between three large brain networks: a self-focused one, a salience one, and a control one. A hub in the salience network, the right front insula, is thought to switch between the other two.

Resting brain scans of patients and healthy controls were split into network maps. Patients showed weaker links inside the insula hub, and that weakness tracked with worse symptoms. It also tracked with odd links between the self-focused and control networks. The pattern fits the idea that a faulty switch traps patients in self-focused, negative thought and blocks goal-directed focus.
europmc-pmc3915289:
Brian M. Campbell, Erik Charych, Anna W. Lee, and Thomas Möller review a chemical pathway in the brain in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2014. The kynurenine pathway breaks down tryptophan, an amino acid from food, into a family of products that act on nerve cells. Some of these products harm neurons, while others protect them, and two key enzymes steer the balance between the branches.

Several enzymes in the pathway answer to inflammatory signals, which links the pathway to brain diseases marked by inflammation. The review focuses on how those signals tune the pathway in degenerative and psychiatric disorders. Cells such as microglia and astrocytes, the brain's immune and support cells, sit at the center of that control story.
europmc-pmc3952189:
Yuriko Osakabe, Keishi Osakabe, Kazuo Shinozaki, and Lam-Son P. Tran review how plants endure water stress in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2014. Drought cuts photosynthesis first, and if it lasts, growth and yield fall hard. Plants have layered defenses, and decades of work have mapped much of the machinery: the genes, signals, and chemistry that let a plant sense dry soil and adjust.

The review follows that regulatory network end to end. Stomata, the leaf pores, close to save water, guided by hormone balance, above all abscisic acid. Cells adjust their chemistry to hold water, guard against the reactive oxygen that stress creates, and shield themselves from excess light damage. The authors frame the knowledge as the raw material for breeding or engineering crops that yield well on less water.
europmc-pmc3971489:
Sean C. Taylor and Anton Posch explain how to design a western blot experiment that yields real numbers, in BioMed Research International in 2014. Western blotting, a workhorse method for detecting a chosen protein in a messy sample, is over three decades old. It began as a yes-or-no detection tool, but journals now demand quantitative claims, fold changes between samples, read from the glow of the blot's bands.

That shift changes everything upstream: how samples are prepared and loaded, how the blot is run and imaged, and how the numbers are analyzed. Building on their own updated protocol, the authors walk through the full workflow with a focus on preparation and data analysis, flagging where casual habits quietly destroy accuracy. The guide targets researchers whose blots must stand up as measurements, not pictures.
europmc-pmc3975389:
Bo Yu, Xiaomin Zhang, and Xiaorong Li review vesicles shed by mesenchymal stem cells. Their paper appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. These stem cells are studied as treatments for many conditions. Proof increasingly says they act at a distance. They work through what they secrete, not by settling in tissue. Exosomes are a prime part of that package. They are nano-sized bubbles that carry proteins and small RNAs.

Studies report several effects for these exosomes. They can repair tissue damage. They can calm inflammation. They can tune the immune system. In these ways they act much like the cells themselves. Results conflict in places, though. The mechanisms are not settled either. As therapy, bubbles offer practical edges over cells. They store well and carry no risk of abnormal cell division. Rejection is less likely as well. The review weighs the proof and the open questions.
europmc-pmc4022989:
The NSCLC Meta-analysis Collaborative Group pools patient-level data on chemotherapy before lung cancer surgery, in The Lancet in 2014. Lung cancer of the non-small-cell type can often be cut out, yet many patients relapse. Drug treatment after surgery had already been shown to help survival. Whether giving the drugs before surgery helps was less sure.

The group gathered records from fifteen randomised trials, close to twenty-four hundred patients in all. Giving chemotherapy before surgery cut the risk of death, lifting five-year survival from forty percent to forty-five percent. Freedom from relapse and time before spread to distant sites also improved. No drug mix, schedule, or patient type stood out as gaining more or less. The authors call the pooled result the most complete evidence yet for treatment before surgery, with side effects in the trials mostly mild.
europmc-pmc4039489:
Jakob Hedegaard and a large Danish team test whether archived wax-block tissue can feed modern genome sequencing, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Hospitals store vast numbers of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded samples. The fixing process shreds and chemically alters DNA and RNA, which long kept such archives out of sequencing studies.

The team compared fresh-frozen tissue with wax-block samples, including matched pairs from the same patients, across six tissue types. Extraction method strongly shaped yield and quality. DNA libraries for exome reads failed often, succeeding in under a third of tries. RNA libraries fared better and could even be built from blocks two decades old. For blocks stored under three years, most DNA variants matched the frozen pair. RNA profiles matched closely at any age. A fixed gene set read differently in fixed tissue, a bias users must allow for.
europmc-pmc4050989:
Samantha E. Serrano and four colleagues review how much of the phthalate chemical load in bodies comes from food, in Environmental Health in 2014. Phthalates, used to soften plastics, are linked to several health outcomes. Diet is thought to be a main route in, but which foods carry them was scattered across small studies.

The team gathered seventeen food monitoring studies plus a few health and intervention studies. One compound, DEHP, ran consistently high in poultry, cooking oils, and cream-based dairy. Another, DEP, stayed low in nearly all foods. Body burden studies lined up: meat, fatty foods, and dairy tracked with higher DEHP in people. Diet-based estimates put infants highest, above the safety reference dose on a typical diet. Meat- and dairy-heavy diets roughly doubled exposure for older groups too. The review names the food groups that exposure warnings should target first.
europmc-pmc4086089:
Marco Biasini, Torsten Schwede, and colleagues described the latest version of SWISS-MODEL, a fully automated server that builds 3D protein models from related known structures. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Model building had become routine for proteins with no experimental structure, provided the tools stayed simple.

The updated template library now records how protein chains assemble and which helper molecules they bind, so models can include multi-chain structure. The pipeline leans heavily on quality estimates to pick the best templates and to tell users how accurate a model should be. Accuracy is also checked continuously by an outside system. A new website lets users search, group, and compare templates interactively before building.
europmc-pmc4155789:
Marie-Claire Arrieta, Leah T. Stiemsma, Nelly Amenyogbe, Eric M. Brown, and Brett Finlay reviewed the gut microbiome in the first years of life. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Colonisation begins at birth, and the community keeps shifting for about three years before it looks adult-like.

Those same years bring big developmental changes to the body and immune system. Imbalances in early gut microbes are now linked to bowel disease, obesity, and asthma, though whether imbalance causes the disease or follows from it is only starting to be answered. The authors describe how the early community is built, what environment shapes it, and its role in immune, metabolic, and brain disease. Better knowledge could yield microbe-based prevention given early in life.
europmc-pmc4246889:
Nan Wang, Hongwei Liang, and Ke Zen reviewed the controls on macrophage polarization in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Macrophages lean toward two poles: M1 cells that attack and damage tissue, and M2 cells that calm inflammation and repair. The balance between them shifts constantly, and diseases from infection to cancer tilt it.

The review maps the machinery that sets the dial. Signal pathways from the cell surface switch on transcription programs for each pole, and small RNAs and chemical gene marks fine-tune the result afterward. Because the poles mirror the Th1 and Th2 split in T cells, the two systems reinforce each other. The authors argue that naming the molecules that move the dial is the step toward drugs that push macrophages the way a disease requires.
europmc-pmc4293489:
Agnieszka Płóciennikowska, Aneta Hromada-Judycka, Kinga Borzęcka, and Katarzyna Kwiatkowska review how the receptor TLR4 teams up with membrane raft proteins to trigger inflammation. Their review appeared in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2015. TLR4 senses LPS, a piece of Gram-negative bacteria, and its response protects the body yet can overshoot into sepsis.

CD14, a protein anchored in fat rich membrane patches called rafts, catches LPS and hands it to TLR4. Other raft proteins, among them Lyn kinase, CD44, and CD36, join the signaling chain, and one branch requires the receptor to be pulled inside the cell. The review assembles this cast into one account of how a bacterial alarm is raised.
europmc-pmc4351889:
Voon and many colleagues published a 2015 study in Molecular Psychiatry on why people with compulsive disorders repeat choices they know are harmful. The team compared two ways of learning: goal-directed choice, which weighs likely outcomes, and habit learning, which repeats past rewarded acts. They tested people with obsessive-compulsive disorder, binge eating, and methamphetamine dependence on a decision task that can separate the two styles.

All three patient groups leaned more than controls toward habit learning, even though their disorders differ in many other ways. Brain scans linked that bias to lower gray matter volume in the caudate and in part of the frontal cortex. The shared tilt toward habit may help explain why fixed, repeated behavior takes hold across these conditions.
europmc-pmc4413189:
Emilia Szymańska and Katarzyna Winnicka reviewed the shelf-life problem of chitosan, in Marine Drugs in 2015. Chitosan is a natural polymer made from shells. Drug and medical firms prize it because it is versatile and kind to living tissue. Many goods based on it are in development. Yet chitosan systems change and break down on the shelf, and that weak shelf life blocks real use. A long shelf life is the field's key test.

The review sorts what shapes long-term stability into three groups: factors inside the material, the storage setting such as heat and damp, and how the goods are made. It then surveys the fixes. Fixes include tighter control of storage, more gentle making, and added stabilizers. Blending chitosan with other polymers is another route. Changing the polymer with chemical or ionic agents is a further route, weighed against the traits that made it attractive.
europmc-pmc4491189:
Naoji Matsuhisa and six co-authors printed a stretchable electrical conductor for electronic textiles in Nature Communications in 2015. Future flexible displays and sensors printed over large areas need inks that conduct well even while stretching. Their ink mixes silver flakes with a fluorine rubber and a fluorine surfactant, a soap-like additive that proved to be the key ingredient.

The surfactant guides the silver flakes to form connected networks at the surface of the printed layer. That gives high conductivity at rest. It also retains a record level for such materials when stretched to more than twice its length. The team demonstrated the ink in a stretchable transistor array on a rubber sheet that kept working under strain, and in a muscle-signal sensor printed directly onto a textile garment. Printed, clothing-integrated electronics come a step closer with this formulation.
europmc-pmc4541289:
Ulf Andreasson leads a twelve-author practical guide to checking lab test methods, in Frontiers in Neurology in 2015. Biomarkers measured in blood or spinal fluid guide diagnosis and drug trials, including for Alzheimer's disease. The workhorse test, ELISA, varies in quality between labs, and sloppy checks let both steady bias and random error slip into results.

Validation means proving a method meets the needs of its planned use. Much has been written on which traits to test, but little on how to run the tests. The guide fills that gap with step-by-step standard procedures for each validation trait, plus a report template. It targets research, clinical routine, and drug development alike.
europmc-pmc4555089:
Kyle R. Barnes and Andrew E. Kilding review running economy in Sports Medicine — Open in 2015. Economy is the oxygen cost of holding a set speed, and it separates good endurance runners from great ones. Comparing values between studies is tricky, though, since test protocols, gas analysis gear, and averaging methods all differ.

The review gathers representative values for trained, highly trained, and elite men and women across speeds, giving coaches a usable yardstick. It then unpacks what drives economy: fuel use, breathing and heart work, stride mechanics, and nerve-muscle traits combine in a mix unique to each runner. The authors stress that economy is simple to measure yet anything but simple in origin.
europmc-pmc4571289:
Stuart Ibsen and four co-authors switch neurons on with sound, in Nature Communications in 2015. Neuroscience needs ways to fire single neurons, especially deep ones. Light-based optogenetics works but demands surgery to deliver light into tissue. Ultrasound crosses tissue without cutting, so the team tested it on the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans.

Normal worms ignore low-pressure ultrasound unless gas-filled microbubbles help transduce it. Putting a touch-sensing channel protein, TRP-4, into chosen neurons made those neurons answer the sound with behavior changes. With that trick the team drove sensory neurons and interneurons and found a new role for the PVD sensory neurons in shaping movement. They propose the method, sonogenetics, for broader use in living animals.
europmc-pmc4623689:
In 2015, Yujie Fang and colleagues' rice study identifying a gene switch, SNAC3, that raises tolerance to heat and drought appeared. Rice often faces high temperature and water shortage together. Switch proteins called NAC factors control many stress response genes. The work appeared in the Journal of Experimental Botany.

SNAC3 acts directly on genes that keep reactive oxygen species, damaging oxygen byproducts, in balance. With SNAC3 active, rice plants handled both heat and water shortage better. The authors present the switch as a single lever that steadies the cell's internal chemistry under several stresses at once. Breeders and genetic engineers could use such multi-stress switches to protect yields as growing conditions grow harsher.
europmc-pmc4631089:
Zhiping Xu and colleagues' 2015 mouse study centres on aquaporin-4, a water channel in the brain, and Alzheimer's disease. The channel helps clear soluble amyloid-beta, the protein that builds up in the disease, along fluid pathways in the brain. Direct proof of its role was missing. The team used mice bred to develop amyloid build-up, with and without the channel gene. The work appeared in Molecular Neurodegeneration.

Mice lacking aquaporin-4 at twelve months showed worse memory, more amyloid deposits, more vessel amyloid, and loss of synaptic proteins and a growth factor in memory regions. Their star-shaped support cells also shrank. Despite some inflammatory side effects linked to the channel, the balance favoured protection, and the authors name it a promising treatment target.
europmc-pmc4720289:
Matthew T. Agler, Jonas Ruhe, Samuel Kroll, and five colleagues studied the microbes living on plant leaves in PLoS Biology in 2016. A plant's surface hosts bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes together, and weather plus plant genes shape that crowd. The team sampled wild Arabidopsis plants, planted different plant genotypes in the field, and ran lab colonization tests. Their question was how outside forces reach the whole community.

The answer ran through hub microbes. A few highly connected species transmit the effects of weather and host genes to everyone else. One hub, the pathogen Albugo, cut bacterial diversity and steadied community makeup. Another, a yeast called Dioszegia, interacted directly with leaf bacteria. The study shows community control can be indirect: press the hub, and the network moves. That idea may guide efforts to steer crop microbes toward plant health.
europmc-pmc4813189:
Hafiz Maher Ali Zeeshan and four co-authors review the tie between a stressed protein-folding shop and damaging oxygen forms, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016. The shop, the endoplasmic reticulum, folds the cell's exported proteins. Its chemistry is redox-based: folding helpers pass electrons along, and oxygen species leak as a by-product.

When misfolded proteins pile up, the shop strains, and the leak grows into cascades that involve calcium release and several named enzyme systems. The review follows those cascades into a long disease list: brain degeneration, diabetes, artery disease, kidney and liver failure, and tissue damage after blocked blood flow. The shared thread, the authors argue, makes the folding shop's redox balance a drug target worth joint study across those fields.
europmc-pmc4854589:
Ian T. S. Coyle-Gilchrist and co-authors counted frontotemporal lobar degeneration syndromes across two British counties in 2016, in Neurology. The group covers frontotemporal dementia and two movement syndromes, progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal syndrome. Cases were gathered from many sources over two years in a population of 1.69 million, then checked against current diagnostic rules.

Counts give prevalence, new-case rates, lifetime risk, and survival for each syndrome, scaled to a standard European population. Rarer middle-ground forms were counted too, not just textbook cases. Firm numbers help plan clinics and trials for these less-known dementias, which strike younger than Alzheimer's disease and are often missed.
europmc-pmc4994089:
Baohong Wang and seven co-authors compare gut microbes in nonobese patients with fatty liver disease and healthy controls. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2016. Gut imbalance is tied to obesity and to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, but nonobese patients were unstudied. The team enrolled more than one hundred and twenty nonobese adults, about a third with the disease, and profiled stool microbes by two sequencing methods.

Patients' gut communities were less diverse, with a clear shift at the phylum level. They carried more Bacteroidetes and less Firmicutes than controls. Several families that make short chain fatty acids fell sharply. Gram negative bacteria, a source of inflammatory toxins, were more prevalent. The disturbed pattern tracked with liver blood test markers of disease. The authors say gut profiling may help flag fatty liver risk even without obesity.
europmc-pmc5016889:
Bethany N. Hannafon and nine co-authors test blood-based markers for breast cancer in Breast Cancer Research in 2016. Small RNAs called microRNAs show cancer-linked patterns, but blood holds a jumble of them from many sources. The team focused on exosomes, tiny parcels that cells shed with a cargo matching their cell of origin, and read the microRNAs packed inside.

Several microRNAs were packed into breast cancer exosomes far above their levels in the cells' surroundings. One, miR-1246, also ran high in blood exosomes from mice carrying human breast tumors, proof that tumor parcels reach the blood. In people, miR-1246 and miR-21 were both higher in blood exosomes from 16 breast cancer patients than from healthy controls. Together, the two separated patients from controls well, hinting at a future blood test for the disease.
europmc-pmc5040989:
Sharanbir K. Sidhu and John W. Nicholson review glass-ionomer cements for dentistry in the Journal of Functional Biomaterials in 2016. These filling materials set by an acid-base reaction in two to three minutes, forming a hard, tooth-colored solid. The review updates the literature on their structure, properties, and clinical uses, with weight on the last five years of work.

Once set, the cement is bioactive: it slowly forms an ion-exchange layer where it meets the tooth, and that layer gives it its strong, lasting grip. It also releases fluoride over long periods, a benefit dentists value even though the proof is not fully settled. Two modified forms are covered. Resin-modified versions match the original's physical strength but sit less well with living tissue. Glass carbomer is more brittle and weaker, and how its bioactivity compares is still unclear.
europmc-pmc5073889:
Etienne Becht and ten co-authors introduce MCP-counter in Genome Biology in 2016, a method that counts cell populations inside a tissue from its gene activity alone. Knowing how many immune and stromal cells infiltrate a tumor or organ guides prognosis and therapy, but direct measurement needs fresh samples and lab assays. MCP-counter instead reads marker genes in a bulk transcriptome and returns abundance scores for eight immune and two stromal populations.

The team validated the scores against lab-made RNA mixtures of known makeup and against stained tissue sections, and showed the method avoids weaknesses of earlier computational approaches. Applied broadly, it sketched immune landscapes across healthy tissues and non-blood cancers, recovering patient groupings tied to survival in lung, colorectal, and breast cancers. Running on existing data, it lets researchers mine old datasets for such clues and may help select patients for immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc5120989:
Artur Krężel and Wolfgang Maret reviewed the chemistry of zinc ions in Archives of Biochemistry and Biophysics in 2016. Zinc never changes its charge in the body and sits inside an estimated tenth of human proteins, holding shapes or driving reactions. Yet the chemistry of zinc ions moving freely between proteins is barely explored.

The review explains how zinc's grip on partner molecules differs from calcium's. Zinc binds far more tightly. It prefers nitrogen and sulfur partners. And it exchanges them at rates suited to signaling, transport, and storage. Small molecules such as ATP, citrate, and glutathione carry much of this mobile zinc. Knowing which form zinc takes, the authors argue, is basic to sound experiments and to designing zinc delivery or removal drugs.
europmc-pmc5210589:
Stefan Bienert, Andrew Waterhouse, Tjaart A. P. de Beer, Gerardo Tauriello, Gabriel Studer, Lorenza Bordoli, and Torsten Schwede reported new features of the SWISS-MODEL Repository in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017. The repository stores three-dimensional protein models built by an automated pipeline that copies the known shape of a related protein. It held over 400,000 quality models covering nearly a fifth of Swiss-Prot entries.

Recent work widened target coverage and improved the quality scores attached to each model, along with functional notes and in-page viewing. A new update scheme refreshes core organism models on a regular cycle and any single model on user request. The modeling pipeline now offers a program interface, and model coordinates moved to open licensing, so groups can download sets of models in bulk and reuse them elsewhere.
europmc-pmc5219689:
Lan Lin and Jianqiong Zhang reviewed gut microbes and immune balance in BMC Immunology in 2017. Trillions of microbes live in the human gut, and their products help build and tune the innate immune system, the body's fast first line of defense. The review asks how these microbes and their chemical outputs keep the gut stable, and what goes wrong when the mix is disturbed.

Friendly gut bacteria do more than crowd out germs: they strengthen the gut wall and calm or prime immune responses inside and beyond the gut. The review covers microbe-derived nucleic acids and metabolites, the small molecules microbes release, as routes of that influence. A disturbed community, called dysbiosis, is tied to inflammatory bowel disease, type 1 diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis, and further links reach metabolic disorders and brain function. Knowing these pathways could point to new prevention and treatment targets.
europmc-pmc5364389:
Alexis R. Barr and co-authors traced how cells weigh damage before they copy again, in Nature Communications in 2017. A cell that copies flawed DNA passes the flaws to its heirs. The tumor guard p53 can halt the cycle by raising the brake protein p21. That brake was known from outside blows like radiation. Its role in plain growth, where damage creeps in as DNA is copied, was unclear.

Watching single living cells, the team saw copying-phase damage raise p21 in the mother cell and on into its daughters. High brake levels froze the daughters before their next copy round. Low levels let them pass. Two cleanup enzymes chew the brake down just before copying starts, and that chew-down locks the go choice in place. Math models of the switch match the cell films. The brake, they show, is a scale that weighs last round's harm.
europmc-pmc5370189:
Yu Huang and co-authors measured weak electric fields inside the living human brain in eLife in 2017. A care method sends mild current through the scalp to nudge brain work. Its trials have grown fast, but no one knew how strong the field in the brain truly is, or where it lands. Computer models guessed at it, with no human checks to prove them.

Ten patients with epilepsy, who bore probes in their brains for care, gave the team direct reads. At the standard dose, field strength in the outer brain just reached the floor that animal work deems the least that can act. Models built on each person's own head shape matched the reads well, in both outer and deep probes. Set tweaks to the tissue flow values in books were needed, while finer splits of skull and fiber paths added nothing.
europmc-pmc5402289:
Yongfeng Deng, Yan Zhang, Bernardo Lemos, and Hongqiang Ren report a 2017 Scientific Reports study of microplastics in mice. Microplastics are plastic bits smaller than a few millimeters, found in seas, rivers, soil, and even table salt. Little was known about their harm in mammals. The team fed mice marked plastic beads of two sizes and traced where the beads settled in the body.

Beads built up in the liver, kidney, and gut, with the pattern set by bead size. Blood and tissue tests showed upset energy and fat handling, plus signs of oxidative stress, the harm done by reactive oxygen forms. Markers tied to nerve harm shifted too. The authors say the spread and effects point to broad health risks from such exposure.
europmc-pmc5427689:
Singh and co-authors explain why bacterial biofilms shrug off drugs that kill free cells. Their review appeared in The Open Microbiology Journal. A biofilm is a cluster of microbes glued to a surface. The cells build their own matrix of proteins, sugars, and DNA. Biofilms grow on medical devices and living tissue. They seed stubborn infections in patients. They also foul water systems and food plants.

The review breaks resistance into parts. The matrix slows and traps antimicrobial agents. It can soak up a large share of its own weight in such drugs. Cells deep inside grow slowly and dodge attacks. Neighbors swap genes and chemical signals. Those exchanges spread resistance traits. The matrix itself changes as conditions shift. The authors point to a hopeful route. Blocking the genes that build biofilms could prevent colonies. That would help patients with implanted devices most.
europmc-pmc5437289:
Elia and co-authors find that proline breakdown fuels metastasis and can be blocked to stop it. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Metastases cause ninety percent of cancer deaths. Spreading cells must adapt their phenotype. How metabolism supports that shift was poorly defined. The team compared breast cancer cells in flat culture. Spheroid culture forced a phenotype shift. Proline catabolism rose sharply in spheroids. The enzyme proline dehydrogenase drives that breakdown.

The same pattern held in real tumors. Metastases showed higher enzyme expression than primary cancers. The comparison covered patients and mice. Blocking the enzyme impaired spheroid growth. In two mouse models it cut lung metastasis formation. The effect was dose dependent. Healthy tissues showed no adverse effects. Organ function stayed normal under inhibition. Non-transformed mammary cells were spared in dishes. The authors nominate the enzyme as a drug target. It offers selectivity against metastasizing cells.
europmc-pmc5439289:
Mustapic and co-authors describe a blood test route into the living brain's disease processes. Their methods review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Brain diseases such as Alzheimer's start years before symptoms. Trials need cheap, gentle ways to spot them early. Spinal fluid tests are invasive. Brain scans are costly. Plain blood tests cannot show which tissue a signal came from. Vesicles shed by neurons may solve that.

Cells release tiny vesicles into the blood. The team pulls out the share that came from neurons. Those vesicles carry proteins from inside brain cells. Past studies used them to diagnose and predict Alzheimer's disease. The authors detail their isolation method here. They add proof that the catch is truly neuron-rich. The enriched vesicles beat plain plasma as a biomarker base. Their cargo is rich in signals for cell survival and repair. Such cargo could track drug response in trials.
europmc-pmc5459889:
Clausen and co-authors review the isoforms of the sodium-potassium pump in health and disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. The Na,K-ATPase maintains steep ion gradients across cell membranes. Those gradients power transport, signaling, and nerve firing. The brain spends most of its energy on this pump. Kidneys pack up to 50 million pumps per cell. Different tissues need different tuning. Evolution answered with isoforms of each subunit.

The pump has alpha, beta, and FXYD subunits. Each comes in several versions. Versions differ in kinetics, regulation, and partners. The review maps sequence variation onto structure. It charts where each isoform is expressed. Sperm carry a unique isoform vital for fertility. Mutations in alpha subunit genes cause distinct diseases. Many are neurological and severe. Plants and toads weaponize pump blockers. Prey animals counter with resistant pump mutations.
europmc-pmc5480189:
Seif and co-authors present a review in Cell Communication and Signaling. Their topic is the JAK-STAT signaling pathway in T helper cells. This pathway carries signals from cytokine receptors to the cell nucleus. It helps decide which type a T helper cell becomes. Faults in its control can lead to immune disorders.

The review first explains how the pathway starts, runs, and stops. Regulator proteins such as SOCS, PIAS, and phosphatases set its timing and strength. Later sections detail the pathway in each T helper subset. The authors close with new drug strategies that target the pathway. Such drugs may treat immune disease, they say. More regulators remain to be found.
europmc-pmc5485789:
Mosier-Boss presents a review in Nanomaterials on SERS substrates for chemical sensing. SERS boosts the faint light signal of molecules stuck to rough metal surfaces. The boost can reach single-molecule levels. Cheap portable Raman devices have widened its reach. This review covers only chemical detection, not biological uses.

Silver, copper, and gold are the workhorse metals. Substrates come as floating particles, fixed particles, or surfaces built by fine fabrication. Ready-made commercial options are listed as well. Weak points include poor selectivity and aging surfaces. Tricks for reuse and for picking one target from a mix are surveyed.
europmc-pmc548689:
Pollitt, Rose, and Kaufman present a systematic review in BMC Public Health on social status and heart disease. Low status tracks with more heart disease in study after study. The authors ask when in life status does its damage. Four life-course models frame the rival answers. They sorted 49 observational studies by design.

Low status early in life showed moderate support as a risk factor, they report. A lifetime pile-up of disadvantage showed consistent support. Moving up or down the social ladder showed little unique effect. Weak study designs limit firm verdicts, they caution. Cohorts followed from childhood would sharpen the picture.
europmc-pmc5691689:
Van Herck and co-authors present a starter's guide in Nutrients. It surveys animal models of fatty liver disease. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease now affects up to 30 percent of people. It tracks closely with obesity and diabetes. Animal models have been key to probing its mechanisms. Many models exist, each with strengths and weaknesses. Choosing the right one shapes what results can mean.

The guide sorts models into three broad families. Dietary models use feeds like high-fat diets. Chemical models use drugs or toxins to drive disease. Genetic models alter pathways tied to fat and inflammation. Each entry lists the traits a model reproduces. Body, blood, and tissue features are covered. Combined models that mix approaches are included too.
europmc-pmc5753389:
Papatheodorou and co-authors report the state of Expression Atlas, a database of gene and protein activity. The database gathers public data sets and reworks them with one standard pipeline. Users can ask where a gene is active across tissues, diseases, and species. By August 2017 it held 3,126 studies from 33 species.

The update adds plant data and large cancer and stem cell projects. Users can view big RNA studies side by side and download the data in plain tables. A new R package lets users search and pull data by script. Fresh tools show gene set overlap and genes that rise and fall together.
europmc-pmc5795289:
Negrini and co-authors present the 2016 SOSORT guidelines in Scoliosis and Spinal Disorders. SOSORT is an international society for non-surgical care of scoliosis. The guidelines cover idiopathic scoliosis in children and teens who are still growing. Idiopathic means the curve in the spine has no known cause. The document updates two earlier SOSORT guideline editions with fresh study proof.

The team built the guidelines from fresh reviews of studies on non-surgical care. They then used a Delphi process and a consensus meeting to agree on the advice. The result is 68 recommendations in total. Most deal with bracing and with scoliosis-specific exercises. Others cover assessment, other treatments, breathing, and sport. The authors note that strong proof is still new and uneven. They call for shared research methods, so future advice can rest on firmer ground.
europmc-pmc5823889:
Duchamp de Lageneste and co-authors find potent stem cells in the periosteum. The periosteum is the skin-like wrap around bones. Bone repair depends on skeletal stem cells. Marrow stem cells were the usual suspects for that job.

In mice, periosteal cells outgrew marrow cells in lab tests. They also formed cartilage and bone more readily. After transplant, they joined repair sites and stayed long-term. Gene profiles flagged periostin as a key partner. Mice lacking periostin healed fractures poorly. Their periosteum also failed to rebuild its stem cell pool. Readers get a new address for the skeleton's repair crew.
europmc-pmc5832789:
O'Leary and co-authors test whether early shifts in blood-borne tumor DNA predict benefit from a breast cancer drug pair. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. It draws on the PALOMA-3 trial of palbociclib plus fulvestrant. No marker yet tells who will gain from CDK4/6 blockers.

The team tracked PIK3CA mutations in circulating tumor DNA. Their level after 15 days of treatment strongly foretold progression-free survival. ESR1 mutations, picked up after hormone therapy, were often minor subclones. Their early shifts predicted outcome far more weakly. Subclones thus answered the same drugs in divergent ways.
europmc-pmc5860089:
Tian and co-authors present an updated version of ChAMP, a methylation analysis pipeline. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. ChAMP works on data from Illumina BeadChips, tools that measure DNA methylation. The new EPIC chip covers over 850,000 sites in the genome. That is about twice the reach of the older 450K array. The update lets the package handle both chip types.

New features include correction for mixed cell types in a sample. The package can now find large methylated blocks and gene modules. It also adds network analysis and gene set enrichment. Interactive graphic interfaces guide users through the steps. ChAMP is free through Bioconductor for R users. The update targets genome-wide studies of epigenetic change.
europmc-pmc5905289:
Jeevanandam and co-authors review nanoparticles and nanostructured materials. Their review appeared in the Beilstein Journal of Nanotechnology. These tiny materials offer tunable traits beyond bulk forms. They are sorted by size, makeup, shape, and origin. Wider production makes harm questions hard to avoid. The team set out to compare natural and engineered kinds.

The review traces the history and sources of these materials. Toxic effects on mammal cells and tissues are summed up. Types of toxic reaction are set out in detail. Rules in different countries to curb risks are compared. Knowledge gaps for risk assessment are named plainly. Readers get history, hazard, and regulation in one survey.
europmc-pmc5943489:
Yang and co-authors profile how the oral microbiota changes as oral squamous cell carcinoma advances. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. This cancer is aggressive and common among men in Taiwan. Some bacteria link to gum disease and to oral cancer. The team sampled oral rinses from 197 patients and 51 healthy people. They sequenced the 16S rRNA V3V4 region to name the microbes.

Stage 4 patients held more complex oral communities than controls, they report. Fusobacteria rose steadily from health through stage 4. Other genera, such as Streptococcus, fell as cancer progressed. A three-bacterium marker panel separated stage 4 cases from controls well. Its area under the curve reached 0.956.
europmc-pmc6088389:
Ludwig and co-authors offer a tutorial on SWATH-MS for quantitative proteomics. Their guide appeared in Molecular Systems Biology. Many fields need protein counts that stay accurate across hundreds of samples. SWATH-MS fragments every peptide inside set mass windows. Nothing is picked in advance.

That approach pairs deep coverage with steady numbers. Analysis leans on spectral libraries built beforehand. The tutorial walks through planning an experiment. It covers instrument settings step by step. Data analysis uses peptide-centered scoring. Trade-offs and alternate strategies get honest space. Readers get a working manual for a demanding method, from design to results.
europmc-pmc6089889:
Arvaniti and co-authors automate Gleason grading of prostate cancer with deep learning. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Gleason scoring predicts patient outlook better than any other tool. Yet grading is slow and varies between pathologists. Middle scores vary most.

The system trained on tissue samples from 641 patients. Expert annotations taught it the patterns. It then graded an independent set of 245 patients. Agreement with each pathologist matched their agreement with each other. Its scores also split patients into clear survival groups. Mixed-pattern cases, the hardest kind, graded well. Readers get evidence for more objective cancer grading.
europmc-pmc6143589:
Al-Shahi Salman and co-authors offer a systematic review and meta-analysis in The Lancet Neurology on bleeding growth in the brain. When a spontaneous brain haemorrhage grows, patients tend to fare worse. Growth is also a target for treatment. The team set out to pin down how often growth happens and what predicts it.

They pooled individual data from cohorts and trials that used repeat brain scans. The search covered studies from 1970 to 2015. From these data they built and validated models that predict growth. They also tested whether CT angiography, a scan of blood vessels, improves the models. The results help doctors judge risk early after a bleed.
europmc-pmc6161189:
Gänger and Schindowski wrote a review in Pharmaceutics on designing drug formulations that travel from nose to brain. The blood-brain barrier blocks most molecules from entering the brain. Other routes, such as injections into the spine, are invasive. The nasal route offers a gentler bypass.

At the roof of the nasal cavity sits the olfactory mucosa, close to the brain. Drugs placed there can head toward the brain along this area. The review describes the tissue's architecture and its physical and chemical traits. It also explains mucociliary clearance, the cleaning flow that sweeps drugs away. Formulations must be tailored to these facts to work. The review guides that design work.
europmc-pmc6197289:
MacParland and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications mapping the cells of the human liver. The liver is the body's largest solid organ, central to metabolism and immunity. Yet its full cell makeup was poorly known. The team profiled fresh tissue from five human livers.

Single-cell RNA sequencing of 8,444 cells revealed 20 distinct populations. They span liver cells, vessel and bile duct cells, stellate cells, and many immune types. Two resident macrophage populations stood out, one inflammatory and one calmer. Flow tests and tissue staining confirmed the map. This atlas gives researchers a reference for liver disease, from hepatitis to cancer immunology.
europmc-pmc6270789:
Priyadarsini reviews the chemistry of curcumin, the yellow pigment in turmeric. Her review appeared in Molecules. Curcumin has drawn wide study for over four decades. Most reviews cover its biology, not its chemistry. This one fills that gap. It tracks curcumin from first isolation in 1815 to today.

Methods for pulling it from turmeric open the account. Lab synthesis routes follow. The review then covers how curcumin breaks down in light and in the body. Reactions with other molecules are also explained. Metal binding and new nano forms get a closing section. Tiny metal and oxide carriers may fix curcumin's poor uptake. The author names where chemistry work should go next. That chemical view may unlock the biology that follows.
europmc-pmc6274989:
Sonnweber and co-authors review arachidonic acid and its products in heart and metabolic disease. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Arachidonic acid is a fat found in cell membranes. Its breakdown products link food intake to immunity and inflammation. That link sits at the start of many common diseases. Obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver are among them.

The review maps how the body makes and uses these products. It then traces their roles in tissue balance and immune defence. Disease sections cover atherosclerosis, heart attack, and stroke. Cholesterol handling is also discussed. Obesity has nearly tripled worldwide in forty years. That rise makes this fat pathway more important, not less. The authors give a concise tour of a crowded field. It can guide both diet research and drug design.
europmc-pmc6300389:
Day and co-authors run a large genome-wide meta-analysis of polycystic ovary syndrome. The study appeared in PLoS Genetics. It pooled 10,074 cases and 103,164 controls of European ancestry. The syndrome involves excess male hormones and faulty ovulation. Two rival rule sets are used to diagnose it.

The team found three new risk loci for the syndrome. They also confirmed 11 loci reported before. Genetic patterns barely differed between the two diagnosis rules. Linked traits included obesity, insulin levels, and type 2 diabetes. Analysis pointed to body mass and other factors playing a causal role. The work also gave first genetic hints of a male form.
europmc-pmc6324489:
Osseo-Asare and co-authors ask minority resident doctors how race shapes training. Their qualitative study appeared in JAMA Network Open. Black, Hispanic, and Native American doctors remain rare in medicine. They form about a third of the population. They are only a small share of practicing physicians. The team interviewed 27 minority residents about workplace life.

Three themes ran through the interviews. Residents faced a daily stream of slights and bias. They were often made spokespeople for their whole race. Many also struggled to merge personal and professional identity. They felt marked as outsiders while doing so. Residency is already a high-stress stage of training. These extra burdens add to that strain. The authors urge schools, hospitals, and accreditors to act.
europmc-pmc6335289:
Lassmann reviews why multiple sclerosis takes different courses in different patients. His review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Most patients start with relapses and remissions. Many later slide into steady progression. A minority progress from the very start. Evidence suggests these courses differ in key ways.

Two kinds of inflammation seem to run side by side. One floods white matter with T and B cells. It breaks the blood-brain barrier and leaves classic plaques. The other gathers immune cells slowly in brain coverings. It causes damage without major barrier leaks. Progressive forms share much of this slow pattern. They differ mainly in the load of focal lesions. The split view helps explain why relapse drugs fail in progression.
europmc-pmc6335389:
Chen and co-authors review polyamines, small molecules that steer plant growth. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science. Polyamines carry several amino groups each. They occur in almost all living cells. In plants they guide flowering and embryo growth. They also shape ageing and responses to harsh conditions.

Stress from drought, salt, and cold all involve polyamines. Plants make more of them or receive them from outside. Both routes can raise yield and stress tolerance. Genetic engineering can boost their production as well. The review sorts what each approach has shown. It also flags how these molecules do their work. Many of those pathways remain unclear today. The authors call polyamines a promising class of plant biostimulants.
europmc-pmc6369189:
Weech and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Psychology on two linked experiences in virtual reality. Presence is the feeling of being inside a virtual space. Cybersickness is the discomfort that VR can cause, much like motion sickness.

The review gathers studies that measured both factors at once. On balance, the authors conclude the two are negatively related. When presence rises, sickness tends to fall, and shared sensory integration processes may drive both. System immersiveness may shape the link as well. They note a lack of large, strong studies and close with advice for future work.
europmc-pmc6391789:
Li and co-authors present a methods article in Genome Biology on finding where transcription factors bind. A lab method called ATAC-seq maps open chromatin, the parts of DNA a cell can read. Bound factors leave small dips, or footprints, in that signal.

Past tools read those footprints poorly because the cutting enzyme has its own biases. Their method, HINT-ATAC, learns those biases and corrects for them. It also accounts for how nearby DNA packaging shapes cuts. In tests it beat rival methods at naming true binding sites. The tool is offered for standard genome pipelines.
europmc-pmc6420889:
Bolte and co-authors review environmental causes of autism in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences. Autism has mixed roots, with genes and environment both at play. The pathways by which outside factors raise risk are still poorly understood.

The review maps parental age, drugs and toxins in pregnancy, and birth risks. It also covers smoking, alcohol, nutrition, and vaccination claims. Protective factors like folate and fatty acid intake get space too. Older parents and the drug valproate stand out among supported risks. The authors call for work that joins exposure records with biology.
europmc-pmc6451189:
The Early Breast Cancer Trialists' Collaborative Group pools data from 26 randomized trials and 37,298 women with early breast cancer. The question: does squeezing chemotherapy into shorter gaps, or giving drugs one after another at full dose, beat standard scheduling? Total drug amounts were broadly similar between arms, which isolates timing as the thing being tested.

Dose-intense treatment cut ten-year recurrence from about 31 to 28 percent and breast cancer mortality from about 21 to 19 percent. The gains held across the two-weekly trials, the sequential anthracycline-taxane trials, and trials combining both tricks. Deaths without recurrence did not rise. For cancer doctors, the patient-level proof favors tighter schedules where patients can tolerate them.
europmc-pmc6497989:
Millwood and co-authors use genetics to settle whether moderate drinking protects the heart, exploiting two alcohol-metabolism variants common in China that sharply change how much people drink. The China Kadoorie Biobank followed 512,715 adults for about ten years; 161,498 were genotyped. Conventional analysis reproduced the familiar story, a U-shaped risk curve with men drinking about 100 grams weekly showing the fewest strokes and heart attacks.

Genotype-predicted intake, ranging from 4 to 256 grams weekly, showed no U-shape at all. Because genes are assigned before lifestyle can confound them, the missing dip undercuts the causal reading of the conventional curve. The lower risk of moderate drinkers in observational data is not confirmed when drinking is predicted by genotype instead of self-report.
europmc-pmc6498789:
Angelakis, Gillespie and Panagioti present a systematic review and meta-analysis in Psychological Medicine. It asks whether abuse and neglect in childhood are linked to suicidal thoughts and attempts in adult life. The authors searched five databases for studies up to January 2018. They pooled data from 68 studies covering 261,660 adults, and weighed study quality in their checks.

All forms of maltreatment raised the odds of a suicide attempt. Sexual abuse showed odds about three times higher. Physical and emotional abuse each raised the odds about two and a half times. Abuse that combined several types carried the highest risk, at over five times the odds. Similar links held for suicidal thinking. Age, health and study quality did not change the main findings, and the authors say how maltreatment leads to suicidality is still poorly understood.
europmc-pmc6520689:
Paoli and co-authors review meal frequency, timing and fasting in human health. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Population studies have linked more meals with lower disease risk. Some trials point the other way. Recent work found higher risk at six or more meals a day.
