The authors treat the fasting gap between meals as a central factor. Eating out of step with body clocks may harm health. Breakfast use and the spread of daily energy intake also matter. So do calorie limits and night-time eating. The authors suggest a regular pattern may help. That means breakfast, more energy early, two or three meals, and steady fasting gaps.
europmc-pmc6619389:
Shrestha and co-authors review how cancer patients trade quality of life against length of life. Their systematic review appears in Psycho-Oncology. Treatment choices often force that trade. Strong therapy may add months yet cost comfort and function. Little was known about what patients themselves prefer.

The authors searched studies published up to October 2018. From 4,393 articles, 30 met their rules. Older patients leaned toward quality over length of life. Younger patients more often chose aggressive care to gain years. Sex, education, faith, and cancer type showed no clear sway. Patients in better health valued length more. Those in poorer health favored quality. The authors call for deeper study of these hard choices.
europmc-pmc6717989:
Otasek and co-authors describe Cytoscape Automation, a bridge between Cytoscape and workflow tools. Cytoscape is a popular program for viewing and analyzing biological networks. Its point-and-click style, though, makes work hard to repeat or scale. The new system exposes Cytoscape functions to code instead.

More than 270 core functions and 34 apps can now be called through a standard web interface. Python and R libraries in tools like Jupyter wrap those calls. Published workflows already use the system. The change lets researchers script network analysis, share exact steps, and rerun the same work on new data without clicking through menus.
europmc-pmc6779789:
Bian and co-authors tested a gut bacterium, Akkermansia muciniphila, against ulcerative colitis in mice. This bacterium is linked to a healthy gut lining, but its role in colitis was unknown. Twenty-four male mice received the bacterium or a salt solution daily for 14 days. Colitis was triggered with a chemical, DSS, in their drinking water.

Treated mice fared better on every measure. They lost less weight, kept longer colons, and scored lower on tissue damage. Their gut barrier worked better too. Inflammatory signals in blood and tissue fell, including TNF-alpha and several interleukins. The bacterium also reshaped the gut community, raising its diversity. Higher diversity tracked with lower inflammation.
europmc-pmc6891889:
Zhou and co-authors report a systematic analysis in The Lancet on health in China. China holds a fifth of the world's people, and its government sets health policy province by province. Planners need province-level evidence, not just national averages. The team applied Global Burden of Disease 2017 methods to all 34 province-level units.

They estimated deaths, years of life lost, years lived with disability, and combined burden for hundreds of causes from 1990 to 2017. Risk factors from diet to air pollution were scored the same way. The picture shows a country mid-transition, with infectious disease retreating and chronic disease advancing at different speeds in different provinces.
europmc-pmc6928789:
Matica and co-authors review chitosan as a wound dressing material. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Chitosan is a natural polymer with antimicrobial power. It is biocompatible, non-toxic, and cheap. It is also biodegradable and aids wound healing.

The authors explain how chitosan attacks microbial cells. They then cover its contact with mammalian cells. That contact shapes the healing process itself. Bacterial resistance makes such natural agents attractive. Antibiotics remain the main tool against infection. Yet microbes keep gaining resistance to them. The review ends with dressing applications. It surveys chitosan-based products already on the market.
europmc-pmc6998289:
Wu and co-authors review small proteins hidden inside RNAs long labelled non-coding. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. Long non-coding RNAs and circular RNAs were thought to make no proteins. They regulate cancer processes and serve as markers. New computing and translation studies are overturning that assumption.

Some of these RNAs do encode tiny functional peptides. The authors first set out the computer and lab methods used to find candidate peptides. They then catalogue specific examples from both RNA classes. Each peptide's mechanism is explained, whether it pushes cancer growth or restrains it. Such peptides could become tools for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment in their own right. The field is young, and the authors flag challenges ahead, but the payoff could be a fresh family of cancer targets.
europmc-pmc7012389:
Taillie and co-authors evaluate Chile's food labelling and advertising law on drink purchases. Their study appeared in PLOS Medicine. The 2016 law was the first anywhere to combine three tools at once. It mandated front-of-package warning labels, limited marketing to children, and banned school sales of foods and drinks high in sugar, salt, saturated fat, or calories.

Using purchase records from 2,383 urban households between 2015 and 2017, the team compared what people bought after the law with what pre-law trends predicted. Purchases of high-in drinks fell by about a quarter against that forecast. Most flagged drinks were high in sugar. Richer and poorer households cut back by similar amounts, though the study tracks purchases, not what people drank. Education levels in the sample rose over the study period, which the models account for. The results offer evidence that a bundled policy can shift buying at national scale.
europmc-pmc7031489:
Khan, Arooj, and Wang review natural killer cell checkpoints in Frontiers in Immunology. Immune checkpoint blockade has changed cancer care, but most work has aimed at T cells. Natural killer cells, another arm of anti-tumour defence, are catching attention as a newer target. Tumours exploit checkpoints on these cells to escape attack, as happens in chronic infections too.

Beyond the classical receptors KIRs, LIRs, and NKG2A, newer checkpoints such as PD-1, CTLA-4, TIGIT, TIM-3, and members of the Siglec family can all disable natural killer cells. The review gathers the evidence on each one. Blocking two checkpoints at once may produce synergy, and pairing blockade with other methods that restore killer cell strength could raise efficacy further. The authors map a fast-growing route for cancer immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc7042389:
Enaud and co-authors review the gut-lung axis in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. Gut and lungs sit far apart, yet their microbial communities influence each other through immune and chemical signals. Lung microbes were recognised only recently and form a quieter community than the gut's. Most studies follow bacteria, but fungi and viruses at both sites also take part.

The review explains how gut and lung microbiota shape immune responses and can steer the course of respiratory disease. Crosstalk runs between host and microbes and also between microbial kingdoms, with effects both local and long-range. The authors focus on bacteria and fungi, since knowledge of the human virus community is still limited. Understanding this axis could open new ways to treat lung disease by tending the gut.
europmc-pmc7072889:
Mazini and co-authors weigh stem cells in wound healing in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Fat tissue holds mesenchymal stem cells, called ADSCs, at several sites in the skin and beneath it. These cells can multiply and turn into skin cells to replace damaged ones. They broadcast signals that switch on regeneration in their neighbours, which may matter more than the cells they become.

During healing, ADSCs enter wounds and mature into dermal fibroblasts, blood vessel lining cells, and keratinocytes. Together with fibroblasts they are the main source of the extracellular matrix proteins that hold skin together. Their secretions shift macrophages out of their inflammatory mode, encourage new vessels and granulation tissue. The review balances those hopes against the limits: results vary, standard preparations are lacking, and long-term safety data are thin. It is a field with real biology still waiting on clinical discipline.
europmc-pmc7179689:
Hördt and co-authors use genome data to redraw the family tree of Alphaproteobacteria. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. This class of bacteria is diverse in shape, lifestyle, and habitat. Some members matter greatly for medicine and ecology. Older classification leaned on a few physical traits and one gene.

The team analyzed draft genomes from more than 1,000 type strains. Whole genomes give far richer comparisons than a single gene tree. Their results sharpen the borders between groups in the class. Many species descriptions gain new genomic details, such as DNA composition and genome size. The work gives taxonomists a firmer base for naming and grouping these bacteria. It shows how genome sequencing is reshaping bacterial classification.
europmc-pmc7191289:
Kitajima and co-authors review what was known about SARS-CoV-2 in wastewater. Their article appeared in The Science of the Total Environment. The virus spreads mainly through droplets and close contact. Yet its RNA had been found in sewage. That raised questions about risk and about tracking the disease through wastewater.

The review gathers evidence on how the virus reaches sewage and how long it survives there. Detecting it reliably in such samples is a technical challenge. The authors discuss faster tests for places with limited lab equipment. They also ask whether the virus in wastewater stays infectious. Sewage monitoring could warn of outbreaks early. The article maps the research still needed before that promise is secure.
europmc-pmc7195489:
Coutzac and co-authors report that gut bacteria products in the blood can blunt a cancer immunotherapy. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Gut microbes make short-chain fatty acids when they ferment dietary fiber. These compounds shape immune responses throughout the body. The team studied mice and patients treated with CTLA-4 blocking antibodies.

High blood levels of butyrate and propionate tracked with resistance to the treatment. Those patients also carried more regulatory T cells. The fatty acids weakened the immune activation the drug tries to spark. Memory T cell buildup after treatment stayed low. The results suggest diet and gut microbes can sway cancer therapy. Measuring these compounds might one day help predict who responds.
europmc-pmc7243089:
Lai and co-authors study COVID-19 infections among health care workers at a major Wuhan hospital. Their case series appeared in JAMA Network Open. The hospital tracked 9,684 staff during the early outbreak. Of them, 110 caught the virus. Infection rates ran higher in supposedly low-contagion areas early on, before defenses tightened.

Nurses younger than 45 were hit especially hard in that first phase. Most infected staff had nonsevere disease. The share of silent carriers and the death rate both measured 0.9 percent. Tests of 90 surface samples around the hospital found no virus. The authors argue most infections happened before protection caught up. Their lesson: guard every area, not only the obvious hot zones, from day one.
europmc-pmc7245089:
Xu and co-authors report treating severe COVID-19 patients with tocilizumab, an antibody that blocks the interleukin-6 receptor. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. In severe disease, immune cells flood the body with cytokines such as IL-6. That storm drives the lung damage that kills patients. The antibody stops IL-6 from docking on its target cells.

All 21 treated patients saw their fever return to normal. Before treatment, 20 of them needed extra oxygen. Afterward, 15 were able to lower their oxygen intake. Blood levels of the inflammation marker CRP fell sharply in most. Scans and symptoms improved alongside. The authors present the drug as an effective option for severe cases. The small, uncontrolled design still called for bigger trials.
europmc-pmc7247289:
Gebhard and co-authors review how sex and gender shape COVID-19 outcomes in Europe. Their article appeared in Biology of Sex Differences. Early data from China showed the disease killing men at higher rates. Fatality there was reported at 2.8 percent in men versus 1.7 percent in women. European data showed similar case counts by sex but worse outcomes in older men.

Men with existing heart and vessel disease fared worst of all. Why women are partly protected remains unclear. Hormones, immune differences, and behavior all enter the discussion. One suspect is TMPRSS2, a protein the virus uses for entry, which male hormones can influence. Blocking it stopped the virus in lab tests. The authors argue the gap could guide risk scoring and treatment choices for both sexes.
europmc-pmc7280589:
Liu and co-authors test whether interleukin-6 levels can track the course of severe COVID-19. Their study appeared in EMBO Molecular Medicine. Sixty-nine patients with severe disease were followed. Severe cases showed low lymphocyte counts and raised levels of several markers, including C-reactive protein, ferritin, and D-dimer.

Patients' starting IL-6 levels were tied to how severe the disease became. Higher starting IL-6 went with higher peak fever and worse chest scan findings. During recovery, IL-6 fell and scans improved. In patients whose condition worsened, IL-6 rose further instead. Watching IL-6 change over time, the authors conclude, gives doctors a practical marker for monitoring severe cases and judging whether treatment is working.
europmc-pmc7315789:
Hartnett and co-authors measure how sharply emergency department visits fell in the United States during the first pandemic weeks. Their report appeared in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. The country declared a national emergency on March 13, 2020. Using national syndromic surveillance data, the team compared March 29 to April 25, 2020 with the same weeks in 2019.

Total emergency visits were 42% lower than the year before. Declines were largest among children aged 14 years and under, among females, and in the Northeast. Many missing visits were likely for real emergencies, not only minor complaints. The authors urge health messages telling people to seek care immediately for symptoms of serious conditions such as heart attack, alongside virtual visits and triage lines to keep departments safe.
europmc-pmc7353689:
Lücking and co-authors ask how reliably fungi can be identified, in IMA Fungus. Fungi may number around 3 million species, yet their simple, often hidden forms make naming them hard. DNA barcoding, reading a standard gene stretch, is the usual first tool, especially the internal transcribed spacer region.

No single tool fits all fungi, the authors argue, because each lineage evolved differently. They propose an integrative approach that combines family trees, visible traits, ecology, and, where possible, breeding biology. Checking old identifications also matters and is often skipped. Their framework grades how accurate and precise barcoding really is. Readers get a field guide to a quiet problem: naming most of life's second largest kingdom.
europmc-pmc7385189:
Lei and co-authors review why checkpoint cancer drugs stop working, in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. Drugs blocking PD1 or PDL1 free T cells to attack tumors and have scored major successes. Yet most patients never respond, and many who do later relapse.

The review sorts resistance into kinds present from the start and kinds acquired under treatment pressure. Early resistance can come from tumors that attract little immune attention, broken antigen display, exhausted T cells, or a suppressive neighborhood. Acquired resistance grows through tumor editing, backup inhibitory signals, and fresh T cell exhaustion. Understanding each route, the authors argue, is the path to better combinations. Readers get a map of an immunotherapy bottleneck.
europmc-pmc7385689:
Puntmann and co-authors scan the hearts of people recently recovered from COVID-19 in JAMA Cardiology. Reports had hinted the virus harms the heart, but most evidence came from the severely ill. The team recruited 100 unselected recovered patients from a test center and ran cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.

The scans showed cardiac involvement in 78 of the 100 patients, and ongoing heart muscle inflammation in 60. These findings did not depend on preexisting conditions, on how severe the illness had been, or on time since diagnosis. Many participants had never been hospitalized. The authors call for long-term study of the heart after COVID-19. The paper shaped early concern about silent damage in ordinary recoveries.
europmc-pmc7407889:
Hong and co-authors review protein-based nanoparticles for drug delivery in Pharmaceutics. Nanoparticles ferry anticancer drugs and therapeutic proteins through the body, but most are built from synthetic polymers. Natural proteins offer a safer alternative, being compatible with tissue and biodegradable.

Candidate building blocks range from silk fibroin and albumin to gelatin, ferritin, and plant proteins such as gliadin and legumin. Making methods include emulsion, electrospray, and desolvation, all under mild conditions without toxic solvents. The review compares each protein and method's advantages and disadvantages honestly. Controlled release is a recurring prize. Readers get a buyer's guide to a gentler class of drug carriers, and to what still limits them.
europmc-pmc7426189:
Hawryluk and a large guideline panel update advice on a brain surgery used after severe head injury. The surgery, decompressive craniectomy, removes part of the skull to ease pressure inside it. The update revises one chapter of the Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines.

Two major trials drive the change. RESCUEicp tested the surgery for stubborn high pressure, and DECRA shared 12-month outcome data. Folding both into the evidence gave three new level-IIA recommendations. One older level-IIA statement still stands and is repeated. A new section helps doctors apply the evidence at the bedside. The update shows a living guideline model, where chapters change as strong new proof appears.
europmc-pmc7497289:
Stenson and co-authors explain how to get the most from the Human Gene Mutation Database. The database gathers published inherited mutations in nuclear genes. Curators pull them by hand from journal papers.

By June 2020 it held over 289,000 gene lesions in over 11,100 genes, drawn from 72,987 articles in over 3100 journals as counted at that time. Two user groups lean on it most: research scientists and clinical diagnosticians. The review shows how each group can filter and use the data well. It covers new mutations, variant reclassification, and automated retrieval tools. It also points to partner resources and future plans. Sound use, the authors argue, turns a vast archive into firm answers for patients.
europmc-pmc7536089:
Wilkinson and Hardman review the cellular basis of wound healing. Skin repair needs many cell events in tight order. When those events fail, wounds can stay open for months.

Age and diabetes are the main risk factors for chronic wounds. Venous ulcers and diabetic foot ulcers are common types. The review explains normal repair step by step. It then shows which cell behaviors break down. Those faults explain slow or failed closure. New research tools may reveal more detail. The authors link that detail to better future therapies. Readers get a clear account of both healing and its failure.
europmc-pmc7614889:
Fatumo, Chikowore, Choudhury, Ayub, Martin and Kuchenbaecker set out a roadmap to raise diversity in genomic studies. Genome work has grown fast over two decades. Most studies still draw on European ancestry samples.

As of June 2021, European samples made up 86.3% of genome-wide studies. East Asian samples made up 5.9% of the total. African samples were just 1.1% of studies. South Asian and Hispanic shares were smaller still. That gap means medical gains may miss many groups. Causes of the imbalance are laid out in depth. The authors draw on work setting up diverse cohorts. Their plan stresses global teamwork toward genomic equity. Equal health gains from genomics are the stated goal.
europmc-pmc7641189:
Depuydt and co-authors map the microanatomy of human atherosclerotic plaques with single-cell methods. Plaques drive most cardiovascular disease through chronic inflammation. Cell-level detail on human plaques was still lacking.

The team ran single-cell RNA and ATAC sequencing on plaques. Samples came from carotid surgery in patients. They charted all cell types in advanced plaques. Activation states of those cells were also mapped. The picture showed active, ongoing inflammation in tissue. Many cell interactions and flexible cell states appeared. Vessel lining cells and macrophages showed such plasticity. Risk gene sites from genome studies were placed by cell type. That placement may help turn genetic hits into new therapies.
europmc-pmc7654589:
Quinn and co-authors review two genes tied to inherited Parkinson disease, PINK1 and PARKIN. The two proteins work as a pair. They tag damaged mitochondria so the cell can clear them, a process called mitophagy.

The authors first explain how this pair keeps cell energy systems in good shape. They then trace failed cleanup in Parkinson and Alzheimer diseases. The review also covers eye diseases such as glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration. It closes with ways to boost this pathway, including gene-based approaches, as a route to new treatments. The review also covers amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and Huntington disease.
europmc-pmc7708389:
Fan and co-authors test whether a frailty score predicts death in Chinese adults. The frailty index counts health deficits as a share of those checked. It gauges fast biological aging. It predicts death well in Europe and the United States, but data from other groups were thin.

The study used the China Kadoorie Biobank, with adults aged 30 to 79 years from ten areas. The index was built from 28 health items. In all, 512,723 people were followed through death records to the end of 2017. The authors test links to death from all causes and from each major cause, by frailty class.
europmc-pmc7714689:
Wang and co-authors pool studies on mood and breast cancer outcomes. Depression and anxiety are common in women with breast cancer. Whether they worsen the disease course was unclear. The team searched the literature for studies that tracked recurrence and death.

They kept 17 studies with 282,203 patients in total. Depression linked to higher recurrence and to higher death from all causes and from cancer. Anxiety linked to recurrence and to all-cause death, but not to cancer death. Both together raised death rates most. The authors urge care plans that treat mood as part of cancer care, not as a side issue.
europmc-pmc7737089:
Madewell and co-authors estimate how often SARS-CoV-2 spreads within households. The household secondary attack rate is the share of household contacts who catch the virus from a first case. Homes are crowded, close settings where spread can thrive. Lockdowns raised time spent at home, which made this rate key.

The pool held 54 studies with 77,758 participants. The overall household rate was 16.6%. That tops rates seen for SARS and MERS. Rates ran higher from cases with symptoms than without. Adult contacts and spouses caught it more than child contacts and other kin. Households stay key venues for spread, the authors warn.
europmc-pmc7738889:
Chen and co-authors review the metabolic talk between tumors and the macrophages inside them. Tumor-associated macrophages can suppress immune attack on the tumor. Many products of tumor metabolism shape how these cells behave. The traffic runs both ways: macrophage products also steer tumor cells.

Past work stressed cytokines as the messengers between these cells. New work shows that metabolites carry much of the signal. Bulk tumor cells, immune cells, and support cells all shed such compounds. These set macrophage state and, in turn, tumor growth or spread. The authors argue that grasping this loop is a step toward reversing immune suppression in tumors.
europmc-pmc7822889:
Tan and co-authors build a nanoparticle vaccine candidate against SARS-CoV-2. Cheap, effective vaccines were in high demand. Their design displays the spike protein's receptor-binding domain. Many copies stud a synthetic virus-like particle. A linking system called SpyTag/SpyCatcher locks them on.

Low doses in a prime-boost plan raised strong antibodies in mice and pigs. Those antibodies beat samples from recovered patients. Tests showed they blocked the ACE2 contact point. They also stopped live and test viruses from infecting cells. The response hit several key sites on the domain. That spread lowers the odds of escape mutants. The vaccine stays stable under heat and can be freeze-dried. Cold-chain needs drop as a result.
europmc-pmc7824389:
Lafuse and co-authors review the role of heart macrophages in inflammation, scarring, and repair. The immune system starts, drives, and ends inflammation after damage. Heart failure often follows lasting heart tissue injury. Immune cells pour into the heart muscle after harm.

Macrophages sit at the center of that response. Some live in the heart long term, and others arrive from blood. They change form and job as repair proceeds. Good repair needs them to calm inflammation on cue. Failed control means excess scar tissue and lasting injury. The authors trace how macrophages talk to other heart cells. They argue these cells are prime targets for new heart failure care.
europmc-pmc7832889:
Kumari and co-authors show that SARS-CoV-2 invades the brain in mice bred to carry the human ACE2 receptor. The virus can cause brain disease in people. Its path inside the nervous system was little known. The team gave the virus through the nose.

All mice died by day 6 after infection. The dose was 105 plaque-forming units. Lung virus levels peaked on day 3, then fell. Brain levels, by contrast, were very high on days 5 and 6. Disease onset matched the brain peak. Brains showed inflammation, bleeding, and neuron death. Virus also grew in the nose lining and the smell center. The authors trace entry to that smell route.
europmc-pmc7850989:
Pidwill and co-authors review how macrophages deal with Staphylococcus aureus infection. This bacterium lives harmlessly on many people. It can also cause grave disease. To infect, it must slip past innate immune cells. Macrophages and neutrophils stand as gatekeepers.

Macrophages kill the bacteria with many weapons. The bacterium fights back with its own tricks. It can survive inside macrophages and bend them to its ends. It can even escape from them. Each stage of infection turns on this duel. The balance decides how the illness ends. The authors gather the newest findings on both sides. Better grasp of the fight could seed new treatments.
europmc-pmc7862389:
Durazzi and co-authors compare two DNA methods for naming gut bacteria. One reads the 16S rRNA gene alone. The other sequences all DNA in the sample. The team used the chicken gut as test ground. Samples spanned two gut zones and two time points.

The single-gene method found only part of the community. Shotgun sequencing revealed many more kinds. With enough reads, it caught rare bacteria the gene method missed. Those rare kinds still carried real signals. They split the test groups as sharply as common kinds did. The authors warn that cheap profiling can mislead. Method choice shapes what a microbiome study can claim.
europmc-pmc7862989:
Shah and co-authors estimate nurse burnout in the United States and its linked factors. The team reused survey data on over 3.9 million registered nurses. They asked how many left jobs over burnout. Work setting and hours were checked as risks.

Among nurses who left a job, a large share blamed burnout. Leavers were 9.5% of the sample. Of them, 31.5% named burnout as the cause in 2018. Hospital work carried higher odds of burnout. So did working more than 20 hours per week. The authors flag an urgent need for fixes. Pandemic demands only raised the pressure on nurses.
europmc-pmc7888189:
Jiang and co-authors report a comparison study on how computers represent molecules for drug discovery. A model must first turn a molecule into numbers it can learn from. Older methods use fixed descriptors. Newer graph neural networks learn the form straight from the molecule's structure. The team tested which approach works better.

They ran eight machine learning algorithms on 11 public datasets. Four models used descriptors, and four used molecular graphs. On average, the descriptor-based models won on both accuracy and speed. Support vector machines did best on the regression tasks. Random forests and XGBoost were strong and fast on classification tasks. Some graph models still shone on larger datasets. The authors also tested the models in virtual screening against HIV.
europmc-pmc7897289:
Nakao and co-authors report a laboratory study on treating gum disease with tiny vesicles from stem cells. Periodontitis destroys the tissue and bone that hold teeth in place. Stem cells from gum tissue release small packets called exosomes. The team tested whether priming those cells first could make the packets heal better.

Priming the cells with TNF-α made them release more exosomes. The packets also carried more CD73, a protein that calms inflammation. In mice with induced gum disease, injected exosomes cut bone loss. Primed exosomes worked even better. They pushed macrophages toward a healing state and slowed the cells that eat bone. A small RNA in the packets, miR-1260b, blocked a pathway that drives bone loss. The work sketches a cell-free treatment path for gum disease.
europmc-pmc7938889:
McDonald and co-authors report a research study that overturns a standard view of bone-eating cells. Osteoclasts are large cells that dissolve bone. They form by the fusion of smaller precursor cells. Once their work was done, they were thought to die. Live imaging in this study showed a different fate under the signal RANKL.

Instead of dying, the cells split into daughter cells the team calls osteomorphs. Blocking the RANKL signal stopped this recycling and made osteomorphs pile up. Gene readings showed these daughters form a distinct cell type. They carry genes whose loss in mice alters bone form and strength. Human versions of those genes link to bone density and to rare skeletal disorders. The finding names a new target for treating bone disease. It also rewrites a basic step of bone renewal.
europmc-pmc7961389:
Jang and co-authors present a review of recent updates on osteoarthritis of the knee. The disease wears down joint cartilage and distorts the joint. Pain, swelling, and stiffness follow. It is a major cause of disability, and its rate will climb as populations age and obesity spreads. The review covers diagnosis, disease process, and treatment in light of fresh research.

Cell therapy draws much of the attention. Stem cells from embryos or reprogrammed skin can become cartilage cells. Mesenchymal stem cells are the most studied option for injection into the joint. They can form cartilage-like cells and calm the immune response. Trials of such therapies are summed up in brief. Non-cell treatments get their due as well. The authors say real needs remain unmet despite the gains. The review lays a base for the next round of clinical work.
europmc-pmc7967389:
Fernández-de-Las-Peñas and co-authors present a paper proposing a shared language for symptoms that follow COVID-19. The pandemic produced a second wave of patients with lasting complaints, often called long-haulers. Terms for their state vary and blur together. The authors offer one classification that sorts symptoms by time since infection. Clear time points are the heart of the scheme.

Symptoms tied to the infection itself run to about 4–5 weeks. Acute post-COVID symptoms cover week 5 to week 12. Long post-COVID symptoms run from week 12 to week 24. Anything past 24 weeks counts as persistent. The scheme also folds in personal risk factors and hospital data. Because symptoms come and go, the time frame matters more than any single check. The authors aim to align care and research on one set of names.
europmc-pmc8167089:
Pedrera and co-authors show how membrane pores shape the pace of ferroptotic cell death. Ferroptosis is an iron-driven form of cell death tied to lipid damage. How the cell membrane finally breaks was unclear.

The team found a lasting rise in cell calcium before the cell bursts. Damage takes the form of tiny pores a few nanometres wide. Protective compounds delayed death without stopping lipid damage. Calcium flow switched on the ESCRT-III repair machinery. That repair bid slows the death process. The findings explain why ferroptosis unfolds over time, not at once.
europmc-pmc8226689:
Bossi and co-authors survey malnutrition, cachexia, and sarcopenia across cancer care. These states differ by cancer type and treatment setting. Knowing their spread helps teams act early.

The narrative review searched literature from January 2010 to December 2020. It weighed tumour factors and treatment factors together. Both can drain weight, muscle, and strength. Early handling may protect quality of life and treatment strength. It may also shape disease outcomes. The authors draw practical steps for team-based care. Diet and muscle checks belong in routine oncology, they argue. Treatment setting shapes risk as much as tumour type does.
europmc-pmc8346589:
Zhang and co-authors build an omics-based frame for ranking the risk of resistance genes. Antibiotic resistance genes spread widely among bacteria. Only some pose a grave threat to public health.

Their framework weighs three traits per gene. It counts enrichment near humans, gene mobility, and host harmfulness. Mobile, human-linked genes formed 3.6% of all genes screened. Those split into current threats at 3% and future threats at 0.6%. The frame named 73 current threat gene families. Most matched earlier expert lists. Watch systems can now rank new genes by evidence, not alarm.
europmc-pmc8410789:
Zhang and co-authors show how a common metabolite can trigger a fiery form of cell death in cancer cells. Pyroptosis is a regulated death path run by gasdermin proteins. The role of one member, GSDMC, was not clear before this work.

The team found that alpha-ketoglutarate sets off pyroptosis through caspase-8 cutting GSDMC. A cell-ready form of the metabolite raised reactive oxygen levels. That oxidized the death receptor DR6 and pulled it inside the cell. There it gathered caspase-8 and GSDMC into one complex. In mouse models, this death path slowed tumor growth and spread. Acidic settings made the effect stronger.
europmc-pmc8563889:
Lei and co-authors review ferroptosis and its place in radiotherapy and combined cancer care. Ferroptosis is an iron-driven form of cell death. It works through peroxide damage to fatty cell membranes. Recent work ties it to radiation-driven tumor death.

It also helps explain the synergy between radiotherapy and immunotherapy. The review sets out known and likely links between radiation and this death path. It treats talks between ferroptosis and other death forms that radiation triggers. Plans that target ferroptosis join the survey. Pairing such drugs with radiation or immune therapy is the prize. The authors frame open questions for the next studies.
europmc-pmc8759089:
Borissov and co-authors survey recent progress in polycyclic heteroaromatic compounds, a class of ring-rich molecules with atoms beyond carbon in their frames. The review covers work from 2016 to 2020. It updates an earlier survey of the same field. Structural variety and new synthesis methods form the twin focus.

These molecules matter for materials and for basic chemistry. New routes have widened the shapes that chemists can build. Nanographenes with heteroatoms form a highlighted group. The authors sort advances by structure type and method. Readers get a compact map of five busy years in this corner of organic chemistry.
europmc-pmc8831689:
Huang and co-authors engineer exosomes into a vaccine that primes immune defenses inside the tumor. Dendritic cells start and steer immune attacks. Vaccines that reach them in the body could work well. The team loaded breast cancer exosomes with two agents. One, ELANE, helps kill cancer cells in an immune-stirring way. The other, Hiltonol, alarms the immune system. An engineered protein targeted the package.

The loaded exosomes, called HELA-Exos, triggered immunogenic death in breast cancer cells. Dying cells exposed tumor antigens and the alarm signal. Local dendritic cells woke and primed killer T cells. Tumors shrank in a hard-to-treat mouse model. Patient-derived tumor organoids responded too. The authors propose this as a vaccine strategy for many cancers.
europmc-pmc8894389:
Zhang and co-authors trace how escaped mitochondrial DNA drives disc degeneration and back pain. Low back pain often starts with a wearing spinal disc. Its core cells, nucleus pulposus cells, die off over time. Loose DNA inside cells acts as a danger signal. The cGAS-STING axis watches for exactly that signal. It can trigger pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death. The team linked these threads in human tissue and rats.

Imaging and tissue tests tied the axis to degeneration grade. Oxidative stress in human disc cells switched the axis on. Mitochondrial pores opened and mitochondrial DNA leaked out. That leak fired the NLRP3 inflammasome and pyroptotic death. A drug blocking the pore calmed the process. Treated rats showed slower disc degeneration. The authors offer this axis as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc9171489:
Joudeh and Linke comprehensively review nanoparticles for biologists, from types and traits to uses. Nanoparticles show new or stronger physical and chemical traits than bulk material. Those traits have sparked uses in medicine, electronics, farming, and food. Greener routes now make them with plants or microbes.

The review sorts nanoparticle classes and explains traits like magnetic, optical, and catalytic behavior. It lists common methods to measure and characterize those traits. Many examples of biologically made particles are given with their uses. The authors aim to make complex methods accessible to bio-oriented readers. Researchers get help to pick the right method for a given nanoscience problem.
europmc-pmc9289789:
GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators quantify how alcohol risk varies by amount, place, age, and sex. They built burden-weighted risk curves across 22 health outcomes. Data cover 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2020 for ages 15 to 95 and older. Two yardsticks result: the lowest-risk drinking level and the level equal in risk to not drinking.

For ages 15 to 39, the lowest-risk level in 2020 ran from zero to 0.603 standard drinks per day. For ages 40 and older, the risk curve was J-shaped in every region. Among people drinking harmful amounts, 59.1% were aged 15 to 39 and 76.9% were male. The team says advice should vary by age and region. Stronger action aimed at younger drinkers is urged.
europmc-pmc9618889:
Kerneur, Cano, and Olive review the major pathways that drive macrophage polarization in cancer. Macrophages guard tissue balance and help remodel tissue. They also shape how tumors progress. Their great asset is plasticity, the power to change role on cue.

Most accounts sort them into two poles of one spectrum. M1-like cells stir inflammation and fight tumors. M2-like cells calm inflammation and aid tumor growth. Tumor linked macrophages can fill 50 to 80% of non-tumor stromal cells. Signals from the tumor setting push them toward either pole. The review follows those signals receptor by receptor. Interferon and interleukin receptors get full treatment. Toll-like receptors, NOTCH, and TGF-beta routes also feature. Signals end by rewiring gene programs in the nucleus. The authors map each path to the cell fate it favors.
europmc-pmc9763089:
Liu and co-authors give an overview of PROTACs as a fresh drug discovery approach. These molecules destroy target proteins instead of just blocking them. They hijack the cell's own protein shredding system to do it. A PROTAC has two gripping ends joined by a linker.

One end holds the target and the other holds a tagging enzyme. Brought together, the target gets marked for destruction. The whole protein vanishes, not just one active site. That opens targets long called undruggable to drug work. Scaffolding proteins and gene switches become reachable this way. Two such drugs showed strong results in mid stage trials. The review lays out design rules for the linkers and ends. It sorts uses by protein class, from kinases to receptors. Oral dosing and target choice remain open challenges. The authors weigh those limits against the gains.
famous-affinities-of-history-the-romance:
Lyndon Orr begins Famous Affinities of History with Antony and Cleopatra, in this first of four volumes. Their story, he writes, has been the most remarkable love story for nineteen centuries. Antony flung away mastery of the world at Actium for Cleopatra's sake. No private ruin, Orr argues, matches that sacrifice.

Abelard and Heloise bring medieval scholarship into the romance of devotion. Queen Elizabeth and the Earl of Leicester, then Mary Queen of Scots and Bothwell, raise the stakes to thrones. Christina of Sweden and Monaldeschi end in murder. Charles II and Nell Gwyn lighten the set, while Maurice of Saxony and Adrienne Lecouvreur join war to the stage. The story of Prince Charles Edward Stuart closes the volume. Orr writes brisk narrative history for readers who like their past in love stories.
fichte-science-knowledge-1889:
Johann Gottlieb Fichte published his Wissenschaftslehre, The Science of Knowledge, in 1794, and A E Kroeger's English translation of 1889 is the text here. W T Harris wrote the preface to this edition. Fichte had heard Kant and aimed to rebuild philosophy from a single first principle, with system and certainty.

That principle is the self-positing Ego: the I that sets itself in being, and in doing so sets a world over against itself. From that act Fichte spins consciousness, nature, and duty in ordered steps. The Science of Knowledge founded German idealism after Kant and set the path for Schelling and Hegel. It is dense, electric, and still fought over.
fichte-science-rights-1889:
Fichte's Grundlage des Naturrechts, The Science of Rights, appeared in 1796, and A E Kroeger's translation of 1889 gives it here. Johann Gottlieb Fichte built the work on his Science of Knowledge, asking what law must be if free beings are to live together. It is the first systematic idealist philosophy of right ever written.

Fichte grounds right in mutual recognition: I can claim my freedom only as I grant yours. From that seed grow property, contract, the state, and the limits of its power. The deduction is strict, and its picture of citizens who make each other free still provokes thought. Kroeger's version carried the system to English readers entire.
french-declaration-rights-man-1789:
The French National Assembly voted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen on 26 August 1789. The French Revolution was weeks old, and the Assembly wanted a statement of principles before writing a constitution. Deputies debated every clause, drawing on Enlightenment thought and the American example.

The seventeen articles declare that men are born free and equal in rights. Liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression are named as natural rights no government may take away. The text also promises free speech, fair law, and taxes set by consent. The declaration became the French Revolution's immortal charter and a model for rights statements everywhere. Critics noted at once that its promises skipped women and the enslaved, a gap later generations fought to close.
frus-1861-d189:
Writing on 30 April 1861, William H. Seward addressed Mr. Stockton in a broad sweep of spring orders. The letter is document 189 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Stockton, like King the day before, gets no post in the record heading. Seward's end of April letters went out in a broad sweep of appointments and orders. This one shows the Secretary filling the ranks of the service as the war took hold. A broad sweep of spring orders reached posts from London to the smallest court. A sweep of that breadth left no post to guess at the new chief's mind.
frus-1861-d289:
A dispatch dated 29 May 1861 carried word from Mr. Morgan to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 289 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d89:
On 4 October 1861, Charles Francis Adams sent a further dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 89 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

October opened the season when Southern agents grew bold in British ports. Adams watched for ships and guns bought with Confederate gold. His early October report belongs to that quiet counter work, done with notes and calls rather than arms. Adams used consuls in the ports as his eyes in the hunt for Southern ships. Eyes in the ports were the first line of a blockade that began on land.
frus-1862-d189:
On 14 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams in London, printed as Document 189 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams was then in his second year as American minister to Britain.

That week the British cabinet formally set aside the idea of acting with France on the war. The choice removed the sharpest foreign threat the Union faced that year. Seward's letter of 14 November was written before the news could reach him. Part of the long effort that had helped bring the safer outcome about. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d289:
Document 289 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 20 June 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to Paris in the same mail.

Same-day pairs let the Secretary divide orders from information, so the envoy could act on one and file the other. The practice also doubled the paper trail, which is why single weeks in this file can look crowded. For the Paris story, the 20 June pair marks the calm desk work done just before the war's summer crisis. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d389:
Simon Cameron wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 August 1862, in a report printed as Document 389 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron was the American minister in Russia.

Cameron's August report traveled from St. Petersburg as the Virginia campaign moved toward its climax. News and envoy moved at the same slow pace, both overtaken by events. For the reader, the Russian letters of this month are a study in distance. A friendly post, faithfully kept, reporting on a war an ocean and a continent away. Russian goodwill gave Washington one capital where it need not argue its right to exist.
frus-1862-d489:
James Shepherd Pike reported from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 March 1862. The dispatch is Document 489 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Pike's reports mixed court business with the talk of Dutch merchants and editors, whose trade suffered when American commerce suffered. In March 1862 he wrote as the war's naval side widened and the ironclad news crossed the ocean. His letters home gave Seward a reading of Dutch feeling that was generally fair to the Union. For the reader, the Hague file shows how much a working minister's weekly judgment mattered. It mattered to a government fighting a war three thousand miles from its sources of news.
frus-1862-d589:
Thomas Corwin sent this report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 May 1862, though the volume prints it after Seward's later instruction. It is Document 589 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Corwin's May report belongs to the weeks after Puebla, when Mexican hopes rose and French plans hardened. From the capital he could describe both the government's resolve and its poverty. His letters kept Washington honest about what sympathy alone could not do. The slight disorder of the printed file, reports and answers interleaved out of date, mirrors the real delays of the correspondence itself. Read by date, Corwin's May letter answers a Mexico transformed by battle.
frus-1862-d689: On 5 March 1862, a Mr. De Long wrote again to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 689 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the third of his letters in a span of two weeks. The evidence for it gives the writer, the date, and its place in the volume, but no post or topic.
frus-1862-d89:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 30 June 1862. Congress received it as Document 89 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d189:
The mail from London dated 7 May 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 189 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d289:
An instruction dated 10 September 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 289 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

In the fall of 1863 two ironclad rams built for the Confederacy waited in a British yard. Washington's orders to Adams that season pressed hard for the ships to be held. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d389:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 10 February 1863. It appears as document 389 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Trade bound the countries tightly, from Southern cotton to British mills. Both sides had much to lose from a break, and the notes reflect that caution. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d489:
From Secretary of State William H. Seward to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons: a letter dated 4 May 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d589:
Among the day's business on 17 July 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d689:
The date is 11 November 1863, and the two men are Secretary of State William H. Seward and Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Their exchange is kept as document 689 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Routine mail of this kind is the spine of the record for the Civil War years. Grand speeches get the fame, but notes like this one did the steady work. They shared facts, lodged protests, and kept each side aware of the other's view. A reader who follows them in order can track the mood between Washington and London almost day by day through the fall of 1863.
frus-1863p1-d89:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 20 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 89 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, a lone sheet after a three-letter day.

A single letter after a flood often tidied a loose end or sent a late piece of news. Adams's February mail kept Washington wise to a court whose mood could shift with each debate. This dispatch is a quiet piece of that watch. It holds its place in the run, between the clusters of mid-February and the fresh orders soon to come from Washington.
frus-1889:
Harrison opens the 1889 volume with a hemisphere in conference. Delegates of all the American states sit in Washington, he notes. They meet to expand mutual interest across the continents. The country files follow. China again runs long, with two legation blocks. Haiti and Mexico hold their usual weight. One section stands outside the country order. Samoan Affairs gets its own heading and file.

Its papers sketch a future government for the islands. Native rule should stand, one memorandum argues. Foreign advisers should assist, not replace, that rule. One power should control, with the others' consent. Triangular control, it warns, would never work. The governor could call warships from any partner. The volume thus holds a Pacific experiment in draft. Samoa joins China as its eastern theme.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d189:
John Winant, the American ambassador in London, sent President Roosevelt a short personal telegram on 4 November 1943. Winant had spent the past weekend at Chequers, the prime minister's country house, with Churchill and South Africa's Jan Smuts, and he reports what was weighing on Churchill's mind.

Four worries stood out: pulling landing craft out of the Italian campaign, the threat of German rocket guns, the Greek islands, and the timing of the second front in France. Winant warns Roosevelt that the coming staff meetings will bring real differences over near-term and long-term war plans to the surface. Those differences, he warns, will need to be settled at the top.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d289:
President Roosevelt wrote a short letter of orders to General Patrick Hurley at Cairo on 23 November 1943. Hurley, his personal representative, is directed to proceed to Tehran in Iran on a mission set out in two messages from the Secretary of State, dated 5 and 19 November.

Those messages charged Hurley with coordinating the work of the several American agencies operating in Iran, and with drawing the American, British, Soviet, and Iranian agencies there into closer cooperation. Roosevelt adds that Hurley must also perform further duties, of a nature and object he has outlined to him in person. The editors judge those extra duties concerned the choice of quarters where Roosevelt would stay in Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d389:
President Roosevelt handed Marshal Stalin a secret paper at Tehran on 29 November 1943 on advance planning for naval operations in the northwestern Pacific. It pairs with his air planning paper of the same day, and it makes the same opening argument about shortening the war.

The more preliminary planning that can be done now, without undue risk, Roosevelt writes, the sooner the war as a whole can be ended once Germany is eliminated. Four specific requests follow. America would welcome combat intelligence on Japan. Should American bases be enlarged to shelter the Soviet Far Eastern submarine and destroyer force if its ports were threatened? What help could the Soviets give an American attack on the northern Kuriles? And which Soviet ports, if any, could Allied forces use, with data on their capacity? The questions can be taken up with the American military mission in Moscow.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d489:
A second exchange between Harry Hopkins and Anthony Eden, message and reply together, is dated December 5, 1943, at the Second Cairo Conference. Hopkins acted for President Roosevelt; Eden was Britain's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. The State Department printed the pair in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Two Hopkins-Eden exchanges in one day show how much conference business flowed through this channel while the leaders met face to face. Eden was Churchill's chief diplomatic adviser, and Hopkins was Roosevelt's eyes and ears. For readers, the paired texts capture the speed of summit work: a question raised by one side and answered by the other inside the same day's record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d89: A further Churchill message to Roosevelt bears the date November 2, 1943, and it is Document 89 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Three Churchill or Roosevelt letters of that single day appear in this run, beside the Chiang and Hull letters of the same date. The record for this note gives no subject. It is preserved in the Foreign Relations series as part of that crowded day.
frus-1944-quebec-d189:
An editors' note traces the paperwork of the lend-lease committee decision. After Morgenthau and Cherwell met on the morning of September 14, 1944, Cherwell, Weeks, and White drafted the directive creating the committee. By late afternoon it was ready. The note also follows a side conversation between White and Weeks about the information Washington would need to decide lend-lease quickly.

That thread surfaces in minutes of a Washington conference on September 20. White listed the key questions he had put to Weeks. They covered Britain's increase in peacetime goods, exports, and employment. They also covered the net transfer of workers from war production to civilian jobs. There were, he said, about a dozen such questions.
frus-1944-quebec-d289:
Roosevelt and Churchill reported the Quebec decisions to Stalin on September 16, 1944, in a joint top-secret message. For northwest Europe, they intended to press on with all speed, strike at the Ruhr and Saar, open Antwerp and Rotterdam before bad weather, and make the main effort on the left. For Italy, they set out Wilson's two alternatives: rout and pursuit toward the Ljubljana Gap, or an orderly German withdrawal and a Lombardy campaign.

Air and commando operations would continue in the Balkans. Against Japan, further operations would intensify the offensive in all theaters. The ultimate aim was invading the homeland. Plans for the prompt transfer of power to the Pacific after Germany's collapse had also been agreed. Harriman and Clark Kerr delivered the message to Stalin jointly on September 23.
frus-1944-quebec-d89:
Secretary Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on September 8, 1944. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It dates from the final days before the conference in Canada. Hull had served as Secretary of State since 1933.

Presidents rely on written advice when a summit nears. Hull's letter put the State Department's view before Roosevelt directly. Four days later, the President met Churchill at Quebec City. Their agenda ran from Germany's defeat to the Pacific war. For readers, the message shows the department's chief making his case. He wrote while the last briefings were being packed.
frus-1945-50-intel-d189: "Central Intelligence Group Paper" bears the date 12 March 1947. It survives in print as document 189 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time. The text belongs to the daily flow of paper that ran the early Cold War state.
frus-1945-50-intel-d289:
A memorandum dated 16 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan). The reader was the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) and Secretary of State Marshall. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 289 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d389:
General Joseph T. McNarney addressed a memorandum to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 22 July 1949. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 389 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Dulles Report had landed in January 1949, and Washington was arguing over which of its fixes the CIA should adopt.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d89:
Russell wrote to Byrnes again two days later, on 20 April 1946. Two papers to the secretary in three days mark a question being closed. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Quick follow-up papers usually carry decisions requested, answers supplied, or loose ends tied. In the State intelligence story, April 1946 tied many ends: staff, funds, and the office's place under the new central system. Readers should read the pair of Russell papers together, as the department's final word in this thread. After them, the volume's center of gravity shifts for good to the central group and its growing quarrels and duties.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d189:
Stettinius briefed Ambassador Winant on the end of the Italy quarrel on 14 December 1944. His secret cable, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, shares Eden's reply to the personal message Winant had delivered. It also gives Winant the inside story of the American statement.

Eden thanked him, called the message helpful and understanding, and wished keenly for close work together. The statement itself, Stettinius explains, came under heavy pressure from the American press, and it played well at home, with newspapers and Congress alike. British officials here admit they should have consulted Washington first, but they blame Washington in turn for not consulting them. Eden's speech in the Commons, he adds, forced the public break.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d289:
The President's own trip log is introduced by this editorial note in the Malta and Yalta volume. The log forms the major part of an eighty-three page booklet, “The President's Trip to the Crimea Conference and Great Bitter Lake, Egypt.” The booklet covers 22 January to 28 February 1945.

Lieutenant Rigdon prepared the booklet, and the President's naval aide, Vice Admiral Wilson Brown, approved it. Its contents run from the list of the President's party and the itinerary to charts of the Atlantic and Mediterranean crossings. A report of the Crimea Conference is included. So is the memorandum of conversations between King Ibn Saud and President Roosevelt of 14 February. The Malta Conference opened on 30 January, but Roosevelt arrived only on 2 February, its last day; the log for that day follows.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d389:
General Kuter kept the minutes of the first American-Soviet staff meeting on the Far East, held February 8, 1945. Admiral Leahy opened by stating the business. The two staffs would discuss military problems in the Far East. The Americans needed firm data for long-range planning across the Pacific's great distances.

Leahy then read a prepared list of questions, drawn from a paper by General Deane of the Moscow military mission. Antonov asked that all questions be put before any answers or debate. The record shows the careful choreography of a first meeting between allies who were also watching each other closely.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d489:
Athens, Moscow, and Belgrade share these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 9, 1945. Observers in Athens judged the trial and sentencing of EAM members during peace talks a mistake. No action had yet been taken against collaborationists. Athens papers now announced that nine leading collaborationists held by the British were being returned for trial.

From Moscow came word on China: Chiang Kai-shek had been told to postpone Soong's visit until late March or early April, given the war in Europe. On Yugoslavia, Tito believed King Peter was playing for time in hope of American support. Grew's digest kept three crises on one page for the traveling Secretary.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d89:
Britain said yes to Roosevelt's voting compromise on 14 January 1945. Michael Wright, acting counsellor of the British Embassy in Washington, confirmed it in a letter to Leo Pasvolsky. The letter is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

His Majesty's Government, Wright writes, is prepared to accept the President's proposed compromise on Security Council voting. London is still unsure of the rule's exact effect on one passage about regional settlement, but expects no difficulty there. The Foreign Office adds a caution. Voting is not the only question left open. Conference invitations, it notes, should go out in the names of the sponsoring powers, after they consult.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d189:
Secretary Byrnes sent London the President's own list of topics on July 5, 1945. The telegram to Ambassador Winant is document 189 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The same list went to Harriman in Moscow at the same hour, for delivery to the Soviet side.

The President may raise, first, machinery for the peace negotiations and territorial settlements. Then comes policy toward Germany: the Control Council, treatment of Germany in the first control period, local administrations, and Germany as an economic unit. The list goes on to carrying out the Yalta Declaration on Liberated Europe, policy toward Italy, joint work on Europe's economic problems, and freedom of communication and information in Europe. Some discussion of the Far East is also expected, and the list is not closed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d289:
The Acting Secretary of State sent Harriman a plan for fixing the Hungary control body in a despatch dated June 21, 1945. The despatch and its enclosures form document 289 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The papers were passed to the Moscow embassy for background, with copies also sent to London.

The enclosure holds Major General William Key's recommendations for reorganizing the Allied Control Commission in Hungary for the armistice's second period, the stretch from Germany's defeat to the peace treaty. Key, the American member of the commission, supplied a revised draft of its statutes with his own comments. Under the draft, a Soviet chairman still heads the body, but the American and British mission chiefs sit as vice chairmen. The statutes were meant to give the Western members the real voice they lacked.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d389:
Pauley's view on dividing the German fleets is reported in Murphy's cable from Hoechst of June 22, 1945. The four powers were to divide Germany's naval and merchant fleets by agreement. Pauley, as American representative on the Reparations Commission, had told General Eisenhower where he stood on the question.

While the United States remained at war with Japan, Pauley held, dividing both fleets was strictly a military matter. The merchant fleet's division, though, ultimately concerned the Reparations Commission. He wanted a careful record and description of the ships kept for future reparations accounting, and he asked leave to place his man, Captain John Faigle, as observer at the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d489:
Harriman's opinion is asked in Grew's cable of June 26, 1945, on the British suggestion about Poland. The suggestion is simple. Recognition would be granted when the new Warsaw government notifies the three governments. Its notice would state that it has been established under the Yalta agreement. It would add a pledge that it will hold free elections. The Department wants the ambassador's reactions.

The Yalta declaration, Grew argues, is clear. The new government shall be pledged to the holding of free and unfettered elections. It must also have been properly formed in conformity with the agreement. Any reasonable reading, he says, makes the election pledge a condition of recognition. He asks whether Harriman judges the pledge already given sufficient.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d589:
A briefing paper extract dated June 29, 1945, proposes a joint statement of Allied aims for Japan. It is document 589 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. State and War Department staff were already drafting such a statement when this paper was written.

The paper argues that Japan's people would accept surrender more readily if told what to expect. The Allies need not drop the words unconditional surrender. They can still spell out the treatment in store and promise that Japan may keep political forms that fit a peaceful life. That would calm fear of the unknown and counter tales that surrender means slavery. It might also split hard-line militarists from those who want the war ended before Japan is destroyed. The fate of the throne, it notes, is the chief block of all.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d689:
The Acting Secretary of State instructed Ambassador Wilson in Ankara on the Turkey dispute, June 23, 1945. The secret wire is document 689 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It explains why Washington would not join Britain in a firm protest to Moscow.

The wire first restates Britain's case for joint action. Molotov's demands, London argued, defied Stalin's explicit Yalta assurances on Turkey's independence and integrity. Washington answers with two doubts of its own. Its men at Yalta do not recall Stalin taking so definite a position. The Moscow talk of June 7, moreover, was sought by the Turkish ambassador himself. It appears to have been friendly and free of threats. A protest now, the Department holds, would be premature treatment of an exploratory exchange.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d89:
President Truman agreed to Churchill's press plan in a six-word telegram sent from Olympia, Washington, on June 23, 1945. The message is document 89 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had proposed that reporters be barred from the Berlin conference, as at Yalta, while photographers were allowed in.

Truman's entire reply reads: your 97, I am in agreement. A note explains the cable went by way of the White House Map Room and Navy channels. Stalin accepted the same plan a few days later. The terse exchange settled how the world would see Potsdam: through official photographs and government statements, not through the eyes of independent reporters at the scene.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1089:
The United States delegation tabled this policy paper on Italy at the first plenary meeting on July 17, 1945. Its aims are Italy's early political independence and economic recovery. In time, the Italian people should choose their own form of government. Italy's double status, both co-belligerent and surrendered enemy, is called anomalous and harmful.

Only a full peace treaty can end that anomaly, and drafting one should be an early task for the proposed council of foreign ministers. Meanwhile, an interim deal should scrap the outdated surrender terms. Italy would pledge no hostile action against the United Nations, and keep only armed forces the Allies allow. Allied control would shrink to military needs and fair settlement of border disputes.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1189:
The Secretary of State wrote to Morgan, chief of the Aviation Division, on 21 August 1945, weeks after Potsdam closed. Civil aviation was becoming a prize of the peace. Which nations' planes could fly where, and under whose rules, would shape trade and travel for decades.

A note to his air-policy chief tasked the expert desk as the postwar order took shape. The subject had moved from war to routes, fields, and flags. This message shows the department turning to that work in the summit's wake. The war's end opened the skies, and papers like this one began to divide them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1289:
A memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff bears the date 18 July 1945. It joins the thick stack of staff papers from the summit's first days. The chiefs' office wrote at a pace that matched the talks themselves.

These papers were the staff mind in fixed form: facts weighed, options ranked, risks named. The envoys who bargained by day read them by night. This one is a single sheet in that stack, from the second day of the conference. Its place in the run is its meaning: steady, expert pressure behind the men at the table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1389:
On 28 July 1945 Mikołajczyk wrote a fifth memorandum for the record of the Potsdam weeks. The Polish deputy prime minister's papers form the most personal run in this part of the volume. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

By the last days of July, the shape of the settlement was plain, and Mikołajczyk wrote against time. His memoranda speak to posterity as much as to the men at Potsdam. Since he could guess how little room he had to change their minds. Readers get the human scale of the conference here: one statesman, shut out of the room, filling pages while empires drew lines through his homeland.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-89:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff met during the Potsdam Conference. These minutes record their session of July 24, 1945. The chiefs were the top United States military body. The chiefs had come to Germany with President Truman. War against Japan still ran, and military advice fed straight into the Big Three talks. The minutes were printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

Military minutes differ from the diplomats' records in tone and focus. They weigh forces, plans, and timing in plain terms. Readers can see how the chiefs framed the choices put to the President. The record links the strategy talks to the politics of the conference table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d789:
Byrnes wrote to Winant in London on July 30, 1945, in document 789. The letter dates from the conference's final days. The Secretary kept his London ambassador close to the end. This exchange joined the others in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

End-of-conference letters carry early word of results. Winant would need the outcome before the public did. Readers see Byrnes preparing an ally's envoy for what was coming. The document shows the alliance being managed to the last hour. Potsdam's deals would land in London first, and this letter softened the ground.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d889: American staff answered the British first charge paper in this memorandum dated July 31, 1945. No author is named. It suggests placing the British wording at the end of section 14(b) of the Economic Principles. That section covers goods needed by occupying forces and displaced persons. It also covers keeping German living standards at or below the European average. The memo quotes the full revised section, with the added sentence in italics. The Americans accept the British language except for one word: approved.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d989: The Acting Secretary of State sent this one-line telegram to William Clayton at Potsdam on July 24, 1945. It adds a fresh fact to Washington's earlier message about Soviet claims on German property in Rumania. Bucharest now reports that the Soviets demand German bank stocks in Rumania as well. The earlier message had dealt with German-held shares in Rumanian oil companies, which Moscow claimed as its own compensation. The cable is marked for Clayton's information and carries no request for action.
frus-1961-63v05-d89:
A private memorandum of conversation at Vienna, on June 4, 1961, records the hardest talk of the summit. President Kennedy asks Khrushchev not to force a Berlin choice on him. Access rights, he stresses, differ from a peace treaty's form.

Khrushchev answers that force will meet force. A six-month interim deal is offered, after which troops must leave. Token forces under a UN-registered pact are the most he grants. The treaty, he says, will be signed in December. Kennedy leaves saying he came to prevent a clash, and fears he has failed.
galton-natural-inheritance-1889:
