Francis Galton, a cousin of Darwin, spent years measuring human bodies and family records to study how traits pass down. His 1889 book Natural Inheritance sums up that work with tables, charts, and family histories. Galton wanted heredity studied with numbers, not guesses.

His key find was regression to the mean: very tall parents tend to have children closer to average height. He showed the same pull toward the middle in seeds, stature, and other measured traits. That simple pattern became a base tool of statistics and of the study of inherited traits. His methods let later workers treat inheritance as a thing that could be counted.
gao-gaoreports-b-295589:
In GAO ruling B-295589 and B-295589.2, dated March 22, 2005, Park Tower Management Ltd. was the protester. The Social Security Administration had awarded LB&B Associates a contract for building maintenance services. Park Tower claimed the technical offers were wrongly judged equal and that the winner had misled the agency on staff commitments. GAO denied the protest. The agency fairly found the winner's past building comparable, though some gear it kept up sat in a building next door.

On maintenance plans, neither offer was complete, and the protester's was scored higher for holding more detail. Price and technical tradeoffs of this kind, the decision notes, are the agency's to make.
gao-gaoreports-b-295989:
Front Line Apparel Group protested Defense Logistics Agency awards for Army combat uniform trousers in GAO decision B-295989, dated June 1, 2005. The firm said the scoring was wrong. It also said talks with bidders were not fair. The fight was over two line items for trousers.

GAO sustained the protest. The agency held a fresh round of talks with the winners. It gave no such chance to this firm. GAO said that gap was not fair. When an agency reopens talks on the same points with one firm, it must give like firms the same chance. The ruling is a clear guide on fair talks.
gao-gaoreports-b-296489:
Digital Healthcare protested a Veterans Affairs call for insurance ID services in GAO decision B-296489, dated August 24, 2005. The firm said the agency stole facts from its own pitched plan. It said the call terms were built from that plan. The pitched plan dealt with how health plans match shared costs.

GAO denied the protest. The firm did not meet its load of proof. It had to show the facts were its own trade facts. That proof was not made. A claim of theft of a pitched idea needs clear proof of a trade right. With that proof absent, the call could stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-297789:
Three print firms protested the axing of a bid call in GAO decision B-297789, dated March 21, 2006. The buyer was the Government Printing Office. The work was Army books and pamphlets. The call went to 22 firms and 16 firms bid. One long-time firm had been left off the list by slip. A check found more flaws in list and post steps.

GAO denied the protest. The office broke its own rules on the list and the post. That breach gave a strong cause to axe the call after bids opened. A fresh call could cure the flaws. Fair play for left-out firms outweighed the cost of a re-run.
gao-gaoreports-b-297889:
AshBritt protested the terms of an Army Corps call for storm clean work in GAO decision B-297889, dated March 20, 2006. The work was tear-down and debris clear in Mississippi. The storm was Hurricane Katrina. The call gave a tilt to firms in Mississippi. Firms in other hit states were shut out of that tilt. Law for aid was the base.

GAO denied the protest. The Stafford Act tells agencies to tilt debris deals to firms in the hit zone. A set-aside for state firms is a fair way to give that tilt. The choice to tilt to Mississippi firms for Mississippi work was in the agency's room to act. No abuse of that room was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-298889:
U.S. Dynamics Corporation protested an Air Force award to U.S. Technologies, Inc. The contract covered a stock of exciter radios. Those parts serve in radar transmitters. GAO ruled in B-298889 on December 19, 2006.

The fight turned on the winner's price offer. The firm said the agency judged that price in a flawed way. GAO read the record for support. The file backed the call that the prices were fair and sound. The buy used a lowest-price, technically-fit method. Under that method, a fair price plus a fit offer wins. No flaw in the price review was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-302789:
The Coast Guard Finance Center asked GAO to rule on its electronic certification path in B-302789. The center sends voucher schedules to the Treasury for payment. One officer confirms the totals on each schedule. GAO issued its legal ruling on July 6, 2005.

The doubt was a clash of roles. At times, that same officer had certified a single voucher in the set. GAO found no bar to that overlap. Risk of loss from error or wrong acts is not raised by it. The officer who backs a schedule owns just the schedule-stage errors. That split of duties is fair as drawn. The center need not split the two steps.
gao-gaoreports-b-303689:
Members of the House asked GAO for a legal opinion in B-303689. The plea hit a gift to the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences. The American Chemistry Council gave funds for grants on toxicants. GAO issued its ruling on September 30, 2005.

GAO found the gift path lawful. The Health and Human Services Secretary may take gifts, even with terms. The pact's terms gave the council a voice in grant review. They did not hand it the power to award grants. That line kept the gift inside the law. GAO urged the institute to set clear donor rules. Such rules would guard the grants process from doubt.
gao-gaoreports-b-310489:
Superlative Technologies, Inc. won its protest — GAO decision B-310489, dated January 4, 2008. The Justice Department's grants office had sought help for its data safety work. It then killed the call for quotes. It said leaks of pick facts gave one firm an unfair edge. The office next bought the work with no race. The no-race team held the same firm that got the leak.

GAO sustained the protest. The kill lacked a fair base on these facts. An agency cannot plead a taint it then rewards. If the leak was the flaw, the cure can not hand the work to the firm the leak is said to have helped.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-189:
DOD Systems Modernization, GAO-05-189 of February 11, 2005, reviews a Pentagon plan to fix its tangled troop and pay systems. Each service has long kept its own staff and pay tools, with known flaws. The new joint system, called DIMHRS, would give all branches one shared tool for staff records and pay. The design for phase one won approval in November 2004.

GAO tests how the Pentagon set the tool's needs. It tests the shape of the team that runs the build. More fixes to that management are needed, the title warns. The stakes are plain: pay and records for every person in uniform ride on this build.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-289:
Environmental Justice, GAO-05-289 of July 25, 2005, asks if clean air rules weigh fair play for all groups as they are built. An order from the President made fair play part of the Environmental Protection Agency's task. Fair play means no race, culture, or pay level bears more harm than its share. The agency wrote guides for its rule teams.

GAO tracks three clean air rules through two stages. It tracks the draft stage, from work team to cost check to public view. It tracks the final stage, from public views to the last cost check. The agency should give fair play more heed, the title finds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-789:
Health care for Native Americans is examined in GAO-05-789, a report issued August 31, 2005. A federal service arranges care at its own sites and buys care outside when needed. Gaps in care have long drawn concern. GAO visited 13 sites and spoke with officials from all 12 regions. It checked basic care first. Then it checked lab, drug, and specialist care.

GAO found basic care was offered at most sites. All 13 sites offered medical care, and 12 offered dental and vision care. But waits, travel distance, and lack of transport often blocked access. Some specialty care was missing on site, such as care for joint pain or behavior health. Bought care was rationed by need at 12 sites. Five sites could pay only for urgent cases.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-189:
Phone and Internet access on tribal lands is studied in GAO-06-189, a report GAO issued on January 11, 2006. A core goal of the 1934 Communications Act is access for all Americans. Native Americans on tribal lands have long had the lowest subscription rates in the nation. The Federal Communications Commission has worked to lift those rates. GAO reported on subscription levels, federal aid programs, and the barriers tribes face.

Some tribes have found ways around the barriers. Distance, rough terrain, and low incomes raise the cost of service. Thin data make the problem hard to size or track. Federal programs exist, but tribes must thread them together with their own funds and plans. The report shows both the gap and the paths tribes use to close it. It gives Congress a base for judging the grant idea then under debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-289:
Fish quota programs and the voices heard in building them fill GAO-06-289, a report issued on February 23, 2006. Dedicated access programs cap a fishery's total catch and hand shares to chosen fishers. The tool can end overfishing and guard stocks. It also reshapes whole fishing towns, since a share can decide who keeps working. Fair process in drawing the lines is thus vital. GAO asked how far regional fishery councils use a sound framework for public input. It also gathered ways that fishers and experts say input could improve.

Core principles and a planned approach would lift participation, GAO found. Councils vary in how they draw in the people hit by quota choices. The report collects methods that stakeholders back, though it makes no recommendation on those methods. The study treats process as part of conservation: rules that fishers help shape are rules they are likelier to obey.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-389:
Radiation detectors at border crossings are a front line against nuclear smuggling. Dated March 22, 2006, GAO-06-389 tracks the Department of Homeland Security's deployment work. The department began placing detection gear at U.S. ports of entry in October 2002. The goal was to stop radioactive material from being smuggled into the country.

GAO reviewed progress in placing the gear in the field. It checked how staff use the gear and how its skill is tested and improved. It also studied teamwork with other federal agencies. GAO found real progress in deployment. Concerns remained, it said. Readers get a port-by-port sense of the shield and its limits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-989:
Navy shipyard funding shifts are judged in GAO report GAO-06-989, dated September 14, 2006. The Navy is merging repair sites and moving its yards from a working capital fund to direct yearly funding. Puget Sound Naval Shipyard made that switch in 2003.

Law told the Navy to grade the switch, and told GAO to review the Navy's report. That report, sent in March 2006, held direct funding the better path. GAO weighed the proof behind that claim. It checked open issues from past studies. It looked for other flaws in how the switch was run. Gains need better proof and follow-through, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-889:
A new citizenship proof rule for Medicaid is surveyed in GAO-07-889, dated June 28, 2007. The Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 ended self-attestation of citizenship. States must now see documents before granting coverage. GAO surveyed Medicaid offices in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Forty-four states replied, covering 71 percent of enrollment. GAO asked about access, workload, and cost effects.

Twenty-two states reported enrollment declines tied to the rule. Most blamed delays or lost coverage for people who seemed to be eligible citizens. One state counted 18,000 denials or terminations in the first seven months. Twelve states saw no effect, and 10 did not know. States also reported heavy paperwork burdens from the rule. Effects past the first year were unclear to many. The report gives Congress the states' own account of the change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-89:
Teamwork at Homeland Security operations centers is assessed in GAO-07-89, dated October 20, 2006. The department runs 25 centers that work around the clock. Four of them need staff from many agencies to do their jobs. GAO visited the centers and read their reports. It described each center's mission, products, and customers. It then graded joint work against proven collaboration practices.

Three centers hold tactical missions, such as tracking flights and travelers. The fourth, the National Operations Center watch, gives a national overview. All four share tasks like situational awareness and incident management. They differ in the reports they produce and the clients they serve. GAO found room to deepen joint habits at the centers. Shared goals, clear roles, and common tools mark the path. The report details each center in turn.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-189:
A program that employs former Soviet weapons scientists is reassessed in GAO report GAO-08-189 (December 12, 2007). The Energy Department set up the program in 1994. It funds peaceful work for scientists who might otherwise sell their skills. The aim is to cut the spread of weapons know-how. Short-term grants were meant to grow into private jobs.

GAO found that the department overstates what the program achieves. In a sample of 97 projects covering about 6,450 scientists, more than half of those paid had never claimed weapons experience. Institute leaders said the funds help them recruit staff instead. GAO urged a full reassessment, with a clear exit plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-289:
Utility merger oversight after a legal shift is studied in GAO report GAO-08-289 (February 25, 2008). For decades, a 1935 act limited who could own or merge with utilities. The Energy Policy Act of 2005 repealed that act. The energy regulator now holds the main federal watch. New owners could try to pass unfair affiliate costs to captive customers. That risk is called cross-subsidization.

GAO asked how the regulator changed its merger reviews after the repeal. It also checked the follow-up reviews done once deals close. State commissions shared their own oversight picture in a survey. The title urges improved vigilance under the new law.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-389:
College students' health coverage is surveyed in GAO report GAO-08-389, dated March 28, 2008. Students can lose a parent's cover as they age and may lack a job that offers a plan. GAO used national survey data and gathered plan details from 340 colleges.

About 80 percent of students aged 18 through 23 had coverage in 2006. Most, 67 percent, were covered through employer-sponsored plans, often as a dependent on a parent's policy. About 20 percent, or 1.7 million students, had no coverage, with part-time and lower-income students most at risk. Over half of colleges offered their own student plans in the 2007-2008 academic year. Yearly premiums ranged from $30 to $2,400, and benefits varied widely.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-589:
GAO-08-589, a GAO report dated June 23, 2008, covers workload strain at the job bias agency. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission enforces federal laws against workplace discrimination. It was created under title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Within 4 years, all of its senior executives and senior managers will be eligible to retire.

Private sector charges keep growing while budgets stay tight. Some field offices still resolve cases fast with good quality, but their methods are not shared. The agency's strategic human capital plan remains unfinished, so skill gaps in the current and future workforce go unmapped. GAO urged the agency to name what its best offices do, spread those practices, and finish the plan with steps and measures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-889:
A new courthouse for Los Angeles federal judges has been planned since 2000, with about $400 million set aside. GAO-08-889, dated September 12, 2008, explains why nothing has been built and why cost guesses have nearly tripled to over $1.1 billion.

Occupancy slipped 8 years, to fiscal year 2014 at the earliest. Planners designed a bigger building than Congress allowed, then cut scope slowly as prices rose. Weak builder interest killed the 41-courtroom project outright. About $366.45 million still sits unspent, but no plan fits the budget now. Congress must bless any new path forward, GAO notes in closing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-89:
Arms exports worth billions need State Department licenses. GAO-08-89, dated November 30, 2007, tracks how the licensing office's workload and waits moved from fiscal years 2003 to 2006, and what drove the strain. Industry and foreign buyers had griped that reviews drag.

Case counts rose 20 percent, and median waits nearly doubled. Open cases climbed 50 percent, from about 5,000 in October 2002 to about 7,500 in April 2007, peaking above 10,000. A crash push cut open cases 40 percent in 3 months by halting training and outreach. That pace cannot last, GAO says. It urges steady study of where the process clogs.
gissing-nether-world-1889:
George Gissing knew London poverty from the inside, having lived in cheap rooms on a tiny income. He set The Nether World, published in 1889, in the slums of Clerkenwell. Gissing wrote it as a plain record of working-class life, without the consolation of a happy plot.

Families crowd into courts and workshops, fighting over wages, drink, and a small inheritance that promises escape. A returned emigrant's money stirs hope in several households, but the money mostly spreads new misery. Gissing refuses villains and heroes; the trap is the world itself. The novel stands among the bleakest and most honest pictures of Victorian slum life.
glanvill-saducismus-triumphatus-english-:
Joseph Glanvill, a fellow of the Royal Society, wrote Saducismus Triumphatus to defeat Sadducism, his age's doubt about spirits. This edition of 1689 appeared after his death, with fresh material added. Glanvill offers full and plain evidence concerning witches and apparitions, gathered like a scientist's casebook.

His most famous case is the Drummer of Tedworth, a poltergeist that beat drums in a Wiltshire house. Glanvill treats testimony for ghosts as data, to be weighed like any observation. The book is science's strangest defense of the spirit world. It shows the new philosophy of experiment turned, in earnest, toward proving that witches exist.
glauber-works-1689:
Christopher Packe gave England the complete Glauber in 1689, translating The Works of Johann Rudolf Glauber, the famous German chemist. Furnaces, mines, metals, saltpetre, and the mending of barren land all fall within his restless program. Glauber wrote from decades at the bench, and his pages smell of the laboratory.

New philosophical furnaces open the collection, designs meant to work metals cleanly and cheaply. Later parts teach the separation of metals, the making of salts, and ways to enrich poor soil. The volume stands as the great seventeenth-century chemical corpus in English, prized by historians of early industry and craft.
gore-lux-mundi-1889:
Charles Gore edited Lux Mundi, the 1889 essay collection that brought biblical criticism inside Anglo-Catholic faith, and shocked Victorian England. Gore, later a bishop, gathered younger Oxford churchmen to write on faith in a new age of science and history. The book's title means Light of the World.

The essays accept evolution and the critical study of scripture while holding fast to the incarnation and the sacraments. Gore's own essay on the Holy Spirit and the church set the volume's daring, loyal tone. Lux Mundi split church opinion and marked the start of a more open Anglo-Catholicism.
grinnell-pawnee-hero-stories-and-folk-ta:
Before his Blackfoot tales, Grinnell spent time among the Pawnee of Nebraska, who shared their hero stories and folk tales with him. His 1889 book prints what he heard, making it one of the earliest published collections of Pawnee narrative.

The tales tell of Tirawa, the great power behind the world, and of heroes who fought monsters and won sacred gifts for the people. Grinnell also describes the morning star sacrifice and the warrior societies that guarded tribal life. These stories carry the Pawnee view of courage, duty, and the sacred, recorded before the tribe's old order broke apart.
hartmann-principles-of-astrological-geom:
Franz Hartmann taught an old art of fate in The Principles of Astrological Geomancy, his guide of 1889. Geomancy reads fate from marks in earth or dots cast at chance. Scribes of old joined those marks to the stars. Hartmann bases his rules on Agrippa, a sage of the age of print's dawn.

Steps, charts, and worked cases fill the guide. A keen fan could cast a chart by its rules at once. The art had near died out by his day. Hartmann's guide is the chief text of its late new life. Casters cast four rows of dots, then read the forms they make. Hartmann shows each step with care, so a new hand can learn fast.
henry-dunbar-a-novel-pg9189:
M E Braddon wrote this novel of crime and doubt in the banking house of Dunbar and Balderby. Henry Dunbar returns from India a very rich man. An old clerk who knew his youth is found dead. The house, the town, and Dunbar's own daughter must face the charge.

The long chapter list runs through flight, weddings, and hidden letters. Margaret hunts proof while Clement Austin risks his place for love. A portrait found abroad helps crack the case at last. The story mixes court scenes, home scenes, and a chase across two lands.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol9-1889:
Volume IX of Hering's Guiding Symptoms, from 1889, stands second to last in the ten-volume row. By now the editorial hands are practised, and the pages hold the same dense, well-sorted wealth. Each remedy's record runs from mental signs down to skin, fever, and sleep.

Hering began the harvest of provings decades before, and his name still heads the work. The grading signs, his own device, mark what practice confirmed most often. For the working homeopath the set served as both library and tool, and this volume carries its full share of the load.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1588-8:
Chapter twenty of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands follows Alexander Farnese against Bergen-op-Zoom. Parma besieges the town while Pallavicini attempts to seduce its garrison's loyalty. Zeeland's fierce amphibious bands have just held Farnese's fleet in prison. The invading party picks its way by night along the Vosmeer's drowned bottom.

The landing fails, and the rising tide swallows four hundred of the Spaniards. The rest fight back half-drowned along their dangerous path. Motley narrates the episode as a parable of the whole war. Spain's veterans could beat any army in Europe on dry land. In the Netherlands the land itself fought for the Dutch, with tide, mud, and flood as their oldest allies. Bergen-op-Zoom holds, and the Armada year's land campaign ends in water.
hobson-physiology-of-industry-1889:
Hobson wrote The Physiology of Industry in 1889 with the businessman A. F. Mummery. It was Hobson's first book, and it launched the heresy he defended for the rest of his life. Orthodox economics taught that saving was always a virtue and spending a danger; the two authors argued the opposite could be true.

They claim that saving can outrun the need for new capital goods, leaving goods unsold and workers idle. Thrift, pushed too far, then causes the very slumps it was meant to prevent. The economics profession tried to bury the book, and Hobson was shut out of academic posts. Decades later, Keynes praised it by name as a seed of his own theory. The volume remains a landmark of dissent inside economics.
in-the-year-2889:
Michel Verne is now believed to be chiefly the author of In the Year 2889, first printed in the Forum in February 1889. It appeared under his father Jules Verne's name and echoes the elder Verne's ideas. The tale pictures a twenty-ninth century of giant towns. Streets run three hundred feet wide, and houses rise a thousand feet.

Aerial travel crosses the sky, and the season's temperature is held the same all year. Mr. Smith funds a young chemist who hopes even to manufacture a human being. Another plan would move a whole city at once. The piece is early future speculation.
janet-automatisme-psychologique-1889:
Pierre Janet maps the hid mind in L'Automatisme psychologique, his French thesis of 1889. Janet was a young sage at work in the wards of Paris. His sick wrote, spoke, and acted with no sense of their own deeds. He calls such acts the work of a split off part of the self, out of the main mind's sight and rule.

Cases fill the book, each probed with great care. His scheme came ere Freud's fame and fed it in part. In French, the book is a root text of mind science. Its reach is vast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdallah-ibn-sa:
Abdallah ibn Saba was a Jew of Yemen, in Arabia, in the seventh century. He settled in Medina and took up Islam. Banished for his attacks on Calif Othman's rule, he went to Egypt. There he founded a sect against Othman, working to lift Ali into power. His teaching held that each prophet had a helper who followed him, and that Ali was that helper for Mohammed.

Tradition in the entry goes much further. It says Abdallah gave Ali divine honors, and taught after Ali's death that Ali still lived. Part of the Godhead, he said, lay hid in Ali, who would return to fill the earth with justice. The entry traces this whole scheme to the hope of a Messiah, joined with the legend of Elijah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigdor-ben-men: Abigdor ben Menahem was a German Talmudist who lived at the beginning of the fifteenth century. Responsa by him are held in the Bodleian collection of manuscripts. From the place given him in that set, he seems a man of the age of Jacob Mölln, who died in 1427, and of Jacob Weil. One point is sure, the entry says. He was no longer living when the responsa were gathered up. The man who gathered them set a memorial blessing after his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abitur-joseph-b:
Joseph ben Isaac ibn Abitur was a Talmudist and liturgical poet born in Merida early in the tenth century. He died in Damascus about 970. At Cordova he studied under Rabbi Moses and became one of his best pupils.

When Rabbi Moses died, his son Hanok won the succession, backed by the calif. Abitur's party was excommunicated, and he left Spain. Later friends offered him the Cordova post, but he refused to take it by wronging Hanok. Few of his works survive. His fame rests chiefly on complex liturgical poems, above all his Abodah for the Day of Atonement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-jud: Abraham ben Judah Elimelech, called Almalik, was a cabalistic writer at Pesaro in Italy. He lived about the end of the fifteenth century and was probably a Spanish exile. His book Likkute Shikhah u-Peah, or Gleanings, comments on haggadic parts of the Talmud in Cabala terms. Its preface gives some detail of his own life. The book was printed at Ferrara in 1556. It appeared with works by Joseph ben Hayyim and Joseph Giquitilla on like subjects.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abudarham-arabi:
Abudarham is a family name borne by Spanish Jews. The entry says David Abudarham bore it first. He was a tax man and an elder of the Jews of Tudela. He served under Sancho the Great of Castile and Leon, who ruled from 1258 to 1295. Sancho set the taxes each Jewish town owed the crown. A board of four chief men met at Huete in September, 1290, to fix the sums.

If the board could not agree, the king sent the case to David. Both sides had to accept his call. The entry links a Toledo synagogue name to him as its builder. Later notes trace kin in Rome in 1524. One man of the name copied a Hebrew text of Aristotle in 1444. The name still shows up in North Africa, Gibraltar, Marseilles, and Tunis in much later years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-addison-joseph-:
Joseph Addison was an English essayist born at Milston on May 1, 1672. He died on June 17, 1719. He has been called the chief shaper of English public opinion in his age. For that cause his views on Jews hold weight. Laws and court thought for a century came from the class that read him.

Five spots in his work treat Jews and Judaism. All show a warm view and fair knowledge for his day. The key piece is "Spectator" No. 495, of September 27, 1712. It treats the spread of the Jews through the trade world. It praises their worth as links between far lands. He likens them to pegs and nails in a great frame. They are small in themselves, he says, yet the whole build needs them. His Ode on Gratitude was later turned into Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agate-889: Agate is a precious stone named four times in the King James Bible. Twice it stands for kadkod, and twice for shebo. Its name comes from the river Achates in Sicily, where it was first found. It is found in many lands, though. Kinds take in the white stone of Chalcedon, the brown sard, and the red carnelian. Onyx and sardonyx are forms of it too. Rabbinic lore tells of two angels in dispute over kadkod. One held it for beryl, and one for jasper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alcan-eugene-10:
Eugene Alcan was a French man of letters, painter, and poet who embraced Christianity. He was born in Paris in 1811 and died about 1898. He was a brother of Alphonse Alkan. No one has explained why the family name is spelled two ways.

His books run from 1879 to 1892. They include "La Legende des Ames," drawn from talks of Saint Vincent de Paul, and two flower-titled works of early life and of suffering. "Les Cannibales et Leur Temps" tells of a sea campaign in Oceania under Captain Marceau. His last book listed is "Recits Instructifs du Pere Balthazar," of 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfaquin-solomo: Solomon Alfaquin was a physician to King Sancho the Wise of Navarre. The king prized his art so highly that he loaded him with gifts. He gave him seven acres of land. He added twelve measures of vineyards at Mosquera and Fontellas, two villages near Tudela. He also granted him the infanzon privileges, the rights of nobility, kingdom-wide. In 1193 the king transferred to him the baths near the Albazares gate at Tudela. The entry names no dates for the physician's own life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-american-jewess: American Jewess was a magazine for Jewish women. It was printed in Chicago and in New York. It began as a monthly and turned to a quarterly. Nine volumes came out in all. The first came out in April 1895. The last came out in March 1899. Its aims were threefold and clear. It gave women a field for their gifts. It drew Jewish women of the land closer. It spoke for the groups Jewish women had formed. Rosa Sonnenschein served as its editor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anchias-juan-de:
Juan de Anchias was an associate and first private secretary of the Inquisition in Spain from 1485 to 1490. The entry says he knew well the wills and marriage contracts used by Maranos accused of Judaism.

In 1507, at Belchite, he wrote the Libro Verde de Aragon, a genealogy of rich, respected baptized Jews. In 1623 Philip IV ordered all copies found and destroyed, and only one old copy survives at Seville. When the book was printed in 1885, that issue was seized at once and stayed banned. Its material later fed Francisco Mendoza y Bovadilla's attack on the Spanish nobility.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antiochus-iv-ep:
Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Illustrious, was king of Syria from 175 B.C. until his death in 164. A son of Antiochus the Great, he took the throne after his brother Seleucus was murdered, though it belonged to his nephew Demetrius. Rabbinic sources call him simply the wicked.

Jewish and heathen sources agree on his character, the entry says, so the portrait is likely true. He mixed the worst Greek and Roman faults: vain, showy, free with money, and cruel at heart. The entry rejects the claim that he meant to reform the Jews. His aim, it argues, was to strip them of their national life altogether. His rule thus shaped Jewish history and religion for good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arabic-poetry-1:
Arabic poetry of the Jews, to judge from what survives, is about as old as Arabic poetry itself. It shares the same form and stamp. The entry splits it into two ages: the pre-Islamic age of lyric song, and the age of Mohammed, which turns to polemic.

The oldest known verses are by Sarah of the Banu Kuraiza, a dirge for her people treacherously slain near the end of the fifth century. The age's height is Samau'al ibn Adiya, who held the castle Al-Ablak in Taima in the middle of the sixth century. Arabs of all ages make him the pattern of fidelity. He let his own son die rather than break a pledge made to the poet Imr al-Kais, the entry recounts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-armilus-1789:
Armilus stands in later Jewish legend as the king who rises at the end of time against the Messiah. The entry calls him a Jewish Antichrist figure who brings great distress on Israel before the Messiah defeats him. His origins, growth, and links to Christian legend are all treated as open questions. Saadia, born in 892 and dead in 942, is the earliest firm authority who names him.

In Saadia's tradition, persecution first drives Israel to repent. A leader of the tribe of Joseph retakes Jerusalem, then Armilus conquers the city, kills that leader, and drives the Jews into the desert. After suffering purifies them, the Messiah comes, retakes Jerusalem, and slays Armilus. Other Midrashim give the figure a darker shape and join him with Satan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asch-abraham-18:
Abraham Asch, a German rabbi and author, was born at Posen and served as rabbi of Zell toward the end of the eighteenth century. He came from a learned family that traced its line to Meir of Lublin. His father Joseph had been rabbi of Dessau, and the scholar Isaiah Berlin was a relative. Asch's book Mareh Esh, The Appearance of Fire, came out after his death.

His son Moses Jacob published the work in 1803. It holds critical notes on the texts of several Talmudic treatises. The entry adds a caution about identity. This Asch is probably not the Abraham Asch who wrote Torah Kullah, The Whole Law, at Berlin in 1796. That writer campaigned against the custom of hasty burial, a different mark on a shared name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asnapper-11789:
Asnapper is named in Ezra chapter 4 as the man who moved a mixed crowd of tribes from Babylon to Samaria after that city fell. The name has been guessed to be a misreading of Assurbanipal, the Assyrian king, though the passage in Ezra points to Esarhaddon. A form in First Esdras suggests a letter has dropped out of the word.

If that guess is right, Asnapper holds the only reference to Assurbanipal in the whole Bible. The Revised Version prefers the form Osnappar. Rabbinic reading takes another path: the Talmud matches Asnapper to Sennacherib and says that king bore eight names, as did his foe Hezekiah. The entry leaves the name balanced among king, misreading, and tradition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-atlanta-2089:
Atlanta has been the capital of Georgia since 1868. United States troops captured and burned the city in 1864, and its civic and synagogue records were lost. By the best tradition the entry could gather, the first Jewish settler was Jacob Haas. He came with his family about 1846. Moses Sternberg followed soon after.

The Hebrew Benevolent Congregation formed during the war and met in the Masonic Temple. Other bodies followed: Ahawat Achim, Gemilath Chesed, and aid societies for women and the poor. In 1889 a Hebrew Orphans' Home opened under B'nai B'rith auspices. In 1900 it cared for sixty-eight children. The entry puts the Jewish population at 1,500 to 2,000 in a total of 100,000. It lists the trades Jews worked in, from paper boxes and furniture to cotton goods and clothing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ayllon-solomon-:
Solomon ben Jacob Ayllon was haham of the Sephardic congregations in London and Amsterdam. He was born in the Orient in 1664 and died in Amsterdam on April 10, 1728. He followed Shabbethai Ẓebi, the false messiah. The entry is blunt about his learning: his legal answers show he was no great scholar and no Talmudist of standing.

Ayllon spent his youth in Salonica among Shabbethaian circles. He later traveled in Europe collecting funds for the poor of the Holy Land, and he seemed to have broken with the movement in public. London made him haham on June 6, 1689. Within a year a member attacked his past, and the exposure wrecked his standing with the learned men of the flock. In Amsterdam he later clashed with the Polish rabbi Ẓebi Ashkenazi over a new Shabbethaian teacher. The entry traces that fight and the part Ayllon played in it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-babylonish-garm:
The Babylonish garment is a piece of dress named in the book of Joshua. Achan stole one from the spoil of Jericho, along with silver and gold. Its place in that company shows it was a thing of real worth. That such a garment reached Jericho points to trade with Babylonia. Other evidence shows that trade began long before Joshua's day. What sort of garment it was cannot be fixed with certainty.

Rabbinic voices differ. One calls it a purple robe, and Josephus says it was made of gold. Two Talmudic views split the point. One speaks to the stuff, fine wool, the other to the dyeing, with alum at a town near Pumbedita.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bakri-jacob-coh: Jacob Cohen Bakri was French consul at Algiers before France conquered it. Born in Algiers in 1763, he died at Paris on Nov. 23, 1836. Rich and well regarded, he was made consul under the Restoration. In 1827 he argued a French claim with the dey Hasan and pressed it hard. The dey insulted him, France took the act as a national affront, and war followed. Algiers fell and the dey was banished. Bakri then settled in Paris, dogged by creditors, since a Spanish debt of 35,000,000 francs owed him stayed out of reach.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bear-2689:
Bear is an animal named often in the Old Testament and once common in Palestine and Syria. Next to the lion it ranked as man's most dreaded foe. Guarding flocks from lions and bears was the shepherd's hardest task, the entry notes.

A mother bear robbed of her cubs stands in the prophets for fierce wrath. In Daniel the bear stands for the Median empire and its greed for land. The entry closes with the Syrian bear, smaller and lighter than the brown bear, and notes the animal is now gone from Palestine proper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bekiin-hebrew-2: Bekiin was a small town in Palestine, set between Jabneh and Lydda. The entry is short and gives the town a single claim on notice. Bekiin was the seat of a Talmud school founded by Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah. That founding fell in the days when Gamaliel the Second held the lead. Three sources are cited for the report, from the Babylonian Talmud, the Jerusalem Talmud, and the Tosefta.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-avigdor-pen:
Ben-Avigdor, pen name of Abraham Leib Shalkovich, was a Russian Hebrew novelist and publisher born in 1867 at Zheludok, in Wilna. Trained for the rabbinate, he chose modern Hebrew letters and Zionism instead. In 1891 he went to Warsaw as secretary of a Zionist society.

There he issued a penny book series of short stories, thirty-one numbers in four years. Six were his own tales; the rest came from leading Hebrew writers of the day. He later helped found one publishing house and then ran his own. Critics fought over his plain new style.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-willia: William Benjamin, often called Bill Bainge, was an English prize fighter born at Northleach, in Gloucestershire, in 1826. His first match pitted him against Tom Sayers, champion of England, in January 1858. Sayers beat him in three rounds. A second bout that April went eleven rounds before Benjamin was counted out. His stronger showing there partly restored his name. In July 1861 he proved his growth as a boxer by beating Dick James of Aberdare in two rounds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bet-din-pl-batt:
Bet din is the rabbinical term for a court. The entry explains that it held civil and religious power together. That union came from the theocratic view of Jewish law. The Great Bet Din sat at Jerusalem. It acted as the supreme court of the country. Its rulings had to be obeyed. It also appointed judges and approved wars of offense.

After 70 the court moved its center to Jabneh. There it led Jewish life until the late third century. Its power faded as Babylonian scholarship rose. The entry then describes local courts of later times. A court of twenty-three heard capital cases. Three members decided money disputes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bigamy-3289:
Bigamy in rabbinical law differs from the common definition. A second union must be lawful to count. Only a man can commit it, the entry says. In Biblical and Talmudic times polygamy was recognized. No question of bigamy could arise then. A man could take wives as he could support them.

The ban dates from the eleventh century. Rabbi Gershon forbade bigamy under excommunication. French and German Jews accepted his decree. Oriental and Spanish Jews questioned his authority. The entry lists permitted exceptions. They cover levirate marriage and a childless union of ten years. A wife's madness needs rulings from 100 rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-josef-338: Josef Bloch was a violin virtuoso and composer. He was born at Budapest on January 5, 1862. He first performed in public at twelve. Huber was his most famous teacher. At barely sixteen he taught at the National Conservatory. Seven years at the Paris Conservatoire followed. Back home he joined the Hubay-Popper String Quartet. It lasted until its dissolution in 1892. In 1889 he became professor at two Budapest schools. Since 1899 he has served the Academy alone. He composed violin pieces and two orchestral suites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boskowitz-3589:
Boskowitz is a town in Moravia, about 21 miles north of Brünn. It held one of the oldest and largest communities in the province. By 1880 its Jewish residents had fallen to 1,967 in number.

Its model school trained many pupils who later won fame. Samuel Levi Kolin, author of a noted ritual commentary, came from Boskowitz. The cabalist Nathan Adler became rabbi there in 1783. His strict ways brought a clash with townsfolk, and he had to leave. Later rabbis also fought with the sharp laymen of the town. Rich foundations from the Löw-Beer family served the community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breslaur-emil-3:
Emil Breslaur was a German musician and writer on music teaching. He was born at Kottbus on May 29, 1836. He first served as preacher and religious teacher in the Jewish congregation of Kottbus.

In 1863 Breslaur moved to Berlin for a four-year course at Stern's Conservatory. He taught piano method at Kullak's academy from 1868 to 1879. He founded a society of Berlin music teachers that grew into a national union. His 1874 work on the technique of piano playing won him the title of professor. From 1883 he was choirmaster of Berlin's Reformed Synagogue. His journal Der Klavierlehrer ran from 1878, and his piano school reached an eighteenth edition by 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buchner-wolf-b-:
Wolf Buchner, son of David Hakohen, was a Hebrew stylist born at Brody in the later eighteenth century. As a boy he lived on the hospitality Talmud students found in study houses. As a man he traveled with Hebrew books through Germany, Galicia, Poland, and Lithuania. At times he earned his living writing letters for people who could not write.

His works include an imitation of Al-Harizi, a book of poems, and hymns modeled on Gabirol. A collection of his private letters appeared at Prague in 1805. The entry calls him a modern voice of the medieval school of artificial poetry. It faults his flowery prose and his care for letter counts over sense. His books sold well in his day, then fell into neglect.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cagliari-hebr-3:
Cagliari, capital of the island of Sardinia, held a Jewish community from early times. When a baptized Jew placed saints' images in its synagogue, Gregory I ordered the bishop to remove them at once. Little else is known of the early centuries. Under Aragonese rule Jews fared well and were received at court.

King Martin I visited in December 1408 and invited a Jew to join games held in his honor. The community's rabbi then was Judah ben David, a physician and Talmudist from Marseilles. He reached Sardinia in 1390 and was confirmed as rabbi of the whole island. A large synagogue served the city. In 1492 the Jews of Cagliari were expelled, like those of Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantonists-3989:
Cantonists were sons of Russian private soldiers schooled from 1805 to 1827 in special canton schools for army service. After 1827 the term took in Jewish boys as well. A statute of Sept. 7, 1827, drafted them at age twelve. They were sent to canton schools in far provinces for their military training.

Under Nicholas the first, officials prized Jewish cantonists as easier to convert than grown men. Distance from home was the chosen tool: boys from Kiev went to Perm, boys from Brest to a distant eastern city. Witnesses told of cruel treatment, and protests changed nothing, since the fault lay in the system itself. Europe's outcry helped end the schools when Alexander the second abolished them in 1857.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carvajal-antoni:
Antonio Fernandez Carvajal, a Portuguese merchant, was the first endenizened English Jew. Born about 1590, probably at Fundão, he fled Inquisition persecution to the Canary Islands, then settled in London about 1635. By 1653 he owned ships trading to the Indies, Brazil, and the Levant. His yearly silver imports averaged £100,000.

In 1655 Carvajal and his two sons gained denizenship as English subjects. He backed Manasseh ben Israel's petition for the return of the Jews to England. The first Jewish burial ground after the readmission stood in his name and two others. Cromwell used his Continental contacts for news of Royalist plans. Carvajal also advanced money to Parliament and broke open a customs warehouse in 1648 to recover a seized cargo of logwood.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caucasus-or-cau:
Caucasus, or Caucasia, was a division of Russia set between European Russia, the Caspian Sea, Persia, Asiatic Turkey, and the Black Sea. It held six governments, four provinces, and two districts. The census of 1897 counted 58,471 Jews there, or 6.3 per cent of all people. The entry warns that the figure is probably too low.

Counts are hard, the account explains. Some southern Jews had taken Islam, and some Georgian Jews had taken Christianity. Native Jews are also mixed in counts with newcomers from European Russia. One estimate puts native Caucasian Jews near 100,000. Some of these Jews claim descent from the Lost Ten Tribes. Others trace their line to Israelites taken by Shalmaneser. The entry weighs a link between the river Habor and Iberia, and a view that Media was the cradle of these Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cervera-4189: Cervera is a hill town in Catalonia, Spain, with a Jewish community in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. In 1328 King Alfonso IV assigned Jews a quarter near San Miguel, with full freedom to trade. Four years later they gained leave to live in the Traders' street. In 1349, at the Black Death, a riot killed eighteen Jews and looted the rest, who fled and later returned. In January 1479, Jews from several towns gathered at Cervera for memorial services for Don Juan II, carrying a coffin with the royal arms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cinnamon-4389: Cinnamon is the bark of Cinnamomum Zeylanicum, a plant named for Ceylon, where it grows best. A common stand-in, cassia, comes from China. The Hebrews knew cinnamon early, the entry notes. It went into the anointing-oil of Exodus xxx. 23. It also served as a plain perfume in Proverbs vii. 17. The Song of Solomon iv. 14 lists it among fragrant woods. On the word itself, Gesenius and Lagarde treat the Hebrew as a Greek loan. Herodotus, though, says the Greeks borrowed it from the Phoenicians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-leonce-44: Leonce Cohen, a French musician, was born at Paris on Feb. 12, 1829, and died in 1884. He studied at the Paris Conservatory under Leborne. In 1851 he won the Prix de Rome. Soon after, he joined the violinists of the Theatre Italien at Paris. The short entry credits him with some operettas. It also names one book, Ecole du Musicien. Riemann's music lexicon of 1900 is the only source given for these few facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-conegliano-also:
Conegliano, also spelled Conian, was a leading Jewish family of northern Italy, named for the town of Conegliano once held by Venice. A branch flourished in Ceneda, and the line seems to start at Asti in the sixteenth century. Learning marked its members.

Israel Conegliano fills most of the entry. A Padua-born physician, he practiced at Venice, then won the trust of the Sultan and Grand Vizier Kara Mustapha at Constantinople. Venice made him physician extraordinary to its embassy on Oct. 10, 1682, at one hundred zecchinos a year. He ran messages between the two powers in wartime. In 1693 Venice freed him and his brothers from the yellow hat and made them citizens. In 1698 he sat at the Carlovitz peace congress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-costa-benjamin-: Benjamin Mendez da Costa was a philanthropist born in 1704. He died in England in 1764. His family ranked among the oldest and most honored of the Portuguese Jews. He stood in the front rank of the Hebrew merchants of his day. His giving was wide: he handed out £3,000 a year to the poor of all creeds. In 1762 he joined Isaac de David Levy to endow a yeshibah. A codicil to his will ordered his gifts to needy families to go on after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-csillag-rosa-47: Rosa Csillag was a Hungarian opera singer, born about 1840. She first drew notice in the chorus of the Hungarian National Theater at Budapest. Trained by Professor Proch, she made her debut in 1858. She sang Fides in Meyerbeer's Le Prophète at the Vienna court opera house. Her fine mezzo-soprano voice delighted audiences there. She stayed with the Vienna Royal Opera until 1873 and toured with success. Her husband was the noted conjurer Hermann. When her voice failed, she taught singing at the Vienna Conservatoire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-danon-berakah-b: Berakah ben Yom-Ṭob Danon was a Talmudical scholar of Jerusalem. He lived in the first half of the nineteenth century. His one work is Bad Ḳodesh, meaning Holy Linen. It holds sermons, together with fresh comments on Maimonides' great code, the Yad. The book came out at Salonica in 1846. It was printed with a work by his father on the same code, called Kebod Yom-Ṭob. Two catalog sources close the entry. Nothing is said of his teachers, posts, or family beyond his father.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davidsohn-georg:
Georg Davidsohn was a German journalist born at Danzig, Prussia, on December 19, 1835. Meant for a merchant's career, he went to Berlin in 1856 and reported on business news. In 1860 he joined the "Berliner Börsen-Zeitung," where he ran its commercial side and founded a weekly literary supplement. Music and opera criticism became his specialty.

In 1868 Davidsohn founded the "Berliner Börsen-Courier" and edited it until his death in Berlin on February 6, 1897. He was a close friend of Richard Wagner and the first Berlin press advocate of Wagner's operas. He helped found the first Berlin Wagner society and championed the Bayreuth theater.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-denis-dionis-al:
Denis, also called Dionis Albertus, was one of the first members of the Portuguese Jewish community in Hamburg. On May 31, 1611, he signed the agreement that secured the community its cemetery at Altona. In 1612 the Senate formally admitted him to the town. He banked for Count Ernest of Schauenburg and supplied silver for the count's mint.

That work brought him into conflict with Hamburg. The Senate accused him of buying up city coins to melt at Altona and ordered him jailed. He escaped to Altona under the count's protection. In 1619 the Danish king gave him charge of the royal mint at Glückstadt. In 1637 he still acted for the Hamburg community in cemetery matters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dienesohn-jacob:
Jacob Dienesohn was a Yiddish novelist born in Zagory, Russia, in 1859. The entry calls him one of the most popular Yiddish novelists of the later nineteenth century. He began to write in 1877 with a story whose second title means The Dark Young Man. Many novels followed, almost all widely read, "Eben Negef" (Stumbling-Stone) among the best known.

Dienesohn pictures the fight between the old and young generations of Jews, between haskalah, or enlightenment, and Ḥasidism. He knew his readers and avoided harsh attacks on fanaticism, showing instead the sufferings of the Maskilim, the enlightened. His later novels are more sketches of Jewish life than romances. He also wrote a world history in Yiddish and good Hebrew pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dosa-also-known: Dosa, also called Dosai, was a Palestinian amora, probably of the fourth century. The Jerusalem Talmud keeps two of his rulings on religious law. Midrashic writings keep several of his sayings as well. One saying calls the work of judging in religious law the dangerous snare God guards men from. Dosa died on the new moon of Nisan. The date was noted because mourners that day were given refreshments, against the usual custom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dyvin-5389:
Dyvin is a village in the government of Grodno, Russia, with a very old Jewish community. No one can say when Jews first settled there. When the town sought the Magdeburg Law, its Jews gave fifty gold coins toward the cost. In return they were promised a share in the town's rights.

Burghers still tried to trim Jewish rights. In 1634 King Ladislaus IV confirmed Jewish ownership of houses, markets, baths, and land. He also upheld their synagogue, burial-ground, and free worship. Royal commissioners in 1656 gave Jews a one-third share in farming town revenues. A tax quarrel with the burghers was settled by agreement in 1661.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eisenstadt-hung:
Eisenstadt, in Hungarian Kis-Márton, is a city in Hungary's Oedenburg county. Its Jewish community stands alone in Hungary. It governs itself politically, electing its own mayor. The town once belonged to the Seven Communities. Its Jews are named as early as 1388.

Leopold I expelled Eisenstadt's Jews in 1671. Prince Paul Esterhazy soon settled Nikolsburg Jews on his land there. His privilege of Jan. 1, 1690, gave them twenty houses. For a yearly tax they could worship freely and elect their own judge. They paid thirty pounds of pepper a year for their cemetery. Israel Hildesheimer's yeshibah later made the town an Orthodox center.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elias-julius-55: Julius Elias was a German author born at Hoya in Hanover. His birth date was June 21, 1861. He studied at schools in Berlin and at Munich University. He took his doctor's degree there in 1888. His first book treated the writer Christian Wernicke. As an editor he brought out letters and a Shakespeare translation in part. With two partners he edited the full works of Ibsen. Since 1891 he has run a yearly review of German literary study. The entry names that post as his chief role.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephesus-5789:
Ephesus was the capital of Ionia in Asia Minor. Under Rome it ruled as capital of Asia Proconsularis. Many Jews lived in that great Greek city for ages. Josephus traces their civic rights to the Diadochi kings. The Greeks of the city gave the credit to Antiochus the Second. He reigned from 261 to 246 before Christ. Equal rights for the Jews most likely date from him.

In 49 B.C. a Roman consul raised troops in Asia Minor. The Jews of Ephesus were Roman citizens by law. Still they were let off army service for their faith's sake. Four years later Dolabella gave the same grant again. He told Ephesus to spread the word to other towns. The grant took hold in Alexandria and Sardis as well. A town decree also guards their Sabbath rest. The entry collects each such decree in its order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fernando-aaron-:
Aaron Fernando was a teacher and reformer at Leghorn, Italy, who died in 1830. He held a post under Napoleon, whom he greatly admired. In that heady age he decided the dawn of world brotherhood had come. Jews, he held, must fall in line by trimming their rites. The commandments should shrink to sixty, and most ceremony laws should go.

His plan was printed at Tiberias in 1810, though only the first of two volumes appeared. Jews denounced the book as a danger to religion. On July 14, 1814 the authorities banned it, and the congregation bought up and burned the copies. One copy, the author's own, survives in Frankfort's city library, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flexner-simon-6:
Simon Flexner is an American physician and pathologist born at Louisville, Kentucky, on March 25, 1863. He took his medical degree at the University of Louisville. He went on to study at Johns Hopkins and at Strasburg and Prague. He was once assistant professor of pathology at Johns Hopkins. By 1903 he held the same chair at the University of Pennsylvania. He has just been named head of the Rockefeller Institute of Preventive Medicine in New York.

Flexner served on a medical commission to the Philippine Islands in 1900. In 1901 he sat on the National Plague Commission. He belongs to many learned societies in America and abroad. His many papers deal chiefly with new research in pathology and bacteriology. One short source line, to Who's Who in America of 1902, closes the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-elkan-6:
Elkan Fränkel was a court Jew to the margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach from 1703 to 1712. He died in the state prison of Wülzburg in 1720. His family had been among the Vienna exiles of 1670. He is first mentioned in 1686 as a member of the Fürth community. There he took charge of the margrave's money interests. He became parnas of Fürth in 1704 and chief parnas of Ansbach in 1710.

Fränkel won the margravate's Jews a remission of a heavy fine in 1708. He also boasted of stopping a seizure of Hebrew books in 1702. Enemies used that boast against him, for his proud manner made him hated. In 1712 a converted Jew denounced him for blasphemous books and fraud. A partial inquiry found all charges true without proof. The margrave had him scourged in the market-place and jailed for life. His fortune was seized and his family expelled.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedmann-paul-:
Paul Friedmann was a German giver of good works, born at Berlin in the middle of the nineteenth century. He was of Jewish descent and kin to the family of Moses Mendelssohn. The fate of the Russian Jews after the attacks of 1882-90 troubled him much. In 1890 he visited the land of Midian and made up his mind to plant a colony there. He had a steam yacht built in Scotland for the plan. He went to Cracow to pick the first settlers.

In November 1891 twenty-four settlers sailed from Cairo under Friedmann and two Christian partners. They landed on the east side of the Gulf of Akabah. The colony broke up in less than two months. The Christian leaders quarreled with the Jews, and Egypt feared trouble with Turkish troops nearby. Friedmann had sunk 170,000 marks in the plan. He sued Egypt and printed a book on Midian in 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-galveston-6489:
Galveston, the chief trade city of Texas on the Gulf of Mexico, was founded in 1836. Its people numbered 32,745 in 1903. Jews settled there in 1840. First services met in 1856 at the home of Isadore Dyer. Congregation Bnai Israel, a Reform body, formed in 1868. Its temple, opened in 1870, later grew to seat 764 people.

A great storm struck on September 8, 1900. About 8,000 people died across the city. Forty-one Jews were among the dead. Temple Bnai Israel was one of few houses of worship left standing. Jews across the land sent 26,427 dollars to aid local sufferers. Galveston Jews also held city posts, and one served as mayor in 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geographers-658:
Geographers are those skilled in describing the surface of the earth. Jews have aided that science in sundry ways. In Bible times such knowledge came chiefly as birth lists, as in the table of nations in Genesis x. Jewish thought also put Jerusalem at the center of medieval maps. That habit grew from a plain reading of Ezekiel v. 5.

Benjamin of Tudela stands as the chief Jewish traveler of the Middle Ages. His notes add much on the Levant in the twelfth century. Jafuda Cresques of Palma made the Catalan map and helped found modern map making. Jews also played a large part in the finding of America and in the quest for a sea road to India.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-girth-of-the-ch:
Chest girth among Jews is measured here against stature, using figures gathered from recruiting officers and doctors in several countries. Goldstein had claimed that Jewish chest girth falls below half the stature, unlike most other races, and so marked a lesser "index of vitality." Tables in the entry cover 7,944 Jews, drawing on reports such as Snigiref's measurements of 6,592 Jews in Poland and Lithuania from 1875.

The entry argues that the low figures for young recruits mislead. A Jewish youth at twenty has not finished growing, and chest width keeps rising long after height stops. By ages forty to fifty, girth reaches 54.5 per cent of stature. The practical point drawn is that Jews are still undeveloped at the age when military service begins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grosser-julius-: Julius Grosser was a German physician. He was born at Freistadt, Prussian Silesia, on Oct. 25, 1835. He died at Prenzlau on Oct. 25, 1901, his birthday. Berlin University gave him his medical degree in 1859. In 1861 he set up practice at Prenzlau. He served as a surgeon in the Franco-Prussian war. That service won him the Iron Cross. In 1880 he founded the "Deutsche Medizinal-Zeitung." He edited it until his death and wrote for it and other medical journals. The entry is a short professional notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananiah-hanina:
Hananiah (Hanina) b. Teradion was a teacher and martyr of the second century. He lived at Siknin, where he ran a school ranked among the distinguished academies. He handled the communal charity funds with great scruple. Once his own Purim money chanced to mix with the charity funds. He distributed the whole amount among the poor. Few halakot survive from him.

During the Hadrianic persecutions he kept convening assemblies and teaching the Law. Jose b. Kisma warned him that Rome was upheld by God. Hananiah answered, "Heaven will have mercy on us." Arrested while teaching with a scroll before him, he replied, "I do as my God commands me." He was burned wrapped in the scroll. Wet wool was laid on his chest to prolong the pain. He told his disciples the power avenging the Law would avenge him too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hartog-edouard-:
Edouard de Hartog, born in Amsterdam on Aug. 15, 1826, was a Dutch composer. He trained with several teachers in Holland and Paris. In 1852 he settled in Paris and taught piano, harmony, and composition. His first opera waited years for a stage, reaching performance in 1868.

De Hartog won his name chiefly through orchestral works from 1857 and 1859. He wrote more operas, a setting of the Forty-third Psalm, string quartets, and pieces for many instruments. Honors came from Belgium and the Netherlands. He also helped add to a standard dictionary of musicians' lives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-abraham-: Abraham ben Judah ibn Hayyim was a Spanish scholar and scribe of the thirteenth century. He wrote a Spanish treatise on making gold foil and colors for small painted pictures. A second work, likely in Hebrew, dealt with the Masorah. It also treated the crowned letters found in a Torah scroll. Scholars named here disagree on whether he is the same man as a French liturgist of a like name. The entry leaves that question open and cites two Italian catalogs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ben-nath: Hayyim ben Nathan was a German scholar of the seventeenth century. He rendered the story parts of the Bible into Judeo-German. In his preface he says he worked from Luther's German version. To that he added tales from the Midrashim and the commentaries. The work came out about 1630, with later printings at Prague and Dyhernfurth. He also published "Sefer ha-Maasim," a Judeo-German version of the Apocrypha. The entry names no town or dates for his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilbronn-josep: Joseph ben Elhanan Heilbronn was a German Hebrew scholar who lived at Posen in the sixteenth century. Three of his works are listed. "Em ha-Yeled" is a first Hebrew grammar for children, with verb tables and German explanations. A second book sets out the 613 commandments in Maimonides' order. A third is a short Hebrew grammar for schools. The entry warns against mixing him up with a Joseph Heilbronn who died at Padua in 1622. They were not the same man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hladik-abraham-: Abraham Hladik was a Bohemian Talmudist who flourished about 1230. His name points to a Czech origin, the entry says. In his comment on penitential prayers he often explains Hebrew with Bohemian words. Yet Zunz held that he lived in France. He taught Hezekiah, son of Jacob, of Magdeburg. Manuscripts quote his rulings often. His customs for the whole year and a prayer comment also survive in manuscript. One scholar tries to identify him with another Abraham, author of a named work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horwitz-aryeh-l: Aryeh Lob ben Zebi Halevi Horwitz, known as Rabbi Lob Zietiler, was a Lithuanian Talmudist of the seventeenth century. He headed schools in several German towns. He was then called to head the school at Minsk while Jehiel Heilprin was chief rabbi there. His known book defends Maimonides. Margenita Taba answers Nahmanides' attacks on the Sefer ha-Mizwot and was printed with that work in 1756. A note in the preface says he also wrote Talmudic novellae and another defense of Maimonides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-ezra-moses-:
Moses ben Jacob ibn Ezra was a Spanish philosopher, linguist, and poet born at Granada about 1070. He died after 1138. He came from one of Spain's leading families and was a kinsman of Abraham ibn Ezra. A lost love for a niece who wed his brother left a sad tone in his verse and may have driven him from Granada.

His philosophy book treats God, man, and the intellect in seven chapters, citing Greeks and Arabs alike. Far greater is his book on rhetoric and poetry, the only work of its kind in Hebrew letters. It answers eight questions from a friend and sums up the literary life of Spanish Jewry. Poets rated his verse above even Judah ha-Levi's. His Tarshish ran to 1,210 lines.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-immanuel-siegmu:
Siegmund Solomon Jacob Immanuel was a German philologist born at Hamburg on September 4, 1792. He died at Minden on December 28, 1847. He embraced Christianity in 1809. He studied theology and philology at Helmstadt, Gottingen, and Leipsic, graduating in 1813. In 1821 he became principal of the gymnasium at Minden and held the post until death.

His school work mattered widely. He was the first principal to put gymnastics into the school plan, in 1831. In 1840 he split the gymnasium into arts and science tracks for the upper classes. Other German states later took up that split. His books treat the Reformation at Minden, classroom speaking, and history teaching. One opinion of his weighs in on health in schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-intermarriage-1:
Intermarriage, marriage between persons of different races or tribes, is barred with the Canaanites in Deut. vii. 3, for the stated reason that they would turn Israel's sons to other gods. The patriarchs had already forbidden it with Canaanites. From Ezra onward the ban was extended to all Gentiles, and Maimonides codified it so. Ammonites and Moabites drew a special ban; Idumean and Egyptian converts' offspring entered the congregation in the third generation.

Christian emperors and councils later banned such marriages under heavy penalties, Constantius in 339 under pain of death. The Great Sanhedrin of 1807 allowed marriages with Christians concluded under civil law. The entry ends with statistics: mixed marriages averaged about one child against three or four for Jewish marriages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ha-kohen-: Isaac ha-Kohen of Narbonne was a French Talmudist of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, a disciple of Abraham ben David of Posquières. He wrote a commentary on several treatises of the Jerusalem Talmud. That commentary no longer survives, but Isaac de Lattes and Menahem Me'iri both mention it. Gross identified him with the Isaac ha-Kohen whose rulings on ritual matters Aaron ha-Kohen often invokes in the "Orhot Hayyim." The entry is short and offers no dates from his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-bar-aha-8: Jacob bar Aha is the name of two Palestinian amorae in this entry. The first, of the third generation, was a contemporary of R. Ze'era. He rarely speaks for himself; mostly he repeats rulings and sermons in older men's names. In his name stands one warm reading: "Hide not thyself from thine own flesh" means a divorced wife, whom her former husband must still support. The second Jacob bar Aha, of the fourth generation, was a contemporary of Hezekiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacopo-jacomo-s: Jacopo Sansecondo, also written Jacomo, was an Italian musician born about 1468. He was an eminent violinist of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. In 1502 he played at the wedding of Lucrezia Borgia, a fact noted in Castiglione's Il Cortegiano. He held a prominent place at the court of Pope Leo X. The entry also reports that he was known as a handsome man and is said to have been the model for Raphael's Apollo on Parnassus, now in the Galleria Sciara at Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joachimsthal-fe: Ferdinand J. Joachimsthal was a German mathematician born on May 9, 1818, at Goldberg in Silesia. He took his doctorate at Berlin in 1842 and taught that year at a Berlin trade school. In 1846 the university there admitted him as a private lecturer. He became professor of mathematics at Halle in 1856 and at Breslau in 1858. His essays appeared in Crelle's Journal across many years and in a French math journal as well. He died at Breslau on April 5, 1861.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-ben-halaft:
Jose ben Halafta was a Palestinian tanna of the fourth generation, in the second century. He was born at Sepphoris to a family of Babylonian origin. He was one of the five main pupils of Akiba, called the restorers of the Law. After his ordination, which broke a Roman edict, he fled to Asia Minor. He later settled at Usha and then returned to Sepphoris, where he built a strong school and died.

His legal rulings fill much of the Mishnah, the Baraita, and the Sifra. He disliked disputes and often chose a middle path between rival views. He was known as the likely author of Seder Olam Rabbah, a chronicle from Creation to Hadrian. He worked as a tanner and prized the study of Torah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-solo: Joseph ben Solomon, called Joseph Darshan of Posen, was a German preacher born at Posen in 1601 who died there in 1696. As a youth he studied in Russia and was present in 1648 when the Chmielnicki massacres struck. He escaped to his home town and became its preacher in 1676. Three of his books came out in 1679, among them Yesod Yosef, against certain sins, and a set of psalms and prayers. Other works, sets of sermons and gathered notes, stayed unpublished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-juma-i-bala-908: Juma-i-Bala is a Turkish city on the Bulgarian frontier, four hours from Dubnitza. Its Jewish community dates from the middle of the eighteenth century and was once weighty and rich. When the rebel chief Pazvan-Oglu and his band rose against Sultan Salim III, the town's Jews had to pay the bandits a ransom of six thousand silver aspers. By 1902 the community was very poor and held no more than thirty families. It kept a small school, and services met in a house fitted out as a synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaidanover-aaro:
Aaron Samuel ben Israel Kaidanover was a Polish rabbi. He was also known as Samuel Kaidanover. He was born at Wilna in 1614. He died at Cracow on Dec. 1, 1676. During the Chmielnicki rising of 1648-49, Cossacks looted his goods. They took his library and his writings. They also killed his two young daughters. He reached Moravia as a poor refugee.

Kaidanover then served as rabbi in town after town. His posts included Nikolsburg, Glogau, and Fürth. He also served at Frankfort-on-the-Main. In time he returned to Poland. The entry lists his books. They include notes on Talmud tractates. They include sermons on the Pentateuch, with some cabalistic matter. Sixty rulings on marriage cases are also named. His son brought several of the books out after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaidanover-zebi:
Ẓebi Hirsch Kaidanover was a native of Wilna. He died at Frankfort-on-the-Main on March 23, 1712. His father was Rabbi Aaron Samuel Kaidanover. His teacher was Joseph ben Judah Jeidel of Minsk and Dubno. From that teacher he took a strong bent toward cabala. In law he followed his father's path more closely.

At Wilna a false charge put Kaidanover in prison with his whole family. He stayed in chains for years before he was pardoned. Fearing a second arrest, he settled at Frankfort. There he published his father's works, adding notes to some. He also wrote "Ḳab ha-Yashar," a book on morals. It mixes ethics with stern calls to a plain life. It first came out at Frankfort in 1705. Many later editions followed, one with his own Judæo-German version.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kanitz-august-9: August Kanitz was a Hungarian botanist. He was born on April 25, 1843, at Lugos. He died on July 12, 1896, at Klausenburg. As a student at Vienna he wrote a history of botany in Hungary. Later works cover the plants of Slavonia, Montenegro, Bosnia, Servia, and Rumania. The Rumania book won him a seat in the Academy of Sciences of Budapest. He also took a Rumanian order of knighthood. In 1872 he became professor of botany at Klausenburg. He founded a botany journal in 1877.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kletzk-9389:
Kletzk is a Russian town in the government of Minsk. It is believed to have been founded in the eleventh century. The earliest known mention of its Jewish community is dated 1522. In that year King Sigismund leased the town's inns to Isaac Jesofovitch, a Jew of Brest-Litovsk. A census of 1552-55 shows Jewish householders living chiefly on Wilna street. In 1670 the Jews of Kletzk were accused of murdering a baptized Jewess. Her body was never found.

Fires destroyed the town repeatedly in the nineteenth century. The large synagogue, built by Prince Radziwil in 1796, always escaped the flames. The town also keeps a bet ha-midrash fully two hundred years old. The philosopher Solomon Maimon lived at Kletzk for several years. In 1903 the town had a population of about 8,000. About 6,000 of them were Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kovner-saveli-g: Saveli Grigoryevich Kovner, a Russian physician born at Wilna in 1837, died at Kiev on Sept. 22, 1896. He graduated from the University of St. Vladimir at Kiev in 1865. Posts as city and county physician followed in Siberia and at Nezhin. From 1873 he led the Nezhin hospital. In 1879 he quit post work to give himself to science, settling at Kiev in 1890. His chief work is a three-volume history of ancient and medieval medicine dated 1879. One chapter covers medical practice among the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lambert-mayer-9: Mayer Lambert, a French Orientalist born on Dec. 23, 1863, at Metz, came from a line of chief rabbis. He studied at the Metz lycée, the Paris Talmud Torah, and the Séminaire Israélite. His rabbi diploma came in 1886. From 1887 he taught Arabic and Syriac at the Séminaire. Hebrew posts at Alliance and Séminaire schools followed. From 1886 to 1895 he worked closely with Joseph Derenbourg. His books give Hebrew grammars dated 1890 and 1900 and Saadia editions dated 1891 and 1894. Many journal pieces treat Hebrew stress, plurals, and syntax.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lamentations-85:
Lamentations holds five poems on the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., called Ekah in Hebrew copies after its first word. City, Temple, king, and people all suffer in its lines. The first poem lacks a clear line of thought and leans on sharp images of pain. The second poem is laid out in a far more ordered way.

Authorship takes up much of the entry. Tradition names Jeremiah, backed by a note in Chronicles and by rabbinic teaching. Critics answer with the book's place in the canon, its late verse forms, and clashes in its content. They spread the poems across decades, with Babylon as a likely home. Reading the book on the Ninth of Ab closes the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lazarus-moritz-:
Moritz Lazarus, a German philosopher born at Filehne in Posen on Sept. 15, 1824, died at Meran on April 13, 1903. Destined for trade, he left an apprenticeship for gymnasium and Berlin study from 1846 to 1849. Herbart's thought shaped him. His doctorate came in 1850.

Lazarus founded Völkerpsychologie, the study of the mind of peoples, in an essay of 1851 and a journal begun with Steinthal in 1860. Bern made him professor that year; Berlin followed in 1874. He led Berlin Jewish bodies for decades and fought the anti-Semitism rising from 1878. His Ethics of Judaism appeared in part in 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-letter-carriers:
Jewish letter-carriers delivered mail to Jews apart from the regular post. In big trade centers like Hamburg, Prague, Breslau, and Frankfort, Jews, and at times Jewesses, did this work under state control. One reason was plain: Christian carriers could not read addresses written in Hebrew. Jews also faced special postal laws.

The fullest records come from Breslau and Frankfort. At Breslau the Post-Jude is first named in a paper of Dec. 13, 1722, though the post was older. He took no oath and drew no salary. His pay was the postage handed over by each person who got a letter. The sums were so small that he needed a second trade. His wife could fill in when he was away.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-jacob-9889:
Jacob Levy, a German rabbi and dictionary maker, was born in May 1819 at Dabrzyze, Posen. He died at Breslau on Feb. 27, 1892. His father and Akiba Eger taught him Talmud. He studied philosophy and Oriental tongues at Breslau and took his doctorate at Halle in 1845.

Levy served as rabbi at Rosenberg until 1850, then moved to Breslau. In 1857 he became associate rabbi there. His Chaldaic dictionary of the Targums came out in 1867-68. His chief work is a four-volume dictionary of Talmud and Midrash, printed from 1876 to 1889. The entry calls him the first to use modern methods in rabbinic lexicography. All later work in that field rests on his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lima-moses-b-is: Moses ben Isaac Judah Lima was a Lithuanian rabbinical scholar, one of the later authorities called Aharonim.
