Identifying which identity gap tracks adaptation most closely tells universities where counseling and community support will do the most good for mobile students.
plos-pone-0349389:
Diana Yaneth Vargas and Fred Russell Kramer describe a lab test that can tell whether two mutations in the same gene sit on the same copy of a chromosome. It can also tell when they sit on opposite copies. That detail matters in lung cancer care, because a second change in a gene can make a targeted drug stop working. Their method uses two specially designed primers that only multiply DNA when both changes are present together on one strand.

Working with two well-known changes in the EGFR gene, the team showed the test stays silent when only one change is present or when the changes sit apart. The test is sensitive enough to guide an early switch to a better drug, and it can run on DNA from a simple blood sample using common lab machines.
plos-pone-0349489:
Kuenyoul Park, Joonsang Yu, Wonho Choe, and Soo Jin Yoo published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It evaluates blood collection tubes from a system called UNI-VAC, covering serum separator, EDTA, sodium citrate, and sodium fluoride types. The comparison benchmark is the widely used Vacutainer tubes from Becton, Dickinson and Company.

Tube choice can quietly shift laboratory results, since each additive preserves blood differently. A head-to-head evaluation tells hospital laboratories whether a newer supplier's tubes match the standard they trust. Laboratory managers weighing purchasing decisions, and clinicians who depend on comparable results, are the readers for this practical test.
plos-pone-0349589:
Android malware keeps mutating and hiding its code, so Vu Minh Manh, Cho Do Xuan, and Nguyen Thi Khanh Van built a detector that reads an app two ways at once. Their 2026 PLOS One framework, HybFusion, fuses behavior traces with permission meanings.

One branch maps how the app's functions call each other, learning the shape of its behavior. The other reads the permissions the app requests as a sentence, catching suspicious combinations. A stacked team of classifiers then votes on the combined picture. Wide testing showed stronger detection and fewer false alarms than single-view rivals, which the authors credit to the two views covering each other's blind spots.
plos-pone-0349689:
Anjana Maharjan and Shobha Laxmi Bajracharya surveyed one hundred twenty-nine caregivers at a Nepali teaching hospital who look after frail elderly relatives with mental disorders. Their 2026 study measured how caregivers cope and how heavy the burden feels, using Nepali versions of two standard questionnaires during face-to-face interviews.

Caregivers leaned on both problem-focused and emotion-focused coping. Nearly half reported little or no burden, but about fifteen percent felt a severe burden, split between personal strain and the strain of the role itself. Women, caregivers in nuclear families, and the employed carried significantly higher burden levels. Coping style and burden showed no firm statistical link, though problem-focused coping trended protective. The authors call for targeted counseling and support for the most pressed caregivers.
plos-pone-0349789:
Abdullah A Aljughaiman and colleagues traced how volatility shocks pass between Europes carbon trading market and stock markets in five emerging European economies. A quantile based model let shock strength differ in calm, falling, and booming conditions. Carbon price swings matter for firms that must buy pollution permits, so spillover strength guides portfolio choices.

Shocks ran far stronger in booming, high volatility states, where total connectedness neared ninety percent, versus about thirty percent in calm or falling states. Greece, Poland, and Hungary absorbed more carbon shocks, while Slovakia absorbed least in every state. Slovak shares thus act as a useful hedge when carbon markets turn wild, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0349889:
Francesca Bettio, Fernando Flores Tavares, and Elisa Ticci revisited a grim question from the pandemic: did violence between partners get worse under lockdown in Tuscany, Italy? They drew on a large phone survey run in twenty twenty-one, described as the only locally representative one of its kind in Italy. They also asked which pandemic shock mattered most, money trouble or being stuck at home.

Respondents said violence had, on balance, grown more frequent or more severe. Among the shocks, the strain of caring for children at home weighed heaviest, job loss came next, and crowding without privacy showed no clear effect. How violence was measured also changed the answers: a measure counting severity picked up effects a simple yes-or-no missed.
plos-pone-0350089:
Natalia Ioannou and Iliatha Papachristou Nadal interviewed midlife women in the United Kingdom living with type two diabetes in 2026. General studies blur how gender and life stage shape the illness, and midlife brings its own pile of roles and changes.

Thirteen women recruited through social media and a research panel spoke in depth online. Four themes covered the daily practical work of the condition, its emotional and social weight, its place in identity and relationships, and how women look ahead. The accounts show diabetes woven into work, family, and ageing, a fuller picture than blood sugar numbers alone give services.
plos-pone-0350289:
Aimee Haley, Alebachew Haybano, and Gun-Britt Wärvik outline in 2026 a review plan mapping research on what happens to doctoral graduates' careers in Africa. Little joined up evidence exists on whether graduates stay in universities or move elsewhere, and what helps or blocks each path. Four databases were searched for English peer reviewed work with no year limit.

Screening against set criteria will sort which studies count, and charting will cover theories used, methods used, and how far non academic careers appear. Conditions at system, institution, and personal levels are a special focus. University leaders could use the map to build better career support and spot research gaps.
plos-pone-0350389:
Mandy H M Chu, William K K Wu, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for a phase two trial of taurine supplements in healthcare workers. Taurine, a nutrient the body makes in small amounts, falls with age in animal studies, and restoring it improved metabolic health in those experiments. The planned trial will randomly assign about eighty workers to daily taurine or an identical placebo for six months, with patients, staff, and assessors all blinded.

The main question is whether more participants on taurine see their long-term blood sugar marker fall at all over six months. Secondary measures include blood fats, blood pressure, weight, a biological age estimate, and a skin marker of sugar damage. The design checks results at intervals and can stop early for success or futility. Findings will decide whether a larger trial is justified.
plos-pone-0350989:
Monalisa M J Faulkner and colleagues charted sickle cell disease in Sierra Leone from 1990 to 2023 in work published in 2026. The inherited blood disorder kills many African children, yet country level figures for this high burden nation were scarce.

Using global burden estimates, they tracked cases, deaths, and lost healthy years. Estimated cases nearly doubled over the period, and deaths rose too, even though the death rate for each age group fell. Population growth drove much of the rise. The split matters: clinics face more patients even as care slowly improves, so services must expand, not just improve.
plos-pone-0351189:
Marzieh Asadi and colleagues designed, entirely on a computer, a new test ingredient for a worm infection called strongyloidiasis. The parasite Strongyloides stercoralis is most dangerous for people with weak immune systems, and current blood tests miss cases or give false alarms. A sharper test could help doctors find infections earlier.

The team picked the most telling pieces of four parasite proteins and joined them into one fusion protein, choosing parts that react strongly but do not cross-react with other germs. Computer checks covered its shape, stability, and how well bacteria could be made to produce it, and they prepared the gene code for a standard lab vector. Lab testing would be the next step beyond this design study.
plos-pone-0351589:
Lingyao Sun and six colleagues published this study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. A protocol sets out a research plan before the work is done. Here the planned work is a systematic review, combined with a network meta-analysis, of treatments for adults with simple obesity.

The document explains how the team will search for trials, judge their quality, and compare many treatments against each other, including ones never tested head to head. Publishing the plan in advance keeps the later review honest and open to checking. Clinicians who treat obesity will be the main readers of the finished review this protocol describes.
plos-pone-0351689:
Mika Allyssa Esquillo and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One secondary analysis of guilt in sixty-one veterans with combat-related post-traumatic stress disorder enrolled in a clinical trial. The authors separated two kinds of guilt: guilt over one's own actions, and survivor guilt over living when others died, then tested how each relates to symptom severity and depression.

Both kinds of guilt independently predicted overall symptom severity. Action guilt alone predicted avoidance and emotional numbing, but that link ran substantially through depression, which carried part of its effect. The authors argue therapists should assess the two guilts separately, and that treating depression may be one route by which action guilt loosens its grip on the numbing symptoms of the disorder.
plos-pone-0351989:
Kora Tushune Godana and seven colleagues review what holds back Ethiopia's community health programme, in this 2026 PLOS ONE scoping review. Since 2003, health extension workers have carried basic preventive care into villages across the country. The reviewers gathered studies, government reports, and partner documents to map the obstacles at every level of the system.

One deep tension stood out: the programme offers prevention, while communities ask for treatment, which erodes trust. The mostly female workforce faces barriers in some cultural settings, and training, retention, and digital skills all lag. The authors recommend adding basic curative services, balancing the workforce, and improving workers' conditions before expecting better results.
plos-pone-0352089:
Touitou-Burckard and colleagues set out an expert consensus plan in 2026 on joined-up care for people with severe mental illness and physical disease. Such patients often fall between mental and physical services. Stakeholders from six European countries, including patients and relatives, will vote through up to three online rounds.

The aim is agreement on what good integrated care must include to last in real systems. Patients, families, clinicians, and officials rarely define best practice together, so this process builds the definition jointly. Agreed features can then guide services that treat mind and body in one plan rather than in competing silos.
plos-pone-0352189:
Donath Valerian and colleagues swabbed the furniture and fittings of Tanzania's national cancer institute, hunting for two families of drug-resistant bacteria. Cancer patients stay long in hospital and have weakened defenses, so germs waiting on bed rails and keyboards are a real threat. Two hundred forty-seven samples came from six kinds of surfaces, from sinks to nursing station tables.

About one surface in twelve carried MRSA, the resistant staph germ, and about one in four carried bacteria that defeat a wide family of antibiotics. Two species dominated the second group, and some isolates resisted nearly every drug tested, though all staph still answered to one reserve antibiotic. For a hospital serving highly vulnerable patients, the findings turn routine deep cleaning and hand hygiene from housekeeping into treatment.
plos-pone-0352589:
Chiodi and colleagues studied wheat fields shaded by solar panels in a 2026 field study. Pairing panels with crops lets one field yield both food and power, but shade changes the soil below. The team compared open sun with two panel layouts, one covering a small share of ground and one covering a much larger share.

Soil under the wider layout held more carbon, nitrogen, and key minerals than soil in open sun or under the sparse layout. Microbe communities in the soil also shifted with panel cover at two points in the season. The results suggest panel spacing shapes soil health, not just crop yield, so farm designs should weigh both outcomes together.
plos-pone-0352689:
George Allison and three colleagues automate a computer pipeline that estimates children's bone strength from CT scans, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The existing method predicts how much bending a child's thigh bone can bear, useful in bone-fragility care, but demands a trained operator clicking through many steps. Their Python application automates the process, including the fiddly job of marking anatomical landmarks, and packages everything into one contained tool.

Scans of sixty-nine children ran through both the old and new pipelines. The automatic landmarks landed almost exactly where human ones did, the strength results matched published experiments, and the whole job finished in about thirteen minutes instead of thirty-five. Automation of this kind is what lets a research method serve whole clinic cohorts.
plos-pone-0352889:
Dan Feng Huang and Dennis Tay present this 2026 PLOS One study on the distinctive style of translated language, using speeches from United Nations meetings as their test case. Translated text carries subtle fingerprints that differ from originally written text, and earlier classifiers could spot them without explaining how. The authors built a deep learning framework designed to reveal its own reasoning through a perturbation method that tests which features drive its decisions.

Their model separated translated from non-translated texts with strong accuracy. More importantly, the explanation step showed the decisions rested on style patterns deeper than surface word choice or sentence structure. The authors offer the framework as a proof of concept for other language studies where researchers need to know not just what a model decides, but why.
plos-pone-0353189:
Kouchaki and colleagues tracked recovery after traumatic brain injury in a registry study in a 2026 paper. Nearly three thousand survivors were scored at hospital discharge and again six months later. Change was classed as recovering, stable, or slipping back, then linked to early clinical, lab, and scan factors.

Movement in both directions was common after discharge, so a single early score misleads. Some early factors predicted which path a patient would take, even within the same discharge score group. Families and rehab teams can plan better when likely paths are known, and follow-up visits can target those at risk of slipping back.
plos-pone-0353389:
Paige Copeland and colleagues charted, hour by hour, how eating cannabis affects thinking and movement. Edible cannabis is common, yet the timing of its effects was poorly mapped. Their 2026 study gave fifteen infrequent users a standard dose and ran a test battery eleven times across six hours, with some repeating the session drug-free.

Users felt drug effects from the first hour through the sixth. Reaction time slowed across that same span. Accuracy on a response-control task dropped from about ninety minutes onward, and short-term memory performance dipped for several hours. Heart rate and blood pressure rose in the middle window. Copeland and colleagues identify three to four hours after eating as the peak testing window.
plos-pone-0353489:
Francis Okyere and Michael Nyanney published this 2026 statistics study of breast cancer risk models built from tumor measures in a classic Wisconsin data set. They compared three penalized regression methods that shrink or drop predictors, judging not only accuracy but whether repeated samples keep choosing the same tumor features.

All three separated cancer from non-cancer almost perfectly, and more honest risk scores than plain regression. Ridge kept every feature steadily, lasso was sparse but jumpy, and elastic net balanced both. Okyere argues stability checks belong in medical prediction, not accuracy alone.
plos-pone-0353689:
Liu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, untangle the two-way link between thinking ability and depressive symptoms in older British adults, with physical activity in the middle. Earlier work showed each can worsen the other, but not the order of events or the mechanism. The team used a national aging study that measured the same people three times across about five years.

Nearly seven thousand adults aged fifty and over took part. Thinking and mood each predicted the other at the next wave, in a negative loop: weaker thinking foretold worse mood, and worse mood foretold weaker thinking. Thinking was the stronger driver of the pair. Activity carried a small part of the effect: weaker thinking led to less activity, which then led to worse mood. The authors suggest that keeping older adults moving may soften one path from cognitive decline into depression.
plos-pone-0353789:
Shao, Gao, and Sun modeled greener delivery of fresh farm goods at varied temperatures in a 2026 study. Foods needing different cold levels often travel in separate trucks, wasting space and fuel. Their model plans routes and three-dimensional truck loading together, aiming to cut both cost and carbon output.

A hybrid search method mixing two classic techniques solved the plan efficiently. Tested on real data from a fresh goods supply firm, joint delivery cut running costs by about three tenths and carbon output by a similar share versus separate delivery. The savings show that sharing trucks across temperature needs can pay, when loading is planned with care.
plos-pone-0353989: Li and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how stock markets react to drug policy news in China. Reactions were not uniform: they varied across drug industry subsectors and across time scales. A policy that lifts one branch, like vaccine makers, may dent another. Investors and policy makers alike benefit from knowing which parts of the sector move, and for how long.
plos-pone-0354089:
Katrin Kochems and a Dutch team merged two separate palliative care tools into one shared working method. They then tested how to get twenty care teams actually using it. Their study ran from 2020 to 2022 and appeared in 2026. It covered primary care practices, hospices, and nursing homes. Nurses, doctors, and other professionals adjusted the method through three rounds of trial and feedback.

Teams found the shared method workable and welcome. They said it helped them spot palliative needs earlier. It kept care centered on the person, and it gave nurses a stronger voice in planning. Fourteen content changes came out of the trials. The study shows how merging rival tools, with the users in the room, can improve end-of-life care teamwork.
plos-pone-0354489:
Nian and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a review of what women should be allowed to eat and drink during labor. For decades, many hospitals kept laboring women fasting, fearing food might enter the lungs under anesthesia. Modern anesthesia has made that event rare, while fasting can leave women hungry, thirsty, and worn out. Guidelines now disagree.

The planned review will search a wide set of English and Chinese databases for trials that compare ways of managing oral intake in labor. A network method will rank the options against each other, even ones never tested head to head. Outcomes include how birth happens, newborn health scores and blood sugar, and mothers' comfort, thirst, and satisfaction. Two reviewers will screen and rate the studies separately. As a protocol, the paper sets out the plan and questions; the answers will come when the review itself is done.
plos-pone-0354589:
Zuo and colleagues report a 2026 review of past cases of a rare, benign bone tumor in the upper arm of children. The tumor, called chondroblastoma, was treated at one center over ten years. Care used scraping out the tumor, heat treatment of the cavity walls, and packing the space with bone graft.

Seventeen young patients were followed for at least seven years after surgery. One child needed a second operation when the tumor came back. More than half saw the treated arm end up a bit shorter than the other, and this was more common in younger children. Even so, arm and shoulder function scores stayed good in both groups. The authors present the method as a sound option, while warning that return of the tumor and uneven growth remain real risks.
plos-pone-0354689:
Ping Zou led a team of seven authors on this 2026 pharmacy study building a two-speed painkiller tablet. Ketorolac is a strong pain reliever whose effect fades fast, forcing frequent doses. Their tablet-in-tablet design wraps a slow-release core in a fast-dissolving outer layer, tuned through systematic formulation experiments.

The finished pill released about a third of its dose within half an hour for quick relief, then kept releasing past ninety percent over a full day. Zou presents the design as a practical way to stretch strong pain relief without extra pills.
plos-pone-0354889:
Mohammed Kebede and five colleagues published this 2026 community study of parents in Dire Dawa, eastern Ethiopia, who treated their children with traditional medicine during COVID-19. Nearly a thousand parents answered surveys, and interviews explored how families learn, prepare, store, and dose herbal remedies, and why they hide that use from health workers.

Almost nine in ten parents had used traditional remedies for their children, usually alongside clinic medicine, and almost none told health staff, fearing blame. Kebede urges stronger traditional medicine policy and open conversation instead of silence that can endanger children.
plos-pone-0354989:
Marina Treskova led a team of eight authors setting out a trial protocol in rural Thailand, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Diseases that jump from animals to people, called zoonotic diseases, pose a daily risk where families live close to livestock. The Saan Suk trial will test an education program tailored to each community, built on One Health ideas.

Treskova's protocol describes a cluster randomized trial in Chanthaburi province, comparing villages that receive the tailored teaching with those that do not. Outcomes cover both knowledge and daily practices. Local tailoring is the bet: generic leaflets rarely change habits. If the trial shows real change, its design can guide zoonotic prevention across rural Southeast Asia.
plos-pone-0355189:
Laura Henry, Julie S Wilson, Jason J Wilson, and Esther R Beck map what exercise programs for breast cancer survivors actually contain, focusing on the arm swelling that can follow treatment. Activity is advised in survivorship care, yet fear of worsening the swelling keeps many women inactive, and program details vary wildly. The review gathered dozens of primary studies across five databases plus grey sources.

Most programs were controlled trials built around resistance training, commonly running about three months under supervision. Participants had usually had armpit node surgery, radiation, or both. Henry and colleagues chart how swelling was measured and where programs were delivered, exposing gaps in reporting and variety. Their map gives designers a base for building programs survivors can trust.
plos-pone-0355289:
Perpetual Arthur and co-authors interview in 2026 traditional medicine practitioners in Ghana who often see women first with breast concerns. These healers work outside formal services yet hold strong community trust. Talks explored how they learned their craft, what they believe causes breast cancer, which signs they watch for, and how they judge a case.

Healers mixed inherited knowledge with workshops and some contact with formal medicine, and they named key signs such as lumps and nipple changes. False beliefs about spiritual causes and reliance on feel and intuition risked missed or wrong calls. Training and referral links could turn their reach into earlier detection, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0355389:
Kittipan Tharakhet and colleagues test in 2026 a messenger RNA vaccine in mice aimed at all four types of dengue virus at once. Four distinct types make dengue hard to vaccinate against, since protection must cover each one. Their design blends parts of a viral protein from every type into one shared version, packed into tiny fat droplets for delivery.

Even a low dose raised antibodies that recognised the protein from all four types. Immune cells also reacted to pieces from several types, though each single type response was weaker than a focused vaccine might give. The authors see the shared design as a useful addition to future dengue vaccines.
plos-pone-0355489:
Leanna Silva Aquino and co-authors probed health care access in Quilombola towns in the Santarém part of the Brazilian Amazon. Quilombola towns were founded by Afro-Brazilian forebears who fled slavery. Brazil vows care for all, but rivers, miles, and want ration it in fact. Their 2026 survey asked five hundred twelve adults in nine rural and riverside towns.

Five forecast models, from tree-based to shrunk regressions, were ranked on how well they foresaw self-reported access. Layered models and part-picking tools split the roles of self, clinic, and land. Aquino and colleagues pair machine learning with plain stats to show which walls bind most, so policy can aim at Amazon facts, not state-wide means.
plos-pone-0355689:
Nuri Peker and colleagues examined what becomes of IVF embryos that fertilize in an odd way. These embryos show one or three pronuclei instead of the normal two. The patients had no normal embryos to use. Their 2026 study tracked fifteen hundred eggs' worth of outcomes at a fertility center. It compared blastocyst formation, genetic test results, and pregnancy across the normal and abnormal groups.

Abnormal embryos reached the blastocyst stage less often for the one-pronucleus group. Every genetically tested abnormal blastocyst came back chromosomally abnormal. So none was transferred on test results. A handful of untested transfers followed, yielding a single pregnancy from a combined transfer. The data counsel great caution. Abnormal fertilization rarely means a usable embryo, and genetic screening is decisive.
plos-pone-0355989:
Charleen Silcock and co-authors heard Pacific people with Parkinson's in Aotearoa New Zealand, plus their kin. Few brain ills are spreading faster than Parkinson's. Yet Pacific voices on it were near absent. Their 2026 study used talanoa, a Pacific way of learning through shared talk, with Pacific staff in the lead.

One big picture held the talks: life with the illness as a trip the whole kin group takes as one. Folks told of first signs, daily care, and help sought, all through that trip lens. The team took findings back to the group to plan next steps. Silcock and colleagues say care must be built with Pacific kin, not just sold to them.
plos-pone-0356389:
Marie Anne El Khoury led a team of six authors validating a psychology scale in Arabic, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fear of happiness is the belief that joy invites disaster, a real pattern that is under-studied in Arabic-speaking populations. The team tested the scale's Arabic version with a sample of adults in Lebanon.

El Khoury's psychometric work checks whether the translated scale measures the trait steadily and truly. A validated tool lets researchers study how this fear relates to depression and daily choices in Lebanon and beyond. Translation alone is not enough; beliefs about emotion differ across cultures, so local testing matters. The study gives Arabic-language mental health research a firmer instrument.
plos-pone-0356689:
Roberta Z J McGuinness, Nichole Fairbrother, and Fiona L Challacombe published a review protocol on anxiety around childbirth, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Perinatal anxiety affects many mothers, and it does not always fade after delivery; for some it lasts for years. Their protocol sets out a systematic review and combined analysis of its long-term course.

McGuinness and her colleagues published the plan in advance, defining what studies count and how results will be merged. That advance plan keeps the later synthesis rigorous and open to checking. Clinicians who screen new mothers need to know how long anxiety can persist to plan follow-up. A sound synthesis will show whether services should extend support well beyond the first months.
plos-pone-0356789:
Issued by the PLOS One staff in 2026, this short notice corrects an earlier study of hepatitis B reactivation during lymphoma treatment. The patients in that study had both surface antigen and viral DNA tests negative. It fixes a results table, removes a duplicated percent sign from treatment-duration data, and replaces several sentences in the abstract and results with their correct wording.

The corrected text states that reactivation rates did not differ significantly by patient gender or by how long treatment lasted. Readers who cite the original study should use these corrected figures. The underlying clinical question matters for doctors deciding how closely to monitor lymphoma patients for a hepatitis B flare during therapy.
plos-pone-0356889:
Fei Meng and colleagues present ASWBoost, a strengthened version of the classic AdaBoost classification algorithm, aimed at messy real-world data where examples are noisy and one class vastly outnumbers the other. Their 2026 paper modifies the penalty function that decides how hard the algorithm pushes on hard examples, adding a tunable parameter that softens the pull of likely mislabeled outliers.

New update rules follow from that change, and the authors prove bounds on training error and analyze how the parameter shapes convergence. Across synthetic and public datasets, ASWBoost beat AdaBoost and several other boosting variants on balanced accuracy and related measures, matching a leading commercial-grade method overall. Fraud detection and medical screening are typical tasks where such stubborn, lopsided data is the norm.
plos-pone-0356989:
Charlotte Verbeke and seven colleagues surveyed people living with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer, and the professionals who treat them, across several countries in late 2023. Their 2026 study asked how much patients know about shared decision-making, how involved they currently feel in treatment choices, and how involved they want to be.

Nearly every patient wanted a say in treatment decisions, and patients reported feeling more involved at recent appointments than at diagnosis. Yet over half of patients, and more than a quarter of professionals, had never heard of shared decision-making as a concept. No personal trait predicted who wanted involvement. The gap is practical, the authors argue: willingness is there on both sides, but clinics need routines that turn willingness into real conversations.
plos-pone-0357089:
Sanchit Vashisht, Shalli Rani, and Fazlullah Khan wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on road safety. It presents TRIDENT-Risk, an AI-driven framework for forecasting high-severity accident risk before crashes happen. The system is a temporal ensemble, combining several models whose inputs unfold over time, built for intelligent transportation systems.

Forecasting severe crashes, rather than all accidents, targets the events that kill and maim. City traffic centers could use advance risk warnings to adjust signals, patrols, or speed limits at dangerous hours. Transport authorities and smart-city engineers are the audience for a proactive system of this kind.
plos-pone-0357289:
Chenxiao Yue led a team of six authors comparing two ways of looking at the world, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. We scan scenes freely when browsing, but hunt in a focused way when searching for something. The team used eye tracking to compare free viewing with goal-directed search and their effects on visual attention.

Yue's gaze patterns reveal precisely how purpose reshapes seeing: where eyes land first, how long they linger, and what they skip. Designers of displays, advertisements, and safety signs all depend on such knowledge. Search behavior also matters for training, from radiology to baggage screening, where missing a target has costs. The study offers clean basic evidence on a skill humans use every waking hour.
plos-pone-0357589:
Frederick Grinnell, Simon Dalley, and Joan Reisch published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on what high school science fair students actually do to communicate their research. National science standards treat communicating information as a core practice, yet nobody had mapped how fair participants use it. They surveyed students nationally across two school years, asking which of seven communication activities, from keeping a notebook to facing judges, their projects involved.

Nearly eighteen hundred answered. Poster preparation was the most common activity, used by about two-thirds, while only about one in six had done a literature review. Students reported three skills on average. Poster boards and judge interviews were picked far more often than notebooks and literature reviews, the quieter work behind a project. Students using more communication skills reported better fair outcomes, the research notebook standing out. The pattern suggests fairs reward showmanship over documentation, a gap teachers could close.
plos-pone-0357789:
Abdulah J Alqahtani led a team of eight authors tracking drug-resistant staph in Saudi Arabia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Staphylococcus aureus that resists methicillin is a standing threat in hospitals. The team reviewed lab isolates from the Aseer region across the years 2013 to 2024, a span of more than a decade.

Alqahtani's retrospective study charts how resistance and non-susceptibility to other drugs moved over time. Clinicians choosing antibiotics need exactly this local trend data, since national averages can mislead. Rising resistance argues for tighter prescribing and infection control; stable trends show where current policy works. A long record from one region gives Saudi health officials a firm base for their next steps.
plos-pone-0357889:
Thomas E Diaz and three colleagues hunted for radiation protection among existing drugs, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Astronauts face cosmic radiation that raises cancer and other risks, and developing new drugs takes decades. The team used bioinformatics to reposition approved drugs, screening them for protective potential against space radiation.

Diaz's computational screen searches among medicines whose safety is already known. A hit could move toward testing far faster than a new compound. Space agencies need such options as missions aim for the Moon and Mars, where radiation exposure grows. Repositioning also suits rare Earth uses, such as protecting staff in nuclear incidents. The study lays out candidates and a method others can extend.
plos-pone-0357989:
Yuan Ding led a team of five authors studying a plant compound and joint cartilage, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The compound, isoquercitrin, comes from plants and belongs to a group known for protective effects in cells. The team studied worn cartilage cells, the kind that fail in osteoarthritis.

Ding's group found that the compound eased cell dysfunction by acting on a protein called AKT1 and on how the cells manage their mitochondria, their energy centers. Healthier cartilage cells in the lab mark the compound as a candidate worth further testing. Osteoarthritis has few drugs that slow it, so even early cell-level leads draw interest from researchers hunting for gentler options.
plos-pone-0358589:
Reinhard Fuchs leads a team of eight testing a hands free way to measure blood flow during resuscitation, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Chest compressions vary in quality, yet rescuers have no easy meter for the blood those compressions actually move. The group mounted an ultrasound Doppler probe on a standard neck collar, using an inflatable cushion to hold steady pressure, aiming for semiautomatic readings without a free hand.

One hundred two healthy volunteers wore the device for about half an hour on average. Pain ratings were very low, support ratings near the top of the scale, and no skin irritation appeared. Clear Doppler sounds were captured in over ninety percent of volunteers, and usable flow curves in about three quarters. The study is an early usability step toward feedback that could tell rescuers whether their compressions are working.
plos-pone-0358689: Buffardi and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on housing as a route to better health. As a scoping review, it maps policy actions that aim to improve health by changing homes or housing access. The map shows what kinds of programs exist and where evidence is thin. Housing shapes health through damp, cold, crowding, and cost, so a clear map helps funders choose wisely.
plos-pone-0358789:
Sophie Merrick leads a team of eight listening to kidney cancer patients who took immune therapy after surgery, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The interviews sit inside RAMPART, a large international trial testing whether checkpoint inhibitors after kidney removal can stop the cancer returning. Standard quality of life questionnaires predate this drug class. So the team interviewed twenty-three UK participants, chosen to span good and bad treatment experiences. They wanted to learn what the therapy actually does to a life.

Two themes organized their accounts. The first was living in a changed body and mind, as immune side effects altered energy, gut, and mood. The second was context: the same side effect landed differently depending on a person's work, family, and stage of life. How long effects lasted weighed heavily with participants. The study argues that trial measurement must catch duration and life context, not just symptom checklists.
plos-pone-0358989: Aji and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tiny zinc oxide particles made in a greener way. The particles are meant to help waxy crude oil keep flowing. Wax can thicken oil and clog pipes as it cools. The team made the particles and described their traits in detail. Flow helpers made sustainably could cut the cost and waste of keeping oil moving.
plos-pone-0359089: Tian and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on forecasting the course of acute pancreatitis. Pancreatitis is a sudden, painful swelling of the pancreas that can turn deadly. The team tested two blood-based scores: one built from glucose and fat levels, the other a ratio tied to inflammation and nutrition. They asked how well each predicts severity and death within twenty-eight days.
plos-pone-0360189:
Innocent Ayesiga, David Tenywa, and Moses Ntaro wrote this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a scoping review of how facilities across sub-Saharan Africa's health services run their systems for reporting workplace hazards and incidents. A scoping review maps what systems exist and what is known about them.

Health workers face needle injuries, infections, and violence at work, yet incidents often go unreported where systems are weak. Mapping reporting systems first shows where evidence and practice stand before deeper reviews follow. Hospital safety officers and African health ministries are the audience for this groundwork on protecting staff.
pmc-10671589:
Anja Feldmann and co-authors use targeted tiny carriers to dissolve calcium deposits in pig heart valves in two thousand twenty-three. Hardened aortic valves narrow the heart's outlet, and surgery is the only care for the final stage. A drug that binds calcium can clear the deposits, but free drug harms living cells.

The team bound that drug to protein-based carriers and tagged them with an antibody that seeks elastin in the valve. Deposits grown in the lab over five days shrank under the targeted carriers at a low drug dose. Plain drug at like doses hurt cell survival, while the targeted form did not. Control carriers without the tag cleared far less. The work is a step toward drug care for valve hardening.
pmc-10696789:
Mingqi Wang and colleagues published a large cohort study in 2023. They compared early and late onset type two diabetes. Early onset means diagnosis before age forty. A population database supplied the patient records. Over six hundred thousand patients were included overall. The team compared traits and disease burden carefully. Disease progression was tracked over time as well. Blood sugar control at diagnosis drew special attention.

Early onset patients showed poorer sugar control overall. Their blood sugar readings were higher at diagnosis. Insulin was prescribed to them more often too. The pattern suggests a more aggressive disease course. Younger patients may accumulate complications over longer lives. Health systems often plan around older patients instead. The findings argue for earlier, stronger intervention. Long-term burden could fall if control improves early.
pmc-10700489:
Weiyin Zhou and a large team survey in 2023 patchy chromosome changes in the blood of African children. Such mosaic changes, where some cells carry altered chromosomes, are linked to blood cancer risk in rich countries but barely studied in Africa. The team tested children with and without Burkitt lymphoma, plus adult men in Ghana.

Mosaic changes appeared in about 3 percent of healthy children and 8 percent of those with the lymphoma. In the cancer cases they often involved gains on chromosomes 1 and 8, the latter covering the MYC gene central to this cancer. Among Ghanaian men, 14 percent carried such changes, rising with age. The authors flag the topic for more study.
pmc-10701589:
Karin Fieten and co-authors measure allergy sensitization in children raised in the Swiss Alps, long assumed to be a low-allergen refuge. Their study appeared in 2023. The team collected questionnaires, house dust samples, and lifetime pollen and pollution exposure from national monitors, then profiled each child's sensitivities with a component-level blood test. Sensitization to airborne allergens proved common anyway, at thirty-eight percent, led by grass at a third of children and cat at sixteen percent.

Dust mite allergen turned up in over a third of homes, yet mite sensitization was rare, at two and a half percent. The authors say alpine air does not spare children from sensitization, though the pattern differs from lowland cities, and exposure alone does not explain who reacts.
pmc-10704089:
Zheng, Koyama, and Mertz improved HiLo microscopy in twenty twenty-three, a method for crisp optical sectioning with fluorescence microscopes. HiLo combines one evenly lit image and one lit with laser speckle to slice a sample optically. Speckle leaves residual noise that is hard to control, though the method resists optical flaws well.

Their fix applies non-local means denoising, which averages similar speckle grains to clean the image without blurring detail. A z-splitter prism lets one camera capture nine focal planes at once, adding multiplane imaging. Tests used synthetic data plus live imaging of heart and brain activity in zebrafish larvae at forty frames per second. The authors offer the setup as a simple tool for fast volumetric imaging in many labs.
pmc-10706389:
Jun Wang and four co-authors show how the liquid used to extract mushroom sugars changes what those sugars can do. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. The mushroom is the straw mushroom, eaten widely in Asia, and its long sugar chains have many uses in food.

The team pulled the sugars out with plain water, with an alkali, or with citric acid. Water gave the heaviest chains and the thickest, stretchiest extracts. The acid extract held water best, foamed well, and mixed oil and water smoothly. It also most strongly blocked two enzymes that break down starch and sugar, a trait tied to blood sugar control. The alkali extract held oil best. Choosing the liquid, the authors say, tunes the product.
pmc-10708189:
Angela Mitchell and nine co-workers tracked guard cell marks in blood DNA as at risk men and women moved toward type 1 diabetes. T cells that hit the body's own cells that make insulin drive the ill. Each T cell bears its own mark, and ill tied marks have been logged. The team hunted near 1,700 known germ bound marks in blood bits kept past years. At risk cases that moved on, matched controls, and fresh ill cases were set side by side.

Virus bound marks showed up in all at all ages. Islet bound marks piled up in split ways by which food mark they knew. A set of 73 islet marks was more plain and more rich in ill bits than controls. More of them linked with a young age at the ill's start. The 2023 finds back cell marks as signs to foretell this ill.
pmc-10708389:
Xinyan Fang and co-authors dial in the fertilizer mix that grows the best chrysanthemums by way of soil microbes, in a 2023 study. Nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium steer plant growth, but their route through the root-zone community was murky. Field plots varied the three nutrients while the team tracked plant uptake, soil chemistry, and bacterial diversity across the season.

One recipe, the heaviest nitrogen with moderate phosphorus and potassium, grew plants ten to forty percent larger on several measures. It also enriched the microbe community most. Mapping showed the nutrients reshaped the soil largely by reshaping its microbes. The authors frame feeding the crop as gardening the underground workforce, not just feeding the plant.
pmc-10710189:
Yan-Hua Sha and a large team mapped tiny circular RNA molecules released by kidney cells under high sugar, in a study from twenty twenty-three. These rings are stable and ride in small packets cells shed, called exosomes. They have been tied to diabetic kidney disease, but their role in the kidney's tubule cells was not fully known.

Cells fed high sugar shed more exosomes than normal cells. Hundreds of the rings rose or fell in those packets. Lab tests on a handful of them showed they could reverse high sugar's effects on swelling and scarring signals in the cells. Their parent genes cluster in sugar, fat, and inflammation pathways, all central to the disease.
pmc-10711589:
Melisa Zisan Karslioglu, Afsun Sahin, and Orkun Muftuoglu followed healing after a simple needle procedure for a painful eye condition in which the cornea surface repeatedly tears loose. Writing in twenty twenty-three, they treated a series of patients whose most common cause was prior eye injury. A special microscope that images living tissue at cell level was used on the treatment day and at set points over six months. The team also tracked symptoms, repeat procedures, and complications.

The surface layer closed within a week. Immune and repair cells rose early, nerve fibers showed bead-like changes, and by six months a scar remained while surface cells and nerves looked normal again. Most eyes ended symptom free, though some needed the procedure a second or third time. The authors call the treatment safe, practical, and low cost.
pmc-10713789:
Flavio Del Santo and Nicolas Gisin propose, in a 2023 philosophy of physics paper, an interpretation that treats potentialities as real parts of the world. On their view, every event carries an inborn tendency to happen, and those tendencies exist alongside the properties things actually show. Physics, classical or quantum, then stays realistic while remaining truly open-ended.

Their tendencies are not plain probabilities at the formal level, though they still yield normal statistics in bulk. The authors argue that famous quantum puzzles, like the measurement problem, are not quantum at all. Any theory with built-in chance faces them. The view thus aims to heal the classical-quantum split.
pmc-10716389:
Buys and Zambidis review how engineered myeloid cells could serve as precise immune therapies. Granulocytes and macrophages form the innate system's front line. They kill germs and tumors and help steer later immune responses. When these cells vanish, as in newborn sepsis or after chemotherapy, infection risk soars. Beyond simple replacement, tailored cells could carry drugs to inflamed sites. Neutrophils home to inflammation by nature, a trait therapy could exploit.

Cells could also bear tumor-targeting receptors or boost killing of blood cancers. The catch is supply: these cells live briefly and are hard to harvest in bulk. Lab-grown progenitors offer a way around that limit. The review weighs promise against that practical hurdle.
pmc-10717189:
Max Ferguson and co-authors study who survives opioid overdoses in British Columbia, Canada. Overdose deaths rose sharply after the pandemic began in the province. Harm reduction sites took surveys in 2018, 2019, and 2021 from their clients. The analysis held 1,447 people who said yes or no to a recent overdose.

About twenty-two percent had overdosed in the prior six months. The share rose from eighteen percent in 2019 to twenty-seven percent in 2021. Men faced higher odds than women, and unstable housing raised odds a great deal. Survey year 2021 alone tripled odds next to 2019. Links with stimulant overdose and seeing an overdose faded over the years. The authors urge swift policy action.
pmc-10726089:
Abhimanyu Singh, Vaibhav Anjankar, and Bhagyesh Sapkale review how obsessive-compulsive disorder is diagnosed, which other conditions it appears with, and how it is treated. The disorder brings back unwanted thoughts and repeated acts that can badly disrupt daily life. It affects adults, children, and teens, and it is often missed or poorly treated. The review sets out why diagnosis is hard and what care looks like today.

The authors note that many patients do not respond well to standard drug or talk therapy, which pushes interest in other options, such as higher doses or combined treatment. The disorder also overlaps often with bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. That overlap hints at shared roots and makes diagnosis harder still. The review closes by arguing that new treatment methods and more research are needed, since many people still live with chronic symptoms.
pmc-10727689:
Bethan Hughes and her team sift how day-night life traits may set if drugs that free the self-attack check can work well for sick folk with tumours. Their 2023 review takes in day rounds in sleep, food, sport, and light.

These check-free drugs changed tumour care, yet lots of sick folk still gain less than they hoped. Trials found time and time again that the hour of the day when a drug is given sways ends. The body clock rules lots of self-attack work, both in a straight way and through when life acts fall. Germs in the gut may pass life trait acts on to the self-attack kit as well. The team joins proof from care and from lab tests to put forth timed life acts for each one. Good time picks could lift ends by a good tune of self-attack work.
pmc-10729089:
Lavergne and co-authors set out a protocol to study the growing paperwork load on family doctors in Canada. Many Canadians struggle to get primary care, while providers report record stress. More doctors per person has not meant easier access to care. One suspect is the shift of tasks from hospitals to primary care teams. Rising administrative duties may also eat into clinic time.

The mixed-method study starts by tracking how service volume changed in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Numbers and interviews will combine to trace what drives the load. The team aims to name fixable causes of reduced access. Findings should inform reforms for strained primary care systems.
pmc-10729189:
Yixin Wei and co-authors set out a plan for reviewing whether gentle brain stimulation over one motor area helps people with Parkinson's disease. Patients often struggle with starting movements, slowness, poor balance, and standing problems. Two stimulation methods, one using magnetic pulses and one using weak electric current, are widely tried, and the supplementary motor area is a promising target. Results so far are mixed and have never been gathered in one place.

The protocol describes a systematic search of five databases for randomized trials comparing real stimulation with sham treatment. Two reviewers will screen studies, judge their quality with a standard scale, and extract results on movement, daily activities, and participation. The finished review is meant to settle how well the approach works.
pmc-10729289:
Rene Cheung and co-authors checked whether the length of a bright band in the outer retina, seen on eye scans, can be measured reliably and means anything clinically. Such bands break up in many retinal diseases, but no easy, trusted scoring method existed. The team studied six hundred patients at a Sydney eye clinic.

Two graders using magnitude estimation agreed well with themselves and each other. Band length shrank with age and varied with refractive error and, in places, with eyesight quality. Glaucoma seemed linked at first pass, but the link vanished once other factors were weighed. The authors say the measure is reliable and may stand in for visual acuity, provided readings are adjusted for the factors that sway it.
pmc-10735489:
Xiang Qi and Bei Wu wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It asks how much dementia could be prevented by fixing poor oral health, using a large national survey of older Americans followed for a decade.

The study covered 15,474 adults aged fifty and up who started with intact thinking. Losing all one's teeth raised dementia risk by roughly a third in both men and women. About 4.6 percent of new dementia cases were attributable to tooth loss, a bigger share than hearing loss or high blood pressure in this analysis. In a smaller group with detailed dental data, broader oral problems carried an attributable share near twelve percent in men, second only to low education. The authors argue oral health belongs in dementia prevention policy.
pmc-10735589:
Hua and seven colleagues link assisted living rules and traits to who gets admitted or discharged in twenty twenty-three. Data covered two hundred fifty communities in seven states, matched to a rule database. Three daily tasks anchored the checks: bathing, rising from bed, and eating. Admission and discharge habits were modeled against rules and community traits.

Looser license types went with looser admission practice, though not past doubt in joint models. Communities heavy on Medicaid payers admitted fewer residents with bathing needs. Ties to nursing homes raised discharge odds for bathing and feeding needs. The authors ask if practice fits resident needs well enough.
pmc-10736489:
Yuval Palgi, Ehud Bodner, and Dikla Segel-Karpas introduce a symposium on the benefits of chosen solitude in later life, in a 2023 summary. Positive solitude means picking time alone and enjoying it, rather than suffering loneliness. The session gathers new theory and findings on this capacity in the second half of life.

Five talks make up the session. One sets out the theory and a new scale for measuring positive solitude. Another shows how calming emotions through music links mindfulness to enjoying alone time. A diary study of couples finds that one partner's chosen solitude goes with the other's better mood, while forced solitude cuts the other way. A fourth talk weighs solitude and loneliness against mental health. A fifth uses language analysis to spot solitude in older adults' own reports. The group closes by proposing programs that build this capacity.
pmc-10737189:
Ittay Mannheim, Cynthia Neiertz, and Eveline Wouters test whether age bias shapes tech-based therapy offers in two thousand twenty-three. Digital tools could widen care for older adults. Yet therapists who view older patients as poor tech users may quietly withhold those options.

Seventy-eight physiotherapists in Luxembourg filled an online survey. Bias was scored on a scale about older adults using technology. Nearly a third admitted they had once skipped a tech-based treatment because of a patient's age. Those one step more negative on the scale were about twice as likely to have withheld it. Warm views of workplace tech also cut the withholding. The study urges training that targets this specific bias.
pmc-10741089:
Simon Kobalter and colleagues published a 2023 study engineering yeast to make tailored fatty acids. Industry usually sources fatty acids from plant oils and animal fats. Demand for sustainable supply keeps rising. Yeast can ferment cheap carbon leftovers instead. This yeast species needed tuning for one scarce fatty acid.

The team reworked the yeast's fat metabolism step by step. Some changes helped output. Others hurt it and were dropped. Engineered yeast released the target acid into the broth. That release simplifies harvesting the product. The work shows how fermentation could replace food-linked supply chains.
pmc-10742989:
Yinan Chen and co-authors improve the hunt for communities in networks with a kernel built from word-statistics math, in a 2023 paper. Spectral clustering groups nodes by the patterns in a network's matrix form, but standard versions miss some structural detail. Their method scores each pair of nodes by point-wise mutual information, rebuilds the network from those scores, and clusters the rebuilt version. A companion algorithm guesses how many communities a network holds.

The guessing algorithm rebuilds the network, samples it many times, and infers the count by Bayesian reasoning. In tests it ran faster and hit the true count more often than rival estimators. The full clustering method, PMIK-SC, also beat other community finders and spectral methods on accuracy and stability. The authors present the pair as a practical upgrade for network analysis.
pmc-10744389:
Milena Zamurovic and ten colleagues report a forty-five-year-old woman whose leg pain turned out to be endometriosis growing into her sciatic nerve. She had three years of growing right leg pain, tingling, weakness, and trouble walking. The pain got worse around menstruation. Standard exams of her nerves, bones, and pelvic organs found nothing.

Magnetic resonance imaging showed a lesion growing into the nerve, and tissue testing confirmed endometriosis. Hormone-blocking treatment shrank the lesion and brought remission. Ongoing hormone therapy, rehab exercises, and follow-up managed her mild remaining symptoms. The authors warn this rare isolated form mimics ordinary sciatica. If missed, it causes permanent nerve damage, so leg pain that follows the monthly cycle deserves imaging.
pmc-10745589:
Julia Blaurock and colleagues published a 2023 methods study on shortening diet questionnaires. Long food lists burden survey respondents. Short lists risk missing key nutrients. The team used mathematical optimization to choose foods. German national nutrition data supplied the test case.

The algorithm sought high nutrient coverage per item. Foods eaten very differently between people scored higher. The optimized lists came out shorter than a validated questionnaire's list. Accuracy targets still constrained the choices. This proof of concept suits large population studies. Shorter forms could raise response rates. Nutrition surveys depend on volunteers finishing long forms, so brevity matters.
pmc-10747889:
Jurasz and coauthors give a new method to turn time spans into digital counts. The method uses a stepwise balance trick like a scale. It needs no reference clock to run at all. That lack makes it apt for low-power chip designs.

Direct conversion keeps the circuit quite small and plain. The method suits long spans, in the range of large microsecond counts. Such spans occur in body signal work with time-based chips. Tests show the stepwise search lands on the right count. Low part count may cut cost for medical sensors. More work will test noise and speed limits.
pmc-10756089:
Parthasarathi Barik and co-authors tested whether boosting a helper protein in stem cells could protect the aging, high-pressure heart. The protein, known as CHIP, helps manage growth signals. The team raised CHIP levels in stem cells taken from rat fat tissue and checked the effects in dishes and in rats bred for high blood pressure. The boosted cells released more of a growth factor called IGF1 and its binding partner, and the growth factor's receptor lasted longer because CHIP steadied it. A signaling protein moving into the cell nucleus drove the extra release.

When the boosted cells were transplanted into nine-month-old hypertensive rats, the hearts pumped better. Ejection measures rose by about fifteen percent against untreated rats, and the hearts were smaller with slower rates. The authors argue that stem cells tuned this way could blunt the thickening and decline that late-stage hypertension causes.
pmc-10757089:
Randa Saeed and five colleagues hunted for survival predictors in advanced lung cancer patients receiving nivolumab. Second-line immunotherapy helps only a subset of people with non-small cell lung cancer. The twenty twenty-three retrospective study covered patients treated with palliative intent in Scotland between twenty sixteen and twenty nineteen. Records came from three health boards. CT scans supplied body composition measures, and blood markers captured systemic inflammation.

Most patients were sixty-five or older, slightly more were women, and about half had adenocarcinoma. The team related clinical features, inflammation, and body composition to survival. Knowing which host and tumor traits predict benefit could spare unlikely responders a futile treatment. It could also focus support on patients whose body composition or inflammation signals a rougher course.
pmc-10781489:
Yingjing Zhao, Yuxue Mu, Yujia Zou, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It mines gene data to find the key drivers of intervertebral disc degeneration, the wearing down of spinal discs, and then hunts for natural compounds that might slow it.

The team combined bulk gene data, single-cell data, and network analysis to spotlight the genes that matter most. Four hub genes emerged, tied to blood vessel growth, tissue breakdown, and immune signals. Attention then turned to a signaling protein called JAK3. Computer screening of natural compound libraries surfaced three candidates that docked well with JAK3, with fair safety and absorption profiles. Stability simulations suggested the pairings hold up in the body. The authors offer the genes as targets and the compounds as starting points for new disc treatments.
pmc-10800989:
Coral Sanfeliu and co-authors review animal models where toxins drive brain cell loss, in an overview from two thousand twenty-three. Such models speed the hunt for drugs against diseases like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Most mimic those two illnesses, the most common in older adults.

Three toxins that kill dopamine cells are compared, with one regime judged most useful for Parkinson's work. Other agents model memory-cell loss, swelling-driven decline, and diabetes-linked damage. A bacterial toxin suits trials of anti-swelling drugs for Alzheimer's. Toxin models beat gene models for Parkinson's drug hunting but not for Alzheimer's, the authors conclude. All model types should serve, they urge.
pmc-10803189:
Crick Lund and a large team lay out a study on teen mental health in poor city areas, in work from 2023. Depression and anxiety drive much of the disease burden in youth, yet proof on prevention in poorer nations is thin. The ALIVE study spans Colombia, Nepal, and South Africa.

The plan pairs poverty relief with training in self-control for teens at high risk. Steps run from building a cause map, to crafting the mixed program, to checking the test tools, to a pilot trial with four arms. Teens take part in shaping the work. The team aims to build proof for blending mental health into broader aid.
pmc-10824989:
Stefano Rosa and co-authors deploy a robot that guides museum visitors while its brain sits in the cloud, in work the text dates to 2023. The catalog lists 2024. The 5G link lets the robot offload its thinking to a remote machine. Localization, mapping, route planning, and visitor interaction are all standard parts; the novelty is running them through a live public network amid real crowds.

The paper walks through the problems the network and the visitors created, and how the team answered them. Results are reported on both method and field performance. The full software stack is public. The authors present the guide as a proof that heavy robot intelligence can live off-board when the connection is fast enough.
pmc-10863789:
Yuqing Ren and a team of co-authors studied heart health scores and kidney disease in American adults, in two thousand twenty-three. The score, called Life's Essential Eight, rates habits and health factors tied to the heart. Kidney disease is closely linked to heart disease, yet its tie to the new score was unclear.

The team used national survey data from more than a decade, with close to twenty-five thousand adults. Higher scores went with lower odds of kidney disease, in a curved rather than straight pattern. Blood sugar and blood pressure scores showed the clearest links on their own. The link was strongest among middle-aged adults, men, and people in couples.
pmc-10915089:
Hye-Shin Kim and three colleagues published a mouse study in two thousand twenty-three on a probiotic strain for allergic airways. Allergy-driven airway inflammation brings excess mucus and a damaged airway lining. The team tested a lactic acid bacterium taken from green tea.

Mice with induced airway allergy received the strain by mouth. Their type-two inflammation eased and mucus overproduction fell, with the main mucus gene switched down. The treatment also raised butyrate, a helpful gut fat, and the gut bacteria that make it. In human airway cells, butyrate alone cut the same mucus gene. The authors propose a gut-to-lung route for the benefit and call for more work on dosing.
pmc-11536389:
Magdalena Riedl Khursigara and three colleagues published a narrative review in two thousand twenty-four on diabetes drugs for a dialysis problem. In peritoneal dialysis, fluid is drawn from the belly using sugar solutions. Over time the membrane can fail at pulling fluid, ending the treatment. Sugar transporters in the membrane help drive that failure.

Drugs blocking one such transporter, SGLT-2, protect heart and kidneys in earlier disease stages. They are untested in dialysis patients. Animal work shows the transporters increase in the membrane and the drugs may cut sugar uptake. Several trials in dialysis patients are now running. The authors discuss trial designs and a patient-centred approach for a future large trial.
pmc-11536589:
Xu and co-authors traced drug resistance in pancreatic cancer for this study from twenty twenty-four. A new drug blocks the KRAS G12D driver found in many of these tumors. Resistance emerges fast, as with other targeted drugs. The team built resistant cell lines and hunted the escape route.

Gene scans pointed at ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death the drug normally triggers. A detox enzyme, MGST1, stood guard in resistant cells by blocking fat damage. Raising or lowering the enzyme dialed resistance up or down. A growth pathway upstream kept the enzyme switched on. Adding a blocker of that pathway restored the drug's punch in cells and in mice. The pairing is offered as a rescue strategy.
pmc-11547789:
Maree Gould, Xiaoxuan Deng, Karl Lyons, and Azam Ali test a dental scaffold in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Tooth pulp holds stem cells that could repair the tooth from within. Their scaffold blends polymers for strength, antibacterial action, and cell support, mixed into a standard dental cement.

Human pulp cells grew faster with the blend than with either part alone, and viability rose. The blend was placed in drilled rat molars for up to forty-five days. New pulp-like tissue grew into the scaffold, lined by cells forming a dentin-like deposit. No infection or sealing-off of the implant was seen. Stem cells moved into the implant over time. The authors call it a promising start, needing more study.
pmc-11573589:
Sameh Saber and colleagues published a review in 2024 on PU-H71, a drug that blocks a protein called HSP90. HSP90 helps other proteins fold and stay stable inside cells. When cancer cells lean on it, they grow and spread more easily.

The review explains how PU-H71 forces key growth proteins to break down. That shuts off several signal routes that tumors use to live and spread. The authors cover work on hard cases such as triple-negative breast cancer, myeloma, blood cancers, and liver cancer. They also note the drug may help carbon-ion beam therapy work better. Readers get a clear map of where this drug might fit in future cancer care.
pmc-11603689:
David Zezai and colleagues mapped what helps and what blocks person-centered care for people living with several long-term conditions at once in poorer countries. Care for single diseases is the norm, while patients with many conditions need joined-up primary care. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team ran a scoping review of studies from low and middle income settings over more than a decade. The team sorted findings by parts of the health system: people, service platforms, workforce, tools, and governance.

Barriers included poverty and low health literacy among patients, split services and missing care guidelines, too few and under-skilled workers, medicine shortages and drug interaction harms, and weak political backing. Helpers included self-management support, integrated services, digital tools, and stronger funding commitment. The authors recommend multimorbidity guidelines, community health workers, and cross-sector integrated care.
pmc-11603989:
Lalique Browne, Irmine Fleury Ayihounton, and Thomas Druetz argue for a negotiation-based feminism to widen abortion access in sub-Saharan Africa in a 2024 paper. Abortion is partly legal in most of the region's countries, yet laws are weakly enforced, and wider rights alone have not opened access. The authors view the gap through reproductive justice, which stresses social context.

Where law and local norms clash, they say, access stalls until norms shift, a slow change. Nego-feminism, an African feminist outlook built on negotiation and relationships, offers a way to work within those norms in the meantime. They point to accompaniment networks that guide safe medication abortion outside formal care. Legal reform stays vital, with the strategy as its partner.
pmc-11607089:
Subhankar Pradhan and five co-authors published a synthetic chemistry study in twenty twenty-four on stitching skipped dienes, the spaced double-bond pattern threaded through natural products and fatty acids, in a single step. Their recipe pairs cobalt catalysis with light-driven photoredox chemistry to couple carbonate building blocks with alkynes.

Regio- and stereocontrol were excellent across terminal, internal, and alcohol-bearing alkynes. The method even extended natural terpene alcohols into longer synthetic cousins by repeated three-carbon additions. Experiments and quantum calculations traced the cobalt catalyst through its oxidation states and a detour through a diene intermediate. One-step access to a motif chemists usually assemble laboriously is the contribution.
pmc-11608889:
Frank Antony Proudlock and Irene Gottlob wrote this commentary in 2024 on the treatment of amblyopia, often called lazy eye. In a healthy child, the brain lines up signals from both eyes to build a sense of depth. When the eyes send unequal signals, the brain may shut down the weaker eye. Two common causes are crossed eyes and a gap in lens strength between the eyes.

The authors review the standard care: glasses first, then a patch over the stronger eye. They note that patching can sting, blur sight for a time, and draw teasing, so many children stop early. They also weigh longer glasses wear, drops that blur the strong eye, and screen-based tasks. About a third of treated children still fall short of good sight, so the piece calls for care matched to each child's age, type, and home life.
pmc-11610089:
Giovanni Cochetti, Michele Del Zingaro, Giuseppe Maiolino, and nine colleagues search for coronavirus in semen in this two thousand twenty-four multicenter prospective study. Whether SARS-CoV-2 reaches semen mattered for transmission and fertility questions, but evidence was muddled. The team enrolled sixty-five men: fifteen with active infection and fifty recovered at least six months earlier. Each gave semen for viral PCR testing and semen analysis, with urinary and sexual function assessed across phases, and the authors also reviewed the published literature.

No semen sample from either group contained detectable virus. Genital or sexual symptoms during active infection were reported by eight patients. Semen quality did not differ significantly between groups, and urinary and erectile function scores stayed stable across infection phases. The authors conclude the virus does not appear in semen of acute or recovered cases, reassuring for sexual transmission concerns while noting the literature remains divided.
pmc-11612289:
Wenji Piao and a large team show how regulatory T cells, immune cells that normally calm immune responses, help tumors grow through a signaling route. Their study came out in 2024. The cells carry a surface molecule that activates a matching receptor on tumor cells and on lymphatic vessel cells.

Activating that receptor turns on a signaling pathway that speeds tumor growth and spread. Drugs that block the pathway slowed tumor growth and movement in laboratory tests. In mice, normal regulatory cells promoted melanoma growth, while cells lacking the surface molecule did not. Blocking the pathway also cut the chemical signals that recruit more regulatory cells to tumors. Fighter immune cells stayed in the tumor longer as a result. The findings suggest a strategy against tumor spread through lymph vessels.
pmc-11613489:
Shaolin Wang and co-authors map where chronic disease gets written down in England's health system, and for whom. They linked family doctor and hospital records for 12.8 million patients and traced 205 long-term conditions over twelve years. Nearly three quarters of patients had at least one diagnosis on record somewhere.

Most diagnoses lived only in primary care records, at about sixty-three percent, while fifteen percent appeared only in hospital records and twenty-two percent in both. Patients of Black, Asian, mixed, and other ethnic backgrounds were less likely than White patients to have a condition recorded at all. Patients in the poorest areas were more likely to have one recorded, across all settings. Recording also varied widely between practices. The authors say linked records give a fuller picture, and that the gaps by ethnicity, poverty, and practice need condition-by-condition study.
pmc-11616489:
Ten authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four on pneumococcal carriage during the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil. The pneumococcus bacterium colonizes the nose and throat and can turn invasive. During the pandemic, invasive cases fell, which made the carriage patterns of that unusual period worth recording with care.

Children and adults who came to emergency clinics with suspected COVID-19 in southern Brazil were invited to join. Swabs were tested with a molecular panel covering the twenty-one most common Latin American types. One type, called 19A, showed a high prevalence. The authors discuss what host and setting factors shaped who carried which type.
pmc-11616689:
Shuang Wang and colleagues describe a 2024 device that sits on a living plant and watches its health. Shaped like a sunflower, the probe runs on sunlight alone, so it needs no battery swaps in the field. It tracks sap flow, a strong sign of how well a plant is doing.

Fold-out solar panels keep the small, light system charged. For sending data, the probe uses faint light pulses modeled on fireflies, which sip power. Drones fly over the field to pick up the signals from many probes at once. Software that learns from images then sorts the readings. The team sees the probe as a cheap tool for plant studies, and the same tricks may suit other tight, remote sensing jobs.
pmc-11616989:
Mirela Zaneva and a large, self-described neurodiverse team of co-authors build an annotated reading list on neurodiversity in two thousand twenty-four. The term has been defined in many ways since it appeared, which confuses newcomers. Well-chosen, well-framed reading on the topic is also scarce.

Nine themes structure the list: the history of the idea, ways to frame it, and the weight of lived experience. Further themes cover autism science under the new lens, views past deficit on ADHD, wider scope, anti-ableism, and sound theory and method. A last theme ties the topic to open and shared research practice. The authors hope the list steers readers and nudges science toward fairer, more open habits.
pmc-11618389:
Huabin He and co-authors link pro inflammatory diets to kidney disease in US adults in this 2024 paper. The dietary inflammatory index scores how much a diet promotes inflammation. Its tie to chronic kidney disease was little studied. Survey data covered 19,317 adults with diet records and kidney measures.

Kidney disease meant low filtration or excess protein in urine. Each step up in diet score raised disease odds in adjusted models. The highest scoring quarter had about half again the odds of the lowest. The team then tested whether the link differs by sex, as the title highlights. Diet quality is a modifiable factor in a disease with few early symptoms. Anti inflammatory eating may protect kidneys at population scale.
pmc-11619689:
Chaojuan Huang and co-authors published this population study in 2024. A new blood index, CTI, blends an inflammation marker with a measure of insulin resistance, two processes suspected in depression. The team tested whether higher CTI tracks with depressive symptoms in American adults. They used national survey data from 2005 to 2010 covering 5,954 participants. Depression was scored with a standard nine-question instrument, with a cutoff marking moderate to severe symptoms.

The link was clear and positive. Each step up in CTI came with higher symptom scores and about thirty percent higher odds of crossing the depression cutoff. People in the top quarter of CTI had double the odds of symptoms compared with the bottom quarter. The pattern held across subgroups and statistical checks. The authors propose CTI as a cheap, routine-blood-based flag for depression risk, marking association rather than cause.
pmc-11621189:
Jimena Lois-Milevicich, Lauriane Rat-Fischer, María Alicia de la Colina, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It asks whether being a clever problem solver also means being good with tools, using plush-crested jays as the test case.

These South American crows are curious and flexible in the wild but have never been seen using tools. The team gave the birds two tasks of like difficulty.
