In one, they had to unlatch a clear box lid to reach food. In the other, they had to rake food out with a tool. Eight of nine birds cracked the latch task. None learned the rake task. The authors say the split hints that tool use draws on its own special skills, not just general cleverness.
pmc-11621489:
Pei-Zhuo Liu and seven co-authors catalog a gene family in celery in two thousand twenty-four. The family, called MORF, helps edit RNA inside chloroplasts, the parts of plant cells that make chlorophyll. Chlorophyll content is a main sign of celery quality, so these genes matter for the crop.

The team found eight MORF genes in celery and named them by subfamily. They predicted each gene's traits, motifs, and partners, and compared the family across four related plants. Four genes were predicted to sit in chloroplasts. Leaf stalk data showed four genes were most active, and more so in green celery than in white. The work lays a base for studying how these genes shape chloroplast growth.
pmc-11622689:
He and co-authors report a child with a rare mixed liver cancer treated with a targeted drug plus chemotherapy. The cancer blends two types and is very rare in children, with poor outcomes. Surgery is the only standard care, and no set drug plan exists for cases that cannot be cut out.

Their patient was a 14-year-old girl with many liver masses and spread to lungs and lymph nodes. Gene testing found an FGFR2-PRDM16 fusion not reported before as a common form. Two blood tumor markers were both raised. The report tracks her lasting response to pemigatinib paired with chemotherapy.
pmc-11624889:
Enhao Wang and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-four on chronic sinus inflammation with nasal polyps. In this condition, soft growths form in the nose and sinuses and often return after treatment. Macrophages, a type of immune cell, seem to play a role, but their molecular marks in the disease were unclear.

The team merged gene data from patients and healthy controls across three public sets. They built a four-gene diagnostic model with high accuracy in both training and test data. One gene, called HMOX1, came mainly from a macrophage type known as M2 and tracked closely with the disease. Cell staining in nasal tissue and mouse cell tests backed the finding. The work points to a marker and a possible treatment target.
pmc-11634689:
Junjie Liu and co-authors hunt the risk factors for leaks where the esophagus is joined to the small intestine after stomach removal, in a 2024 study. The team reviewed 609 cancer patients at one hospital over six years. Leaks struck 48 patients, about eight percent. Simple comparisons flagged sex, illness count, low blood protein, tumor position, and long operations.

The full model kept two independent risks: having two or more other illnesses, and operations lasting at least 260 minutes. Each roughly tripled or doubled the odds. Male sex, junction tumors, and low protein mattered before adjustment. The authors urge extra care for patients carrying several illnesses into long surgery.
pmc-11637989:
Zhou, Li, and Sun review how a protein-tagging enzyme controls two amino acids that cancers crave in this 2024 article. Tumors rewire their metabolism to gather building blocks for growth. Glutamine is the most abundant amino acid in blood, and cancer cells depend on it heavily.

Cells swap part of their glutamine output for cystine from outside, which they convert to cysteine for proteins and antioxidant defense. The CRL3 ligase, part of the cell's protein disposal system, regulates both sides of this trade. The review gathers what is known about that control and its place in the tumor's surroundings. Targeting such a hub could starve tumors of two fuels at once.
pmc-11638489:
Xindi Lin and eight co-authors use brain scans to study why some children wet the bed, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. Waking to the urge to urinate is a key skill that fails in bedwetting. Its brain basis was largely unknown, so the team looked for brain areas whose activity tracks that skill.

Scans came from one hundred seventy-three children with varied scores for the waking skill. Activity in one area, the right angular gyrus, ran lower as the skill worsened. A link between that area and a frontal region ran stronger in the same children, an odd pairing the authors note. The findings give early clues to the brain wiring behind bedwetting and may guide future treatment ideas.
pmc-11639789:
Diming Li and co-authors present a 2024 study of a pea protein emulsion that guards frozen dough. Frozen dough suffers as ice wrecks its gluten web and frees water. The team whipped oil-in-water emulsions held by two, three, and four percent pea protein and folded them into dough. Loaves were judged after four weeks frozen, on water spread, freezable water, web strength, and bake results.

The three percent mix won: its water spread ran most even and its freezable share ran low. The gluten web held together, keeping the dough springy. Baked loaves rose higher, felt softer, and lost less in the oven. A plant protein shield could lift the quality of bake-at-home goods. Freezer time need not mean flat bread.
pmc-11639889:
Minhye Kim and colleagues report two cancers growing together inside a stomach duplication cyst. Their case report from twenty twenty-four concerns a Korean woman in her fifties. Such cysts are rare birth defects, usually harmless. She arrived with stomach bleeding symptoms over time.

Scans showed a protruding mass in the stomach wall. Surgeons removed the whole stomach by keyhole surgery. Tissue study found misplaced pancreas tissue inside the cyst. Two cancer types had grown from that tissue together. The authors call it a world-first combination. Benign cysts can rarely turn malignant in hidden ways. Bleeding plus a cyst mass deserves thorough checking.
pmc-11640589:
Masao Ryu and twelve co-authors compare two ways to silence genes in worn spinal disk cells. The target path helps cells grow but blocks their cleanup work, and it plays a role in disk wear. The team took human disk cells at surgery and treated them with either small RNA pieces or a gene-editing tool, each aimed at three genes in the path. Both methods cut the target proteins.

The editing tool got into far more cells within a day. Silencing any of the three genes sped cell cleanup and slowed cell death and aging, with one gene's edit working best. The paper weighs both routes for future disk care.
pmc-11640989:
Pavlova and seven co-authors build a reusable sensor surface in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The target compounds are polyphenols, plant chemicals with antioxidant power. One key example is chlorogenic acid, found in many foods and health products.

Exact checks of this acid matter for grading raw materials and final goods. The team let gold nanoparticles assemble themselves at a liquid boundary, then printed that film into a sensor. The surface boosts Raman light signals, a method that can name and measure chemicals. A cheap, reusable sensor that works in the field could speed quality checks for food and drug makers.
pmc-11641389:
Xiangying Zhao, Shunan Zhang, Dongyan Nan, Jiali Han, and Jang Hyun Kim map the field of human-computer interaction in health care in two thousand twenty-four. Work in that area has grown fast, yet no full map of its trends had been made. Such a map helps readers see where the field is heading.

The team used a mapping tool on a topic search of a major database, which gave near three thousand six hundred papers from two thousand four to two thousand twenty-three. They chart the most active authors, centers, and countries, plus how each collaborates. Citation links show which journals and papers carry the most weight. Word bursts and clusters reveal the hot themes inside the field.
pmc-11641589:
Masahiro Ikezu and co-authors study knee osteoarthritis in a paper from 2024. They ask how the thigh bone and shin bone line up, in two planes, and how that links to medial meniscus extrusion. That term names the state in which the inner knee pad bulges out past its place. The team first tests if ultrasound can gauge how far the shin bone has turned.

In the test, ten healthy adults get both MRI and the scan, and the scan scores match MRI. The scan gap score tracks the turn angle MRI finds. Next come 63 adults with one worn knee and 16 healthy adults. Bulging was worse when the shin bone had slipped back. It did not shift much with how far the bone had turned. The authors say the scan can judge knee line well in a clinic.
pmc-11641789:
Cuicui Yang and colleagues dissect how a milk-derived peptide blocks a blood pressure enzyme, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. The enzyme is ACE, target of many hypertension drugs. Food-derived inhibitors could offer gentler alternatives or leads.

The peptide, three amino acids long and called LLY, came from casein hydrolysate. It inhibited ACE strongly and stayed stable. Kinetic plots showed it binds away from the enzyme's active site, a non-competitive pattern. Molecular docking agreed with that reading. Spectroscopy and atomic force microscopy watched the enzyme change shape on binding. The systematic interaction map matters for designing peptide-based antihypertensives that survive digestion and reach their target.
pmc-11642189:
Fu-Der Lai, Yen-Ting Lai, and Chang-Song Chen design colored solar absorbers for buildings using big data screening. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. A good absorber drinks in sunlight as heat, but buildings also need colors that please the eye.

The stack is simple: silica, chromium, silica. The team computed how layer thicknesses shift both efficiency and color, then mapped the trade-off on a color chart. When absorption passes ninety percent, heat conversion trails it by only about two points. Seven colored samples were built and tested for optics and materials traits. Oxygen creeping into the chromium layer slowly dulls performance. Surface roughness of the base also shifts rust resistance and color. The work ties looks to physics.
pmc-11642889:
Jiang leads a large team hunting for new tuberculosis drugs in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Tuberculosis still kills many people, and drug resistance keeps growing. Drugs that work in a new way are badly needed.

The team targeted an enzyme called PafA in the TB germ. A computer screen found a first blocker compound. Docking models showed how it binds, and lab tests confirmed the effect. Guided by that structure, they built a stronger second blocker. Both compounds blocked PafA in lab and cell tests in a selective way. The work offers a fresh lead for TB drug design, though human use is far off.
pmc-11643589:
Yong-Xia Li, Li-Xia Bai, and Jin-Chang Guo design tiny clusters with a fluorine atom held flat by four neighbors. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, joins two exotic ideas in chemistry. Superhalogens are groups that grab electrons even harder than single halogens. A flat four-way fluorine center had never been linked to them before.

Their star-shaped clusters pair lithium arms with chlorine, bromine, or iodine helpers. Computer searches show each shape is the lowest-energy form. Motion tests at room heat show the shapes hold together. Bonding study credits shared ionic links, not ring effects, for the strength. The clusters also shed electrons with great reluctance, the mark of a superhalogen.
pmc-11643989:
Wonchang Kim, Taehyung Kim, and Taegyu Lee wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It tests concrete in which part of the cement is swapped for bio-sulfur, a sulfur recovered from landfill gas by microbes, blended with limestone.

Five blends were prepared at different sulfur-to-limestone ratios. Too much limestone wrecked workability and halved strength, so an even ratio won. With that blend, adding more bio-sulfur raised compressive strength by up to twelve percent. Wave speed through the specimens rose in step and did not depend on the water ratio. Statistics confirmed the effects were real. X-ray analysis showed the usual cement crystals early, then new magnesium and calcium sulfur-bearing hydrates by day twenty-eight. The authors say the waste sulfur route is a genuine, greener cement substitute.
pmc-11644489:
Takashi Hatayama and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, a new resin core system built around a monomer that shrinks less as it hardens. After root canal treatment, a tooth is rebuilt from inside, and the filling's grip on the canal wall decides how long the repair lasts. Shrinkage pulls the material off the wall and opens gaps. The new system was measured against three rivals on extracted human teeth, for bond strength and for gaps seen in cross-section imaging.

All systems gripped the crown end alike. Down at the root tip, where bonds usually fail, the new system held significantly stronger than every rival. Its gap share after setting was about eleven percent, roughly a third of two rivals' and matching the best. The authors conclude that taming shrinkage buys exactly what root rebuilds need: adhesion where it is hardest to get.
pmc-11651589:
Jiwoo Park and co-authors study whether short bursts of fine dust in the air link to cases of violence in South Korea. The work, from two thousand twenty-four, uses records from a national survey of hospital injury cases from two thousand fifteen to two thousand nineteen. Past work had leaned on deaths in large cities with air sensors, which left much of the country out.

The team pairs each case with modeled daily dust levels that cover all inland districts. Risk rose in a near straight line in the two days after exposure, and the link was stronger for men and for people aged sixty-four or less. The authors argue that cleaner air may also cut harm from violence.
pmc-11652389:
Thamali Kariyawasam, Martin Petkovich, and Bas Vriens test algae as cleaners of a common drug in wastewater. Their twenty twenty-four article deals with diclofenac, a widely used anti-inflammatory drug that passes through standard treatment and builds up in waterways. Microalgae can break it down, and trapping them in a matrix may keep them working longer.

Two freshwater species were grown free and immobilized for six days. By day three, the trapped algae beat free cells, removing about four fifths of the drug. Mixed cultures did best, above ninety percent. By day six, all setups cleared the drug fully. The team breaks down how much was degraded, stored in cells, or lost by abiotic routes.
pmc-11653589:
Katsuya Maeshima and co-authors look for factors tied to fungal infections in severe COVID-19 care. Fungal infections are a grave side issue when the virus makes people very ill. The team re-used data from a large study of patients at sixty-six hospitals in Japan. All patients in the group needed a breathing machine, and infection was counted when antifungal drugs ran for five days or more.

Of 559 patients, fifty-seven had a fungal infection by that count. Many factors looked linked at first, such as age and other drugs. After careful checks, only one factor held: each extra day of steroid use raised the risk. Two extra checks with stricter counts gave the same result. The team urges care with long steroid courses.
pmc-11654189:
Prabhat Agarwal and co-authors test a triple drug pill for type 2 diabetes in India. Diabetes affects about eleven percent of adults in India, and many patients stay above sugar targets on two drugs. The study enrolled 215 patients at many centers whose sugar stayed high on a pair of drugs. Each took a fixed pill that joins three drugs in one dose, twice a day.

Blood sugar marks fell a great deal by twelve and twenty-four weeks. At the end, about forty-five percent of patients hit the target level. Kidney measures held steady or improved, and fat levels in blood moved in a good direction. Side effects of note hit under five percent, and none were grave. The authors call the pill safe and effective for this group.
pmc-11654789:
Buchman bids farewell in twenty twenty-four as founding editor of Critical Care Explorations, an open-access journal for critical care. He looks back at how the journal began and at wider shifts in medical publishing. Open access, where all readers can read work for free, moved from rare to common over two decades.

He recalls how the journal was built in just four months and launched in twenty nineteen. A planned shift in Europe toward open access spurred its parent society to act fast. He credits staff at the society and its publisher for the quick launch. His piece closes a founding term by tracing what the experiment showed.
pmc-11655289:
Chen, Farley, and Lassmann build a tool to link cell types to illness. Large maps now show which genes are on in each kind of cell. Those maps may show which cells drive a given illness. The team set up one clear work flow to test such links.

They ran the flow on four large single-cell data sets. The sets span many tissue types and life stages. The flow groups genes that turn on and off as a set. It then checks if those groups match known illness traits. The tests found both known links and new ones worth more study.
pmc-11655889:
Xiaoyang Wang and five colleagues present a way to purify dual-target antibodies without the standard costly capture step, in a twenty twenty-four paper. These antibodies bind two targets at once and hold great drug promise. Making them yields look-alike waste, including wrong pairings from the host cells. The team used a mixed-mode resin to catch the product, then an ion-exchange column to polish it.

The two-step method reached ninety-eight percent purity on two tests. Host cell protein waste fell to ten parts per million. About sixty percent of the product was recovered. The authors offer the platform as a simpler, cheaper rival to the usual affinity route for these drugs.
pmc-11656789:
Povilas Kavaliauskas, Evaldas Kazlauskas, and Giedre Smailyte survey the mental health of Lithuania's nurses, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Nurses face elevated burnout and suicide risk worldwide. National data guide whether interventions are warranted.

Five hundred thirty-three nurses completed validated scales for depression, anxiety, and stress, plus a suicide risk questionnaire. High distress was common: roughly a fifth reported high depression, nearly a third high anxiety. About one in five carried increased suicide risk. Almost two-thirds had considered leaving for non-medical work within a year. The authors frame the numbers as a retention emergency as much as a health one: systems lose their most experienced staff first.
pmc-11657689:
Qing-Qing Tan and nine colleagues test a short screening routine for eye coordination problems in cataract patients, in a twenty twenty-four study. Cataract surgery changes how the two eyes work together, and hidden coordination faults can cause trouble after surgery. A full exam takes long, so the team checked whether a few quick tests could match it. Patients took the full battery before surgery and again after the second eye was done.

One measure stood out: the shift in eye alignment between distance and near gaze, from a simple cover test. It matched the full battery on its own. Adding a push-up fusion test at both distances raised accuracy further. The authors say this brief routine can flag at-risk patients without the long exam.
pmc-11658989:
Hao Jiang and his six co-authors, publishing in 2024, revisit a puzzle in fatty liver disease: heavier patients sometimes seem to outlive thinner ones. The team re-examined a national health survey from 1988 to 1994. They tracked deaths over a median of twenty years. Two measures of body size were compared, the standard body mass index and the waist-to-height ratio.

At first glance the paradox appeared. Overweight and obese patients showed slightly lower death risk than normal-weight patients. But the effect vanished once smoking was accounted for and early deaths were excluded. Then extra weight raised risk as expected. The waist-based measure showed the paradox more weakly, and it too disappeared after the same fixes. The authors conclude the paradox is an artifact of smoking and reverse causation, and that waist-to-height is the sharper tool.
pmc-11660089:
Amirah Nasr, Bianca Lourenço, Amanda Coleman, and Joseph Bartges track a kidney marker in dogs on two common drugs. The dogs had kidney disease with protein leaking into urine. The drugs ease pressure inside the kidney's filters but can briefly lower how well the kidney cleans the blood. The team used stored samples from twenty-nine dogs, taken before treatment and at one week and one month on one of two drugs.

The marker, called SDMA, barely moved on average, while two older markers rose. The pattern varied when a third drug was added for high blood pressure. The paper helps vets read early marker shifts when starting these drugs.
pmc-11669989:
Ding, Lin, and Liang review a gel system that may help large bone breaks heal. Bone healing needs calm swelling, new blood flow, and new bone growth. Zhang and a team built a gel that holds tiny packets from marrow stem cells. Those packets can guide nearby cells as they heal.

In lab tests, the packets boosted blood vessel growth and bone cell growth. The gel also pushed immune cells toward a calm, heal-helping state. That mix may suit big bone gaps that heal poorly on their own. The review weighs strengths and gaps for next tests in animals and people.
pmc-11670789:
Saurabh Jain and nine colleagues test how cigarette smoke affects temporary crown materials, in a twenty twenty-four lab study. They made 112 discs by four routes: printed, milled, standard resin, and classic acrylic. Half sat in artificial saliva for thirty days, while half faced smoke in a custom chamber twice daily. Color and surface roughness were measured before and after.

Smoke changed both color and roughness more than saliva did. The classic acrylic stained the most. The printed resin changed color the least. The authors say smokers' temporary crowns may age faster, and printed materials may hold their look best under smoke.
pmc-11672689:
Boonkum, Chankitisakul, Kananit, Tuntiyasawasdikul, Sirisan, and Kenchaiwong estimate in twenty twenty-four how genes jointly shape growth and meat chemistry in Thai slow-growing chickens. Breeders want faster growth without loading meat with purines, which raise uric acid in eaters. The team recorded weights and breast size in several hundred native birds, then sampled meat, liver, and blood from a subset for purine, uric acid, and a protective enzyme.

Growth traits proved moderately heritable, while the chemistry traits were weakly to moderately so. Total purine content ran strongly against growth at the genetic level, a helpful sign. Other chemistry links varied in direction. The authors say joint genetic evaluation can pick birds that grow well with cleaner meat.
pmc-11672989:
Zhihao Zhang, Yuying Yan, and Seong Min Kang study how tiny pillar patterns on a surface change wetting and droplet drying, in a twenty twenty-four paper. Such patterns copy nature, like the water-shedding leaves and insect wings (biomimetic surfaces). The team used light-based printing to make resin pillars in varied shapes and layouts. They then watched how droplets sat, heated, and dried on each surface.

Round pillars let the team tune wetting by layout and roughness. These surfaces also cooled the drying droplet less and sped its drying by about thirteen percent. Hotter bases changed wetting on every design. The results guide the design of surfaces for cooling and water control.
pmc-11674689:
Dagnija Grabovska and colleagues present two patients whose neck lumps turned out to be a harmless body variant, in this case series from twenty twenty-four. The mylohyoid muscle forms the floor of the mouth, but it often has small gaps. Through such a gap, a saliva gland from under the tongue can slip down and feel like a lump under the jaw.

The first patient, a woman in her forties, had a slow-growing lump on the right side for two years. The second, a woman of seventy, had vague neck discomfort and no lump that could be felt. Ultrasound and CT scans left both cases unclear. MRI then showed the gland poking through the muscle gap in each case. The authors urge doctors to keep this variant in mind when a lump under the jaw defies a quick label, since full imaging can spare needless alarm.
pmc-11674889:
Huanyu Li and colleagues described a new sensor design in 2024 for spotting tiny amounts of a urine marker. Terahertz sensing can identify molecules without labels, but bulky optics have limited its use. The team built a stretchable patterned surface on a soft silicone base that strengthens the signal from very small samples. Stretching the surface or tilting the incoming beam tunes its response, which simplifies the setup and lets it match the target molecule.

Tests showed sharp, high-quality responses and strong overall sensing scores. The sensor could detect the marker, a compound found in urine, at very low surface amounts. The authors link the marker to conditions such as diabetes in pregnancy, where a urine test could help screening. They present the design as a step toward practical terahertz tools for medical testing outside large laboratories.
pmc-11676789:
Yansong Gao leads a team that tracks metabolite change in fermented whey. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with Kluyveromyces marxianus fermentation. Fermented whey can gain health linked traits.

A non targeted scan read the small molecule mix over time. One yeast strain did the fermenting work here. Metabolites grew richer as fermentation ran longer. More than a hundred changed compounds were identified. Groups spanned amino acids, fatty acids, and sugars. The peak content point sat at forty-eight hours. Peptide and amino groups rose by set folds.  Fold gains differed by compound group.
pmc-11677889:
Evgeny Morkovin and co-authors review two dietary compounds, resveratrol and extra virgin olive oil, as guards against age-related disease, in an overview from two thousand twenty-four. A literature search gathered findings on how each compound works and what health gains follow. Both compounds fight cell damage and swelling, and they protect brain tissue.

Their actions pair well, the authors note, and may lift each other's uptake and effect. Longevity and thinking health gains are the headline claims. The review urges long trials in varied older groups and deeper work on the pathways involved. Gut microbes and body chemistry links also need study, they add.
pmc-11679789:
Jyoti Joshi and co-authors show that feeding double-stranded RNA to wireworms can silence their genes. Their 2024 paper targets the larval stage of click beetles, among the most destructive soil pests of garden and field crops. Gene silencing by RNA interference needs two things: the right target genes and a delivery route that works in these tough larvae.

The team built a liquid feeding method that gets the RNA into the worms reliably. They then tested four target genes tied to cell energy, structure, and shell building. Silencing the top target killed half the worms and cut its gene activity sharply. The other three targets killed roughly a third each. Feeding-based control could one day protect crops without broad insecticides.
pmc-11680089:
Caroline Lacorte Rangel and co-authors hunt hantavirus traces in bats of Brazil's Atlantic Forest, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Three hundred thirty-six blood samples from five states over near a decade were tested. Four test proteins came from bat and rodent virus kinds.

One bat virus protein caught over a third of samples, far above the rodent ones. The usual test protein for the Americas cross-reacted, which can blur counts. The team backs the bat protein as the sharper tool for bat checks. Unknown kin viruses likely ride these bat crowds. Readers get a call for better watch tools where bats and people meet.
pmc-11685089:
Jingjing Shao, Tianye Zhao, Jibin Liu, and Peipei Kang published a 2024 study on a gene that may mark hard-to-treat liver cancer. Liver cancer kills heavily worldwide, and its usual blood marker is unreliable for early detection. The team hunted among genes tied to cancer stem cells, the stubborn subpopulation blamed for relapse. Single-cell analysis pointed to MRPL17, a gene for a mitochondrial protein.

They tested its power to predict survival and response to immunotherapy. Clustering methods sorted tumors by related gene programs, and a diagnostic model was built and checked across several datasets with varied machine-learning tools. A marker that forecasts who benefits from immunotherapy would sharpen treatment choices in a cancer with few. The authors position MRPL17 as both prognostic sign and possible target. As with many such studies, the claim now awaits wet-lab and clinical confirmation, but the computational case is laid out.
pmc-11688089:
Ching-Hsiang Yu, Hsiang-Kuang Tseng, Ding-Kuo Chien, and En-Chih Liao report an older woman harmed by taking far too much vitamin D. Their case report and literature review were published in twenty twenty-four. Deficiency is common in the elderly, but overshooting carries its own dangers.

Over three days the woman grew weak in the legs, confused, and swollen in the belly. Brain bleeding was ruled out; blood tests showed several mineral imbalances and severe excess calcium. Questioning revealed she had swallowed large amounts of liquid vitamin D for three weeks, past the poisoning threshold. Fluids to flush calcium through the kidneys began her recovery. The authors urge better teaching on safe doses, especially when caregivers give the supplements.
pmc-11688889:
Ashley Curtis and Christina McCrae introduce a symposium in two thousand twenty-four on theory-guided ways to improve behavioral treatments for older adults. Too few geriatric mental health providers exist, drugs for thinking and sleep problems work only modestly, and drug side effects pile up in older patients. Behavioral approaches are a promising answer.

The session's papers share one theme: using psychosocial theory to tune treatments to the people who will use them. One paper applies a biopsychosocial model to cognitive training and weighs how expectations shape gains. Another describes step-by-step refinement of a wellness program for older adults.
pmc-11688989:
Joann Montepare, Rowena Gomez, and Harvey Sterns write about how large groups for scholars can help staff who are near the end of their work lives, or past it. Their piece comes from two thousand twenty-four and centers on higher schools of learning.

More staff now work past age sixty-five, so schools are places where people age on the job. The authors share a survey of three hundred ninety-one members, all aged fifty-two or more, from a large mind and behavior group. Members asked for talks and plans on job change, money strain, health, and ways to stay linked to peers. The paper urges groups to use a full life-span view for their own members.
pmc-11689689:
Patricia Heyn, writing in two thousand twenty-four, looks at short skill badges, called micro-credentials, at schools that serve many Hispanic students. Such schools enroll at least a quarter Hispanic undergraduates and form one of the fastest growing groups in higher learning.

Heyn argues these badges can widen access for Hispanic learners. They give bendable paths that respect culture and life duties, and they link school gains to skills firms want. Tied to fields with high demand, they may raise the pay of Hispanic graduates. Yet she flags hard gaps: bosses and schools still do not grant the badges full weight, and their worth needs proof. The piece weighs real gains against work still to be done.
pmc-11689889:
Keri Christensen, Jennifer Severance, and Lesca Hadley published a study in 2024 on training medical students in rural clinics. Early practice in quality improvement readies students for complex care systems. The team built a course on an age-friendly frame that stresses four themes in elder care.

Seventy-five third-year students took the course during a twelve-week rural family medicine rotation. Online lessons covered improvement cycles and the elder-care frame before the rotation. In clinic, each student ran a small project to make care more age-friendly in their practice. Weekly video meetings with geriatrics faculty gave support. In surveys, fifty students reported real gains in improvement skills and grasp of why process matters. The authors say the frame spreads well through student projects.
pmc-11690989:
Eunju Lee, Kyungmin Kim, Yin Liu, and Steven Zarit published a study in 2024 on daily stressors, positive experiences, and daily fatigue among family caregivers of people with dementia. Caregivers often feel exhausted in body and mind, yet little was known about how that fatigue rises and falls from day to day.

The researchers tracked 173 caregivers through daily interviews over eight consecutive days. On days with more care-related stress or more stress from the rest of life, caregivers felt more fatigued. On days with more positive experiences, they felt less fatigued. Conflict with family members about caregiving made the link between care-related stress and fatigue worse. The findings show that support for caregivers needs to consider the whole day, not only the care tasks.
pmc-11691889:
Hisashi Kawai and seven colleagues published a 2024 study tracking how functional competence declines with age in Japan. Competence here means the higher-level abilities needed for independent daily life, such as using transport, managing money, and engaging with society. A newer index, the JST-IC, was designed to measure higher levels of competence than the older Tokyo index.

The study followed 775 community-dwelling older adults in the Otassha study who attended health check-ups at least three times between 2014 and 2019. It compared the aging trajectories of the two indices over time. Knowing the normal trajectory of each index helps clinicians spot decline that is faster than expected and intervene earlier.
pmc-11692289:
Miseon Kang, Seolah Lee, Inhye Jung, and Hyo Jung Lee published a study in 2024 on changes in digital literacy among older adults. They also examined what those changes mean for life satisfaction. Society's rapid digitalization requires technology use in daily life, and the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated that shift.

The researchers used a Korean media panel survey. It covered 1,924 adults over sixty-five who responded from 2019 to 2021. Four patterns of change emerged. Most people belonged to a group whose skills rose from a low starting level. About a third rose from a medium level. Smaller groups maintained a high level or rose rapidly. All three of those groups reported greater life satisfaction than the low-level group. The team finds that most older adults did gain digital skill during those years. They argue that support should be tailored to each skill level, because the variation is wide.
pmc-11692889:
Khalil Iktilat, Roy Tzemah-Shahar, and Maayan Agmon published a 2024 study of physical capacity and attention in middle-aged adults. Links between fitness and thinking are well studied in the young and the old, but not in the years just before old age. The participants were 255 Muslim adults in Israel, a group facing long-running health gaps.

Two physical tests were used: a six-minute walk and a 30-second sit-to-stand count. Attention was measured with the Stroop test and a trail-making test. Sit-to-stand performance tracked with Stroop scores, even after accounting for age, sex, education, and blood sugar. Walking distance tracked with neither attention test. The authors suggest that more demanding physical tasks may better protect focused attention.
pmc-11696789:
Moritz Hartleb and co-authors tested whether a cross-section indentation method can measure how strongly thin film layers stick together in chip making. Reliable numbers are scarce for stacks with very sticky or soft plastic layers, such as polyimide. The team weakened one inner interface on purpose and varied the test settings step by step.

The shape of the indenter tip and its distance from the interface mattered most. With the best settings, thirty percent of tests gave usable results, a high rate for this kind of testing. A staged computer model accounted for the soft layer's bending, yielding energy release rates near ten joules per square meter. The team presents the tuned method as a promising way to test such stacks.
pmc-11698589:
Benni Iskandar and colleagues reviewed herbal nanoemulsions for cosmetics in two thousand twenty-four. Nanoemulsions are blends with extremely tiny droplets. They help poorly soluble ingredients mix and stay stable. Plant extracts often suffer both problems. The review covers design, preparation, and testing methods.

Key checks include droplet size, charge, and thickness. Microscope methods confirm structure and spread. Such blends sink into skin well and last longer. That makes them attractive for creams and lotions. The authors call herbal versions effective and promising. Cosmetic makers gain a full formulation guide. It collects scattered know-how in one place.
pmc-11699089:
Charles Jonassaint and co-authors trial a phone-based therapy against plain lessons for pain in sickle cell disease in two thousand twenty-four. Chronic pain burdens many adults with the blood disorder, and drug-free options are scarce. Both arms of the trial ran through an app with chat-style lessons and a personal health coach.

Seven centers and community groups across the United States enrolled adults with chronic pain or daily opioid use. Of those screened, three hundred fifty-nine were split between therapy and education for twelve weeks. The main score was change in how much pain disrupts life at six months. Mood, life quality, and confidence were also tracked. About seventy percent finished the follow-up.
pmc-11709589:
Basilio Cieza and co-authors build, in a 2025 study, a risk score for Alzheimer's disease out of gene activity rather than gene variants. Static DNA scores miss much of the disease's heritability. Their score instead weighs how strongly candidate genes are expressed in the brain's prefrontal cortex. The candidates were picked by a random forest from five hundred sixty-five donated brains across six American brain banks.

The donors spanned white, Hispanic, and African American groups, deliberately. The score separated low from high pathology stages with accuracy near eighty percent, and, unusually, it held when trained on one ethnic group and tested on another. Checked in a second large cohort of over a thousand brains, it performed the same. The authors argue that expression-based scores, built diverse from the start, can travel across populations where DNA scores often fail.
pmc-11710089:
Margaret A Pericak-Vance gives a progress report, published in 2025, on the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project. The project began after a national law on Alzheimer disease was passed. The National Institute on Aging set it up to read the full gene sets of many people. Its aims are to find gene changes that raise or lower risk, to learn how those changes act, and to turn the findings into treatment ideas.

The report sums up how the project is built and how far it has come. Its newest release holds over thirty-six thousand genomes. Those genomes come from more than forty study groups around the world. The author stresses the project's push for global inclusion and diversity. She frames that breadth as key to treatments and prevention that work for everyone, not just for the groups studied most in the past.
pmc-11712989:
Dennis J Selkoe, Shobha Dhadda, Michael C Irizarry, and Lynn D Kramer review the case, published in 2025, for keeping patients on lecanemab, an antibody drug for Alzheimer disease. The drug targets protofibrils, a toxic mid-size form of amyloid. It binds that form far more strongly than single amyloid units or mature plaques. A large trial found that it slowed decline over eighteen months in early disease.

The authors lay out how the drug works and why stopping early may waste its gains. Alzheimer disease keeps producing amyloid, they argue, so treatment must keep pace. They review the latest data on the drug's action and on tau, the protein that may predict later nerve damage. They also cover the newest rules for diagnosing the disease. Open questions are named plainly. The paper aims to give doctors a reasoned basis for continued dosing.
pmc-11714889:
Andrea Zammit and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on brain proteins tied to resilience, the power to keep thinking well despite age or disease. Past work found such proteins in the cortex, some linked with slower decline and some with faster.

The team used two long studies of older adults, with more than a thousand people who took yearly thinking tests and gave brain tissue after death. They found forty proteins whose effects on decline spread across up to twenty-five years of follow-up. For the proteins tied to slower decline, effects could start more than two decades before death. For those tied to faster decline, effects bunched in the last seven years of life. The authors say the timing of each protein's effect varies a great deal.
pmc-11715789:
A team led by Pablo Aguero tested a lab assay in this study, published in two thousand twenty-five. The assay measures neurofilament light chain, or NfL, a protein that rises when nerve fibers are harmed. High NfL is a known sign in dementia, above all in frontotemporal dementia.

The team ran the test on spinal fluid from seventy people: some with Alzheimer's disease, some with frontotemporal dementia, and a small healthy group. NfL ran much higher in the frontotemporal group than in the Alzheimer's group or the healthy group. Blood NfL, checked with a second method, matched the spinal fluid values well. One cut point split the two dementia types with strong power to rule cases in. The authors say the assay could help clinics tell dementia types apart.
pmc-11727489:
Gkintoni and Michou reviewed the evidence in twenty twenty-four on therapy for primary progressive aphasia, a condition where language skills fade slowly while other thinking stays stronger at first. Help exists, but care is often generic rather than tuned to the brain changes behind each subtype.

The review gathered sixty-three studies from the past decade. Brain imaging tools such as EEG and MRI scans, the authors found, sharpen therapy by showing which language circuits are failing. Classic speech therapy helped, and so did computer-aided programs and gentle brain stimulation. Watching the brain also helped tell the subtypes apart, which guided better-matched treatment. Gains from steady, focused practice could last. The authors urge clinics to weave brain science into routine care. They also call for studies on long-term benefit in everyday settings.
pmc-11728389:
Wang and co-authors report a 2024 study of the microbes living in soil around the roots of a medicinal plant grown in Northeast China. The plant, Acanthopanax senticosus, is farmed across a wide area, and the team asked how place shapes the bacteria and fungi in its root-zone soil. They also asked what forces build those communities at each site.

Gene sequencing showed that both diversity and community makeup shifted strongly with location. Bacteria were mostly assembled by chance-like processes, while fungi showed a mix of chance and set rules. Networks linking bacteria and fungi also changed with longitude and latitude. Soil traits such as acidity and carbon levels tracked the patterns, and a few microbe groups stood out as drivers of the differences between sites.
pmc-11728489:
Silva Monteiro and coauthors hunt germ pairs that eat oil waste in soil. Microbes offer a low-cost way to clean oil-tainted land. Ring compounds in oil resist breakdown and linger for years. The team sought native germs from tainted soil samples.

Soil came from land dosed with diesel and biodiesel blends. Growth on diesel as sole food enriched oil eaters. Gene reads named seven fungi and twelve bacteria in all. All fungi made soap-like compounds that lift oil. Four bacteria made those soap compounds as well. Paired sets may break oil faster than single strains.
pmc-11728789:
Maruti Nandan Rai and Rikky Rai published a review in 2024 on gene switches in harmful fungi. Fungi that infect people and crops use chemical tags on their DNA spools to tune gene activity. One tag, placed on a key spool protein, has drawn wide study. The review gathers what that tag does in fungal disease.

The tag helps fungi change shape, guard their DNA, and adapt their chemistry to a host. It also aids wall upkeep, film growth, drug resistance, and attack strength. The enzymes that add and remove the tag are alike across many fungi. That likeness makes them tempting drug targets. The authors map the proof and point to gaps where new antifungal drugs might arise.
pmc-11729189:
Davison, Morin, and the Darwin Tree of Life teams present a genome note from twenty twenty-four for the striped dolphin. The assembly comes from a single male dolphin. Its total length runs to about two point seven billion bases. Most of it sorts into twenty-three chromosome-scale pieces. Both sex chromosomes, X and Y, are included in that set. The small mitochondrial genome is assembled as well. The note follows the project's standard genome report format.

Reference genomes like this one support study of dolphin biology and conservation. Chromosome-level detail lets researchers compare species and track population health. The assembly is released for open use by the wider field. It joins a growing catalog of species genomes from the project.
pmc-11729489:
Kulkarni, Accoto, and Campolo damp wrist tremor with a wearable robot using an optimized mechanical metamaterial, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Pathological tremor disrupts daily life, especially in wrist bending motions. Their robot's interface is a custom metamaterial shaped to each user's wrist. The material follows hand paths while minimizing skin shear for comfort.

Viscous damping uses wrist velocity to oppose tremor in real time. An interaction model guides the control design. Simulation and test-bed trials show twenty to thirty decibel attenuation. Tremor amplitude falls significantly at various tremor frequencies. The approach promises discreet, wearable relief for tremor patients.
pmc-11804989:
Koushik Mukherjee and co-authors compare gels applied under the gumline as add-ons to deep cleaning for chronic gum disease. Their 2024 clinical study enrolls well over a hundred patients. All receive scaling and root planing, the standard removal of plaque and tartar from root surfaces. The question is which local agent helps healing most.

Patients were split into three groups receiving ozonated olive oil, plain olive oil, or a chlorhexidine gel, applied at set visits over three weeks. Gum health, pocket depth, and attachment level were recorded at the start and after one month. All three measures were tracked for change within each arm. Local plant-based agents appeal because they are cheap and gentle, but they need evidence against the standard antiseptic gel.
pmc-11810689:
Sujatha Baddam and co-authors review whether the diabetes drug pioglitazone raises the risk of bladder cancer. Their review appeared in 2024. Bladder cancer rates vary widely by place, sex, and wealth, and a drug link has long been debated. The team searched three databases for studies from 2018 to mid-2024. From 212 candidate papers, screening left six that met the rules and had usable data.

Two of the six found a possible link between the drug and higher cancer risk; four found no clear tie. The authors say the split verdict means the question stays open. They call for studies that handle confounders better, especially how long patients took the drug and who the patients were. Until then, they advise care rather than alarm in prescribing.
pmc-11813789:
Li and five co-authors pooled in twenty twenty-five risk tools that guess spread of pale lung lumps by a plain math form. Such lumps can be an early lung cancer sign, and spread risk guides care. They searched major data banks for all such tools built to that date.

Thirty risk traits came up in the works they kept, with sixteen used more than once. Big size, dense core, spiky edge, and vessel signs all raised spread risk in the pool. Age and lump kind raised it too. The tools guessed spread well in their tests, the team finds.
pmc-11888689:
Asha Pogula and co-authors review gene variants in vessel swelling paths as early marks of preeclampsia, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The pregnancy illness brings new high pressure and urine protein past mid pregnancy. Four genes were pooled from case and cohort studies across three databases.

Variants in all four genes tied to higher odds of the illness in the pooled counts. Named forms in growth, swelling, calm, and fat genes each carried part of the signal. The authors frame the marks as leads for early checks and targeted care. More work on how the variants act is still owed. Readers get a short gene list with pooled weight behind each entry.
pmc-11894989:
Ting Xu and co-authors test a plant alkaloid against poxvirus infection, in a research paper from 2024. The work follows the 2022 mpox outbreak, which the World Health Organization declared a global emergency. Drug options against poxviruses remain few and slow to arrive.

The compound, narciclasine, blocked vaccinia virus, a model poxvirus, at very low doses in cell tests. It chiefly cut the output of the wrapped form of the virus that spreads between cells. The effect seems to run through activation of the RhoA signaling pathway, which shapes the cell's inner frame. The authors present narciclasine as a promising lead for new poxvirus drugs and urge further development.
pmc-12670789:
Isabella Kimmeswenger and co-authors present a 2025 study of exercise, taste buds, and sweet taste in adults. Hard training sparks low-grade inflammation, which may dull taste. The team compared 34 highly active adults with 31 low-activity ones. They logged tongue bud size and count, sweet taste thresholds, sweet food habits, saliva and urine markers, body makeup, and food-drive hormones.

The active group needed about 36 percent more sugar before they could taste it. Their saliva held about 26 percent more of an inflammation signal. Their taste buds were also fewer and smaller on average. A summary model split the main traits into two axes, one for body and buds, one for taste and signal levels. Sweet taste may dim as a side effect of hard training.
pmc-12690089:
Johanna Dudek and co-authors test whether a lab-made mineral can stand in for real tooth enamel in studies of dental plaque. Enamel is mostly hydroxyapatite, but its exact makeup differs from person to person, which clouds comparisons. The team grew the mouth's first biofilm on synthetic hydroxyapatite pellets and on natural enamel, side by side, inside volunteers' mouths.

The films formed at the same speed, with the same structure, and each person's film kept its personal stamp on both materials. Protein patterns matched as the films matured, and the later bacterial films looked alike in shape and timing. One difference favored the stand-in: bacteria stayed more alive on the mineral, which suits tests of germ-fighting agents. The authors call synthetic hydroxyapatite a perfect substitute for enamel in biofilm research.
pmc-12692589:
Afnan Alotaibi and colleagues assessed nurse handovers after surgery in two thousand twenty-five. Poor handovers lose critical patient information. They contribute to errors and broken care continuity. Four hospitals in Jeddah took part. Nurses worked in theaters, recovery, intensive care, and wards. An online form rated handover quality.

Overall quality reached roughly three-quarters of the maximum. Conduct and quality items scored highest. Female nurses performed better on teamwork measures. Older nurses scored better on conduct and quality. Education and experience shaped results further. Standardized handover training could lift the weakest areas. Surgical patients depend on these transitions daily.
pmc-12705689:
Michael Fridén and a large team of co-authors race two designed diets against usual care for liver fat in diabetes. Their trial appeared in twenty twenty-five. Fatty liver shadows type two diabetes and prediabetes, and polyunsaturated fat had shown promise against it.

One hundred fifty adults ate freely for twelve months on one of three plans. The anti-lipogenic diet swapped carbohydrates for polyunsaturated fat. The healthy Nordic diet leaned on whole grains and low fat. Both cut liver fat by roughly one and a half percentage points more than usual care. The Nordic plan also shed more weight and blood sugar. No winner emerged between the two diets on the main measure.
pmc-12706189:
Iris van de Voort and co-authors study in 2025 how hospital work wears down the people who give care. When staff cannot stay in their jobs in a healthy way, care quality suffers, and poor care in turn wears staff down. The team watched two teams in a Dutch hospital, in the emergency room and the operating room.

They found three habits that set the cycle in motion. Staff were stretched too thin as a routine. Workers felt far from decision makers. And raised concerns were often ignored. Over time these bred quiet feelings of discontent, distrust, and apathy, which the authors call an undertow. They urge leaders to treat such feelings as warning signs, not noise.
pmc-12706489:
Devan Patel and a team of co-authors describe a case, published in twenty twenty-five, of a nail gun injury to the brain. A man in his forties shot a nail into the left side of his own head at work, by accident. He arrived with no loss of movement or feeling, which is rare for such injuries.

Scans showed the nail in the brain with a small bleed around it and no clear damage to blood vessels. Doctors checked the vessels with a catheter test before surgery, then removed the nail in a room fitted for both surgery and vessel imaging. A repeat vessel check during surgery showed no leak. He went home the day after surgery, and later checks found no weak spot on a vessel.
pmc-12709789:
Qian Yao, Bin Zhan, Huimin Liu, Liu Luo, and Lin Tang report three cases of heart myxoma in one family line, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Myxomas are the most common benign heart tumors, yet they can break loose and block vessels. Two cases formed a father-daughter pair; a third was found after a sudden worsening.

Scans showed growths inside the heart, and surgery removed them under bypass. Tissue checks confirmed the diagnosis. Gene testing found a PRKAR1A mutation passed from father to daughter, an uncommon route. All recovered well, and the authors urge steady follow-up for recurrence.
pmc-12712089:
Mina Fahim and three co-authors found exact wave forms for a hard math model of light pulses. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, works on a sixth order form of the Schrödinger equation. This model tracks strong nonlinear and spread effects in fiber optic lines. The team used an improved tanh function method to solve it. They sought full exact forms, not rough numeric ones.

Their work yields a broad family of wave forms. It holds bright and dark solitons, sharp singular forms, and waves that repeat. Some forms rest on special elliptic functions, and some on plain growth curves. Readers in optics get new exact tools to test how pulses move in fiber systems.
pmc-12714689:
Jose Ramirez led a team building a tool to find variants in ribosomal DNA in a 2025 paper. This DNA repeats many times in the genome and varies a lot between people. Standard variant callers were built for two-copy regions and had never been properly checked here. The team built a simulator that mimics real variation to test common callers fairly.

Their tuned pipeline reached high precision on real data. Applied to a large public genome project, it found thousands of new variant positions across populations. African participants showed the most variants. The authors offer the tool as a robust way to study this neglected part of the genome and its role in human diversity.
pmc-12716089:
Gao and eleven co-authors review tiny tech for burn-away cures of liver tumors in this twenty twenty-five paper. This liver type is rife and grave, and it oft comes back past a cut or burn. Burn cures kill the lump with heat, cold, shock, or light at its spot.

Inside, tiny trucks can haul drugs to the lump and drop them on a set cue. They can also guide the burn by scan and wake the guard net at the spot. The review sorts those gains by burn type, from heat wave to light heat. Force and safe grades rose in test work the team pools here. The team ends with what still bars such trucks from wide ward use.
pmc-12716789:
Li and seven co-authors show that a DNA repair protein also helps run the body clock in fish in this twenty twenty-five study. The protein is best known for fixing sun harm in DNA when light hits it. Its kin serve as clock parts in many species, which raised the ask of shared roles.

Inside, fish cells that lack the protein show weak clock beats in a key clock gene. The protein can both lift and curb gene use at two types of gene switches. It also binds clock parts in ways that block them from pairing as they should. The work shows that DNA repair and clock work meet in this one protein.
pmc-12717689:
Inkster and co-authors probe marks on DNA in womb tissue from a rare flare ill. The ill, called CIUE, sends dam cells into the gap space of the womb sac. No clear cause is known for the cell flood. The ill links to sac harm, loss of the child, and stunted growth. The team guessed the sac would show a set DNA mark script. Marks were read on a chip that scans near 856,000 sites.

Clean data came from 24 ill sacs and 27 sound sacs, plus six wall bits. Ill sacs split as 14 high grade and 10 low grade. Checks flagged dam DNA in the ill sacs by gene reads. Cell mix and cell age scores were also worked from the marks.
pmc-12718389:
Zied Riahi and a large team study the genetics of deafness present from birth in North Africa and Jordan. Their study came out in 2025. The cohort covers four hundred fifty unrelated patients with severe family hearing loss, drawn from five countries where marriage between relatives is common, which concentrates recessive gene variants.

Genome analysis found more than two hundred different mutations across forty-nine deafness genes, and over a third were previously unreported. The analysis fully resolved nine in ten cases of the isolated recessive form. Most mutations were private to single families, with a few shared exceptions. A tricky group of genes can cause either isolated deafness or Usher syndrome, which adds vision loss, depending on the mutation. The team proposes a reclassification that could improve diagnosis and counseling.
pmc-12719589:
Chao Guan and seven co-authors chart how lung cancer's surroundings change at each landing site, in a 2025 paper. Lung adenocarcinoma most often spreads to lymph nodes, brain, bone, and liver. Each site reshapes the tumor's microenvironment, the mix of immune and support cells around it, which in turn steers treatment success.

Node deposits show tired killer T cells and heavy immune braking. Brain deposits form an immune desert behind the blood-brain barrier. Bone deposits stir the cells that dissolve bone, while liver deposits lean on the liver's own guard cells to suppress attack. Shared markers, led by the PD-L1 brake signal, recur across sites. The authors argue that pairing immune therapy with site-specific fixes offers the best path forward.
pmc-12725589:
Siti Roszilawati Ramli and her team set out a case set of three scrub typhus ills that ended in death in Malaysia. Their 2025 work calls the ill, borne by mites, a left-out and death-linked ill. It is oft missed in hot zones.

All three sick folk came in with strain in breath and with more than one part of the body in fail state. Lab tests made the germ that drives the ill firm. Low test marks hint high loads of germs, tied to how grave the ill was. Gene checks showed two clear strains in flow in the zone. The scab-like bite marks were there but missed at first in two cases. The team marks that vague signs make sight of the ill in care key. An early find and gene proof are a must to cut deaths from this ill, which care can cure.
pmc-12727889:
Jiaxin He, Ke Liu, Zhenhui Ma, and Zhiyu He survey Chinese university students on green food buying, in a twenty twenty-five study. Green food choices help health and the planet, yet what drives young buyers is not fully clear. The team asked 836 students about their digital skills, their care for nature, and their plans to buy green food. They tested an expanded model of planned behavior with these factors added.

Digital skill raised buying plans both directly and by lifting attitudes and a sense of control. Care for nature shaped plans through every path in the model. Oddly, digital skill did not move what students felt others expected of them. The authors say digital know-how acts as mental capital while green values form the base.
pmc-12727989:
Bo Song, Shixuan Liang, Peng Wu, Xiaomin Li, and Qian Gong review how immune cells from a simple blood draw could serve breast cancer care. Their review was published in twenty twenty-five. Breast cancer is now the most common cancer worldwide, and current screening has clear limits.

Mammograms miss some cancers, and ultrasound flags too many false alarms, which can lead to needless treatment. The cells reviewed, called PBMCs, patrol the blood and change their inner makeup when disease is present. Reading those changes could aid early detection, judging how treatment works, and forecasting outcome. Since the cells come from a blood sample, tests would be gentle and repeatable. The review maps what is known and what still needs proof before clinic use.
pmc-12728989:
Sujeong Shin and Jongmin Woo published this hospital study in 2025. Carbon monoxide poisoning, from accidents and suicide attempts, is a serious problem in South Korea. Breathing pure oxygen under pressure is the main treatment. The team reviewed records for 288 treated patients from 2020 to 2023. They split patients by whether they arrived alert or with clouded consciousness, and compared the groups' early features and courses.

About two-thirds of patients were men, typically in their mid-forties. Alert patients reached hospital sooner. Suicide attempts were far more common in the non-alert group, at eighty-four percent. Heart damage, shock, and ventilator use also clustered there. Most symptoms eased early in the oxygen protocol for both groups. The authors caution that delayed brain and psychiatric effects can still appear later, even in patients who arrived alert. They urge closest watching for those with neurological signs or heart injury.
pmc-12729189:
Li Li and co-authors validate a mental health knowledge questionnaire in China in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The tool measures how well non-specialists know how to support people with mental health problems. It was built for English-speaking countries, so a Chinese version needs testing before use.

The team translated the tool, adapted it for local culture, and pre-tested it. Then four hundred twenty-five nurses outside mental health care, at a general hospital, completed it. The Chinese version has sixteen items in a single dimension. Scores were steady over time and hung together well, and content checks were strong. The authors say the version is fit for use with Chinese nurses.
pmc-12730489:
Liu and co-authors reviewed an imaging upgrade in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Mass spectrometry imaging maps where molecules sit inside a tissue slice. Ion mobility adds a sorting step that separates look-alike molecules by shape. Fused together, the two give both a map and a structural fingerprint.

The review lays out the principles and the main designs of the combined method. Uses in cancer and brain disorder research get the most attention. The authors also walk through data handling steps and the software tools in common use. They frame the fusion as a sharper route to biomarkers and disease mechanisms. Workflows for beginners are part of the survey's value.
pmc-12732189:
Four authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five on AI reading of swallowing X-ray videos. Swallowing problems from aging, nerve disease, or structural faults harm quality of life, and food or drink entering the airway is the danger sign. Video X-ray studies are the gold standard test, but reading them by hand is slow and costly.

Their model is a vision transformer that watches the video in sliding windows of three-dimensional patches. It trained on over one thousand one hundred studies from one hundred seven people. Its accuracy beat five standard image networks on every measure the team reports.
pmc-12732989:
Nina Russin and co-authors review what is known about art therapy and art making for adults with cancer. Their review appeared in 2025. Cancer and its treatment often bring pain and emotional distress. Drugs help, but many patients want added support. The team searched six databases for peer-reviewed studies on adults with cancer. From more than 1,300 results, 23 studies met their rules.

The studies varied so much in design that the team could not judge how well art helps. Some used trained therapists, others simple art tasks, and outcomes were measured in many ways. The review is clear that art should add to drug care, not replace it. The authors call for larger, better-matched trials so clinics can tell which patients gain most from art-based support.
pmc-12733389:
Orgil Zorigtbaatar leads a team on knee surgery choices in Mongolia. Their study from twenty twenty-five compares repair and partial removal. Both treat tears of the meniscus, the knee's shock pad.

Folks were tracked at two centers over a span of years. Most had partial removal, while a third had repair. Knee scores rose a lot after surgery in both groups. Pain, movement, anxiety, and joy with care were also checked. Short term results are set side by side for both paths. Tailored choice is the theme of the work.
pmc-12733889:
Mohannad Dawary leads a team reviewing children kept alive by an external heart pump while awaiting a donor heart. Their cohort study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The Berlin Heart is the main bridge device for small children in end-stage failure. Its toll in complications is as important as its success rate.

Eleven consecutive children were implanted over three and a half years. Most had weakened, dilated heart muscle and the sickest urgency class. Ten of the eleven reached transplantation successfully. Intensive care stays averaged months, not weeks. Stroke, bleeding, and pneumonia each struck about a third of patients. One child died before transplant from a brain hemorrhage. Survival three years out stood at about two thirds. The authors affirm the device despite its heavy costs. For these children, the alternative is usually none.
pmc-12735189:
Yu Song and eight co-authors report a surprising fatigue result for a common car steel in a 2025 study. The steel has two phases mixed together, and standard rules say finer grains should resist fatigue better. The team compared two hot rolled samples with similar pulling strength but different grain sizes and yield strengths.

Against the usual rule, the coarse grained sample lasted better under repeated loading. Its cracks grew more slowly and needed more force to start moving. Microscope views showed cracks in the coarse sample took a winding path, which blunted their advance and closed them in part. The authors say well designed coarse structures can beat fine ones for fatigue, if the phase mix is right.
pmc-12738789:
Mohamed Radwan and three co-authors made a green catalyst from one fungus, in work published in twenty twenty-five. The fungus, Aspergillus niger, does two jobs at once. It makes lipase, an enzyme that breaks down fats and oils. It also builds the tiny iron oxide grains that hold the enzyme in place.

Because both parts come from one source, they fit well: most of the enzyme stuck, and it kept most of its force. The catalyst worked across a wide range of acid levels and kept over four-fifths of its force after eight uses. In tests it cleared almost all dye from dirty water and lifted oil stains from cloth.
pmc-12748089:
Neel Edupuganti and his team poll how kind of care sways how good life feels in glaucoma sick folk in Augusta, Georgia. Their 2025 care poll sets drug-just care next to care that joins drugs and knife work. It uses forms that have been checked as true.

One hundred eighty sick folk filled sight work forms and glaucoma forms in late twenty twenty-three. File data was added. Near two thirds of sick folk with glaucoma used drugs just. A third had joined care with drugs and knife work. Sight scores split in a firm way by race, ill grade, and age, but not by kind of care. Sick folk with a bad form told of the most low life grade. How bad the ill was swayed lots of score zones. Splits by kind of care showed just in the drive score zone in this check.
pmc-12750689:
Zengyuan Luo, Linlin Zhang, Zaiyu Wang, and eight colleagues propose a blood marker for kidney disease progression in this two thousand twenty-five prospective study. ALCAM is a molecule that activates lymphocytes and guides them into tissues; its role in IgA nephropathy, a common kidney disease, was unknown. The authors enrolled seventy-one patients and forty-one controls, measuring ALCAM in blood and urine, and its expression in kidney tissue alongside its ligand S100B.

Circulating ALCAM ran higher in patients than controls and correlated with proteinuria and worse kidney pathology. Splitting patients at a cutoff of four point seven six nanograms per milliliter, the high group showed more severe clinical and pathological features. Statistical modeling identified high serum ALCAM as an independent risk factor for progression, and that group had lower cumulative kidney survival. The authors offer serum ALCAM as a non-invasive prognostic marker.
pmc-12751189:
Hsuan-Hsuan Yu and six co-authors study hormone therapy after breast cancer surgery in a 2025 paper. The patients had early cancer that tested strongly for one growth signal, called HER2, but only weakly for estrogen response. Doctors were unsure whether hormone pills still help when the estrogen signal is that low.

Using Taiwan's national cancer registry, the team tracked more than ten thousand patients diagnosed from 2011 to 2019. About fifteen percent had the low estrogen pattern. In both the low and higher groups, patients who took hormone therapy lived longer and stayed free of the cancer longer. The authors conclude that the pills still earn their place even when estrogen response is weak.
pmc-12756889:
Niraula and five co-authors pooled evidence on AI prediction in lung disease for this review from twenty twenty-five. Flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease drive hospital visits and deaths. Many machine learning models promise to predict them, but their pooled skill was unclear. The team gathered thirteen studies under standard review rules.

Patient counts ranged from about one hundred to over one hundred thousand. Models of many types were pooled, and overall discrimination was moderate to good. Readmission models varied less than flare-up models across studies. Outside-tested models scored a bit higher than home-tested ones. Most studies carried moderate to serious bias risks, often from thin reporting. The authors call for standard reporting and real-world trials.
pmc-12767389:
Zhang and co-authors test a potato-based calcium salt that may push dental pulp stem cells toward bone. These stem cells hold promise for bone repair, but coaxing them to form bone is hard. The salt, called POs-Ca, is known for helping tooth mineral rebuild.

The team grew the stem cells and checked safety, bone markers, and mineral deposits. Markers such as collagen I and RUNX2 rose with treatment. Calcium flow inside cells was tracked with a glowing dye. The salt switched on AMPK signals and cell recycling, and blocking calcium or AMPK changed the effect.
pmc-12772089:
Weichong Zhou and nine co-authors build a machine learning model to predict early outcomes after a burst brain aneurysm in a 2025 study. This type of bleeding stroke is a life threatening emergency, and early risk sorting guides care. The team used records for more than eleven hundred patients from four large hospitals, treated between 2022 and 2024.

Twenty eight candidate factors were tested, covering clinical grades and blood markers of inflammation and nutrition. A two step selection process narrowed the list, and six learning methods were trained and compared. Extra patients from a fifth hospital served as a check set. The authors assessed accuracy, calibration, and clinical usefulness, and used explanation tools to show which factors drive each prediction.
pmc-12776189:

Trials clash on whether beams help this group, and big real-world proof was thin. A United States cancer registry gave near thirty thousand such patients from 2004 to 2021. About one in five had radiation. The beam group held more mid-stage cases and more chemo use at the start.

Survival curves and risk models, tuned for the start gaps and matched in a second pass, weighed the beam link. Subgroups were probed for who gains most. Registry work cannot kill all bias, and the authors say so plainly. Still, tens of thousands of cases give the debate a firmer floor. Care teams gain real-world odds to set by trial claims.
pmc-12784089:
Jong Han Kim, Jun Hong Park, Hae Sang Lee, and Young Suk Shim published a 2025 study of body fat distribution in Korean children and teenagers. Body scans measured the trunk-to-limb fat ratio, the balance between fat on the torso and fat on the arms and legs. They compared this ratio with waist size, blood pressure, blood lipids, and fasting glucose. The study tests whether this simple ratio flags children at higher risk.
pmc-12785689:
Ali Mostafa, Israa Zeid, Nariman Abu El Kher, Nayla El-Kork, and Mahmoud Korek model the CdBr molecule for laser cooling, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. The team also tracked how the molecule shifts between two states and how long it stays excited. Their numbers show CdBr is a strong pick for direct laser cooling. They lay out a cooling plan with four lasers in the ultraviolet range. The plan gives hands-on guidance for lab work on ultracold molecules.
pmc-12787189:
Pawel Lewinski and co-authors test how well standard models predict slow strain in lightweight concrete under repeated loads, in work from twenty twenty-five. The concrete uses a baked light filler and serves in structures that face cycles of load. Lab tests ran at a Warsaw research institute on two mixes.

The team measured strength, stiffness, shrinkage, and slow creep strain as loads cycled. They then fit four standard models, from older codes to the newest draft. With set correction factors, the models tracked creep growth well. A feared step by step drift did not appear, since plastic strain stayed very low. The work backs use of this concrete in cyclic load structures.
pmc-12787989:
Haijun Zhang and nine colleagues catalog a zinc-finger gene family across three cotton species, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. One member, GhDBB22, received functional testing under salt stress. Salt harms plants through osmotic pressure, ion poisoning, and oxidation simultaneously. A regulator proven to help could be bred or engineered into salt-tolerant varieties. Genome-wide family surveys are the map-making step before such targeting.
pmc-12788089:
Christoph Tremmel and colleagues compare body responses in video calls versus face-to-face conversation. Their study from twenty twenty-five records many signals at once. Eye tracking, movement, heart, breathing, and brain signals were captured. Video chats significantly reduced movement and gaze dynamics. Staying inside the camera frame explains part of that stillness. Pupils dilated more in person, signalling higher arousal. Heart and brain trends pointed the same direction. Interface designers can compensate for the flattened cues. Presence is partly a bandwidth problem for the body.
pmc-12797389:
Hunter and Douglas interview in twenty twenty-five low-income parents in Scotland about feeding babies through the cost-of-living crisis. Seven themes emerged, from skipping their own meals to quiet embarrassment at seeking help. Working parents felt especially unsupported, falling between benefit rules. Breastfeeding was viewed warmly but often defeated by circumstance. Money talk with health professionals was rare, which the authors flag as a missed opening for help. Family and charities filled many gaps.
pmc-12810989:
Karen Goto and Shoji Oura report, published in 2025, a breast cancer case that flags a rare risk of needle biopsy: seeding tumor along the needle track. A woman of fifty-two arrived with a biopsy-proven cancer that scans showed as a neat, pushing mass. It was an expansive-type tumor, growing outward as a solid lump rather than creeping. Surgery followed five weeks after the biopsy. The removed tumor measured seventeen millimeters. Stains showed hormone-sensitive cancer with a growth index.

The warning sat in the tissue around the tumor. Pathologists found clusters of cancer cells inside the blood clot left by the biopsy needle. Such cells could, in time, grow into a recurrence along the track. The patient healed, took radiation and a hormone-blocking drug, and stays on follow-up. The authors urge sampling doctors to plan needle paths with this growth type in mind.
pmc-12823589:
Jin-Kook Lee, Dahngyu Cho, Youngchae Kim, and Yunjeong Mo present a 2025 study on speeding up indoor design in building information modeling, known as BIM. Modeling each object by hand takes much time and effort, so the team tests a space-first approach built on ready-made composite objects.

Their method defines sets of objects that belong together in a room, then places them in the space on its own using a visual, rule-based modeling process inside standard BIM tools. Designers feed in data, pick and place interior items, and get a layout early in the design stage. A demonstration in interior design work shows the approach can cut wasted effort for designers.
pmc-12824389:
Rineke de Jong and six co-authors test a DNA vaccine against bird flu in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The target strain, H7N9, could spark a future pandemic. Seasonal flu shots would do little against such a new virus. Genetic vaccines can be made fast, which suits an outbreak.
