In mice, the vaccine raised strong neutralizing antibodies and protected against a lethal related virus. In ferrets, one dose already sparked antibodies and T-cell responses, and a second dose raised them further. Vaccinated ferrets also withstood a live virus challenge. The study is preclinical proof of concept, a step toward pandemic-ready flu vaccines.
pmc-12827989:
Byeolhee Kim, Jungyo Suh, Young-Hak Kim, Jung-Min Ahn, and Tae Joon Jun predict, published in 2025, which heart patients will die within five years of a stent procedure. Standard risk models use clinical variables and miss much of what doctors see. This team feeds a machine learning model three kinds of data at once. Angiography videos supply the pictures, procedure reports supply the words, and charts supply the numbers. Each kind is turned into an embedding, and a gradient-boosted model joins them. The cohort held over ten thousand patients.

The three-source model scored better than any one- or two-source version. Its discrimination reached a level the authors call strong for this task. An explanation method showed the sources carry complementary signals, with chart variables packing the densest punch. The authors offer the framework as a step toward forecasts that use everything the procedure already records.
pmc-12830589:
Han and four colleagues map how the eye's deep blood layer changes in vein blocked eyes in twenty twenty-five. Retinal vein occlusion is a top cause of vision loss. The deep layer ran thicker and more vessel rich in sick eyes. Its branching pattern, though, grew simpler by a fractal score. In branch type cases, changes hugged the blocked quadrant only. Growth signals and swelling paths may drive the remodel, they suggest. The two blood layers plainly interact in place, the team concludes.
pmc-12830689:
Tatiana Fernandez and co-authors published a 2025 study on an HIV drug that may also suppress a second virus. HTLV-1 infects millions and can cause severe disease, yet it has no dedicated treatment. The team compared people co-infected with both viruses against those with HTLV-1 alone. They measured the proviral load, the share of blood cells carrying the virus's DNA. Statistical matching balanced age, sex, treatment, and immune cell counts between groups. Dolutegravir use was related to lower proviral load in the co-infected group. A lower load matters because it tracks disease risk in HTLV-1. The authors suggest an existing drug may quietly double as the first lever against a neglected virus.
pmc-12830789:
Taha and coauthors make new compounds that may help control blood sugar. Two gut enzymes break down starch and sugar for uptake. Drugs that block those enzymes can blunt sugar spikes. Long use of current drugs can cause side effects, so new choices are due.

The team built a set of oxindole-based compounds and tested each one. All blocked both enzymes at low doses in lab tests. A few blocked them far more strongly than the rest. Computer docking showed how the best ones fit the enzyme pockets. The work gives a base for safer sugar-control drugs.
pmc-12830889:
Saroj Kumar and three co-authors steer teams of wheeled robots with a hybrid of fuzzy logic and a nature-inspired optimizer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Robots that replace human labor must reach several targets while dodging obstacles and each other.

A Petri net controller then fine-tunes the plan to prevent robot collisions, even with moving obstacles. Lab simulations and real runs both succeeded. Against rival methods and earlier papers, the technique improved navigation measures by about ten percent or more. The authors present it as a practical step toward real-time multi-robot work.
pmc-12830989:
Steuten and co-authors present Glyco-PAINT-APP, a tool that tracks how sugars bind to immune cells. Until now, no one could pull single-molecule binding rates from live primary cells. Their method builds on PAINT imaging, which lights up brief binding events.

The pipeline sorts these events by cell region on its own and at high speed. With lab-made sugars and coated antigens, the team linked binding patterns on dendritic cells to uptake and cross-presentation. The tool also spots fine gaps in mannose receptor binding across several cell types and cell states in the immune system.
pmc-12838489:
Zuheng Wang and eight colleagues published a 2025 study on warning of sepsis after kidney stone surgery. Urosepsis is a severe infection that starts in the urinary tract. It is a top cause of death around the time of stone surgery in the upper urinary tract.

The team built a prediction model from lab test values in 7,464 patients. They sifted 155 traits from before and after surgery to find the ones that matter. Eight machine learning methods were trained and compared. An explainer tool, SHAP, shows which values push each prediction up or down. A clear, simple model could help teams watch the right patients closely after surgery.
pmc-12842289:
Srijit Jana and co-authors review the machines that keep a failing heart pumping during cardiogenic shock, in a 2025 paper. Shock still kills at high rates despite modern care. Severity is staged from at-risk to extremis, and the stage steers treatment. The review walks through the through-the-skin options: balloon pumps, impeller devices like Impella, paired-chamber systems, and full heart-lung bypass circuits.

One major trial showed early impeller support saving lives in a narrow group of heart-attack patients, and the authors caution against stretching that result too far. Device choice hinges on shock stage, anatomy, other illnesses, and the center's skill. Team-based, patient-by-patient selection is the modern standard, they argue, with trials still running on open questions.
pmc-12843489:
Melanie Ochoa-Ocampo and nine co-authors review the fungus Trametes polyzona as a tool for cleaning pollution and for industry. Their systematic review came out in 2025. This white-rot fungus digests lignin, the tough polymer in wood, using powerful enzymes.

Forty-six studies over three decades reported strong enzyme activity and efficient breakdown of dyes, pesticides, and phenol pollutants. The fungus also shows promise as a source of antioxidant and antimicrobial compounds. But methods varied so much between studies that results are hard to compare or standardize. The reviewers flag missing checks on whether breakdown products are themselves toxic. They see room to improve growth conditions, scale up reactors, and harvest useful fungal products.
pmc-12845489:
Alina Elena Coman and co-authors build bone like scaffolds from perch fish collagen and a bone mineral, in work from twenty twenty-five. Bone defects are common, and scaffolds that mimic bone matrix can guide regrowth. Fish processing waste offers a cheap collagen source with fewer concerns than mammal collagen.

Four mixes, from pure collagen to mostly mineral, were crosslinked and freeze dried. The scaffolds were porous and linked inside, with even mineral spread. Stiffness rose with mineral share, and heat tests showed stability. Bone forming cells lived and spread well on the material. Breakdown was gradual, and germ fighting action was present but modest. The team calls the scaffolds a strong candidate for bone repair.
pmc-12847989:
Bo Yu and four colleagues test whether the secretions of stem-cell-derived cells can rebuild weakened vaginal tissue, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Pelvic organ prolapse follows failing support tissue. Surgery helps but recurs often and carries risks.

Patient stem cells were converted into progenitors of smooth muscle cells. Their conditioned medium, rich in secreted proteins, was analyzed and found loaded with matrix remodeling factors. Applied to vaginal fibroblasts from prolapse patients, it raised matrix protein production. In rats with surgically injured vaginas it enhanced repair. The approach uses cells' messages without transplanting the cells themselves. A non-surgical adjunct for prolapse is the long-term goal.
pmc-12857089:
Shalini Moningi and seven colleagues published a 2025 study of older men treated for prostate cancer with low dose rate brachytherapy. In this treatment, small radioactive seeds are placed inside the prostate to kill the cancer at close range. Using such treatment in men aged 75 and older is debated, because other illnesses and the risk of over-treatment grow with age.

The study followed 268 men aged 75 or more who received the seeds. Many also got external radiation or hormone therapy. The authors tracked long-term survival and the causes of death, and asked whether other illnesses at diagnosis should guide who gets treated. Their results help doctors weigh cure against burden in older patients.
pmc-12859889:
Matthijs Michielsen and a team of co-authors pool one hundred trials to find which exercise traits best lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. Exercise is a first-line treatment, but the ideal recipe was unclear, and heart risk factors were rarely tracked together.

About seventy-two hundred adults took part across the trials. Every exercise type cut the long-term sugar marker HbA1c. Combined training and high-intensity interval work cut it most, then steady aerobic work, then resistance training. Supervised programs worked best, as did weekly totals between one hundred fifty and two hundred ten minutes. The review also weighs effects on the wider heart risk profile reported alongside.
pmc-12866189:
Six authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five on a diabetes drug and long COVID. The drugs, called SGLT2 inhibitors, lower blood sugar in type 2 diabetes. Long COVID brings lasting symptoms after infection, and people with diabetes face higher risk. Whether these drugs guard against it was unclear.

Using a large health data platform, the team matched more than five thousand pairs of patients with diabetes who had COVID. Users of the drugs had a lower risk of long COVID than non-users. Lower rates showed up across symptoms such as pain, headache, anxiety, low mood, and thinking problems. The study design was retrospective, based on past records.
pmc-12868289:
Meng Kong and four co-authors mine gene data to find the key gene behind liver scarring in biliary atresia, a grave bile duct disease of newborns. Blocked ducts drive swelling, scarring, and in the end liver failure. The study was published in twenty twenty-five.

The team pulled a public gene set with many patient samples and few healthy ones. They screened changed genes, mapped their roles, and built a protein link web to pick core genes by three rank methods. One gene, EDIL3, was then studied in depth with set based tests, checks in fresh tissue, and cell place checks. The authors frame it as a lead for how scarring grows.
pmc-12872789:
María Ángeles de Pedro and co-authors study fluid released by stem-like cells taken from menstrual blood, in work published in 2025. The fluid carries signals that can steer immune cells called macrophages, which shift between states that fuel or calm inflammation. The team compared fluid from plain cells with fluid from cells first exposed to two immune signals.

Both fluids pushed young immune cells partly toward the inflammatory state. During later stages the effects split, with the pre-treated fluid often boosting or switching the state in other ways. A protein scan showed the two fluids differ in key proteins tied to these shifts. The results suggest such cells, once primed, could help tune inflammation in future treatments.
pmc-12877189:
Angel Baudon and a large team of co-authors report in 2025 on how stress changes star-shaped support cells in the brain, called astrocytes. The team focused on the amygdala, a brain area that handles fear and stress. A brain chemical called oxytocin plays a key role in how the body meets stress.

Working with mice, the team used gene tools, drugs, and brain scans of proteins. They found that oxytocin makes the arms of these support cells pull back for a short time. After that, nearby nerve cells react more strongly to a common salt signal in the brain. This chain shapes the freeze response mice show under stress. The work shows support cells help set the brain's stress response.
pmc-12883389:
Miguel Baltazar leads a large team on color compounds in Portuguese red grapes. Their study deals with twenty-seven red grape varieties. Climate change presses growers to find resilient varieties.

All varieties grew in the same Douro region terroir. Berries were checked over two straight growing years. Color compound totals varied a lot by variety. One variety sat at the low end of the range. Another topped the scale by a wide margin. Gene activity for color building was also measured. Most varieties raised color in the second year.  Color measures joined the chemistry in tests.
pmc-12904489:
Shome and three co-authors bare a brown lump trap in a young woman's jaw in this twenty twenty-five case report. The lump is a rare late fruit of a gland ill left bare for years. High gland call makes bone tools eat bone, which forms the lump.

Inside, the woman, in her late twenties, bore the lump on her jaw's right side. Such lumps can grow in any bone, yet face bones host them but rare. Its giant cells and scar webs earn it a string of past names. Blood salt lows drive the gland call that feeds the lump's growth. The case warns teams to test gland acts when jaw lumps look odd.
pmc-12909189:
Oluwatobi Ogundepo and Arrigo De Benedetti study a variant of a DNA repair protein found often in Louisiana prostate cancer patients, in work published in 2025. The protein, ERCC6, helps fix DNA harm that blocks gene reading. The variant is called M1097V, and it turns up mostly in Black patients in that state, who face higher rates of the disease.

Past work found the variant helps cells shrug off light harm, which may raise the risk of new flaws over time. The authors weigh a paired attack on two repair paths at once. They argue gene, place, and care facts must be joined to close the gap in outcomes.
pmc-12950589:
Jingyun Du and co-authors probe a single gene, dltD, in Streptococcus mutans, the germ most blamed for tooth decay. The germ's harm rests on a web of traits: sticking to teeth, building biofilm, and making acid. The team worked with a standard lab strain and a high-decay clinical strain taken from patients with active caries. For each, they built a version with dltD deleted and a version with it restored, to pin any change on that gene alone.

A rat caries model measured real decay in living mouths. Counts of colonies gauged how well each strain colonized. Lab tests covered sticking, surface water-repellence, and biofilm growth, shape, and live-dead makeup under the microscope. The gene sits in a system that tweaks the cell surface, so deleting it can shift both the biofilm scaffold and acid handling.
pmc-13001789:
Austin Nguyen and Matthew Swisher reported a case of removing a contraceptive implant that could not be felt in two thousand twenty-five. Implants that sit on the surface are easy to remove in an office. Deep ones, under tissue layers, raise safety risks and can be hard to find.

Their patient was a twenty-eight-year-old woman whose implant sat inside the biceps muscle. Ultrasound found and mapped it before surgery. The anesthesiologist then used ultrasound to guide a nerve block near the arm, with local drug placed under the tissue layer. The implant was removed with no extra pain relief needed. The case shows a role for ultrasound-trained anesthesiologists in such removals.
pmc-13086889:
Pier-Valerio Mari and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, trial evidence for biologic drugs in a lung disease subtype marked by high eosinophil counts. In this subtype, triple inhaler therapy still leaves patients uncontrolled. These drugs target type 2 inflammation, a driver in this subtype. The review weighs three named agents head to head on the phase 3 record.

One drug gave the steadiest gains, cutting flare-ups and lifting lung function and life quality. A second helped mainly on flare-ups. A third showed no clear benefit. Blood eosinophil counts remain the chief guide for picking patients. The authors urge careful selection and wider profiling, since nose and sinus disease often rides along.
pmc-13092989:
Milica Nestorovic and David Baldwin wrote a short piece in two thousand twenty-five asking what became of research on recurrent brief depression. In this condition, low mood returns in short bouts. More than twenty years ago, an editorial in the same journal called for more study of how common it is and how it feels in daily care.

The authors note that little was known then about causes or proven treatments. Two decades on, they say the last ten years brought no real progress, and study of the condition seems to have faded. Given concern about depressive symptoms in young people, they call again for research in real clinic samples, this time with a focus on younger patients.
pmc-13117689:
Jusselit Estrada, María Angélica Miglino, Nikol Ponce-Rojas, and Mariano del Sol standardize how to measure the stress hormone cortisol in hair across pregnancy, in a two thousand twenty-six methods paper. Hair cortisol reflects cumulative exposure month by month, but inconsistent methods block comparisons.

Three-centimeter samples from each trimester were washed in isopropanol, milled to powder, extracted through four methanol incubations, and measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay. Mean levels came out at four point one units in the first trimester, eleven point five in the second, and six point six in the third. The authors argue a fixed protocol improves reproducibility and could bring hair cortisol into clinical use.
pmc-13146789:
Pierre Seners and nine co-authors examine stroke patients first imaged at primary stroke centers without fast access to clot-removal treatment. Their conference abstract reworks data from the LASTE trial, which enrolled patients with a large area of brain already damaged. The question is whether transfer for endovascular therapy still beats medicine alone.

Of the trial's patients, one hundred fifty-seven fit this subgroup, split between medicine alone and added endovascular therapy. The therapy group had better function at three months, with no clear difference in deaths or serious bleeding. The findings support transferring such patients to larger centers early. That advice matters for hospitals that must decide quickly.
pmc-13148089:
Xinru Wang and Zhaoan Guo review a low-oxygen path that may drive kidney scar growth and could point to new cures. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. The scar state at issue is a key mark of end-stage kidney loss, with no drug yet to slow or turn it. Kidneys are prone to low oxygen by their build, which turns this path on.

The path pairs a sensor gene with a target gene to switch on cell self-eating of worn power parts. That clear-out curbs cell death and flare and keeps cell power in line. The review also traces the path in burn death, strain, and cut-flow harm. Gaps for drug work are laid out.
pmc-13150889:
Duc Trong Quach and seven co-authors compare two scoring tools for bowel cancer risk in a 2026 study from Vietnam. Both scores sort people by their chance of harboring advanced growths in the colon. The newer score adds body mass index to the older one and was said to work better, but it lacked outside testing.

The team studied 714 adults with no symptoms who came for screening colonoscopy at a clinic in Ho Chi Minh City. About nine percent had advanced growths. Both scores flagged the high-risk group well, and the newer score did better in the middle-risk group. Overall accuracy, though, did not differ much, so the authors advise using either score to rank patients, not to rule anyone out.
pmc-13155089:
Yasuhisa Nakamura, Shohei Mori, Shuji Kijima, Masahiro Tanaka, and Osamu Taguchi build a checklist for grading intake interviews in mental health occupational therapy in work dated two thousand twenty-six. A good first interview is a core skill, yet tools for scoring brief watched sessions are scarce. Their checklist has sixteen items, each anchored in plain behavior terms.

Sixty third-year students from two Japanese universities each ran one mock session with an actor patient. Two licensed therapists scored each session on their own across stance, interview skill, and evaluation. Agreement between raters ran from fair to strong across the three test scenes. Inner consistency of each domain was high.
pmc-13155289:
Roberta Santoriello, Francesco Viola, and Vincenzo Citro seek a shared rule behind one style of swimming in a 2026 paper. Squids, jellyfish, and salps move by rhythmic squeezes of the body that push out jets. One form of this motion, peristaltic propulsion, where a squeeze wave travels along the body, is poorly understood, and observations have lacked a single frame.

The team builds a model swimmer modeled on salps and runs detailed flow simulations. The same pattern held across shapes, which let them explain past lab data and match living cases. From that they distill a simple theory that predicts how such swimmers behave in varied forms. The work ties biology to flow physics in one predictive frame.
pmc-13155889:
A large national committee presents an updated guideline in two thousand twenty-six on screening for risky drinking. Older screening tools no longer match newer evidence on how much alcohol harms health. The update revises the screening advice in Canada's national practice guideline on alcohol use disorder.

The committee reviewed studies from two thousand thirteen to two thousand twenty-three on screening tools for heavy drinking and alcohol use disorder. Members included clinicians, researchers, and people with lived experience of drinking problems. Recommendations were graded for strength and certainty with standard tools, and the guideline itself was appraised for quality.
pmc-13166789:
Lale Ozisik and eight co-authors find what drives grave flu outcomes in adults in hospital across nine flu seasons in Turkiye. Flu sends many adults to hospital each year, yet multi season data from mid income lands are scarce. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

Sites in a global flu watch network screened adults soon after admission with flu like ills. Only lab proven flu cases fed the risk study, a few hundred of thousands screened. Grave outcomes were common, with about a fifth needing intense care or a breathing machine and a clear share dying in hospital. Most who died were older adults, and most proven cases had at least two chronic ills.
pmc-13174089:
Rachel L Tulloch and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six study of DNA floating in museum specimen jars. Preserved animals in spirit were long written off for genetics. The liquid around them might carry their DNA, sparing precious specimens from sampling.

Two capture methods plus a harsh extraction were tested on collection media. DNA was recoverable from many samples, including most targets in a mixed jar. Unwanted background DNA from other collection material dominated, though. Success followed jar chemistry, especially near-neutral acidity and low leftover formalin. Jar liquid is a real but messy archive.
pmc-13174389:
Ishtyaq Mahmud and Tania Banerjee survey how artificial intelligence is reshaping genomics. Machine learning, deep learning, language models, and generative systems now help read disease mechanisms, design treatments, and tailor care to the patient. The review maps these methods onto tasks such as sequencing, spotting variants, reading gene activity, and guiding CRISPR edits.

The authors catalog the main tools, benchmark datasets, and open software that support the field. Problems persist: data quality, hard-to-explain models, ethics, and sheer computing scale. They see promise in merging many kinds of biological data through graph networks and multimodal models, and in newer ideas such as synthetic genomes and digital twins of patients.
pmc-13177389:
Tatsuhiko Tanaka and a large team functionally characterise a rare immune disorder presenting without the usual pigment loss, in two Japanese patients. Their 2026 study concerns Griscelli syndrome type two caused by variants in a transport gene.

The syndrome classically combines pale pigmentation with life-threatening immune overactivation. These patients kept normal pigmentation, a presentation called sine albinism. Laboratory systems lacking the gene tested each variant pair's function. Some variants failed to restore pigment granule distribution and lost binding to two partner proteins. Others preserved one partner interaction but weakened the other. The findings show gene variants can separate pigment transport from immune function, so normal pigmentation cannot exclude the syndrome.
pmc-13179889:
Kai Shi and colleagues traced how rain washes phosphorus out of farmland into rivers in two neighboring small watersheds in the Sichuan Basin. Phosphorus loss feeds water pollution, yet its timing across scales and farm types was poorly known. One river drains mostly rice paddies, the other mostly dry fields. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team paired satellite data on rain and land cover with river monitoring of phosphorus. Other quality measures, then applied cross-correlation and fractal tools to link rain patterns with river phosphorus.

The two watersheds behaved oppositely: phosphorus fell downstream in the paddy river but rose downstream in the dryland river. Rain and phosphorus stayed linked over long periods in paddy areas, but only briefly in dry areas before the link flipped and wobbled. Dryland coupling was less stable overall, the fractal measures showed.
pmc-13189589:
Yuanbo Kang, Nanze Yu, Xiao Long, and Jiuzuo Huang report a mass that hid foreign bodies. Their case from twenty twenty-six deals with a woman of fifty-one. A lump under her skin kept coming back after cuts.

First reads called the mass a fibrolipoma, a fat based growth. Later work named it a post trauma hemangioma, a vessel growth. A slingshot wound four decades past had left bits inside. Those bits kept the mass coming back, it turned out. Scans showed odd nodules that hinted at vessel flaws. Full removal with in surgery checks is stressed.
pmc-13190389:
Victoria García and co-authors untangle two phone problems that are often mixed up. One is mobile addiction, a compulsive pull to keep using the phone. The other is nomophobia, the fear of being out of reach of it. They surveyed 366 Spanish workers, aged 18 to 99, and compared levels of both problems across age groups.

Both problems ran higher in younger people, the generation that grew up with the technology, than in older ones. Age also changed how the two problems relate: the link between addiction and fear differed across the age span, so age acts as a moderator. The authors argue the two should be studied as distinct but connected conditions. They call age a key factor for any program that aims to prevent or treat problem phone use.
pmc-13194989:
Pei Li leads a 2026 study of a gene mutation causing inherited enamel defects, a condition called amelogenesis imperfecta. Enamel, the hardest body substance, forms under control of dental epithelium cells. A patient-derived change in the KDF1 gene was suspected, but its disease mechanism was unclear. The team built mice carrying the same change.

Mutant mice showed graded enamel defects, thinner, poorly mineralized, and disorganized, with less enamel protein as gene copies rose. Gene activity scans pointed to weakened cell adhesion and a disturbed growth pathway, Hippo-YAP. Cell tests showed faster growth, weaker sticking, and excess activity of a growth switch. Blocking that switch rescued the cell defects, supporting the proposed mechanism.
pmc-13195889:
Comas-Alberti and coauthors compare protein patterns in brain illness by sex. Protein tests in spinal fluid and blood have taught teams a lot. Yet few studies split those patterns by sex or match both fluids. Gaps are large for Alzheimer disease and two related illnesses.

The team used a sharp test that tracks many proteins at once. They used paired spinal fluid and blood from the same patients. Their aim was to find sex-linked and illness-linked protein shifts. Such shifts may show how each illness harms the brain. They may also guide tests that work well for both sexes.
pmc-13196789:
Yuya Ohga and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a heart attack with open arteries. Their patient was a 76-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis, a disease that thickens skin and harms small blood vessels. She had lasting chest pain, yet scans showed no blocked heart artery.

Heart scans showed a weak patch of heart muscle and signs of tissue stress. Blood tests showed a brief rise in inflammation that cleared with no infection found. Later tests ruled out artery spasm but showed poor flow in tiny heart vessels. Drugs that widen small vessels eased her symptoms. At three months her heart scans were normal, and no relapse came in a year.
pmc-13197189:
Danil Markelov and colleagues present a 2026 theory framework for SABRE, a method that boosts weak magnetic signals. SABRE uses a special form of hydrogen gas to pump up nuclear signals without changing the target substance. At near-zero magnetic fields, the pumping acts in ways that are hard to model for many atoms at once.

Their math rests on symmetry, a sameness in the spin system that lets them shrink the problem. The full motion of spins, swapping, and signal decay fits inside a smaller space. Checks on small systems matched exact math. They then modeled a fourteen-spin complex, far past the reach of standard methods. The tool can help design stronger signal-boosting tests.
pmc-13197289:
Feyza Icoglu Aksakal and colleagues report a 2026 lab study of a copper-based nano pesticide in zebrafish. Tiny copper hydroxide particles are sprayed on crops more and more. The team asked how they harm fish that were never the target, using gene and chemical profiling.

Young and adult zebrafish were exposed at levels below those that kill outright. Gene tests showed shifts in copper handling, stress response, and cell death paths. Effects grew with dose and were strongest in larvae and adult liver. Chemical profiles showed broad shifts in energy and amino acid use, the building blocks of proteins. Liver strain signs rose in adults. The results flag risks for water life near farms.
pmc-13200289:
Walid Hammad presents a four-finger touch method to place a heart protection tube during heart surgery, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The tube feeds a guard fluid backward through a heart vein, but some surgeons struggle to find the vein mouth by feel. Each finger is set to a fixed landmark so the hand maps the target groove.

Two hundred adult patients were treated with the method in a row. First-try success hit ninety-four percent, and mean time fell as surgeons learned. Brief drops in blood pressure or heart rate hit a few early cases and cleared fast. No case switched to open viewing. Readers get a simple hand skill with a short learning curve.
pmc-13206389:
How sure gamblers feel that they can control their own betting may shape how much harm gambling does them. Ainhoa Coloma-Carmona, Cristina Valdivia Blanco, José Luis Carballo, and Antonia Pelegrín-Muñoz surveyed Spanish adults online and focused on nine hundred and twenty-one who had gambled in the past year. They split the group by self-belief scores and measured impulsivity, distorted beliefs about gambling, and problem severity.

Those with low self-belief gambled more widely, scored higher on impulsivity and distorted beliefs, and had worse problem scores. High self-belief softened the link between impulsivity and problem severity, though only slightly. It did not change the link for distorted beliefs. The authors call the buffering role real but modest.
pmc-13210889:
Montassar Aidi Sharif presents a solo 2026 modeling study of artificial skin for robot touch. The skin is built from an ionic polymer-metal composite, a layered material that generates electric signals when bent or pressed. Robot fingers sliding across such skin create friction and shear that shape the signal. Predicting that response calls for models that join contact physics with ion movement.

The author built a three-dimensional simulation pairing finite element methods with equations for ion flow and electric fields. A hard slider moved back and forth over the layered skin, mimicking a finger. The model tracked how normal and sideways contact forces change over time. It then predicted the sliding current the skin would output. Tests varied friction, sliding history, layer sizes, and transport settings. The work offers designers a way to tune touch sensors before building them.
pmc-13211989:
A toddler's first dentist visit goes better when the storybook stars the toddler, and a 2026 pair of case reports headed by Hitoshi Ishitani tests that idea with generated pictures. Two dentally inexperienced toddlers received device-based picture books made with an image generator, tailored to the real clinic, the actual dentist, and each child's own appearance.

Caregivers read the book at home for a week, and the appointment then deliberately mirrored the scenes page by page. Both caregivers reported lower anxiety before the visit and less worry about crying after reading at home. They rated the children as highly cooperative during treatment, though opinions on the reading burden were mixed between the families.
pmc-13214289:
Nele Sommer and colleagues ask in 2026 how well debriefs work in real ambulance training, where crews learn by talking through calls after the fact. They polled 177 trainees and their field teachers on debrief quality, self-review skill, felt safety, and speaking up.

The two groups rated felt safety and speaking up much the same. They split on debrief quality and self-review skill. For teachers, self-review skill tracked debrief quality most. For trainees, felt safety mattered most, since safe rooms made debriefs feel good. Felt safety also linked to speaking up in both groups. The team urges coach training that builds safe, thoughtful talk, not just routine chats.
pmc-13214389:
Tatsuya Horibe and co-authors search in 2026 for warning signs that a heart surgery patient's lungs will oxygenate blood poorly after the heart-lung machine stops. Such lung trouble is frequent after bypass and lengthens intensive care.

Records for 202 patients at a Japanese university hospital split by an oxygen ratio measured on intensive care arrival, with about a quarter impaired. Three features measured before surgery independently predicted trouble: higher body mass index, a history of high blood pressure, and a raised respiratory index from blood gas analysis. Combined, they separated patients with fair accuracy. The index is cheap and already available, so the authors suggest adding it to routine risk checks.
pmc-13216089:
Vanessa Martins Fayad Milken and co-authors present a 2026 case series setting ultrasound reference values for the crab-eating fox, a wild South American canid. Wildlife vets lack normal imaging benchmarks for this species, which turns up often at rescue centres.

Eleven healthy captive adults from the Brazilian Cerrado were sedated and scanned. The team recorded sizes and appearance for the bladder, prostate, spleen, kidneys, liver, gallbladder, gut walls, and testicles; the left kidney averaged 4.08 centimetres long, for example. Overall the images resembled those of domestic dogs. The authors offer the measurements as a baseline for clinical checks and release decisions in this species.
pmc-13217889:
Matthew R. Longo and co-authors present a 2026 psychology study showing that people can pinpoint touches delivered to a tool they are holding, in two dimensions rather than just along a rod's length. The finding extends the familiar fact that a blind person's cane seems to feel at its tip.

Participants held a square wooden board in the left hand while one of thirty-six spots on it was tapped, then marked where they felt the touch. Judged maps matched the true layout far better than chance along both axes of the board. Accuracy was sharper side-to-side than near-to-far, mirroring an anisotropy known from skin itself, and the pattern was organized around the hand. The authors argue that wielded objects are absorbed into the body's own touch system.
pmc-13218089:
Yingyu Pan and co-authors describe the PROGRESS trial in a 2026 protocol: a proactive, graded follow-up plan meant to cut recurrence of acute pancreatitis. A repeat attack is common after the first episode of pancreatic inflammation, and each one adds permanent damage while lowering quality of life. Standard advice at discharge often fades because patients get no continuing reminders.

The multicentre trial will randomize 194 patients to proactive follow-up or to routine care with discharge education and one clinic visit. In the proactive arm, a physician sorts patients into high-risk and low-risk groups and contacts them through the WeChat messaging app every three or six months according to that grade. The main outcome is the number of recurrence episodes within two years of discharge, with chronic pancreatitis, quality of life, mood scores, readmissions, and deaths also tracked. Results will be published once the trial completes.
pmc-13218189:
Quynh Anh Tran and colleagues assess how accurately a contrast enema diagnoses Hirschsprung disease in children when the biopsy service was disrupted by COVID-19, in a 2026 study from Hanoi, Vietnam. Hirschsprung disease, a missing-nerve bowel condition, blocks newborns and infants, and diagnosis leans on a rectal suction biopsy. During the disruption, from May 2020 to October 2021, one children's surgical centre had to rely on imaging.

The study covered 354 consecutive children given a contrast enema for suspected disease, with diagnoses settled by surgical pathology or clinical follow-up. The enema's sensitivity reached 86.75 percent and its specificity 90.64 percent overall. It performed best in babies one month or younger, where sensitivity rose to 96 percent, though specificity fell. Among X-ray signs, the most sensitive was the inverted rectosigmoid index, and an irregular mucosal pattern was the most specific. The authors endorse the enema for triage, not a standalone replacement for biopsy.
pmc-13218489:
Mansoorullah Muradi, Lima Oria, and Tariq Aziz Azizi compare university students' knowledge, attitudes, and habits around e-cigarettes in Afghanistan, the Netherlands, and Turkey in a 2026 study. E-cigarettes were introduced as a harm-reduction tool but have become popular among young adults, who misjudge their safety. An online questionnaire gathered responses across the three countries.

Just over half the students reported using e-cigarettes, and use clustered where close friends or family smoked. Knowledge was poor: more than half showed weak understanding, especially of health risks and the rules for the products. Attitudes were mostly negative, with nearly three quarters voicing concern about vaping, even though most considered it more socially acceptable than smoking. Three quarters of users had friends who vaped, underlining peer influence, and tobacco smokers were more likely to vape, suggesting dual use rather than quitting. The authors recommend targeted education, peer-led campaigns, and regulation.
pmc-13222189:
Misbath Daouda and Carlos F Gould examine government environmental justice screening tools in the United States, in a 2026 review. Rather than scoring the tools' outputs, the authors dissect their structure: which domains they include, how they combine numbers, and what assumptions sit underneath. Use of the tools in research from 2020 to 2025 also comes under review.

Across jurisdictions, designs converged on exposure and vulnerability domains. Adding burdens together versus multiplying them encodes different beliefs about how harms interact, which shifts which communities get flagged. Procedural fairness and recognition of communities stayed weakly represented. The authors warn that these indices govern real eligibility and funding, so their partial view of justice needs democratic context.
pmc-13222889:
Shannon L. Walker and Sarah M. Emery study how a fungal partner inside a dune grass changes the whole plant community's response to added nitrogen, in a 2026 field experiment. The setting is a nutrient-poor coastal dune system where the grass Ammophila dominates, sometimes hosting the fungus Epichloë in its shoots. Nitrogen arrived at real-world and high doses in a long-term experiment.

Extra nitrogen pushed colonizing plants toward larger size and thinner, faster leaves, and high doses first narrowed trait diversity. Root length at community level fell under enrichment, yet that effect vanished when the fungus was present. A microbe inside one grass species thus steered belowground traits of its neighbors, with knock-on effects for erosion and soil function.
pmc-13232789:
Diego Fernando Escobar Escobar and colleagues trial in 2026 planting an Amazon plant beyond its home range as a conservation strategy. Some prized species make seeds that cannot be banked, which blocks the usual storage route. Freezing tissue is costly and immature for many plants, while garden collections hold thin gene pools.

Their inter situ plantings sit in semi-natural forest outside the current range, close enough to wild conditions to keep evolving. The plantings double as enrichment for the understory of recovering forest plots. Tracking seed output and survival plant by plant guides how harvest and sowing improve over time. Practical guidelines close the work for teams guarding other hard-to-bank tropical species.
pmc-13233889:
Mirja M. Wirtz and co-workers issued a 2026 survey study on training doctors to use lung ultrasound for interstitial lung disease, a group of scarring lung conditions. Guidelines call for structured training, so the team ran a six-hour workshop mixing lectures with supervised scanning practice on real patients. Ten physicians, mostly seasoned lung and joint doctors, attended and filled in a survey afterward.

pmc-13239689:

pmc-13240989:

pmc-13241489:

pmc-13241989:

pmc-13242389:

pmc-13242889:

pmc-13242989:

pmc-13243089:

pmc-13243189:

pmc-13245089:

pmc-13246389:

pmc-13246989:

pmc-13250589:

pmc-13250689:

pmc-13253389:

pmc-13253889:

pmc-13256689:

pmc-13256889:

pmc-13259089:
Xu Zhang and colleagues detect land changes in satellite image pairs using frequency information in a 2026 paper. Color images alone often confuse real changes with look alike backgrounds. Their network works in two stages, first locating rough change zones, then refining borders.

A frequency aware module spots blurred change boundaries in the first stage. A fusion module then uses fine color detail to correct those borders. Urban planners and land monitors gain sharper change maps from routine satellite passes.
pmc-13259189:
Emanuel Moisa and colleagues report true liquid fasting times before surgery across Romania in a 2026 analysis. Twenty one centers enrolled over two thousand adults having planned procedures in late November twenty twenty four. Two fasting measures separated last small sips from last larger drinks.

Median fasting reached eight hours to last sips and twelve hours for larger volumes. Guidelines call for far shorter liquid fasts, so most patients fasted far too long. Center practices, care level, and workload were tested as predictors of prolongation. Afternoon scheduling patterns also entered the analysis. Anesthesia teams gain national evidence for tightening local fasting instructions.
pmc-13259289:

A revised mathematical model captures both effects plus large strain hardening. Building simulations showed cold and heating push base forces in opposite directions. Ignoring the coupling can badly misjudge response in long strong quakes. Seismic designers gain a model matched to real service conditions.
pmc-13260189:

Formal developmental care programs existed in eighty-eight percent of centers, and routine breathing tube placement during cooling was reported by seventy-one percent. The most used drugs were midazolam at ninety-four percent, sufentanil, morphine, and paracetamol. pmc-13260789:
Bilton, Knapp, and Tran check whether new urology leaflets for patients are easier to read, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Long lines fell as a share, from ten point one one to six point eight four out of each hundred. Passive phrasing fell, from thirty point five zero down to sixteen point two two out of each hundred. pmc-13261089:
Yehua Dennis Wei and colleagues present a 2026 study of how natural environment and neighborhood context relate to suicidal behavior within Salt Lake City, Utah. Mixed land use near downtown was associated with higher risk, which the authors link to noise, waste, and crime.
pmc-13261689:
Si Wang and co-authors present a 2026 study linking inflammation genes to ischemic stroke, the kind caused by a blocked brain artery. Inflammation plays a key role in the disease. Single-cell analysis showed enrichment patterns varying by cell type, highlighting macrophages and monocytes in the inflammation. The authors offer the genes as potential treatment targets and prediction tools needing further study.
pmc-13261989:
Charles J Ferro and colleagues reviewed in 2026 fish oil supplements in chronic kidney disease, where heart disease drives most deaths. People on dialysis face the highest risk, and standard artery drugs help them little. Their review explains the many actions of omega-3 fats, from calming inflammation to stabilizing plaques.

Events in the main combined outcome fell by forty-three percent, with matching drops in cardiac death, heart attack, and stroke. pmc-13262289:
Hee Sung Moon and colleagues decode why citrus peels from seven cultivars taste and smell so different. Peel, usually discarded, concentrates the sugars, acids, and aromatics that flavor foods and perfumes. Their 2026 study pairs electronic tongues and noses with deep chemical profiling.

Sixty odor compounds were catalogued, with decanal, limonene, and pine-like notes carrying the most scent weight. Sensor patterns separated cultivars cleanly along sour, sweet, and umami lines. Linking instruments to molecules gives producers a shortlist of peels for targeted flavor jobs.
pmc-13262589:
Xinyuan Tian and colleagues show zinc oxide nanocrystals strangling bacterial biofilms by cutting their supply lines. pmc-13263289:
Perla Chebli and colleagues analyze personal writing by Chinese American patients with cancer in a 2026 journal article. Cancer is the leading cause of death in this group, yet supportive care research is scarce. Thirty-one participants in an expressive helping program wrote about their cancer experiences in four 20-minute sessions. The team coded the entries for themes about illness and meaning.

Patients described first disbelief and distress at diagnosis, eased by reframing their experience and finding support. Many worried about burdening their families, then came to value family support more. Dealing with the health system was hard, though trusted clinicians and modern medicine were praised. Participants also offered advice for other patients, summed up in the paper's title about not hiding the illness.
pmc-13263489:
Xiaolu Xu and co-authors report a 2026 journal article using genetics to test whether eating habits cause ischemic stroke, the kind caused by a blocked brain artery. Their method, Mendelian randomization, uses gene variants tied to 32 eating habits as natural experiments. Data came from large genome studies of people of European ancestry.

After strict correction for multiple testing, genetically higher intake of cheese, dried fruit, and muesli each linked to lower stroke risk. The authors call for further studies to confirm the food-specific findings before dietary advice changes.
pmc-13263689:
Kairui Shi and colleagues describe a rare cast of the windpipe that nearly suffocated an elderly patient after surgery. Obstructive fibrinous tracheal pseudomembrane can form where a breathing tube sat, then peel loose. Their 2026 case report follows an eighty-year-old woman two days after lung surgery.

Chest tightness and breathlessness sent her to intensive care after her tube came out. A bronchoscope revealed gray-white membrane and mucus plugging her airway below the vocal cords. Forceps pulled the pieces free through the scope, clearing the passage completely. She left hospital within a week and stayed clear at follow-up. Bronchoscopy both finds and fixes this emergency, they stress.
pmc-13263789:
Chaofan Huang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a nanoparticle system designed to wake up the immune system inside esophageal tumors. This cancer, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, usually resists immunotherapy because its surroundings suppress immune attack. Their platform combines a tumor-targeting aptamer, a short DNA strand, with a danger-signal protein and a STING activator, a drug that triggers innate immune alarms.

In lab and animal models the particles helped macrophages, the immune system's eater cells, engulf tumor cells. They shifted tumor macrophages toward an attack-ready state, matured dendritic cells, and drew in killer T cells. Tumors shrank without obvious whole-body toxicity. The authors present the bridging design as a template for immune-focused cancer nanomedicine.
pmc-13263889:
Bowen Li and a large team studied in 2026 how to judge each tumor separately in patients with several independent lung cancers, a pattern detection keeps finding more often. Telling a second primary tumor from spread changes treatment entirely. Their prospective series profiled sixty-nine nodules from thirty patients with imaging, pathology, gene sequencing, and a fourteen-gene expression assay.

Most patients were women, and family cancer history ran high. Bigger, denser, hotter-scanning, more solid nodules behaved more invasively. Patients whose every nodule scored low risk on the gene assay enjoyed clearly better disease-free survival. A worked case shows the assay flagging the nodule that truly needs action. The authors propose the score as an independent compass for surgery follow-up and added therapy.
pmc-13263989:
Suhail Sapkota and a large team present a 2026 case report on acute myeloid leukemia, a fast blood cancer, in a man who also needed dialysis. Kidney failure limits drug choice, and such patients are often left out of large trials. The report pairs one case with a review of past work.

The patient, a 51-year-old man on dialysis, had very low blood counts and gene changes linked to poor outlook. His team chose two lower-strength drugs, azacitidine and venetoclax, over strong standard chemo. He finished 12 cycles with no major tumor breakdown crisis. Later tests lost two gene changes but kept one, and the cancer came back about a year later.
pmc-13264089:
Cayetano Herrera and colleagues release a 2026 field dataset on bruchid beetles that damage faba bean and lentil crops in France. Daily weather summaries and farm management details, including sowing dates, varieties and pest control, are included. The combined resource supports work on pest ecology and on farming practices that might raise natural parasitism of these seed beetles.
pmc-13264189:

pmc-13264789:
Zhihan Hao, Min Zheng, and Bo Zhang report a case of lymphoma found in both breasts of a 38-year-old woman, in work published in 2026. The diagnosis was revised to systemic Burkitt-like lymphoma at the most advanced stage. Systemic chemotherapy improved her symptoms and cleared the breast lesions. pmc-13264889:
Priyanka Ramesh Jain and Annalie DeLemos wrote a 2026 study on training dentists in Manila, Philippines, to counsel patients to quit tobacco. Interviews showed better skill, more awareness of referral routes, and stronger drive. System barriers like weak referral paths and short visits persisted. The authors urge adding the training to dental curricula with better referral support.
pmc-13264989:
Juncheng Li and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on Coicis Semen, Job's tears seed used in traditional practice, against osteomyelitis, a bone infection most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus. pmc-13266189:

pmc-13266889:

pmc-13267589:

High marker levels on day one tracked with more time under high brain pressure and poor pressure control later. Same-day links were the strongest. pmc-13267789:

pmc-13267889:
Ziad W Elmezayen and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare blood disorder in pregnancy. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura makes tiny clots form across the body while platelets fall. pmc-13268289:

pmc-13269289:

pmc-13269589:

pmc-13269889:

The authors offer the model for studying barrier failure and testing treatments.
pmc-13270189:

pmc-13270589:

pmc-13270689:

pmc-13271589:

pmc-13271889:

pmc-13272089:

pmc-13272189:

pmc-13272289:

pmc-13272389:

pmc-13272889:

pmc-13273389: Correction notice for a 2025 case report on Clostridium difficile peritonitis in a patient formerly on home peritoneal dialysis, a form of kidney treatment. pmc-13273589:

pmc-13273989:

pmc-13274189:

pmc-13275289:

pmc-13275389:

pmc-13275589:

pmc-13280289:

pmc-13280789:

pmc-13282689:

pmc-13283189:

pmc-13283389:

pmc-13283489:

pmc-13284089:

pmc-13284289:

pmc-13284589:

pmc-13287089:

pmc-13287789:

pmc-13289489:

pmc-13290389:

pmc-13290589:

pmc-13290789:

pmc-13290989:

pmc-13291489:
Blocking one immune signal pair may calm gum disease. Sara Di Nicolantonio leads a 2026 mouse study of periodontitis. The signal pair, TL1A and its receptor DR3, stirs mucosal immunity. Their role in gum tissue loss was unknown.

Mice prone to gut and gum disease were the model. Mice lacking DR3 lost far less jaw bone. Their gum structure looked near healthy control mice. Sick gums held more of both signal partners. Harm signals and immune cell counts also ran high. Removing DR3 cut those signals and cell build-up. The pair may thus drive the damage circuit. A blocking drug could help chronic gum patients.
pmc-13291589:
Losing one vessel gene may speed brain aging in mice. Matasha Dhar leads a 2026 study of KLF4 in blood vessel cells. The gene was removed only from lining cells. That loss hit the blood-brain barrier early and hard.

Barrier leaks let vessel and nerve damage build up. Thinking skills then declined in the mice. The model mirrors microvessel failure in aging brains. Such failure is a key step in age-related decline. Guarding this gene could protect the barrier. Its downstream paths offer more drug targets. The work gives labs a ready model of brain vessel aging.
pmc-13291789:
Hanan Alautry surveys Iraqi dental students on oral health knowledge and their own tooth decay, in a 2026 study. The participants were 142 fifth-year students at Wasit University in Kut. A questionnaire covered preventive knowledge and daily habits such as brushing and flossing. Each student also received a decay count using the standard decayed, missing, and filled index. Statistical models linked knowledge and habits to decay scores.

About half the future dentists scored low on preventive knowledge. Roughly half brushed twice a day, and about half had seen a dentist within six months. Low knowledge went with higher decay counts, at an adjusted rate about twenty-three percent above peers. Skipping daily floss also tracked with more decay, near thirty percent higher in adjusted terms. Mean age in the group was twenty-three years. The author argues that dental training should model the habits it teaches.
pmc-13291889:
Fei Ding, Jirong Yue, and Yong He built a 2026 screening score for sarcopenia that leans on thyroid-related measures in Chinese adults with normal thyroid function. Their multicenter cross-sectional study enrolled 3,858 middle-aged and older adults at hospitals in western China. Participants were split into exploratory and validation groups, and statistical selection narrowed the candidate variables.

The final score runs from 0 to 14 and uses age, body mass index, calf circumference, the AST/ALT ratio, and free T4. Accuracy was solid, with area-under-curve values of 0.845 in the exploratory group and 0.854 in the validation group. At the best cutoffs, sensitivity and specificity traded off between catching cases and avoiding false alarms. The authors present the score as a handy first-pass screen.
pmc-13292389:
Xuteng Wang and colleagues review a 2026 food technology challenge: swapping dairy caseinate for plant proteins in non-dairy creamers without losing performance. Creamer powder must wet fast, whiten drinks, stay stable, resist oxidation, and taste right. Plant proteins often dissolve poorly, adsorb slowly at oil surfaces, form films that are too weak or too stiff, and carry off-flavors.

The review follows the full path from emulsion to spray-dried powder, weighing protein source, oil loading, wall materials, and processing together. Physical, enzymatic, and chemical tweaks can sharpen interfacial behavior, yet heavy processing may hurt stability, color, digestion, or flavor. The authors push for multivariate optimization and honest testing in real coffee and tea. They frame the swap as promising for plant-based and sustainability goals, but not yet a drop-in fix.
pmc-13292589:
Heskmatollah Khosravinia writes a 2026 letter commenting on a broiler gut-health trial by Khairunnesa and colleagues. That trial tested a plant-based blend against necrotic enteritis damage in 450 chicks. Challenged birds showed more deaths and higher inflammation markers in droppings than unchallenged birds. The blend nudged survival and two markers back toward the unchallenged pattern. Khosravinia praises non-invasive droppings markers as real-time windows on tissue injury.

His caution is statistical: poultry work lacks agreed cutoff values for such markers, so raw group comparisons can mislead. He proposes re-analyzing by spread, flagging birds far below group means and counting them. On design, he argues a two-by-two factorial with a blend-only control group would have been sturdier than three treatments. He closes by offering collaboration on failure-to-thrive causes in young chicks. The letter is a methods critique, not new data.
pmc-13292689:
Carlos M Nogueira, Filomena Azevedo, and Carmen Lisboa follow a 2026 Portuguese case series asking whether childhood lichen sclerosus really melts away at puberty, as tradition claims. Their tertiary dermatology service traced patients diagnosed before eighteen and before 2010, reviewing records and phoning participants about symptoms, treatments, and life impact in adulthood. Five patients qualified: three female, two male, diagnosed at a mean age of eleven.

Every child had reached remission at first, yet three of the five relapsed during adolescence or early adulthood. One man's course ran severe, with scarring, urethral surgeries, and depression requiring psychiatric support. The authors place their small series beside larger studies reporting relapse in 60 to 75 percent of girls after puberty. Their verdict: childhood disease can be chronic, and families deserve honest long-term follow-up rather than reassurance of a cure.
pmc-13293389:
Irina Vartanova and co-authors chart, in a 2026 study, worldwide shifts in whether partner violence against women is seen as acceptable, and whether violence itself fell alongside. Views that excuse such harm track closely with how often it occurs.

Survey data spanned 1999 to 2024, with over 1.9 million women in 69 countries and over half a million men in 60 countries. Acceptance fell in most countries for both sexes, by about 1.3 points per year on average, a pace the authors report. Places where broad development rose faster saw faster falls in acceptance, and those places also cut reported physical violence faster.
pmc-13293789:
Yadong Dong and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether poor nutrition before chemotherapy predicts harsher side effects in advanced stomach and bowel tumors. Malnutrition is common in these cancers and may leave patients less able to bear treatment.

Records covered 720 patients treated from 2017 to 2023, split evenly between stomach and colorectal cancers. Blood-related side effects hit about half of stomach cases and nearly two-thirds of bowel cases. Being underweight, with low albumin or low nutrition scores, raised blood side effect odds in both cancers. Age alone predicted other side effects. Nutrition checks before treatment could flag fragile patients.
pmc-13293889:
Huiling Zuo and coauthors review treatments for fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems in a 2026 article centered on mitochondrial quality control. The condition, shortened to MASLD, is now among the most common chronic liver disorders. Insulin resistance, oxidative stress, and inflammation all connect to faulty mitochondria, the cell parts that manage energy.

Quality control covers making new mitochondria, fusion and fission that reshape them, and mitophagy that clears damaged ones. When control slips, fat injury to liver cells worsens, and injury further breaks control. The review explains each pathway in turn and surveys drugs and strategies that target mitochondria to break that cycle.
pmc-13293989:
Maya N. Walker and coauthors give a 2026 stepwise protocol for studying alternative splicing in single cells from SMART-Seq2 data. Splicing lets one gene yield varied transcripts, adding diversity that bulk averages hide. Their example uses pediatric high-grade gliomas carrying the H3.3K27M histone mutation, starting from raw reads through alignment and quantification.

Gene clustering with Seurat sorts cell types, and variant calls flag tumor cells. The MARVEL package with custom scripts then computes percent spliced-in values, finds variable events, and compares splicing between groups. The workflow is reproducible and can move to other SMART-Seq2 datasets beyond brain tumors.
pmc-13294189:
Jia Duan heads a 2026 evidence pooling on hospital-acquired infections during ECMO, the heart-lung support circuit. Reported risk factors conflicted across studies, so five databases were searched for multivariable results in adults. Two reviewers screened and graded work with a standard quality scale, pooling odds with random-effects models.

Thirty-four observational studies held about 8,901 patients. Clear risks included immune suppression, transfer between hospitals, infection before ECMO, higher severity scores, longer ECMO runs, kidney replacement therapy, and catheter placement. Each extra ECMO day and severity point added risk in the reported models. Age, body mass, diabetes, and hypertension showed no clear link.
pmc-13294489:
Işık Sibel Küçükünal and Fulya Yalçınkaya look for a listening problem behind children's speech sound errors, in a 2026 study of five- to eight-year-olds. Children who mispronounce sounds are usually treated as having a production problem. The authors suspected faulty processing in the brain's auditory pathways instead, comparing twenty-five children with articulation problems against twenty-five typically developing peers on hearing and speech tests.

The groups diverged on tests that play different words or sentences into each ear at once. Children with articulation problems scored low only in the left ear on those competing-input tasks, a pattern the authors link to delayed maturation of right-brain auditory pathways. Sounds processed poorly during listening, they observed, were the same sounds produced poorly in speech. They recommend screening central auditory processing in every child referred for articulation difficulties.
pmc-13294689:
Hong-Yan Huang and co-authors revise the mushroom genus Hygrophorus in China in a 2026 taxonomic study. These waxcaps partner with trees and grow mainly across temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere. The team combined physical features with genetic evidence to sort out which species occur in China.

Family trees built from three genetic markers confirmed five species as new, placed across three sections of the genus. Full descriptions, habitat notes, and updated distribution records cover both the new species and several already known ones. The confirmed total for China now reaches 63 taxa, giving a firmer base for future work on the group.
pmc-13294989:
Xinrui Yu, Min Pu, Ruoli Wang, and Haitao Ran survey sonogenetics, a young field that aims to steer cells with sound, in a 2026 review. The idea borrows from optogenetics but swaps light for ultrasound, which reaches deep tissue without wires or fibers. Target cells are first equipped with sound-sensitive machinery, often channels that open under force from sound waves or microbubbles. The review organizes the field around its three working parts and how each can be improved.

Those parts are the sound-responsive agents that convert waves into cell signals, the delivery vectors that install them in the right cells, and the ultrasound emitters whose settings shape the dose. The authors propose a standard operating workflow and size up what blocks clinical use, chiefly control efficiency and safety. They close with the bottlenecks worth attacking and the directions where the method could first prove itself.
pmc-13295389:
Enzo M R Reyes and colleagues map social life in an endangered mockingbird to guide moves in a 2026 study. Floreana mockingbirds breed cooperatively in family groups with strict pecking orders. Shifting birds between islands for conservation could tear those structures apart if key members are taken.

Networks from three family groups were charted, then computer removals tested how each loss rippled through the group. Age mainly set rank, yet highly connected and go-between birds mattered most for holding the group steady. The authors argue that moving plans must weigh network position alongside simple traits, or rescues may create fresh social harm.
pmc-13295489:
Gabriela Meza-Fuentes and colleagues report organ support needs in hantavirus lung disease in Chile in a 2026 analysis. The Andes virus illness can crash from fever into lung failure and shock within days, and no proven specific treatment exists. Fresh national data were gathered to guide intensive care planning.

A public hospital registry covering most of the population captured 31 adult admissions during 2024, the full national count for that year. Records detailed breathing support, heart-lung machine use, kidney support, and transfusions alongside hospital outcomes. Such complete endemic-country data help intensive care teams elsewhere judge the support burden when imported cases arrive.
pmc-13295689:
Casandra Juárez Sarrión and colleagues seek early death warnings in dogs with pancreatitis in a 2026 study. The pancreas illness ranges from mild to deadly, and spotting high-risk dogs on arrival is hard. Records of 192 hospitalised dogs were searched for admission measures tied to short-term death.

Three routine blood values stood out: creatinine, total bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase measured at intake. The first two were already known as poor signs in this illness. The alkaline phosphatase link may be new for dogs, the authors note. Using the trio early could sharpen monitoring choices and help vets speak plainly with owners about risk.
pmc-13295989:
Jennifer Muñoz-Grein and colleagues test whether colostrum can lift rumen fermentation in weaned lambs, in a 2026 lab study. In intensive dairy rearing, young animals leave their mothers at birth and drink milk replacer, which can leave the rumen's microbes underbuilt at weaning. The team added colostrum from sheep, from cows, and a shop-bought bovine product at two doses to rumen fluid from such lambs.

Every colostrum source boosted fermentation and raised butyrate, a fuel that helps the rumen grow. Splitting the colostrum into parts showed that taking the fat out changed little. The antibody part, immunoglobulin G, seemed to drive most of the gain. The authors suggest colostrum works both as food and as a microbial nudge, and they back antibody-rich products for young ruminant diets.
pmc-13296289:
Yue Xu and co-authors describe a 2026 method for creating contrast-enhanced brain scan images without giving a contrast drug. Gadolinium agents help reveal brain tumours but cannot be used safely in some patients, including many with kidney problems. Their network learns from ordinary scans plus one extra sequence to predict the enhanced view.

The system first maps where lesion-related enhancement should appear, then guides a diffusion model to build the final image. Tested on the BraTS 2021 dataset, it scored highest on several image quality measures against rival methods. Radiologists who scored the images blind also rated lesion enhancement as faithful, with fewer false bright spots. Using FLAIR as the extra sequence gave cleaner backgrounds than using T2 images.
pmc-13296389:
Akram Al-Ibraheem and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether scanning patients twice with a fibroblast-targeting tracer helps separate cancer from harmless uptake. The tracer lights up tissue around many tumours, and a delayed second scan has been proposed to sharpen the call.

Across varied cancers, uptake did shift between early and late scans, but accuracy in telling malignant from benign findings did not meaningfully improve. Early imaging alone matched the two-scan approach while saving time and easing workflow. The authors recommend a single early scan for routine practice with this tracer.
pmc-13296489:
Qixuan Li and Marialore Sulpizi simulate, in 2026, how acids steady tiny reversed droplets formed by a common soap-like molecule in toluene. Such reverse micelles serve as miniature reactors for making nanoparticles, and small chemical tweaks decide their size and stability.

Atom-level simulations with four acids showed acid molecules weaving lasting hydrogen-bond networks at the droplet wall. That stiffened the surface, calmed the soap heads and lowered wall tension, favouring larger, steadier droplets. Acids differed in strength of effect, ranked in a clear order. The authors offer the ranking as guidance for tuning nanoparticle recipes.
pmc-13296989:
Jingxian Wu and co-authors mine, in a 2026 study, shared genetics between a faulty heart rhythm and eight core health factors. The rhythm fault, atrial fibrillation, is built from many small genetic effects, and its full architecture is hard to draw. The eight factors, a well-known heart health set called Life's Essential 8, span diet, activity, sleep, and blood measures. The team used the overlap as a net for new loci.

Genetic correlations showed for all eight components. A tuned analysis found 970 pleiotropic loci tied to both the fault and at least one factor. Deeper colocalization checks cut those to 137 distinct regions with shared causal variants. Forty of the top genes were new. The genes cluster in heart development and rhythm control pathways. Blood pressure shared the most ground with the fault of all eight factors.
pmc-13297089:
Merve Huner Yigit and colleagues compare blood and semen lipids in men with poor semen quality in a 2026 prospective study. Ninety-nine men took part, roughly half with combined low count, motility, and shape problems. Blood HDL was split into ten subfractions, while semen cholesterol measures were taken separately.

Blood lipid profiles looked the same in both groups, across every subfraction. Semen told a different story, with total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol both clearly lower in the affected group. Semen HDL tracked sperm concentration, movement, and normal shape moderately well. The authors propose semen HDL as a local metabolic indicator in male infertility, distinct from anything blood tests show.
pmc-13297589:
Michael Klowak and colleagues published a 2026 review of alcohol and nerve pain. Alcohol is a known cause of peripheral nerve damage. Its full relationship with neuropathy was unmapped. The team reviewed observational studies worldwide. Drinking amount, frequency, and dependence were separated.

Seventy-six studies met the criteria. Most were one-time surveys of patients. Cohort and comparison designs were fewer. Links varied by drinking pattern and study type. Dependence showed the most consistent harm signals. The review supports counseling patients with nerve pain about alcohol. It also shows where stronger long-term studies are needed.
pmc-13297989:
Three warning signs can forecast which leukemia patients will resist a common gentler drug pairing, report Qingqing Fan and co-authors in a 2026 study. They examined 74 people with acute myeloid leukemia treated with venetoclax plus a hypomethylating agent, a standard option for older or frail patients.

Mutations in the KIT and TP53 genes, together with the FAB-M5 subtype of the disease, each linked to a higher chance that the combination would fail. Combining the three into a scoring system sorted patients into low, medium, and high resistance risk. The authors suggest the nomogram could help doctors decide sooner who needs a different plan.
pmc-13298689:
Plant-based meats nearly match real meat in a few categories and lag badly in others, shows a 2026 open benchmarking study by Sybren D van den Bedem and colleagues. In blinded tastings, 2,684 consumers rated products across 14 categories, generating over 11,000 evaluations and 800,000 data points.

Plant-based chicken filets, nuggets, and burgers scored within 0.1 to 0.3 points of animal benchmarks on a seven-point liking scale, and almost half of tasters rated the filet and burger versions equal or better. Savoriness, aftertaste, juiciness, and tenderness drove liking most. Categories near parity held 5 to 14% market share, versus under 1% elsewhere. All data were released publicly.
pmc-13299189: A 2026 note from Maria Eduarda Altino de Carvalho and her team fixes wrong sums in a past paper on gels that soak up water for farm use. The gels mix polyacrylamide with white angico gum, kaolin clay, and soapstone. The wrong sums sat in Table 4 of the first print. Since the end notes drew on that table, one part of them has been reworded with the right sums for swell, spring, and water hold. The authors state the gist of the work stands as it was.
pmc-13299489:
Drew Barber, Neha Mishra, Fiona Hegarty, and Aviv Paz reveal how the drug miglustat binds an unintended target, in a 2026 structural biology study. Miglustat treats two rare storage diseases by blocking one enzyme, yet it also inhibits the enzyme that finishes glycogen breakdown. A crystal structure of a yeast version of that enzyme with the drug bound shows exactly where it sits.

The drug occupies the pocket thought to hold a branched sugar unit, and targeted mutations there abolished binding, confirming the hot spots. Computer docking predicted a similar, though not identical, pose in the human enzyme. The template may help design related drugs with less off-target binding.
pmc-13300589:
Light scattered off a molecule can betray the shape of the proteins tangled in a diseased brain. Alice Gualerzi and five colleagues review that idea in a 2026 survey of Raman spectroscopy for Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. The focus falls on the clumped proteins alpha-synuclein and amyloid-beta, hallmarks of the two disorders.

Plain Raman and its surface-enhanced version can read aggregate structure in the lab and, increasingly, in blood-based liquid biopsies. The authors weigh what these optical methods offer over antibody tests that struggle to tell clumps from single molecules. Missing standard protocols remain the chief obstacle, they note, before clinics can adopt the approach widely.
pmc-13301189:
Eremeev Spiridon and co-authors review radiofrequency ablation for hemorrhoidal disease in a 2026 narrative article. The technique sends controlled heat into internal hemorrhoid tissue, shrinking it through scarring and fixing it in place, without cutting away sensitive lining, unlike conventional excision surgery. The authors trace the method's mechanism and technical principles. They give the Rafaelo procedure a special look, and set it beside earlier radiofrequency approaches that the literature still muddles.

Across the studies, patients report less postoperative pain, need fewer pain pills, suffer fewer wound problems, and return to normal activity sooner than after hemorrhoidectomy. Symptom control stays acceptable, especially for grade II and III disease. The catch is evidence quality: designs, techniques, patient selection, results, and follow-up all vary. The authors ask for randomized trials, standardized reporting, long term recurrence data, and cost analysis before the method's proper place can be fixed.
pmc-13301289:
Weakness that waxes and wanes defeats a single examination, so José Pedro Soares Baima and colleagues built a 2026 practice guide around scales for myasthenia gravis. The paper walks clinicians through the MGFA classification, the daily-living MG-ADL score, and the fifteen-item quality-of-life MG-QOL15. A case vignette of a 42-year-old man opens the discussion.

Definitions of remission, minimal manifestation, and high-burden or highly active disease are set beside the scales that measure them. The authors show how paired scores guide severity grading, response checks, and decisions to escalate treatment. Their aim is steadier, comparable assessment in everyday clinics, where patient-reported outcomes now anchor follow-up.
pmc-13301389:
In a 2026 retrospective study, Can Zhao and colleagues show that a yellow pigment building up after repeat heart-valve surgery flags patients in trouble. They reviewed 259 adults who had elective redo valve surgery on bypass between March 2018 and July 2024. High bilirubin meant a total level above 3 mg/dL at any point after the operation.

The problem struck 101 patients, a 39.0 percent share, and those patients spent longer on ventilators and in intensive care. Pneumonia, kidney replacement therapy, and hospital death all ran higher in that group. High direct bilirubin before surgery, long bypass runs, and heavy plasma transfusion independently predicted the rise, making bilirubin a stress gauge worth watching.
pmc-13302189:
A Silva and a large team compare, in a 2026 real-world study, left bundle branch area pacing against conventional right-sided pacing in people paced most of the time. The newer method recruits the heart's own wiring and should protect pumping function. Evidence from routine practice, rather than trials, remained limited.

The single-centre series included 663 patients implanted between 2022 and 2024 who reached at least forty percent pacing. Paced trace width narrowed under the new method while it widened under conventional pacing. Pumping fraction rose by about five points in the new-method group and fell by a similar amount in the other. Right-sided pacing carried roughly double the risk of heart-failure emergency visits and of the combined clinical endpoint.
pmc-13302289:
Zdenka Sunjic Lovric and co-authors follow a hormone-like peptide called catestatin through pregnancy in a 2026 prospective study. The peptide, cut from a larger protein, calms adrenaline release and helps regulate blood pressure and metabolism. How its levels move across a healthy pregnancy was poorly described.

Fifty women with low-risk single pregnancies gave blood in the first trimester and again in the third. Catestatin levels fell significantly by late pregnancy, dropping from a median in the mid-teens to under ten units.
