Changes in the peptide tracked with late-pregnancy insulin levels, and third-trimester levels correlated with systolic blood pressure. The authors suggest the decline reflects normal metabolic and circulation adjustments, pending larger studies with complicated pregnancies.
pmc-13303089:
Mette Q. Ludwig and a large team map, in a 2026 study, the brainstem cells through which an amylin-like obesity drug exerts its effects. Cagrilintide produces strong weight loss, especially combined with semaglutide, but its brain mediators were unclear. The team built a cell atlas of the dorsal vagal complex across rats, mice, and macaques.

The atlas covers over half a million cells in eighty neuronal populations, with spatial mapping in rat tissue. Two conserved cell groups carrying the drug's receptor stood out. Silencing a hormone gene in one solitary-tract group erased cagrilintide's effect on eating and weight in rats, while leaving semaglutide's effect intact. Brief activation of the other group changed gene activity without lasting weight change.
pmc-13304689:
Kirti Sharma, Baani Singh, and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how gene-regulating marks control a neutrophil weapon that wrecks the blood–brain barrier after stroke. Neutrophils arriving at blocked brain vessels can expel sticky DNA webs called extracellular traps. The review argues that forming these traps is licensed by epigenetic changes: loosened chromatin, altered histone marks, shifted DNA methylation, and non-coding RNA control.

Once released, the webs injure vessel-lining cells, chew through tight-junction proteins, and stir further inflammation around the injured tissue. Trap components also reprogram barrier cells themselves, keeping the vessel leaky and delaying repair. The authors frame this axis as a source of drug targets for protecting the neurovascular unit and limiting secondary brain injury after ischemic stroke.
pmc-13305189:
Laura Sofia Aguilera-Ariño leads a 2026 cross-sectional study of nutrition and brain development in preschoolers in El Codito, a low-income Bogotá neighborhood. Food shortages at home can shape growth and learning in the first school years.

Children at community childcare centers were measured against World Health Organization growth charts and tested with a national development scale. Household food insecurity was surveyed as well. Most children showed adequate nutrition and expected development, yet some faced stunting risk or excess weight, and scores varied by skill area. Certain growth measures linked significantly to development scores.
pmc-13307289:
Kornelia Kadac-Czapska reviewed tiny plastic bits in foods made for health in a 2026 survey. Such foods feed babes, old adults and sick people on clinic feeds, groups that may face high risk from such bits.

Bits were found in pills, herbs, plant drinks, honey, babe milk and clinic feeds in the work read. Threads and shards were most seen, in plastics such as nylon and polythene in the reported finds. Bits can come from soil, air and water, plus plant steps, pack wear and clinic feed gear used each day.
pmc-13307389:
Karthik Reddy and Shahzad I Mian review in 2026 how doctors can test for and treat damage to the nerves of the cornea, the clear front of the eye. Their search of PubMed and Google Scholar gathered 112 papers on nerve regrowth, imaging, and care.

New scans can show nerve loss before symptoms start, which allows care to begin sooner. Current care centres on drugs such as cenegermin, while insulin drops, serum drops, and surgery draw growing interest. Care is shifting from easing symptoms toward true nerve repair. Clearer maps of nerve signals and growth factors should help match each patient to the right mix of options.
pmc-13307589:
Haibin Ma, Rongchang Liu, and Ming Liao review in 2026 the two-faced role of cell recycling in four picornaviruses of farm animals. The viruses cause foot-and-mouth disease, duck hepatitis, and other costly illnesses in cattle, pigs, and poultry. Recycling can digest viral parts as a defence, yet viruses also bend it to their own ends.

Some viruses use recycling membranes to copy their genomes, release offspring, and hide from immunity. Host cells deploy selective receptors that tag viral proteins for destruction. Viral cutting enzymes then sabotage those receptors in reply. The review walks through each virus and each recycling step in turn. Understanding the tug of war, the authors argue, could yield antiviral drugs and markers that predict how disease will progress on farms.
pmc-13307689:
Xue Gao and co-authors survey in 2026 the H9N2 bird flu virus in Jiangsu Province, China, across markets, farms, slaughter sites, and bird habitats. From 5779 samples, 6.89 percent tested positive, and 12 full strains were grown and sequenced for gene and binding checks.

All 12 strains fell in one known lineage, and all carried a change that favours binding to human type receptors in the nose. Blood tests found antibodies in 4.05 percent of exposed workers and in 2.5 percent of others, a gap that was not firm in these data. The strains also resisted an older flu drug class, so watch systems and vaccine stores need upkeep.
pmc-13307889:
Chenxi Zhang and co-authors trace in 2026 coxsackievirus A6, a leading cause of hand, foot, and mouth disease, in Baotou, Inner Mongolia, across 2023 and 2024. Throat swabs from sick children were screened, and the VP1 gene plus full genomes of chosen samples were read and compared.

Of 266 samples, 169 held an enterovirus, and 146 of those held the A6 type in this set. Cases peaked in autumn and winter and hit children aged 4 to 6 years most often of all. All local strains fell in one sub type, D3c, with a shared mixed ancestry form. Steady gene watch can guide vaccine work and outbreak plans for the region.
pmc-13308189:
Dan G O’Neill and co-authors chart in 2026 the health of giant dog breeds under normal vet care in the United Kingdom during 2019. VetCompass records held 28,345 giant dogs from 29 breeds, a small slice of more than two million dogs in the full set.

Ear infection and excess weight led the list of single ills, each near 8 percent of giant dogs that year. Skin, muscle and bone, and ear groups led at the broader level of grouping used here. Among 1068 deaths, median age at death was 8.94 years in the records, with cancer the top grouped cause. The authors raise welfare worries about breeding for huge size and float shared limits on height and weight.
pmc-13308489:
Gaetano Santulli surveys in 2026 a new class of joined drugs that hit five targets at once for obesity and type 2 diabetes care. The lead case links gut hormone action on two receptors with a drug that switches on three nuclear receptors inside the cell.

In obese mice, the joined drug cut weight, fat, food intake, and high blood sugar more than each part alone could manage. One nuclear path drove the sugar gain apart from weight loss in their checks. The joined form also dodged harms seen with the loose drug, such as low blood counts and fluid build up. Human proof still lags far behind the mouse data.
pmc-13308889:
Farah Abuazzam and co-authors detail in 2026 a giant tubulovillous adenoma of the small bowel, found by chance in a man aged 58 years with chronic hepatitis B. He came in for lung infection and bladder infection, and scans caught a mass in the small bowel as a side find.

Deeper checks showed a large ring shaped polyp mass that ran from the duodenum into the upper jejunum in one span. Biopsy confirmed the adenoma type, with no sign of cancer change in the samples taken at that time. Surgery was planned due to size and place. Such growths are rare in the small bowel and carry cancer risk, so early finds matter.
pmc-13309189:
Souvik Dubey and co-authors set out in 2026 a network level guess that ties the broader autism phenotype to the default mode network and to brain signal entropy. The phenotype names soft social, sense, and thought traits seen in some kin of autistic people and in the wider public.

Family and twin work gives mixed tales, so the authors frame the traits as a chance mark of shared load, not a missed call. Odd wiring of the default mode web, and its links to two rival webs, may join stiff thought to social strain in their model. Entropy scores, which gauge how wild a brain signal runs, could bridge nerve flux to trait spread. Direct proof in this group stays thin.
pmc-13309489:
Luca Del Sorbo and colleagues test two fungal compounds against a dog coronavirus in a 2026 cell study. The compounds, sphaeropsidin A and sphaeropsidin B, come from plant-attacking fungi and had shown promise against a cattle coronavirus. Natural products are being screened as options beside standard antiviral drugs.

Dog cells grown in dishes were infected, then treated with each compound. Treated cells made far less new virus and showed lower levels of a key viral protein. Treated cells also stayed healthier, kept better shape, and showed lower activity in a receptor path tied to coronavirus infection. Acid levels inside cell compartments moved back toward normal. The authors present both compounds as leads for further antiviral work.
pmc-13309589:
Patryk Adam Wesołowski and co-authors review how protein energy landscapes are pictured across levels of detail in a 2026 article. A landscape sums the shapes, motions, and jobs of a protein as hills and valleys of energy. No study sees the full landscape directly; each model keeps some detail and drops the rest.

From quantum-level surfaces down to coarse maps, each step cuts degrees of freedom and reshapes the landscape picture. Many simple models still work because key features survive the cut: funnel shapes, barriers, and rival basins. The authors spell out the physics behind coarse-graining and solvent handling. Their aim is a clearer guide for mixing levels in simulations.
pmc-13309889:
Weiqiang Sun and colleagues pool six studies in 2026 comparing percutaneous repair of fully blocked heart arteries when the first attempt has already failed against first-time attempts. The analysis covered 15,803 patients, with 2,703 in the repeat-attempt group. Blocked-vessel procedures already succeed far less often than ordinary angioplasty, so every repeat case is a judgement call.

Success ran lower after prior failure: just under seventy-two percent achieved clearance versus about eighty-five percent on first attempts. Major heart events, deaths, and deaths from cardiac causes did not differ meaningfully between groups. Drawbacks include heavy variation between studies and a mostly Eastern evidence base. Repeat procedures expose patients to more radiation and contrast, so selection matters. The authors call for multicentre randomised trials to settle who genuinely benefits from trying again.
pmc-13310389:
Lorenzo Marramiero and co-authors test whether tiny parcels from young muscle stem cells can refresh old ones in a 2026 study. Muscle thins and weakens with age, and muscle stem cells partly drive that decline. Muscle also acts as a signaling organ, releasing parcels called extracellular vesicles that carry gene snippets and proteins.

Vesicles were collected from thigh muscle cells of young and older donors and profiled for markers, size, and cargo. Young vesicles carried renewal signals that eased functional decline in aged stem cells. Old vesicles did the reverse, blunting the renewal capacity of young cells in the swaps performed. The authors frame vesicle cargo as a lever on muscle aging worth pursuing toward therapy.
pmc-13310689:
Lushan Wang and co-authors profile registered severe mental disorders in Quzhou, China, in a 2026 study. Severe mental disorders strain families and services, and fine-grained regional profiles guide local planning. Quzhou records had never been charted in such depth.

The national psychosis registry supplied 11,589 registered patients for analysis of traits, care, and trends from 1969 to 2022. Women made up 52.4 percent of the cohort, and 84.7 percent had junior high schooling or below in the registry data. Schizophrenia dominated at 66.0 percent of diagnoses across six disorder categories. Every measured trait differed significantly across categories. Clustering split the disorders into three groups, and trend analysis traced shifting incidence over five decades.
pmc-13310789:
Nazmin Ahmed presents a 2026 image report on a brain abscess with a striking crescent sign on scans. A man aged 22 years with a history of vein drug use came in with two weeks of headache, fever, right side weakness, and seizures. Scans showed ring shaped lesions near the fluid spaces of the brain with marked swelling.

Detailed scans showed a half moon layer capping the abscess cavity, unlike the classic double rim sign. Surgery drained pus and removed the infected membrane and nearby cover tissue. Strength improved within days. Lab growth found yeast with Staphylococcus aureus, a mixed germ pattern. The sign may aid early spotting with full context.
pmc-13310889:
Lixiao Shi and colleagues test cheap blood ratios as risk markers in childhood neuroblastoma in a 2026 study. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumor outside the brain in children and drives a large share of child cancer deaths. High risk cases still fare poorly, so low cost markers to sort risk could guide care strength.

Past cases from a Beijing children center from 2023 to 2025 were reviewed. Ratios of neutrophils and platelets to lymphocytes rose with higher risk stage. Cut points sorted high risk from lower risk groups, and a paired model sorted best. High starting ratios also linked to worse traits. Wider proof must confirm added value.
pmc-13310989:
Qian Wu led a 2026 study on cross reactive antibodies after COVID-19 and a dual targeting lab antibody. Related animal coronaviruses threaten future outbreaks, so broad antibodies are prized. Blood from recovered patients was tested against seven related spike proteins, and memory cells were mined for strong clones.

Plasma came from 67 recovered patients, with 17 severe and 50 non severe cases. Severe cases held broader and stronger cross responses that lasted a year and rose after vaccination. One cloned antibody gripped both spike parts at once and blocked two viruses, though weakly. The clone proves a dual grip plan for wider design.
pmc-13311289:
Rafel M. Prieto and colleagues outline a 2026 case of kidney stones and crystal-laden urine caused by mesalazine, a drug used for bowel inflammation. The drug dissolves poorly in water, which sets up the problem.

A 13-year-old with ulcerative colitis took 2 grams of mesalazine a day and formed stones when the dose was doubled. High doses raise drug levels in urine until crystals grow into a stone on each other. Low body weight and low urine volume raise the risk in children. The authors stress dose care and strong fluid intake to keep urine dilute.
pmc-13311589:
Ching-Hui Chien and co-authors give their 2026 trial protocol on a joint learning program for men with prostate cancer and their wives in Taiwan. The program builds family resilience through a shared theory-based course.

Sixty patient-spouse pairs from an outpatient clinic will be split evenly between the program plus usual care and usual care alone. The program runs eight weeks, with checks at ten and sixteen weeks. Questionnaires cover resilience, family strength, loneliness, happiness, tiredness, and prostate symptoms. The trial, approved by the Chang Gung board, tests whether couples who learn together cope better than couples left to usual care.
pmc-13311689:
Sahar Alviri, Sara Rahimi, and Pooya Pakzad give a 2026 protocol for a study of nursing students' lived experience during children's ward placements. Caring for sick children and their families carries a heavy emotional load for trainees.

The study will use in-depth interviews with nursing students who finished a pediatric rotation, sampled on purpose until no new themes arise. Interviews will be taped, typed out word for word, and read through Colaizzi's seven-step method by three researchers. Checks with participants and an audit trail guard trust in the findings. Results will go to nursing faculties to improve placement support.
pmc-13311789:
Jixiang Peng and co-authors in 2026 present an interview study from Chongqing, China, on welfare technology meant to prevent solitary death among frail older adults who lost their only child. Home help providers give the view from the front line.

Interviews with sixteen community workers and caregivers, plus a focus group of seven volunteers, covered two city districts. Three themes arose. Devices improved safety through faster risk spotting and response. Daily use faltered over complex controls, low acceptance, glitches, and extra staff workload. Devices also could not meet emotional needs or replace human care. The study tempers tech hopes with ground truth.
pmc-13311989:
Hengshuai Zhang and co-authors present the 2026 study engineering E. coli to make the amino acid l-valine efficiently under low-oxygen conditions. In factory microbes, the cell's own metabolism steals the building blocks.

The team evolved the bacteria under oxygen limits, gaining a strain with better growth and higher valine yield. Gene and protein comparisons showed stronger pyruvate processing and more NADH on hand in the evolved strain. Reverse engineering those gains produced strain VAL19, which reached 93.7 grams per liter in 28 hours in a five-liter tank in this work. The route could cut costs of valine manufacture.
pmc-13312189:
Lauriel F Earley and colleagues write a 2026 commentary arguing that what sits inside a gene therapy virus capsid deserves far more scrutiny than it usually gets. Recombinant adeno-associated virus vectors come as a mixed population: full capsids, empty shells, partly filled capsids, and packages holding stray genetic material.

The authors stress that many current tests never check whether the packaged genome is complete, even though broken genomes add to viral counts without helping patients and may raise immune risk. Different assays often disagree, which muddies comparisons between laboratories. The piece calls for sturdier genome integrity tests, shared reporting habits, and multi-method frameworks that connect capsid content measures to potency and patient safety as gene therapy products move toward the clinic.
pmc-13312489:
ZongHai Huang and co-authors report a 2026 food science study turning cookies into a delivery vehicle for grape seed polyphenols. These plant compounds are strong antioxidants but degrade easily and absorb poorly, and classic butter cookies carry an unhelpful fat profile. The team replaced butter with a camellia seed oil emulsion gel loaded with the polyphenols.

The best gel used a 7 to 3 oil-to-water ratio with 3 percent gelatin, holding 89.5 percent of its oil in a uniform structure, and adding 0.1 percent polyphenols strengthened the network further. Cookies baked with the gel earned the best sensory scores, digested more slowly with about 7.9 percent more resistant starch, and kept 1.6 to 1.9 times longer than controls thanks to antioxidant protection. The authors pitch the system for functional baked goods.
pmc-13312589:
Min Yang and co-authors describe, in a 2026 study, a manganese-based nanoparticle built to wake the immune system against triple-negative breast cancer. This aggressive subtype responds poorly to immunotherapy because its tumors excite little immune interest and sit in a suppressive environment. The team combined two immune triggers in one self-assembled particle.

Their particle, HLM315, assembles from modified hyaluronic acid, the peptide LTX-315, and manganese ions, homes to tumors, and releases its cargo in response to tumor conditions. The peptide ruptures tumor membranes, spilling antigens and danger signals that start immune activation, while manganese generates reactive oxygen species and amplifies the cGAS-STING alarm pathway. Together they drove interferon production, dendritic cell maturation, and T-cell attack, and the treatment strongly slowed tumors in an orthotopic mouse model while building immune memory.
pmc-13312789:
Marijus Giraitis and colleagues survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how people with Parkinson's disease in Luxembourg use the national electronic health record. Parkinson's care spans many specialists, so a shared record could coordinate treatment and support self-management. The researchers questioned 191 patients using validated digital literacy and health information instruments. They then modeled which patient, provider, and technology factors predicted engagement.

Use was low. In the past year, only 29.8 percent had opened their record repeatedly. Most had not used it at all: 70.2 percent, including 40.8 percent who had never accessed it since launch. Engagement ran higher among patients born in Luxembourg, those with milder disease, and those with stronger digital health literacy. Active encouragement from their clinicians also helped. Surprisingly, greater trust in providers and higher general health literacy predicted less use. The authors call for broad fixes so digital records do not exclude the patients who need coordination most.
pmc-13313189:
Eviatar Weizman, Dan Ben-Avraham, and Robert Fluhr describe a 2026 project that built an AI helper to guide users to the right core research facility. Such shared labs hold costly tools and deep skill, yet many students and young scientists never find the unit they need or cannot frame a clear request.

Their system pairs a chat agent with retrieval from a fixed knowledge base built on the facility websites, using Google Gemini File Search for facts about each unit. A web agent handles broad science questions, while routing rules send service questions to the file search and keep the agents inside approved domains. Guardrails block drift into general chat. The authors set out ways to judge the tool, such as truth of answers, cost per chat, and speed, and note it stays current as the source sites change.
pmc-13313489:
Abhijeet S. Barath leads a 2026 mouse study of SWELL1, the core part of a cell channel, in microglia, the brain immune cells. The channel, called VRAC, lets cells handle volume shifts, and seizures changed its makeup in microglia, which raised the question of what it does there.

Mice lacking SWELL1 only in microglia had worse kainate-driven seizures, but only in males, yet lost fewer neurons to those seizures. The loss of the channel cut microglial numbers on its own and lowered release of brain-active chemicals the channel can pass, such as taurine, GABA, and glutamate, in lab cultures. Weakened cleanup of dead cells by microglia also played a part, going by the report. The split result shows how one channel can raise seizure risk yet spare neurons.
pmc-13313889:
Yendraliza Yendraliza, Muhamad Rodiallah, and Jaswandi Jaswandi optimize, in a 2026 study, a cheap sperm sexing method for Bali cattle, Indonesia's breed. Sorting sperm by sex lets breeders steer offspring toward production goals and supports conservation of the breed's germplasm. The albumin gradient method is far cheaper than flow cytometry, but its timing and the donor bull's age were untested. Fifty-six ejaculates from bulls aged eight, nine, and ten years passed through gradients for 30, 45, or 60 minutes. Sperm quality was checked before and after freezing, and sex fractions were verified by gene amplification.

Thirty minutes won. It separated X and Y fractions cleanly and left frozen-thawed sperm in the best shape, beating longer runs. Nine-year-old bulls supplied the best semen across motility, viability, membrane, and acrosome measures. The authors set thirty minutes and nine-year-old donors as the recipe for sexed semen production in Bali cattle programmes.
pmc-13314389:
Yoonjeong Kim and colleagues compare five Korean perilla types for healthy compounds in 2026 work. Perilla seeds and leaves carry lignans, plant compounds with antioxidant power, but levels may vary by cultivar.

Using liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry, the team found six lignans, among them secoisolariciresinol, matairesinol, and pinoresinol. Total lignan content differed by type, with Anyu highest at a level of 88.639 micrograms per 100 grams as stated in the report, and syringaresinol the main single lignan. Dayu and Gayeon held more polyphenols and flavonoids than the rest. Dayu and Neulbora led one radical-scavenging test, while Neulbora led a second such test. Lignan levels tied only weakly to antioxidant strength, so breeders should judge each trait on its own.
pmc-13314789:
Jeyanthi Valaitham and co-workers set out a trial plan for posture teaching in high school students, published in 2026. Teens sit more and sit badly, in poor desk setups that can harm posture, fitness, and mood, yet school programs to fix this lack a standard test.

Their 8-week Posture Education Program will run inside physical education classes for students aged 14 to 17 years. It blends posture awareness, core strength work, desk setup fixes, guided movement, and reflective behavior tasks. A control group keeps standard physical education. Main outcomes are posture alignment, aerobic capacity, and lung function, with activity, mood, and ergonomic knowledge as secondary marks, as the protocol states. The plan, built on standard teaching and function frames, gives schools a ready trial to copy.
pmc-13315389:
Anat Loewenstein and a large team pooled two trials in 2026 to check eye pressure after injections of aflibercept at a higher dose and volume. One trial covered wet age-related macular degeneration and the other diabetic macular swelling, with patients getting 8 milligram or 2 milligram doses on varied schedules through week 96.

The safety set held 1,667 patients, most on the higher dose. The team gathered pressure-related side effects and care, plus pressure readings before and after each injection, and summed them across both trials. The question was whether the larger injected volume, 70 microliters versus 50, raises pressure risk over long treatment.
pmc-13315889:
Fei Yan and colleagues tested in 2026 how colored light during withering changes white tea flavor and aroma. Tea making depends on withering, and natural sunlight fails in bad weather, so red light, blue light, and three red-blue blends were applied for the first twelve hours, followed by indoor withering.

Tasters rated red-heavy treatments highest for aroma and taste, while blue-heavy mixes darkened the brew and raised red and yellow tones. Red light cut tea polyphenols by 12.79 percent and raised free amino acids by 6.24 percent, while blue light lowered total catechins by 9.72 percent. Gas analysis, electronic nose, and liquid checks backed the sensory results.
pmc-13316189:
Liliana C. Wu and colleagues ran a two-year brain imaging study in 2026 on negative self-referential bias in people whose depression had lifted, asking whether the bias forecasts relapse. Eighty-one outpatients took a self-referential encoding task during scans before and after preventive therapy with mindfulness-based or well-being focused cognitive therapy.

Stronger negative bias predicted higher later symptoms, with a coefficient of 0.10 in the reported model, but not relapse itself. Brain activity tied to the bias inside frontal default and salience networks did link with relapse status. Non-relapsers showed distinct treatment-linked brain changes, hinting at protective patterns.
pmc-13316289:
Mykhailo Krolevets and a broad German team report 2026 case-control findings on chemical marks on DNA in people living with heart failure. The study compares patients from the MyoVasc cohort with adults from a general population study, looking at both single marks and signs of faster aging in cells.

Marks were read at 767,735 sites in samples from 2,155 people. Heart failure went with lower marking across the genome and an aging gap near 19 extra years on clock measures, and those clocks also foretold worsening illness and death. Effects differed by chromosome and by region type, strongest near island shores. The results point to altered marking as a core feature of the syndrome and a possible guide for risk care.
pmc-13316689:
Andrew E Craver and colleagues describe, in 2026, a man on dialysis whose eczema treatment with dupilumab later gave way to a thick form of psoriasis. Dupilumab blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signals and helps many people with severe eczema. Blocking those signals can shift immunity toward pathways that drive psoriasis, a change called a phenotype switch.

The 78-year-old began dupilumab in 2021 for severe itching and a widespread eczematous rash, with strong early relief. Thick plaques later returned. Biopsies and cytokine profiling supported ostraceous psoriasis, a form with very thick scale. Switching him to guselkumab, which blocks interleukin-23, resolved the eruption completely, even in the setting of end-stage kidney disease.
pmc-13316789:
Faezeh Ebrahimi leads a 2026 review on extracellular vesicles in glioblastoma, the most aggressive primary brain tumor. These tiny cell-made packages ferry messages between tumor cells and, evidence suggests, help the cancer dodge drugs and the immune system.

The review sorts what vesicles carry, from small RNAs to proteins and fats, and how those loads protect tumor DNA, keep stem-like cells alive, reshape surroundings, and blunt immune attack. It carefully separates dish findings, animal results, and patient evidence, and notes cases where vesicles seem to slow tumors instead. The same packages might serve as markers or drug carriers, yet uneven isolation methods and scale problems block clinical use for now.
pmc-13317589:
Simone Ranieri and colleagues report, in 2026, a water-cleaning material that both captures and destroys a common painkiller. Naproxen sodium, an anti-inflammatory drug, passes through sewage treatment and persists in rivers and groundwater. Practical removal methods need high efficiency without creating new waste.

Their composite joins a lignin-based cationic gel with an iron-containing framework material locked inside during synthesis. The gel took up the drug quickly and held more than the plain gel, thanks to charge attraction and extra binding sites. Under ultraviolet light with hydrogen peroxide, the drug broke down fully into oxidised by-products. No iron leaked out, and the material kept much of its performance over repeated regeneration cycles, supporting reuse.
pmc-13317689:
Andrea Dalle Vedove and co-authors report, in 2026, an unusual folded shape adopted by compounds that bind a hard-to-drug protein domain. BAZ2A helps silence ribosomal DNA and is overproduced in aggressive prostate cancer. Its bromodomain, a pocket that reads chemical marks on proteins, has resisted strong inhibitors because the pocket is shallow.

The team found binders that curl back on themselves into an almost enclosed pose inside the pocket. Such backfolded binding was unexpected for this family of compounds. The authors suggest the pose offers a starting point for ring-shaped macrocyclic inhibitors, a strategy that has worked for other bromodomains. Their structural observations may guide chemists seeking the first potent and selective BAZ2A blockers for cancer research.
pmc-13318089:
Tingting Luo and colleagues present, in 2026, a trial protocol testing acupuncture for thinking problems after COVID-19 related chronic fatigue syndrome. Cognitive dysfunction is among the most disabling features of that condition, and effective treatments are limited. Acupuncture has helped cognition in other diseases, but its mechanism here is unknown.

The planned trial will enrol 129 patients and 30 healthy controls. Patients will be split equally among real acupuncture, sham acupuncture and a waitlist group, with three sessions a week for eight weeks in the treated groups. The main outcome is change on a symbol-digit test of processing speed. Many other cognitive tests are included, alongside brain scans measuring metabolite levels and resting connectivity, plus fatigue, sleep, anxiety and mood scales.
pmc-13318589:
Tamiris Beppler Martins and colleagues examine, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how well common field tests of balance, hopping, and jumping reflect measured knee strength in professional male soccer players. Forty athletes without symptoms completed the test battery, and strength data were available for 38.

Machine-measured thigh strength was taken at a set speed and compared with reach balance, single-leg hop, and jump results, including symmetry between legs. Two-legged jump height related moderately to front thigh strength, while single-leg jumps linked only weakly and unevenly to strength. Hop distance showed no real link at all. The authors conclude these tests capture separate qualities and should sit alongside, not replace, direct strength testing in return-to-play decisions.
pmc-13318689:
Kerui Zhu reports a 2026 trial of high-intensity interval training in obese female college students. The study asked whether short, hard exercise sessions improve body shape and mental health. One hundred twenty students took part. They were randomly split into a training group and a control group.

The training group exercised for twelve weeks, three times a week. Each session lasted 30 minutes. Controls received routine health education without structured exercise. Afterwards, the training group showed lower body mass index and body fat. Waist size and waist-to-hip ratio also fell. Depression and anxiety scores dropped, while self-esteem rose. Fitness, blood lipids, fasting glucose, sleep, and quality of life all improved more in the training group.
pmc-13318789:
Yu Wu and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of lifestyle programmes for young children's daily movement. Preschoolers often move too little, sit too much, watch screens too long, and sleep too little. Trials of structured programmes were pooled. Searches covered five databases through December 31, 2025.

Forty-three trials from 16 countries covered 13,659 children aged two to six. Programmes raised active play by a mean of 5.77 minutes per day in the pooled results. Sleep grew by 0.18 hours per day, while sitting fell by 7.62 minutes daily. Screen time dropped by 0.33 hours per day in the same analysis. Results varied widely between trials, and evidence certainty was low. The authors read the effects as promising directions, not firm numbers.
pmc-13318989:
Fenglin Song and Biao Xu present a 2026 experiment on generative AI in a university character design course in China. One hundred twenty undergraduates were split into three groups. One used AI tools inside a structured design thinking strategy based on the Double Diamond model. Another used AI without that structure. The third learned traditionally.

The structured AI group outperformed both other groups overall. Its students reached higher design achievement scores. They also reported stronger creative self-efficacy and better problem-solving skills. AI alone helped less than AI guided by a clear process. The authors argue the tools need instructional framing to deliver their full value. They discuss what this means for design teaching in higher education more broadly.
pmc-13319089:
Weidong Liu and colleagues present a 2026 framework for segmenting brain tumours on MRI when the contrast-enhanced scan is missing. That sequence is often unavailable because contrast agents are unsafe for some patients or scans fail. Performance of standard tools drops sharply without it. Their system, named UAF-AIMM, tackles the gap in three parts.

One module rebuilds the missing sequence's features from the scans that exist. A second weighs each spot by estimated reliability before fusing features. A third recalibrates the model for each new case at test time. On the BraTS 2021 benchmark, the system reached a Dice score of 89.20 percent in their testing. Gains were largest in the enhancing tumour region, the part most dependent on contrast. The approach outperformed four named baselines.
pmc-13319189:
Yixiao Dong and three co-authors offer a tutorial from 2026 on how to study clashes between goals in mental health and behavior research. Goals such as speed and accuracy often pull in opposite ways, so gains in one can mean losses in the other. Standard tools in the field were not built to map such clashes, and many of them stay hidden as a result.

Core ideas from Pareto methods, long used in biology and related fields, are set out in plain steps. A free web tool called PO-Run lets users run the method, and a score borrowed from economics helps put a number on each clash. A worked case plus notes on limits and next steps round out the guide.
pmc-13319389:
Nobel Norrman and six co-authors present a meta-analysis from twenty twenty-six on prediction processing in autistic brains. Theories claim autism shifts the balance between prior knowledge and raw sensation. Brain scan studies testing that idea had never been pooled. The team gather functional scan and magnetic sensing studies with autistic participants. Contrasts touching predictions or surprise signals are sorted by direction. Stronger autistic activation shows no consistent meeting point. Stronger typical activation converges in one frontal region tied to error monitoring.

That region also handles uncertainty estimates. Many contrasts show no group gap at all. The authors urge caution given the thin evidence base. High-level processing differences remain the supported story.
pmc-13319489:
Jingying Zhou and co-authors group life risk factors for low mood in a 2026 study of a large British health bank. Low mood grows from many strands of strain at once, yet how those strands cluster in one person was poorly known. Brain scans were also checked to see whether each cluster left a distinct mark.

Among 157317 adults who filled in a mental health survey, 24 strain and habit factors fell into three groups. Most people sat in a low risk group, while two smaller groups centered on harm in childhood or harm in adult life. Both strain groups faced far higher odds of low mood, each with its own main symptoms. Brain wiring also looked weaker in both groups.
pmc-13319689:
Xinghe Sun and co-authors link blood fat carrier proteins to eye vessel harm in a 2026 health check study. Stiff small vessels at the back of the eye give an early, painless sign of wider vessel damage. Standard fat tests may miss part of that risk, so two carrier proteins and their ratio were tested as sharper signs.

Eye photos and blood tests came from 4938 adults in a health screening group. Vessel harm showed in about 14 percent of men and about 9 percent of women, using the figures as reported for each sex. Higher levels of one carrier and a higher ratio each tracked with more vessel harm after full checks. The ratio may add value to heart risk checks.
pmc-13319889:
Jing Hu and co-authors study a growth signal that helps gum ligament cells build bone in a 2026 lab and animal study. Cells in the ligament that holds teeth in place can turn toward bone making when teeth are pulled by braces. A bone growth protein and its inner relay chain were tested as the drivers of that shift under stretch.

Rats fitted with tooth moving gear showed more of the protein on the stretched side of the ligament. Human ligament cells under lab stretch also raised the protein, made more bone markers, and formed more mineral knots. Blocking the protein or its relay chain cut those gains. The chain thus helps stretch turn into new bone.
pmc-13319989:
Clemens Clar and co-authors study head scans after brain injury in a 2026 records review from a top level trauma center. Most scans after a head blow show no fresh harm, yet scanning everyone uses time and beds. A blood marker that rises after brain harm was also checked for its power to rule out harm when its level stays low.

Records covered 11504 adults seen from 2016 to 2024, and most scans were clear of fresh harm. Fresh harm showed in about one in ten scans, and urgent steps were rare, most of all among outpatients. The blood marker was on file for 483 people, and low values matched clear scans far better for outpatients than for inpatients. Clear rules could trim needless scans.
pmc-13320289:
Xianlu Zhang and co-authors wrap an immune alarm drug in trainer cell skin for bladder cancer care in a 2026 study. Alarm drugs that trip a cell danger switch hold promise, yet they clear fast, enter cells poorly, and wake trainer cells too weakly on their own. Bubbles made from the skin of trainer cells primed with tumor bits were used as a smart coat for the drug.

The coated bubbles kept the key display gear of trainer cells and held the drug firm on their surface. Trainer cells took the drug up far better, woke more strongly, and primed stronger killer cell attack in lab tests. In mice bred with a human like immune system, shots shrank both skin and bladder tumors and cut lung spread, with good safety.
pmc-13320489:
Xhevat Jakupi leads a 2026 report on a newly found virus carried by sand flies in Kosovo. The virus, named Mirusha virus, was taken from a Phlebotomus perfiliewi sand fly caught in 2022 and sits within the Phlebovirus group. Sand fly viruses in Europe can cause short fevers that are easy to miss or misread.

Full gene reading showed the three-part genome typical of its family, and lab tests found growth in mammal cells but not in mosquito cells. Blood checks found neutralising antibodies in 2.0 percent of dogs and 0.8 percent of people tested across Kosovo. Those signs suggest wider spread and support broader checks for sand fly illness in fever season.
pmc-13320889:
Yu Zhou and colleagues compare carbon storage across seven herb plants and their root zone germs in a 2026 study. Most past work on plant and microbe carbon capture focused on trees, leaving smaller plants underexplored. The team paired plant measures with gene based profiles of soil microbes around roots.

Root zone germ groups carried genes for both breaking down carbon and fixing it, showing linked decay and building work in the same community. Plant performance tracked closely with certain microbe pathways in correlation tests. Plants and their root germs thus act as one carbon storage system. Using that partnership could help lift ecosystem carbon sinks as air carbon dioxide climbs.
pmc-13321089:
Wei Zhou and colleagues pool trials of water based exercise for joint disease in heavier adults in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Water exercise is known to ease pain in lower limb osteoarthritis, but its value for overweight and obese patients, and the best dose, were unclear. The team searched five databases for randomised trials up to February 2026.

Twelve trials with 1057 participants were pooled. Water exercise went with lower pain scores and better physical function, with small to moderate pooled effects. Both overweight and obese groups gained, with slightly larger shifts in obese patients. Shorter, less frequent programmes tended to do at least as well, a dose clue for clinic planning.
pmc-13322189:
Phuong Vo and Yuehua Cui present a new method to unmix cell types in spatial gene data in a 2026 study. Spatial transcriptomics reads gene activity at spots across tissue, but each spot mixes several cell types. Methods that need matched single cell references are often impractical, while reference free methods ignore that neighbours tend to share cell mixes.

Their tool, SpatialCD, extends a topic style model with spatial smoothing so nearby spots favour similar makeups. Across simulated and real data sets, from mouse smell bulb to tumour tissue, it recovered truer cell shares and gene patterns than rival reference free tools. It also revealed fine tissue layers and tumour linked cell groups.
pmc-13322489:
Tatiana Rocha Silva and co-authors discuss cochlear implants for one sided deafness in Brazil in a 2026 article. A 2023 law, number 14,768, recognises people with total one sided hearing loss and guarantees their rights. Yet national health system guidance from 2014 reserves cochlear implants for severe to profound loss in both ears, leaving one sided cases outside cover.

Hearing with one ear loses key benefits when speech and noise sit apart, including head shadow relief and binaural gains that sharpen speech in noise. The authors weigh that gap between legal recognition and implant rules. Aligning guidance with the law would open a proven rehabilitation route for this group.
pmc-13322889:
Na Liu and a large team review stem cell vesicles as drug carriers, in a 2026 article on engineering and safety. Tiny vesicles released by mesenchymal stem cells carry proteins, lipids and nucleic acids between cells, mix well with body tissue and provoke little immune reaction.

Engineering can tune how much drug these vesicles hold and where they travel, through changes to the parent cells or direct loading methods. Clinical reports across lung, skin, nerve, eye and gut conditions give early safety and effect data for such carriers. The authors weigh those results against hurdles in production and control, and map where careful trials could move this delivery route toward routine care.
pmc-13323489:
Yuqiong Zhang, Yiming Lyu and Danyang Hou study how conducting gesture complexity loads choir singers' minds, in a 2026 experiment. Two directors were filmed leading one-minute excerpts of Eric Whitacre's Lux Aurumque with simplified, standard and elaborated gestures, paired with set audio tracks.

A total of 120 university choir members, split evenly between novice and experienced singers, rated all six videos for mental load and rehearsal effectiveness and wrote brief observations. Gesture complexity clearly shifted both ratings. Elaborated gestures during sight-reading imposed the heaviest load, while standard gestures won the best effectiveness ratings in both contexts. Written notes focused on the conductor, and elaborated videos drew the most negative comments.
pmc-13323589:
Lorenzo-Lupo Dei and co-authors screen the hearts of elite entertainment wrestlers, in a 2026 study of World Wrestling Entertainment athletes. Routine checks with ECG and ultrasound covered 68 athletes with a mean age near 28 years, about two thirds men, and similar weekly training loads by sex.

Electrical changes were rare, seen in two athletes, and heart geometry was mostly normal in both sexes. Women had smaller absolute chamber sizes but larger size once scaled to body area, and two women showed pumping strength below half. Right ventricle enlargement appeared in a minority of both sexes. The authors describe a largely normal adaptation pattern, with a few athletes needing closer cardiac follow-up.
pmc-13323689:
Xu Liu, Yunxia Zhou, Yingjie Li and Mu Wang study fine particle air pollution and metabolic syndrome in older adults, in a 2026 study. Their group held 1,506 residents aged 60 or older in a Hengyang community in Hunan. Among them, 396 people had metabolic syndrome.

A thirty-day average of PM2.5 exposure gave the strongest link to metabolic syndrome in their window tests. Screening of blood amino acids picked out isoleucine as a shared factor. Mediation analysis supported a small indirect path through that amino acid. Age and diet did not alter the path in any clear way. The authors stress the cross-sectional design. The amino acid route is thus a statistical lead rather than proven biology.
pmc-13325389:
Jinha Shin, Hyunjae Park, and Soo Ouk Jang built binder-free hybrid power-cell electrodes from tungsten disulfide and tungsten oxide on 3D carbon nanowalls. Their 2026 paper tackles a known weakness of the sulfide: limited current flow, complex making, and the need for binders. The team used a plasma-chemical route, laying ammonia-based tetrathiotungstate solution onto them and treating it with downstream hydrogen remote plasma.

Varying starting-mix amount and microwave power routed the scaffold surface through distinct regimes, from nanowall-rich to tungsten oxide-rich, while preserving the three-dimensional shape. The oxide-rich one delivered the highest areal capacitance, 91.1 millifarads per square centimeter at a slow scan rate, against 4.6 for bare walls, though with higher interfacial and transport resistance. The gain came mainly from diffusion-controlled pseudocapacitive storage, and the authors present the route as a practical plan for high-performance binder-free parts.
pmc-13325889:
Jin Guo and co-authors trace how lactate blocks liver regrowth in acute liver failure in a 2026 study. The failing liver drowns in lactate while its repair stalls, and the link between the two was unclear.

Gene data showed liver Kupffer cells shifting to heavy sugar burning, flooding the tissue with lactate. Neutrophils pulled that lactate in through the MCT1 transporter and cast out DNA traps in response. Liver cells swallowed the trap DNA, and their TLR9 sensor then shut down the factor KLF15. Losing KLF15 freed YAP1 activity in a way that halted cell division. Restoring KLF15 rescued growth in cell tests. The chain names drug targets.
pmc-13325989:
Jenny Gentizon and colleagues run Rasch checks on a medication literacy scale for older adults and their caregivers in a 2026 study. Managing complex drug regimens safely depends on skills that few tools measure for this group.

The MED-fLAG scale was answered by 582 hospitalized adults aged 65 and over in Switzerland, Belgium, and the Netherlands, with 563 responses analyzed. Mean age was 73.9 years across the sample. The functional part, with 19 items, and the interactive part, with 13 items, held up well on fit and reliability. The critical part, with 21 items, split into several dimensions and behaved differently across French and Dutch speakers.
pmc-13326989:
Trina Kellar and team give the Gastroenterological Society of Australia stance on idiopathic gastroparesis. Their 2026 paper says past advice focused too tight on slow stomach emptying. That hallmark lines up weakly with signs like nausea after meals, vomiting, feeling full fast, fullness, and pain. Emptying care works weakly.

Mix-ups with functional gut and eating disorders make care harder still. A country-wide team of many fields read past work. By a staged vote with patient voices, expert review, and public comment, it drew up twenty agreed notes, graded for proof and advice strength, plus a care path. The stance reframes idiopathic gastroparesis as a sense-and-motion gut disorder on a line with functional dyspepsia, seen through a body-and-mind lens. The team calls for a fresh take on the disorder and for study to turn to new care targets.
pmc-13327389:
Elham Yousief and colleagues published a 2026 clinic study linking grip strength to insulin resistance in women with early blood sugar problems. They recruited 44 women aged 40 to 60 with prediabetes or newly found type 2 diabetes. Scans measured belly fat and back muscle, and a hand device measured grip.

Stronger dominant-hand grip went with lower insulin resistance scores, even after other factors were taken into account. Belly fat volume and body mass index showed no clear link once adjusted, and back muscle thickness showed only a weak trend. Findings suggest a cheap grip test may flag metabolic trouble early, though longer studies are needed to test cause and effect.
pmc-13327689:
Abhiram Kanneganti and team marked World Ovarian Cancer Day by untangling a silent killer's molecular shape. Their 2026 paper notes ovarian cancer has no known ribbon, screening plan, or star-backed drive, and kills quietly, with about 80% of women found at a late stage. It ranks seventh for new cases and eighth for deaths. The awareness day, set up on May 8, 2013, by groups across eighteen countries, now draws backing from over two hundred groups.

As an immune-cold cancer, it has few T cells moving in, weak vessel growth, and mixed biology. It gives no steady shed marker for screening or guard care. The paper weighs treatment debates. Drug-first care then interval debulking surgery versus upfront surgery at high-volume centers. Second debulking fits chosen platinum-sensitive returns. Heated belly chemo has trial gains, but limits come from fit to other settings, side harms, and special center needs.
pmc-13327789:
David A Haslett and colleagues test sound-meaning clusters in English words in a 2026 study. Phonesthemes are starting sounds that recur in words with linked senses, such as the gl- in glow, gleam, and glitter. Whether they shape how adults handle familiar words, not just made-up ones, was unclear.

In word-judgment tasks, people spotted real words with phonesthemes faster and more accurately than matched controls. Brain responses differed early, and large pooled datasets showed the same speed edge for seen words but not heard ones. Meaning judgments suffered slightly when a sound cluster misled, as gl- does in glove. Such clusters sit between full word parts and empty letter strings, the authors conclude.
pmc-13327889:
Thanat Tantinam and a large team test machine learning against standard regression for forecasting rectal cancer return in a 2026 study. Records covered 581 patients with rectal adenocarcinoma treated at two Thai university hospitals between 2013 and 2022. Seventeen routine features fed five models, from logistic regression to boosted trees.

All models performed moderately, with AUC values from 0.626 to 0.662 across the set, XGBoost topping the list and random forest giving the best balance of precision and recall. Logistic regression caught every recurrence at its tuned threshold but at a cost in false alarms. Tumor marker level ranked among the key predictors, and the authors weigh accuracy gains against clarity for clinical use.
pmc-13327989:
Ruixin Shi and colleagues build an explainable learning tool for grading thyroid eye disease in a 2026 study. Grading now rests partly on judgment and varies between observers. The team used measured eye features from MRI, such as protrusion and muscle thickness, in 443 patients giving 1,054 orbital scan units.

Six learning models were trained to sort eyes into mild, moderate-to-severe, and sight-threatening bands. Two datasets were compared, all scans versus first visits only, to stop repeat scans from flattering the scores. Plain anatomical features, aligned with how clinicians judge, keep the tool readable. Honest data handling, the authors argue, matters as much as model choice for tools that clinics can trust.
pmc-13328189:
Pretty Ponnachan and co-authors review mechanisms behind long COVID in a 2026 article. About one in five COVID-19 survivors develops lingering symptoms such as brain fog, breathlessness, fatigue, pain, and anxiety or depression, with risk raised by smoking, age, obesity, female sex, and prior hospitalization. The authors sort the candidate explanations.

Proposed drivers include reawakened Epstein-Barr virus, molecular mimicry that turns immunity against the body, virus persistence, autoantibodies, and failing mitochondria, the last of which could explain crushing fatigue. Brain and mental effects get their own focus, as does how vaccination may shift risk. Naming the routes is a step toward treatments matched to each patient's pattern.
pmc-13328789:
Yeong-Jik Kim and Tae-Beom Seo test a combined recovery plan after spinal cord injury in rats in a 2026 study. Forty male rats were placed in four groups of 10: uninjured, injured with rest, injured with naringenin, and injured with both naringenin and treadmill work. Injured rats rested for 2 weeks first, then the exercise group trained for 4 weeks at low intensity.

Tissue checks looked at support cell activity, surviving motor neurons, and regrowth in cord pathways below the injury. Combined care preserved more motor neurons than rest alone and raised markers tied to fibre regrowth. Support cell activity also rose with treatment. The authors propose the pairing as one option to aid nerve recovery after cord injury.
pmc-13329389:
Andrija Savić and colleagues report results of distal nerve transfers for shoulder repair in a 2026 single-centre study. The operations help people who lost shoulder lift and outward turn after brachial plexus or armpit nerve injury. Donor nerves were joined to shoulder nerves through an approach from the back, and outcomes were checked two years later.

Most patients regained useful shoulder lift, and most also regained useful outward turn, the authors report. Quality of life scores moved from mostly poor or fair before surgery to mostly good or better after surgery. Pain eased as well. Full plexus injury gave the weakest outward turn results. Younger age and surgery within 6 months leaned toward better recovery. The team calls the transfers effective and repeatable.
pmc-13329589:
Özgür Özcan and Serdal Dikmen pooled how heat stress hits milk yield and make-up in dairy cattle. Their 2026 study, run by PRISMA rules and the PICOS frame, gathered 35 stand-alone studies from 2010 to 2023, pooling results with an inverse variance heterogeneity model fit for high mix. Effect sizes used Cohen's d, and spread sources were probed through Temperature-Humidity Index group checks and meta-regression.

Heat stress tracked with lower milk yield at minus 0.723, next to falls in milk fat at minus 0.633, in protein at minus 0.555, and in lactose at minus 0.404 in turn for these traits. Yield falls grew sharper once the Temperature-Humidity Index passed 72. Given heavy mix, the team warns pooled figures should be read as broad world trends, not exact world cut-offs. Future work should weigh total exposure time and local farm microclimates to better foretell yield responses.
pmc-13330689:
Omar Alaqeeli mines large genetic datasets for other repeat expansions tied to Huntington disease in a 2026 study. The CAG repeat expansion is held to be the sole marker for Huntington and like disorders. Alaqeeli compared samples from patients and controls, with 83 patient and 74 control datasets in the reported totals.

Association rule mining scanned all three-letter repeat types across the data. Most repeats showed no meaningful expansion in patient samples. A few, such as AAA, GAA, and TGC, appeared more often in patients but far below a significant level in the analysis given. CAG thus stands alone as a usable marker, Alaqeeli concludes.
pmc-13331689:
Yuanning Ye and colleagues present a 2026 endoscopy case report of a healthy 34-year-old man whose routine stomach examination found a roughly 30 mm lump under the stomach lining. Ultrasound imaging suggested a benign fat tumor, though its deep edge could not be seen clearly.

The team removed the lump by endoscopic submucosal dissection, cutting it out in one piece without perforation or later bleeding, and careful control of the many blood vessels inside it proved essential. Tissue study showed mature fat mixed with growing blood vessels, confirming a rare gastric angiolipoma rather than a plain lipoma. A check three months later showed full healing, supporting dissection as both a diagnostic and a treatment option for such uncertain lumps.
pmc-13332789:
Shuna Zhang and colleagues review how an excess of reactive oxygen in the ovary undermines fertility, in a 2026 synthesis. Reactive oxygen species are normal signals in follicle growth and egg release, but when production outruns antioxidant defenses, the ovary's high metabolic rate makes it especially vulnerable.

The review traces the damage routes: failing mitochondria, stressed protein-folding compartments, inflammatory switches such as NF-κB and NLRP3, and changes in gene control marks. These paths converge on cell death programs including apoptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis in granulosa cells and eggs. Links are drawn to polycystic ovary syndrome, early ovarian insufficiency, and endometriosis, along with biomarker options. Treatment ideas range from mitochondria-targeted antioxidants and stem cell exosomes to traditional Chinese medicine and lifestyle steps. The authors also flag conflicting evidence and open gaps.
pmc-13333389:
Dandan Song and Shaning Yang map a proposed overhaul of atrial fibrillation care in a 2026 review. They argue that pairing digital twins with artificial intelligence could turn one-off decisions into continuous management. Care today is fragmented, with each choice made from a single moment's data.

A digital twin is a patient-specific virtual heart. The review reports the chain for building one is now complete. Anatomy matching reaches Dice scores of 93 percent or higher, and activation timing predictions correlate above 0.96 in the cited work. AI tools run through every stage. ECG reading raised detection 2.3-fold, and models predicting relapse after ablation scored AUC values ranging from 0.72 up to 0.85 in the review. In-procedure 3D rebuilding dropped to 65 s. A loop of sensing, modeling, in-silico testing, deciding, and feedback has support in drug screening, ablation planning, and clot risk checks. The authors want multicenter proof before routine use.
pmc-13333689:
Man Li and co-authors describe in a 2026 case report how they treated infected pancreatic necrosis caused by a carbapenem-resistant bacterium in a gravely ill man. The 51-year-old patient had severe acute pancreatitis with organ failure, abdominal compartment syndrome, and kidney injury needing dialysis support.

Blood cultures on day 5 grew enterococci, and drainage on day 7 showed necrosis infected with carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, which then entered the bloodstream. Because the companion Enterococcus faecium resists all carbapenems, the team paired sulbactam-durlobactam with tigecycline as a salvage regimen. The patient began to improve by day 13, with cultures clearing as treatment went on. The report records an early use of this drug pairing and sums up past reports for doctors facing similar infections.
pmc-13334789:
Shoji Kikui and colleagues report a 2026 label change from PD to multiple system atrophy based on over-time medical and imaging findings. Telling apart PD from multiple system atrophy, notably the PD-like subtype, is often hard in early stages because of shared medical signs. The patient was a 72-year-old man first found with PD, later moved to multiple system atrophy PD-like subtype after autonomic failure and typical MRI findings emerged.

He presented with tremors, stiffness, slow movement, and balance wobble, and dopamine scans showed two-sided early dopamine failure. Cardiac MIBG scans showed reduced uptake on initial check, considered in favor of PD disease, yet levodopa response was limited. During follow-up, unusual signs appeared, including Pisa syndrome, early balance wobble, standing low blood pressure, and nerve bladder. Follow-up MRI findings detailed in the full report supported the revised label.
pmc-13335489:
Kiara Quinn and co-authors show, in twenty twenty-six, that reinnervating muscle targets makes motor unit signals easier to separate after nerve transfer surgery. After amputation, prostheses often decode intent from pooled muscle signals, which limits natural control. Splitting the signal into single motor units promises finer control, but overlapping units blur together. The team tested direct nerve-to-muscle implantation in a rodent hindlimb model. Tissue and electrical analyses followed the reinnervation.

Structural changes after surgery spread motor unit signals farther apart in space than in intact muscle. That separation meant fewer complex, overlapping signals in recordings. The team used the cleaner signals for a first proof-of-concept: precise control of a virtual prosthesis after direct nerve-to-muscle implantation.
pmc-13335789:
Qingyi Hu and co-authors identified the RNA-modifying enzyme METTL3 as a driver of autoimmune thyroiditis in a 2026 mechanistic study. In this disease, lymphocytes flood the thyroid and destroy its follicle cells, but what sustains the attack was unclear.

METTL3 levels and its m6A marks ran high in thyroid cells from patients and from mice with experimental thyroiditis, tracking with inflammation scores. Blocking METTL3 genetically or with drugs quieted a KDR/VEGFA signaling loop, cut cytokine release and lymphocyte infiltration, restored the Th17 to Treg balance, and eased tissue injury. The team traced the chain upward to reactive oxygen species lifting a SIRT1 brake on METTL3, and downward to the reader YTHDC2 stabilizing KDR's message. The loop marks METTL3 as a drug target for thyroid inflammation.
pmc-13336389:
Kuan Yang and co-authors built a single-cell metabolic atlas spanning seven major metabolic diseases in a 2026 cross-cutting study. How metabolic pathways link up, and which links matter in the clinic, had remained murky.

Pooling public single-cell RNA datasets gave 562,699 cells from 86 patients. Their scoring strategy rated activity across 227 metabolic pathways and found 89 enriched in disease. Those pathways grouped into 15 joint modules whose reshaping tracked with coordinated activity. By tying module behavior to ligand-receptor signaling and transcription factor dynamics, the team mapped cross-cell control circuits and named 63 potential drug targets. An open-access resource goes with the work so others can query the atlas, which argues metabolic diseases share a modular logic beneath their variety.
pmc-13336489:
Chen Shi and co-authors looked at how artificial intelligence, physics simulation, and experiment can be woven together to model protein motion in a 2026 article. Proteins work as shifting ensembles, not statues, and no single method captures their dynamics alone.

Experiments give true benchmarks but blur fast, rare states. Physics-based simulation produces atomic paths yet suffers sampling limits and force field sensitivity. Deep learning predicts structures and ensembles fast but explains itself poorly and trains on scarce dynamics data. The review lays out each approach's principles, then maps the integrations: experimental constraints steering simulations, AI cleaning experimental data and building ensembles, physics lending plausibility to AI output, and AI speeding sampling. The trio framing aims at sound dynamics models.
pmc-13336589:
Jordan Gillespie and colleagues review 2026 new non-steroid skin creams for child skin care: atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, alopecia areata, vitiligo, and seborrheic dermatitis. The aim is to review current books on child non-steroid skin creams (NSTT) for these five conditions. Current child skin creams are few for these conditions. In the past, first-line care used steroid creams (TCS).

The FDA approved difamilast and widened the approved age ranges for roflumilast, tapinarof, and ruxolitinib to treat AD. Recent studies show good results with delgocitinib. In psoriasis, current work shows promise for tapinarof and roflumilast in a wider age range. Among new AA treatments, relevant writing supports both ruxolitinib and tofacitinib. Work in child vitiligo now focuses on roflumilast and latanoprost. The FDA widened age ranges for roflumilast in SD care, and data show efficacy and safety with long-term use.
pmc-13337489:
Vignesh Sundararajan leads a large 2026 team finding a drug weakness in the most aggressive ovarian cancer subtypes. High-grade serous ovarian cancer splits into expression subtypes, and the mesenchymal and stem-like A groups fare worst. These tumors also carry heavy replication stress, the strain of copying damaged DNA.

Cell lines of those subtypes showed higher replication stress and greater sensitivity to ATR inhibitors, drugs that block a stress-response kinase. Fiber assays confirmed faster forks and more exposed single-stranded DNA. Patient-derived graft models echoed the vulnerability in living tumors. The subtype's stress profile could serve as a biomarker, steering ATR inhibitor treatment toward patients most likely to benefit.
pmc-13337889:
Si-yi Li and colleagues chart second cancers after cervical or womb cancer in a 2026 hospital study. Records covered 253 cervical cases and 102 endometrial cases with a later separate cancer at Fujian Cancer Hospital from 2014 to 2024. Timing, age, and cancer sites were mapped.

Median age at first diagnosis was 52 years for cervical and 55 years for endometrial cases as reported. Second cancers appeared after a median of 2 years and 0.5 years in the two groups. Lung, thyroid, and breast were common after cervical cancer, while thyroid and ovary led after womb cancer. Most second cancers were found early, supporting tailored follow-up scans.
pmc-13339189:
Junli Wu and colleagues frame fatty liver disease as a driver of stiff-heart failure in a 2026 review. Heart failure with preserved pumping action is now the dominant form worldwide and travels with metabolic trouble. Fatty liver linked to metabolism is common in these patients yet often missed.

Shared paths include low-grade inflammation, insulin resistance, faulty fat handling, and vessel lining damage. Signals from the gut, liver, and liver-made mediators reach the heart and reshape it. Together they explain why standard heart drugs often disappoint here. The authors propose joint liver-heart diagnosis and treatment rather than organ-by-organ care.
pmc-13341489:
Whole brain slices as a living stage for tumor growth are established by Katharina Fuchs's team in a 2026 methods study. Existing slice cultures usually come from adult animals or single regions like the hippocampus, limiting how faithfully they mimic the brain.

Slices 300 µm thick were cut from 6- to 9-day-old mice, yielding many sections per brain, and kept alive 7 to 14 days. Rat glioblastoma spheroids seeded onto the slices grew and invaded like tumors. Viability assays and live/dead staining showed the tissue stayed healthy for about a week before gradual decline, a workable window for studying invasion.
pmc-13343389:
Wenrui Bao and co-authors follow brain structure and mental symptoms in long COVID over a year, in a 2026 longitudinal study. All 144 patients had mild infection without hospital care, and scans plus psychiatric and thinking tests ran at one, two, and twelve months, with heart-healthy controls scanned for comparison.

Symptom patterns tied to coordinated structural patterns across wide brain regions, and the links grew stronger over the first months while controls showed none. Volume ties stayed in frontal-limbic circuits, whereas thickness ties spread toward frontoparietal zones. Smaller volume in the right cuneus and upper frontal areas at three months foreshadowed worse executive function and fatigue a year later, marking early warning signs.
pmc-13344389:
Dewei Zhao leads an expert panel issuing a 2026 consensus on blood supply in adult femoral neck fractures. Broken femoral necks often starve the ball of the hip joint, causing bone death and failed healing, so surgeons from orthopedics and reconstruction pooled evidence and experience into a vessel-first plan.

The statement maps the head's arterial network, reviews perfusion imaging with digital subtraction angiography as the sharpest tool, and proposes a four-type classification blending CT and angiography findings. Treatments scale with vessel damage, from careful fixation with porous tantalum screws to joint replacement, plus microvascular grafting when supply is fully cut. A scoring system using age, displacement, and vessel injury aims to forecast trouble early.
pmc-13345789:
Teresa Zumarraga-Lizundia, Arantzazu Barquin-Garcia, and Ainhoa Madariaga weigh a two-drug pairing for advanced cervical cancer in a 2026 commentary. Cervical cancer still ranks among the top killers of women worldwide, and once disease returns or spreads, about a third of patients worsen within six months of first-line chemo combinations.

The authors map second-line gains from immune drugs and antibody-drug conjugates, citing survival edges for cemiplimab and tisotumab vedotin over standard chemo, then place camrelizumab plus famitinib inside that crowded field. Response rates for plain chemo sit at just 5 to 10 percent, so any pairing must prove real added benefit against its side-effect cost. Careful patient selection will decide where the combo fits.
pmc-13347389:
Tülin Deniz Çiftçi and co-authors coat waste keratin fibres with magnetite to pull many toxic metals from water at once, in a study from 2026. Most cleanup tests use one metal at a time, which misses real mixed pollution. So batch tests challenged the coated waste with 14 metal and metalloid ions together across a wide acidity range.

Removal ran from about 80 to 99 percent across the ion set under mixed conditions in the reported tests. Uptake paths varied by element. Clear rivalry among ions for sites appeared too. Real drinking water and wastewater runs gave average recoveries near 90 percent, supporting the cheap waste-based sorbent for messy real samples rather than clean lab water alone.
pmc-13348189:
Yaoyao Shen and colleagues produce a red bacterial pigment in record yield. Their study was published in 2026. They also show the pigment revives a last-line antibiotic. A high-making variant supplied the pigment. The variant belongs to Streptomyces spectabilis. Yield reached up to 300 mg per litre. That supply let the team test the pigment widely. It served as a helper for colistin. Targets were resistant Gram-negative germs from four species groups.

The test dose was 5 micromolar. At that dose, colistin needs fell sharply. Cuts reached up to 32,768-fold across isolates. Plasmid-borne resistance carriers were included. Early probes point to one part of the boost. Reactive oxygen rises inside the cells. Ring pigments thus look like strong partners. They may help fight drug resistance.
pmc-13350389:
Yuichi Saito and colleagues tracked heart failure markers long after heart attack, in a 2026 prospective study from Chiba, Japan. Early rises and falls in BNP and NT-proBNP after acute myocardial infarction are well charted, but their path beyond the first months was unclear. The team followed patients across ten hospitals in the Chiba AMI and heart failure registry.

Eligibility centered on patients who received primary percutaneous coronary intervention within 48 hours of their heart attack. Repeated natriuretic peptide measures let the team map mid- to long-term trajectories and link them to later heart failure events. The work fills a monitoring gap for clinicians deciding how long to watch survivors closely after discharge.
pmc-13350589:
Kai Zhao and colleagues built a prediction model in 2026 for death of the hip ball bone after neck-of-femur fractures, using three-dimensional displacement measured on CT scans. They reviewed 302 patients fixed with screws after closed repositioning.

Within three years, 68 patients, 22.5 percent, developed bone death. Fracture type, age, delay to surgery, bone thinning, fragmentation, implant removal, and several displacement measures all tracked with the outcome. Vertical shift and separation stayed predictive in the final model, presented as a scoring chart checked for accuracy and usefulness. Gauging displacement in 3D could warn surgeons which healed fractures still threaten the joint.
pmc-13351389:
Woo Sik Yu wrote a 2026 commentary on using drain fluid enzyme trends to decide when patients may eat again after oesophagus removal surgery. Leaks where the stomach is rejoined to the remaining gullet are among the operation's most feared complications, delaying recovery and further treatment.

The traditional swallow X-ray a week after surgery misses most leaks, with one study finding sensitivity of only 28.6 percent, so a normal result cannot reassure. Measuring amylase in drain fluid is painless and can be repeated daily. Yu weighs the study's trend-based approach as a gatekeeper for safe first meals, potentially replacing a test that often gives false comfort.
pmc-13351889:
Josefine Wassermann leads a 2026 field study on whether droppings found outdoors can support tracking of the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis in wild meat-eaters. Foxes and raccoon dogs are the main hosts. Between November 2023 and March 2025, hunters on the island of Rügen in north-eastern Germany supplied 84 carcasses for lab checks.

Combined tests found the parasite in 37.9 percent of foxes and 15.4 percent of raccoon dogs. Teams also gathered 365 droppings on 13 trips in early 2025, and species tests showed most came from foxes. Parasite DNA appeared in 18.1 percent of fox droppings. The comparison shows what outdoor sampling can and cannot replace in wildlife tracking.
pmc-13352189:
Tsachi Tsadok Perets leads a 2026 national consensus guideline on hydrogen and methane breath tests in Israel. Bloating, gas, pain, and changed bowel habits can stem from sugar malabsorption, small bowel bacterial overgrowth, or gut-brain disorders. Breath tests are cheap and non-invasive, yet varied methods produce uneven diagnoses. A broad panel met 8 times under the Israeli Gastroenterology Association.

Experts included adult and child gut doctors, dietitians, nutrition specialists, and lab heads. Standards cover measuring both gases at once, recording symptoms during the test, and uniform preparation before it. Care is urged where anatomy or transit speed is altered. Lactulose is named the preferred test substance, giving clinics a shared routine for adults and children.
pmc-13352889:
Burak Kizilcay and co-authors traced how candidemia, a bloodstream illness caused by Candida fungi, changed over time in heavy care people, in a 2026 study. These sickness carry high deaths among critically ill people, and the mix of species, drug pushback, and results may shift across years. The team matched two periods to see what actually moved.

The look-back study covered 250 heavy care people treated between January 2018 and January 2022, split into an earlier group of eighty and a later group of one hundred seventy. Species patterns, antifungal pushback, medical traits, and deaths were matched, with multivariable study seeking independent signs of deaths. The results help heavy care teams spot the people at greatest risk and adapt antifungal plan.
pmc-13354389:
Fei Zhou and co-authors use genetics in 2026 to probe cancer risks tied to GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs. The diabetes and obesity drugs carry disputed long-term cancer signals in observational data. Gene variants near the GLP1R gene stood in for drug exposure in a Mendelian randomisation design, with summary data for 21 cancer types from public genome consortia.

Proxied drug use linked to lower breast and prostate cancer risk but higher head and neck plus thyroid cancer risk. Body mass explained about 3 percent of the endometrial cancer effect, while blood sugar explained small shares for two other cancers. United Kingdom Biobank checks matched the directions without reaching significance. Cancer-specific monitoring is advised.
pmc-13354989:
Carlos Acosta-Batista writes a 2026 letter to the editors about the glass ceiling in medical education. He praises a study of women's lived barriers to leadership roles in academic medicine. Then he argues that schools should go past describing unfairness and start measuring its size with a clear number.

He proposes the Gini coefficient, a tool his group has used in fields from surgery scheduling to heart data. Plotted for a faculty, it would show what share of leadership roles a share of staff holds. A score near one would expose stark imbalance. Tracking the score over time, he argues, would show if policy truly levels the field.
pmc-13355689:
