Luis Moreno and colleagues reply to a critique of their heat-based treatment for pelvic vein disorders, in a 2026 letter. The first study proposed heat ablation through basilic vein access as a new option where proof stays thin. Commentator Mark Whiteley raised concerns about applying heat inside deep belly veins.

The authors agree that heat in that area demands careful technique and careful choice of patients. They stress their study, which followed patients forward in time, aimed to show the method can be done safely, not that it beats the established blocking treatment. Larger multi-hospital trials with longer follow-up and set energy rules, they write, must come before broad use.
pmc-13356689:
Yoshinori Osaki and co-authors used gene-edited mice in 2026 to trace how statin-linked muscle disease arises. Statins block an enzyme that makes cholesterol, but they also cut a fat-like compound needed by muscle. The team made mice lacking that enzyme, or a partner transfer enzyme, only in skeletal muscle, and tested a rescue compound.

Blocking the main enzyme caused strong muscle disease, starting in slow, mitochondria-rich fibers, and the rescue compound reversed it. Loss of the transfer enzyme alone caused later disease, and loss of both was far worse and faster. Mitochondria failed early in all models, before clear signs, hinting they help drive the disease.
pmc-13357089:
Yanqiang Xiong and co-authors tested in 2026 a retargeted virus as a gene therapy carrier for ovarian cancer, one of the deadliest cancers of the female reproductive system. Normal carrier viruses drift to the liver, causing off-target harm. The team fitted a virus shell with a binder that seeks a surface molecule common on ovarian tumors, then loaded it with a suicide gene system.

The retargeted virus infected ovarian cancer cells precisely and lit up tumors strongly in mice, while sparing heart, liver, and other organs. With its partner drug, it shrank tumors far more than the normal virus, with much lower liver enzyme signs of damage.
pmc-13357389:
Shuo Li and co-authors present a 2026 study on esophageal cancer, a cancer of the food pipe. They looked at genes tied to lactylation, a change to proteins driven by lactate, a by-product of how cells burn sugar. The team searched big public gene databases to find which of these genes link to how long patients live.

From hundreds of candidate genes, four stood out as strong signs of outlook: GADD45B, HMGB3, LMNB2, and MFAP5. The team checked these genes against immune cell patterns and drug response, and confirmed them in lab tissue tests. The four genes could help doctors sort patients by risk and choose treatment more wisely.
pmc-13358489:
Nicolas Ajkay wrote a 2026 commentary on pain control after breast cancer surgery. Strong pain after mastectomy is common, and opioid drugs, while they work, carry a real risk of long-term use. Ajkay weighs two numbing methods that can cut the need for opioids: the erector spinae plane block and the paravertebral block.

Both methods place numbing medicine near nerves by the spine, but they differ in depth, ease, and spread. Ajkay reviews the proof behind each and what guidelines now advise for breast surgery. The piece helps surgical teams pick a method that fits their skill and their patients, keeping pain low while opioid use falls.
pmc-13359089:
Isaac W Babcock and others helped the truth of brain cells genetic aiming at using a CSF1R blocker, in 2026. Brain cells, the brain's local white cells, are central to brain immunity, but aiming at them by genes is hard because widely used Cre lines also affect outer white cells. Those outer cells fail to turn over within the standard four-week window meant to improve truth.

The team joined tamoxifen start in Cx3cr1CreERT2 mice with CSF1R blocker care to deplete outer white cells while keeping brain-cell aiming at. The joined approach helped truth without losing brain-cell tagging. Neuroscientists gain a useful method for attributing experimental effects to brain cells rather than to outer immune cells.
pmc-13360589:
Feng Gao and co-authors published a 2026 study of a gene chain that drives colon cancer growth. At the center sits TDGF1, a growth factor first found in a tumor type. A long non-coding RNA called OLMALINC soaks up a small RNA that normally holds TDGF1 down, so TDGF1 levels rise. The team used data analysis and lab tests to map this chain and its effects.

With TDGF1 freed, two signal paths switch on and push the cancer forward. High TDGF1 levels also tracked with a tumor setting that shuts out immune attack, later stage, and worse outlook for patients. The authors say TDGF1 could serve as a marker for judging a patient's likely course. The whole chain offers fresh targets for future colon cancer drugs.
pmc-13360789:
İsa Can and co-authors compare two ways to close a hole in the heart in a 2026 single-center study. The hole, a secundum atrial septal defect, sits between the heart's upper chambers. It can be closed with a device threaded through a blood vessel, or by robot-assisted surgery. The team reviewed 635 patients: 290 treated with the robot and 345 with the catheter method.

Robot cases took longer in the procedure room and kept patients in hospital longer. The team also compared care, problems, and follow-up results between the groups, with a closer look at patients treated after 2019. Both routes are in wide use, so a direct comparison helps heart teams match each patient to the safer, simpler option. The study adds a large set of real cases to that choice.
pmc-13361589:
Menglan Li and co-authors built a physics-style model to predict gene marks in liver cancer cells in a 2026 study. Chemical tags on histones, the spools DNA wraps around, help switch genes on and off. At the start regions of long non-coding RNAs, odd tag patterns link to cancer behavior. Past models could not explain results at exact positions, so the team scored DNA by the energy of its local letter patterns.

They trained the model on windows of 600 DNA letters centered on true signal peaks, for both rising and falling tag states. Repeated cross-checks showed the energy gap between the two states sorts sequences very well. The result ties local DNA structure energy to histone marking. A readable, physics-based model can guide studies of gene control in liver cancer.
pmc-13361889:
Shelby Brage and co-authors listened to people aging with HIV in a 2026 qualitative study. Modern treatment controls HIV well, yet people aging with it face early aging and extra chronic illness. The team asked how these adults see their HIV alongside normal aging. Interviews explored their lived experience and worries about the future.

Many described HIV as separate from their other health conditions, not blended into one aging story. A large share voiced concern about growing isolation and about future loss of thinking ability. The authors urge clinicians to learn these mental models of aging. Asking about social support early can flag who will need extra resources later. The study gives a voice to a group whose numbers keep rising.
pmc-13362089:
Peng Cui and co-authors traced a gene circuit that drives kidney cancer growth in a 2026 study. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma makes up over three-quarters of kidney cancers and causes most deaths from the disease. The team focused on CDC6, a gene that helps cells copy DNA and is tied to tumor grade and outlook. In paired patient samples, CDC6 was overactive in the tumor in nearly every case.

Silencing CDC6 in cancer cells cut their viability by about 60 percent and halved a marker of DNA copying. Two chemical tags on histones, the spools of DNA, were shown to switch CDC6 on. A partner gene, EXOSC5, completes the axis named in the work. The circuit offers fresh drug targets for a cancer that badly needs them.
pmc-13363089:
Zhe Fan and colleagues report a 2026 study on weaving fiber optic sensors inside composite panels, the stiff layered materials used in aircraft. The hair-thin fibers carry light signals that report strain from within, turning the panel into its own health monitor. The worry is that the fibers themselves weaken the panel. The team varied how many fibers were embedded, then bent, pulled, and crushed the panels, with computer models alongside.

Up to five sensors could be embedded without hurting the panel's core strength in their tests. The embedded sensors tracked strain as well as surface gauges stuck on the outside. The results set practical limits on fiber count and placement, and they support smart panels that report damage in real time during service.
pmc-13363589:
Sarit Nov and colleagues report a 2026 study, the second part of a series, on using ash from a semi-industrial waste incinerator in Israel as a concrete ingredient. The ash, burned at mid-range furnace heat, was checked for its minerals and grain shapes, then swapped into industrial concrete in place of some cement or sand. Fresh flow and hardened strength were both tested against plain mixes.

The ash was rich in calcium phases, above all a cement-like mineral that made up over half the crystal content. Ash mixes flowed better and held their flow longer. As a sand swap, strength stayed within a hair of the plain mix, while as a cement swap it fared worse. The authors back ash as fine aggregate to cut landfill loads.
pmc-13363689:
Guokai Dai and colleagues report a 2026 study on titanium monoxide, Ti2O, as a saturable absorber for ultrafast fiber lasers. Such absorbers act as light valves that shape laser output into short pulses, and broadband, stable options are still wanted. The team baked phase-pure Ti2O crystals, coated them onto devices by light-driven deposition, and verified steady light-swallowing behavior with a twin-detector setup.

Placed in two fiber lasers, the absorbers gave stable pulsed output in both. One laser gave picosecond pulses near one micrometer. The other gave far shorter femtosecond pulses near 1.5 micrometers. The authors claim the first systematic use of Ti2O this way and offer it as a base for broadband ultrafast photonics.
pmc-13364289:
Martina Tosi and a large team report a 2026 survey of how people in the United Kingdom take sapropterin, a drug for the rare food disorder known as PKU. A 31-part form went out through a national PKU group site and social feeds. It asked about dose, form, food, and daily use.

Of 124 users who took part, most were care givers of young people. Most took the drug once a day, most used pills, and three in four took it with food. The spread of habits shows a need for clear, shared advice on how to give this drug.
pmc-13369889:
Paulius Gibieža and co-workers tie in 2026 two cell movers that must meet for a cell to split in two clean. One is a ves ship chief on loop pods. The next is a track motor that hauls loads to the bridge that joins young cells. Their meet at that bridge was not well set.

The pair crowd at the bridge in split cells. Drop either one and the pair link fades, with more twin core cells, stray mini cores, and long split spans. A cut crew chief fails to reach the bridge. The pair act as one axis for clean splits.
pmc-13372189:
Jose Rodrigo Alcantara Dzib and co-authors tell of a rare ear tumor in a 2026 case report. A man aged 43 had fluid behind his left ear drum for five years, with no lasting gain from care. A tube had been placed to drain the fluid, yet the trouble stayed.

Surgery on the bone behind the ear took a sample for lab tests. The tests showed a rare tumor made of nerve-type cells. Such growths are easy to miss, since they look like plain long-term ear fluid. The report urges ear teams to test odd, stuck cases, since full removal and long follow-up are the main care.
pmc-13373689:
Shin and colleagues report a fulminant case of streptococcal toxic shock syndrome that presented as a suspected spinal abscess, in a 2026 emergency care case report. The syndrome, caused by Group A Streptococcus, can crash organ function within days. A 75-year-old man arrived with days of neck and shoulder pain on both sides and a suspected cervical epidural abscess, an infected collection pressing on the spinal cord. He was short of breath on arrival.

Despite intubation before respiratory failure, the patient worsened to cardiac arrest and died within hours of arrival. Blood cultures taken at arrival grew Streptococcus pyogenes, reported after 3 days, confirming the toxic shock diagnosis only after death. Shin stresses that an epidural abscess is not a typical face of this syndrome, yet the infection can collapse catastrophically in its phase. A high index of suspicion and immediate workup, the authors argue, are the defenses.
pmc-13374289:
Mariam Ali and colleagues test whether migraine adds to artery stiffness and heart strain in middle-aged women after stroke in a 2026 study. Migraine raises stroke and heart disease risk in women, possibly through body-wide vessel dysfunction. Three groups of women aged 40 to 60 were compared: stroke alone, stroke with migraine, and neither condition.

Aortic stiffness was measured as arch pulse wave velocity on MRI, and heart function was judged by stroke volume, cardiac output, and ejection fraction. Among 118 women, with 44 in each stroke group, multivariable models estimated differences against the healthy reference group. The study asks whether migraine leaves a measurable macrovascular signature beyond stroke itself.
pmc-13375389:
Asayel S Almutairi and Saulat Jahan scored daily sugar care and life quality in Saudi Arabia in a 2026 study. The work sat in the Qassim zone and used health center patients. A web form in Arabic held two checked scales, one for care acts and one for life feel.

A total of 155 patients took part, with a mean age of 53 and a near even sex split. Care acts like food picks, moves, and sugar checks were logged next to life feel scores. The team hunted what drives life feel most. Such maps help clinics spend aid on the acts that lift daily life, not just blood marks.
pmc-13377689:
Ben Zion Vider puts forth a loop view of cell talk and cancer in a 2026 piece. Talk paths in cells run from face parts down to gene switch parts. The piece holds that those two ends oft boost each, in a loop that sets cell fate.

Such loops may be a core rule of growth, plain cell life, and the shift cells make when they turn spread-ready. Famed growth paths and their switch outs are the chief tales told. If loops rule, care could pair path drugs with gene-state drugs to break the loop. The piece is a frame to test, not a proof as yet.
pmc-13377789:
Madhu Bala and colleagues assess genetic diversity in twenty chrysanthemum genotypes in India in a 2026 study. Trials at Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana, in 2022 to 2023 covered cut, loose, and pot types grouped by early, mid, and late maturity. Vegetative traits, flowering traits, ray floret traits, and reproductive biology were measured.

Plant height, spread, branching, and stem girth varied significantly, with Ratlam Selection and Solan Shringar tallest and Punjab Mohini most branched. Early types initiated buds earliest, while late types took longer. Punjab Mohini yielded the most flowers per plant, and Jaya had the most ray florets. Pollen viability and pistil receptivity peaked on day three after flowering. The survey guides breeders toward high-yield, diverse parents.
pmc-13377889:
Kliti Grice and co-authors read a fossil fly-lizard bone from Brazil in a 2026 study. The wing bone is 113 million years old and kept its 3D shape, soft bits, and cure-like marks in one find, a rare trio. Fine scans and chem reads were pooled for the tale.

A shift to sour, air-rich states round the corpse was the key turn. Germ rot made sour states that laid down a hard bone mineral fast, which locked the soft bits in. That mineral sat with two rare salt stones. The step tale shows how a corpse can turn to a time vault, and what to hunt in next finds.
pmc-13379489:
Ninon Le Goaziou and a large French team report a 2026 nationwide study of whole-body treatments for severe alopecia areata in children. The condition causes major hair loss, and strong treatments are often used off-label, with little data on how well they work or how safe they are in children. The study fills that gap with real-world records.

It followed 262 children under eighteen who received at least one such treatment between 2010 and 2023. The main measure was how long each treatment was continued before stopping. The authors also recorded why treatments stopped and what happened over the long term. Most children were girls, and the typical age when hair loss began was nine years.
pmc-13380489:
Huimin Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 report of two patients with stubborn sunken scars treated by combining two regenerative materials. The scars followed inflamed lumps caused by cosmetic injections, which can destroy tissue under the skin and leave depressions that resist standard care such as laser treatment or ordinary fillers.

Treatment combined concentrated growth factor, prepared from the patient's own blood, with a collagen filler. The aim was to restore lost volume while prompting the skin to rebuild itself. Both cases involved scars that had failed to respond to earlier approaches. The report describes the technique and outcomes, and suggests this pairing may help a difficult and under-recognised problem.
pmc-13382389:
Sabrina Luettschwager and co-authors present a 2026 study of tummy-tuck surgery after massive weight loss, focusing on how much tissue is removed and whether that predicts complications. Removing loose skin and fat after major weight loss is demanding surgery. Higher removed weight has been linked with more problems, but the evidence was incomplete.

The study reviewed 217 adults operated on at a university hospital in Graz between 2012 and 2023, all after losing at least half their excess weight. It recorded weight history, tissue removed, and complications graded on a standard scale. Statistical models tested which patient and procedure factors drove resection weight, and whether resection weight itself predicted complications.
pmc-13382789:
Colleen Byrnes and colleagues trace how unusual fatty lipids harm nerve-like cells in a 2026 genome-wide screen. The lipids at issue lack a key hydroxyl group, so they cannot be broken down in the normal way. Their build-up is tied to nerve damage in several metabolic and brain disorders.

The screen pointed to the pathway that builds very long chain ceramides, fats with chains of 22 to 26 carbons. Cells lacking genes for that pathway resisted the toxic lipid and showed far less stress in the cell's protein-folding compartment. The results mark that pathway as a possible drug target for diseases driven by these lipids.
pmc-13382989:
Bijay Guragain's team reviews how to wire transplanted heart muscle cells into host tissue safely, in a 2026 review. Stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes promise repair after heart attack, but large-animal studies show arrhythmias from spontaneous beating and poor electrical coupling. Safety hinges on graft and host beating as one.

The review covers the basics of cardiac electrical activity and new tools for triggering and imaging it, including heart tissue slices with high-resolution optical mapping and optogenetic pacing. It also surveys biological fixes for coupling. The synthesis aims to guide the next generation of cell therapy trials toward grafts that integrate rather than irritate.
pmc-13383389:
Ziliang Deng's team built a single fusion-protein blood test to improve neurosyphilis diagnosis, in a 2026 study. An earlier luciferase assay for antibodies against Tp17 and Tp47 showed promise but needed simplification. The team fused Tp15, Tp17, and Tp47 into one tripartite antigen and tested serum from 434 HIV-negative patients suspected of neurosyphilis in Beijing and Guangzhou.

Antibodies against the fusion protein gave moderate diagnostic power alone, with 79 percent area under the curve in the development cohort. An optimized prediction model swapping in the fusion antibody improved accuracy further. The single-antigen format could make neurosyphilis testing simpler and more reliable in routine labs.
pmc-13383889:
Hwang and colleagues describe a simpler arthroscopic operation for irreparable tears at the back and top of the shoulder's rotator cuff, in a 2026 technique paper. Such tears in younger, active patients resist ordinary repair because the tendon is too damaged to reattach. The technique combines restorations: superior capsular reconstruction, which rebuilds the shoulder's static capsule, and lower trapezius tendon transfer, which reroutes a muscle to restore rotation. Together they address both systems in one procedure.

An Achilles tendon graft serves both repairs, easing graft preparation and fixation compared with using separate grafts. The approach works through small portals rather than an open incision. Hwang argues pairing the static and dynamic fixes restores the balance that isolated repairs leave lopsided. It also recovers external rotation strength that patients need for overhead activity. The paper presents steps and pearls rather than outcome data, positioning the method for case-series testing.
pmc-13386789:
Heinrike Schmeling's team sought serum markers tied to eye inflammation in German children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, in a 2026 cohort study. Uveitis threatens vision in juvenile arthritis, yet markers predicting its onset were unclear. The team tested baseline serum from newly diagnosed JIA patients in a cohort followed prospectively, using multi-analyte arrays for conventional and novel autoantibodies.

The analysis covered 52 patients with uveitis and 141 without. About 26 percent of uveitis patients already showed complications at first documentation. Younger age at diagnosis, higher ANA titers, and the AC-30 staining pattern tracked with uveitis presence, but not with complications. The AC-4 pattern appeared more often in children without uveitis. The markers may sharpen early risk detection and eye monitoring in juvenile arthritis care.
pmc-13387789:
Yoshihiro Ono and colleagues describe an awareness effect on a treatment fever reaction in syphilis in a 2026 letter. Their clinic began giving structured explanations before penicillin therapy in April 2025, covering likely symptoms, timing, and self-care steps. Earlier, some patients had mistaken the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction for drug allergy and stopped treatment.

In the prior year, the reaction appeared in 5 of 26 men treated for early syphilis at the clinic. The letter sets that baseline against the period after fuller explanations began, arguing awareness changes detection. Reported rates in the wider literature range widely, which frames why reporting habits matter.
pmc-13389289:
Lonike K. Faes's team used layer-resolved brain imaging to watch how the human cortex predicts sounds, testing predictive coding theory at mesoscopic scale. They played listeners a cascading oddball sequence, where repeated sounds set up expectations that occasional deviants break, while scanning with laminar blood-oxygen imaging.

Broken predictions lit up superficial planum polare layers and middle layers of lateral temporal cortex in an organised hierarchy, while updating the brain's internal model tracked changes in deep layers. The results ground auditory forecast in the layered architecture of temporal cortex and show laminar imaging can probe such fine-grained processes.
pmc-13389389:
Adrián García-Martínez's team simulated pyrophosphate hydrolysis in water. It is the model reaction behind ATP and GTP energy use, and the work settles how protonation and magnesium ions speed it up. Experiments and models had both left the workings and the metal's true speed boost unclear.

Machine-learning models trained to match quantum results, plus wide path sampling, showed several pathways, with a main route in which P-O bond making and breaking occur at once, then solvent-aided proton transfer. Both protonation and magnesium tightened the transition state and lowered barriers, though the metal's intrinsic effect proved smaller than previously thought.
pmc-13390689:
Kathrine M Jakobsen leads a 2026 effort to build a predictive model that helps clinicians tell typical from atypical positional vertigo. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is the most common cause of dizziness, yet reading the direction and strength of eye movements during attacks is hard, leading to uncertain diagnoses.

The retrospective study drew on 26 patients with typical or atypical disease plus two control subjects who had dizziness without vertigo. Eye and head movement data fed a data-driven model judged on how well it separated the variants. Balance specialists gain a decision aid aimed at the exact point where treatment often goes wrong, since repositioning manoeuvres only help when the correct canal is identified.
pmc-13391989:
Megan D Johnson and co-authors examine, in 2026, how everyday healthcare experiences may feed a cycle of genomic health disparities. Genetics is used ever more widely, yet racial minority groups, rural residents, and poorer patients are repeatedly left behind in access to genetic care and research.

Using the national All of Us research programme in a cross-sectional study, the team links reported healthcare experiences with engagement in genomic healthcare. The argument is that negative experiences compound access barriers, which in turn deepen underrepresentation. Health equity researchers gain evidence for treating patient experience itself as an intervention point, not merely a background factor.
pmc-13392189:
Tummala Mohit and colleagues report, in 2026, a shinbone fracture after partial knee replacement that they trace to the angle of the new component. The Oxford partial knee system is widely used for one-sided knee arthritis, usually with durable results.

A 70-year-old woman had both knees replaced with the cementless device. On the left, the tibial component sat in valgus, tilted outward, relative to a slightly inward resection cut. Postoperative scanning revealed an undisplaced tibial fracture, which was fixed internally and healed uneventfully. The authors argue the mismatch created eccentric loading and a wedging effect. Knee surgeons gain a specific alignment warning for cementless fixation.
pmc-13392289:
Daifei Shen, Runji Chen, and Shu Ye review, in 2026, the two-way link between fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction and cardiovascular disease. Evidence connecting the liver condition, now called MASLD, with adverse heart outcomes keeps growing as both burdens rise worldwide.

The review summarises epidemiological and clinical proof. It explains why the rename from NAFLD to MASLD shifts risk thinking toward metabolism. It also discusses liver fibrosis scores. Those scores may refine heart risk prediction beyond traditional factors. Cardiologists and liver specialists gain a shared framework for a patient group each specialty often sees separately.
pmc-13392989:
Ali Bahadur, Shahid Iqbal, Hashem O Alsaab, Nasser S Awwad, and Hala A Ibrahium face retraction of their study designing a photocatalyst meant to break down coloured pollutants under visible light. The catalyst paired nickel-zinc oxide with sulfur-doped carbon nitride. The notice from RSC Advances, signed by executive editor Laura Fisher in July 2026, replaces an earlier expression of concern. The authors supplied fresh data during the inquiry but could not produce the original raw records.

Editors list three faults: Infrared spectra in one figure had already appeared in an earlier paper described as a different experiment. X-ray patterns for supposedly distinct samples partly match in two figures. Given the scale of the overlap, the journal declares the findings no longer reliable. Iqbal opposes the retraction, while the remaining authors never answered the journal's letters.
pmc-13393689:
Emine Şimşek and Selimcan Satar test haptic virtual reality training before dental students treat real patients in a 2026 study. Preparing an access cavity in endodontics demands precise hand skill, anatomical knowledge, and confidence, and students usually first practice without live patients.

Thirty fourth-year students facing their first endodontics clinic cases were split into two groups of 15. One group received touch-feedback virtual reality training first, while the other went straight to clinic. Performance on real patients and student perceptions were then compared. Dental schools gain evidence on whether simulated touch practice transfers to the chair.
pmc-13394189:
Yuxu Wu and colleagues build a sustained-release microneedle patch for diabetic wounds in a 2026 study. Diabetic foot ulcers persist because oxidative stress stays high and new blood vessel growth stays weak throughout healing, and current treatments rarely address both at once.

The team loaded dihydrocapsaicin into cerium-based metal-organic frameworks inside a gelatin hydrogel microneedle patch, releasing drug across the whole healing course. Treated wounds showed lower oxygen radicals, a shift from inflammatory to healing macrophages, and stronger vessel growth. The patch offers a single platform for the full course of diabetic wound care.
pmc-13394489:
Maria Vamvini and colleagues test whether pre-ablation iodine levels predict thyroid cancer outcomes in a 2026 study. Radioactive iodine ablation after surgery needs high thyroid stimulating hormone and a low-iodine diet, yet the diet's effect on long-term outcomes was uncertain.

Among 304 patients treated at one center from 2007 to 2020, urinary iodine-to-creatinine ratio was measured after two weeks of low-iodine diet, with recurrence at twelve months as the main outcome. Positive pre-treatment thyroglobulin strongly predicted recurrence. Endocrinologists gain guidance on which pre-ablation markers actually matter for prognosis.
pmc-13395889:
Caroline Just and co-authors review, in 2026, how Alzheimer's disease differs in women, who make up near two thirds of cases. A gene variant named APOE4 raises risk more in women than in men. Menopause, depression, chronic stress, poor pregnancy outcomes, and metabolic faults may add to the load. The review covers markers, thinking tests, and care.

Amyloid build-up looks alike across sexes, but tau spreads earlier or faster in women once amyloid is present. Women often keep word memory longer despite hidden damage, which can delay diagnosis. A blood marker named p-tau217 may sharpen early spotting. The authors urge sex-aware testing and treatment.
pmc-13396189:
Yalan Yu and others show self-fixing high-detail two-photon printing in a 2026 study. This print craft builds 3D shapes at 100-nanometer fine scale, but shaky repeat runs and hand tuning have curbed factory use.

One laser comb printed while the twin-comb set gauged phase all over the work field at 360 hertz, feeding a live model that fixed height slips on the fly. A full fourteen-hour run made millimeter-scale light-bending parts with under 100-nanometer true slips. Makers gain a self-fixing route to nano-scale factory craft.
pmc-13396389:
Aggeliki Sotiriou and others study CYLD tag-trimming in brain cell talk and cell cleanup in a 2026 paper. Lysine63 tag chains are rife in the brain, and loss of the CYLD trim enzyme is tied to synapse faults and brain wasting, but its levers were dim.

The team shows CYLD-1 trim work boosting long-term synapse and cell upkeep, tying tag edits to signal pass and to cell cleanup, the cell's trash crew. By easing age-linked slide in these jobs, CYLD stands as a guard of aging synapses. The paper ties one small tag edit to brain aging fate.
pmc-13397089:
Parsa Ahsan and co-authors measured how well new mothers in Lahore, Pakistan, understand and use health information, and whether that skill tracks with how their pregnancies ended. Their 2026 cross-sectional study enrolled 374 postnatal women at the University of Lahore between January and June 2025.

A dedicated questionnaire recorded health literacy alongside social background and pregnancy history, and statistics were run in standard software. Mothers with low literacy may struggle to act on advice about danger signs, nutrition, or follow-up care, with costs for both mother and newborn. Local numbers, rather than imported assumptions, are what antenatal services need to target teaching where it is weakest.
pmc-13397689:
Guillaume Mulier and others compare information borrowing strategies in phase II oncology dose-ranging trials in a 2026 study. Stock phase I dose picking based on toxicity alone has led to poor approved doses, as with ibrutinib, whose lower doses later matched response rates.

Spurred by that case, the team adapted the Bayesian Optimal Phase II design to multiple doses and compared borrowing strategies for sharpening statistical power. Dose tuning is now urged in oncology, and borrowing across doses can sharpen dose picking without bigger trials. Trial designers gain a methods comparison for modern dose-ranging studies.
pmc-13397789:
Basile Njei and co-authors propose a scoring index for judging whether health artificial intelligence treats all groups fairly. Their 2026 viewpoint responds to tools trained on narrow data that can perform badly elsewhere and deepen existing gaps, above all in poorer countries. Good intentions, they argue, need a yardstick that regulators and buyers can actually use.

The AI in Healthcare Equity Index grades systems across five areas: whose data trained them, fairness of the algorithm, openness about how it works, oversight, and how benefits reach communities. One standard score would let hospitals compare products, push makers to improve and inform funding and publishing choices. The authors outline pilot tests across varied settings as the next step.
pmc-13398489:
European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), with Fernando Álvarez first among the listed authors, reports a 2026 peer review of the fungus Trichoderma atroviride strain 77B as a crop pesticide. The Netherlands acted as the lead assessing country under European Regulation 1107/2009. The microbe serves as a fungicide on nightshade crops such as tomato and pepper, plus strawberry and grapevine.

Reviewers checked the first national assessment, settled reliable endpoints for regulatory use and judged whether residue limits could be waived under Annex IV rules. Gaps where required information is still missing are listed in the conclusions. Such peer reviews form the evidence spine for European decisions on whether a pesticide stays on the market.
pmc-13398689:
Yuechuan Luo and co-authors find a natural gene variant that makes soybeans grow bigger, richer seeds. Their 2026 genome-wide scan for seed length landed on a locus on chromosome 20, named SL20. Seed size drives yield, yet its genetic control in soybean was only partly mapped.

The gene, GmSL20, codes for a TGA-type bZIP transcription factor. Knocking it out shrank seeds and cut lipid making, while boosting it enlarged seeds and raised oil content. It works by switching on two partner genes that route carbon into the seed. A superior allele born during domestication binds DNA harder, and seed collections carrying it run larger, a ready marker for breeders.
pmc-13399289:
Di Wang and colleagues traced a molecular brake on blood vessel regrowth after stroke in mice, reporting in 2026. The team focused on a long noncoding RNA called Gpr137b-ps. Computer predictions linked it to the messenger of the enzyme 15-PGDH, raising the question of how they interact in the brain's smallest vessels.

The researchers blocked a brain artery in mice to model stroke. They also starved cultured vessel cells of oxygen and glucose, then restored both. Ischemia raised levels of both the enzyme and the RNA. Silencing the enzyme reduced cell growth, movement, and tube formation, marking it as pro-vessel growth. Extra copies of the RNA lowered the enzyme's protein level and suppressed vessel formation. Restoring the enzyme rescued that suppression. The authors describe a feedback axis in which the RNA reins in the enzyme. Blocking the RNA might aid vascular repair, they suggest.
pmc-13399789:
Mikalyn T. DeFoor and colleagues outline a systematic approach to revision surgery after a failed Latarjet procedure for front shoulder instability. Their 2026 technical paper addresses a rare but difficult problem: graft misplacement, bone loss, broken hardware, or infection can leave the shoulder unstable after the first bone block operation. Scar tissue, shifted landmarks, and limited socket space complicate any redo.

The method centers on careful removal of prior hardware and graft, followed by thorough preparation of the front socket for a new distal tibial bone-cartilage allograft. A video case shows a 34-year-old man with more than 15 years of recurrent dislocation after earlier Bankart repair and Latarjet, still unstable despite physical therapy. The paper gives revision surgeons an organized sequence, while revision outcomes for this pathway need follow-up data.
pmc-13400089:

pmc-13400389:

pmc-13400489:

pmc-13400989:

Some checks used bacteria expressing the targets.
pmc-13401189:

pmc-13401289:

pmc-13401689:
Atal Saha and a large team wrote a 2026 genomic analysis of the white anglerfish, a species fished for sale, ranging widely across the North Atlantic and Mediterranean. pmc-13402089:

pmc-13402289:

The student model performed favorably against its own teachers across that spread. Wang and the team present the result as evidence that careful distillation can yield one sturdy, general tool for medical image work instead of many narrow ones.
pmc-13402689:

It held that output for 1000 hours at a factory-grade current density of 1 ampere per square centimeter. Pure cobalt, stuck on the worse pathway, managed only about 50 percent efficiency and worsened at high nitrate levels.
pmc-13402889:
Delphin Murhula Katabana and a team at the University Clinics of Bukavu follow a young girl with multierosive juvenile idiopathic arthritis that tests positive for rheumatoid factor. Disability follows in 20 to 30 percent of cases, often with slowed growth. A multierosive case managed in the Democratic Republic of Congo, they argue, deserves a record, since reports from such settings are scarce.
pmc-13403589:

Nine models were tested, with XGBoost performing best, reaching AUCs of 0.8423 in training and 0.7871 in validation. The team released an online tool for real-time prediction. The paper offers a practical triage aid, while prospective validation should confirm performance in new clinics.
pmc-13403889:

Better local blood flow followed in diabetic mice, and swelling plus cell stress in the wound calmed. Healing pace in the mice returned toward normal. pmc-13404089:
Evelin Despot-Slade and team weighed centromere layout across root-knot nematodes with different breeding and chromosome sets. pmc-13404489:

Adjusted analysis left heart glucose uptake as the only factor tied to advanced fibrosis risk. pmc-13404789:

pmc-13404989:

Plans differ in staffing, data systems and region, so responses were expected to vary.

Gains were larger in HMO plans, at 20.8 percent in the reported figures, than in PPO plans at 7.6 percent, and bigger in cities than in rural areas. pmc-13405589:

pmc-13406189:

Photographs and clinical details capture how lesions present on Filipino skin. Educational videos built from the cases aim to help general doctors recognise these diseases earlier.
pmc-13407589:

pmc-13407889:

pmc-13408089:

pmc-13408289:

pmc-13408689:

pmc-13409089:

pmc-13409989:

pmc-13410589:

pmc-13410889:

pmc-13411989:

pmc-13415289:

pmc-13415789:

pmc-13415889:

pmc-13415989:

pmc-13416189:

pmc-13416289:

pmc-13416389:

pmc-13416589:

pmc-13417289:

pmc-13418189:

pmc-13419189:

pmc-13419689:

pmc-13420089:

pmc-13420289:

pmc-13421189:

pmc-13421689:

pmc-13424089:

pmc-13445889:
Quan Wen and coauthors develop a 2026 rating tool, AFLE-HIV, for age-friendly housing for older adults living with HIV in China, a group lacking proven housing tools. pmc-13446189:
Paola Naal-Chan and colleagues report two Mexican teenagers with Sanfilippo syndrome, a rare storage disease that erodes the mind, in a 2026 case series. It is little diagnosed in Latin America, and no cases of these two subtypes had been confirmed in Mexico.

Her history held regression from age four and hard seizures. The pair marks the first confirmed cases of their subtypes in the land.
pmc-13446289:

pmc-13446889:
Julia G. Lebovitz and Sohee Park study how people with strong depersonalization, a felt split from self and world, register emotions in the body, in a 2026 survey study. The state often travels with trouble naming feelings, called alexithymia. The team set thirty-three adults with high scores beside sixty-six with low scores from the general population.

Higher depersonalization also went with higher alexithymia scores. pmc-13447289:
Darong Lu and colleagues build a prediction model for pneumonia after bleeding stroke in a 2026 study. Lung infection is a serious and common complication that worsens recovery. Five learning algorithms were trained and compared on held-out cases, with plain logistic regression performing best. Explanation scores ranked leg muscle strength, cholesterol measures, white cell count and alertness among the strongest signals. The authors offer the model as a quantitative aid for sorting patients and targeting prevention early.
pmc-13447789:
Lynn Addington argues that age subgroups matter in partner homicide against older women in a 2026 brief research note. Firearms featured in most cases at every age, with their share rising as age rose. Age-aware risk research is the note's central plea.
pmc-13448489:
Zhang and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract BSLD-08, a hunt for what lets lung and breast cancer cells colonize the leptomeninges. The authors propose MAL2 as both a prognostic marker and a possible drug target.
pmc-13449789:
Maren Hülsemann and a large Berlin team audit in 2026 how well the flood of COVID-19 studies using human organ models reported their methods. The systematic review covered 558 studies, split into pandemic and post-pandemic periods, and judged how each investigated host factors, viral replication, and immune responses.

Post-pandemic papers improved only partly. The authors link the gaps to harder bias assessment and shakier evidence synthesis, exactly when pooled answers mattered most. pmc-13449989:
Serna and colleagues report a 2026 study of gut bacteria inside tumors and survival in bowel cancer that can be removed by surgery. Nine centers enrolled stage I to III patients, and a central lab tested tumors for Fusobacterium. The team tracked recurrence and survival for about four years.

About one in five of 740 patients had Fusobacterium-positive tumors, which were more often right-sided, high-grade, and invasive, with less immune cell entry. Positive patients relapsed sooner, with recurrence risk near double that of negative patients even after other factors were weighed. Added chemotherapy after surgery clearly helped bacteria-negative patients but showed no clear gain in positive ones.
pmc-13450189:
Xiaoyan Zhang and co-authors characterize in 2026 Campylobacter bacteria collected from chicken farms and shop-bought poultry across ten regions of Jiangsu Province, China. The genus is a leading cause of foodborne diarrheal disease, and chicken meat is its main route to people. Nearly half the isolates, 46.6 percent, resisted multiple drugs, and the species split sharply: Campylobacter coli hit 75.4 percent multidrug resistance against only 17.5 percent in Campylobacter jejuni. The commonest resistance gene rode in a pump variant carried mainly by jejuni. Seven jejuni isolates carried wlaN, a gene linked to the paralyzing Guillain-Barré syndrome, a finding the authors flag for surveillance.
pmc-13451589:
Arko Dhar and co-authors link in 2026 a heart health score to vessel function in the Jackson Heart Study, a large Black adult cohort. Higher scores went with slower pulse waves in stiff main arteries, lower center pressure, and better flow surge in the arm after a squeeze test. Blood sugar and blood pressure grades drove most of the links. The authors read the pattern as proof that a healthy daily life leaves a mark on vessel walls, and they call for work on whether raising scores repairs vessels.
pmc-13451789:
Aarno Hatsala and co-authors release in 2026 a data set from lab tests on a layered timber floor built with glued wood trusses. The floor was built step by step, adding board skins, ceiling panels, a concrete cap, and light walls. Each stage was loaded and shaken so the effect of each layer could be read on its own.

Weight tanks drove bend tests, read by dial gauges, while heel drops set off shakes caught by motion sensors at many spots. Files hold raw and cleaned measures, sensor maps, and diagrams for free reuse. The team offers the data for checks of floor comfort rules, design guides, and new timber floor studies.
pmc-13452089:
Hannah Rowe and Frank Guenther review in 2026 a brain model of speech control called DIVA and what it says about speech disorders. The model maps how the brain turns word plans into mouth moves through three loops: a preset move plan, hearing feedback, and touch feedback. Each loop is tied to named brain zones and paths.

That map lets the team read disorders such as stuttering as faults in set loops, rather than as vague breakdowns. The review walks the model's build, its uses across speech ills, and how it could steer care and speech tech. Rival models are set beside it so readers can judge where DIVA fits in the field.
pmc-13452189:
Reshmi Talwar and a large team report in 2026 on a joint eye clinic set inside a cancer center for transplant patients at risk of an eye attack by donor cells. The eye form of graft-versus-host disease hits about half of stem cell transplant patients, yet watch rules are vague. The Maryland clinic opened in 2021, and the team set 76 later patients against 107 earlier ones.

Eye disease struck about a fifth of the earlier group and near an eighth of the later group within two years of transplant. Adjusted odds ran lower after the clinic opened, though the gap fell short of firm proof. First-visit eye treatments were also checked for links. The authors back built-in eye watch as part of transplant care.
pmc-13453489:
Kor and colleagues used gene editing in 2026 to change how rice builds starch in its grains. They disabled a gene called OsSBEIIb, which helps branch starch chains, in the widely grown IR64 variety.  The team then measured starch shape, cooking traits, protein, and small chemicals in the grain.

The edited rice had fewer short starch chains and more long chains, plus much more resistant starch, which resists digestion. Its predicted glycaemic index, a score for how fast food raises blood sugar, fell from 80 to 57 in the edited lines. Protein content rose by up to a tenth, with more of several essential amino acids. The trade-offs were chalkier grains and lighter seeds. The authors see these lines as a base for healthier rice, once grain quality improves.
pmc-13453589:
Ram and Damodaran review a class of small RNA molecules in cancer and argue that where and when they act matters as much as which ones are present. These molecules, called oncomiRNAs, tune gene activity after a gene is copied, and they can push tumors to grow or hold them back. The 2026 review stresses that most past work ground up whole tumor samples, which hides how these molecules vary across regions, spread sites, and stages of disease.

New tools such as spatial gene mapping, single cell profiling, and repeat blood tests now reveal that variation. The review links shifting oncomiRNA patterns to drug resistance, escape from the immune system, and mixed patient outcomes. The authors urge studies that sample many tumor regions over time, feed the data into shared models, and design trials that adapt treatment to each patient's changing pattern.
pmc-13453789:
Ge Li and Wenshi Wei test a nutrition score as a death risk signal in critically ill stroke patients and build a machine learning model around it. The score, called CONUT, blends albumin, cholesterol, and a white cell count to grade nourishment. Their 2026 study draws 1,103 patients from a large intensive care database and checks the result in 659 patients at a Chinese hospital.

Each one point rise in the score came with a 14.1 percent rise in 30 day death risk and a 15.9 percent rise over a year. Survival curves sank step by step as nourishment grades worsened. Of six learning methods, a model called CatBoost sorted risk best, holding up in the outside hospital check. The authors present the simple score plus model as an early warning pair for stroke units.
pmc-13454289:
Helgi Winther Olsen and others tested the FIT FIRST FOR ALL school activity program in the Faroe Islands in 2026, measuring acute physiological and perceptual responses. The structured program offers three weekly forty-minute sessions for ten weeks alongside physical education, aiming to promote engagement. A non-randomized cluster study enrolled 179 pupils aged seven to sixteen.

In a subsample of fifty-three, sessions consistently reached moderate-to-vigorous intensity, with mean heart rate at 67.2 to 69.9 percent of maximum and 57.9 to 64.9 percent of session time at moderate-to-vigorous intensity. Enjoyment was comparable across fitness groups despite higher exertion in low-fitness pupils. Cardiorespiratory fitness improved in the intervention sample of 117, with greater gains tending toward the lowest fitness group. Schools gain evidence the program engages all fitness levels.
pmc-13454389:
Thibault Schutz, Nezha Badi, and Filip E. Du Prez introduce, in 2026, molecular tags that let makers trace plastic goods through production and recycling. The tags are short chains built from a four-letter chemical alphabet, mixed into plastic at less than 0.05 percent by weight. Each chain spells a code that marks the batch or product.

Light-based checks give a first read of the tag, and a scripted mass spectrometry routine confirms the full sequence. The team compared two backbone designs to find which survives heat better. Tags stayed intact inside both soft plastics and hard resins, enduring extrusion at up to 270 degrees and full curing steps. The authors present the system as a practical tool against fakes and for sorting plastics by origin.
pmc-13454589:
William Z. Zhang leads a large team studying, in 2026, an iron-storage protein that worsens severe lung failure. The team found both ferritin parts enriched in the blood and lung macrophages of patients, and matched the pattern in mice with oxygen-driven lung injury.

The authors name macrophage ferritin handling as a lever for future lung therapies.
pmc-13454989:
Fu and colleagues tested in 2026 crocin I, a pigment from saffron, for its power to slow cell ageing in human lung fibroblasts. pmc-13455189:
Ramesh R Allam and others read care-place choice for HIV patients in Andhra Pradesh, India, in 2026, for 2023 to 2024. Among two hundred thirteen thousand three hundred seventy-five patients alive in care, twenty thousand seven hundred sixty-one, or nine point seven percent, trekked far and were offered near care. Poisson models with firm errors picked traits tied to taking near care, given as adjusted relative risks. Twelve-month stay-in-care was set side by side by Kaplan-Meier curves for near and far care groups. Programme planners gain take-up traits and stay-in-care proof for spread-out care.
pmc-13457389:

pmc-13457589:

pmc-13457789:

The authors conclude the four products work about equally in the short term, with none clearly superior.
pmc-13457889:

pmc-13457989:

pmc-13458089:

pmc-13458389:

pmc-13458489:

pmc-13459089:

pmc-13459789:

That reference helps them compare how related strains divide labor with different partners.
pmc-13461489:

pmc-13462389:

A decision tree picked out the key factors, and a second modelling step confirmed how the parts relate. Fit scores for the final model were good by standard cut-offs.
pmc-13462889:

pmc-13463889:

pmc-13464989:
Ji and colleagues studied in 2026 a puzzling pattern after treatment for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, a pregnancy-related tumor: the hormone hCG stays mildly raised during follow-up. pmc-13465189:

The review ties lab chemistry to clinic and field use, arguing the hybrids fit a greener materials future.
pmc-13465289:
Lillian G. Maxwell and colleagues built a DNA test in 2026 for deerpox virus, a spreading pox disease of wild and captive deer. pmc-13465389:

pmc-13465489:

pmc-13465589:
