pmc-13465789:
Maksimovic and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how economic thinking explains decisions in dementia care and similar life-limiting illness. Such decisions are shared among patients, family carers, and professionals, and they drive much of the cost. The search spanned four databases plus targeted economics sources. From 9,854 studies, 62 were kept for close reading.

Six economic concepts organized the evidence. They are the principal-agent problem, uncertainty, and asymmetric information. The empathy gap and hyperbolic discounting follow, and the non-linear value of time completes the set. Together they help explain familiar patterns, like high spending at the end of life. They also explain why advance care planning works unevenly. Global dementia costs were estimated above 1.3 trillion dollars, half of it unpaid family care time. The authors call for dynamic three-way communication as the practical fix.
pmc-13465889:
Akın Özdemir, Mehmet Altay Sevimay, and Ercan Karakaş ran matching surveys of dental implant patients and their dentists to see where expectations line up and where they part, in a 2026 study. Two hundred fifty patients and two hundred dentists answered parallel sixteen-item questionnaires. Items covered hopes for the final result and worries about the surgery itself, each rated on a five-point scale.

The two groups differed clearly on thirteen of the sixteen items. Total scores, though, came out nearly equal because gaps in opposite directions cancelled each other. The surgical worry section held several of the sharpest mismatches. For clinics, the lesson is practical: asking about single topics beats trusting an overall score that hides real gaps in understanding.
pmc-13466289: Hector Guadalajara and colleagues issued a correction in 2026 to their rectal cancer study from the FOREST project. The notice is a correction only. It adds missing affiliation lines for three of the authors. The added lines name doctoral programs in Madrid, at the Autonomous University of Madrid in Spain. No data, methods, or findings change. The authors state that the study's conclusions stand as before. The journal's academic editor approved the fix, and the original article was updated to match.
pmc-13466689:
Eui-Jong Kwon, Bong-Woo Lee, and Ji Hyeon Ju map the cytokine networks that drive Sjögren's disease and differ between its many faces, in a 2026 narrative review. The autoimmune condition dries the eyes and mouth as immune cells invade glands, yet many patients also suffer effects far beyond the glands. Signaling proteins from both the innate and adaptive arms sustain that attack.

In glands, interferon signals and helper T cell cytokines keep inflammation alive and even build lymphoid clusters. Across the body, the BAFF and APRIL signals plus interferon signatures drive antibody production. Sorting patients by which network dominates could guide targeted therapy, the direction the authors favor.
pmc-13466789:
Hatice Duman and colleagues produce a gut bacterium's sugar-cutting enzyme and test how broadly it can strip complex sugars from proteins, in a 2026 study. Such sugars, called N-glycans, shape how proteins fold and behave, yet freeing them intact usually demands harsh pre-treatment. The enzyme, EndoBI-1, comes from a Bifidobacterium strain that lives in infant guts.

Two very different test proteins were used: bovine lactoferrin from milk and soy protein from plants. Precise mass analysis showed the released sugar sets differed by source, with complex and sialic-acid-bearing forms among them. A versatile, gentle release tool matters because sugar profiles are read as clues in food science and disease research alike.
pmc-13466889:
Wang and co-authors describe a cheap, sunlight-driven material for cleaning antibiotic-contaminated water in this 2026 study. Powdered catalysts that break down pollutants under light are often costly and hard to handle. So the team set bismuth tungstate, a light-active compound, into a geopolymer. That is a stone-like material made from inexpensive industrial ingredients. Their target was tetracycline hydrochloride, a common antibiotic found in wastewater.

With only four percent bismuth tungstate in the mix, the composite removed 82.7 percent of the antibiotic after 300 minutes under visible light. The test ran at a mildly alkaline pH of 8. Scavenger tests, which block specific reactive species, showed that positively charged holes and superoxide radicals did most of the breakdown work. The material also kept its structure and performance in real water samples.
pmc-13467289: Beigi Kheradmand and colleagues published a correction in 2026 in Materials to their 2022 article on heat treatment of an aluminum alloy with scandium and zirconium. Editors confirmed that reference 73, a 2021 paper on photoacoustic pumps, was off topic. That citation was removed, and later reference numbers shifted. The authors state the article's conclusions are unaffected. It was approved by the Academic Editor, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13467589:
Martin Sedlmajer and colleagues open a 2026 research program on how polymer fibre insulation actually burns, starting at the scale of single fibres. Fire safety classes for building materials in Europe rest largely on empirical test methods, which makes results hard to use when developing new insulation, much of it made from recycled textile fibres. Burning in these materials mixes physical and chemical processes in ways the standard classes do not capture.

Instead of offering a finished predictive model, the authors lay out the basic relationships that should govern fibre combustion and report their first experimental results. The goal is a physics-based path from fibre behavior to the fire class a finished product earns. Such a path would let manufacturers design insulation for fire performance rather than discovering it in late, expensive tests.
pmc-13467689:
Víctor Huebla-Concha and colleagues present a 2026 draft genome for Ecuadorian plantain, Musa paradisiaca, and track two genes behind fruit browning. Browning, driven by enzymes called polyphenol oxidases, cuts the market value of fruit from one of the world top banana exporters. The team sequenced the genome with a portable nanopore device and assembled it into 13,239 contigs, or DNA segments.

Within that draft they found two browning enzyme genes, named MpPPO1 and MpPPO2, and deposited them in a public gene bank. Gene activity tests across three stages of green fruit showed MpPPO1 rising sharply in physiologically mature green fruit, while the second gene behaved differently. Knowing which gene switches on as fruit matures gives breeders and handlers a target for slowing the browning that downgrades the harvest.
pmc-13467889:
Qin and colleagues stress-test a candidate Moon construction material in this 2026 study: fabric woven from basalt fiber, a thread spun from melted volcanic rock. Lunar surfaces swing from minus 196 to plus 125 degrees Celsius and endure harsh ultraviolet radiation, conditions that degrade ordinary polymers, so the team simulated those extremes in the laboratory.

Fabric samples and natural basalt rock powder went through repeated thermal shock cycles and ultraviolet exposure, then faced a battery of structural checks. The fiber surfaces stayed intact with no cracking or etching, the internal silicate network showed no recrystallization, and color measurements stayed stable even under combined heat and ultraviolet attack. Most importantly, the yarns' tensile strength showed no downward trend as cycles accumulated. The authors conclude the fabric's durability rivals natural basalt rock itself, supporting its use in future lunar composites.
pmc-13468289:
Azzurra Annunziata, Artur Kraus, and Angela Mariani survey in 2026 the willingness of Italian university students to try cultured meat, lab-grown meat that is not yet sold in their country. Cultured meat promises sustainability and animal welfare gains, but acceptance is unproven where consumers cannot buy it. An online survey of 335 students was analyzed to find which perceptions and values actually drive openness to a first taste.

Willingness was driven mainly by familiarity with the product, perceived safety, and ethical concern for animal welfare. Demographic traits and general resistance to new food technologies mattered far less. For policymakers and producers, the lesson is that information and safety assurance, plus the animal welfare case, will move young consumers more than novelty marketing. The authors draw practical lessons for launching a controversial food in a traditional food culture.
pmc-13468489:
Dinh Quang Ngoc and colleagues test in 2026 a visual reaction training system for the footwork of badminton players under twelve. Thirty-four young players were randomly split between the light-based training system and a control group for six weeks. Performance was scored with star-pattern footwork tests under both fixed and random light sequences, capturing reaction time and total movement time separately.

The training system produced significant gains in reaction time and movement time for the elementary school boys in the trial. Because the lights both cue the movement and record it, the system doubles as a measuring tool, giving coaches objective numbers for agility and coordination instead of stopwatch impressions. Fast, accurate first steps decide junior badminton rallies, and a low-cost light system that trains and tests them together is an attractive addition to school programs.
pmc-13468689:
Ahmet Turgut and co-authors let a machine learning surrogate design in 2026 an extremely small dual-band MIMO antenna for sub-6 gigahertz 5G and Internet of Things devices. Shrinking multiple antennas into a tiny footprint while keeping the ports isolated normally demands endless full-wave simulations. Their framework trains a deep neural network on 440 simulated designs, then actively proposes new candidates, refining the search boundaries as it learns.

At the 83rd active learning cycle the system found its best candidate, later validated in the standard simulator and built. The nested-loop antenna, with a deliberately defected ground structure, fits in 1,634 square millimeters on a Rogers circuit board and works across two bands. Autonomous design loops like this one attack the real bottleneck of antenna engineering, which is expert time spent babysitting simulations.
pmc-13468789:
Zhuang and co-authors map the evidence for rehabilitation in chronic bone and joint pain. Their 2026 critical narrative review uses a structured evidence-mapping approach across studies from 2021 to 2026, sorting interventions and hunting gaps rather than pooling numbers. Exercise therapy anchors the findings.

Exercise supported functional outcomes and pain relief in selected musculoskeletal conditions, though the best dose and which patients match which programme remain uncertain. Manual therapy and physical modalities offered short-term relief as adjuncts, with effects conditional on technique and context. Digital and virtual-reality rehabilitation improved access and engagement, but functional and lasting benefits varied. Low-load blood-flow-restriction training looked promising for patients who cannot tolerate heavy loads. The authors resist a universal precision model, proposing phenotype-informed matching as a research agenda and noting heterogeneity and publication bias throughout the base.
pmc-13468889:
Mao and co-authors simulate transformer oil breaking down, hunting earlier warning gases. Their 2026 paper models mineral insulating oil with reactive molecular dynamics. The team built a multi-component oil of alkanes, ring compounds, and aromatics. They exposed it to heat alone and to heat plus electric field. Standard dissolved gas analysis watches only the smallest gases, which appear late in a fault's development.

The simulations, backed by bench experiments, spotlight mid-size three- and four-carbon hydrocarbons as earlier sentinels. Heat sped breakdown overall; the mid-size gases accumulated at moderate temperatures and appeared in a specific mid-temperature window. An added electric field supplied reaction energy and boosted their generation. Crucially, their concentrations fluctuated measurably in incipient, non-breakdown faults long before the conventional gases moved. The authors propose adding these intermediates to monitoring practice for earlier transformer fault detection.
pmc-13469189:
Bowen Tian and colleagues fuse infrared and visible images in 2026 with a method that asks how much each pixel region of each source can be trusted. Fusion must keep visible texture while preserving the hot silhouettes only infrared sees, and forcing one source over the other destroys real information. Their framework, ARC3Fusion, decomposes the pair into what both agree on, what each adds, and where they conflict.

A progressive encoder with modality-specific adapters produces the features first. Candidate details from each side are verified. Infrared extras are checked against heat intensity and edge evidence. Visible extras are checked against source cues and learned frequency patterns. A conflict estimator maps the incompatible zones so the fusion can handle them deliberately instead of smearing them. Surveillance, night driving, and rescue imaging all consume fused pictures, and a fusion that knows which source to believe where is the advance claimed.
pmc-13469589:
Zhang and colleagues propose a 2026 security scheme for groups of small internet-connected devices that must prove their identity to each other without heavy computation. Quantum computers threaten today's codes, and tiny devices cannot store secret keys safely. Their design combines three tools to solve both problems at once.

Each device carries a physical unclonable function, a hardware fingerprint that cannot be copied, so no secret key sits in memory. Quantum key distribution supplies session keys that are secure in principle, and a gossip method spreads group agreement through neighbor chats instead of one broadcast storm. Pseudonyms hide real identities, and keys refresh when members join or leave. Formal logic checks supported the design, which beat rival schemes on cost in tests.
pmc-13469989:
Martinez and colleagues in Canada asked in 2026 whether a stand in score can speed kidney cancer trials: time free of disease in place of time alive. Trials for such tumors use the free of disease mark as their main score, but its link to life span was unproven. The team swept the banks for past drug trials round surgery and kept 25. Of those, 13 gave both scores, near ten thousand patients in all.

The two scores tracked each other with strength: where drugs cut the return of disease, they cut death in step. The link let the team set a bar. A drug that cut the disease return risk by near a tenth or more could be read as a life gain. No slant showed in which trials saw print. The authors back the stand in score for new trials, with long checks still run.
pmc-13470189:
Aishwarya S Borkar, Yvanna Todorova, and Oonagh Markey pool trial evidence in 2026 on whether a component of milk fat can improve heart, metabolic, and brain markers in adults. The milk fat globule membrane and its polar lipids are bioactive parts of dairy fat. Their review searched three databases for randomized trials comparing foods or supplements rich in these components against similar dairy products low in them.

Thirteen studies passed screening, with quality rated low to moderate concern. Pooled results over two to sixteen weeks showed modest drops in total cholesterol and in the harmful LDL fraction. A protein marker tied to cholesterol particles and the ratio of total to protective cholesterol also fell. The reviewers graded the certainty behind each key outcome, giving readers a cautious summary of what is known.
pmc-13471389:
Romano and colleagues built a drug carrier from red blood cell vesicles, tiny bubbles shed by red cells, to deliver two cancer drugs together against triple-negative breast cancer. Their 2026 study loaded the vesicles with cisplatin, a chemotherapy drug, and cetuximab, an antibody drug, and tested the pairing in cells and patient-derived organoids.

Because the vesicles carry no DNA and lack the receptor cetuximab targets, the two drugs did not interfere with each other inside the carrier. The combined formulation boosted cisplatin's cancer-killing power by up to 50% in laboratory tests and in organoids grown from patient tumors. Gene-readout data point to ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, as part of how the treatment kills tumor cells.
pmc-13471489:
Liu and colleagues dissected how four variants of the NR5A1 gene, a master switch for adrenal and sex-organ development, disrupt its function in 46,XY disorders of sex development. Their 2026 study examined two newly found variants and two known ones from patients at a Shanghai children's hospital, testing protein behavior and gene activity in cells.

All four variants sat at conserved positions and cut the amount of NR5A1 protein while keeping it out of the cell nucleus where it works. The truncating variant broadly switched down hormone-making genes, including CYP11A1, STAR, and CYP17A1, which build steroids. Two further target genes, AMHR2 and STARD8, lost both expression and the variant protein's binding signal. Such variants explain roughly 10 to 15% of these disorders.
pmc-13471589:
Bae and colleagues used topic modeling, an algorithm that clusters word patterns, to map seven decades of home health care research and find its blind spots. Their 2026 analysis ran latent Dirichlet allocation over 39,548 PubMed papers published from 1952 to April 2025, distilling them into ten coherent topics.

Healthcare resource utilization was the steadiest theme across the whole period, anchoring the field's agenda. Telehealth, end-of-life services, and technology-assisted caregiving grew fastest, a shift visible from the 2010s and supercharged by the pandemic, when telehealth visits leapt from 0.2% of medical claims in 2019 to 15.4% in 2020 nationally. Pediatric home care and screening of high-risk groups stayed notably underrepresented throughout.
pmc-13472889:
Ngo and colleagues replied in 2026 to a letter critiquing their study of glutamate inputs into the sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus, a small brainstem hub that drives REM sleep, the dreaming stage. Their work mapped excitatory inputs from cortex and brainstem and identified neurons in a nearby gray area whose activity pattern suggests they help launch REM sleep. The letter questioned the fiber photometry method, which reads bulk calcium glow from many cells at once.

The authors concede the method's low cellular resolution but argue the cited weakness came from the striatum, a region whose dense branching cells differ sharply from their brainstem targets. They cite work showing photometry signals track cell-body activity well elsewhere. They thank the critics, accept the stated limits of their tracing, and welcome the proposed follow-up directions. The exchange, they suggest, sharpens how the field should hunt the true sources of REM-triggering input.
pmc-13473289:
Changjiu Liang and colleagues build a tool in 2026 to flag early death risk in a fast-moving blood cancer. The cancer, called peripheral T-cell lymphoma not otherwise specified, often turns deadly within months. Data came from a United States registry for 1,156 people diagnosed between 2016 and 2021. Seven factors stood out, among them age, stage, symptoms, and whether chemo or radiation was given.

Seven learning methods were trained and checked on held-out cases. One method, called XGBoost, gave the best balance of accuracy and clear risk scores. Charts in the report show how each factor pushes risk up or down for a given person. Doctors could use such a tool to plan closer watch or stronger care for those at highest risk.
pmc-13473489:
Rui Bai and six colleagues optimised in 2026 riverbed dredging for a mixed pumped-storage power station in China, where hydropower, wind, and solar are combined. Such stations face a pumping funnel problem in the lower reservoir, a swirling dip that threatens reliable pumping, yet engineering fixes for it had barely been studied. Using the Lianghekou station as a case study, the team paired numerical modelling with physical experiments, choosing the best scheme by balancing pumping improvement against cost.

The chosen scheme was then verified in a large physical model of the whole lower reservoir. It widened the river cross-section by 15 to 23 percent, cut reverse flow by 30 to 42 percent, and shrank pumping funnel depth to 65 percent of its original value. Continuous pumping lengthened by 61 percent. The authors offer the numbers as a basis for design at Lianghekou, with lessons for other mixed pumped-storage projects.
pmc-13473689:
Anil Utku and three colleagues built in 2026 a data-driven index for judging how well European cereal systems withstand climate stress. Most earlier work tracked average yield responses, leaving resilience itself poorly measured. Their index separates long-term yield trends from short-term climate-driven swings.

Annual yield series were split into trend and anomaly parts, and several machine and deep learning models tested which climate signals predicted them. A combined TCN-LSTM model predicted best, and a principal-component framework captured most climate variation in one factor. Lagged yield anomalies and rolling volatility led the predictors. Country results varied widely, and rankings held up under different weights. The index gives planners a consistent way to compare resilience across countries.
pmc-13474689:
Yi Liu and co-authors report a plant biochemistry study, published in 2026. It traces how moringa sprouts make glucomoringin. This sulphur-rich compound is valued as the source of moringin. Moringin is studied for anticancer potential. The pathway in sprouts was largely unknown. The team combined gene activity profiling with chemical analysis. Sprout extracts were analysed.

The team compared germinating seeds under two conditions. Some received added tyrosine. Tyrosine is an amino acid building block. They mapped a proposed tyrosine-based route. Candidate genes were named for each step. Several enzyme genes were among them. Two further genes were flagged as likely converters. They would turn glucomoringin into moringin. Breeders and growers now have targets for raising levels of the compound.
pmc-13474889:
Yalcin and co-authors looked for warning signs that womb cancer has spread to the para-aortic lymph nodes, glands high in the abdomen whose involvement worsens the outlook. Their 2026 review covered 598 patients with stage I to III disease who had full surgical staging at Bursa Uludag University Hospital between 2000 and 2025. The team tested which tumor and patient features predicted spread to those upper glands.

Para-aortic spread appeared in 64 patients, or 10.7 percent of the staged group, and in 3.5 percent it was the only nodal disease found. Cancer already in the pelvic nodes was by far the strongest predictor, raising the odds of upper spread about 25-fold in the adjusted analysis. A raised blood marker called CA-125 added independent risk, as did deep invasion into the womb muscle. Tumor cells inside small vessels mattered too, and the authors say these signs can guide who needs full node removal.
pmc-13476889:
Caroline Kokorudz and co-authors show in 2026 that an imprinted gene called Peg3 guards DNA marking in placenta precursor cells. Mice lacking the gene grow small placentas and fetuses, yet its molecular job was vague. Stem cells from the placenta lineage without Peg3 made more copying errors and DNA breaks. Two repressive marks, one on DNA and one on histones, both ran low.

Without Peg3, cells failed to silence genes that should stay off at their stage. Mark loss hit a set of control islands that wire gene networks through a looping protein. Peg3 thus acts as part of the silencing machinery itself. Placenta growth faults gain a molecular thread to follow.
pmc-13477389:
Gaetano Pinnacchio and coauthors published a 2026 validation study of seven scoring systems meant to predict hidden atrial fibrillation after unexplained stroke. Finding this rhythm disorder matters because it changes stroke prevention treatment. Implantable heart monitors can detect it, but cost and logistics limit their use, so scores aim to pick who benefits most from monitoring.

The study followed 132 patients with cryptogenic stroke or transient ischemic attack who received implantable monitors. Each published score was applied to the same patients and judged on how well it separated those who developed atrial fibrillation from those who did not. Threshold versions of the scores were also tested for ruling out the condition with high confidence. The work gives clinicians an outside check on tools mostly tested only by their creators.
pmc-13478389:
Pranda Prasanta Gupta and six colleagues planned in 2026 wind-storage capacity for high-mountain irrigation pumping using an improved whale algorithm. Wind and solar vary unpredictably, and storage must cover pumping demand without inflating lifetime cost.

Their scenario-free chance model weighed wind, pumping, and storage options, comparing single-battery against hybrid battery-gas storage. The hybrid cut lifetime cost by 5.4 percent, eased battery stress, and kept pumping efficiency. A dependability model for wind generation underpinned the planning. The approach shows clear money and technical gains for renewable irrigation systems.
pmc-13478489:
Jimin Pei and two colleagues mapped in 2026 predicted protein links across the human proteome in structural detail. Their earlier work had listed nearly 18,000 high-confidence predicted links; this follow-up turns selected links into testable ideas about how proteins work together.

Case studies cover DNA repair, mitochondrial function, and the building of cilia and other cell parts, showing how paired links join into larger multi-protein machines and reveal new candidate parts. Disease-linked mutations often sit right inside predicted contact zones, suggesting how a single change can break a network and drive illness. The work thus turns bulk predictions into concrete leads for lab tests and fuller maps of cell machinery.
pmc-13479889:
Xu Han and colleagues present a 2026 study building machine learning models to predict whether bile duct stones return after endoscopic removal. Recurrence is common enough that follow-up planning matters, and a risk estimate could target surveillance. Records from 1,130 patients were split seventy-thirty into training and test sets.

Automated feature selection and logistic regression narrowed the predictors to eight risk factors. Three model families were tuned by random search with ten-fold cross-validation: random forest, gradient boosting, and logistic regression. Accuracy measures and decision curve analysis compared their clinical usefulness. The winning model was then opened up with Shapley explanations, which show how much each factor pushes an individual prediction up or down.
pmc-13481489:
João Prada and co-authors describe a 2026 study of soil bacteria around grapevine roots in Portugal's Douro valley, famed for port wine. Climate shifts threaten the valley, so knowing what shapes root microbes may guide rescue plans. The team sampled four vineyards from mid-2022 to early 2024, profiling soil chemistry, rootstock type, and bacterial communities by gene barcoding.

Soil traits ruled the mix, led by organic matter and acidity. Rootstock type played a second role, sorting microbes by what they do rather than who they are. One stock drew versatile, fast-growing bacteria keen to expand, while the other favoured tight specialists that squeeze energy from scarce fare. Each vineyard thus grows its own microbial terroir. Vine managers gain a baseline for seeding helpful microbes as the climate warms.
pmc-13482189:
Eugene Kim and eight colleagues linked in 2026 MRI patterns to gene programs in a mouse model of multiple system atrophy. MRI captures regional shrinkage and microstructure change in this Parkinson-like disorder, but the molecular roots of those patterns were unclear.

Pairing detailed structural and diffusion MRI with gene mapping in PLP-αSyn mice, they tied imaging traits to programs for oligodendrocyte work, energy metabolism, and neuroinflammation, with distinct signatures per scan type. Independent RNA sequencing backed the links, which also matched human disease findings. The work benchmarks MRI-gene links for this disorder and frames how imaging markers can be read in related synuclein disorders.
pmc-13482289:
Suvera and colleagues fine-tune a hybrid ice cream in 2026, blending dairy milk with coconut milk at three ratios to find the mix tasters like best. The blends, three to two, one to one, and two to three, held fat, sugar, stabilizer, and emulsifier constant so only the milk balance changed between batches. Each batch was scored for composition, thickness, hardness, melting, airiness, plant compounds, and flavor by a sensory panel.

More coconut milk steadily raised fat, total solids, thickness, hardness, melting resistance, and phenolic content, the plant compounds linked to antioxidant value in foods like this. It also lowered overrun, the air whipped into the mix, making a denser product at the highest coconut share in the trials run. The equal blend won overall, scoring 93.60 of 100 for flavor and total sensory quality, with about 19 percent fat and 4.30 percent protein in the finished ice cream.
pmc-13482589:
Wang and colleagues design a two-layer lock in 2026 for vector map data, the coordinate files behind national mapping. Older scrambling tricks leave numbers readable, and simple chaos systems wear out into predictable cycles. Their scheme first scrambles coordinates with sequences from a four-dimensional hyperchaotic system. That reshapes the map's layout. The values are then encrypted with the SM4 national cipher, using keys the chaos generates.

Tests covered all three map element types, points, polylines, and polygons, and protected files yielded their structure only to the right keys. The authors report strong resistance to brute-force guessing and to differential attacks, which probe how small input changes alter the encrypted output of a cipher. The hyperchaotic layer also avoids the period collapse that weakens low-dimensional chaos, making the scheme fit for storing and sending geographic data.
pmc-13482789:
Cara Monroe and others describe an eight-week summer program in Oklahoma that brings American Indian high school students into cancer and biomedical research. In 2026, the account covers the Youth Enjoy Science Oklahoma Scholars program, run through the University of Oklahoma health and cancer centers with tribal and university partners. Its teaching model ties lab work and public health lessons to students' home communities and cultural contexts.

The program pairs campus lectures and lab research with two university courses that carry general education credit, while virtual teaching widens access for students far from campus. Near-peer mentors and former scholars help recruit new students and keep community links alive. The authors also report the logistical and institutional problems of building a place-based curriculum, and the adjustments that produced a plan other programs could adapt with care.
pmc-13482989:
Indupalli and Pradeepini designed a way for hospitals to train one shared disease-classification model without pooling private patient records. Their 2026 framework uses federated learning, where each site trains locally and only model updates travel. An autoencoder, a network that compresses data into key features, extracted the strongest signals at each hospital. Extra synthetic examples balanced rare diseases against common ones.

The combined system classified diseases with 92.5 percent accuracy in the experiments the authors ran for this study. That beat a standard image-style network and a sequence-based network tested under the same conditions. Performance held up even when hospitals held uneven mixes of patients, a common real-world problem. Indupalli argues the design shows privacy rules and strong accuracy can coexist, though hospitals would still need to test it on their own data.
pmc-13483389:
Enci Liu and co-authors report a 2026 survey of how deeply ultrasound has soaked into vein access training in Eastern China. The multicentre poll drew 682 valid replies, split between 454 trainees and 228 teachers across anaesthesia programs. Questions probed confidence, habit, and views on the older landmark method that uses surface anatomy alone.

Trainees trusted ultrasound far more than landmarks. Those who first learned with ultrasound were several times more likely to favour it now for both neck vein and wrist artery lines. Nine in ten trainees still called landmark skill important, yet over forty percent felt anxious working without the screen. Three quarters of teachers saw landmark skill fading in fresh graduates. Programs should drill and test both arts side by side, the authors urge.
pmc-13483489:
Qian Wang and co-authors present a 2026 study of a combined blood index that forecasts heart disease in people with early heart-kidney-metabolic syndrome. The index fuses inflammation, insulin resistance, and belly fat measures into one score. The team followed 6,728 Chinese adults aged forty-five and up from a national ageing survey across nine years.

Nearly a quarter developed heart or vessel disease during follow-up. Risk climbed in a straight line with the score: each standard step up raised risk by about a third after full adjustment. The top quarter faced roughly double the risk of the bottom quarter. The score also sorted people into risk groups slightly better than its single parts. Built from cheap routine tests, it could help clinics flag high-risk patients early for prevention.
pmc-13483689:
Ying Yang and colleagues build a computer model of one patient's airway to show how a jaw-advancing mouthpiece treats sleep apnea. Published in 2026, the proof-of-concept study uses computed tomography scans taken during natural sleep before and after two months of device use in a man with moderate apnea. Three-dimensional models track bones, soft tissues, and airflow.

Forward jaw movement pulled the tongue, soft palate, throat flap, and hyoid bone forward and upward, widening the airway in two directions and raising its volume. Airflow pressure and speed fell and evened out at peak breathing in and out, while tissue wobbling lessened. Effects were strongest during inhalation. A single case cannot prove benefit for everyone, yet the simulation makes the mechanical chain from jaw position to airflow visible.
pmc-13484989:
Seongje Lim shows how a pinch of ruthenium switches on two neighboring metals at once inside a mixed-metal hydrogen catalyst. Published in 2026, the high-entropy alloy work targets alkaline water splitting, where breaking water apart is the slow step. Spectroscopy reveals ruthenium pulling electrons away from cobalt and nickel neighbors, pushing them into higher oxidation states.

Calculations confirm cobalt and nickel as the main working sites, with their energy levels shifted to ease water breaking and to hold hydrogen just tightly enough. The tuned catalyst needed only 29 millivolts of extra push at a standard current level and beat both the plain alloy and a commercial ruthenium catalyst despite low ruthenium content. Ruthenium acts as an electronic conductor here, not the star performer, which stretches a scarce metal further.
pmc-13486489:
Umar and colleagues proposed a leak detector for pipelines that watches how signal patterns shift overall instead of chasing single spikes. Pipeline signals wobble with operating conditions, so spike-based alarms cry wolf, and labeled leak examples are rare. Their 2026 framework summarizes short windows of vibration data with time, frequency, and wavelet features, then compares the whole feature distribution against a reference built from normal operation.

Three statistical distance measures team up to flag when the live distribution drifts too far from normal. Because the method needs no library of leak examples, it can start protecting a pipeline from its first day of normal data. The multi-domain features catch changes that any single view would miss. Umar presents the design as a reliability-first alternative to black-box learning models for safety-critical monitoring.
pmc-13487389:
Hortuma A Habteslasie hunts the genes behind small body size in Eritrea's village chickens, a trait prized where feed runs scarce. Published in 2026, blood from 384 birds across sixteen local types is genotyped, then filtered down to 141 birds and 42,356 markers for analysis. Three suspected short-bodied types face five heavier control types, with body measures feeding parallel quantitative scans.

Small size in these birds travels with lower feed needs, heat tolerance, disease resistance, and fit to low-input farming. Ancestry mapping shows extensive sharing among types, which the mixed models handle through kinship correction. Separate scans per type plus a combined scan structure the search in the full report. Native chicken genetics tuned by centuries of scarcity could inform breeding far beyond Eritrea.
pmc-13487989:

pmc-13490389:

pmc-13493689:

pmc-13495389:

pmc-13495489:

pmc-13498589:

pmc-13499189:

pmc-13499689:

pmc-13502389:

pmc-13503489:

pmc-13503689:

pmc-13503789:

pmc-13503989:

pmc-13504289:

pmc-13504789:

pmc-13507089:

pmc-13507189:

pmc-13507289:

pmc-13511289:

pmc-13511689:

pmc-13511789:

pmc-13517389:

pmc-13518789:

pmc-13521889:

pmc-13522489:

pmc-13522589:

pmc-13522689:

pmc-13522789:

pmc-13523389:

pmc-13524089:

pmc-13524589:

pmc-13524689:

Programs with night float had more fellows and covered more hospitals overnight. Most suspended continuity clinic and lecture attendance during night rotations. Directors most often praised improved trainee wellness and satisfaction, while lost clinic continuity and missed teaching were the commonest drawbacks. The authors call for balancing rest with educational continuity.
pmc-13524889:
Xingnan Yi and colleagues use a 2026 cross-sectional survey of 40,600 Hong Kong households to examine who provides family care for people with disabilities and what drives caregiver stress. In East Asian societies, filial expectations and limited formal services place much care on families. Data came from the 2019-2020 Hong Kong General Household Survey.

Among weighted respondents in households including a person with disability, 14.5 percent were family caregivers. Women and unmarried respondents were more likely to provide care. Helping with daily living activities more than doubled the odds of longer weekly hours, and women also reported more hours. Severe mental stress was tied to being female, helping with daily activities, and caring for a relative with mental health disability. The authors urge targeted support that addresses gendered expectations.
pmc-13525189:
Adnan Imran and colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, evidence linking vitamin D deficiency with heart, metabolic, and kidney outcomes in autoimmune rheumatic diseases. These chronic immune diseases carry extra cardiovascular and renal burden, and vitamin D deficiency is common within them. Searches covered five databases through March 2026 without language limits.

The cardiovascular event estimate was large but imprecise, and the link between vitamin D level and protein in the urine in children with lupus was inconclusive. Other metabolic and vascular studies pointed adverse but could not be pooled because measures differed. The authors flag confounding and varied definitions.
pmc-13525289:
Surender Himral and colleagues examine, in a 2026 retrospective study, how often a completely blocked culprit artery hides inside heart attacks that lack the classic electrocardiogram pattern. Such occlusive infarctions can be missed when patients are sorted by tracing alone. The cohort came from an Indian tertiary cardiac center.

The study included 340 patients arriving within a day of chest pain who underwent angiography. A blocked or near-blocked culprit artery defined occlusion, found in 112 patients, about one third. Heart pumping fraction was lower in the occlusive group at presentation and stayed lower at three months despite improvement in both groups. Baseline features were otherwise similar, and death rates by nine to twelve months did not differ significantly. Lower pumping fraction was the strongest correlate of occlusion.
pmc-13525689:
Abdulrahman Arabi leads a large team in a 2026 nationwide analysis of trends in emergency angioplasty for major heart attacks in Qatar over nine years. This procedure, primary percutaneous coronary intervention, is the standard for ST-elevation heart attacks, yet long-term Middle Eastern trend data were scarce.

In-hospital mortality dropped from four point four percent in 2016 to one point five percent in 2023. Shock, cardiac arrest, older age, and delay predicted death.
pmc-13528089:
Haiou Yang and eight colleagues uncover how low oxygen helps bowel cancer resist a key drug in a 2026 study. Tumors often sit short of oxygen, which rewires their chemistry. The team screened RNA strands active in low-oxygen cancer cells. One long non-coding RNA stood out. They named it lnc-IRP.

The metal then stayed locked in storage form instead of the loose pool cells use. That shift blocked two death routes, apoptosis and iron-driven ferroptosis. Cancer cells survived the drug oxaliplatin more easily. The authors propose lnc-IRP as a drug target. Freeing the iron switch could restore sensitivity, they argue.
pmc-13528389:
Si and co-authors diagnose why clinical prediction tools powered by artificial intelligence so rarely reach patients, despite thousands of published models. Their 2026 narrative review argues the failure is planned in from the start: researchers build models first and wonder about deployment later. The authors propose reversing the direction, a bedside-to-bench discipline. It begins by defining the clinical question, the intended user, and the exact point in the care pathway where a score would change a decision.

Around that core they arrange the neglected homework: early and continuing engagement with clinicians and patients, and a programme theory linking model outputs to changed outcomes. Regulatory routes, funding models that keep software alive, equity checks, and the engineering of implementation and monitoring complete the list. Methodological hygiene still matters, they note, since reviews keep finding sloppy methods and incomplete reporting, but rigour alone cannot cross the translational gap.
pmc-13529189:
He and colleagues mined the Food and Drug Administration's adverse event database for safety signals of acyclovir, in a 2026 analysis. Acyclovir is the first-line drug for herpes simplex infection in newborns. Safety evidence in babies under one month old is thin despite wide use at high doses. The team screened reports from 2004 through late 2024 with acyclovir as the suspect.

He found 130 neonatal reports covering 409 adverse events and applied four statistical signal methods at once, keeping only signals positive on all four. Four organ groups stood out: skin and tissue under it, general and injection-site problems, liver and bile disorders, and kidney and urinary disorders. The strongest signals involved tissue death or swelling at the infusion site and skin peeling or death. Three reported events, including Kawasaki disease and gut inflammation, do not appear in product labeling, which the authors say warrants confirmation and monitoring.
pmc-13529789:
Cláudio M Lousada presents a two thousand twenty-six computational study of grain boundaries in uranium nitride and uranium carbide. Uranium nitride is a candidate nuclear fuel. Its behaviour depends on the seams where crystal grains meet inside the material.

Fourteen symmetric tilt boundaries were modelled with quantum calculations for both materials. One boundary type proved most stable in each. Boundary energy bottomed out at a shared tilt angle. Extra volume at the seam predicted energy well in the nitride. The calculations also yielded a first stacking fault energy for the carbide, aiding future fuel modelling.
pmc-13530189:
Yi Zhang and co-authors build a 2026 low-cost method for generating traditional decorative patterns with artificial intelligence, using ancient Egyptian designs as the test case. Training image models normally demands heavy computing and large pattern collections, both scarce for heritage material. Their route adapts a big image model through small trainable add-on layers only.

Pattern sorting by content and form cleaned the training set before fine-tuning. Judging covered shape, color, beauty, novelty, and use value, backed by numeric image scores. Trainable parts shrank by over 99 percent, and memory needs fell sharply. Trials on Chinese patterns held steady.
pmc-13530389:
Shiva Ebrahimi and colleagues manage a rare lung disease crisis during pregnancy. Their case report from twenty twenty-six concerns lymphangioleiomyomatosis, called LAM. The disease grows abnormal muscle-like cells through the lungs. It mostly strikes women of childbearing age.

The young patient arrived at seventeen weeks pregnant, struggling to breathe. Both lungs had collapsed almost completely on imaging. Small cysts scattered through her lung tissue suggested LAM. Chest drains and specialist input stabilised the emergency. Decisions balanced mother and fetus in a low-resource setting. Several teams coordinated the ongoing care plan together. The case shows rare disease care under extreme constraints.
pmc-13530589:
Pianka and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 149, ten-year results after hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement, split by where the pain sits. The condition is a painful hip shape conflict. Classic pain is in the front groin; lateral or posterior pain is called atypical and sometimes prompts doubts about operating.

The retrospective cohort covered primary arthroscopies from 2010 to 2013 with at least ten years of follow-up, matched three-to-one into 81 typical and 27 atypical pain patients. Both groups improved greatly on two standard hip scores, and the improvements, near forty points on each scale, did not differ between them. Revision surgery and conversion to a hip replacement each occurred in about six percent of the typical group and four percent of the atypical group. Success thresholds were met at similar rates.
pmc-13531789:
John Y Rhee and co-authors untangle in 2026 an ethics puzzle around limited feeding at the end of life. Minimal comfort feeding gives food or fluids only when a dying patient shows hunger or thirst. The same practice can mean comfort care during active dying or a deliberate step to hasten death.

Two clinical cases show how intention and timing change the moral reading under a virtue ethics framework and the doctrine of double effect. The authors propose split names: proportionate comfort feeding when death is foreseen yet unintended, versus minimal feeding to hasten death when speed is the goal.
pmc-13532289:
Dingxiang Zhu and colleagues report in 2026 how the silkworm virus protein GP64 reaches the cell surface. GP64 helps the virus infect cells, and in silkworm cells it keeps a small tag called a signal peptide. The team asked whether GP64 needs the normal route through the Golgi, a part of the cell that sorts proteins.

Blocking that route had no clear effect in silkworm cells, yet it cut GP64 surface levels in cells from another moth. A control protein that needs the Golgi route was blocked in both settings. Readers learn how a virus protein can bypass a main cell route in its true host.
pmc-13532889:
Peyton M Day and colleagues track in 2026 heart forces inside the left ventricle in mice with reversible pressure overload. The forces come from ultrasound measures of heart motion and blood flow, and they can flag poor pumping earlier than standard scores. Eight male mice had scans before narrowing, after narrowing, and after release.

Forces along the long axis during systole shifted clearly with overload and with recovery. One new ratio of early to late systolic force linked most strongly to both states. Sideways force during the impulse phase also hinted at who would recover well after release.
pmc-13534189:
Armaan Raina and John Meitzen published a 2026 study using machine learning on hormone-driven brain changes. Female rats' reward neurons shift across the fertility cycle. The electrical fingerprints of those shifts are subtle. Public data covered four cycle phases. Several learning models were trained to classify phase.

The best model reached high classification accuracy. Accuracy depended on which electrical features were supplied. Passive membrane properties carried strong signal. Firing burst length and synaptic baseline also mattered. Within one neuron type, state changes are learnable. That finding validates machine listening for gentle biological modulation. Similar methods could track drug or disease states.
pmc-13534489:
Sankhanava Kundu and colleagues traced how the brain builds and keeps a learned rule for telling smells apart. Published in 2026, the mouse study trained rodents on a hard odor-discrimination task until a sudden light-bulb moment when rule learning clicked. Whole-cell recordings from smell cortex tracked neurons switched on during learning.

From training onset, activated neurons showed higher intrinsic excitability, followed by coordinated rises in synaptic excitation and inhibition across each cell. Meanwhile the density of activated neurons fell sharply, with nearly two thirds of the rule-memory ensemble active from the start. Silencing those tagged neurons erased rule memory entirely. The authors propose a discrete learning moment stabilized by gradual cellular tuning. Readers get a biophysical portrait of learning how to learn.
pmc-13534889:
Ciara Rhodes and colleagues compare in 2026 two ways to prepare historic human bone for DNA identification work. Grinding bone to powder is standard, yet it can harm fragile genetic profiles in aged remains. Paired bones from the 19th century were either ground or softened and sliced without powder.

Slices gave far more human DNA on average than ground samples from the same bones. No ground sample produced a standard profile, while slices gave partial profiles and much higher marker recovery in targeted sequencing. Labs gain a workflow built from common reagents that lifts success on hard cases.
pmc-13536189:
Taylor N Breddy and colleagues surveyed how reward pathways link binge eating and harmful drinking. Published in 2026, the planned review pulled together 25 papers on shared and distinct reward pathways, sorted by reward type and testing method. The two habits often occur at once and worsen each other's harms, yet their joint reward pathways were poorly mapped.

Higher self-rated looking-forward to rewards in general and for food or drink tracked both joint and apart use of binge eating and harmful drinking. Longer use of either habit linked to stronger habit-based reward learning. The authors propose adding checks of reward craving and learning to treatment plans for both habits. Readers get a joint map for aiming at reward pathways in care for both habits.
pmc-13537889:
João Pedro Araújo Teixeira and co-authors compare two forms of gastric bypass surgery in a 2026 study from a high-volume center. In the standard operation, part of the stomach is bypassed but left in place. In the other form, that leftover part is removed at the same time, which is sometimes needed for early disease, stubborn infection, or repeat surgery.

Records covered more than two thousand patients, of whom a small share had the removal form. That group had more leaks, collections of fluid, trouble eating, and repeat procedures, mainly in first-time surgery. No deaths occurred within ninety days. Weight loss tended to be a bit greater with removal, but the edge was not steady across measures. The authors urge careful patient choice for the bigger operation.
pmc-13538389:
Rasheed Omobolaji Alabi and colleagues build a learning model for early death in head and neck cancer in a 2026 population study. Death within six months stays common despite better care for early to mid-stage tumors. Registry data for 4,802 patients supplied model building, with checks in near two thousand German registry cases and a small Finnish hospital group. Risk factors were ranked for death at six months, two years, and five years.

The model predicted early death fairly in the main registry and moderately in outside checks, weaker in the smallest group. Older age, prior other cancers, unmarried status, larger tumor stage, and throat or voice box sites led early death factors. Rankings shifted modestly at later time points. The authors propose the model to flag high-risk patients for faster, tailored decisions.
pmc-13538689:
Su-Jung Ji and colleagues sequence the first complete mitochondrial genomes of underground aquatic crustaceans in a 2026 phylogeny study. The tiny eyeless order lives only in subterranean waters, yet none of its roughly 340 species had a full mitochondrial genome before. Four species from two families were sequenced and placed within a broad crustacean family tree.

The genomes showed extensive gene shuffling, strong composition biases, and fast evolution. Tree analyses firmly supported the group as one lineage, though very long branches hint that underground simplification blurs deep relationships. The two orders once grouped as close kin landed far apart, suggesting their shared traits evolved independently. The authors offer the genomes as resources for rethinking crustacean classification.
pmc-13542589:
Chang and co-authors upgrade sorghum for meat ducks by fermenting it with microbes and an enzyme. Their 2026 paper prepares the feed with Bacillus subtilis, Candida utilis, and phytase, an enzyme that unlocks phosphorus bound in phytic acid. Two experiments followed: a digestibility trial in 128 young ducks and a 21-day growth trial in 240 ducks where the treated sorghum replaced most of the corn.

Fermentation raised the sorghum's protein and ash while cutting phytic acid and fibre. Ducks digested its protein, fat, zinc, phosphorus, and energy better, and absorbed several amino acids more completely. In the growth trial the fermented diet beat plain sorghum on final weight and daily gain with a leaner feed conversion ratio. Gut enzyme activities rose, caecal fermentation acids increased, and gut microbe diversity improved with a shift toward Firmicutes. The authors endorse the co-fermentation strategy.
pmc-13543489:
Xiaoyan Wang and colleagues published a 2026 cohort study asking what happens when frailty and metabolic syndrome occur together, tracking fatty liver disease, diabetes, and death in the UK Biobank. More than 165,000 participants were grouped by having neither condition, one, or both. A multi-state model followed them from health into metabolic fatty liver disease, onward to diabetes, or to death across nearly thirteen years of follow-up.

People with both frailty and metabolic syndrome faced almost triple the risk of developing fatty liver disease compared with those who had neither. Their risk of progressing from fatty liver to diabetes was higher still, at over four times. Survival curves confirmed the ordering of the groups. Frailty alone is easy to overlook beside laboratory measures, yet pairing the two assessments, the authors argue, sharpens early identification of people on the road to liver and metabolic disease.
pmc-13543589:
Xinming Hu's team published a 2026 study of why kidney cancers stop responding to sunitinib, a standard targeted drug, using tumour organoids grown from patient tissue. Gene profiling of treated organoids flagged ALDH1L2, a metabolic enzyme, which also ran high in real tumours and marked worse survival. Removing it had the opposite effect, restoring sensitivity. A ferroptosis-triggering drug cancelled the protection. Screening then found a plant-derived compound, hederacolchiside A1, that binds and reduces the enzyme and strengthened sunitinib's attack in the models. Shield proteins like this one may explain, and eventually reverse, drug resistance.
pmc-13544089:
Run Wang and colleagues published a 2026 perspective proposing an equity-centred version of PEDALs, a staged model for getting proven health practices into routine use. The know-do gap, the lag between evidence and practice, persists worldwide, and implementation work that ignores equity can widen the very disparities it hopes to close. Their adaptation threads fairness through every stage, from problem definition to long-term scale-up.

At the problem stage, root causes of inequity come first. A later stage admits practice-based knowledge and even the removal of harmful practices. Determinants are analysed with marginalised voices in the room, actions are co-designed for context, and long-term outcomes are measured through an equity lens. The authors commend hybrid designs and rapid, participatory methods, under a philosophy of radical incrementalism: steady, equity-driven steps rather than revolutions, especially for lower-income health systems.
pmc-13545689:
Aljahdali and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2026 the use of a patient's own fat-derived products in nose surgery and nasal reconstruction, where thin or scarred skin makes outcomes fragile. The review followed standard guidelines and searched five databases to mid-2025 for human studies of products such as microfat, nanofat, stromal vascular fraction, and fat enriched with platelet fibrin.

Twelve studies covering 768 patients qualified. Most reported better scar appearance, skin quality, and tissue pliability after grafting, with pleasing aesthetic results and high patient satisfaction, and complications were rare and minor. The catch is measurement: only one study used objective three-dimensional imaging, while the rest relied on subjective judgment, and the studies varied too much to pool. The authors judge the products well tolerated and promising as surgical adjuncts, and call for standardized, objective outcome tracking.
pmc-13547289:
Sara Darabi, Gholamreza Heidari, and Payman Salami compared in 2026 poultry manure with chemical fertilizer across three cereal crops at a university farm in Iran over two growing seasons. Pearl millet, sorghum, and maize each received no fertilizer, manure alone, full chemical fertilizer, or blends of manure with urea and phosphate. Soil chemistry and enzyme activity, a sign of living, working soil, were measured.

Manure alone gave the richest soil carbon in every crop and the strongest activity of both phosphatase enzymes, which free up phosphorus for plants. The full chemical treatment led on potassium but lagged on biology. Manure also raised soil salinity somewhat, so the authors advise controlled rates with regular monitoring rather than abandoning a practice that clearly feeds the soil.
pmc-13547389:
Massimo Apicella and colleagues studied in 2026 whether poor control of emotions adds risk for suicide attempts in teenagers beyond depression itself. Their clinic sample held 182 adolescents, average age near sixteen, of whom 41 had recently attempted suicide. Teenagers who had attempted suicide scored higher on both facets and had more depressive episodes. Stepwise models showed raw reactions to others predicted a recent attempt on their own, even after depression was counted, and part of that effect ran through depression. The full model explained about a third of the differences between groups. The authors argue suicide risk checks should cover emotion control, not mood alone.
pmc-13547889:
Afsar Murat and Çelik Çetin followed in 2026 an invasive red-eared slider turtle population in a wetland in western Turkey. They asked how the animals handle heat in a habitat that suits them poorly. The species ranks among the world's worst invaders. Habitat quality was suboptimal during the turtles' active hours, yet the animals held their bodies close to their preferred range with high precision, scoring strongly on effectiveness measures. Body temperature tracked water and air temperature closely. The authors read this skillful behavioral regulation as a built-in advantage that helps the invader thrive and may expand with warming.
pmc-13548489:

The authors recommend the scores for early sorting and clear communication rather than as stand-alone prognostic tools.
pmc-13548589:
Asli Bahar Ucar and colleagues study how visible agitation shapes emergency care for adults in substance-related crises, in a 2026 chart review from a Turkish referral hospital. Many such visits now involve unsteady behavior rather than a clear poisoning picture. The team analyzed ninety visits where patients got calming drugs. They scored agitation on a standard scale and tracked whether treatment had to step up or the patient went to a psychiatry ward.

Most patients arrived severely agitated. About a quarter needed a second calming drug, and seven in ten were admitted to psychiatry, with both outcomes rising step by step across agitation levels. Severe agitation independently predicted admission with nearly eightfold odds, while older age lowered the odds. The authors suggest a set agitation score at the door could help teams plan sedation and placement earlier.
pmc-13548689:
Dagyeong Kwon and colleagues hunt for apple genes that resist anthracnose, a fungal disease complex rotting fruit and spotting leaves, in a 2026 genetic association study. Breeders need resistance that holds up in real orchards. The team scored 440 apple genotypes, mostly offspring of six crosses, across several years of natural orchard exposure. They then challenged fruit and leaves with the fungus under controlled conditions, using wounded and unwounded tissue.

Disease severity swung strongly with the year's weather, underlining how environment steers infection. The region sits far from a previously known resistance region on the same chromosome, so it is likely new. Controlled inoculation scores produced no such signal. The authors stress that field testing across seasons is what reveals resistance worth breeding for.
pmc-13548789:
McKay and colleagues reviewed bone health in advanced prostate cancer and how to protect it within care, in a 2026 narrative review. Hormone therapy that lowers testosterone accelerates bone loss from the moment it starts, and once cancer spreads to bone. happens in the great majority of resistant cases, patients face fractures, spinal cord compression, and other skeletal events that erode quality of life.

McKay recommends assessing every man on hormone deprivation with bone density scanning and a bone-quality score. Options include bisphosphonate drugs and denosumab, which blocks a bone-breakdown signal, with monitoring for jaw bone damage and low calcium. Several cancer drugs, including abiraterone, enzalutamide, and radium-223, help bone. pmc-13549689:

The baby was seven days old when brought in with a hard mass present since birth. The mass stuck out from the gum ridge, pushed her lip outward, and blocked full mouth closure. It also interfered with sucking and bled when touched. Surgeons removed it two days later under general anesthesia. Tests on the tissue showed a marker pattern seen in only a few such cases. The report reviews how doctors tell this growth apart from others.
pmc-13550489:
M. Siva Ramkumar and colleagues coordinate electric vehicle charging with a hybrid control system meant to keep a renewable-fed smart grid steady, in a 2026 engineering paper. The other, a spiking deep residual network, forecasts the best operating parameters as conditions change.

The proposed system posted converter efficiency of ninety-nine point seven percent, energy use efficiency near ninety-nine percent, and the lowest system error at one and a half percent. The authors claim the coordination smooths charging while solar and wind inputs fluctuate, though all results come from simulation rather than hardware.
pmc-13550989:
Yuyao Yi and a large team of co-authors test whether a Chinese-made hormone therapy for prostate cancer matches its reference product. Their study appeared in 2026. Blood levels and safety were then tracked for a month.

Peak levels and total exposure over the month landed within a few percent of each other, inside the usual equivalence margins. Earlier healthy-volunteer data pointed the same way. The authors conclude the home-grown formulation behaves like the reference in patients, widening supply options.
pmc-13551389:
Abhishek Bisht, Gokulprasanth Murugan, Jun Tae Kim, and Soottawat Benjakul review metal-organic frameworks for seafood preservation. Some kill microbes through released ions or reactive oxygen. Others trap spoilage compounds or release protectors slowly. The authors weigh benefits against risks like metal migration into food. pmc-13551689:

Twelve factors held up, including diabetes, hypertension, mouth infection, prior radiotherapy, smoking, and alcohol history, plus several blood measures. The authors advise tailored prevention and closer monitoring for patients carrying these risks.
pmc-13551989:
Abolfazl Rezaei, Maryam Jahanbakhsh, and Hamid Reza Dehghan published a 2026 review on electronic medical records in developing countries. Paper records still rule in many such settings. pmc-13554189:

Higher scores followed senior titles, more schooling, hands-on catheter work, and past training. Workplace guidelines and felt training needs mattered in big hospitals, less so in smaller ones. Big-hospital employment itself lifted scores. The authors call for training tailored to hospital level, since the drivers of knowledge clearly differ between settings.
pmc-13555889:
Hoon Kim leads a five-author team measuring the energy cost of bounce squats versus standard squats in a 2026 study. Computer models of the body then estimated energy use for the whole body and for single muscles, split by movement phase.

Thigh muscles called the vasti drove the saving during descent across all loads. The rising phase gained nothing from bouncing. Tendon recoil at the quick reversal likely explains the cheaper lowering.
pmc-13556789:

The team combined EEG and MRI recordings while participants slipped between alert and drowsy states. Some actively worked on a listening task; others just heard tones passively. As alertness fell, passive listeners showed more local synchrony in the parietal lobe. Active task users instead boosted long-range links between frontal and parietal areas. pmc-13557089:

pmc-13558389:

pmc-13558489:

The survey gives Brazilian planners a baseline picture of unmet need by severity and by care route.
pmc-13558589:
Seong Duk Do, Yeonhui Lee, and Jae-Sung Rhee sequenced in 2026 the first complete mitochondrial genome of the sea cucumber Ocnus glacialis and compared it across its order. This group of sea cucumbers is species rich, yet scarce mitochondrial data leave its family history fuzzy. The circular genome held the standard 37 genes, and the authors analysed base composition, selection pressure, gene order, and divergence timing against relatives.

The species showed the highest share of A and T bases in the group and the most scrambled gene order, built through repeated duplication and loss events. Several genes carried signs of relaxed or positive selection, and evolution ran faster on this branch. The authors tie the pattern to a move into Arctic cold and deep water combined with small population sizes. Their timeline gives the order a firmer evolutionary framework.
pmc-13558889:
Najirman Najirman and two colleagues measured in 2026 how blood markers of the bone-remodelling command chain relate to a marker of bone breakdown in people with rheumatoid arthritis. The disease speeds bone loss through a signalling trio that governs the cells dissolving bone, and the breakdown marker CTX-1 shows how fast skeleton is being eaten away. Their cross-sectional study at a referral hospital in Padang, Indonesia, recruited patients over six months of 2024 and assayed all four quantities from blood.

The two activating members of the trio correlated almost perfectly with the breakdown marker. The trio's brake protein also correlated strongly. A brake rising alongside breakdown is notable, since it suggests the system is straining to compensate. Average patient age was about forty. The authors conclude that circulating levels of the whole pathway track skeletal turnover in this disease, a possible handle for spotting patients whose bones need protection.
pmc-13559589:
Mengxiang Huang and colleagues trace a small regulatory RNA that reins in exosome release and movement in pancreatic cancer. Their 2026 study began by comparing microRNA profiles in blood from patients and healthy controls, which singled out miR-27b-5p as a factor lost in the disease. Exosomes are tiny parcels cells shed to signal neighbors, and pancreatic tumors release them in unusual numbers.

Reporter experiments confirmed the microRNA binds directly to RAB27A, a protein that ferries exosome carriers to the cell surface. Restoring the microRNA in cancer cells lowered RAB27A, cut exosome output, and slowed migration in dish and animal tests, without changing growth. Putting RAB27A back undid those effects, proving the chain of control. The authors present the pair as a regulatory axis behind exosome-driven spread. They suggest it as a foothold for future anti-metastasis strategies in a cancer that badly needs them.
pmc-13560389:
Shuai Zhang and colleagues report a multi-omics study, published in 2026. It maps how mouth microbes and body chemistry change as upper digestive tract cancers develop. A screening programme supplied the participants. The team enrolled 420 people in four equal groups. They ranged from healthy through two precancerous stages to cancer. Saliva microbes were profiled. Saliva and blood metabolites were profiled too.

Each stage carried a distinct signature. Saliva microbes remodelled strongly early. This was at the low-grade precancer stage. Whole-body metabolic shifts marked the move to high-grade lesions. Disordered mouth bacteria may feed early tissue changes, the team proposes. A fuel pathway related to acetyl-CoA is involved. Their combined classifier suggests a saliva-based triage test for high-risk screening.
pmc-13561089:
Gupta, Yoon, and Josic inferred gene regulatory networks from steady-state cell data with Bayesian statistics in twenty twenty-six. Such networks decide which genes are on or off. Their wiring limits how signals flow through a cell. Most methods for inferring them skip the basic chemistry behind noisy gene activity.

Their method models gene activity with the chemical Langevin equation at a random steady state. So no time-course data are needed. A regularized horseshoe prior, a tool that shrinks weak links toward zero, fits the known sparseness of real networks. Strong regulatory edges still stand out. On synthetic data with known truth, the method found the network's structure and its kinetic parameters. It even found regulatory cycles. The authors argue the Bayesian path reads clearly in biology terms. It pins down structure in a way plain statistics or deep learning methods do not.
pmc-13562589:
Alexandra Mitlehner and co-authors present a 2026 study of how the cell's display stand swaps its cargo. The stand, MHC class I, shows cell-made scraps to T cells so threats can be spotted. A helper protein, tapasin, edits which scraps stay. Using locked bonds, ice-cold microscopy, and atom motion sims, the team caught the stand mid-swap. Its grip groove partly caves in during the swap.

The scrap's head end tucks against a set of ring-shaped side chains. One wall of the groove frays while the other holds firm, braced by the helper. Deep time has made the fraying wall looser, the team note. Looseness may tune which scraps get shown. Display editing is a drug aim for immune tuning.
pmc-13562689:
Nimra Iman and five colleagues train a neural network to outline narrowed heart arteries in X-ray angiograms, a task that eats expert time and invites human error. Coronary stenosis, a partial blockage of the heart's own arteries, can kill if missed. The gains came despite tiny vessels and low contrast, the classic hardships of these images. The authors present the system as an assistant to flag narrowed regions for a cardiologist's final judgement.
pmc-13563589:
Jinting Liu and others put out a flavor science study in 2026. They studied Luzhou-flavor baijiu, a Chinese sorghum spirit. Brewing mixes raw and fermented grains during distillation. How cooking grain shapes final flavor was unclear. The team studied four sorghum cooking styles. They also studied base spirits from unlike ways. A joint pulling and chromatography method named the compounds. Key aroma chemicals were set side by side across samples, with care.

Cooking brought in several new flavor things at once. It also raised seven key flavor compounds greatly. Esters linked to fruity notes were among them. Heat converts grain chemicals during the process itself. Grains also ferment with the mash. Raw stuff thus shapes flavor, and is not just a bystander. Makers can tune cooking to steer aroma. Old process steps gain a plain explanation.
pmc-13563789:
Sina Meisamy and six colleagues listen to tumour temperature as an early whisper of whether cancer treatment is working. Tumours run metabolically hot or cold as therapy bites, well before they shrink. Their 2026 study implanted telemetric sensors in mice carrying three cancers, melanoma, breast, and colon, then compared each tumour's temperature against the body's through treatment. Melanoma received a vaccine-style immunotherapy, breast cancer a standard chemotherapy pairing, and colon cancer an anti-PD-1 immune drug.
