pmc-13563889:
Li-bing Liang and five colleagues set out the protocol for a trial pairing an exercise with brain training for older adults whose memory is slipping. Mild cognitive impairment is the last station before dementia, and remedies have disappointed. Their 2026 protocol describes a twelve-week, three-arm randomised trial of 186 patients. One arm performs Baduanjin, an eight-movement exercise, then does cognitive training in sequence. The other arms receive the exercise alone or the training alone.

Global cognition, scored on the Montreal assessment, is the main outcome. A light-based scan will track oxygenated blood in the prefrontal, premotor, and supplementary motor areas at rest, before and after. Balance, daily-living ability, heart rate, and variability fill out the battery, repeated at week twelve and four weeks later. The trial is registered in China. The team hopes the brain data explain any synergy, guiding non-drug care.
pmc-13567989:
Yen-Wei Chen and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six feasibility study of a new way to monitor dental implant stability in a pig jaw model. Dentists need to know when an implant loosens. A flex constant, measuring how much the implant bends per unit force, is their candidate.

A commercial implant was placed in a pig jaw by standard protocol. Freezing the jaw mimicked high stability, thawing mimicked low. A small motor shook the implant while a sensor measured movement. The standard resonance method ran alongside for comparison. The study tests whether the simpler flex measure tracks stability changes reliably.
pmc-13570289:
Jessica Stockhausen and eight co-authors compare shin bones in the stiff and free limbs of children with one-side spastic cerebral palsy. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The palsy is known for poor bone build, but whether the flaw is local to the stiff side was open. They scan both shins of young walkers with a fine CT tool.

The stiff limb's shin is smaller in total, inner, and shell area, with a thin shell and a short rim. It tests weaker and less stiff, at like bone density. Habit reads of play and sport barely track the gap, save one link to limb length. Shape, not density, drives the weak side.
pmc-13570889:
Mansour Mohamed and colleagues match the mechanical and electrical traits of zinc oxide nanoparticles, pure or doped with silver. The team studied three mixes, no doping and two levels of silver, from thirty to one hundred fifty degrees Celsius.

All samples showed the wurtzite crystal structure, tensile stress, and a brittle nature. Silver doping raised crystallite size a bit. It cut dislocation density, micro-strain, surface area, porosity, and particle size. Elastic moduli, hardness, wave speeds, and Debye temperature all rose bit by bit with doping. The dielectric constant, dielectric loss, and AC conductivity rose with heat and with doping. The activation energy of charge carriers fell as doping rose. Peaks of relaxation, absent in the loss curves of the lighter mixes, showed up clearly at the highest doping.
pmc-13571389:
Takeshi Niizeki and colleagues demonstrate, in a 2026 technique report, a balloon trick that stops a guidewire from buckling out of place. The trick opens a completely blocked heart artery from the far side. Their patient, a 70-year-old man with a blocked right coronary artery, was approached backward through a small connecting channel. The wire kept prolapsing at a steep exit angle.

A small balloon advanced along the backward route was inflated just past the exit fork. The balloon screened the opening so the wire could be steered in a controlled way into the blockage. A standard reverse tracking method then completed the opening. The authors note the connecting channel may first need gentle widening to deliver devices.
pmc-13571689:
Yu Zeng, Li Bao, Jian Li, and Yanyan Hong build a prediction tool for a common swelling complication after rectal cancer surgery in older patients, in a 2026 paper. The surgery often adds a protective ileostomy, an opening that diverts waste, and the lining there can swell early on, burdening recovery. No good tool predicted who would swell. The team studied 296 patients and let several machine learning methods vote on which facts about a patient mattered most.

Five predictors survived every method: a nutrition index, a blood ratio tied to inflammation, fluid given during surgery, the size of the abdominal opening, and the wait for the first bowel movement. These fed a plain logistic regression model, kept readable on purpose. The model was checked by resampling, cross-checks, and a small outside group of forty patients. The authors offer it as an interpretable aid for spotting high-risk patients before surgery.
pmc-13572089:
Zhenzhen Lu and co-authors present a 2026 study of diabetes risk in adults with borderline high blood sugar. People at this stage often move on to type 2 diabetes, but death from other causes can cloud long studies. The team followed 913 adults in Liuzhou, China, for up to 20 years. They asked whether the choice of stats model changes which risk factors stand out.

Three model types were run side by side on the same data. Blood sugar level, body fat share, and older age raised risk in all three. Being female lowered risk in all three as well. Weight measures split the models, giving unlike answers by method. Blood pressure showed no firm effect in any model. The authors urge readers to run more than one model when death competes with the outcome.
pmc-13573489:
Que-Anh Truong-Le, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 food system that shields probiotic bacteria in a printed core-shell bead. Friendly bacteria die fast in storage and in stomach acid, so few reach the gut alive. The bead wraps a starch gel core in an alginate-pectin shell, printed layer by layer for exact shape.

A ten-strain mix of two bacteria families filled the core, and printing itself cost no survival. Cold storage at fridge level kept near two thirds alive after 33 days, while free bacteria fell below five percent far sooner. In mock digestion, the beads held over 97 percent through the mouth phase and above 82 percent in stomach and gut phases. Free bacteria crashed to near six percent by the gut phase. The authors back the shell as real protection.
pmc-13574789:
Alexandru Stihi and Christopher Yau mapped where aggressive ovarian cancer cells sit inside tumours, not just how many there are. The Oxford Classic signature sorts high-grade serous ovarian cancer into five transcriptional programs, with the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition program marking poor prognosis. Their 2026 study built a deep-learning method for spatial transcriptomics and applied it to 94 tumours.

Transition-program cells formed dense clusters walled off from stromal and immune neighbours, except for selective monocyte contact at cluster edges. Tumours rich in those cells showed stronger spatial reorganisation. Crucially, spatial measures of immune organisation predicted survival better than the transition share alone. The authors conclude that tumour architecture, not just composition, drives outcomes in this cancer.
pmc-13575189:
Jiazhen Liu, Gonglin Yuan, and Zhongyu Mo propose a faster training algorithm for machine learning in a 2026 paper. Classic conjugate gradient methods use only first-order slope data, which limits how well they sense the curve of a loss surface. Their method, TASCG, adds a third-order curvature estimate to the search direction.

The authors prove the method keeps a proper downhill step and settles at a solution under standard assumptions. Its cost bound matches the best known rate for plain stochastic gradient methods. A second version adds variance reduction to sharpen gradient estimates. Tests on nonconvex problems, including support vector machines, beat standard methods on speed and final accuracy, and coped better with step size choices. The work frames a new route for using geometry in stochastic training.
pmc-13575389:
Masachika Niimi and five colleagues test a new bedside scale for delirium and thinking problems in intensive care in a 2026 study from Japan. Their Jikei Command Following Scale scores eight simple actions. Patients hold and release a hand, open and close the eyes, follow an object with the gaze, and carry out a two-step command, among other tasks.

Fifty intensive care patients were assessed. Scores were highly consistent within the scale, and two examiners agreed closely on total scores, though agreement varied across single items. Scores tracked strongly with two established delirium tools used in intensive care. They also correlated with a standard thinking test given two weeks after leaving the unit. The authors judge the scale reliable and valid for this setting.
pmc-13575489:
Basran and Richtsmeier test a new kind of CT scanner for use in planning radiation care in twenty twenty-six. Most scanners sum up the energy of X rays in each scan. The new scanner counts single photons, which can give sharper images with more detail. No one had yet checked it as a tool to plan cancer treatment.

The team ran standard checks on shape, image quality, dose, and safety. Shape checks matched the true sizes, and dose checks were close to the set values. Some image values shifted a bit with scan settings and place in the scanner. On the whole, the scanner met the rules for planning use.
pmc-13576389:
Anam Anjum and three colleagues review extracellular vesicles as a therapy route for peripheral nerve injury in a 2026 paper. Vesicles are tiny parcels that cells release to pass messages and cargo to neighbours. Repair of nerves outside the brain and spinal cord stays poor, with limited working treatments.

What a vesicle carries depends on the cell it came from, and that cargo decides whether it protects nerves, calms immune reactions, or drives regrowth. The review compares vesicle sources side by side, tracing how each source's contents map onto repair pathways after injury. It also covers recent technical advances for loading and targeting vesicles. The authors argue that picking the right source, rather than vesicles in general, is the key design choice for future treatments, and they set out what clinical use would require.
pmc-13577289:
Taowen Pan and colleagues published a laboratory study in two thousand twenty-six on how human cytomegalovirus gets inside fibroblast cells. Their focus was a sugar coating added to a surface protein called integrin beta three. An enzyme named ST6Gal1 attaches that coating, and the team asked whether the virus needs it to enter.

pmc-13578189:
Anne Frisch and co-authors survey emergency radiologists on CT-guided procedures that drain infection sources in sepsis. Their 2026 paper draws on a European society's membership survey. Sepsis care often hinges on removing or draining the infection's source, and CT both finds it and guides the needle.

Most emergency radiologists strongly agreed that CT is important for planning these interventions. Both groups leaned toward acting within a few hours. pmc-13578489:
Surya P Rednam and colleagues chart the care load for children with nerve sheath tumors tied to a genetic condition, in a 2026 United States chart review. pmc-13579089:
Do and colleagues described a 2026 materials study on a stretchy piezoelectric composite, a material that makes electric signals when pressed or bent. Soft sensors need such materials to stay stretchy while keeping a strong electric response. The team built their film from a fluorinated polymer mixed with treated barium titanate particles.

pmc-13579889:

pmc-13579989:
Yifei Xu and a large team of co-authors test whether routine blood work, split by an inflammation marker, can tell bipolar disorder from major depression in women, in a 2026 study. White cell counts and several liver and thyroid values pulled in opposite directions across groups. pmc-13581689:
Samer Abdulkader-Sande and six co-authors report a brain tumour case that widens the known range of a rare fusion type. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The tumour sits high in the brain of an adult man. It joins two genes, EP300 and BCOR, in a swapped fusion. Tumours with such fusions form a new and still fuzzy group.

pmc-13581989:

pmc-13582689:
Sandra Rubio Bernabé and colleagues compared face-to-face and online mock workshops on care in the last hours of life for final-year med students at the University of Navarra. Forty-six students were split by chance, seventeen to face-to-face work and twenty-nine to online work, with mock patients, debrief talks, and shared aims. pmc-13583689:
Danielle Dunnett leads a team that reviews finger prick tests at point of care. Their review from twenty twenty-six asks how such tests are received. It covers both patients and the staff who give them.

The team searched six data sets from the start to a set date. Work had to share views, joy, or ease with the test. Counts, talks, and mixed study forms all could join. Two reviewers pulled data and judged study quality. A small set of studies met the rules. Themes pull the views into one clear tale.
pmc-13583789:
Biksegn Asrat Yirdaw and co-authors evaluate mental health support inside outbreak response in western Uganda in this 2026 paper. Outbreaks bring grief, fear, and social strain along with disease. Thematic analysis mixed planned and emergent coding. District health leaders joined as participants, not just overseers. Findings inform whether such support belongs in standard outbreak toolkits. pmc-13584289:

pmc-13584389:

Game-based students scored a touch higher on every test and rated their method a bit better, with the clearest gain among students whose past grades were lower. None of those gaps, though, reached the level statisticians call solid. The authors conclude that either method works well in a virtual flipped class.
pmc-13584489:
Deniz Sarel, Nilgün Yerli, and İlker Büyük catalogue a hidden class of genes in hemp plants under drought in this 2026 study. Fifty-one of them shifted clearly with drought, near genes for wood-like wall building, a dry-stress hormone, and ion storage. pmc-13585689:
Thirteen authors present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on high blood calcium caused by cancer. A protein made by tumors, related to parathyroid hormone, is a main driver of this dangerous complication. Evidence on it has come mostly from small case series, leaving the clinical picture fuzzy.

The team mined records from eight hospitals in Korea, gathering adults with cancer and raised calcium between two thousand thirteen and two thousand twenty-two. Cases driven by the protein were separated from other causes by a blood threshold. Two hundred eighty-nine patients had the protein-driven form; most had solid tumors, and the paper profiles their course.
pmc-13586789:

Genetic analyses backed selected links, including chronic pancreatitis. The authors say follow-up care should watch for this staged pattern.
pmc-13587389:
Uriel Palacios-Barahona and Juan Felipe Combariza track deaths from sickle cell disease in Colombia over twelve years. Using national death records from 2012 to 2023, the pair counted 675 deaths tied to the disease and mapped rates by region, sex, and local development.

Places with low development scores saw triple the mortality of the best-off areas, and the gap widened further after adjusting for sex and town or country living. Deaths dipped below forecast in the pandemic years, which the authors read as missed registration rather than real improvement. Their call is for care and counting that reach the poorest regions first.
pmc-13589389:

The authors call the stress state reversible and drug-targetable.
pmc-13590589:
Yulun Zhang and colleagues rebuilt Greenland's surface mass balance from 1950 to 2020 with machine learning. Their 2026 study trained a CNN-Transformer model on compiled field observations plus ERA5-Land reanalysis and MAR regional climate model outputs, producing gridded yearly maps at 0.1-degree resolution.

The best models correlated 0.96 and 0.93 with observations for the two input versions, and spatial cross-checks cut errors by about half versus the original datasets. Independent checks against IceBridge airborne radar confirmed robustness, cutting relative error by 35 and 50 percent. The authors offer the complete yearly datasets as inputs for ice-sheet and hydrology models.
pmc-13591189:
Carmine Petrasso and colleagues asked if one survey query can spot move faults in people with cancer that cannot be cured. They read start data from 206 adults with solid tumours and poor function scores in a multi-land rehab trial. Move skill was scored both with one query from a palliation survey and with the move part of a WHO disability scale.

The two scores moved in step, at 0.650, and five move groups came out that mainly ran from mild to bad trouble, not from distinct types. Young people and aid-device users showed up more in the bad groups. One query may thus help clinic staff screen for move loss and judge when full tests or rehab help are due.
pmc-13591489:
Samuel Martínez-Alcalá and co-authors compare, in a 2026 study, the inner architecture of two very different RNA virus populations. A single dominant variant sits at the center, ringed by layers of ever rarer variants as their distance from the center grows. The networks match in both shape and measured detail, forming a clear hierarchy. The authors argue that this common blueprint flows from the geometry of sequence space itself, and that network thinking can forecast viral evolution better than diversity counts alone.
pmc-13591889:
Lianlian Yang, Fan Yang, and Qiaoyun Ji weigh, in 2026, whether food supplements help the social and behavioral troubles of autism. Hints of gain also appeared for irritability, while hyperactivity showed no clear shift. The authors urge caution: trials were small, links sparse, and results fuzzy. They conclude no supplement yet earns a firm recommendation, and call for large, well run trials.
pmc-13592689:

pmc-13608489:

pmc-13610889:
